title: Biology
description: High school biology for one full credit, written for learners studying on their own: the chemistry of life, cells and membranes, photosynthesis and respiration, cell division, Mendelian and molecular genetics, biotechnology, evolution and population genetics, the diversity of life, human body systems and homeostasis, and ecology, with the math biologists use (probability, Hardy-Weinberg, chi-square, population growth). Optional honors material goes further: 22 honors lessons inside the modules and three honors modules (research and biostatistics; development, stem cells and the genome; behavior, disease and conservation).
author: Erudior
changelog: 34 optional honors lessons (22 in the modules, three honors modules), pictures and diagrams in every lesson, and new question types: fill in the blank, match, put in order, label the picture, and select all that apply.

Honors: Development, stem cells, and the genome

lessons.title: What biology studies: life and its levels
lessons.body:
## What this course is about

Biology is the science of living things: how they are built, how they get and use energy, how they grow and reproduce, how they pass traits to their offspring, how they interact with each other and their surroundings, and how they have changed over Earth's long history. This first lesson answers two questions every later lesson depends on. What makes something alive? And how is life organized, from molecules up to the whole planet?

Neither question is as easy as it sounds. A flame grows, "feeds" on fuel, gives off heat and can spread to new places, yet no biologist calls fire alive. A dormant seed can sit in a drawer for decades doing almost nothing, yet it is alive. Working out why gives us a usable definition.

## The characteristics of life

No single property separates living from nonliving things. Instead, biologists use a set of characteristics that living things share. A living thing shows all of them, at least at some stage of its life or across its lineage.

1. *Made of cells.* Every living thing is built from one or more cells, the smallest units that can carry out all the processes of life. A bacterium is one cell; you are tens of trillions of them. (Module 2 is all about cells.)
2. *Uses energy: metabolism.* Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in an organism: breaking down food to release energy, and using that energy to build the molecules it needs. A plant captures light energy; you get energy from food. Either way, the organism is constantly taking in matter and energy and transforming them.
3. *Maintains a stable internal state.* **[[Homeostasis]]** is keeping internal conditions (temperature, water content, pH, sugar levels) within the narrow range the cells need, even when the outside changes. You sweat when you are hot and shiver when you are cold; a single-celled organism pumps out excess water that leaks in.
4. *Responds to stimuli.* A stimulus is any change in the environment an organism can detect. Plants bend toward light; bacteria swim toward food; your hand jerks away from a hot stove.
5. *Grows and develops.* Living things increase in size and change form according to instructions they carry, as a fertilized egg becomes a frog.
6. *Reproduces.* Organisms make more organisms, either sexually (two parents) or asexually (one parent).
7. *Has heritable genetic information.* Instructions stored in DNA are passed from parent to offspring and direct how the organism is built and run.
8. *Populations evolve.* Over many generations, the inherited traits of a population change, and populations become adapted to their environments. This happens to groups, not to an individual during its own lifetime.

Some characteristics apply to individuals and some to groups. A mule (the offspring of a horse and a donkey) is almost always sterile, but it is obviously alive: it has cells, a metabolism and homeostasis, and it came from reproduction. Reproduction and evolution are properties of the lineage, not requirements every individual must meet.

### Example 1: Is it alive?

Apply the checklist to a flame, a dormant bean seed and a crystal of salt growing in a saturated solution.

- *Flame.* It "grows" and gives off energy, but it has no cells, no DNA, no homeostasis (it cannot keep its temperature steady against the surroundings) and no inheritance: a new fire is not built from instructions copied from the old one. Not alive.
- *Bean seed.* It looks inert, but inside is an embryo made of cells, with DNA and a very slow metabolism (it still uses a little oxygen). Given water and warmth it grows, develops and eventually reproduces. Alive, though dormant.
- *Salt crystal.* It grows by adding ions to its surface, but growth alone is not enough. It has no cells, no metabolism and no genetic information. Not alive.

One characteristic is never enough; living things show the whole set.

## Detecting life by its chemistry

Because metabolism is so central, it is what scientists look for when they hunt for life. When the two Viking landers reached Mars in 1976, one experiment (the "labeled release" test) dripped nutrient broth containing radioactive carbon onto soil samples. The idea: if microbes were present, they would metabolize the nutrients and release radioactive carbon dioxide gas. Gas did come off. But a control sample, heated first to kill anything living, gave almost none, and other instruments found no organic molecules in the soil. Most scientists concluded that reactive chemicals in the soil, not organisms, released the gas. The episode shows two things you will see again: a single sign of life is not proof, and a well-chosen control is what lets you interpret a result.

## Levels of organization

Life is organized in a hierarchy, each level built from the one below. The picture runs through the twelve levels in order, and the table gives an example of each.

![Twelve numbered tiles, read left to right and top to bottom: 1 atom, 2 molecule (a water molecule), 3 organelle (a mitochondrion), 4 cell, 5 tissue (a sheet of similar cells), 6 organ (a heart), 7 organ system (a heart inside a loop of vessels), 8 organism (one person), 9 population (three people), 10 community (a tree, an animal, a mushroom and a person), 11 ecosystem (living things with sun, water and ground), 12 biosphere (the globe).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Level | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Atom | Smallest unit of an element | A carbon atom |
| Molecule | Atoms bonded together | A protein, DNA, water |
| Organelle | A structure inside a cell with a job | A mitochondrion |
| Cell | Smallest unit that is alive | A muscle cell |
| Tissue | Similar cells working together | Heart muscle tissue |
| Organ | Different tissues forming one structure with a job | The heart |
| Organ system | Organs working together | The circulatory system |
| Organism | One complete living individual | A person |
| Population | All the members of one species in one area | The deer in a forest |
| Community | All the populations of different species in an area | Deer, oaks, wolves, fungi together |
| Ecosystem | A community plus its nonliving surroundings | The forest with its soil, water and climate |
| Biosphere | All the ecosystems on Earth | The whole living planet |

Unicellular organisms such as bacteria skip the tissue-to-organ-system levels: the cell is the organism. Plants have the same levels as animals, with their own tissues (such as the xylem that carries water) and organs (roots, stems, leaves).

Two of these levels are worth separating carefully. A population is one species; a community is every species. And an ecosystem adds the nonliving (abiotic) parts, such as sunlight, water and minerals, to the living (biotic) community.

### Example 2: Ordering the levels

Put these in order from smallest to largest: a pancreas, an insulin molecule, all the people in a city, a pancreatic cell, the digestive system, one person.

Work up the table, asking "what is this made of?" at each step:

1. Insulin molecule (a protein: a molecule).
2. Pancreatic cell (makes the insulin: a cell).
3. Pancreas (made of several tissues: an organ).
4. Digestive system (pancreas, stomach, intestines and more: an organ system). The pancreas also belongs to the endocrine system; organs can serve more than one system.
5. One person (an organism).
6. All the people in a city (one species in one area: a population).

The tissue level was skipped because none of the items is a tissue; that is fine, the order still holds.

## Emergent properties

At each level, new abilities appear that the parts on their own do not have. A single heart muscle cell can contract, but only a whole heart, with tissues arranged into chambers and valves, can pump blood. A water molecule is not wet; wetness is a property of many water molecules together. These **[[emergent properties]]** arise from how the parts are arranged and interact, not from any one part.

That is why biologists study every level: knowing every molecule in a cell does not tell you how the cell behaves.

## Homeostasis in action

Homeostasis usually works by negative feedback: a change triggers a response that pushes the condition back toward its set point. (Module 9 studies feedback in detail; here you only need the idea.) The diagram traces the loop for body temperature on a hot day: the response (sweating) undoes the change that triggered it, and as the temperature returns to normal the response winds down.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Negative feedback keeps body temperature near its set point
  accDescr: A loop of five steps. Body temperature rises above the set point of about 37 °C. Sensors in the skin and brain detect the rise. The brain signals the sweat glands to release more sweat. Sweat evaporates and carries heat away. Temperature falls back toward the set point, the sensors detect the return, and sweating slows. The response opposes the change that triggered it.
  A["Stimulus: body temperature rises above about 37 °C"] --> B["Sensors in skin and brain detect the rise"]
  B --> C["Control center: the brain signals sweat glands"]
  C --> D["Response: sweat evaporates and carries heat away"]
  D --> E["Temperature falls back toward the set point"]
  E -- "sensors detect the return; sweating slows" --> B
```

### Example 3: Reading homeostasis data

A student records her body temperature and her skin's sweat rate during a 40-minute run on a hot day.

| Time (min) | Body temperature (°C) | Sweat rate (relative) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 37.0 | 1 |
| 10 | 37.6 | 4 |
| 20 | 37.9 | 7 |
| 30 | 37.9 | 7 |
| 40 | 37.8 | 7 |

What does the table show?

1. Running releases heat from muscle metabolism, so temperature rises at first (37.0 to 37.6 °C).
2. Sweating increases as the temperature rises. Sweat evaporating from skin carries heat away.
3. After 20 minutes the temperature stops rising and levels off near 37.9 °C even though she keeps running. The rise in heat production is now balanced by the increased heat loss.

The temperature changed by less than 1 °C during heavy exercise. That small change, held in check by a response that grows with the disturbance, is the signature of homeostasis by negative feedback. If sweating failed (for example, from dehydration), the temperature would keep climbing, which is how heat stroke happens.

## Is a virus alive?

Viruses are the classic hard case. They carry genetic information and evolve, but they are not made of cells, have no metabolism of their own and reproduce only by hijacking a living cell. Most biologists therefore do not classify them as living organisms, while recognizing that they sit near the boundary (Lesson 7).

## Common mistakes

- *Using one characteristic as the definition.* "It grows, so it's alive" makes crystals and fires alive. Check the whole set.
- *Thinking every individual must reproduce.* Sterile organisms (mules, worker bees) are alive; reproduction is a property of the species.
- *Saying individuals evolve.* An individual's inherited traits do not change during its life. Populations evolve across generations.
- *Mixing up population and community.* Population: one species. Community: all species in the area.
- *Forgetting the nonliving parts of an ecosystem.* Sunlight, water, soil and temperature are part of an ecosystem, not of a community.

## Key points

- Living things are made of cells, carry out metabolism, maintain **[[homeostasis]]**, respond to stimuli, grow and develop, reproduce, carry heritable DNA, and evolve as populations.
- No single characteristic defines life; nonliving things can show one or two.
- Levels of organization: atom → molecule → organelle → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.
- New **[[emergent properties]]** appear at each level, so every level needs its own study.
- Homeostasis usually works by negative feedback, which returns a condition toward its set point.
- Viruses have genes and evolve but have no cells or metabolism of their own, so most biologists do not consider them alive.

lessons.title: How biologists know: experiments, data, and theories
lessons.body:
## From "what is life" to "how do we know"

The last lesson listed what living things have in common. Every one of those statements was established by evidence: observations, experiments and measurements that other people could check. This lesson is about that process. You will learn how to design a fair experiment, how to read and summarize its data, and what scientists mean (and don't mean) by the words hypothesis, theory and law. These skills come back in every module, because a large part of this course is reading the data from classic experiments and deciding what they show.

## Observations, questions and hypotheses

Science starts with an observation that raises a question. In the 1600s most people believed that maggots arose from rotting meat by "spontaneous generation": life appearing from nonliving matter. The Italian physician Francesco Redi noticed that flies hovered around meat before maggots appeared, and he asked whether the maggots came from the flies.

A **[[hypothesis]]** is a proposed, testable explanation for an observation. Redi's hypothesis: maggots develop from eggs laid by flies, not from the meat itself. A good hypothesis makes a prediction you could check, often written as "if…then": *if* maggots come from fly eggs, *then* meat that flies cannot reach will not develop maggots.

Notice what a hypothesis must be: testable and falsifiable, meaning some possible result would show it is wrong. "Maggots come from an undetectable life force" cannot be tested, so it is not a scientific hypothesis.

The flowchart shows how these pieces fit into an investigation. It is a loop, not a straight line: a hypothesis the data don't support is revised and tested again, and a supported one is checked by other scientists before it is accepted.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How a scientific investigation proceeds
  accDescr: An observation raises a question. A testable hypothesis is proposed, leading to an if-then prediction. A controlled experiment tests the prediction, and the data are analyzed. If the data do not support the hypothesis, it is revised or replaced and tested again. If the data support it, the results are shared for peer review and other scientists try to replicate them; many supported tests can build into a broad theory.
  A["Observation raises a question"] --> C["Hypothesis: a testable explanation"]
  C --> D["Prediction: if... then..."]
  D --> E["Controlled experiment"]
  E --> F["Analyze the data"]
  F -- "does not support" --> H["Revise or replace the hypothesis"]
  H --> C
  F -- "supports" --> G["Share results: peer review, replication; many tests can build a theory"]
```

## Designing a controlled experiment

Redi's experiment (1668) is a model of good design. He put pieces of meat in jars. Some jars were left open; others were covered with fine gauze that let air in but kept flies out. Maggots appeared on the meat in the open jars. In the covered jars no maggots appeared on the meat, though flies laid eggs on the gauze itself. The picture shows the two setups side by side.

![Two glass jars, each with a piece of meat at the bottom. The left jar, labeled open jar (control group), has flies flying in and maggots on the meat. The right jar, labeled gauze-covered jar (experimental group), has a gauze cover that lets air in but keeps flies out; flies sit on the gauze and have laid eggs on it, and there are no maggots on the meat.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every controlled experiment has the same parts.

- The **[[independent variable]]** is the one factor the experimenter deliberately changes. For Redi: whether flies can reach the meat (open jar or gauze).
- The **[[dependent variable]]** is what is measured to see the effect. For Redi: whether maggots appear on the meat.
- A **[[controlled variable]]** (also called a constant) is anything else that could affect the result, kept the same in every group. Redi put the same kinds of meat (he used several, including fish and veal) in both groups, used similar jars and the same room and time. The gauze still let air in, so "lack of air" could not explain the difference, which answered critics who said sealed jars lacked a "vital" air.
- The **[[control group]]** is the group used as a baseline for comparison, usually the normal or untreated condition (here, the open jars). The experimental group gets the treatment being tested.

The logic: if the groups differ in only one way, then a difference in the results must be caused by that one factor. Change two things at once and you cannot tell which caused the effect.

Two more features make results trustworthy. *Replication* means using many individuals or repeating trials, because living things vary; one plant that grows tall might just be a big plant. *Sample size* is how many individuals are in each group. Larger samples make it less likely that a difference is just chance.

### Example 1: Identify the parts

A student wants to know whether a fertilizer helps bean plants grow. She plants 20 bean seeds in identical pots with the same soil. Ten get 50 mL of water with fertilizer each day; ten get 50 mL of plain water. All pots sit on the same windowsill. After three weeks she measures each plant's height.

- Independent variable: whether the water contains fertilizer.
- Dependent variable: plant height after three weeks.
- Controlled variables: type of seed, pot, soil, volume of water, light (same windowsill), length of time.
- Control group: the ten plants given plain water.
- Experimental group: the ten plants given fertilizer.
- Replication: ten plants per group rather than one.

A common slip is to call the plain-water group "controlled variables." Controlled variables are factors held constant; the control group is a set of individuals.

## Summarizing data: means and percent change

Raw data are the individual measurements. To compare groups, we summarize them. The *mean* (average) is the sum of the values divided by how many there are:

$$\text{mean} = \frac{\text{sum of values}}{\text{number of values}}$$

To describe how much something changed relative to where it started, use *percent change*:

$$\text{percent change} = \frac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%$$

A positive result is an increase, a negative one a decrease. Always divide by the original value, not the new one.

### Example 2: Analyze the fertilizer data

Five of the plants in each group (heights in cm):

| Group | Plant 1 | Plant 2 | Plant 3 | Plant 4 | Plant 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain water | 12 | 15 | 14 | 11 | 13 |
| Fertilizer | 18 | 16 | 19 | 17 | 20 |

*Step 1: means.* Plain water: $(12 + 15 + 14 + 11 + 13)/5 = 65/5 = 13$ cm. Fertilizer: $(18 + 16 + 19 + 17 + 20)/5 = 90/5 = 18$ cm.

*Step 2: percent change.* Taking the control mean as the original:

$$\frac{18 - 13}{13} \times 100\% = \frac{5}{13} \times 100\% \approx 38\%$$

*Step 3: look at the spread.* The control heights run 11–15 cm and the fertilizer heights 16–20 cm. The ranges do not overlap, so the difference is unlikely to be chance. If the ranges overlapped a lot, the difference in means would be much less convincing. (Scientists use statistical tests to make this judgment precise; Module 5 introduces one, the chi-square test.)

*Step 4: graph it.* For comparing groups, a bar graph of the means works well; for a variable that changes continuously (like height over many days) a line graph is better. The independent variable goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis.

```plot
{"x": [0, 3], "y": [0, 22], "xLabel": "treatment", "yLabel": "mean height (cm)", "bars": [{"x": 1, "height": 13, "width": 0.6, "label": "plain water"}, {"x": 2, "height": 18, "width": 0.6, "label": "fertilizer"}], "caption": "Mean height of bean plants after three weeks"}
```

*Conclusion:* in this experiment, plants given fertilizer grew about 38% taller on average. That supports the hypothesis that the fertilizer increases growth under these conditions. Note the careful wording: data *support* a hypothesis; they never prove it for all conditions.

## Correlation is not causation

Some questions cannot be tested with a controlled experiment, for ethical or practical reasons. Biologists then use observational studies: they measure variables in a population and look for patterns. If two variables rise and fall together they are *correlated*. But correlation alone does not show that one causes the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated because both rise in summer; ice cream does not cause sunburn. A third, hidden variable (here, sunny weather) can drive both. Controlled experiments, where only one factor differs between groups, are the strongest way to show cause and effect.

### Example 3: Spot the flaw

A student tests whether music helps plants grow. She plays music to plants on a sunny windowsill and keeps a second group, with no music, in a dim closet. The music group grows more. What can she conclude?

Nothing about music. The groups differ in two ways: music and light. Light is a known cause of plant growth, so it could explain the whole result. To fix the design, keep both groups in the same light (and temperature, water and soil), and vary only the music. She should also use several plants per group.

## Hypothesis, theory and law

These three words have specific meanings in science that differ from everyday speech.

- A hypothesis is a testable explanation for a specific observation, before much evidence is in.
- A **[[theory]]** is a broad, well-tested explanation that ties together many observations and hypotheses and has survived repeated attempts to disprove it. Cell theory, the theory of evolution and germ theory are among the best-supported ideas in all of science. In everyday speech "theory" means a guess; in science it means close to the opposite.
- A scientific law *describes* a pattern, often as a mathematical relationship, without explaining why it happens. Mendel's law of segregation describes how traits are passed on; the chromosome theory of inheritance explains why.

Theories do not "graduate" into laws with more evidence. They do different jobs: laws describe, theories explain. Both remain open to revision if new evidence demands it, which is a strength of science, not a weakness.

Science is also a community process. Scientists publish their methods and data so that others can repeat the work, and journals use *peer review*, in which other experts check a study before it is published. A result that other labs cannot reproduce is not accepted, however exciting.

## Common mistakes

- *Changing more than one variable.* Then you cannot tell which change caused the effect.
- *Confusing the control group with controlled variables.* The control group is a baseline set of subjects; controlled variables are conditions kept the same.
- *Dividing by the new value in percent change.* Always divide by the original.
- *Saying data "prove" a hypothesis.* Data support or fail to support it.
- *Treating "theory" as "guess."* A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation.
- *Assuming correlation means causation.* A third variable may drive both.

## Key points

- A **[[hypothesis]]** is a testable, falsifiable explanation; it leads to an "if…then" prediction.
- In a controlled experiment, only the **[[independent variable]]** differs between groups; the **[[dependent variable]]** is measured; **[[controlled variables]]** are kept constant; the **[[control group]]** is the baseline.
- Replication and larger samples make results more reliable.
- Mean = sum / count. Percent change = (new − original) / original × 100%.
- Correlation does not show causation; controlled experiments can.
- A **[[theory]]** is a broad, well-supported explanation; a law describes a pattern. Neither is a guess.

lessons.title: Atoms, water, and pH
lessons.body:
## Why a biology course needs chemistry

The first lesson described life as a hierarchy that starts with atoms and molecules, and the second showed how biologists test ideas. Now we start at the bottom of the hierarchy. Every process in this course, from digestion to DNA copying, is chemistry happening inside cells, and most of that chemistry happens in water. This lesson covers the few chemical ideas biology leans on: what atoms and bonds are, why water behaves so unusually, and how acidity is measured with the pH scale.

## Atoms and the elements of life

All matter is made of atoms. An atom has a dense nucleus of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge), surrounded by electrons (negative charge). An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom, defined by its number of protons: every carbon atom has 6, every oxygen atom 8.

About 25 elements are essential to life, but six make up roughly 98% of the mass of living things. A handy memory aid is **[[CHNOPS]]**: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur. Carbon is the backbone of biological molecules, nitrogen appears in proteins and DNA, phosphorus in DNA and in the energy carrier ATP, and sulfur in some amino acids. Smaller amounts of other elements matter too: calcium in bones, iron in the hemoglobin that carries oxygen in your blood, sodium and potassium in nerve signals.

## Chemical bonds

Atoms join into molecules by bonding, which depends on their outer electrons.

- In a covalent bond, two atoms share a pair of electrons. Covalent bonds are strong and hold the atoms of a biological molecule together: the C–H bonds of sugar, the O–H bonds in water.
- In an ionic bond, one atom transfers electrons to another, producing ions (charged atoms) that attract each other. Table salt, NaCl, is Na⁺ and Cl⁻ held by ionic attraction.

Electrons are not always shared equally. Oxygen pulls on shared electrons much harder than hydrogen does. In a water molecule the electrons spend more time near the oxygen, giving it a slight negative charge (written δ−) and leaving each hydrogen slightly positive (δ+). A molecule with an uneven distribution of charge like this is a **[[polar molecule]]**. Water is also bent, not straight, so its two positive ends sit on one side and the negative end on the other.

```shape
{"circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}, {"center": [-1.25, -0.95], "r": 0.6}, {"center": [1.25, -0.95], "r": 0.6}], "labels": [{"at": [0, 0], "text": "O"}, {"at": [-1.25, -0.95], "text": "H"}, {"at": [1.25, -0.95], "text": "H"}, {"at": [0, 1.35], "text": "δ− (oxygen end)"}, {"at": [0, -1.9], "text": "δ+ (hydrogen end)"}], "caption": "A water molecule is bent and polar: the oxygen end is slightly negative, the hydrogen ends slightly positive"}
```

Opposite charges attract, so the slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule is drawn to the slightly negative oxygen of a neighbor. This attraction between a hydrogen on one polar molecule and an electronegative atom (oxygen or nitrogen) on another is a **[[hydrogen bond]]**. A hydrogen bond is much weaker than a covalent bond, roughly a twentieth as strong, and hydrogen bonds constantly break and re-form in liquid water. But there are enormous numbers of them, and together they explain almost everything special about water. They also hold the two strands of DNA together and help proteins keep their shapes, as you will see in the next two lessons.

![Five water molecules. The center molecule's oxygen is joined by dashed hydrogen bonds to the hydrogens of two molecules above it, and its two hydrogens are joined by dashed hydrogen bonds to the oxygens of two molecules below it. Labels point out a covalent bond inside one molecule, a hydrogen bond between molecules, the slightly negative oxygen end and the slightly positive hydrogen end.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the picture, each solid line is a covalent bond holding a single water molecule together, and each dashed line is a hydrogen bond between two molecules. One water molecule can hydrogen bond with up to four neighbors: its two hydrogens each point at another molecule's oxygen, and its oxygen attracts the hydrogens of two more.

## The properties of water

*Cohesion and adhesion.* **[[Cohesion]]** is the attraction of water molecules to each other, through hydrogen bonds. It gives water high surface tension, which is why a water strider can stand on a pond. Adhesion is the attraction of water to other substances, such as the walls of a glass tube. Together they produce capillary action, water creeping up a narrow tube. In plants, cohesion holds a continuous column of water together all the way up the thin xylem tubes from root to leaf, so that evaporation from the leaves pulls the whole column upward.

*High specific heat.* **[[Specific heat]]** is the amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C. For water it is about 4.18 J/(g·°C), one of the highest of any common substance; dry sand is about 0.8 J/(g·°C). Heating water means first breaking many hydrogen bonds, which soaks up energy. The result: water changes temperature slowly. Oceans and lakes keep coastal climates mild, and the water that makes up most of your body buffers you against sudden temperature swings. Water also absorbs a lot of energy when it evaporates, which is why sweating cools you.

*Ice floats.* Most substances are denser as solids. When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open lattice that takes up about 9% more space than the same mass of liquid water, so ice is about 8% less dense and floats. A frozen pond freezes from the top down, and the ice layer insulates the liquid water beneath, letting fish survive the winter.

*Water is an excellent solvent.* In a solution, the substance that does the dissolving is the solvent and the dissolved substance is the solute. Because water is polar, it surrounds ions and other polar molecules and pulls them apart: the δ− oxygens face positive ions and the δ+ hydrogens face negative ions. Sugars, salts, amino acids and many other molecules of life dissolve in water, which is why blood, sap and the inside of cells are all water-based solutions. Nonpolar substances, such as oils and fats, do not dissolve in water; they are hydrophobic ("water-fearing"), while polar and charged substances are hydrophilic.

### Example 1: Using specific heat

How much energy does it take to warm 250 g of water from 20 °C to 30 °C? How much for 250 g of dry sand?

Energy = mass × specific heat × temperature change.

- Water: $250 \times 4.18 \times 10 = 10\,450$ J, about 10.5 kJ.
- Sand: $250 \times 0.8 \times 10 = 2000$ J, about 2 kJ.

The same energy that warms sand by 10 °C would warm the same mass of water by only about 2 °C. That is why a beach's sand is scorching by afternoon while the sea stays cool, and why large bodies of water steady the temperature of the land around them.

## Acids, bases and pH

A small fraction of water molecules split into a hydrogen ion (H⁺) and a hydroxide ion (OH⁻). In pure water these are equal. An acid is a substance that releases H⁺ into a solution, raising the H⁺ concentration; a base lowers it (by releasing OH⁻, which combines with H⁺ to make water, or by taking up H⁺ directly).

**[[pH]]** is a measure of the hydrogen ion concentration on a scale usually running from 0 to 14:

$$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+], \qquad [\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} \text{ mol/L}$$

- pH 7 is neutral (pure water at 25 °C).
- Below 7 is acidic; the lower the pH, the more H⁺.
- Above 7 is basic (alkaline).

The scale is logarithmic: each step of 1 pH unit is a *tenfold* change in H⁺ concentration. A solution at pH 4 has 10 times the H⁺ of one at pH 5 and 100 times that at pH 6.

```numberline
{"x": [0, 14], "points": [{"at": [2, 0], "label": "stomach acid ≈ 2"}, {"at": [5, 0], "label": "black coffee ≈ 5"}, {"at": [7, 0], "label": "pure water 7"}, {"at": [7.4, 0], "label": "blood 7.4"}, {"at": [11, 0], "label": "household ammonia ≈ 11"}], "caption": "The pH scale: acidic below 7, basic above 7"}
```

### Example 2: Comparing pH values

Stomach fluid has a pH of about 2; the small intestine, where the stomach's contents go next, is near pH 8. How many times greater is the H⁺ concentration in the stomach?

The pH differs by $8 - 2 = 6$ units. Each unit is a factor of 10, so the stomach has $10^6 = 1\,000\,000$ times the H⁺ concentration. Equivalently, $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-2}$ mol/L in the stomach and $10^{-8}$ mol/L in the intestine, and $10^{-2} / 10^{-8} = 10^{6}$.

A frequent wrong answer is 6 times (treating the scale as linear) or 4 times (dividing 8 by 2). Neither respects the logarithm.

## Buffers keep pH steady

Living cells tolerate only a narrow range of pH, because pH changes the charges on proteins and with them the proteins' shapes (Lesson 5 shows what that does to enzymes). Human blood is held between about 7.35 and 7.45. Body fluids stay so steady because of a **[[buffer]]**, a pair of chemicals that takes up excess H⁺ when acid is added and releases H⁺ when base is added. In blood, the main buffer is the carbonic acid / bicarbonate pair: bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) soaks up extra H⁺, and carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) gives H⁺ back when the blood becomes too basic. Buffering is a chemical part of homeostasis.

### Example 3: Reading buffer data

A student adds drops of dilute hydrochloric acid to 50 mL of pure water and to 50 mL of a buffer solution, measuring pH after each 5 drops.

| Drops of acid | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pure water (pH) | 7.0 | 3.2 | 2.9 | 2.7 | 2.6 |
| Buffer (pH) | 7.0 | 6.9 | 6.9 | 6.8 | 6.7 |

What do the data show?

1. In pure water, the first 5 drops dropped the pH by almost 4 units: a rise in H⁺ of several thousandfold ($10^{3.8} \approx 6000$). Water alone has nothing to absorb the added H⁺.
2. In the buffer, 20 drops lowered the pH by only 0.3 units. The buffer took up almost all the added H⁺.
3. Conclusion: the buffer resists change in pH. A buffer has a limited capacity, though; if acid kept being added, the buffer would eventually be used up and its pH would fall quickly too.

This is a controlled comparison: same volume, same acid, same drops. The only difference between the two groups is whether a buffer is present.

## Common mistakes

- *Treating pH as linear.* A change of 3 pH units is a $10^3 = 1000$-fold change in H⁺, not 3-fold.
- *Getting the direction backward.* Lower pH means more H⁺, which is more acidic.
- *Confusing hydrogen bonds with covalent bonds.* Covalent bonds hold the atoms within a water molecule together; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between separate molecules.
- *Mixing up cohesion and adhesion.* Cohesion is water to water; adhesion is water to something else.
- *Thinking a buffer keeps pH exactly constant.* It reduces the change, and only until its capacity runs out.

## Key points

- Six elements (CHNOPS) make up about 98% of living matter; carbon is the backbone of biological molecules.
- Water is a **[[polar molecule]]**; **[[hydrogen bonds]]** between water molecules cause its **[[cohesion]]**, high **[[specific heat]]**, floating ice and power as a solvent.
- **[[pH]]** $= -\log[\text{H}^+]$. Below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; each unit is a tenfold change.
- A **[[buffer]]** resists changes in pH; buffers in blood keep it near 7.4.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids
lessons.body:
## Building with carbon

The last lesson ended with water, the medium of life. Now we turn to what is dissolved in and built around that water: the large carbon-based molecules that make up most of a cell's dry mass. Carbon is ideal for building, because each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds. Carbon atoms link into chains, branches and rings, with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and other atoms attached, giving an almost unlimited variety of shapes. Molecules built around carbon are called organic molecules.

Biologists sort the large molecules of life into four classes: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Each class has a characteristic building block, a characteristic set of elements and characteristic jobs. Learning these patterns lets you predict what a molecule does from what it is made of.

## Monomers, polymers and the water rule

Three of the four classes are polymers. A **[[monomer]]** is a small molecule that can link to others like it; a **[[polymer]]** is a long chain of monomers bonded together, like a train made of cars.

Cells build polymers by **[[dehydration synthesis]]**: two monomers are joined by a covalent bond, and in the process a molecule of water is removed (one monomer loses an –OH, the other loses an –H). Cells break polymers apart by **[[hydrolysis]]** ("splitting with water"): a water molecule is added across the bond, separating the monomers. Digestion is mostly hydrolysis. Specific enzymes speed up both reactions, as the next lesson explains.

The bookkeeping is simple. Joining $n$ monomers in a single chain makes $n - 1$ bonds, so it releases $n - 1$ water molecules. Breaking the chain back into monomers uses $n - 1$ water molecules.

![Two ring-shaped monomers, numbered 1 and 2. Monomer 1 carries an OH group and monomer 2 an H, highlighted together. An arrow pointing right, labeled dehydration synthesis (builds; releases water), leads to the two rings joined through an oxygen atom, plus a separate water molecule. An arrow pointing back left is labeled hydrolysis (breaks; adds water).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The diagram shows where the water comes from: an –OH from one monomer and an –H from the other leave as H₂O. Hydrolysis runs the reaction backward.

### Example 1: Counting water and mass

Glucose has a molar mass of 180 g/mol and water 18 g/mol. (a) What is the molar mass of a disaccharide made from two glucose molecules? (b) A short chain of 10 glucose units is built by dehydration synthesis. How many water molecules are released, and what is the mass of the chain?

(a) One bond forms and one water leaves: $180 + 180 - 18 = 342$ g/mol. (Maltose, made of two glucoses, and sucrose, made of glucose and fructose, both have formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ and mass 342.)

(b) Ten monomers make $10 - 1 = 9$ bonds, releasing 9 water molecules. Mass $= 10 \times 180 - 9 \times 18 = 1800 - 162 = 1638$ g/mol.

The usual mistake is to subtract 10 waters instead of 9. Picture three cars in a train: two couplings, not three.

## Carbohydrates

A **[[carbohydrate]]** is a sugar or a polymer of sugars, made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, typically in about a 1:2:1 ratio (glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆). Carbohydrates are the main short-term energy source for cells and also serve as building material.

- *Monosaccharides* are single sugars: glucose (the fuel most cells burn), fructose (fruit sugar) and galactose.
- *Disaccharides* are two sugars joined: sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), maltose.
- *Polysaccharides* are long chains, often hundreds or thousands of glucose units. Starch stores energy in plants (potatoes, grains). Glycogen stores energy in animals, mainly in the liver and muscles. Cellulose builds plant cell walls; it is the most abundant organic molecule on Earth. Chitin forms the exoskeletons of insects and the walls of fungi.

Starch and cellulose are both made of glucose, yet you can digest one and not the other. The glucose units in cellulose are linked in a different orientation, and human enzymes cannot hydrolyze that bond. Cows and termites can live on cellulose only because microbes in their guts make the needed enzymes. Same monomer, different linkage, completely different properties: structure determines function.

## Lipids

A **[[lipid]]** is a member of a diverse group of molecules that are mostly nonpolar and therefore do not dissolve in water. Lipids are not true polymers, because they are not built from repeating identical monomers. They are made mainly of carbon and hydrogen, with relatively little oxygen.

- *Fats and oils (triglycerides)* consist of one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acid chains. They store energy compactly: about 9 kcal per gram, compared with about 4 kcal per gram for carbohydrates and proteins. They also insulate and cushion organs. In a *saturated* fatty acid every carbon holds as many hydrogens as possible, and the chain is straight; the chains pack tightly, so saturated fats such as butter are solid at room temperature. An *unsaturated* fatty acid has one or more carbon–carbon double bonds that, in the usual natural (cis) form, put kinks in the chain; the chains cannot pack tightly, so unsaturated fats such as olive oil are liquid.
- *Phospholipids* have two fatty acid tails and a phosphate-containing head. The head is polar and the tails are not, so phospholipids form the double layer of every cell membrane (Lesson 9).
- *Steroids* have four fused carbon rings. Cholesterol stiffens animal cell membranes and is the starting material for hormones such as testosterone and estrogen.

## Proteins

A **[[protein]]** is a polymer of amino acids folded into a specific three-dimensional shape. An **[[amino acid]]** has a central carbon bonded to an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen and a side chain called the R group. Twenty different R groups, some polar, some nonpolar, some charged, give the 20 common amino acids their different properties. Amino acids join by dehydration synthesis; the bond between them is a peptide bond, and a chain of amino acids is a polypeptide. Proteins contain C, H, O and N, and most also contain sulfur.

![The general structure of an amino acid: a central carbon atom bonded to a hydrogen above, an H2N amino group on the left, a COOH carboxyl group on the right (a carbon double-bonded to O and bonded to OH), and an R group, the side chain, below. Labels name each part and note that the R group differs among the 20 amino acids.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The picture labels the four groups attached to the central carbon. Only the R group changes from one amino acid to another. When two join, the carboxyl group of one meets the amino group of the next and a water leaves, as in the diagram above.

Proteins do more kinds of jobs than any other class: enzymes speed up reactions, hemoglobin carries oxygen, antibodies fight infection, collagen gives structure, actin and myosin move muscles, and insulin carries signals.

A protein's job depends on its shape, which is described at four levels:

1. *Primary structure*: the sequence of amino acids, set by a gene.
2. *Secondary structure*: local coils (α helices) and folded sheets (β sheets), held by hydrogen bonds along the backbone.
3. *Tertiary structure*: the overall 3-D fold of one chain, held by interactions between R groups.
4. *Quaternary structure*: two or more chains assembled together. Hemoglobin has four.

![A four-panel diagram. Panel 1, primary: a chain of beads labeled Met, Ala, Lys, Gly, Leu, Ser, Cys, joined by peptide bonds. Panel 2, secondary: a coiled alpha helix and a beta sheet of three side-by-side arrows linked by dashed hydrogen bonds. Panel 3, tertiary: one chain, including a helix and a strand, folded into a compact shape. Panel 4, quaternary: four subunits, two alpha and two beta, packed together as in hemoglobin.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the picture, each level is built from the one before it.

How do we know the sequence determines the shape? In the late 1950s Christian Anfinsen treated the enzyme ribonuclease with chemicals that broke its internal bonds and unfolded it completely; it lost all activity. When he slowly removed the chemicals, the chains refolded on their own into the correct shape, and nearly all the activity returned. No other information was present, so the amino acid sequence alone must hold the instructions for folding. A single change in sequence can matter enormously: in sickle cell disease, one amino acid substitution in hemoglobin changes how the molecules stack, distorting red blood cells.

## Nucleic acids

A **[[nucleic acid]]** is a polymer of nucleotides that stores and transmits genetic information. Each nucleotide has three parts: a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing base. Nucleic acids contain C, H, O, N and P.

- **[[DNA]]** (deoxyribonucleic acid) stores the hereditary instructions. Its sugar is deoxyribose and its bases are adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). It is usually a double strand.
- **[[RNA]]** (ribonucleic acid) carries out the instructions, chiefly by helping build proteins. Its sugar is ribose, it uses uracil (U) in place of thymine, and it is usually single-stranded.

One nucleotide deserves a mention now. ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is built like an RNA nucleotide, with the base adenine and the sugar ribose, but it carries a chain of three phosphate groups instead of one. It is the cell's main short-term energy carrier (Module 3). Module 6 covers DNA and RNA in depth.

## Identifying the class

| Class | Monomer | Elements | Main jobs | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | Monosaccharide | C, H, O (≈1:2:1) | Quick energy, structure | Glucose, starch, cellulose |
| Lipids | None (glycerol + fatty acids for fats) | C, H, little O; P in phospholipids | Long-term energy, membranes, hormones | Oils, phospholipids, cholesterol |
| Proteins | Amino acid | C, H, O, N (often S) | Enzymes, transport, structure, signals | Hemoglobin, collagen, insulin |
| Nucleic acids | Nucleotide | C, H, O, N, P | Store and express genetic information | DNA, RNA |

### Example 2: Identify the molecule

An unknown molecule is analyzed. It contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur, but no phosphorus. Hydrolysis breaks it into about 300 small molecules of 20 different kinds. What is it?

1. Nitrogen rules out ordinary carbohydrates and fats.
2. No phosphorus makes a nucleic acid unlikely, since every nucleotide contains phosphate.
3. Sulfur is characteristic of proteins (from the amino acids cysteine and methionine).
4. Twenty kinds of monomer matches the 20 amino acids; four kinds would suggest a nucleic acid; one kind would suggest a polysaccharide such as starch.

It is a protein of about 300 amino acids.

### Example 3: Food test results

Standard chemical indicators detect each class: Benedict's solution turns from blue to green, orange or brick-red when heated with simple sugars such as glucose; iodine solution turns blue-black with starch; biuret reagent turns violet with protein; lipids leave a translucent spot on brown paper (or stain red with Sudan III). A student tests four samples:

| Sample | Benedict's | Iodine | Biuret | Paper spot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | brick-red | brown (no change) | blue (no change) | none |
| B | blue (no change) | blue-black | blue (no change) | none |
| C | blue (no change) | brown (no change) | violet | none |
| D | blue (no change) | brown (no change) | blue (no change) | translucent |

Sample A contains a simple sugar (could be glucose solution or fruit juice). B contains starch (a potato extract). C contains protein (egg white). D contains lipid (vegetable oil). A distilled-water sample tested the same way is the negative control: it shows what "no change" looks like for each reagent.

## Common mistakes

- *Subtracting $n$ waters for $n$ monomers.* A chain of $n$ monomers has $n - 1$ bonds.
- *Mixing up the two reactions.* Dehydration synthesis builds and releases water; hydrolysis breaks and uses water.
- *Calling lipids polymers.* They lack a repeating monomer.
- *Thinking starch and cellulose differ in their sugars.* Both are glucose; the linkage differs.
- *Forgetting which classes contain N and P.* Proteins have N (and often S); nucleic acids have N and P; ordinary carbohydrates such as sugars, starch and cellulose have neither (chitin, a sugar polymer with nitrogen added, is the notable exception).

## Key points

- **[[Monomers]]** link into **[[polymers]]** by **[[dehydration synthesis]]** (water released) and are split by **[[hydrolysis]]** (water added); $n$ monomers → $n - 1$ water molecules.
- **[[Carbohydrates]]**: sugars and polysaccharides, for energy and structure.
- **[[Lipids]]**: nonpolar fats, phospholipids and steroids, for long-term energy storage, membranes and hormones.
- **[[Proteins]]**: chains of 20 kinds of **[[amino acid]]**; shape (from sequence) determines function.
- **[[Nucleic acids]]**: **[[DNA]]** and **[[RNA]]**, polymers of nucleotides that store and use genetic information.

lessons.title: Enzymes
lessons.body:
## Proteins that make chemistry fast

The last lesson ended with proteins and the idea that a protein's shape determines its job. The most important proteins of all are enzymes. A cell carries out thousands of chemical reactions every second: digesting food, copying DNA, building membranes. At body temperature, most of these reactions would happen far too slowly to keep a cell alive, taking years or even centuries on their own. Enzymes make them happen in fractions of a second. This lesson explains how, and how temperature, pH, substrate supply and inhibitors change their speed.

## What an enzyme is

An **[[enzyme]]** is a biological catalyst, almost always a protein, that speeds up a specific chemical reaction. A catalyst is any substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up or permanently changed by it. Because the enzyme comes out unchanged, one enzyme molecule can catalyze the same reaction over and over, thousands of times per second for fast enzymes.

The molecule an enzyme acts on is its **[[substrate]]**; what the reaction produces are the products. Enzyme names usually end in *-ase* and often name the substrate: lactase breaks down lactose, protease breaks down proteins, DNA polymerase builds DNA polymers.

The discovery that enzymes are chemicals, not a mysterious "vital force," came in 1897. Eduard Buchner ground yeast cells with sand, filtered the juice so that no living cells remained, and added sugar. The cell-free juice still fermented the sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Something in the juice, not life itself, was doing the chemistry. In 1926 James Sumner purified the enzyme urease into crystals and showed it was a protein. (A few catalysts in cells, called ribozymes, are made of RNA instead; the ribosome's catalytic core is one. But the vast majority of enzymes are proteins.)

## Activation energy

Even a reaction that releases energy needs a push to get started. Old bonds must be strained or broken before new ones form. The energy needed to start a reaction is its **[[activation energy]]**. A match will not light until you strike it; sugar will not burn in air until you heat it.

Enzymes speed up reactions by *lowering the activation energy*. They do not supply energy, and they do not change how much energy the reaction releases or absorbs overall; the starting and ending energies are the same with or without the enzyme. They provide an easier pathway.

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [0, 11], "xLabel": "progress of reaction", "yLabel": "energy", "functions": [{"f": "3.5 - 1.5*tanh(2*(x-5)) + 5*exp(-(x-5)^2)", "label": "without enzyme"}, {"f": "3.5 - 1.5*tanh(2*(x-5)) + 2.5*exp(-(x-5)^2)", "label": "with enzyme", "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [1, 5.6], "text": "reactants"}, {"at": [9, 1.4], "text": "products"}], "caption": "An enzyme lowers the activation energy (the hump) but not the energy of the reactants or products"}
```

## How enzymes work: the active site

An enzyme folds into a shape with a small pocket or groove called the **[[active site]]**, where the substrate binds. The active site's shape and the chemical properties of its amino acid side chains match the substrate, which is why each enzyme is so specific: sucrase acts on sucrose, not on lactose.

The steps are:

1. The substrate binds to the active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex.
2. The enzyme changes shape slightly to grip the substrate more tightly. This is the *induced fit* model; the older "lock and key" picture of a rigid active site is a useful start but leaves this out. The fit strains the substrate's bonds, holds two substrates in the right orientation, or provides a favorable chemical environment, lowering the activation energy.
3. The reaction occurs and the products are released.
4. The enzyme is free to bind another substrate.

![Three panels connected by arrows. Panel 1, substrate meets active site: a substrate shaped like a wedge sits above a matching notch, the active site, in a larger enzyme. Panel 2, enzyme-substrate complex: the substrate sits in the active site, whose edges have closed around it (induced fit). Panel 3, products released: the substrate has split into two pieces that move away, and the enzyme is unchanged and ready to act again.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The picture follows one trip around this cycle. Notice that the enzyme in panel 3 is identical to the one in panel 1: that is what it means for a catalyst not to be used up.

Many enzymes need a helper to work: a *cofactor* such as a metal ion (zinc, magnesium, iron) or an organic *coenzyme*, many of which come from vitamins. That is one reason vitamins are needed in the diet.

## Measuring enzyme activity

Enzyme activity is measured as a reaction rate: how much product forms, or how much substrate disappears, per unit time.

$$\text{rate} = \frac{\text{change in amount}}{\text{change in time}}$$

On a graph of product versus time, the rate is the slope. Biologists usually report the *initial rate*, the slope at the very start, because later the substrate is being used up and the reaction slows.

### Example 1: Catalase and oxygen

Catalase, found in nearly all cells that use oxygen, breaks down hydrogen peroxide (a harmful by-product of metabolism) into water and oxygen gas: 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. A student adds a slice of potato (a source of catalase) to hydrogen peroxide and collects the oxygen.

| Time (s) | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| O₂ collected (mL) | 0 | 8 | 15 | 21 | 25 | 27 | 28 |

*Initial rate (first 10 s):* $\dfrac{8 - 0}{10 - 0} = 0.8$ mL/s.

*Rate from 40 to 60 s:* $\dfrac{28 - 25}{60 - 40} = \dfrac{3}{20} = 0.15$ mL/s.

*Interpretation:* the rate falls over time not because the enzyme wears out (it is not used up) but because the hydrogen peroxide, the substrate, is being consumed. Fewer substrate molecules means fewer collisions with active sites. If the curve flattens completely, the substrate is gone; adding more peroxide would start the reaction again.

## Factors that affect enzyme activity

### Temperature

Raising the temperature makes molecules move faster, so enzymes and substrates collide more often and the rate rises. But above a certain temperature, the vibrations break the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions holding the enzyme's shape. The active site loses its shape and can no longer bind substrate. This loss of shape is **[[denaturation]]**, and it is usually permanent (an egg white does not unboil). The temperature of fastest activity is the *optimum temperature*. For most human enzymes it is near body temperature, about 37 °C. Enzymes from bacteria living in hot springs have optima above 70 °C; their stable proteins are used in the PCR technique of Module 6.

```plot
{"x": [0, 65], "y": [0, 110], "xLabel": "temperature (°C)", "yLabel": "relative activity (%)", "functions": [{"f": "113*exp(0.07*(x-37))/(1+exp(0.5*(x-41)))", "label": "human enzyme"}], "points": [{"at": [37, 100], "label": "optimum ≈ 37 °C"}], "caption": "Activity rises with temperature until the enzyme denatures, then falls steeply"}
```

Notice the shape: a gradual rise, then a steep fall. Cooling an enzyme slows it but does not denature it; warm it back up and activity returns. Overheating destroys it.

### pH

Each enzyme also has an *optimum pH*. Changing the pH changes the charges on R groups, disrupting the bonds that hold the enzyme's shape and the charges in the active site. Far from the optimum, the enzyme denatures. Optima match where enzymes work: pepsin, which digests protein in the acidic stomach, works best near pH 2; trypsin, which continues protein digestion in the small intestine, works best near pH 8.

```plot
{"x": [0, 12], "y": [0, 110], "xLabel": "pH", "yLabel": "relative activity (%)", "functions": [{"f": "100*exp(-(x-2)^2/1.5)", "label": "pepsin"}, {"f": "100*exp(-(x-8)^2/1.5)", "label": "trypsin", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Pepsin works best near pH 2, trypsin near pH 8"}
```

### Substrate concentration

With a fixed amount of enzyme, adding substrate speeds the reaction at first, because active sites find substrates more often. Eventually every active site is busy all the time; the enzyme is *saturated*, and the rate levels off at a maximum. At that point, only adding more enzyme can raise the rate.

### Inhibitors

An **[[inhibitor]]** is a molecule that reduces an enzyme's activity.

- A *competitive inhibitor* resembles the substrate and binds the active site, blocking it. Because inhibitor and substrate compete for the same spot, flooding the reaction with substrate can outcompete the inhibitor and restore nearly the full maximum rate.
- A *noncompetitive inhibitor* binds elsewhere on the enzyme and changes its shape so the active site works poorly. Adding more substrate does not help, because the problem is not competition for the site.

Cells use inhibition to regulate themselves. In *feedback inhibition*, the end product of a chain of reactions inhibits an enzyme early in the chain, so the cell stops making a product when it has enough. The diagram shows the pattern: product D, three steps away, shuts down enzyme 1.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Feedback inhibition of a metabolic pathway
  accDescr: Enzyme 1 converts a starting molecule A into B, enzyme 2 converts B into C, and enzyme 3 converts C into the end product D. When D builds up, it binds enzyme 1 and inhibits it, slowing the whole pathway so the cell stops making D when it has enough.
  A["A"] --> E1{{"Enzyme 1"}}
  E1 --> B["B"]
  B -- "enzyme 2" --> C["C"]
  C -- "enzyme 3" --> D["End product D"]
  D -. "inhibits" .-> E1
```

Many drugs and poisons are inhibitors: ibuprofen blocks an enzyme that makes inflammation signals, and some nerve agents and insecticides block an enzyme needed by nerves.

```plot
{"x": [0, 30], "y": [0, 110], "xLabel": "substrate concentration", "yLabel": "reaction rate", "functions": [{"f": "100*x/(2+x)", "label": "no inhibitor"}, {"f": "100*x/(8+x)", "label": "competitive inhibitor", "dashed": true}, {"f": "50*x/(2+x)", "label": "noncompetitive inhibitor", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Extra substrate overcomes a competitive inhibitor but not a noncompetitive one"}
```

### Example 2: Which kind of inhibitor?

A researcher measures the rate of an enzyme with and without a drug, at low and high substrate concentrations (rates in µmol/min).

| Substrate | No drug | With drug |
|---|---|---|
| Low | 40 | 15 |
| Very high | 95 | 93 |

At low substrate the drug cuts the rate sharply (from 40 to 15), but at very high substrate the rate with the drug almost reaches the uninhibited maximum (93 versus 95). Extra substrate overcomes the drug, so it competes for the active site: it is a *competitive inhibitor*. A noncompetitive inhibitor would lower the rate at high substrate too.

### Example 3: Predicting an experiment

A student boils a potato slice for 5 minutes, cools it to room temperature, then adds it to hydrogen peroxide. Predict the result, and name the control.

Prediction: little or no oxygen is produced. Boiling denatured the catalase, and cooling does not restore its shape. The control is an unboiled potato slice of the same size in the same volume and concentration of peroxide at the same temperature; it should bubble vigorously, showing that the peroxide and procedure work and that any difference comes from boiling.

## Common mistakes

- *Saying enzymes are used up.* They are released unchanged and reused; the substrate is used up.
- *Saying enzymes add energy or change the overall energy released.* They only lower the activation energy.
- *Saying high temperature "kills" enzymes.* Enzymes are molecules, not living things; they denature.
- *Thinking cold denatures enzymes.* Cold slows them reversibly; heat and extreme pH denature them.
- *Assuming all enzymes have the same optimum.* Optima match each enzyme's normal environment.
- *Confusing the two inhibitors.* Only competitive inhibition is overcome by adding substrate.

## Key points

- An **[[enzyme]]** is a reusable biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds a specific reaction by lowering its **[[activation energy]]**.
- The **[[substrate]]** binds the **[[active site]]**; induced fit strains bonds and brings substrates together.
- Rate = change in amount ÷ time; the initial rate is the slope at the start.
- Activity rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme undergoes **[[denaturation]]**; each enzyme has an optimum pH too.
- More substrate raises the rate until the enzyme is saturated.
- A competitive **[[inhibitor]]** blocks the active site (overcome by extra substrate); a noncompetitive inhibitor changes the enzyme's shape from elsewhere.

lessons.title: Protein structure and folding
lessons.body:
## From four levels to a mechanism

Lesson 4 described protein shape at four levels and told the story of Anfinsen's ribonuclease, which refolded on its own. This honors lesson asks the harder questions. Why does one stretch of chain become a helix and another a sheet? What holds a folded protein together? How does a chain find its one correct shape among an astronomical number of wrong ones, and what happens in the cell, and in disease, when it doesn't? The picture below recaps the four levels from Lesson 4.

![A four-panel diagram of protein structure. Panel 1, primary: a chain of beads labeled Met, Ala, Lys, Gly, Leu, Ser, Cys, joined by peptide bonds. Panel 2, secondary: a coiled alpha helix and a beta sheet of three side-by-side arrows linked by dashed hydrogen bonds. Panel 3, tertiary: one chain, including a helix and a strand, folded into a compact shape. Panel 4, quaternary: four subunits, two alpha and two beta, packed together as in hemoglobin.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The backbone: flat plates joined by swivels

When two amino acids join by dehydration synthesis, the carboxyl carbon of one bonds to the amino nitrogen of the next. This C–N bond is the **[[peptide bond]]**. A polypeptide therefore has a repeating backbone, N–C–C, N–C–C, with an R group on each central (alpha) carbon. One end has a free amino group (the N-terminus), the other a free carboxyl group (the C-terminus); sequences are written from N to C, the direction the ribosome builds them.

The peptide bond is not an ordinary single bond. Electrons are shared partly across the C=O and C–N bonds, giving the C–N link partial double-bond character. Double bonds don't rotate, so the six atoms around each peptide bond lie flat in one plane. The chain can only twist at the single bonds on either side of each alpha carbon: picture flat playing cards joined at the corners by swivels. In 1963 G. N. Ramachandran showed that most combinations of swivel angles make atoms bump into each other; the allowed regions are small, and they include the angles found in the helix and the sheet.

## R groups decide where each part goes

The backbone is the same along the whole chain, so the R groups make each protein different. They fall into four broad groups at the pH of a cell:

| Class | Examples | Behavior in water |
|---|---|---|
| Nonpolar (hydrophobic) | glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, proline | avoid water; tend to be buried inside |
| Polar, uncharged | serine, threonine, asparagine, glutamine, tyrosine, cysteine | hydrogen bond with water or each other |
| Acidic (negative) | aspartate, glutamate | charged; usually on the surface |
| Basic (positive) | lysine, arginine (histidine is partly charged) | charged; usually on the surface |

Three have special jobs. Glycine's R group is a single hydrogen, so the chain is flexible there (common in tight turns). Proline's R group bonds back to its own backbone nitrogen, locking its swivel and removing the N–H a helix needs, so proline usually breaks or kinks a helix. Cysteine's –SH group can bond covalently to another cysteine.

## Secondary structure: patterns in the backbone

Secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms (the C=O of one amino acid and the N–H of another), not between R groups, which is why the same few patterns appear in almost every protein.

In an **[[α helix]]** (alpha helix) the backbone winds into a right-handed coil. The C=O of each amino acid forms a hydrogen bond with the N–H of the amino acid four positions further along the chain, so every backbone group in the middle of the helix is paired. There are 3.6 amino acids per turn, and each amino acid raises the helix by 0.15 nm, so one turn is about 0.54 nm tall. The R groups point outward like bristles on a bottle brush. Linus Pauling, Robert Corey and Herman Branson predicted this structure in 1951 from careful models of the peptide bond, years before any whole protein structure was seen: a risky, testable prediction that was later confirmed.

In a **[[β sheet]]** (beta sheet) the chain runs in nearly straight, stretched-out segments called strands, about 0.33 to 0.35 nm per amino acid. Strands lie side by side, running in opposite directions (*antiparallel*) or the same direction (*parallel*), and hydrogen bond to each other; R groups stick alternately above and below the sheet. Loops and turns connect helices and strands. Some amino acids favor one pattern or the other, but only as tendencies.

### Example 1: How long is a helix?

A protein has a helix of 18 amino acids. (a) How many turns does it make, and how long is it? (b) If the same 18 amino acids formed a β strand instead (about 0.34 nm each), how long would that be? (c) The oily core of a cell membrane is about 3.0 nm thick. How many amino acids must a helix have to cross it?

(a) Turns: $18 \div 3.6 = 5$ turns. Length: $18 \times 0.15 = 2.7$ nm.

(b) Strand length: $18 \times 0.34 \approx 6.1$ nm, more than twice the helix, because the strand is stretched out instead of coiled.

(c) $3.0 \div 0.15 = 20$ amino acids. This matches real membrane proteins, whose membrane-crossing parts are typically helices of about 20 mostly nonpolar amino acids.

## Tertiary structure: burying the oily parts

The main force that makes a chain fold up is the **[[hydrophobic effect]]**. Nonpolar R groups can't hydrogen bond with water, so the water around them is forced into more ordered arrangements. When the chain folds so that nonpolar R groups cluster in the interior, that ordered water is released and the system as a whole becomes more disordered, which is favorable. A typical soluble protein ends up with an oily core and a polar, charged surface. (Membrane proteins are nonpolar on the surface where they touch the lipid tails.)

Other interactions fine-tune the shape (the picture after this list shows one of each):

- hydrogen bonds between polar R groups;
- ionic bonds (salt bridges) between negative R groups (aspartate, glutamate) and positive ones (lysine, arginine);
- van der Waals attractions, weak but numerous, between closely packed atoms in the core;
- a **[[disulfide bond]]**, a covalent S–S bond between two cysteines. These are common in proteins that work outside cells, such as antibodies and insulin; the inside of a cell is chemically reducing, which breaks S–S bonds.

![A diagram of one folded polypeptide backbone, drawn as a thick gray line that runs back and forth three times. Between the first and second passes, two cysteine sulfur atoms are joined by a disulfide bond, and nonpolar side chains cluster together as hydrophobic interactions. Between the second and third passes, a negative COO minus group faces a positive NH3 plus group in an ionic bond, and an OH group lines up with an O atom in a hydrogen bond.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Apart from disulfides these interactions are individually weak, which explains denaturation (Lesson 5): heat shakes them apart, and a pH change alters which R groups are charged. The covalent backbone, and so the primary structure, survives.

Large proteins are usually built from several **[[protein domains]]**, compact regions of about 50 to 250 amino acids that fold on their own and often have their own job, such as binding DNA.

A caution: not every protein has one fixed shape. Many proteins contain long *intrinsically disordered* regions that stay floppy until they bind a partner. "One sequence, one stable fold" holds for most enzymes and structural proteins, but it is a simplification.

## Quaternary structure: subunits that talk to each other

The same interactions hold separate chains together. Hemoglobin's four chains (two α, two β) each carry a heme group that binds one O₂, and they influence each other: when one binds oxygen its shape shifts, making the others bind more readily. This *cooperativity* helps hemoglobin load oxygen in the lungs and unload it in the tissues; single-chain myoglobin shows none. The next honors lesson shows enzymes using the same trick.

## How does a chain find its fold?

Ribonuclease has 124 amino acids, including 8 cysteines that form 4 disulfide bonds. Anfinsen unfolded it with urea (which breaks the weak interactions) and β-mercaptoethanol (which breaks S–S bonds); removing both slowly gave back active enzyme. But when he let the S–S bonds re-form while urea still kept the chain unfolded, only about 1% of the activity returned. A trace of mercaptoethanol added later let the wrong bonds break and re-form, and activity crept back to full. His conclusion: the native shape is the most stable one the sequence can adopt, and the chain will find it if wrong bonds can be undone.

### Example 2: Why about 1%?

How many different ways can 8 cysteines pair up into 4 disulfide bonds? What fraction is correct?

The first cysteine can pair with any of the other 7; the first of the 6 left with any of 5; the first of the 4 left with any of 3; the last 2 pair with each other.

$$7 \times 5 \times 3 \times 1 = 105 \text{ pairings}$$

Only one is native, so random pairing gives the right set $1/105 \approx 0.95\%$ of the time, matching the roughly 1% activity: without the folded chain to guide them, the sulfur atoms paired at random.

### Example 3: Levinthal's paradox

In 1969 Cyrus Levinthal posed a puzzle. If each amino acid of a 100-amino-acid chain could take just 3 positions, and the chain tried shapes at random at $10^{13}$ per second, how long would a full search take?

Number of shapes: $3^{100} \approx 5.2 \times 10^{47}$.

Time: $\dfrac{5.2 \times 10^{47}}{10^{13} \text{ per s}} = 5.2 \times 10^{34}$ s. Dividing by $3.16 \times 10^7$ s per year gives about $1.6 \times 10^{27}$ years, some $10^{17}$ times the age of the universe.

Real proteins fold in microseconds to seconds, so folding is not a random search. Local pieces such as helices form quickly and are kept because they lower the energy, and the chain collapses to hide its hydrophobic R groups; each step narrows the options. Biophysicists picture an energy *funnel* sloping from many unfolded shapes down to the one native state.

## Folding in a crowded cell: chaperones

The cytoplasm is crowded, and a new chain leaves the ribosome one amino acid at a time, its hydrophobic stretches exposed before the rest of the chain can cover them. Exposed patches on different chains stick together into useless, sometimes toxic clumps.

**[[Molecular chaperones]]** help other proteins fold. The Hsp70 family grabs exposed hydrophobic stretches and releases them in ATP-powered cycles, giving the chain repeated chances. Chaperonins (GroEL with its lid GroES in bacteria) form a barrel-shaped chamber where one chain folds alone. Many chaperones are *heat shock proteins*, made in larger amounts when heat threatens to unfold proteins. Chaperones carry no instructions for the final shape; they prevent wrong interactions, consistent with Anfinsen's finding.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The possible fates of a newly made polypeptide
  accDescr: A ribosome releases a new, unfolded polypeptide. Most chains fold into their native shape, often with help from chaperones. Some misfold, leaving hydrophobic patches exposed. A misfolded chain can be refolded by a chaperone, tagged and broken down by the proteasome, or stick to other misfolded copies and form aggregates such as amyloid fibrils, which are linked to diseases like Alzheimer's and prion diseases. Stress such as heat, a change in pH or a mutation can push a native protein toward misfolding.
  R["Ribosome releases a new, unfolded chain"] --> N["Native fold: working protein"]
  R --> M["Misfolded: hydrophobic patches exposed"]
  N -. "heat, pH change or mutation" .-> M
  M -- "chaperone helps it refold" --> N
  M -- "tagged and destroyed" --> P["Proteasome breaks it down"]
  M -- "sticks to other misfolded copies" --> A["Aggregates and amyloid fibrils"]
```

The diagram shows the cell's three answers to a misfolded chain: refold it, destroy it in the proteasome, or, when both fail, live with aggregates.

## When folding goes wrong

*Sickle cell disease.* In hemoglobin's β chain, the sixth amino acid, glutamate (charged), is replaced by valine (nonpolar). The change is on the surface, so each molecule still folds and carries oxygen. But after releasing oxygen, the valine's oily patch fits a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring molecule, and the molecules link into long fibers that bend red blood cells into rigid sickles.

*Cystic fibrosis.* The most common mutation deletes one phenylalanine (position 508) from CFTR, a chloride channel. The channel misfolds and the cell's quality control destroys most copies before they reach the membrane. Newer "corrector" drugs help it fold well enough to get there.

*Amyloid and prions.* Some misfolded proteins stack into β-sheet-rich fibrils called amyloid, found in Alzheimer's disease (amyloid-β, tau) and Parkinson's disease (α-synuclein); how far they cause these diseases is still being researched. A **[[prion]]** is a misfolded form of a normal brain protein (PrP) that converts normal copies to its own shape, so misfolding spreads like an infection, causing Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and "mad cow disease" (BSE). Stanley Prusiner's claim that a protein with no DNA or RNA could be infectious was doubted at first and earned the 1997 Nobel Prize.

## Seeing and predicting structures

Structures are determined by X-ray crystallography (myoglobin and hemoglobin were solved this way around 1958–1960), NMR for small proteins, and cryo-electron microscopy (2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry). The public Protein Data Bank holds well over 200,000 structures. In 2020 the AlphaFold program, trained on them, predicted many proteins' shapes from sequence alone, often close to experimental accuracy; its developers shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Predictions are weaker for disordered regions, complexes and single mutations, so experiments remain essential.

## Common mistakes

- *Saying secondary structure is held by R groups.* Helices and sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups; tertiary structure is where R groups take over.
- *Treating the hydrogen bond as the main reason proteins fold.* The hydrophobic effect, hiding nonpolar R groups from water, is the main driving force.
- *Thinking denaturation breaks peptide bonds.* Heat and pH break the weak interactions; the primary structure is intact.
- *Assuming chaperones hold the folding instructions.* The sequence does; chaperones prevent wrong interactions.
- *Using 0.15 nm per amino acid for a strand.* That rise is for a helix; a strand is about 0.34 nm per amino acid.

## Key points

- The **[[peptide bond]]** is flat and rigid; the chain folds by rotating at the alpha carbons, and only certain angle combinations are allowed.
- The **[[α helix]]** has 3.6 amino acids per turn, rises 0.15 nm per amino acid and is held by C=O to N–H hydrogen bonds four amino acids apart; the **[[β sheet]]** is made of extended strands hydrogen bonded side by side.
- The **[[hydrophobic effect]]** drives folding; hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals contacts and covalent **[[disulfide bonds]]** refine it. Large proteins are built of **[[protein domains]]**.
- Sequence determines shape (Anfinsen; random disulfide pairing, $1/105$, explains his 1% result). Folding follows a funnel, not a random search (Levinthal).
- **[[Molecular chaperones]]** prevent misfolding and aggregation in the crowded cell.
- Misfolding underlies sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, amyloid diseases and **[[prion]]** diseases.

lessons.title: Enzyme kinetics and regulation
lessons.body:
## From a curve to an equation

Lesson 5 showed that, with a fixed amount of enzyme, the reaction rate rises with substrate concentration and then levels off when the enzyme is saturated, and that a competitive inhibitor can be outcompeted by extra substrate while a noncompetitive one cannot. *Enzyme kinetics* turns those pictures into numbers. Two numbers per enzyme let you predict its rate at any substrate concentration, compare enzymes fairly and tell from a few measurements how a drug works. The second half of the lesson turns to how cells switch enzymes on and off.

## The Michaelis–Menten model

In 1913 Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten, studying the enzyme invertase, proposed that enzyme (E) and substrate (S) bind reversibly to form a complex (ES), which either falls apart or goes on to make product (P):

$$\text{E} + \text{S} \rightleftharpoons \text{ES} \rightarrow \text{E} + \text{P}$$

The rate is proportional to how much enzyme is in the ES form. For the *initial* rate, with far more substrate than enzyme molecules, this gives the **[[Michaelis–Menten equation]]**:

$$v = \frac{V_{\max}\,[\text{S}]}{K_m + [\text{S}]}$$

Here $v$ is the initial rate and $[\text{S}]$ the substrate concentration. The two constants describe the enzyme:

- **[[Vmax]]**, written $V_{\max}$, is the maximum rate, reached when every enzyme molecule is busy all the time. It depends on how much enzyme is present: double the enzyme and $V_{\max}$ doubles.
- The **[[Michaelis constant]]**, $K_m$, is the substrate concentration that gives half the maximum rate.
