- *Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)* hands the electrons to oxygen, making water, and pumps 2 H⁺ per pair of electrons. Cyanide and carbon monoxide poison you by binding here.

![The inner mitochondrial membrane drawn across the middle, with the intermembrane space above and the matrix below. Complexes I, III and IV span the membrane and pump 4, 4 and 2 hydrogen ions upward. Electrons from NADH enter complex I, and electrons from FADH2 enter complex II; both pass to Q in the membrane, then to complex III, to cytochrome c on the outer face, to complex IV and finally to oxygen, forming water. Hydrogen ions flow back down through ATP synthase, whose head in the matrix makes ATP from ADP and phosphate.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Adding up: electrons from NADH pass through complexes I, III and IV and move $4 + 4 + 2 = 10$ H⁺. Electrons from succinate skip complex I and move $4 + 2 = 6$. That difference, rather than anything about FADH₂ itself, is why the two carriers are worth different amounts of ATP.

## Storing energy in a gradient

Pumping protons stores energy in two forms at once: a chemical part, because the matrix becomes less acidic than the intermembrane space (a pH difference, $\Delta\text{pH}$), and an electrical part, because each H⁺ is charged, so the matrix side becomes negative (a membrane potential, $\Delta\psi$). Together they make up the **[[proton-motive force]]**, $\Delta p$, usually given in millivolts:

$$\Delta p = \Delta\psi + (61.5 \text{ mV}) \times \Delta\text{pH} \quad \text{(sizes only, at 37 °C)}$$

In a working mitochondrion both parts push protons back into the matrix: roughly 150–180 mV of membrane potential plus 0.5–0.8 pH units, for a $\Delta p$ of about 180–220 mV, mostly electrical. In chloroplasts other ions (Cl⁻, Mg²⁺) cross the thylakoid membrane and cancel much of the charge, so more of the force is a pH difference. Isolated thylakoids reach about 3 pH units; in living leaves the difference is smaller, and the exact split is still studied.

The free energy released when one mole of H⁺ flows back is $F\,\Delta p$.

### Example 1

A mitochondrion has $\Delta\psi = 160$ mV and $\Delta\text{pH} = 0.65$. Find $\Delta p$, the free energy per mole of H⁺, and the smallest number of H⁺ that could pay for one ATP if making ATP in the matrix costs about 50 kJ/mol.

Step 1: $\Delta p = 160 + 61.5 \times 0.65 = 160 + 40 = 200$ mV, or 0.200 V.

Step 2: Energy per mole of H⁺: $96.5 \times 0.200 = 19.3$ kJ/mol.

Step 3: $50 \div 19.3 = 2.6$. At least 2.6 protons must flow back for each ATP. Real synthases use a little more than this minimum, as the next section shows.

## ATP synthase: a rotary motor

ATP synthase has two parts. F₀, in the membrane, contains a ring of identical c subunits. F₁ is the knob: three α and three β subunits around a lopsided central stalk, on the matrix side in mitochondria and the stroma side in chloroplasts. Protons ride on the c subunits as the ring turns, and the ring spins the stalk. As the stalk turns, it forces each β subunit through three shapes in turn: one that loosely binds ADP and Pᵢ, one that clamps them so tightly that ATP forms, and one that opens and releases ATP. This is Paul Boyer's **[[binding-change mechanism]]**. Its surprise is that the energy is spent mainly on releasing ATP from the enzyme, not on forming the bond.

Three ATP are made per full turn (one per β subunit), so protons per ATP = (number of c subunits) ÷ 3. Ring sizes differ: 8 in animal mitochondria, 10 in yeast mitochondria and E. coli, 14 in spinach chloroplasts. Mammalian synthase needs about $8/3 \approx 2.7$ H⁺ per ATP, just above the minimum from Example 1. In mitochondria about one more H⁺ per ATP is spent bringing phosphate in and swapping the new ATP out for ADP.

## How many ATP per NADH?

The **[[P/O ratio]]** is the number of ATP made per oxygen atom reduced, that is, per pair of electrons sent down the chain. The common textbook accounting uses 4 H⁺ per ATP (about 3 through the synthase plus 1 for transport):

- NADH: $10 \div 4 = 2.5$ ATP
- Succinate (FADH₂): $6 \div 4 = 1.5$ ATP

These are the core lesson's 2.5 and 1.5, close to measured values. They are not whole numbers because the gradient sits between electrons and ATP, and some protons leak back without making ATP. Using ring sizes instead: mammals need $8/3 + 1 = 3.67$ H⁺ per ATP, so NADH is worth $10 \div 3.67 = 2.7$ ATP. A synthase with a 10-subunit ring (as in yeast mitochondria) needs $10/3 + 1 = 4.33$, so 10 H⁺ buy only 2.3 ATP. (Baker's yeast actually lacks complex I, so its NADH pumps fewer protons and yields even less.) That is one reason the total per glucose is a range (about 30–32), and why the older figures of 3 and 2 per carrier (36–38 per glucose) were revised.

## The chloroplast version

The thylakoid runs a similar chain powered by light. Photosystem II (reaction center P680) pulls electrons from water, releasing O₂ and H⁺ into the thylakoid space. Plastoquinone (PQ), a cousin of ubiquinone, carries them to the cytochrome b₆f complex (a cousin of complex III), which pumps more H⁺ inward. The copper protein plastocyanin (PC) carries them to photosystem I (P700), where a second photon boosts them to ferredoxin (Fd), and the enzyme FNR makes NADPH. Protons flow back out through ATP synthase, whose knob faces the stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses the ATP.

![The thylakoid membrane drawn across the middle, with the stroma above and the thylakoid space below. Light strikes photosystem II, which splits water into oxygen and hydrogen ions on the thylakoid-space side. Electrons pass through plastoquinone, the cytochrome b6f complex, plastocyanin, photosystem I (which receives more light), ferredoxin and the enzyme FNR, which makes NADPH in the stroma. Hydrogen ions are pumped into the thylakoid space at the b6f complex and flow back out to the stroma through ATP synthase, making ATP.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The orientation looks reversed: chloroplasts pile protons up inside the thylakoid and make ATP in the stroma outside it; mitochondria pile them up outside the matrix and make ATP inside it. But in both, the knob faces the compartment that matches the cytoplasm of their bacterial ancestors, just as bacteria pump protons out and make ATP in their cytoplasm.

### Example 2

In linear electron flow, the passage of 4 electrons from 2 H₂O to 2 NADP⁺ moves about 12 H⁺ into the thylakoid space (4 from splitting water, 8 at the b₆f complex). The chloroplast ATP synthase has 14 c subunits. Does linear flow make enough ATP for the Calvin cycle, which uses 3 ATP for every 2 NADPH?

Step 1: Protons per ATP $= 14/3 = 4.67$ (no transport cost: the ATP is made and used in the stroma).

Step 2: ATP per 2 NADPH $= 12 \div 4.67 = 2.57$, a ratio of $2.57 \div 2 = 1.29$ ATP per NADPH.

Step 3: The Calvin cycle needs $3 \div 2 = 1.5$ ATP per NADPH. Linear flow falls short by about 0.2 ATP per NADPH. Chloroplasts make up the gap with **[[cyclic electron flow]]**: electrons from photosystem I return from ferredoxin to the plastoquinone pool and the b₆f complex instead of going to NADP⁺. This pumps protons and makes ATP without making NADPH or splitting water.

## The experiments behind chemiosmosis

When Peter Mitchell proposed chemiosmosis in 1961, most biochemists were hunting for a high-energy chemical intermediate linking electron transport to ATP synthesis, as in substrate-level phosphorylation. None was ever found. Mitchell's idea made testable predictions: the membrane must be sealed, electron transport must move protons, and an artificial proton gradient alone should make ATP.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The Jagendorf acid-bath experiment
  accDescr: Thylakoid membranes are soaked in an acid solution at about pH 4 in the dark, so the space inside each thylakoid fills with hydrogen ions. They are then moved quickly into a pH 8 buffer containing ADP and phosphate, still in the dark. Hydrogen ions flow out of the thylakoids through ATP synthase, and ATP is made with no light and no electron transport. If an uncoupler is added, the hydrogen ions leak out across the membrane instead and almost no ATP is made.
  A["Thylakoids soaked in pH 4 acid, in the dark"] --> B["Thylakoid space fills with H+ (about pH 4)"]
  B --> C["Moved quickly into pH 8 buffer with ADP + Pi, still dark"]
  C --> D["H+ flows out through ATP synthase"]
  D --> E["ATP made: no light, no electron transport"]
  C --> F["With an uncoupler: H+ leaks out across the membrane"]
  F --> G["Almost no ATP made"]
```

In 1966 André Jagendorf and Ernest Uribe did this acid-bath experiment with spinach thylakoids. In the dark, the membranes made a burst of ATP, up to about one ATP per four chlorophyll molecules, far more than any hidden intermediate could have stored; the yield grew with the size of the pH jump, and substances that make membranes leaky to protons abolished it. In 1974 Efraim Racker and Walther Stoeckenius made ATP in light using artificial vesicles holding only two proteins: a light-driven proton pump from an archaeon (bacteriorhodopsin) and a mitochondrial ATP synthase. No electron transport chain was present at all. Mitchell received the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In 1997 a Japanese team filmed the stalk of ATP synthase rotating, and that year Boyer and John Walker, whose group had solved the structure of the F₁ knob, shared half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (the other half went to Jens Skou for the sodium-potassium pump).

## Uncouplers, inhibitors, and brown fat

Because the gradient links the chain to the synthase, the two normally run together: electrons flow only as fast as protons can get back in. This coupling is called **[[respiratory control]]**.

An **[[uncoupler]]** lets protons back across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase. The classic one, 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), is a weak acid that picks up H⁺ outside the matrix, crosses the membrane and releases it inside. Electron transport and oxygen use speed up, ATP synthesis collapses, and the energy appears as heat. DNP was sold as a diet drug in the early 1930s, caused deaths from overheating, and was soon taken off the US market; it still kills people who buy it illegally.

Mammals also uncouple on purpose. Mitochondria in **[[brown adipose tissue]]** (brown fat), found in newborns, hibernating animals and, in smaller amounts, many adults, are packed with uncoupling protein 1 (thermogenin), a channel that lets protons leak back and makes heat without shivering.

Inhibitors act at specific points: rotenone on complex I, antimycin A on complex III, cyanide and carbon monoxide on complex IV. Oligomycin plugs the proton channel of ATP synthase; through respiratory control it slows electron transport too, because the gradient can no longer be spent.

### Example 3

Isolated mitochondria are given succinate in a sealed chamber, and their oxygen use is measured (illustrative data). Explain each rate.

| Condition | O₂ use (nmol O₂/min) |
|---|---|
| Succinate only | 10 |
| + ADP | 48 |
| + ADP, then oligomycin | 11 |
| + oligomycin, then DNP | 70 |

Step 1: Succinate only: with no ADP the synthase cannot run, so the gradient builds up and pushes back on the pumps. The slow rate reflects protons leaking back.

Step 2: Adding ADP lets protons flow through the synthase, lowering the gradient, so electron transport speeds up about fivefold. This is respiratory control.

Step 3: Oligomycin plugs the synthase, so the gradient builds again and oxygen use falls back to the leak rate, even with ADP present.

Step 4: DNP gives protons a route around the plugged synthase. The gradient collapses and oxygen use is the highest of all, yet no ATP is made: respiration has been uncoupled.

## Common mistakes

- Saying the electron transport chain makes ATP. It makes the proton gradient; ATP synthase makes ATP.
- Forgetting why FADH₂ is worth less: its electrons enter at Q and skip complex I, so they move 6 protons, not 10.
- Placing the gradient backwards. H⁺ is high in the intermembrane space (ATP made in the matrix) and in the thylakoid space (ATP made in the stroma).
- Thinking oligomycin and DNP have the same effect on oxygen use. Both stop ATP synthesis, but oligomycin slows oxygen use and DNP speeds it up.

## Key points

- Mitochondrial chain: NADH → complex I → Q → complex III → cytochrome c → complex IV → O₂. Protons pumped per pair of electrons: 4 (I), 4 (III), 2 (IV); 10 from NADH, 6 from succinate.
- Proton-motive force = electrical part + pH part; about 200 mV in mitochondria. Each mole of H⁺ flowing back releases $F\Delta p$, about 19 kJ.
- ATP synthase is a rotary motor: 3 ATP per turn, so H⁺ per ATP = (number of c subunits) ÷ 3, plus about 1 for transport in mitochondria.
- P/O ratios of about 2.5 (NADH) and 1.5 (FADH₂) follow from proton counting; they depend on ring size and leaks.
- Thylakoids run a similar chain (PSII → PQ → b₆f → PC → PSI → Fd → FNR); cyclic electron flow adds ATP without NADPH to reach the 3 ATP : 2 NADPH the Calvin cycle needs.
- Evidence: Jagendorf's acid bath (1966) and Racker–Stoeckenius vesicles (1974) showed that a proton gradient alone makes ATP.
- Uncouplers (DNP, thermogenin) give fast oxygen use, little ATP, much heat; oligomycin blocks ATP synthase and slows oxygen use.

lessons.title: The Calvin cycle in depth: photorespiration, C4 and CAM
lessons.body:
## The enzyme at the center of life

The core photosynthesis lesson gave the Calvin cycle in three steps and one fact about its key enzyme: rubisco attaches CO₂ to RuBP. This lesson follows every carbon atom around the cycle, then looks at rubisco's great weakness, its tendency to grab O₂ instead of CO₂. The corn in a field, the cactus in a desert and the pineapple on a farm photosynthesize differently because of that one problem.

## The cycle, carbon by carbon

It is easiest to follow three turns of the cycle, which fix three CO₂ and produce one spare three-carbon sugar.

1. *Fixation.* Rubisco joins each CO₂ to a molecule of RuBP (ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate, five carbons). The six-carbon product is unstable and splits at once into two molecules of **[[3-phosphoglycerate]]** (3-PGA, three carbons). For three turns: 3 RuBP + 3 CO₂ → 6 3-PGA. Carbon count: $15 + 3 = 18 = 6 \times 3$.
2. *Reduction.* Each 3-PGA is phosphorylated by ATP and then reduced by NADPH to G3P. This is the step where light energy, carried by ATP and NADPH, becomes chemical energy in sugar. Six 3-PGA use 6 ATP and 6 NADPH to make 6 G3P (18 carbons).
3. *Leaving.* One G3P (3 carbons) leaves the cycle. It is the actual product: exported to the cytosol to make sucrose, or kept in the stroma to make starch.
4. *Regeneration.* The other five G3P (15 carbons) are reshuffled through a series of three-, four-, five-, six- and seven-carbon sugars into three five-carbon molecules, and 3 more ATP phosphorylate them back into 3 RuBP (15 carbons). The cycle is ready to turn again.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Carbon bookkeeping in three turns of the Calvin cycle
  accDescr: Three RuBP, five carbons each and 15 carbons in all, combine with three CO2 in the fixation step catalyzed by rubisco, giving six 3-PGA with 18 carbons. In the reduction step, 6 ATP and 6 NADPH turn these into six G3P, still 18 carbons. One G3P, 3 carbons, leaves the cycle as product. The other five G3P, 15 carbons, are rearranged using 3 more ATP into three RuBP, and the cycle repeats.
  R["3 RuBP (15 C)"] -- "fixation by rubisco: + 3 CO₂" --> P["6 3-PGA (18 C)"]
  P -- "reduction: 6 ATP, 6 NADPH" --> G["6 G3P (18 C)"]
  G --> O["1 G3P leaves (3 C)"]
  G -- "5 G3P (15 C)" --> X["Regeneration: 3 ATP"]
  X --> R
```

Totals per G3P: 9 ATP and 6 NADPH. Per CO₂: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. The 3 : 2 ratio of ATP to NADPH matters: as the last honors lesson showed, linear electron flow alone makes slightly too little ATP, and cyclic electron flow tops it up.

Several Calvin cycle enzymes, rubisco included, switch on in the light and off in the dark. Light makes the stroma more alkaline (about pH 8, as protons are pumped into the thylakoids) and raises its Mg²⁺ level, and electrons from ferredoxin activate other enzymes through a small protein, thioredoxin. So the cycle does not waste ATP at night.

### Example 1

In the 1950s, Calvin's group followed the radioactive label in algae and then changed the conditions suddenly. Predict what happens to the amounts of 3-PGA and RuBP (a) when the light is switched off, with CO₂ still present, and (b) when the CO₂ supply is cut, with the light still on.

Step 1: (a) In the dark, ATP and NADPH run out within seconds, so 3-PGA can no longer be reduced and starts to pile up. Rubisco keeps fixing CO₂ for a short while, consuming the remaining RuBP, and no new RuBP is made (regeneration also needs ATP). So 3-PGA rises and RuBP falls.

Step 2: (b) Without CO₂, rubisco has nothing to attach to RuBP, so RuBP accumulates. The 3-PGA already present is still reduced by ATP and NADPH from the light reactions and drained away. So RuBP rises and 3-PGA falls.

Step 3: This is what the experiments found, and the opposite responses were key evidence that RuBP is the CO₂ acceptor and 3-PGA its product.

## Rubisco's weakness and photorespiration

Rubisco is slow, catalyzing only a few reactions per second per active site, compared with thousands for many enzymes. Plants make up for this with sheer quantity; rubisco is often a third to half of the soluble protein in a leaf and is probably the most abundant protein on Earth. Its bigger problem is that it is not choosy. Its active site also accepts O₂, which competes with CO₂ for the same position on RuBP.

When rubisco adds O₂ to RuBP instead of CO₂, the products are one 3-PGA and one two-carbon molecule, 2-phosphoglycolate, which the Calvin cycle cannot use and which inhibits some of its enzymes. The plant salvages it through a long pathway that runs through the chloroplast, the peroxisome and the mitochondrion. For every two 2-phosphoglycolate (4 carbons), the salvage pathway returns one 3-PGA (3 carbons) to the Calvin cycle and releases one CO₂, plus ammonia that must be refixed using ATP. This whole process is called **[[photorespiration]]**: it uses O₂ and releases CO₂ like respiration, but it makes no ATP; it costs ATP and NADPH.

How often does rubisco make this mistake? In a typical leaf at 25 °C in today's air, roughly one oxygenation for every three or four carboxylations. The ratio climbs with temperature, because CO₂ becomes less soluble relative to O₂ as water warms and rubisco's preference for CO₂ weakens. It also climbs when stomata close to save water on a hot, dry day: CO₂ inside the leaf falls while O₂ from the light reactions builds up. In hot conditions, photorespiration can cut a plant's net carbon gain by a quarter or more.

Why would evolution leave such a flaw? Rubisco arose billions of years ago, when the air held far more CO₂ and almost no O₂, so the side reaction hardly mattered. Its CO₂ and O₂ reactions seem chemically linked, so a faster, more selective rubisco may not be possible without trade-offs; this is still debated, and engineering a better one is an active research goal. Photorespiration may have some uses (supplying amino acids, protecting the light reactions under stress), but on balance it lowers yield.

### Example 2

A leaf's rubisco carries out 400 carboxylations per second, and the ratio of oxygenations to carboxylations is 0.3. Find the net CO₂ fixed per second, and the percentage of fixed carbon lost to photorespiration.

Step 1: Oxygenations: $400 \times 0.3 = 120$ per second.

Step 2: Each 2 oxygenations release 1 CO₂ in the salvage pathway, so $120 \div 2 = 60$ CO₂ are released per second.

Step 3: Net fixation: $400 - 60 = 340$ CO₂ per second. Loss: $60 \div 400 = 0.15$, or 15% of the carbon fixed. And that ignores the extra ATP and NADPH spent on the salvage pathway.

## C4 plants: concentrating CO₂ in space

Plants that fix CO₂ directly with rubisco, making the three-carbon 3-PGA as their first product, are called **[[C3 plants]]**; they include most plants, among them wheat, rice, soybeans and trees. In the mid-1960s, Hugo Kortschak's group in Hawaii and then Marshall Hatch and Roger Slack in Australia found that sugarcane fed radioactive CO₂ put the label first into four-carbon acids (malate and aspartate), not into 3-PGA. These are **[[C4 plants]]**, and they work by pumping CO₂ to rubisco.

![Two cells side by side. In the mesophyll cell, carbon dioxide from the air, as bicarbonate, is attached to PEP by PEP carboxylase, giving oxaloacetate, which becomes malate. Malate moves into the bundle-sheath cell, where it releases carbon dioxide and becomes pyruvate. The carbon dioxide, now concentrated around rubisco, enters the Calvin cycle, and sugars go to the vein. Pyruvate returns to the mesophyll cell, where ATP is used to turn it back into PEP.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The trick uses two kinds of cell arranged in rings around each vein, an arrangement called **[[Kranz anatomy]]** (German for "wreath"). In the outer mesophyll cells, the enzyme **[[PEP carboxylase]]** attaches CO₂ (as bicarbonate, HCO₃⁻) to the three-carbon PEP, making four-carbon oxaloacetate, which is turned into malate. PEP carboxylase has no reaction with O₂ and grabs bicarbonate even at low concentrations. Malate moves into the inner **[[bundle-sheath cells]]**, tightly packed around the vein, where it is broken down to release CO₂ and pyruvate. Rubisco and the Calvin cycle are found there, bathed in CO₂ at several times (by some estimates up to ten times) the level in the outside air, so oxygenation becomes rare. The pyruvate returns to the mesophyll and is turned back into PEP.

The C4 pump is not free. Regenerating PEP uses one ATP but breaks it down to AMP, which costs the equivalent of 2 ATP. So a C4 plant spends 5 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed instead of 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. In cool, moist or shady conditions, where photorespiration is low, that extra cost can make C4 the losing strategy. In hot, bright and dry conditions it pays off. Because C4 plants keep CO₂ high around rubisco, they can also keep their stomata less open, losing less water per sugar made, and they need less rubisco, so less nitrogen.

C4 photosynthesis has evolved independently more than 60 times, in grasses (corn, sugarcane, sorghum, millets, crabgrass) and in many other families. C4 species are only about 3% of flowering plants, but they carry out roughly a quarter of all photosynthesis on land.

### Example 3

Compare the ATP and NADPH a C3 plant and a C4 plant spend to make one glucose (6 CO₂), ignoring photorespiration.

Step 1: C3: $6 \times 3 = 18$ ATP and $6 \times 2 = 12$ NADPH (as in the core lesson).

Step 2: C4: $6 \times 5 = 30$ ATP and $6 \times 2 = 12$ NADPH.

Step 3: The C4 plant pays 12 extra ATP per glucose, two-thirds more ATP. It comes out ahead only when the C3 plant would otherwise lose enough carbon and energy to photorespiration, which happens at high temperature and when stomata are closing. In experiments, C4 grasses usually beat C3 grasses in full sun above roughly the mid-20s °C, and C3 plants usually win in cool climates.

## CAM plants: concentrating CO₂ in time

Desert plants face a sharper trade-off: open stomata and lose water, or close them and starve. **[[CAM]]** (crassulacean acid metabolism, named for the stonecrop family, Crassulaceae, which includes the jade plant) solves it by opening the stomata at night, when air is cool and humid, and closing them during the hot day.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: CAM plants separate CO2 uptake and the Calvin cycle in time
  accDescr: At night the stomata are open. CO2 enters the leaf, PEP carboxylase fixes it into oxaloacetate, which becomes malic acid stored in the vacuole. During the day the stomata are closed. Malic acid leaves the vacuole and releases CO2 inside the leaf, and the Calvin cycle fixes that CO2 using ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.
  subgraph Night["Night: stomata open"]
    direction TB
    N1["CO₂ enters leaf"] --> N2["PEP carboxylase makes oxaloacetate"] --> N3["Malic acid stored in vacuole"]
  end
  subgraph Day["Day: stomata closed"]
    direction TB
    D1["Malic acid leaves vacuole"] --> D2["CO₂ released inside leaf"] --> D3["Calvin cycle, powered by the light reactions"]
  end
  N3 --> D1
```

At night, PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into four-carbon acids, stored as malic acid in the large central vacuole; the cell sap becomes steadily more acidic through the night. As early as 1815 a botanist noted that leaves of one such plant tasted sour in the morning and much less so by afternoon. During the day, with the stomata shut, the malic acid is broken down to release CO₂ behind closed doors, and the Calvin cycle fixes it using ATP and NADPH from the light reactions. C4 plants separate the two carboxylations in space (two cell types); CAM plants separate them in time (night and day, in the same cell).

CAM plants include most cacti, agaves, pineapple, jade plants and many orchids and bromeliads, together roughly 6% of plant species. Their growth is usually slow, because the vacuole can store only so much acid each night, but their water economy is unmatched. Many CAM plants can also switch to ordinary C3 fixation when water is plentiful.

| | C3 | C4 | CAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| First product of CO₂ fixation | 3-PGA (3C) | Oxaloacetate (4C) | Oxaloacetate (4C) |
| How the steps are separated | Not separated | In space: mesophyll and bundle sheath | In time: night and day |
| Stomata open | Day | Day (less widely) | Night |
| Photorespiration | Significant, worse when hot | Very low | Very low |
| ATP per CO₂ fixed | 3 | About 5 | About 5 or more |
| Examples | Wheat, rice, oaks | Corn, sugarcane | Cacti, pineapple |

### Example 4

A rough, often-quoted comparison: a C3 plant loses about 500 molecules of water through its stomata for every CO₂ molecule it fixes, a C4 plant about 250, and a CAM plant about 50 (real values vary a lot with weather and species). How many moles of water does each lose while fixing enough CO₂ for 1 mole of glucose?

Step 1: One glucose needs 6 CO₂, so 1 mol glucose needs 6 mol CO₂.

Step 2: C3: $6 \times 500 = 3{,}000$ mol water. C4: $6 \times 250 = 1{,}500$ mol. CAM: $6 \times 50 = 300$ mol.

Step 3: In mass (18 g/mol), that is about 54 kg, 27 kg and 5.4 kg of water for 180 g of glucose. The CAM plant uses a tenth of the water of the C3 plant, which is why CAM dominates in deserts despite growing slowly.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking C4 and CAM plants do not use the Calvin cycle. They all do; C4 and CAM add a CO₂-concentrating step in front of it.
- Thinking CAM plants run the Calvin cycle at night. It needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so it runs in the day; only CO₂ uptake happens at night.
- Calling photorespiration a kind of respiration that makes ATP. It consumes ATP and NADPH and releases CO₂ that had already been fixed.
- Thinking C4 is always better. It costs extra ATP; C3 plants do as well or better in cool, moist, shady places.
- Mixing up the enzymes: PEP carboxylase does the first fixation in C4 and CAM plants; rubisco still does the fixation that feeds the Calvin cycle.

## Key points

- Three turns of the Calvin cycle: 3 RuBP + 3 CO₂ → 6 3-PGA → 6 G3P; 1 G3P leaves, 5 regenerate 3 RuBP. Cost per CO₂: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH.
- Rubisco is slow and also reacts with O₂; the salvage pathway (photorespiration) releases 1 CO₂ per 2 oxygenations and costs ATP.
- Photorespiration rises with temperature and when stomata close.
- C4 plants (Kranz anatomy): PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ in mesophyll cells into a four-carbon acid that delivers CO₂ to rubisco in bundle-sheath cells. About 5 ATP per CO₂.
- CAM plants: take in CO₂ at night and store it as malic acid; release it to the Calvin cycle by day with stomata closed. Highest water-use efficiency.
- Which strategy wins depends on temperature, light and water.

lessons.title: The cell cycle and mitosis
lessons.body:
## Why cells divide

The last module followed energy through the cell: light captured in photosynthesis, sugar broken down for ATP. One of the biggest jobs that ATP pays for is making new cells. You began as a single fertilized egg and are now made of roughly 30 trillion cells. Your body replaces roughly 330 billion cells every day, most of them blood cells: skin flakes away, the lining of your gut is renewed every few days, and red blood cells last about four months. A cut heals because cells near the wound divide. Single-celled organisms such as amoebas and yeast divide to reproduce.

There is also a size reason, from module 2: as a cell grows, its volume rises faster than its surface area, so a large cell cannot move nutrients and wastes across its membrane fast enough. Dividing restores a workable surface-area-to-volume ratio.

Every division must solve one problem perfectly: each new cell needs a complete, accurate copy of the DNA. This lesson shows how eukaryotic cells do that.

## Chromosomes and chromatids

A eukaryotic cell's DNA is divided among several long molecules, each wrapped around proteins to form a **[[chromosome]]**. Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. Most of the time chromosomes are long, thin, and tangled in the nucleus, which is ideal for reading genes but terrible for sorting them. Before division they coil up tightly, becoming short and thick enough to see under a light microscope.

Before a cell divides, it copies each chromosome. The two identical copies, still joined together, are called **[[sister chromatids]]**. They are held together most tightly at a constricted region called the **[[centromere]]**, which gives a duplicated chromosome its familiar X shape. The counting rule that trips people up: a duplicated chromosome is still one chromosome, even though it contains two chromatids (two DNA molecules). When the sister chromatids separate, each becomes a chromosome in its own right. The drawing shows one chromosome before and after it is copied.

![A single chromosome drawn as one rod before S phase, and after S phase as two identical rods side by side joined at a dark dot. Labels mark the two sister chromatids and the centromere.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The cell cycle

The **[[cell cycle]]** is the life of a cell from the moment it forms by division to the moment it divides again. It has two main parts.

**[[Interphase]]** is the long stretch between divisions, typically 90% or more of the cycle. It is not a resting stage; the cell is working hard. Interphase has three phases:

- G1 (first gap): the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and does its normal job.
- S (synthesis): the cell replicates its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids.
- G2 (second gap): the cell keeps growing and makes the proteins needed for division, such as the components of the spindle.

The M phase (mitotic phase) is division itself. It includes **[[mitosis]]**, the division of the nucleus, and **[[cytokinesis]]**, the division of the cytoplasm into two cells. The diagram traces one turn of the cycle; cells that stop dividing leave it for a resting branch called G0 (lesson 15).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The cell cycle
  accDescr: A new cell enters G1, where it grows. It then enters S phase, where the DNA is copied, then G2, where it prepares to divide, then mitosis, where the nucleus divides, then cytokinesis, which makes two new cells that each start again in G1. From G1 a cell can instead leave the cycle and enter G0, a non-dividing state, and some cells can return from G0 to G1.
  G1["G1: growth"] --> S["S: DNA copied"]
  S --> G2["G2: prepare to divide"]
  G2 --> M["Mitosis: nucleus divides"]
  M --> C["Cytokinesis: two cells"]
  C -- "each new cell" --> G1
  G1 -. "stop dividing" .-> G0["G0: not dividing"]
  G0 -. "some return" .-> G1
```

For a typical human cell growing in culture, a full cycle takes about 24 hours: roughly 11 hours in G1, 8 in S, 4 in G2, and only about 1 in M. Cycle length varies enormously. Early frog embryo cells divide every 30 minutes or so; some liver cells divide only once a year or two.

```plot
{"x": [0, 26], "y": [0, 2.6], "xLabel": "time (hours)", "yLabel": "DNA per cell (relative)", "segments": [{"from": [0, 1], "to": [11, 1]}, {"from": [11, 1], "to": [19, 2]}, {"from": [19, 2], "to": [24, 2]}, {"from": [24, 2], "to": [24, 1], "dashed": true}, {"from": [24, 1], "to": [26, 1]}], "labels": [{"at": [5.5, 1.25], "text": "G1"}, {"at": [14, 1.8], "text": "S"}, {"at": [21, 2.25], "text": "G2"}, {"at": [24.6, 2.3], "text": "M"}], "caption": "DNA content of one cell through a 24-hour cycle: it doubles during S and halves when the cell divides"}
```

## The stages of mitosis

Mitosis was first described in detail by Walther Flemming in 1882. He stained cells from salamander larvae with dyes, saw thread-like structures in the nucleus (he named the stainable material chromatin), and drew the threads splitting and moving apart. Biologists divide the continuous process into four stages.

1. **[[Prophase]]**. The chromosomes condense and become visible, each as two sister chromatids. Outside the nucleus, the **[[spindle]]** begins to form: a framework of protein fibers (microtubules) that grows from two organizing centers moving to opposite ends of the cell. Near the end of prophase, the nuclear envelope breaks apart, and spindle fibers attach to each chromosome at its centromere, one fiber from each pole.
2. **[[Metaphase]]**. The spindle lines the chromosomes up along the middle of the cell (the metaphase plate). Each chromosome's two sister chromatids face opposite poles. This is the easiest stage to recognize in a micrograph and the best moment to count chromosomes.
3. **[[Anaphase]]**. The proteins holding sister chromatids together are cut, and the chromatids are pulled to opposite poles as the spindle fibers shorten. Each separated chromatid is now a chromosome, so the chromosome count in the cell briefly doubles. Anaphase is short, often only a few minutes.
4. **[[Telophase]]**. A complete set of chromosomes arrives at each pole. Nuclear envelopes re-form around them, the chromosomes uncoil, and the spindle breaks down. There are now two nuclei in one cell.

Cytokinesis usually overlaps telophase. In animal cells, a ring of protein filaments pinches the cell in two, forming a cleavage furrow, like pulling a drawstring. Plant cells have rigid walls and cannot pinch; instead, vesicles gather at the middle and fuse into a cell plate that grows outward into a new wall.

The result: two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent and genetically identical to it (apart from rare copying errors). The drawing follows an animal cell with four chromosomes through the whole process. The red and blue colors mark chromosomes inherited from the mother and from the father; in mitosis they do not pair up, they simply line up one by one.

![Five drawings of an animal cell with four chromosomes. Interphase: a nucleus with thin tangled chromatin. Prophase: four X-shaped duplicated chromosomes inside a breaking nuclear envelope, with two spindle poles starting to separate. Metaphase: the four chromosomes lined up in a column at the middle, attached to spindle fibers from both poles. Anaphase: single chromatids pulled toward the two poles. Telophase and cytokinesis: two new nuclei in a cell pinching in two.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Prokaryotes have no nucleus and usually a single circular chromosome. They divide by a simpler process, binary fission: the chromosome is copied, the copies move apart as the cell lengthens, and the cell splits.

### Example 1

A cell from a fruit fly has 8 chromosomes in G1. How many chromosomes and how many chromatids (DNA molecules) does it have in G2, metaphase, anaphase, and each daughter cell?

Step 1: G1. 8 chromosomes, each one DNA molecule: 8 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules.

Step 2: G2. The DNA was copied in S, so each chromosome now has 2 sister chromatids: still 8 chromosomes, but 16 chromatids.

Step 3: Metaphase. Nothing has separated yet: 8 chromosomes, 16 chromatids.

Step 4: Anaphase. Sister chromatids separate, and each counts as a chromosome: 16 chromosomes in the cell (8 heading to each pole), 16 DNA molecules.

Step 5: Each daughter cell: 8 chromosomes, each a single DNA molecule. The count matches the parent's G1, as it must.

## Measuring the cycle from a snapshot

You cannot easily watch one cell for a whole day, but you can take a snapshot of many cells at once. In a growing onion root tip, cells divide constantly and are not synchronized, so at any instant each cell is at a random point in its cycle. The fraction of cells caught in a stage is proportional to the time that stage takes. A stage that lasts 10% of the cycle should contain about 10% of the cells.

The **[[mitotic index]]** is the percentage of cells in a sample that are in mitosis:

$$\text{mitotic index} = \frac{\text{cells in mitosis}}{\text{total cells counted}} \times 100\%$$

A high mitotic index means cells are dividing rapidly, which is why pathologists use it in grading tumors.

### Example 2

A student counts 200 cells in an onion root tip micrograph:

| Stage | Interphase | Prophase | Metaphase | Anaphase | Telophase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cells | 180 | 10 | 4 | 3 | 3 |

Find the mitotic index. If the whole cycle takes 24 hours, about how long does prophase last?

Step 1: Cells in mitosis: $10 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 20$.

Step 2: Mitotic index: $\dfrac{20}{200} \times 100\% = 10\%$.

Step 3: Time in prophase is the same fraction of the cycle as the fraction of cells in prophase: $\dfrac{10}{200} \times 24 = 1.2$ hours, or 72 minutes.

Step 4: Check it makes sense: interphase holds $\dfrac{180}{200} = 90\%$ of cells, so it lasts about 21.6 of the 24 hours, the longest stage, as expected.

## Common mistakes

- Calling interphase a "resting phase." The cell grows, works, and replicates its DNA during interphase.
- Thinking DNA is copied during mitosis. It is copied in S phase, before mitosis starts.
- Counting chromatids as chromosomes. Count centromeres: each centromere marks one chromosome, whether it holds one chromatid or two.
- Treating mitosis and cytokinesis as the same thing. Mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cell.
- Thinking daughter cells get half the chromosomes. Mitosis keeps the number the same; halving is the job of meiosis (lesson 16).

## Key points

- The cell cycle = interphase (G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation) + M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis).
- After S, each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
- Mitosis: prophase (condense, spindle forms), metaphase (line up in the middle), anaphase (chromatids separate), telophase (nuclei re-form).
- Cytokinesis: cleavage furrow in animal cells, cell plate in plant cells.
- Mitosis gives two genetically identical cells with the parent's chromosome number.
- Mitotic index = cells in mitosis ÷ total × 100%; a stage's share of cells estimates its share of the cycle time.

lessons.title: Regulating the cell cycle; cancer and stem cells
lessons.body:
## Knowing when to divide

The last lesson showed how a cell divides. Just as important is when. A skin cell near a cut should divide until the wound closes and then stop. A nerve cell in your brain should almost never divide. If cells divided whenever they could, your body would lose its shape and function; if they never divided, wounds would not heal. This lesson is about the control system that makes these decisions, what happens when it breaks (cancer), and the special cells that keep supplying new cells for the body (stem cells).

## Checkpoints: the cycle's inspections

The cell cycle has built-in inspection points called **[[checkpoints]]**, where the cell checks conditions and either continues or stops. There are three major ones.

- *G1 checkpoint.* Is the cell big enough? Are there enough nutrients? Have neighboring cells sent signals to divide? Is the DNA undamaged? In many cells this is the main decision point. A cell that does not get the go-ahead may leave the cycle and enter a non-dividing state called G0. Mature nerve cells and heart muscle cells stay in G0 essentially for life; liver cells sit in G0 but can be called back into the cycle after an injury.
- *G2 checkpoint.* Has all the DNA been copied, and copied correctly? Damaged DNA is repaired before the cell is allowed into mitosis.
- *Spindle (metaphase) checkpoint.* Is every chromosome attached to spindle fibers from both poles? Anaphase is delayed until they are, so that each daughter cell gets exactly one copy of every chromosome.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The three main checkpoints of the cell cycle
  accDescr: At the G1 checkpoint the cell asks whether it is big enough, has growth signals, and has undamaged DNA. If yes, it goes on through S phase and G2; if not, it pauses or leaves the cycle for G0. The G2 checkpoint asks whether all the DNA was copied completely and correctly; if yes, mitosis begins, and if not, the cell pauses for repair. During mitosis the spindle checkpoint asks whether every chromosome is attached to both poles; if yes, anaphase and division follow, and if not, anaphase waits. If damage is too great to repair, the cell undergoes apoptosis.
  A["G1 checkpoint: big enough, growth signals, DNA undamaged?"] -- yes --> B["S phase, then G2"]
  A -- no --> C["Pause, or leave the cycle for G0"]
  B --> D["G2 checkpoint: DNA copied completely and correctly?"]
  D -- yes --> E["Mitosis begins"]
  D -- no --> F["Pause for repair"]
  E --> G["Spindle checkpoint: every chromosome attached to both poles?"]
  G -- yes --> H["Anaphase and division"]
  G -- no --> I["Anaphase waits"]
  F -. "damage too great" .-> J["Apoptosis"]
```

If the damage at a checkpoint is too great to fix, the cell can trigger **[[apoptosis]]**, a tidy, programmed cell death in which the cell dismantles itself and is eaten by neighbors without causing inflammation. Apoptosis also sculpts the body during development: the webbing between your fingers disappeared before birth by apoptosis.

## The molecular clock: cyclins and CDKs

How does a cell "decide"? In 1970 Potu Rao and Robert Johnson fused pairs of cultured human cells at different stages into single cells with two nuclei. When an S-phase cell was fused with a G1 cell, the G1 nucleus immediately began copying its DNA, ahead of schedule. When a mitotic cell was fused with an interphase cell, the interphase nucleus's chromosomes began to condense, as in prophase. The conclusion: the cytoplasm contains chemical signals that drive the cell into the next phase.

Those signals turned out to be two kinds of proteins working together. **[[Cyclins]]** are proteins whose concentration rises and falls in each cycle; Tim Hunt discovered them in sea urchin eggs, where one protein built up steadily and then vanished at every division. Cyclin-dependent kinases (**[[CDKs]]**) are enzymes that are present all the time but active only when bound to a cyclin. An active cyclin–CDK complex adds phosphate groups to target proteins (phosphorylation, from lesson 11), switching on the machinery for the next phase. Destroying the cyclin switches the CDK off again. Different cyclin–CDK pairs act at different points; the one that triggers mitosis was first detected in frog eggs as "maturation-promoting factor." Leland Hartwell, Tim Hunt, and Paul Nurse shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for this work.

```plot
{"x": [0, 48], "y": [0, 1.2], "xLabel": "time (hours)", "yLabel": "relative level", "functions": [{"f": "0.5 - 0.5*cos(pi*mod(x,24)/24.5)", "label": "M cyclin"}, {"f": "0.35", "label": "CDK", "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [24, 1.1], "text": "mitosis"}, {"at": [47, 1.1], "text": "mitosis"}], "caption": "Cyclin builds up through interphase and is destroyed at mitosis; the CDK level stays roughly constant"}
```

Signals from outside the cell also matter. Growth factors are proteins released by other cells that bind receptors on the cell's surface and push it past the G1 checkpoint. Platelets release one at a wound, which is part of why cells there start dividing. Normal cells in a dish also show density-dependent inhibition: they divide until they form a single layer touching their neighbors, then stop.

## Cancer: division without control

**[[Cancer]]** is a group of diseases in which cells divide uncontrollably, ignoring the checkpoints and signals that restrain normal cells, and can invade other tissues. It is caused by changes (mutations) in the genes that control the cell cycle. Two kinds of genes are involved.

- **[[Proto-oncogenes]]** code for proteins that stimulate division, such as growth-factor receptors and the RAS protein that relays their signal. They are the cell's gas pedal. A mutation that makes such a gene overactive turns it into an **[[oncogene]]**, like a stuck accelerator. One mutated copy is enough to push the cell to divide.
- **[[Tumor suppressor genes]]** code for proteins that slow or stop division, repair DNA, or trigger apoptosis. They are the brakes. The most famous is p53, which halts the cycle at G1 when DNA is damaged and triggers apoptosis if repair fails; it is mutated in about half of all human cancers. Because one working copy usually still brakes, both copies must be damaged.

In 1971 Alfred Knudson studied retinoblastoma, a rare eye cancer in children. Children with the inherited form often got tumors in both eyes, at a young age; children with the non-inherited form got a single tumor, later. Knudson's "two-hit" explanation: inherited cases start life with one damaged copy of a tumor suppressor gene (later identified as RB) in every cell, so a single new mutation in any retinal cell is enough. Non-inherited cases need two separate mutations in the same cell, which is much less likely.

One mutation is almost never enough. Most cancers need several, in both kinds of genes, which is one reason cancer risk rises sharply with age. Mutations come from copying errors, from mutagens such as tobacco smoke and ultraviolet light, and from certain viruses (for example, some types of HPV cause cervical cancer, which is why the HPV vaccine prevents many cases). Some people inherit a mutation that raises their risk, such as a faulty BRCA1 gene.

A mass of abnormally dividing cells is a tumor. A benign tumor stays in one place and can often be removed completely. A malignant tumor invades nearby tissue, and its cells can break away, travel in blood or lymph, and form new tumors elsewhere, a spread called **[[metastasis]]**. Most cancer deaths are caused by metastasis. The drawing traces these steps in a layer of tissue.

![A cross-section of tissue. On the left, an orderly layer of cells sits on a thin basement membrane. In the middle, a benign tumor forms a dome of extra cells that stays above the membrane. On the right, irregular malignant cells break through a gap in the basement membrane, invade the tissue below, and one enters a blood vessel. An arrow leads from the vessel to a distant organ, where a small secondary tumor has formed.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Treatments include surgery, radiation and chemotherapy (which damage rapidly dividing cells, explaining side effects in hair follicles and the gut lining), and newer drugs targeting specific mutated proteins or helping the immune system attack cancer cells.

### Example 1

A tumor becomes detectable at about 1 billion ($10^9$) cells. Starting from a single cell, how many doublings does this take? If the cells double every 60 days, how long does it take?

Step 1: After $n$ doublings, one cell becomes $2^n$ cells. We need $2^n \approx 10^9$.

Step 2: $2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$, so $2^{30} = (2^{10})^3 \approx 10^9$. About 30 doublings. (Exactly: $2^{30} = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824$.)

Step 3: Time: $30 \times 60 = 1800$ days, about 4.9 years. A tumor can grow silently for years before it is found. And only 10 more doublings give $2^{40} \approx 10^{12}$ cells, roughly a kilogram of tissue. This is why early detection matters.

### Example 2

Researchers grow two cultures of cells. Culture A has a mutation that leaves RAS permanently switched on. Culture B has lost both copies of p53. Both are exposed to a dose of radiation that damages DNA. Predict what happens in each, compared with normal cells.

Step 1: Normal cells: p53 detects the DNA damage, halts the cycle at G1 for repair, and triggers apoptosis in cells that cannot be repaired.

Step 2: Culture A: RAS keeps sending a "divide" signal even without growth factors, but p53 still works. Damaged cells are still stopped or eliminated, so the damage is mostly not passed on, even though the cells divide too often.

Step 3: Culture B: there is no p53 brake. Damaged cells keep dividing and pass on new mutations, so this culture accumulates mutations much faster. This is why p53 is called the "guardian of the genome."

## Stem cells

Most of your cells are specialized and divide rarely, if at all. **[[Stem cells]]** are unspecialized cells that can divide to renew themselves and can also produce cells that specialize (differentiate). They differ in how many cell types they can become, their potency:

| Potency | Can become | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Totipotent | Every cell type, including the placenta | Zygote and the first few cells of an embryo |
| **[[Pluripotent]]** | Every cell type of the body | Embryonic stem cells from an early embryo |
| Multipotent | Several related cell types | Blood stem cells in bone marrow |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Stem cell potency from the zygote to specialized cells
  accDescr: The zygote is totipotent. It gives rise to the early embryo, whose inner cells are pluripotent embryonic stem cells. These give rise to multipotent adult stem cells such as blood stem cells in bone marrow, which make red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. A separate path shows that a specialized skin cell can be reprogrammed in the lab into an induced pluripotent stem cell, which is pluripotent again.
  Z["Zygote: totipotent"] --> E["Embryonic stem cells: pluripotent"]
  E --> B["Blood stem cell: multipotent"]
  B --> RBC["Red blood cells"]
  B --> WBC["White blood cells"]
  B --> PL["Platelets"]
  SK["Skin cell: specialized"] -- "reprogrammed in the lab" --> IPS["iPSC: pluripotent"]
```

Adult stem cells, such as those in bone marrow and the skin, replace cells that wear out; bone marrow transplants treat leukemia by supplying healthy blood stem cells. In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka showed that adding just four genes could reprogram ordinary mouse fibroblasts (connective-tissue cells, such as those in skin) into induced pluripotent stem cells (**[[iPSCs]]**), which behave much like embryonic stem cells; in 2007 his team and others did the same with human skin cells. He shared the 2012 Nobel Prize. iPSCs avoid the use of embryos, which some people object to on ethical grounds, and can be made from a patient's own cells.

## Common mistakes

- Calling cancer a single disease with a single cause. It is many diseases, each driven by several mutations.
- Mixing up oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Oncogenes are overactive accelerators (one copy enough); tumor suppressors are lost brakes (usually both copies).
- Thinking all tumors are cancer. Benign tumors do not invade or spread.
- Thinking G0 cells are dead or dormant. They are fully active; they just are not dividing.
- Thinking adult stem cells can become anything. Most are multipotent.

## Key points

- Checkpoints at G1, G2, and the spindle (metaphase) check size, signals, DNA integrity, and chromosome attachment.
- Cyclins rise and fall; they activate CDKs, which phosphorylate targets to move the cycle forward.
- Cancer: uncontrolled division from accumulated mutations in proto-oncogenes (become oncogenes) and tumor suppressor genes (such as p53).
- Malignant tumors invade and metastasize; benign tumors do not.
- Stem cells self-renew and differentiate: totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent; iPSCs are reprogrammed body cells.

lessons.title: Meiosis and sexual reproduction
lessons.body:
## A division that halves

Mitosis, from lesson 14, copies a cell exactly: same chromosome number, same genes. That is perfect for growth and repair, but it creates a puzzle for sexual reproduction. A human egg and a human sperm combine to make a new person. If each carried 46 chromosomes, the child would have 92, the grandchild 184, and so on. That does not happen, so something must halve the chromosome number before fertilization.

Biologists in the 1870s and 1880s saw this directly. In 1876 Oscar Hertwig, watching transparent sea urchin eggs, saw a sperm nucleus enter the egg and fuse with the egg's nucleus: fertilization is the joining of two nuclei. In 1883 Edouard van Beneden counted chromosomes in a roundworm (Ascaris) whose cells have very few: the egg nucleus and the sperm nucleus each brought 2 chromosomes, and the fertilized egg had 4. August Weismann then argued that a special "reduction division" must halve the number when sex cells form. That division is **[[meiosis]]**. This lesson explains how it works and why it makes every offspring genetically unique.

## Pairs of chromosomes

Look at the 46 chromosomes of a human body cell arranged by size and you will see they come in 23 pairs. One chromosome of each pair came from the mother's egg and one from the father's sperm. The two members of a pair are **[[homologous chromosomes]]** (homologs): they are the same size and shape, have their centromeres in the same place, and carry the same genes in the same order. They are not identical, though, because they can carry different versions of those genes; your mother's copy of a gene for a blood protein might differ slightly from your father's.

Of the 23 pairs, 22 pairs are autosomes, matched in everyone. The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes: two X chromosomes in most females, an X and a Y in most males. The X and Y differ in size but pair up during meiosis through a small shared region. (Module 5 covers how sex chromosomes affect inheritance.)

A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, is **[[diploid]]**, written 2n. A cell with one set is **[[haploid]]**, written n. In humans 2n = 46 and n = 23. Body cells are diploid. Sex cells, or **[[gametes]]** (eggs and sperm), are haploid. Fertilization joins two haploid gametes into a diploid zygote, the first cell of a new organism: n + n = 2n. Every species has its own number: fruit flies 2n = 8, dogs 2n = 78, garden peas 2n = 14. The diagram shows how meiosis and fertilization alternate in the human life cycle.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: The human life cycle
  accDescr: A diploid adult with 46 chromosomes makes haploid eggs or sperm with 23 chromosomes by meiosis. At fertilization an egg and a sperm join to form a diploid zygote with 46 chromosomes. The zygote divides by mitosis many times to grow into a diploid adult, and the cycle repeats.
  A["Adult: diploid, 2n = 46"] -- meiosis --> G["Eggs or sperm: haploid, n = 23"]
  G -- fertilization --> Z["Zygote: diploid, 2n = 46"]
  Z -- "mitosis, many times" --> A
```

## Meiosis step by step

Meiosis starts after a normal interphase, so the cell enters it with every chromosome duplicated into two sister chromatids. Then it divides twice: meiosis I and meiosis II.

*Meiosis I separates the homologous pairs.*

1. Prophase I. Chromosomes condense, and each pairs up with its homolog along their whole length. The paired homologs (four chromatids in all) form a tetrad. While paired, chromatids from the two homologs exchange matching segments, a process called **[[crossing over]]**. The X-shaped places where they cross can be seen under a microscope.
2. Metaphase I. The homologous pairs line up at the middle of the cell as pairs, side by side. Which homolog faces which pole is random for each pair.
3. Anaphase I. The homologs of each pair are pulled to opposite poles. Sister chromatids stay joined. This is the key difference from mitosis.
4. Telophase I and cytokinesis. Two cells form, each with one chromosome from every pair: they are haploid, although each chromosome still has two chromatids.

*Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids.* No DNA replication happens between the two divisions. Each haploid cell goes through prophase II, metaphase II (chromosomes line up singly), anaphase II (sister chromatids separate), and telophase II. Meiosis II works just like mitosis, but in a haploid cell.

The result: four haploid cells, each genetically different from the parent cell and from each other. The drawing follows a cell with 2n = 4 through both divisions. Red marks the chromosomes inherited from the mother and blue those from the father; the small patches of the other color are the segments swapped by crossing over.

![Seven drawings of a cell with two pairs of chromosomes, one long and one short, each pair with a red and a blue homolog. Prophase I: homologs paired side by side with tips swapped. Metaphase I: the pairs lined up side by side at the middle. Anaphase I: whole duplicated homologs pulled to opposite poles. Telophase I: two cells, each with one long and one short duplicated chromosome. Metaphase II: in each cell the two chromosomes line up singly. Anaphase II: sister chromatids separate. Result: four small cells, each with one long and one short single chromosome in different color combinations.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1

A fruit fly cell has 2n = 8. Track the number of chromosomes and chromatids from the start of meiosis I to the end of meiosis II.

Step 1: Before meiosis (after S phase): 8 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids, so 16 chromatids.

Step 2: Metaphase I: still 8 chromosomes (4 homologous pairs), 16 chromatids.

Step 3: After meiosis I: each of the 2 cells has 4 chromosomes (one from each pair), each still with 2 chromatids: 8 chromatids per cell. The cells are now haploid (n = 4).

Step 4: Anaphase II: in each cell the sister chromatids separate, so each pole receives 4 chromosomes of one chromatid each.

Step 5: After meiosis II: 4 cells, each with 4 single-chromatid chromosomes. Halved from 8, ready to combine with another gamete (4 + 4 = 8).

## Mitosis and meiosis compared

| | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Making gametes for sexual reproduction |
| Divisions | One | Two |
| Homologs pair up? | No | Yes, in prophase I |
| Crossing over? | No | Yes |
| Daughter cells | 2, diploid (2n → 2n) | 4, haploid (2n → n) |
| Genetically | Identical to parent | Different from parent and each other |

## Three sources of variation

Siblings with the same parents (other than identical twins) are never genetically identical. Meiosis and fertilization shuffle genes in three ways.

1. **[[Independent assortment]]**. At metaphase I, each homologous pair lines up independently of the others. For each pair there are 2 ways it can face the poles, so with n pairs the number of different chromosome combinations in a gamete is $2^n$. For humans, $2^{23} = 8{,}388{,}608$. This chromosome-level shuffle is the physical basis of Mendel's law of independent assortment (lesson 18): genes on different chromosomes end up in gametes independently of one another. Genes close together on the same chromosome travel together unless crossing over separates them.
2. Crossing over. Exchanging segments between homologs makes recombinant chromosomes, mixing the mother's and father's versions of genes on the same chromosome. Every pair normally has at least one crossover, and longer chromosomes often have two or three, multiplying the possibilities far beyond $2^{23}$.
3. Random fertilization. Any one of the millions of possible sperm can fertilize any one of the millions of possible eggs. Ignoring crossing over, one couple could produce $2^{23} \times 2^{23} \approx 7 \times 10^{13}$ (about 70 trillion) different chromosome combinations.

Why does variation matter? A population whose members differ is more likely to include some individuals who survive a new disease or a change in climate. This variation is the raw material for natural selection (module 7).

### Example 2

A plant species has 2n = 6. How many genetically different gametes can independent assortment alone produce? How many different chromosome combinations could a zygote have from two parents of this species (ignoring crossing over)?

Step 1: n = 3 pairs, so gamete combinations $= 2^3 = 8$.

Step 2: Each parent can make 8 kinds of gametes, so the zygote combinations number $8 \times 8 = 64$.

Step 3: Check by thinking about one pair: each pair lines up 2 ways, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Doubling the number of chromosome pairs to 6 would square the gamete count, giving 64, not double it.

## When meiosis goes wrong: nondisjunction

Sometimes a homologous pair (in meiosis I) or a pair of sister chromatids (in meiosis II) fails to separate. This is **[[nondisjunction]]**. The result is gametes with an extra chromosome (n + 1) or a missing one (n − 1). If such a gamete is fertilized, the zygote has 47 or 45 chromosomes instead of 46.

- Nondisjunction in meiosis I: both homologs go to one cell, so all four gametes are abnormal: two n + 1 and two n − 1.
- Nondisjunction in meiosis II: only one of the two cells is affected, so two gametes are normal, one is n + 1, and one is n − 1.

Most embryos with a missing or extra chromosome do not survive. A well-known exception is trisomy 21 (three copies of chromosome 21), which causes Down syndrome; people with Down syndrome share some physical traits and some degree of intellectual disability, and many live full lives into their 60s. The chance of nondisjunction rises with the age of the egg, which is why trisomy 21 is more common in children of older mothers. Module 5 returns to chromosome disorders and how karyotypes reveal them.

## Making eggs and sperm

In males, each cell that completes meiosis produces four sperm, and sperm are made continuously from puberty on. In females, meiosis divides the cytoplasm unequally: one large egg cell keeps nearly all the cytoplasm (stored nutrients for the early embryo), and the other products are tiny polar bodies that break down. So one meiosis yields one egg. Human egg cells begin meiosis before birth and pause in prophase I for years or decades, finishing only around ovulation and fertilization; that long pause is thought to be part of why nondisjunction rises with maternal age.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking meiosis II halves the chromosome number. The halving happens in meiosis I, when homologs separate.
- Calling homologous chromosomes identical. They carry the same genes but can carry different versions. Sister chromatids are the identical ones.
- Saying the DNA is copied again before meiosis II. It is copied only once, before meiosis I.
- Treating independent assortment as $2 \times n$. The count is $2^n$, because each pair's choice multiplies the possibilities.
- Thinking nondisjunction in meiosis I and II give the same results. Meiosis I nondisjunction makes all four gametes abnormal; meiosis II, only two.

## Key points

- Meiosis turns one diploid cell (2n) into four haploid gametes (n); fertilization restores 2n.
- Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes, one from each parent; they pair and cross over in prophase I.
- Meiosis I separates homologs (the reduction step); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
- Variation comes from crossing over, independent assortment ($2^n$ combinations), and random fertilization.
- Nondisjunction gives gametes with n + 1 or n − 1 chromosomes; trisomy 21 is one result.
- Sperm: four per meiosis. Egg: one per meiosis plus polar bodies.

lessons.title: Molecular control of the cell cycle and apoptosis
lessons.body:
## Opening the control box

Lesson 15 described the cell cycle's controls from the outside: checkpoints, cyclins that rise and fall, CDKs that switch on when a cyclin binds, p53 as a brake, and Knudson's two hits. This lesson opens the box: how the mitotic trigger was found, why a cell flips into mitosis all at once, how Rb and p53 turn the clock into decisions to divide, pause or die, and how a cell carries out its own death.

## Frog eggs and maturation-promoting factor

A frog oocyte (an immature egg) is a giant cell, over a millimeter across, paused for months in prophase of meiosis I, a G2-like state with a large intact nucleus. A hormone signal makes it mature: the nucleus breaks down, the chromosomes condense, and meiosis runs on until it pauses again at metaphase II to wait for a sperm.

In 1971 Yoshio Masui and Clement Markert (and, independently, Dennis Smith and Robert Ecker) injected a little cytoplasm from a mature egg into an immature oocyte that had received no hormone.

![Two rows of frog egg cells. In the experiment row, cytoplasm from a mature egg paused in metaphase II is injected into an immature oocyte with a large nucleus; hours later its nucleus has broken down and condensed chromosomes sit on a spindle. In the control row, cytoplasm from an immature oocyte is injected into another immature oocyte, which still has its intact nucleus hours later.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The injected oocyte matured on its own; cytoplasm from an immature oocyte did nothing. Masui named the active substance **[[maturation-promoting factor]]** (MPF). Cytoplasm from the newly matured recipient could trigger another oocyte, then another, through many serial transfers without diluting away, even with protein synthesis blocked: MPF activates more MPF already stored in an inactive form. Extracts of dividing yeast, clam and mammal cells worked too, so MPF was a universal trigger, soon read as "M-phase promoting factor."

Three lines of work then met. Paul Nurse had found *cdc2*, a fission yeast gene needed to enter mitosis, and in 1987 showed that the human version could replace it in yeast, a control gene conserved across about a billion years. Tim Hunt had found cyclin in sea urchin eggs. MPF was purified from frog eggs in 1988, and within two years it was shown to be a CDK (CDK1, the product of *cdc2*) bound to cyclin B.

## Switching a CDK on and off

Cyclin binding is necessary but not sufficient. A CDK is fully active only when:

1. a cyclin is bound;
2. an activating phosphate group has been added at one site;
3. inhibitory phosphates at a second site are absent. A kinase called Wee1 adds these, and a phosphatase (an enzyme that removes phosphate groups) called Cdc25 takes them off.

During G2, cyclin B accumulates and binds CDK1, but Wee1 keeps the complexes switched off, like a loaded spring. Once a little cyclin B–CDK1 becomes active, it phosphorylates Cdc25 (activating it) and Wee1 (inactivating it), which frees more CDK1, which activates more Cdc25. This positive feedback makes entry into mitosis an all-or-none switch, and it explains the serial transfers: a little injected MPF converts the recipient's stored MPF into active MPF.

Leaving mitosis needs the opposite. The **[[anaphase-promoting complex]]** (APC/C) tags cyclin B with chains of the small protein ubiquitin, the label that sends a protein to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder. Without its cyclin, CDK1 goes quiet and the cell can rebuild nuclei and divide. The APC/C also destroys securin, which guards an enzyme called separase; freed separase cuts **[[cohesin]]**, the protein rings holding sister chromatids together, and anaphase begins. The spindle checkpoint holds the APC/C back: every **[[kinetochore]]** (the protein structure on a centromere where spindle fibers attach) that is still unattached sends a "wait" signal. When Conly Rieder's group destroyed the last unattached kinetochore in a waiting cell with a laser, the cell went straight into anaphase.

Animal cells use several cyclin–CDK pairs:

| Pair | When active | Main job |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclin D – CDK4/6 | G1, made in response to growth factors | Starts phosphorylating Rb |
| Cyclin E – CDK2 | Late G1 into S | Commits the cell to S phase |
| Cyclin A – CDK2 | S | Drives DNA replication and helps block a second round |
| Cyclin B – CDK1 (MPF) | G2 to M | Condenses chromosomes, breaks down the nuclear envelope, builds the spindle |

Cells can also block CDKs with **[[CDK inhibitor]]** proteins such as p21, which binds and blocks cyclin–CDK complexes, and p16, which binds CDK4 and CDK6 and keeps cyclin D from activating them.

### Example 1

In 1989 Andrew Murray and Marc Kirschner made frog egg extracts that cycle in a test tube, repeatedly building and breaking down nuclear envelopes around added sperm DNA.

```plot
{"x": [0, 90], "y": [0, 1.1], "xLabel": "time (minutes)", "yLabel": "relative level", "functions": [{"f": "min(0.1 + 0.8*mod(x,30)/28, 0.9 - 0.4*(mod(x,30)-28))", "label": "cyclin B"}, {"f": "0.05 + 0.85*exp(-(mod(x,30)-27.5)^2/2)", "label": "MPF activity", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Schematic of a cycling egg extract: cyclin builds up gradually, MPF activity switches on sharply near the top, and cyclin is then destroyed"}
```

Predict the result of each change: (a) all mRNA is destroyed, then only cyclin B mRNA is added back; (b) a cyclin B that cannot be tagged with ubiquitin is added; (c) Wee1 is removed.

Step 1, (a): CDK1, Wee1, Cdc25 and the APC/C are already present as proteins, and cyclin B can still be made. Cyclin builds, MPF switches on, cyclin is destroyed, and the cycle repeats. This is what Murray and Kirschner saw: cyclin is the only protein that must be newly made each cycle.

Step 2, (b): MPF switches on, but the APC/C cannot destroy this cyclin, so CDK1 stays active and the extract is stuck in M phase. Destroying cyclin is required to leave mitosis.

Step 3, (c): Nothing holds cyclin B–CDK1 inactive, so MPF switches on before the usual amount of cyclin has built up, and mitosis comes early. (Yeast lacking *wee1* divide at about half the normal size, hence the name.)

## Rb and the restriction point

Late in G1 is the **[[restriction point]]**: after it, a cell goes on through S, G2 and M even if growth factors are removed; before it, removing them sends the cell into G0. The Rb protein (from the retinoblastoma gene in lesson 15) runs this switch.

Unphosphorylated Rb binds and blocks a transcription factor called **[[E2F]]**, which switches on S-phase genes, including cyclin E. Growth factors lead to cyclin D, and cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb, loosening its grip. Freed E2F makes cyclin E, and cyclin E–CDK2 phosphorylates Rb further, freeing more E2F: another positive feedback loop that makes commitment abrupt.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Rb and E2F at the restriction point
  accDescr: Growth factors cause the cell to make cyclin D, which activates CDK4 and CDK6. These phosphorylate Rb, which releases the transcription factor E2F. E2F switches on S-phase genes, including cyclin E. Cyclin E with CDK2 phosphorylates more Rb, releasing more E2F in a positive feedback loop. Once enough E2F is free, the cell passes the restriction point and enters S phase.
  GF[Growth factors] --> CD[Cyclin D with CDK4 and CDK6]
  CD -- phosphorylates --> RB[Rb releases E2F]
  RB --> E2F[E2F switches on S-phase genes]
  E2F --> CE[Cyclin E with CDK2]
  CE -- phosphorylates more Rb --> RB
  E2F --> S[Restriction point passed: enter S phase]
```

High-risk HPV jams this switch: its E7 protein binds Rb and releases E2F (and its E6 protein sends p53 to the proteasome). Many cancers have instead lost p16, the CDK4/6 inhibitor, with the same result.

## p53: responding to damage

p53 is made all the time but destroyed within minutes, because the protein MDM2 tags it with ubiquitin. DNA damage activates sensor kinases (ATM and ATR) that phosphorylate p53 so MDM2 can no longer bind it. p53 accumulates and, as a transcription factor, switches on:

- the CDK inhibitor p21, which blocks cyclin–CDK complexes, keeps Rb unphosphorylated, and holds the cell in G1;
- DNA repair genes;
- genes that start apoptosis (such as BAX) if the damage is too great.

p53 also switches on the MDM2 gene, a negative feedback loop that lowers p53 again after repair. People who inherit one faulty copy of *TP53* (the gene for p53) have Li-Fraumeni syndrome and a very high lifetime risk of several cancers.

## Apoptosis: how a cell dismantles itself

The word apoptosis ("falling off," as leaves fall) was coined in 1972. Its genetics came from the roundworm *C. elegans*: as a hermaphrodite develops, exactly 1,090 somatic cells are made and the same 131 always die. Robert Horvitz found that the genes *ced-3* and *ced-4* are needed to kill and *ced-9* protects cells that should live. Humans have related genes for all three (Nobel Prize 2002, with Sydney Brenner and John Sulston).

The killers are **[[caspases]]**, protein-cutting enzymes (proteases) that use a cysteine to cut just after an aspartate. Each is made as an inactive procaspase. An initiator caspase cuts and activates executioner caspases, so a small signal becomes a large, irreversible cascade. Executioners cut hundreds of proteins, including the lamins that support the nuclear envelope and an inhibitor that holds a DNA-cutting enzyme in check. The DNA is cut between nucleosomes, so on a gel it forms a "ladder" of fragments in multiples of about 180 base pairs, a classic test for apoptosis.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The two main pathways of apoptosis
  accDescr: In the intrinsic pathway, DNA damage or stress, acting through p53, activates proteins such as BAX, which make pores in the outer membrane of mitochondria, while Bcl-2 opposes this. Cytochrome c leaks out and joins Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates caspase 9. In the extrinsic pathway, a killer cell's Fas ligand binds the Fas death receptor, which activates caspase 8. Caspase 9 and caspase 8 both activate executioner caspases 3 and 7, which cut hundreds of proteins, and the cell breaks into fragments that phagocytes eat.
  D[DNA damage or stress, via p53] --> BAX[BAX opens pores in mitochondria]
  BCL[Bcl-2] -. blocks .-> BAX
  BAX --> CYT[Cytochrome c released]
  CYT --> AP[Apoptosome: Apaf-1 activates caspase 9]
  FAS[Killer cell signal binds Fas receptor] --> C8[Caspase 8]
  AP --> EX[Executioner caspases 3 and 7]
  C8 --> EX
  EX --> END[Cell cut apart and eaten by phagocytes]
```

- Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway: proteins such as BAX open pores in the outer mitochondrial membrane, and cytochrome c, the electron carrier from the electron transport chain (lesson 13), leaks out. It binds Apaf-1, forming a wheel-shaped apoptosome that activates caspase 9. **[[Bcl-2]]** and its relatives block the pores. (In the worm, CED-9 is the Bcl-2 relative, CED-4 the Apaf-1 relative, and CED-3 a caspase.)
- Extrinsic pathway: a killer T cell's Fas ligand binds a "death receptor," Fas, on the target cell, activating caspase 8.

The dying cell shrinks, its chromatin condenses, and it buds off small sealed packets. Phosphatidylserine, a phospholipid normally kept on the membrane's inner face, flips outward as an "eat me" signal for phagocytes. Nothing spills out, so there is no inflammation. **[[Necrosis]]**, death from injury such as a burn or lost blood supply, is the opposite: cells swell and burst, and their contents trigger inflammation.

Escaping apoptosis is a hallmark of cancer. Bcl-2 was discovered in follicular lymphoma, where a translocation makes B cells overproduce it so they fail to die; a Bcl-2-blocking drug (venetoclax) now treats some leukemias.

## Cancer genes and the arithmetic of two hits

In 1976 Harold Varmus and J. Michael Bishop's group found that *src*, the cancer gene of a chicken sarcoma virus, has a close match in the DNA of normal chickens. The virus had picked up a normal cell gene: proto-oncogenes are ordinary growth-control genes. One becomes an oncogene by a gain of function: a point mutation that leaves the protein stuck on (RAS), extra copies (amplified *HER2* in some breast cancers), or a gene fusion (BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia, blocked by the drug imatinib). One altered copy is enough, so oncogenes act dominantly in a cell.

Tumor suppressors (Rb, p53, p16) fail by loss of function and act recessively in a cell. Yet inherited predisposition, as in familial retinoblastoma, shows up in pedigrees as dominant. The two-hit model resolves this: a carrier has millions of cells each needing only one more hit, so some cell almost surely loses its good copy. That second hit is often **[[loss of heterozygosity]]**: the good copy is deleted, or the whole chromosome is lost by nondisjunction in mitosis, or replaced by mitotic recombination. Tumors in carriers often have two bad copies and no good one.

### Example 2

Knudson treated the number of tumors in a child who inherits one bad RB copy as a Poisson count with a mean of about 3 per carrier. For a Poisson count with mean $m$, $P(k) = \dfrac{m^k e^{-m}}{k!}$. What fraction of carriers get no tumor, and what fraction get two or more?

Step 1: No tumor: $P(0) = e^{-3} = 0.0498$, about 5%. About 95% of carriers get at least one tumor: a dominant-looking trait with high but incomplete penetrance.

Step 2: Exactly one: $P(1) = 3e^{-3} = 0.149$.

Step 3: Two or more: $1 - P(0) - P(1) = 1 - 4e^{-3} = 0.801$. Most carriers get several tumors, which is why inherited cases usually affect both eyes.

Step 4: Compare a noncarrier. If a carrier's expected number of second hits is $m = N\mu = 3$ ($N$ cells at risk, chance $\mu$ per cell of losing a copy), a noncarrier cell needs two independent hits, chance about $\mu^2$, so the expected number of tumors is about $N\mu^2 = 3\mu$. With $\mu$ near one in a million, that is a few in a million: sporadic cases are rare and almost always in one eye. (This simplest model underestimates sporadic cases, because a cell with one hit can divide into a clone of many one-hit cells before the second hit.)

## Reading the cycle with a flow cytometer

A flow cytometer measures the DNA content of thousands of dye-stained cells. G1 cells have the diploid content, written 2C; G2 and M cells have 4C; S-phase cells are in between. As with the mitotic index (lesson 14), the fraction of cells in each group estimates the fraction of the cycle spent there. (Growing cultures have slightly more young cells than old, which careful work corrects for.)

### Example 3

A culture with a 20-hour cycle is analyzed before and after 16 hours with a drug that inhibits CDK1.

```plot
{"x": [0, 6], "y": [0, 100], "xLabel": "DNA content per cell", "yLabel": "percent of cells", "bars": [{"x": 1, "height": 50, "width": 0.8, "label": "2C"}, {"x": 2, "height": 30, "width": 0.8, "label": "2C-4C"}, {"x": 3, "height": 20, "width": 0.8, "label": "4C"}, {"x": 4.2, "height": 5, "width": 0.4}, {"x": 4.6, "height": 7, "width": 0.4}, {"x": 5.0, "height": 88, "width": 0.4}], "labels": [{"at": [2, 70], "text": "untreated"}, {"at": [4.6, 95], "text": "after CDK1 inhibitor"}], "caption": "Left: an untreated culture (50% 2C, 30% between, 20% 4C). Right: the same culture after the drug (5% 2C, 7% between, 88% 4C)."}
```

How long are G1, S and G2 + M, and what did the drug do?

Step 1: Untreated: G1 $= 0.50 \times 20 = 10$ h, S $= 0.30 \times 20 = 6$ h, G2 + M $= 0.20 \times 20 = 4$ h.

Step 2: After the drug, 88% of cells have 4C DNA. Cells kept moving through G1 and S but could not enter mitosis without active CDK1, so they piled up in G2.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking cyclin binding alone activates a CDK. Phosphates added and removed by other enzymes (Wee1, Cdc25) also set the timing.
- Thinking the spindle checkpoint counts chromosomes. It senses unattached kinetochores; one is enough to wait.
