Only 10 were seen. The **[[coefficient of coincidence]]** is observed ÷ expected double crossovers, $10 / 17.1 \approx 0.58$, and **[[interference]]** is $1 - 0.58 = 0.42$. Positive interference means one crossover makes another nearby less likely, which is common in many organisms.

## Using a map to predict offspring

A map distance works backward as a prediction. Genes 18 map units apart produce 18% recombinant gametes, split equally between the two recombinant types, and 82% parental gametes, split equally between the two parental types.

### Example 4

Genes A and B are 20 map units apart. A plant that is Ab / aB (A on the same chromosome as b) is test-crossed with ab / ab. How many of 500 offspring are expected in each class?

The parental gametes here are Ab and aB, each $\tfrac{80\%}{2} = 40\%$: 200 Ab/ab and 200 aB/ab offspring. The recombinant gametes are AB and ab, each $\tfrac{20\%}{2} = 10\%$: 50 of each. In this plant the "all dominant" and "all recessive" phenotypes are the rare ones. The arrangement with both dominant alleles on one chromosome (AB / ab) is called coupling, and the arrangement in this example (Ab / aB) is called repulsion.

## What maps do and don't tell you

A genetic map shows order and recombination distance, not physical distance in DNA. Crossovers are more common in some regions ("hotspots") than others, and rates differ between the sexes; female human meiosis produces more crossovers overall than male meiosis. Across the human genome, one map unit corresponds very roughly to a million base pairs, but the local ratio varies a lot.

Mapping still matters. In 1983 the Huntington's disease gene was placed on chromosome 4 because, in large families, the disease allele was inherited along with a nearby DNA marker; the gene itself was identified ten years later.

```mermaid
timeline
  accTitle: Milestones in linkage and gene mapping
  accDescr: 1905, Bateson, Saunders and Punnett see coupling of traits in sweet peas. 1909, Janssens describes chiasmata between paired homologs. 1911, Morgan explains linkage and crossing over in fruit flies. 1913, Sturtevant publishes the first genetic map. 1931, Creighton and McClintock in maize, and Stern in fruit flies, show that genetic recombination goes with a physical exchange between chromosomes. 1983, the Huntington's disease gene is mapped to chromosome 4 using a linked DNA marker.
  1905 : Coupling seen in sweet peas
  1909 : Chiasmata described
  1911 : Morgan proposes linkage and crossing over
  1913 : Sturtevant's first genetic map
  1931 : Recombination shown to be physical exchange
  1983 : Huntington's gene mapped to chromosome 4
```

## Common mistakes

- Calling the "all dominant" and "all recessive" classes parental by default. Parental classes are the most common ones; which phenotypes they are depends on coupling or repulsion.
- Dividing recombinants by the number of parental offspring instead of the total.
- Leaving out the double crossovers when calculating each interval in a three-point cross. They are recombinant in both intervals.
- Expecting recombination frequencies above 50%, or reading 50% as proof that genes are on different chromosomes.
- Using a heterozygous male fruit fly in a mapping test cross. Male *Drosophila* don't cross over, so you would see no recombinants.
- Treating map units as physical distance. They measure crossover frequency, which varies along a chromosome.

## Key points

- Linked genes are close together on one chromosome and are inherited together more often than chance; crossing over in prophase I makes recombinants.
- In a test cross, the two most common classes are parental and the two least common are recombinant. Recombination frequency = recombinants ÷ total × 100%.
- 1% recombination = 1 map unit = 1 centimorgan. Distances are roughly additive over short intervals, so the largest distance spans the outer genes.
- Recombination frequency approaches but doesn't meaningfully exceed 50%, because one crossover affects only two of four chromatids and multiple crossovers cancel out.
- In a three-point cross, the rarest classes are double crossovers; the gene that switches between parental and double-crossover classes is in the middle.
- Coefficient of coincidence = observed ÷ expected double crossovers; interference = 1 − coefficient of coincidence.

lessons.title: Epistasis, pleiotropy, and quantitative traits
lessons.body:
Lesson 19 met three complications in passing: epistasis (yellow Labradors and the 9 : 3 : 4 ratio), pleiotropy (the sickle-cell allele) and polygenic traits (the bell curve of height). This honors lesson takes each further: where modified ratios such as 9 : 7 and 12 : 3 : 1 come from and how to spot them in data, how one allele can affect both coat color and survival, and how geneticists measure how much of the variation in a trait comes from genes. That last number, heritability, is one of the most useful and most misunderstood in biology.

## Reading a modified ratio

Every two-gene ratio in this lesson starts from the same 16 equally likely F2 outcomes of AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance at each gene: 9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb (the blank means "either allele"). Mendel's genes acted on separate traits, so all four classes looked different. When two genes act on the *same* trait, some classes look alike and merge. The alleles still segregate and assort normally; only the mapping from genotype to phenotype changes.

So if an F2 falls into classes close to sixteenths, such as 9 : 7 or 12 : 3 : 1, suspect two genes and a doubly heterozygous F1.

![Five rows of 16 boxes, grouped as 9 A_B_, 3 A_bb, 3 aaB_ and 1 aabb, with boxes of the same phenotype in the same color. 9:3:3:1 (no interaction) has four colors. 9:3:4 (recessive epistasis) merges aaB_ with aabb. 9:7 (duplicate recessive epistasis) merges everything except A_B_. 12:3:1 (dominant epistasis) merges A_B_ with A_bb. 15:1 (duplicate dominant genes) merges everything except aabb.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The figure shows which classes merge in each of the four ratios below.

## Recessive epistasis: 9 : 3 : 4

In **[[recessive epistasis]]**, two recessive alleles at one gene hide the effect of another gene. In mice, the agouti gene controls the pattern of pigment in each hair: A gives banded "agouti" hairs (the wild grayish-brown color), and aa gives solid black hairs. A second gene controls whether any pigment is made: it encodes tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin synthesis. Mice that are cc make no melanin and are albino, whatever their agouti genotype.

AaCc × AaCc gives 9 A_C_ agouti : 3 aaC_ black : 3 A_cc albino : 1 aacc albino, or 9 agouti : 3 black : 4 albino. The gene that does the hiding (C) is called epistatic; the hidden gene (A) is hypostatic.

## Duplicate recessive epistasis: 9 : 7

Around 1905, Bateson and Punnett crossed two true-breeding white-flowered strains of sweet pea. Surprisingly, every F1 plant had purple flowers, and the F2 came out about 9 purple : 7 white.

The explanation is a two-step pathway in which each step needs a different enzyme:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A two-step pigment pathway behind the 9 to 7 ratio
  accDescr: A colorless precursor is converted to a colorless intermediate by an enzyme made by the dominant allele C. The intermediate is converted to purple pigment by an enzyme made by the dominant allele P. A plant that is cc is blocked at step 1, and a plant that is pp is blocked at step 2, so either one is white.
  A["Colorless precursor"] -- "step 1: enzyme from C, missing in cc" --> B["Colorless intermediate"]
  B -- "step 2: enzyme from P, missing in pp" --> D["Purple pigment"]
```

A plant needs at least one working allele at both genes (C_P_) to be purple. One white strain was CCpp and the other ccPP; the F1 is CcPp and purple. In the F2, the 9 C_P_ are purple and the other 7 sixteenths (3 C_pp, 3 ccP_ and 1 ccpp) are white. Genes that must both work to produce one phenotype like this are called **[[complementary genes]]**.

The white × white → purple F1 is the logic of a **[[complementation test]]**: cross two individuals with the same recessive mutant phenotype. Normal offspring mean the mutations are in different genes (each parent supplies the working allele the other lacks); mutant offspring mean both mutations are in the same gene.

### Example 1

A cross of two different true-breeding white-flowered lines gives purple F1 plants. The F2 has 176 purple and 144 white plants. Which hypothesis fits better: one gene (3 : 1) or two complementary genes (9 : 7)?

Total 320. For 3 : 1, expected 240 purple and 80 white:

$$\chi^2 = \frac{(176 - 240)^2}{240} + \frac{(144 - 80)^2}{80} = 17.07 + 51.20 = 68.27$$

For 9 : 7, expected $\tfrac{9}{16} \times 320 = 180$ and $\tfrac{7}{16} \times 320 = 140$:

$$\chi^2 = \frac{(176 - 180)^2}{180} + \frac{(144 - 140)^2}{140} = 0.089 + 0.114 = 0.20$$

Both tests have df = 1 (critical value 3.84). The one-gene hypothesis is firmly rejected; the 9 : 7 data fit well. Two genes, each needed for color, explain the result.

## Dominant epistasis: 12 : 3 : 1

In **[[dominant epistasis]]**, a dominant allele at one gene hides the other gene. In summer squash, fruit color depends on two genes. A dominant W allele blocks pigment production early, so W_ fruit are white whatever the second gene. In ww plants, the second gene decides: Y_ gives yellow fruit and yy gives green.

WwYy × WwYy: 9 W_Y_ and 3 W_yy are white (12), 3 wwY_ are yellow and 1 wwyy is green: 12 : 3 : 1.

## Duplicate dominant genes: 15 : 1

Sometimes two genes do the same job, and one dominant allele at either gene is enough. In shepherd's purse, a small weed in the mustard family, seed capsules are heart-shaped (triangular) if the plant has a dominant allele at either of two genes, and narrow and oval only when it is homozygous recessive for both. AaBb × AaBb gives 15 triangular : 1 oval. Such genes are called **[[duplicate genes]]**; they often arise when a gene is copied during evolution and both copies keep working.

## Pleiotropy and lethal alleles

Lesson 19 described pleiotropy: one gene affecting several traits. Pleiotropy can even reach survival. In 1905 Lucien Cuénot found that yellow mice never bred true. Crossing two yellow mice always gave yellow and non-yellow offspring, in a ratio near 2 : 1 instead of 3 : 1.

The yellow allele, $A^Y$, is dominant for coat color: $A^YA$ mice are yellow. But $A^YA^Y$ embryos die early in development, so that genotype never appears among the pups. For survival, $A^Y$ acts as a recessive **[[lethal allele]]**. The molecular story is now known: the $A^Y$ mutation is a deletion that switches on the agouti gene in every tissue (which also makes yellow mice prone to obesity, a third effect of the same allele) and removes the working part of a neighboring gene that embryos need.

### Example 2

Two yellow mice ($A^YA$) are mated many times and produce 120 pups. How many are expected to be yellow, and why are their litters smaller than usual?

The Punnett square gives $\tfrac14\ A^YA^Y : \tfrac12\ A^YA : \tfrac14\ AA$. The $A^YA^Y$ quarter dies before birth, so among the surviving pups, yellow is $\dfrac{1/2}{3/4} = \tfrac23$ and agouti is $\tfrac13$. Expected yellow: $\tfrac23 \times 120 = 80$, agouti 40. The litters are about a quarter smaller than litters of non-yellow parents because a quarter of the embryos are lost.

A 2 : 1 ratio among the offspring of two parents with the same dominant phenotype is a classic sign of a recessive lethal. A human example of pleiotropy is Marfan syndrome: one dominant allele of the fibrillin-1 gene (a connective-tissue protein) affects the skeleton, the eyes and the aorta.

## Quantitative traits

A **[[quantitative trait]]** is measured on a continuous scale (height, milk yield, kernel color, blood pressure) rather than sorted into a few classes. Lesson 19's additive model explains the shape of the distribution. The model also works backward: you can estimate how many genes are involved from the extremes.

In 1909 Herman Nilsson-Ehle crossed wheat with dark red kernels and wheat with white kernels. The F1 was intermediate, and in some crosses about 1 in 64 F2 kernels was as white as the white parent. With $n$ additive genes, each F2 extreme requires homozygous recessive at all $n$ genes, probability $\left(\tfrac14\right)^n$, and the number of phenotype classes is $2n + 1$ (0 to $2n$ "adding" alleles). Since $\left(\tfrac14\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{64}$, those crosses involved three segregating genes.

### Example 3

Two true-breeding plant lines differ in height: 40 cm and 72 cm. The F1 is 56 cm. Of 1024 F2 plants, about 4 are 40 cm tall. Assuming additive genes with equal effects and no environmental effect, how many genes differ between the lines, and how much does each "adding" allele contribute?

The fraction as short as the short parent is $\tfrac{4}{1024} = \tfrac{1}{256} = \left(\tfrac14\right)^4$, so $n = 4$ genes. The tall line carries $2n = 8$ adding alleles and the short line none, so each allele adds $\dfrac{72 - 40}{8} = 4$ cm. The F2 should fall into $2 \times 4 + 1 = 9$ height classes, from 40 to 72 cm in steps of 4 cm, and the F1 with 4 adding alleles is $40 + 4 \times 4 = 56$ cm, as observed.

Real estimates are rougher, because gene effects are unequal and the environment blurs the classes.

## Genes and environment: norms of reaction

The same genotype can give different phenotypes in different environments. The range of phenotypes one genotype produces across environments is its **[[norm of reaction]]**. In a classic study in the 1940s, Jens Clausen, David Keck and William Hiesey split single yarrow plants into clones and grew them in gardens at different elevations in California. Different genotypes responded differently to the same gardens, so no single "genetic height" describes a plant without saying where it grows.

```plot
{"x": [0, 3], "y": [0, 60], "xLabel": "garden (1 low, 2 middle, 3 high elevation)", "yLabel": "plant height (cm)", "functions": [{"f": "50 - 15*(x - 1)", "from": 1, "to": 3, "label": "genotype 1"}, {"f": "30 - 2*(x - 1)", "from": 1, "to": 3, "label": "genotype 2"}], "caption": "Invented norms of reaction for two clones: genotype 1 is taller low down but shorter high up"}
```

## Heritability

Variation in a quantitative trait has genetic and environmental sources. Geneticists split the total (phenotypic) variance $V_P$, a measure of spread, into a genetic part $V_G$ and an environmental part $V_E$ (ignoring interactions between them):

$$V_P = V_G + V_E$$

**[[Heritability]]** in the broad sense is the fraction of phenotypic variance that is genetic:

$$H^2 = \frac{V_G}{V_P}$$

Only part of $V_G$ passes predictably from parent to offspring: the additive part $V_A$, from alleles whose effects simply add up. Dominance and epistasis effects depend on combinations of alleles that are broken up each generation. **[[Narrow-sense heritability]]** is $h^2 = V_A / V_P$, and it predicts the response to selection with the **[[breeder's equation]]**:

$$R = h^2 S$$

where $S$, the selection differential, is how far the chosen parents' mean is from the population mean, and $R$, the response, is how far the offspring mean moves.

### Example 4

(a) Two inbred lines of corn and their F1 are each genetically uniform, and their ear lengths have a variance of 4.0 cm². The F2, which is genetically varied, has a variance of 10.0 cm². Estimate $H^2$ for ear length.

In the genetically uniform groups, all variation is environmental, so $V_E \approx 4.0$. In the F2, $V_G = V_P - V_E = 10.0 - 4.0 = 6.0$, so $H^2 = \tfrac{6.0}{10.0} = 0.6$. (This assumes the environment varies as much for the F2 as for the other groups.)

(b) In another population with a mean plant height of 120 cm and $h^2 = 0.4$, a breeder plants seed only from plants averaging 130 cm. Predict the offspring mean.

$S = 130 - 120 = 10$ cm, so $R = 0.4 \times 10 = 4$ cm, and the offspring mean is about $120 + 4 = 124$ cm. Selection works, but only the heritable part of the parents' advantage is passed on.

In humans, heritability is estimated from relatives, especially twins: identical twins share all their genes, fraternal twins about half. If identical twins are much more alike than fraternal twins, genes account for much of the variation. Height in well-nourished populations has a heritability of about 0.8 by such estimates.

## What heritability does not mean

Heritability is easy to misread:

- It describes variation in a population, not an individual. $H^2 = 0.8$ for height does not mean 80% of your height comes from genes.
- It belongs to one population in one environment. Make the environment more uniform and $V_E$ shrinks, so heritability rises; the same trait can have different heritabilities in different places.
- High heritability doesn't mean a trait can't change. Average heights rose a lot in many countries during the 1900s as nutrition improved, though heritability stayed high, and PKU (lesson 19) is strongly genetic yet fully treatable by diet.
- Heritability within groups says nothing about the causes of average differences between groups, which may be entirely environmental.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a 9 : 7 or 12 : 3 : 1 ratio as a sign that Mendel's laws failed. The alleles segregate and assort normally; only the genotype-to-phenotype mapping changes.
- Mixing up which gene is epistatic. The epistatic gene is the one whose genotype hides the other (cc albino mice hide the agouti gene).
- Using 3 : 1 for two parents with the same dominant phenotype when one allele is a recessive lethal; the surviving offspring come out 2 : 1.
- Reading heritability as "how genetic a trait is in each person," or as fixed and unchangeable.
- Using broad-sense $H^2$ in the breeder's equation. Response to selection depends on narrow-sense $h^2$.

## Key points

- Two genes acting on one trait merge the 16 F2 outcomes into modified ratios: 9 : 3 : 4 (recessive epistasis), 9 : 7 (complementary genes), 12 : 3 : 1 (dominant epistasis), 15 : 1 (duplicate genes). Ratios in sixteenths point to two genes.
- Two true-breeding mutants with the same phenotype whose F1 is normal carry mutations in different genes (complementation).
- Pleiotropic alleles can be dominant for one trait and recessive lethal for survival, giving 2 : 1 among survivors (yellow mice).
- With $n$ additive genes, each F2 extreme has probability $(1/4)^n$, and there are $2n + 1$ phenotype classes.
- $V_P = V_G + V_E$; $H^2 = V_G/V_P$; $h^2 = V_A/V_P$; breeder's equation $R = h^2 S$.
- Heritability describes variation in a particular population and environment, not individuals, not fixedness and not differences between groups.

lessons.title: DNA structure and replication
lessons.body:
In the last module you followed genes through crosses and pedigrees without asking what a gene physically is. Mendel never knew; he only saw the ratios. This module opens the box. This lesson answers two questions: how do we know genes are made of DNA, and how does the shape of the DNA molecule let it be copied every time a cell divides?

## How biologists showed that genes are DNA

By the 1940s genes were known to sit on chromosomes, which are made of DNA and protein. Most biologists bet on protein: proteins use 20 different amino acids, while DNA has only four kinds of nucleotide, which seemed too simple to carry instructions. Three experiments changed their minds.

*Griffith, 1928.* Frederick Griffith worked with two strains of pneumonia bacteria. The S strain has a smooth sugar coat and kills mice; the R strain lacks the coat and is harmless. Heat-killed S bacteria were harmless too. But when he injected heat-killed S bacteria *mixed with* live R bacteria, the mice died, and live S bacteria came out of their blood. Something from the dead S cells had permanently changed the R cells, and the change was passed on to their descendants. Griffith called this transformation. He did not know what the "transforming principle" was.

*Avery, MacLeod and McCarty, 1944.* They purified extract from S cells and destroyed one kind of molecule at a time with enzymes before mixing it with R cells.

### Example 1

Here is the logic of the Avery experiment as a data table. Which molecule is the transforming principle?

| S-cell extract treated with | Live S cells appear? |
|---|---|
| Nothing | Yes |
| Protease (destroys protein) | Yes |
| RNase (destroys RNA) | Yes |
| DNase (destroys DNA) | No |

Reason through each row. Destroying protein did not stop transformation, so protein is not needed. The same holds for RNA. Only destroying DNA stopped it. The transforming principle is DNA. The untreated extract is the control: it shows transformation works at all.

*Hershey and Chase, 1952.* Some biologists still doubted, so Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase used a virus that infects bacteria (a bacteriophage). A phage is just protein wrapped around DNA, and it injects its genes into the bacterium. Protein contains sulfur but almost no phosphorus; DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur. So they grew one batch of phages with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S, labeling protein) and another with radioactive phosphorus (³²P, labeling DNA). After infection, they shook the empty phage coats off in a blender and spun the bacteria down. The ³²P was found inside the bacteria; the ³⁵S stayed outside with the coats. The material that enters the cell and directs new phages is DNA.

## The structure of DNA

Recall from module 1 that DNA is a nucleic acid, a polymer of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a phosphate group, the five-carbon sugar deoxyribose, and one of four nitrogen bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). A and G are purines, with a double ring; T and C are pyrimidines, with a single ring.

Nucleotides link into a strand through sugar–phosphate bonds, forming a backbone with the bases sticking out to one side. The two ends of a strand differ: one ends in a phosphate attached to the sugar's 5′ (five-prime) carbon, the other in the sugar's 3′ carbon. So every strand has a direction, written 5′ → 3′.

Two strands make the **[[double helix]]**, a twisted ladder. The sugar–phosphate backbones are the rails; pairs of bases are the rungs, held together by hydrogen bonds. The pairing follows strict rules, called **[[complementary base pairing]]**:

- A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds);
- G pairs with C (three hydrogen bonds).

Each rung is one purine plus one pyrimidine, so every rung is the same width and the helix is a uniform 2 nm wide. The strands are **[[antiparallel]]**: they run in opposite directions, one 5′ → 3′ and its partner 3′ → 5′.

The figure shows the helix and, beside it, four rungs untwisted into a flat ladder: phosphates and sugars alternate along each backbone, and the bases meet in the middle. Follow the arrows to see that the strands point opposite ways.

![Left: a double helix drawn as two twisting strands joined by rungs, 2 nm wide, with one full turn of 3.4 nm holding about 10 base pairs. Right: four base pairs untwisted into a ladder. Each backbone alternates phosphate circles and pentagon-shaped deoxyribose sugars. The pairs from top to bottom are A–T, G–C, T–A and C–G; A–T pairs are joined by two dashed hydrogen bonds and G–C pairs by three. The left strand runs 5′ to 3′ downward and the right strand runs 5′ to 3′ upward. A dashed box marks one nucleotide: a phosphate, a sugar and a base.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The model came together in 1953. Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photographs, taken at King's College London (where Maurice Wilkins also studied DNA), showed a helix of constant width with a repeating pattern every 3.4 nm. James Watson and Francis Crick, who saw her data without her knowledge, combined it with a key clue from chemistry, Chargaff's measurements, and built the model.

## Chargaff's rules

Erwin Chargaff measured the base composition of DNA from many species. He found two patterns, now called **[[Chargaff's rules]]**: in any double-stranded DNA, the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of G equals the amount of C; but the proportion of A + T versus G + C varies from species to species. Base pairing explains the first rule at once: every A on one strand has a T across from it.

Human DNA is about 30% A, 30% T, 20% G and 20% C.

### Example 2

A sample of double-stranded DNA is 22% guanine. Find the percentages of the other three bases.

- G pairs with C, so C = 22%.
- G + C = 44%, so A + T = 100% − 44% = 56%.
- A = T, so each is 56% ÷ 2 = 28%.

Answer: A 28%, T 28%, G 22%, C 22%. Check: 28 + 28 + 22 + 22 = 100.

Chargaff's rules apply to the double helix as a whole, not to one strand. One strand can have far more A than T; its partner then has the extra T.

### Example 3

Write the strand complementary to 5′-ATGCCGTT-3′.

Pair each base in turn: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G. Under the given strand, the partner bases are T A C G G C A A. Because the strands are antiparallel, the partner runs the other way, so its left end is 3′:

| Given strand | 5′- A T G C C G T T -3′ |
|---|---|
| Complement | 3′- T A C G G C A A -5′ |

If you are asked to write the complement in the usual 5′ → 3′ direction, read it from its 5′ end (the right): 5′-AACGGCAT-3′. Both descriptions are the same molecule. The safest habit is to write the complement directly under the original with its ends labeled.

## Replication is semiconservative

Watson and Crick noticed that base pairing suggests a copying method: separate the two strands, and each one is a template for building its partner. Each new double helix would then have one old strand and one new strand. This is **[[semiconservative replication]]**. Two other ideas were possible: conservative (the original helix stays intact and a wholly new one is made) and dispersive (old and new pieces mixed along both strands).

In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl tested them. They grew bacteria for many generations on heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), so all their DNA was heavy, then moved them to normal light nitrogen (¹⁴N) and let them divide. They spun DNA samples in a dense salt solution, where DNA settles in a band at its own density.

### Example 4

Predict the bands after one and two generations in light nitrogen if replication is semiconservative.

- Generation 0: all DNA is heavy/heavy: one heavy band.
- Generation 1: each helix has one old heavy strand and one new light strand: one band, halfway between heavy and light (hybrid). This alone rules out the conservative model, which would give separate heavy and light bands.
- Generation 2: the two strands of each hybrid separate. The heavy strand gets a light partner (hybrid); the light strand gets a light partner (light). Half the DNA is hybrid, half is light: two bands of equal amount.

![Three centrifuge tubes with dashed reference lines for light (14N/14N) DNA at the top, hybrid (15N/14N) in the middle and heavy (15N/15N) at the bottom. Generation 0 has one heavy band, generation 1 one hybrid band, and generation 2 two equal bands, one hybrid and one light.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

That is exactly what Meselson and Stahl saw, as the tubes above show. The dispersive model predicts a single band that just drifts lighter each generation, so the two bands in generation 2 ruled it out too. In general, after $n$ generations the two original heavy strands sit in exactly two of the $2^n$ helices, so the hybrid fraction is $2/2^n$.

## The replication machinery

Copying is done by a team of enzymes:

1. Replication starts at specific sites called origins. A bacterial chromosome has one origin; a human chromosome has hundreds to thousands, so the work is split among many replication forks.
2. Helicase unwinds the helix, breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases and forming a Y-shaped replication fork.
3. Primase lays down a short RNA primer, because the main copying enzyme cannot start a strand from nothing.
4. **[[DNA polymerase]]** reads the template and adds matching nucleotides. It can only add to the 3′ end of a growing strand, so new DNA is always built 5′ → 3′.
5. Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand (the leading strand) is built continuously toward the fork. The other (the lagging strand) must be built in short pieces, working away from the fork each time a new stretch opens up. These pieces are **[[Okazaki fragments]]**, named for Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki, who found them in the 1960s.
6. The RNA primers are replaced with DNA, and DNA ligase seals the gaps between fragments.

The drawing puts these steps in one picture: the leading strand grows in one piece toward the fork, while the lagging strand is a row of Okazaki fragments, each started from its own primer and pointing away from the fork.

![A replication fork. On the right, unopened parent DNA; at the fork, helicase (a hexagon) separates the strands. The top template, 3′ at its left end, has a new leading strand built continuously toward the fork by DNA polymerase. The bottom template, 5′ at its left end, has a lagging strand made of Okazaki fragments that each grow away from the fork: the newest fragment has an RNA primer and a DNA polymerase at its growing end, primase lays down a new primer near the fork, and DNA ligase seals the nick between the two oldest fragments.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

DNA polymerase also proofreads: it backs up and removes a wrongly paired base. With proofreading and later repair, the final error rate is roughly one mistake per billion bases copied. Errors that slip through are mutations, a topic in lesson 24.

## Common mistakes

- Pairing A with G or C with T. The pairs are always A–T and G–C (purine with pyrimidine).
- Applying Chargaff's rules to one strand. A = T and G = C hold for double-stranded DNA, not for a single strand or for RNA.
- Forgetting that A + T and G + C both add to 100%. If G is 22%, A is not 78%; G and C together are 44%, leaving 56% to split between A and T.
- Ignoring direction. The complement of a 5′ → 3′ strand runs 3′ → 5′; label the ends.
- Thinking the lagging strand is made in the 3′ → 5′ direction. Every new strand grows 5′ → 3′; the lagging strand is made in fragments precisely because of that rule.
- Saying Meselson and Stahl's first generation ruled out the dispersive model. Generation 1 rules out conservative; generation 2 rules out dispersive.

## Key points

- Griffith found transformation; Avery's enzyme tests identified DNA as the transforming principle; Hershey and Chase showed phage DNA, not protein, enters the cell.
- DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands with sugar–phosphate backbones and base pairs A–T and G–C.
- Chargaff's rules: in double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C; the A + T to G + C ratio differs between species.
- Replication is semiconservative: each new helix keeps one old strand (Meselson–Stahl, 1958).
- Helicase unwinds, primase primes, DNA polymerase builds 5′ → 3′ (leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments), ligase joins, and proofreading keeps errors near one per billion bases.

lessons.title: From gene to protein
lessons.body:
The last lesson showed how DNA is copied. But a gene is not useful just sitting in the nucleus being copied; it has to *do* something. Almost everything a gene does, it does through a protein: an enzyme, a channel, a hormone receptor, a structural fiber. This lesson follows the path from a stretch of DNA to a finished protein, and explains how a four-letter alphabet spells out sequences of 20 amino acids.

## The central dogma

Francis Crick summed up the flow of genetic information in 1958 as the **[[central dogma]]**: DNA → RNA → protein. Information is copied from DNA into RNA by **[[transcription]]**, and the RNA's message is decoded into a chain of amino acids by **[[translation]]**. Using a gene's information to make its product is called gene expression.

There are exceptions to the simple arrow. Retroviruses such as HIV copy RNA back into DNA, and many genes make RNA molecules that are never translated but do jobs of their own. Still, the main traffic of information goes DNA → RNA → protein, and it never goes from protein back to nucleic acid.

Why use an RNA middleman at all? In eukaryotes the DNA stays in the nucleus, while ribosomes work in the cytoplasm. A gene can be transcribed into many RNA copies, each translated many times, so one gene can make thousands of protein molecules quickly while the master copy stays protected.

The diagram traces that path in a eukaryotic cell, with the steps this lesson covers in order.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  accTitle: Gene expression in a eukaryotic cell
  accDescr: Inside the nucleus, DNA is copied by replication and transcribed into pre-mRNA. The pre-mRNA gets a cap and tail and its introns are spliced out, giving mature mRNA. The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore. In the cytoplasm a ribosome translates its codons into a polypeptide, which folds into a working protein.
  subgraph N[Nucleus]
    DNA -- transcription --> PRE[pre-mRNA]
    PRE -- "cap, tail, splicing" --> MRNA[mature mRNA]
  end
  subgraph C[Cytoplasm]
    RIB[Ribosome reads codons] -- translation --> POLY[Polypeptide]
    POLY -- folding --> PROT[Working protein]
  end
  DNA -- replication --> DNA
  MRNA -- "leaves through a pore" --> RIB
```

## RNA is not DNA

RNA is a nucleic acid too, but it differs from DNA in three ways:

| | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | deoxyribose | ribose |
| Bases | A, T, G, C | A, U, G, C (uracil replaces thymine) |
| Strands | usually two (double helix) | usually one |

Uracil pairs with adenine, just as thymine does. Three kinds of RNA do the main work of protein synthesis:

- **[[mRNA]]** (messenger RNA) carries a gene's sequence to the ribosome.
- **[[tRNA]]** (transfer RNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome; each tRNA carries one specific amino acid.
- **[[rRNA]]** (ribosomal RNA) makes up much of the ribosome and catalyzes the bonds between amino acids.

## Transcription

Transcription copies one gene, not a whole chromosome, and it uses only one of the two DNA strands as a pattern.

1. *Initiation.* The enzyme **[[RNA polymerase]]** binds to a **[[promoter]]**, a DNA sequence just upstream of the gene that marks where to start and which strand to read. It unwinds a short stretch of the helix.
2. *Elongation.* RNA polymerase moves along the template strand, adding RNA nucleotides that pair with the template bases (A with U, T with A, G with C, C with G). Like DNA polymerase, it builds 5′ → 3′, so it reads the template 3′ → 5′. Unlike DNA polymerase, it needs no primer.
3. *Termination.* At a terminator sequence the polymerase releases the RNA and the DNA rewinds.

The DNA strand that is read is the template strand. The other strand is called the coding strand, because its sequence matches the mRNA (with T in place of U).

![A stretch of double-stranded DNA with a bubble where the strands are pulled apart inside an RNA polymerase. A shaded promoter sits upstream on the left. The top coding strand runs 5′ to 3′ left to right; the bottom template strand runs 3′ to 5′. Inside the bubble a new RNA strand pairs with the template strand, and its 5′ end trails out of the polymerase to the upper left. An arrow shows the polymerase moving to the right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the picture, notice which strand the RNA pairs with (the template), and that the RNA's free end is its 5′ end: the RNA was started first at that end and is growing at its 3′ end inside the polymerase.

In eukaryotes the new RNA is processed before it leaves the nucleus. A protective cap is added to its 5′ end and a tail of many A's to its 3′ end. Most genes also contain **[[introns]]**, stretches that are cut out, and **[[exons]]**, the stretches that are spliced together and expressed. Splicing can join exons in different combinations, which is one reason humans make far more kinds of protein than their roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.

### Example 1

A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACGGATCC-5′. Write the mRNA.

Pair each template base with its RNA partner: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→U, T→A, C→G, C→G. The mRNA is antiparallel to the template, so its left end is 5′:

5′-AUGCCUAGG-3′.

Check with the coding strand: it would be 5′-ATGCCTAGG-3′, the same as the mRNA with T for U. A common error is to write the DNA complement (ATGCCTAGG) and forget that RNA uses U.

## The genetic code

Four bases cannot code for 20 amino acids one at a time, or even two at a time ($4^2 = 16$). Three at a time gives $4^3 = 64$ combinations, enough with some to spare. Each group of three mRNA bases is a **[[codon]]**. In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei cracked the first word: they added an artificial mRNA made only of U's (UUUUUU…) to a cell-free extract, and it made a protein made only of phenylalanine. So UUU means Phe. Within five years all 64 codons were assigned.

| First base | Second U | Second C | Second A | Second G | Third base |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U | UUU Phe | UCU Ser | UAU Tyr | UGU Cys | U |
|  | UUC Phe | UCC Ser | UAC Tyr | UGC Cys | C |
|  | UUA Leu | UCA Ser | UAA Stop | UGA Stop | A |
|  | UUG Leu | UCG Ser | UAG Stop | UGG Trp | G |
| C | CUU Leu | CCU Pro | CAU His | CGU Arg | U |
|  | CUC Leu | CCC Pro | CAC His | CGC Arg | C |
|  | CUA Leu | CCA Pro | CAA Gln | CGA Arg | A |
|  | CUG Leu | CCG Pro | CAG Gln | CGG Arg | G |
| A | AUU Ile | ACU Thr | AAU Asn | AGU Ser | U |
|  | AUC Ile | ACC Thr | AAC Asn | AGC Ser | C |
|  | AUA Ile | ACA Thr | AAA Lys | AGA Arg | A |
|  | AUG Met | ACG Thr | AAG Lys | AGG Arg | G |
| G | GUU Val | GCU Ala | GAU Asp | GGU Gly | U |
|  | GUC Val | GCC Ala | GAC Asp | GGC Gly | C |
|  | GUA Val | GCA Ala | GAA Glu | GGA Gly | A |
|  | GUG Val | GCG Ala | GAG Glu | GGG Gly | G |

To read the table, find the first base in the left column, the second base in the column headings, and the third base on the right. The code has four features worth knowing:

- *Start and stop.* AUG codes for methionine (Met) and is also the start codon where translation begins. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons: no tRNA matches them, and they end translation.
- *Redundant.* 61 codons code for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons (Leu has six). The extra codons usually differ in the third base, so many third-base changes don't change the protein.
- *Unambiguous.* Each codon means exactly one thing.
- *Nearly universal.* Bacteria, plants and people read codons almost the same way, which is strong evidence that all life shares a common ancestor, and the reason a human gene can be expressed in bacteria (lesson 25).

## Translation

Translation happens on ribosomes. Each tRNA has, at one end, an **[[anticodon]]**: three bases that pair with an mRNA codon. At the other end it carries the amino acid that codon specifies. The tRNA is the adapter that connects the nucleic acid language to the protein language.

1. *Initiation.* The small ribosomal subunit attaches to the mRNA near its 5′ end and slides to the first AUG. A tRNA with anticodon UAC, carrying Met, pairs with it, and the large subunit joins. The AUG sets the reading frame: from here the mRNA is read in non-overlapping groups of three.
2. *Elongation.* The next tRNA whose anticodon matches the next codon enters the ribosome. The rRNA joins its amino acid to the growing chain with a peptide bond. The ribosome shifts one codon along the mRNA (toward the 3′ end), the empty tRNA leaves to be reloaded, and the cycle repeats.
3. *Termination.* When a stop codon enters the ribosome, a release factor (a protein, not a tRNA) binds, the finished chain is let go, and the ribosome comes apart.

The figure freezes one moment of elongation on the mRNA from Example 2 below. The tRNA holding the chain Met–Phe sits on codon UUU, and the next tRNA, carrying Gly, has just paired its anticodon CCG with codon GGC. Next, the chain will be moved onto Gly, the ribosome will shift one codon to the right, and the tRNA on UUU will leave, just as the empty tRNA for AUG is leaving on the left.

![A ribosome with a large upper subunit and a small lower subunit clamped around an mRNA that reads 5′ AUG UUU GGC AAA UGA 3′. Two tRNAs sit in the ribosome: one with anticodon AAA paired to codon UUU and carrying a chain of Met and Phe, the other with anticodon CCG paired to codon GGC and carrying Gly. An empty tRNA with anticodon UAC drifts away on the left. An arrow shows the ribosome moving toward the 3′ end.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The new chain then folds into its three-dimensional shape, sometimes helped by other proteins, and may be modified or sent to the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus you met in module 2.

### Example 2

Translate the mRNA 5′-GCAUGUUUGGCAAAUGAUC-3′.

- Find the start codon. Scanning from the 5′ end, the first AUG begins at the third base: GC AUG UUU…, so the reading frame starts there and the GC before it is not translated.
- Split into codons from AUG: AUG | UUU | GGC | AAA | UGA | UC.
- Look up each: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, AAA = Lys, UGA = Stop.

The polypeptide is Met–Phe–Gly–Lys: four amino acids. The stop codon adds nothing, and the bases after it are not read.

### Example 3

A tRNA has the anticodon 3′-AAG-5′. Which amino acid does it carry?

The anticodon pairs with the codon, so the codon is the complement: A pairs with U, A with U, G with C, giving 5′-UUC-3′. From the table, UUC codes for Phe. Don't look up the anticodon itself in the table; the table is written in codons.

## Common mistakes

- Writing T in an mRNA. RNA uses U; the mRNA matches the coding strand, not the template strand.
- Translating from the first base instead of the first AUG.
- Looking up anticodons or DNA triplets in the codon table. The table lists mRNA codons.
- Counting the stop codon as an amino acid. A coding region of $n$ codons, start to stop, makes $n - 1$ amino acids.
- Saying ribosomes are made of protein only. rRNA forms the core and catalyzes peptide bonds.
- Thinking each gene makes exactly one protein. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several.

## Key points

- Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → RNA → (translation) → protein.
- RNA has ribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded; mRNA, tRNA and rRNA work together to make proteins.
- RNA polymerase starts at a promoter and builds an RNA complementary to the template strand. Eukaryotic RNA gets a cap and tail, and its introns are removed.
- The genetic code uses triplet codons: 64 codons, AUG = start (Met), three stops, redundant, unambiguous and nearly universal.
- tRNA anticodons pair with codons; the ribosome links amino acids in codon order from AUG to the stop codon.

lessons.title: Gene regulation and mutation
lessons.body:
Your skin cells and your nerve cells carry the same DNA, copied from the same fertilized egg. Yet one makes keratin and the other makes neurotransmitter receptors. The last lesson showed how a gene becomes a protein; this lesson asks when it does. Cells constantly decide which genes to express, and that control is what makes cell types different. The second half of the lesson looks at what happens when the DNA sequence itself changes.

## Why cells regulate genes

Making RNA and protein costs energy and raw materials. A bacterium that made every one of its roughly 4,000 proteins all the time would waste resources on enzymes it has no use for. A multicellular organism has a different problem: hundreds of cell types must each express the right set of genes, at the right time in development, in the right amount. Most regulation happens at the first step, transcription, because it is cheapest to not start making something you don't need.

## The lac operon: a switch in bacteria

The first gene switch to be understood was found by François Jacob and Jacques Monod in the bacterium *E. coli*, work that earned a Nobel Prize in 1965. *E. coli* prefers glucose, but it can live on lactose (milk sugar) if it has to. To use lactose it needs enzymes, including one that splits lactose into glucose and galactose. Those enzymes are made only when lactose is around.

In bacteria, genes that work together are often grouped into an **[[operon]]**: a cluster of genes controlled by a single promoter and transcribed together as one mRNA. The lac operon has:

- a promoter, where RNA polymerase binds;
- an operator, a short DNA sequence overlapping the promoter that acts as the on/off switch;
- three genes for lactose-handling enzymes, transcribed together.

A separate gene, always on, makes a **[[repressor]]** protein that binds the operator.

- *No lactose:* the repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. The genes are off.
- *Lactose present:* a form of lactose binds the repressor and changes its shape, so it falls off the operator. RNA polymerase can now transcribe the genes. When the lactose is used up, the repressor binds again and the genes switch off.

The figure shows the two states side by side.

![Two drawings of the lac operon DNA. Each shows, from left to right, the lacI gene, a promoter (P), an operator (O), and the three genes lacZ, lacY and lacA. Top, no lactose: a repressor protein sits on the operator and RNA polymerase waits on the promoter, unable to pass, so the genes are off. Bottom, lactose present: lactose is bound to the repressor, which has left the DNA, and RNA polymerase moves along the genes making mRNA, so the genes are on. The lacI gene makes the repressor all the time.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The system is a negative feedback loop: the enzymes destroy the very signal that turns them on. (A second control, through an activator protein, keeps the operon low when glucose is also present, because the cell prefers glucose.)

### Example 1

Jacob and Monod worked out this model largely by studying mutant bacteria. Predict whether the lac genes are on or off in each case.

| Strain | Lactose absent | Lactose present |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | off | on |
| Repressor can't bind DNA | ? | ? |
| Repressor can't bind lactose | ? | ? |
| Operator changed so repressor can't bind it | ? | ? |

- Repressor can't bind DNA: nothing ever blocks the operator, so the genes are on in both conditions (always on).
- Repressor can't bind lactose: it stays on the operator even when lactose arrives, so the genes are off in both conditions (never induced).
- Operator mutated: the repressor has nowhere to bind, so the genes are on in both conditions, just like the first mutant.

Patterns like these, where the gene is stuck on or stuck off, are how the parts of the switch were identified.

## Gene regulation in eukaryotes

Eukaryotic cells regulate at many more steps, but the main control is still transcription.

- **[[Transcription factors]]** are proteins that bind to DNA near a gene and help or block RNA polymerase. Some bind the promoter; others bind enhancers, control regions that may sit thousands of bases away and loop over to touch the promoter. A gene is usually controlled by a combination of factors, so a few hundred transcription factors in different combinations can specify many cell types.
- *Packing.* DNA is wound around histone proteins. Tightly packed regions are hard for RNA polymerase to reach and stay silent; loosely packed regions can be transcribed. Chemical tags such as methyl groups on DNA, and tags on histones, change packing. These tags can be copied when cells divide, so a liver cell's daughters stay liver cells. Inherited changes in gene activity that don't change the DNA sequence are called epigenetic.
- *After transcription.* Cells also control RNA splicing (lesson 23), how long an mRNA lasts before it is broken down, whether it is translated (small RNAs called microRNAs can block it), and whether the finished protein is activated or destroyed.

In development, cell differentiation is gene regulation. Early embryonic cells switch on different transcription factors depending on their position, and those factors switch on further genes. Master regulators such as the Hox genes, which set up the head-to-tail body plan of animals from flies to people, are themselves transcription factors. A mutation in one Hox gene of a fruit fly can grow legs where its antennae should be.

## Mutations

A **[[mutation]]** is any change in the DNA sequence. Mutations arise in two main ways:

- *Spontaneously,* mostly from rare copying errors that slip past proofreading and repair (lesson 22).
- *From a* **[[mutagen]]**, an agent that damages DNA or raises the error rate: ultraviolet light (which links neighboring thymines), X-rays and other ionizing radiation, and chemicals such as some in tobacco smoke.

Where the mutation happens matters. A mutation in a body (somatic) cell is passed only to that cell's descendants; it can contribute to cancer (module 4) but is not inherited by children. A mutation in a cell that makes eggs or sperm (a germline mutation) can be passed on.

### Point mutations

A **[[point mutation]]** changes a single base. When one base is swapped for another (a substitution), the effect on the protein depends on the codon it lands in:

| Type | What changes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Silent | Codon changes but still codes for the same amino acid | GAA → GAG: Glu → Glu |
| Missense | Codon now codes for a different amino acid | GAA → GUA: Glu → Val |
| Nonsense | Codon becomes a stop codon; the protein is cut short | UGG → UGA: Trp → Stop |

Sickle cell disease comes from a single missense mutation in the gene for a hemoglobin chain: codon 6 changes from GAG to GUG, putting valine where glutamic acid should be. That one change makes the hemoglobin molecules stick together into stiff fibers when oxygen is low, bending red blood cells into a sickle shape. One base out of hundreds in the gene changes how the protein behaves.

### Insertions and deletions

Adding or removing bases is more drastic. Because the ribosome reads in fixed groups of three from the start codon, inserting or deleting one or two bases shifts every codon after the change. This is a **[[frameshift mutation]]**. The amino acids downstream are all different, and a stop codon usually turns up early.

An insertion or deletion of exactly three bases (or any multiple of three) keeps the reading frame. The most common cystic fibrosis mutation is a deletion of three bases that removes one phenylalanine from a protein of about 1,480 amino acids. The protein misfolds, but the rest of its sequence is intact.

### Example 2

The normal mRNA is 5′-AUG GAA UGG CUA AAA UAA-3′, which codes for Met–Glu–Trp–Leu–Lys. Classify each mutation.

1. Codon 2 GAA → GAG. GAG still codes for Glu: silent.
2. Codon 2 GAA → GUA. GUA codes for Val: missense (Glu → Val).
3. Codon 3 UGG → UGA. UGA is a stop codon: nonsense. The protein is Met–Glu only.
4. The G of codon 2 is deleted. Re-read in threes from AUG: AUG AAU GGC UAA. The protein is Met–Asn–Gly, then stop. Every codon after the deletion changed, and a stop codon appeared early: frameshift.

Notice the method: write the new sequence, re-split it into codons starting from AUG, and translate. Don't just translate the one codon you think changed.

The flowchart sums up the decisions you just made.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Classifying a mutation in a coding region
  accDescr: Start by comparing the mutant and normal sequences. If one base was swapped for another and the number of bases is unchanged, ask whether the new codon codes for the same amino acid. If yes, the mutation is silent. If not, ask whether the new codon is a stop codon. If yes, it is nonsense; if no, it is missense. If bases were added or lost, ask whether the number is a multiple of three. If not, it is a frameshift. If it is, the reading frame is kept and amino acids are added or removed.
  A[Compare mutant and normal sequence] --> B{Bases added or lost?}
  B -- "no: one base swapped" --> C{Same amino acid?}
  C -- yes --> S[Silent]
  C -- no --> D{New codon is a stop?}
  D -- yes --> N[Nonsense]
  D -- no --> M[Missense]
  B -- yes --> E{Multiple of 3?}
  E -- no --> F[Frameshift]
  E -- yes --> G[In frame: amino acids added or removed]
```

## Mutations are the raw material of variation

Most mutations are neutral (in DNA that doesn't code for anything, or silent) or harmful. A few are helpful in a particular environment. A mutation that keeps the lactase gene switched on in adults spread in human populations that kept dairy animals. Mutations are the ultimate source of new alleles; meiosis and fertilization (module 4) only reshuffle alleles that already exist. Module 7 shows how natural selection acts on that variation.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking different cells have different genes. Nearly all cells in a body have the same DNA; they express different parts of it.
- Mixing up the operator and the promoter. RNA polymerase binds the promoter; the repressor binds the operator.
- Saying lactose turns on the operon by binding the DNA. Lactose binds the repressor, which then lets go of the DNA.
- Calling every deletion a frameshift. Deleting three bases removes one amino acid and keeps the frame.
- Assuming every mutation is harmful. Many are neutral and some are beneficial.
- Thinking a somatic mutation is inherited. Only germline mutations reach the next generation.

## Key points

- Cells regulate which genes they express, mostly at transcription; different cell types differ in gene expression, not in genes.
- The lac operon: a repressor bound to the operator blocks transcription; lactose binds the repressor and releases it, switching the genes on.
- Eukaryotes use transcription factors, enhancers, DNA packing and epigenetic tags, plus control after transcription.
- Mutations come from copying errors and mutagens; only germline mutations are inherited.
- Substitutions can be silent, missense or nonsense; insertions and deletions not in multiples of three cause frameshifts.
- Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles, the variation evolution works on.

lessons.title: Biotechnology
lessons.body:
The last three lessons described what DNA is, how it is copied, how it is read and how it changes. Every one of those facts became a tool. Biotechnology is the use of living things and their molecules to make products or answer questions, and modern biotechnology mostly means handling DNA directly: copying a gene, cutting it, sorting the pieces, moving it into another organism, or editing it in place. This lesson covers the core tools and the math that goes with them.

## Cutting DNA: restriction enzymes

Bacteria defend themselves against viruses with enzymes that cut foreign DNA. A **[[restriction enzyme]]** recognizes a specific short sequence, usually 4 to 8 base pairs, and cuts both strands there. The enzyme EcoRI, for example, recognizes

5′-GAATTC-3′
3′-CTTAAG-5′

and cuts between the G and the A on each strand. Notice the site reads the same 5′ → 3′ on both strands; most recognition sites are palindromes like this. Because the cuts are offset, each piece is left with a short single-stranded tail (AATT). These "sticky ends" can pair with any other piece cut by the same enzyme. (The bacterium protects its own DNA by adding methyl groups at its sites.)

Since a restriction enzyme cuts at every copy of its site, cutting a known DNA molecule gives predictable fragment sizes.

### Example 1

A linear DNA molecule of 10,000 base pairs (bp) has EcoRI sites at positions 3,000 and 7,500. What fragments does EcoRI produce? What if the same DNA were a circle?

- Linear: two cuts make three pieces. From the left end to the first cut: 3,000 bp. Between the cuts: 7,500 − 3,000 = 4,500 bp. From the second cut to the right end: 10,000 − 7,500 = 2,500 bp. Check: 3,000 + 4,500 + 2,500 = 10,000.
- Circular: a circle has no ends, so two cuts make only two pieces: 4,500 bp, and 10,000 − 4,500 = 5,500 bp.

In general, $n$ cuts give $n + 1$ fragments of a linear molecule and $n$ fragments of a circular one.

## Sorting DNA: gel electrophoresis

**[[Gel electrophoresis]]** separates DNA fragments by size. The DNA is loaded into wells at one end of a slab of gel (usually agarose, a jelly made from seaweed), and an electric current is run through it. DNA's phosphate backbone is negatively charged, so every fragment moves toward the positive electrode. The gel is a tangle of fibers, and short fragments slip through it faster than long ones. After a set time, fragments have spread out by size: the smallest are farthest from the wells. A dye makes the bands visible.

To measure size, one lane holds a ladder: a mixture of fragments of known sizes. Distance traveled is close to a straight line when plotted against the logarithm of size, so you can read an unknown off the ladder.

```plot
{"x": [25, 60], "y": [2.5, 4.2], "xLabel": "distance from well (mm)", "yLabel": "log of size (bp)", "functions": [{"f": "(110 - x)/20", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [30, 4], "label": "10,000"}, {"at": [36.02, 3.699], "label": "5,000"}, {"at": [43.98, 3.301], "label": "2,000"}, {"at": [50, 3], "label": "1,000"}, {"at": [56.02, 2.699], "label": "500"}], "caption": "Ladder bands: log of fragment size falls along a straight line as distance increases"}
```

### Example 2

On the gel above, the ladder bands sit at these distances:

| Ladder band (bp) | 10,000 | 5,000 | 2,000 | 1,000 | 500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance (mm) | 30.0 | 36.0 | 44.0 | 50.0 | 56.0 |

An unknown band traveled 47.0 mm. Estimate its size.

- It lies between the 2,000 bp band (44 mm) and the 1,000 bp band (50 mm), so its size is between 1,000 and 2,000 bp. Farther means smaller.
- Use the straight line: every 6 mm here is a factor of 2 in size, and every 20 mm is a factor of 10. The unknown is 3 mm short of the 1,000 bp band, so its log-size is $3 + 3/20 = 3.15$, and the size is $10^{3.15} \approx 1{,}400$ bp.

A linear guess halfway between 1,000 and 2,000 (1,500 bp) is close but not right; on a gel, halfway in distance means halfway in the logarithm.

## Copying DNA: PCR

Often there is too little DNA to study: a drop of blood at a crime scene, a single virus in a swab. **[[PCR]]** (polymerase chain reaction), invented by Kary Mullis in 1983, copies one chosen stretch of DNA billions of times in a few hours. A tube holds the DNA, two short primers that match the ends of the target stretch, free nucleotides, and a heat-resistant DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase, from a bacterium that lives in hot springs). A machine cycles the temperature:

1. Denature, about 95 °C: the two strands separate.
2. Anneal, about 50–65 °C: primers bind to their matching sequences on each strand.
3. Extend, about 72 °C: the polymerase builds new strands starting from the primers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: One cycle of PCR
  accDescr: Each PCR cycle has three temperature steps. Denature at about 95 degrees Celsius, which separates the two DNA strands. Anneal at about 50 to 65 degrees, which lets the primers bind. Extend at about 72 degrees, as Taq polymerase builds new strands from the primers. The number of target copies doubles, and the cycle repeats, usually 25 to 35 times.
  D["Denature, about 95 °C: strands separate"] --> A["Anneal, about 50-65 °C: primers bind"]
  A --> E["Extend, about 72 °C: Taq builds new strands"]
  E --> X["Target copies double"]
  X -- "repeat 25-35 times" --> D
```

Each cycle takes a few minutes and, ideally, doubles the number of copies of the target. Starting with $N_0$ copies, after $n$ cycles there are

$$N = N_0 \times 2^n.$$

### Example 3

A sample has 50 copies of a target sequence. How many copies are there after 20 cycles, assuming perfect doubling?

$N = 50 \times 2^{20} = 50 \times 1{,}048{,}576 = 52{,}428{,}800$, about 52 million copies. Ten more cycles would multiply that by another $2^{10} = 1{,}024$. Real reactions run a bit below perfect doubling and level off once primers and nucleotides run low, so the formula gives the ideal maximum.

PCR is the basis of COVID-19 and other infection tests (after the virus's RNA is first copied into DNA), paternity tests, forensic work and studies of ancient DNA.

## Recombinant DNA and genetic engineering

Because the genetic code is nearly universal (lesson 23), a gene from one species can be expressed in another. **[[Recombinant DNA]]** is DNA joined together from different sources. The classic recipe uses a **[[plasmid]]**, a small circle of DNA that bacteria carry apart from their chromosome and copy on their own:

1. Cut the plasmid and the human insulin gene with the same restriction enzyme, so their sticky ends match.
2. Mix them; the ends pair, and DNA ligase seals the joints.
3. Put the recombinant plasmids into bacteria. Plasmids usually carry an antibiotic-resistance gene, so growing the bacteria on that antibiotic keeps only those that took up a plasmid.
4. Grow the bacteria in large tanks; they make human insulin.

Human insulin made this way was approved in 1982 and replaced insulin taken from pigs and cattle. An organism carrying a gene from another species is a **[[transgenic organism]]**. Examples include corn with a bacterial gene for an insect-killing protein (Bt corn), and Golden Rice, engineered to make beta-carotene to help prevent vitamin A deficiency.

## Editing genes: CRISPR

**[[CRISPR]]**-Cas9 also came from bacterial defense: bacteria store snippets of viral DNA and use a protein, Cas9, guided by a matching RNA, to cut that virus if it returns. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that the guide RNA could be designed to match almost any sequence, so Cas9 could cut a chosen gene in any organism. The cell's repair system then either disables the gene or inserts a supplied replacement. They received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In 2023 the first CRISPR-based treatment was approved, for sickle cell disease: doctors edit a patient's own blood stem cells outside the body to turn back on a fetal form of hemoglobin. Editing human embryos, whose changes would be inherited, remains widely opposed by scientists and regulators.

## Reading DNA: profiling and sequencing

Your genome differs from a stranger's at millions of places. **[[DNA profiling]]** compares a few highly variable regions. Forensic labs use short tandem repeats (STRs), places where a short sequence such as GATA is repeated a different number of times in different people. PCR copies about 20 STR regions, and electrophoresis measures their lengths. The chance that two unrelated people match at all of them is extremely small. Identical twins, though, share their profile.

### Example 4

At one STR region, evidence from a crime scene shows bands at 9 and 12 repeats. Suspect A has 9 and 12; suspect B has 9 and 14. What can be concluded from this one region?

The gel below shows this result. The ladder lane holds fragments with 8 to 15 repeats, so each sample band can be read against it like a ruler.

![A gel with the negative electrode at the top and the positive electrode at the bottom; DNA moves down from the wells. Four lanes: a ladder with bands for 8 to 15 repeats (8 farthest from the wells, 15 nearest), the evidence with bands at 9 and 12, suspect A with bands at 9 and 12, and suspect B with bands at 9 and 14. Longer pieces stay near the wells and shorter pieces travel farthest.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Suspect B has a 14-repeat allele not in the evidence, so B is excluded as the source. Suspect A matches, but many people share any one pair of alleles, so one region can't identify A. Labs compare all regions; a match at every one is strong evidence, while a single mismatch excludes.

DNA sequencing reads the bases directly. The Human Genome Project finished a nearly complete human sequence in 2003, after 13 years and about $3 billion; today a genome can be sequenced in a day or two for a few hundred dollars.

## Common mistakes

- Saying DNA moves toward the negative electrode. It is negatively charged and moves toward the positive one.
- Thinking big fragments travel farthest. Small fragments move farthest from the wells.
- Using $N_0 \times 2n$ instead of $N_0 \times 2^n$ for PCR. Copies double each cycle; they don't add two.
- Forgetting that a circle cut $n$ times gives $n$ pieces, while a line gives $n + 1$.
- Treating a match at one STR region as proof of identity. One mismatch excludes; identity needs a match at every region.

## Key points

- Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific (often palindromic) sequences, many leaving sticky ends.
- Gel electrophoresis separates negatively charged DNA by size; small fragments move farthest, and sizes are read from a ladder on a log scale.
- PCR copies a target by repeated denature–anneal–extend cycles; ideally $N = N_0 \times 2^n$.
- Recombinant DNA in plasmids lets bacteria make human proteins such as insulin; transgenic crops carry genes from other species.
- CRISPR-Cas9 edits chosen sequences; DNA profiling compares STR lengths; sequencing reads genomes base by base.

lessons.title: Operons, transcription factors, and epigenetics
lessons.body:
Lesson 24 showed the lac operon as a single switch: a repressor sits on the operator until lactose pulls it off. That is only half of the lac story, and some bacterial switches work the other way around. Eukaryotes add more layers: proteins acting from thousands of bases away, DNA packing that hides or exposes genes, chemical marks copied when cells divide, and control after transcription. This lesson takes each layer, with the experiments behind it, at AP or first-year college depth.

## Inducible and repressible operons

The lac operon is an **[[inducible operon]]**: it is normally off and is switched on by a small molecule, the inducer. (Strictly, the inducer is allolactose, a rearranged form of lactose made inside the cell; it binds the repressor and changes its shape so it can no longer grip the operator.)

The trp operon of *E. coli* works in the opposite direction. Its five genes encode the enzymes that build the amino acid tryptophan. It is a **[[repressible operon]]**: normally on, switched off by a small molecule. The trp repressor protein is made in an inactive form that cannot bind the operator. When tryptophan is plentiful, tryptophan itself binds the repressor and changes its shape so that it *can* bind the operator. A small molecule that activates a repressor like this is a **[[corepressor]]**. When tryptophan runs low, the repressor loses its tryptophan, falls off, and the genes are transcribed again.

The logic follows from what each pathway is for. A pathway that breaks down a food (lactose) should run only when the food is present, so it is inducible. A pathway that builds a product (tryptophan) should run only when the product is scarce, so it is repressible and shut off by its own end product. Both are negative control: in each, a repressor protein blocks transcription.

## Positive control: CAP and glucose

*E. coli* prefers glucose. Even with lactose around, it makes few lac enzymes while glucose is available. The reason is an activator. The **[[CAP]]** protein (catabolite activator protein) binds a site just upstream of the lac promoter, bends the DNA and helps RNA polymerase bind, raising transcription many-fold. CAP can bind only when it is holding a small signal molecule, cyclic AMP (cAMP), and cAMP levels rise when glucose is scarce. So CAP is a "glucose is low" signal and the repressor is a "lactose is absent" signal, and the operon reads both:

| Glucose | Lactose | Repressor | CAP–cAMP | lac transcription |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| present | absent | on operator | not bound | essentially none |
| present | present | released | not bound | low |
| absent | absent | on operator | bound | essentially none |
| absent | present | released | bound | high |

Only the last row, lactose but no glucose, gives full expression. (Glucose also slows the entry of lactose into the cell, which adds to the effect; current models include both mechanisms.)

## Telling DNA sites from proteins: cis and trans

A "stuck on" lac mutant could have a broken repressor *protein* or a broken operator *site*. To tell them apart, Jacob and Monod made partial diploids: bacteria carrying a second copy of the lac region on a plasmid. Each cell then has two operons, and the question is whether a mutation in one copy affects the other.

- A repressor is a protein. It diffuses through the cell and can bind any operator, on either DNA molecule. A part that acts on other DNA molecules like this is **[[trans-acting]]**.
- An operator is a DNA site. It controls only the genes next to it on the same molecule. A part that acts only on its own DNA molecule is **[[cis-acting]]**.

Geneticists write the alleles as $I^+$ (normal repressor), $I^-$ (no working repressor), $I^S$ (a "super-repressor" that cannot bind the inducer), $O^+$ (normal operator), $O^C$ (a mutant operator the repressor cannot bind) and $Z^+$ or $Z^-$ (working or broken gene for β-galactosidase, the enzyme measured).

### Example 1

Predict β-galactosidase production, with and without lactose, for each partial diploid. Assume no glucose. The two copies are separated by a slash.

| Genotype | No lactose | Lactose |
|---|---|---|
| (a) $I^+ O^+ Z^+$ / $I^- O^+ Z^+$ | ? | ? |
| (b) $I^+ O^C Z^-$ / $I^+ O^+ Z^+$ | ? | ? |
| (c) $I^+ O^C Z^+$ / $I^+ O^+ Z^-$ | ? | ? |
| (d) $I^S O^+ Z^+$ / $I^+ O^+ Z^+$ | ? | ? |

Work through what each protein can reach and which operon has the working $Z$:

- (a) The $I^+$ copy makes normal repressor, which diffuses to both operators. Without lactose both operons are off; with lactose both turn on. Result: **off / on** (normal). The $I^-$ mutation is recessive because the good repressor acts in trans.
- (b) The $O^C$ operon can never be repressed, but its $Z$ gene is broken, so it makes no enzyme. The only working $Z$ sits next to a normal operator. Result: **off / on**. The constant transcription of the $O^C$ copy is invisible here.
- (c) Now the working $Z$ is next to $O^C$. The repressor cannot bind there, with or without lactose. Result: **on / on**. Comparing (b) and (c) shows that $O^C$ affects only the genes on its own molecule: it is cis-acting.
- (d) The $I^S$ repressor cannot bind inducer, so it stays on whichever operator it reaches, and it reaches both. Result: **off / off**. $I^S$ is dominant, because a protein that never lets go blocks the normal copy too.

## Eukaryotic transcription: many proteins, combined

Eukaryotic RNA polymerase II cannot recognize a promoter by itself. A set of **[[general transcription factors]]** binds the core promoter first (many promoters contain a TATA box about 25–30 bases upstream of the start site) and positions the polymerase. On their own they give only a low, basal rate.

Most of the control comes from specific transcription factors. Activators bind **[[enhancers]]**: short DNA control regions that can lie thousands, even hundreds of thousands, of bases from the gene, upstream, downstream or inside an intron, and they work in either orientation. The DNA between them bends into a loop that brings the enhancer-bound activator next to the promoter. A large protein complex called Mediator bridges the activator and the polymerase. Repressor proteins bound to silencer sites work similarly but lower transcription.

![A DNA molecule that bends into a loop. On the upper arm an enhancer is bound by an activator protein. The loop brings the activator down onto a Mediator complex, which sits on RNA polymerase II. The polymerase and general transcription factors sit on the promoter on the lower arm, just upstream of the gene, and an arrow shows the direction of transcription.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each enhancer has sites for several factors, so control is combinatorial: a gene that needs activators A and B stays off in a cell that makes only A. A few hundred factors in different combinations can specify hundreds of cell types.

### Example 2

How do biologists find an enhancer? A common method is a reporter assay. The DNA upstream of a liver gene is joined to a reporter gene, luciferase, whose product glows and is easy to measure. Pieces of the upstream DNA are removed or moved, and each construct is tested in liver cells and kidney cells. Light output (relative units):

| Construct | Liver | Kidney |
|---|---|---|
| A: bases −3,000 to 0 (full region) | 100 | 4 |
| B: −2,000 to 0 | 98 | 4 |
| C: −1,000 to 0 | 5 | 4 |
| D: core promoter only (−200 to 0) | 4 | 4 |
| E: the −2,000 to −1,000 piece, flipped, in front of the core promoter | 96 | 4 |
| F: the −2,000 to −1,000 piece placed after the reporter gene | 90 | 4 |

Reasoning step by step:

1. D gives 4 in both cells: the core promoter alone gives basal transcription.
2. Removing −3,000 to −2,000 (A → B) changes little, so that piece isn't needed. Removing −2,000 to −1,000 (B → C) drops liver activity from 98 to 5, about $98 / 5 \approx 20$-fold. The key element lies between −2,000 and −1,000.
3. E and F show that the piece works backwards and downstream of the gene: the defining properties of an enhancer.
4. Kidney cells stay at 4 with every construct. The enhancer is liver-specific, most likely because liver cells make an activator that binds it and kidney cells don't.

## Chromatin: packing as a gate

In the nucleus, DNA is wrapped around **[[histone]]** proteins. About 147 base pairs coil around a core of eight histones (two each of four kinds) to form a **[[nucleosome]]**, and nucleosomes linked by short stretches of DNA look like beads on a string. The beads fold further into denser fibers. The whole DNA–protein material is **[[chromatin]]**.

Tightly packed chromatin keeps transcription factors and polymerase away from the DNA; loosely packed chromatin lets them in. Cells change packing with chemical marks:

- *Histone acetylation.* The histones' flexible tails carry positively charged lysines that grip the negatively charged DNA. Enzymes that add acetyl groups neutralize those charges, loosening the grip, and the acetyl groups are also docking sites for activator proteins. Acetylated chromatin is usually active; removing the acetyl groups (deacetylation) silences it. Histones can also be methylated, which can mark a gene as active or silent depending on which amino acid carries the mark.
- *DNA methylation.* In mammals, **[[DNA methylation]]** adds methyl groups to cytosines, mostly where a C is followed by a G (CpG). Methylated promoters are usually silent: proteins that bind methylated CpG recruit enzymes that deacetylate histones and compact the chromatin.

![Left: closed chromatin, with nucleosomes (DNA wrapped around histone cores) packed tightly together and methyl groups attached to the DNA, so the gene is silent. Right: open chromatin, with nucleosomes spaced out along the DNA, acetyl groups on the histone tails, and a transcription factor bound to the DNA between nucleosomes, so the gene can be active.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Why does a methylation pattern survive cell division? CpG reads CpG on the partner strand too (5′-CG-3′ pairs with 3′-GC-5′), so both strands are methylated at the same site. After replication, each new helix has one methylated old strand and one unmethylated new strand. A maintenance enzyme recognizes these half-methylated sites and methylates the new strand to match. The pattern is copied along with the sequence.

Changes in gene expression that are passed on through cell divisions without a change in the DNA sequence are the subject of **[[epigenetics]]**. Two well-established examples:

- *X inactivation.* In female mammals, one X chromosome in each cell is coated by a noncoding RNA and packed into silent chromatin early in development, and each cell's daughters keep the same X silent. In a calico cat, orange and black patches are groups of cells that silenced different X chromosomes.
- *Imprinting.* For a small number of genes, the copy inherited from one parent is methylated and silent. The growth gene *IGF2*, for example, is normally expressed only from the father's copy.

Be careful with bigger claims. Marks are reliably copied through cell divisions within one body, but in mammals most are erased and reset in eggs, sperm and the early embryo. Inheritance of acquired marks across generations is well documented in plants and roundworms; in humans it is debated, and popular claims often outrun the evidence.

## After transcription: splicing and microRNAs

**[[Alternative splicing]]** joins a gene's exons in different combinations, as in the figure, where skipping exon 3 gives a shorter protein. About 95% of human genes with several exons are alternatively spliced, and splicing choices differ between tissues.

![A pre-mRNA with exons 1 to 4 separated by introns. Splice pattern 1 keeps all four exons, giving mRNA 1 (exons 1, 2, 3, 4) and a longer protein. Splice pattern 2 skips exon 3, giving mRNA 2 (exons 1, 2, 4) and a shorter protein that lacks the part coded by exon 3.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 3

The fruit fly gene *Dscam* has four clusters of mutually exclusive exons: every mRNA includes exactly one exon from each cluster. The clusters have 12, 48, 33 and 2 alternatives. How many different mRNAs are possible?

Each choice is independent, so multiply: $12 \times 48 \times 33 \times 2 = 38{,}016$. That is more than twice the number of genes in the whole fly genome (about 14,000). Compare an optional "cassette" exon, which is either included or skipped: $n$ independent cassette exons give $2^n$ versions.

A **[[microRNA]]** is a small RNA, about 22 nucleotides long, that turns down the expression of other genes. It is cut from a hairpin-shaped precursor and loaded into a protein (Argonaute) that uses it as a guide. Bases 2–8 of the microRNA, its "seed", pair with matching sites, usually in the 3′ untranslated region of target mRNAs. In animals the pairing is usually partial, and the result is less translation and faster mRNA breakdown rather than a clean cut. One microRNA can tune hundreds of targets. The first microRNA was found in roundworms in 1993, work recognized by the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How a microRNA silences a gene
  accDescr: A microRNA gene is transcribed into a long RNA that folds into a hairpin. In the nucleus the enzyme Drosha cuts out a shorter hairpin, which is exported to the cytoplasm. There the enzyme Dicer cuts it into a double-stranded piece about 22 bases long. One strand is loaded into an Argonaute protein, forming the RISC complex. The microRNA's seed region pairs with a matching site, usually in the 3 prime untranslated region of a target mRNA. The result is less protein, because translation is blocked and the mRNA is broken down faster.
  G[microRNA gene] -- transcription --> P[Long RNA folds into a hairpin]
  P -- "Drosha cuts, hairpin exported" --> H[Short hairpin in cytoplasm]
  H -- "Dicer cuts" --> D[Double-stranded RNA, about 22 bases]
  D -- "one strand kept" --> R["RISC: microRNA + Argonaute"]
  R -- "seed pairs with 3' UTR" --> T[Target mRNA]
  T --> X["Less protein: translation blocked, mRNA decays"]
```

A mutation that destroys a target's seed match frees that mRNA from control, so its protein level rises. Synthetic small RNAs that use the same machinery (RNA interference) silence chosen genes in research, and several are approved drugs.

## Common mistakes

- Treating tryptophan like lactose. Lactose (as allolactose) inactivates its repressor; tryptophan *activates* its repressor as a corepressor.
- Thinking lactose alone gives full lac expression. CAP–cAMP is also needed, so glucose must be low.
