- Calling an operator mutation trans-acting. A DNA site affects only genes on its own molecule; only diffusible products (proteins, RNAs) act in trans.
- Assuming enhancers must sit just upstream of the gene. They can be far away, downstream or in introns, in either orientation.
- Thinking DNA methylation changes the base sequence. A methylated C still pairs with G; the sequence is the same.
- Mixing up the effects of acetylation and DNA methylation. Histone acetylation usually opens chromatin; DNA methylation at promoters usually silences.
- Thinking microRNAs are translated. They are noncoding RNAs that pair with mRNAs.

## Key points

- Inducible operons (lac) are turned on by an inducer that inactivates the repressor; repressible operons (trp) are turned off when a corepressor activates the repressor.
- CAP–cAMP is a positive control: the lac operon is fully on only with lactose present and glucose absent.
- Proteins act in trans and can affect both copies in a partial diploid; DNA sites such as operators act in cis.
- Eukaryotic genes are switched by combinations of activators at enhancers, which reach the promoter by DNA looping and Mediator.
- Histone acetylation opens chromatin; DNA methylation at CpG silences promoters and is copied after replication. Heritable expression states without sequence change are epigenetic.
- Alternative splicing multiplies the proteins one gene can make; microRNAs pair with sites in mRNA 3′ untranslated regions to reduce translation and speed mRNA decay.

lessons.title: Sequencing, genomics, and gene editing
lessons.body:
Lesson 25 gave DNA sequencing and CRISPR a paragraph each. This lesson opens both up. You will see how a sequencing machine actually reads bases, why a genome has to be read many times over, what the human genome turned out to contain, how sequences are compared, and how Cas9 finds and cuts one chosen site among billions. It ends with gene therapy and the ethical questions it raises, presented as the range of views people hold.

## Sanger sequencing: reading DNA by stopping it

The first practical method, published by Frederick Sanger in 1977, uses DNA polymerase's own rules against it. Polymerase adds each nucleotide to the 3′-OH group of the growing strand (lesson 22). A **[[dideoxynucleotide]]** (ddNTP) lacks that 3′-OH. Once one is added, nothing can be attached after it, and the strand stops.

A Sanger reaction holds the template, a primer, DNA polymerase, plenty of the normal nucleotides, and a small amount of all four ddNTPs, each tagged with a different colored fluorescent dye. Most of the time the polymerase adds a normal nucleotide and keeps going; now and then it adds a ddNTP and stops. Across millions of template copies, strands stop at every position, and each strand's last base is marked by its color. Capillary electrophoresis then sorts the strands by length, one base apart, and a detector reads the color of each length in turn. That is **[[Sanger sequencing]]**. It reads about 800–1,000 bases per reaction, very accurately, and is still used to check short stretches.

![Top: a template strand reading 3′-TGCAATC-5′ after a primer-binding region, with a primer bound and an arrow showing the polymerase adding bases 5′ to 3′. Middle: seven new strands, each starting at the primer and ending one base later than the last, each stopped by a colored terminator: A, then AC, ACG, ACGT, ACGTT, ACGTTA and ACGTTAG. Right: the terminators read in order of length, shortest first, spell A, C, G, T, T, A, G. Bottom: the new strand reads 5′-ACGTTAG-3′, the complement of the template.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1

A Sanger run with a 16-base primer gives fragments of these total lengths, with these terminal bases: 21 G, 18 T, 22 A, 19 C, 20 C, 23 T, 17 A, 24 G. What is the new strand's sequence, and what is the template?

- Sort by length: 17 A, 18 T, 19 C, 20 C, 21 G, 22 A, 23 T, 24 G. The 17-base fragment is the primer plus one base, so A is the first base added.
- The new strand, after the primer, reads 5′-ATCCGATG-3′.
- The template is its complement, antiparallel: 3′-TAGGCTAC-5′, which written 5′ to 3′ is 5′-CATCGGAT-3′.

## Next-generation sequencing and coverage

The Human Genome Project (1990–2003) relied on Sanger reads and cost about $3 billion. Today's **[[next-generation sequencing]]** gets its speed from parallel reading. The genome is broken into fragments a few hundred bases long; each fragment is copied into a tiny cluster on a glass slide, and hundreds of millions of clusters are read at once. In the most common method, each cycle adds one fluorescent nucleotide to every cluster, a camera records each cluster's color, and the dye and a temporary block are removed so the next base can be added. The result is billions of short reads (often 150 bases). Newer long-read methods read single molecules tens of thousands of bases long, for example by pulling DNA through a protein pore and measuring how each stretch changes an electric current. Long reads are slower per base but can span long repeated sequences that short reads can't place.

Reads come from random places, so some bases are covered many times and some not at all. The average number of reads covering a base is the **[[coverage]]** (or depth):

$$C = \frac{N \times L}{G}$$

where $N$ is the number of reads, $L$ the read length and $G$ the genome size. If reads land at random, the fraction of bases missed entirely is about $e^{-C}$. At $C = 1$ that is $e^{-1} \approx 37\%$ of the genome unread, so genomes are sequenced to around 30×, which also lets each base be checked many times and shows both alleles at heterozygous sites.

### Example 2

How many 150-base reads give 30× coverage of a 3.1-billion-base human genome? What fraction would be missed by chance?

- Rearrange: $N = \dfrac{C \times G}{L} = \dfrac{30 \times 3.1 \times 10^9}{150} = 6.2 \times 10^8$, about 620 million reads.
- Missed fraction $\approx e^{-30} \approx 9 \times 10^{-14}$: in practice, nothing is missed at random. Real gaps come from regions that are hard to sequence, such as long repeats.

## What genome projects found

A **[[genome]]** is an organism's complete set of DNA. The human genome holds about 3.1 billion base pairs per set of chromosomes; the last gaps were closed in 2022 by the Telomere-to-Telomere project (the Y chromosome followed in 2023), adding about 8% that earlier versions could not read. Some findings surprised biologists:

- Only about 1.5% of the genome codes for protein, in roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, about as many as a roundworm has. Much of the rest is regulatory DNA (enhancers, promoters), genes for noncoding RNAs such as microRNAs, and repeated sequences; about half is derived from transposable elements.
- Two unrelated people differ at about 1 base in 1,000. Most differences are **[[SNPs]]** (single-nucleotide polymorphisms): single positions where people carry different bases. Larger insertions, deletions and duplications add more variation.
- Sequencing is now used in medicine: to diagnose rare genetic diseases in sick newborns, to choose cancer treatments from a tumor's mutations, and to track virus variants during outbreaks.

## Comparing sequences

To compare two sequences, line them up in an alignment, placing a gap where one has an insertion the other lacks. The simplest score is percent identity: identical positions divided by aligned positions. Databases can be searched for sequences similar to a new one, and close similarity points to shared ancestry (homology) and often shared function.

### Example 3

A 20-base stretch of a gene in two species:

| Species | Sequence (codons separated) |
|---|---|
| 1 | ATG GCT AAG CTT GCA GTC GA |
| 2 | ATG GCA AAG CTT GCG GTC GA |

Positions 6 and 15 differ, so 18 of 20 bases match: 90% identity. Both differences are in the third base of a codon: GCT and GCA both code for Ala, as do GCA and GCG. The protein is unchanged. This pattern is common in real comparisons: silent third-position changes accumulate faster than changes that alter amino acids, because natural selection removes many of the harmful protein changes.

## CRISPR-Cas9: how the cut is aimed

In bacteria, CRISPR is an immune memory: stored snippets of viral DNA are transcribed into short RNAs that guide Cas proteins to cut matching viruses. For editing, scientists use Cas9 with a single **[[guide RNA]]** whose first 20 bases (the spacer) are chosen to match the target.

1. Cas9 slides along DNA checking for a **[[PAM]]** (protospacer adjacent motif). For the commonly used Cas9, the PAM is 5′-NGG-3′, where N is any base. Without a PAM, Cas9 moves on, which is also why the bacterium's own CRISPR array, which lacks PAMs, is never cut.
2. At a PAM, Cas9 unwinds the neighboring DNA. If the guide's spacer pairs with one strand, starting with the bases nearest the PAM, it forms an RNA–DNA hybrid.
3. With a full match, Cas9's two cutting domains each cut one strand, about 3 bases from the PAM, leaving a double-strand break.

![Cas9, drawn as a large oval, holds a stretch of DNA whose strands are pulled apart. The guide RNA's 20-base spacer pairs with the target DNA strand, and the rest of the guide RNA, the scaffold, loops inside Cas9. On the other strand, a PAM reading NGG sits just past the end of the matched region. A dashed line marks where both strands are cut, a few bases from the PAM.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The cell then repairs the break, and that repair is what creates the edit:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: What happens after Cas9 cuts DNA
  accDescr: Cas9 makes a double-strand break. The cell repairs it in one of two main ways. Nonhomologous end joining glues the ends back together, often adding or deleting a few bases. Such small insertions or deletions in a coding region usually cause a frameshift that knocks out the gene. If a repair template with matching ends is supplied, homology-directed repair can sometimes copy it, giving a precise edit such as a chosen base change or an inserted sequence. Homology-directed repair is less frequent and works mainly in dividing cells.
  C[Cas9 makes a double-strand break] --> N[Nonhomologous end joining]
  C --> H["Homology-directed repair (needs a supplied template)"]
  N --> I["Small insertions or deletions (indels)"]
  I --> K["Often a frameshift: gene knocked out"]
  H --> E["Precise edit: chosen base change or inserted sequence"]
  H -.- L[Less frequent; mainly in dividing cells]
```

### Example 4

Design a guide for this stretch, using only the strand shown:

5′-TTCAGACTCATGCTAGCTTACAGATGGATCCAGTTCA-3′

- Find a PAM. Scanning for any base followed by GG, the only one is TGG (bases 25–27).
- The target is the 20 bases just 5′ of the PAM: GACTCATGCTAGCTTACAGA.
- The guide's spacer has the same sequence, in RNA: 5′-GACUCAUGCUAGCUUACAGA-3′. It pairs with the opposite strand, as in the figure.
- Cas9 cuts 3 bases from the PAM, between …CTTAC and AGA.

Is a 20-base target unique? There are $4^{20} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{12}$ possible 20-base sequences, and a 3.1-billion-base genome offers about $6.2 \times 10^9$ positions on its two strands. A random genome would contain a given 20-mer about $6.2 \times 10^9 / 1.1 \times 10^{12} \approx 0.006$ times by chance, so a chosen target is usually unique. Real genomes are not random, though, and Cas9 tolerates some mismatches, especially far from the PAM, so guides are screened by computer for near-matches that could cause off-target cuts.

Newer tools avoid the double-strand break: base editors chemically convert one base to another, and prime editors write a short new sequence. A Cas9 with its cutting domains disabled can carry activators or repressors to a chosen promoter, switching genes on or off without changing the sequence.

## Gene therapy

**[[Gene therapy]]** treats disease by adding, repairing or silencing genes in a patient's cells. Genes are delivered by disabled viruses or by lipid nanoparticles, either into cells taken out of the body and returned (ex vivo) or directly into the body (in vivo). Early trials taught hard lessons: a volunteer died from an immune reaction to a viral vector in 1999, and in the early 2000s a vector that inserted itself near a cancer-related gene caused leukemia in some children. Safer vectors followed. Approved treatments now include a virus-delivered gene for an inherited form of blindness (2017) and one for spinal muscular atrophy (2019). In 2023 Casgevy became the first approved CRISPR therapy: patients' blood stem cells are edited to break an enhancer of *BCL11A*, a gene that switches off fetal hemoglobin after birth, so their red cells make enough fetal hemoglobin to make up for the faulty adult form. (Compare the enhancers in the previous honors lesson.)

## Ethics: several perspectives

These questions don't have one scientific answer; people weigh the same facts differently.

- *Somatic treatment* changes only the patient. Most people support it for serious disease, but list prices above $2 million raise questions of fairness and access, and long-term effects are still being followed.
- *Germline editing* would pass changes to future generations. In 2018 a researcher announced twins born from edited embryos; the work was condemned worldwide and he was imprisoned. Some argue germline editing could one day prevent serious inherited disease when no other option exists; others point to off-target edits, the impossibility of consent from future people, and a slide toward enhancement. An international summit in 2023 called heritable editing unacceptable at this time.
- *Disability perspectives* differ. Many families welcome cures; some disabled people, including some in the Deaf community, see certain conditions as differences rather than diseases and worry about who decides which traits to remove.
- *Genetic privacy.* Genome data can reveal information about relatives who never consented. In the US a 2008 law bans genetic discrimination in health insurance and employment, but not, for example, in life insurance.

## Common mistakes

- Saying a ddNTP stops synthesis because it lacks a base. It has a base; it lacks the 3′-OH needed for the next bond.
- Reading a Sanger result as the template. The colors spell the new strand; the template is its complement.
- Using the coverage formula backwards. Coverage rises with more or longer reads and falls with genome size.
- Forgetting the PAM. A perfect 20-base match is not cut without an adjacent NGG.
- Writing the guide as the complement of the target strand you chose. The guide matches the protospacer next to the PAM (with U for T) and pairs with the opposite strand.
- Thinking CRISPR itself makes the precise change. Cas9 only cuts; the cell's repair makes the edit.

## Key points

- Sanger sequencing: ddNTPs stop strands at every position; sorting by length and reading terminal colors gives the sequence.
- Next-generation sequencing reads billions of short fragments in parallel; coverage $C = NL/G$, and about 30× is used so that almost nothing is missed.
- The human genome: about 3.1 billion bp, about 20,000 protein-coding genes, about 1.5% coding; unrelated people differ at about 0.1% of bases, mostly SNPs.
- Alignments and percent identity compare sequences; silent third-position differences are the most common.
- Cas9 needs a PAM and a 20-base guide match, cuts both strands near the PAM, and relies on end joining (knockouts) or template repair (precise edits).
- Gene therapy can be ex vivo or in vivo; somatic and germline editing raise different ethical questions.

lessons.title: Evidence for evolution
lessons.body:
Module 6 ended with mutations: random changes in DNA that create new alleles. This module asks what happens to those alleles over many generations. **[[Evolution]]** is a change in the inherited traits of a population over generations. Over long spans of time, that change produces new species, and all living species trace back through branching lines to common ancestors, which Darwin called descent with modification.

In science, a theory is not a guess. It is a broad explanation supported by many independent lines of evidence, like the cell theory or the germ theory of disease. This lesson lays out the main lines of evidence for evolution and shows how biologists read them. The strength of the case is that the lines are independent: rocks, anatomy, embryos, DNA and geography each tell the same story.

## The fossil record

Fossils are remains or traces of past organisms, mostly preserved in sedimentary rock. Sediment settles in layers, so in undisturbed rock, deeper layers are older. Fossils therefore come in a time order, and that order is consistent worldwide: simple single-celled life in the oldest rocks, then simple animals, fish before amphibians, amphibians before reptiles, and so on. No one has ever found a rabbit in rocks 500 million years old.

The record also contains **[[transitional fossils]]**, which show a mix of features of an older group and a later one. *Archaeopteryx* (about 150 million years old) had feathers and wings like a bird, but teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like small dinosaurs. A series of fossil whales from about 50 to 40 million years ago shows four-legged land mammals gradually becoming fully aquatic, with nostrils moving up the head and hind legs shrinking.

### Example 1

By the late 1990s, fossils showed fish in rocks about 385 million years old and four-legged animals (tetrapods) in rocks about 365 million years old. If tetrapods evolved from fish, where should a researcher look for a fish–tetrapod transition?

Reason from the theory: the transition should be in rocks between those ages, roughly 375 million years old, and formed in shallow fresh water, where the earliest tetrapods lived. Neil Shubin and colleagues searched exposed rock of that age and type on Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada. In 2004 they found *Tiktaalik*: a fish with scales, fins and gills, but also a flat head, a neck, lungs and sturdy fin bones matching our upper arm, forearm and wrist. The point is not just that the fossil exists, but that evolution predicted *when* and *where* it would be.

## Dating rocks: radiometric dating

Layer order gives relative age. **[[Radiometric dating]]** gives actual ages in years, using radioactive isotopes that decay at a steady, known rate. The **[[half-life]]** is the time for half of a radioactive isotope's atoms to decay. After one half-life, $\tfrac12$ is left; after two, $\tfrac14$; after $h$ half-lives, $\left(\tfrac12\right)^h$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 5.2], "y": [0, 1.05], "xLabel": "half-lives", "yLabel": "fraction remaining", "functions": [{"f": "0.5^x"}], "points": [{"at": [1, 0.5], "label": "1/2"}, {"at": [2, 0.25], "label": "1/4"}, {"at": [3, 0.125], "label": "1/8"}, {"at": [4, 0.0625], "label": "1/16"}], "caption": "Radioactive decay: each half-life leaves half of what was there"}
```

Different isotopes suit different ages:

- Carbon-14 (half-life 5,730 years) dates once-living material such as bone, wood or shell, up to about 50,000 years. Living things take in carbon-14 while alive; after death the carbon-14 decays and is not replaced.
- Potassium-40 (half-life 1.25 billion years) and uranium isotopes date volcanic rock, millions to billions of years old. Fossils in sedimentary rock are dated by volcanic layers above and below them.

### Example 2

A bone contains $\tfrac18$ as much carbon-14 as living tissue. How old is it?

$\tfrac18 = \left(\tfrac12\right)^3$, so 3 half-lives have passed. Age $= 3 \times 5{,}730 = 17{,}190$ years.

### Example 3

A volcanic ash layer contains 25% of its original potassium-40. A fossil lies just below it. What can you say about the fossil's age?

25% is $\tfrac14 = \left(\tfrac12\right)^2$: two half-lives, $2 \times 1.25 = 2.5$ billion years. The fossil is below the ash, so it is at least that old. (Carbon-14 is useless here: after 2.5 billion years, essentially none would be left.)

## Comparative anatomy

**[[Homologous structures]]** are body parts that share an underlying structure because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even if they now do different jobs. The forelimbs of a human (grasping), a cat (walking), a whale (swimming) and a bat (flying) all have one upper-arm bone, two forearm bones, a group of wrist bones and five sets of finger bones. An engineer designing each limb from scratch would not use the same parts list; shared ancestry explains it.

The figure colors the matching bones: the upper-arm bone (humerus), the two forearm bones (radius and ulna), the wrist bones (carpals), and the palm and finger bones (metacarpals and phalanges). Sizes and shapes differ enormously, from the bat's long, thin fingers to the whale's short, flat forearm, but the parts and their order from shoulder to fingertip are the same.

![The forelimbs of a human, a cat, a whale and a bat drawn side by side, with the upper-arm bone in blue, the two forearm bones in green, the wrist bones in yellow and the palm and finger bones in pink. The whale's bones are short and enclosed in a flipper; the bat's finger bones are very long and support a wing membrane.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**[[Analogous structures]]** do similar jobs but are built differently and evolved separately. Bird wings and insect wings both fly, but a bird wing is a modified forelimb with bones and feathers, while an insect wing is a thin outgrowth of the body wall. Similar environments can shape unrelated lineages in similar ways, a pattern called convergent evolution. Analogous structures are evidence for natural selection, but not of close relationship.

**[[Vestigial structures]]** are reduced remnants of parts that were functional in ancestors. Some whales and snakes have tiny hip bones not attached to any leg. Humans have a tailbone and small muscles that once moved the ears. "Vestigial" doesn't always mean useless (a tailbone anchors muscles); it means much reduced from its ancestral role.

Embryos show homology too. Early vertebrate embryos, from fish to humans, all have a tail and a series of pouches in the throat region. In fish these pouches become gill structures; in humans they become parts of the ear, throat and glands.

## Molecular evidence

Every living thing uses DNA, the same genetic code (lesson 23) and the same 20 amino acids. That shared machinery is hard to explain except by common descent. Beyond that, the number of differences in a gene or protein between two species is a measure of how long ago they shared an ancestor: the longer two lines have been separate, the more mutations each has collected.

### Example 4

Cytochrome c is a protein of about 104 amino acids used in cellular respiration by nearly all eukaryotes. Approximate numbers of amino acids that differ from the human version:

| Species | Differences from human |
|---|---|
| Chimpanzee | 0 |
| Rhesus monkey | 1 |
| Chicken | 13 |
| Tuna | 21 |
| Baker's yeast | about 44 |

Which species is most distantly related to humans, and which conclusion do the data support?

Yeast, with the most differences, shares the most distant common ancestor with humans. The ranking (primates, then birds, then fish, then fungi) matches the order of relatedness worked out independently from anatomy and fossils. Two separate kinds of evidence agree.

DNA also holds "molecular fossils." Humans, other apes and monkeys carry the same broken copy of a gene for making vitamin C, with some of the same disabling mutations, at the same spot in the genome. The simplest explanation is that the gene broke once in a common ancestor.

## Biogeography

**[[Biogeography]]** is the study of where species live. Its patterns make sense only with history. Species on islands resemble species on the nearest mainland, not species living in similar climates far away: Galápagos finches and mockingbirds resemble South American birds. Australia, isolated for tens of millions of years, has a great variety of marsupials filling roles that placental mammals fill on other continents. Related fossils on now-separate continents fit the slow movement of the continents over time.

## Evolution observed

Evolution is also seen directly. Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics within years. In a long-term experiment started by Richard Lenski in 1988, populations of *E. coli* have been followed for more than 75,000 generations; one population evolved the ability to use citrate as food, something normal *E. coli* cannot do in oxygen. The next lesson explains the mechanism behind such changes.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking "theory" means a hunch. A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation supported by large bodies of evidence.
- Saying humans evolved from chimpanzees. Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 8 million years ago (estimates vary); both lines have evolved since.
- Calling bird and insect wings homologous. They are analogous: same function, different structure and origin.
- Using carbon-14 to date dinosaurs. Dinosaur fossils are tens of millions of years old, far beyond carbon-14's range; their ages come from isotopes in nearby volcanic rock.
- Thinking that after two half-lives nothing is left. Each half-life removes half of what remains: $\tfrac14$ is left after two.

## Key points

- Evolution is change in a population's inherited traits over generations; all life shares common ancestry.
- Fossils appear in a consistent order; transitional fossils such as *Tiktaalik* and *Archaeopteryx* link groups, and some were found by prediction.
- Radiometric dating gives absolute ages: after $h$ half-lives, $\left(\tfrac12\right)^h$ of the isotope remains.
- Homologous structures show shared ancestry; analogous structures show similar selection on unrelated groups; vestigial structures are reduced remnants.
- Molecular similarities and differences, embryos and biogeography independently support the same tree of relationships.

lessons.title: Natural selection and adaptation
lessons.body:
The last lesson showed that evolution happened: life has changed over time and shares common ancestors. This lesson explains the main mechanism that produces the fit between organisms and their surroundings, natural selection. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the idea independently and presented it together in 1858; Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* followed in 1859. Their argument is short enough to check step by step.

## The argument

Natural selection follows from four observations about any population:

1. *Variation.* Individuals differ in their traits: size, color, beak shape, resistance to disease.
2. *Inheritance.* Some of that variation is heritable, passed from parents to offspring through genes.
3. *Overproduction.* Populations produce more offspring than the environment can support. A single cod can release millions of eggs; most die young.
4. *Differential success.* Which individuals survive and reproduce is not entirely random. Individuals whose traits suit the environment better tend to leave more offspring.

Put these together and the conclusion follows: heritable traits that help survival and reproduction become more common in the next generation, and over many generations the population changes. That process is **[[natural selection]]**. The diagram shows how the pieces of the argument fit together.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The logic of natural selection
  accDescr: Two observations, heritable variation in a trait and more offspring than the environment can support, lead together to the conclusion that individuals whose traits suit the environment leave more offspring. As a result, the helpful alleles are more common in the next generation, and repeating this over many generations produces adaptation.
  A["Heritable variation in a trait"] --> C["Individuals with helpful traits leave more offspring"]
  B["More offspring than the environment can support"] --> C
  C --> D["Helpful alleles are more common in the next generation"]
  D --> E["Repeated over many generations: adaptation"]
```

Biologists measure success with **[[fitness]]**: an individual's reproductive success, the number of offspring it contributes to the next generation, compared with others in the population. Fitness is not strength or speed. A strong animal that leaves no offspring has zero fitness; a small one that leaves many has high fitness.

An **[[adaptation]]** is a heritable trait that increases fitness in a particular environment: the thick fur of an arctic fox, the camouflage of a stick insect, the deep roots of a desert shrub. An adaptation is always relative to an environment. Thick fur is a burden in the tropics.

## Variation comes before selection

A common misunderstanding is that the environment *causes* the helpful variation: that bacteria become resistant because they need to. In 1952 Joshua and Esther Lederberg tested this with a clever trick called replica plating.

### Example 1

The Lederbergs grew many bacterial colonies on a dish with no antibiotic. They pressed a velvet pad onto it, picking up a few cells from every colony in the same arrangement, and pressed the pad onto a dish containing the antibiotic. A few colonies grew there, all from cells at the same positions, say positions 7 and 19. Then they went back to the original dish, which had never touched the antibiotic, and tested colonies 7 and 19. Predict: are they resistant?

![Replica plating in four steps. A master plate without antibiotic has many colonies. A velvet pad on a block is pressed onto it and then onto an antibiotic plate, where only two colonies grow. Those two positions are circled on both plates, and an arrow leads back to test the matching colonies on the master plate.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If resistance arose in response to the antibiotic, colonies on the original dish would not be resistant, because they were never exposed. If resistant mutants already existed by chance, colonies 7 and 19 on the original dish would be resistant. The Lederbergs found the second result: cells from those colonies grew on antibiotic even though they had never met it. Conclusion: the mutations arose randomly, before exposure. The antibiotic did not create resistance; it selected the cells that already had it.

Mutation is random with respect to need. Selection is not random: it sorts the variation that mutation and sexual reproduction supply.

## Natural selection measured: Darwin's finches

Peter and Rosemary Grant have studied the finches of Daphne Major, a tiny Galápagos island, since 1973, catching, measuring and banding nearly every bird. In 1977 a severe drought struck. The medium ground finch eats seeds, and as small soft seeds ran out, the remaining food was mostly large, hard seeds that only birds with deep, strong beaks could crack. The population crashed by more than 80 percent. Survivors had deeper beaks on average than the birds that died, and because beak depth is heritable, the next generation's beaks were measurably deeper, by roughly 4 percent.

Later, after very wet years in the early 1980s, small seeds became plentiful and selection favored smaller beaks. Selection tracks the environment, so its direction can reverse.

### Example 2

A moth population has 600 light moths and 400 dark moths, so it is 40% dark. On tree bark darkened by soot, birds see light moths more easily: 40% of light moths survive to reproduce, but 70% of dark moths do. What percent of the survivors are dark?

- Light survivors: $600 \times 0.40 = 240$.
- Dark survivors: $400 \times 0.70 = 280$.
- Dark fraction: $\dfrac{280}{240 + 280} = \dfrac{280}{520} \approx 0.538$, or 53.8%.

One generation of selection moved the population from 40% dark to about 54% dark among the parents of the next generation. This is close to what happened to the peppered moth in England: in polluted industrial areas the dark form rose from rare in the 1840s to about 98% around Manchester by the late 1800s, and it fell again after clean-air laws in the 1950s let the bark lighten.

## Three patterns of selection

For a trait with many values, like beak depth or body size, selection can change the distribution in three ways. In each figure, the solid curve is the population before selection and the dashed curve after.

**[[Directional selection]]** favors one extreme, so the average shifts. Drought finches with deeper beaks are an example.

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [0, 1.2], "xLabel": "trait value", "yLabel": "number of individuals", "functions": [{"f": "exp(-(x-4.5)^2/2)", "label": "before"}, {"f": "exp(-(x-6)^2/2)", "dashed": true, "label": "after"}], "caption": "Directional selection: the average moves toward one extreme"}
```

**[[Stabilizing selection]]** favors the average and removes both extremes, so variation shrinks. Human birth weight was a classic case: very small and very large babies historically had lower survival. (Modern medicine has weakened this selection.)

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [0, 1.6], "xLabel": "trait value", "yLabel": "number of individuals", "functions": [{"f": "exp(-(x-5)^2/2)", "label": "before"}, {"f": "1.5*exp(-(x-5)^2/0.9)", "dashed": true, "label": "after"}], "caption": "Stabilizing selection: the middle is favored and the spread narrows"}
```

**[[Disruptive selection]]** favors both extremes over the middle. In an African finch, the black-bellied seedcracker, birds with small bills handle soft seeds well and birds with large bills crack hard seeds, while intermediate bills do neither well. Over time the population can split into two peaks.

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [0, 1.2], "xLabel": "trait value", "yLabel": "number of individuals", "functions": [{"f": "exp(-(x-5)^2/2)", "label": "before"}, {"f": "0.8*(exp(-(x-3)^2/1.2) + exp(-(x-7)^2/1.2))", "dashed": true, "label": "after"}], "caption": "Disruptive selection: both extremes are favored and the middle declines"}
```

A related process, sexual selection, favors traits that improve mating success rather than survival, such as a peacock's tail. The tail may attract predators, but if it attracts more mates, its genes spread.

## Artificial selection

Darwin opened the *Origin* with breeders, not wild animals. In **[[artificial selection]]**, people choose which individuals breed, based on traits they want. From one species of wild cabbage (*Brassica oleracea*, a relative of mustard), farmers have bred cabbage (selected for the end bud), broccoli (flower clusters), kale (leaves), kohlrabi (stem) and Brussels sprouts (side buds). From ancient wolves came every breed of dog. If people can change a species this much in a few thousand years, natural selection acting over millions of years can do far more. The difference is who does the choosing: in nature, the environment "chooses" through survival and reproduction.

## Selection in medicine

When an antibiotic is used, it kills susceptible bacteria; any resistant cells survive and multiply. Overuse and misuse, such as taking antibiotics for viral colds, speed this up. Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA) and drug-resistant tuberculosis are results of natural selection happening now. The same logic explains insects resistant to pesticides and weeds resistant to herbicides.

## What selection cannot do

- It acts on individuals, but populations evolve. A single moth doesn't change color; the proportion of dark moths in the population changes.
- It has no foresight. Selection favors what works now, not what might help later.
- It works only with existing variation. If no individual has a helpful allele, selection cannot produce it.
- Traits acquired during life are not inherited. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed that a giraffe stretching its neck passed a longer neck to its young. A gym-built muscle isn't coded in your DNA, so it isn't passed on.
- Adaptations are compromises. A bigger beak cracks harder seeds but costs more to grow.

## Common mistakes

- Defining fitness as physical strength. Fitness is reproductive success relative to others.
- Saying organisms evolve because they need to. Mutations arise randomly; selection keeps the ones that happen to help.
- Treating "survival of the fittest" as survival alone. An organism that survives but doesn't reproduce has no effect on the next generation.
- Mixing up stabilizing and directional selection. Stabilizing keeps the average and narrows the spread; directional moves the average.
- Thinking individuals evolve. Individuals are selected; populations evolve.

## Key points

- Natural selection follows from heritable variation, overproduction and differential reproductive success.
- Fitness is relative reproductive success; an adaptation is a heritable trait that raises fitness in a given environment.
- Variation arises randomly, before selection (Lederberg replica plating); selection sorts it.
- The Grant finches and peppered moths show selection measured in wild populations, and its direction can reverse.
- Directional selection shifts the average, stabilizing selection favors the average, disruptive selection favors both extremes.
- Artificial selection by breeders and antibiotic resistance in bacteria show the same process.

lessons.title: Population genetics and Hardy-Weinberg
lessons.body:
In the last lesson, selection changed the share of dark moths and deep-beaked finches. Underneath every such change is a change in the alleles carried by the population. Population genetics puts numbers on this: it measures how common each allele is, predicts what should happen if nothing is changing, and uses the gap between prediction and data to detect evolution and work out its cause. It joins Mendel's genetics (module 5) to Darwin's natural selection.

## The gene pool and allele frequencies

A population's **[[gene pool]]** is all the alleles of all its genes, across every individual. For one gene with two alleles, $A$ and $a$, each diploid individual carries two copies, so a population of $N$ individuals has $2N$ copies of the gene.

The **[[allele frequency]]** of an allele is the fraction of all gene copies that are that allele. By convention, $p$ is the frequency of $A$ and $q$ the frequency of $a$. Since every copy is one or the other,

$$p + q = 1.$$

In these terms, evolution in the narrow sense (sometimes called microevolution) is a change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next.

### Example 1

A population of 1,000 plants has 500 $AA$, 200 $Aa$ and 300 $aa$ individuals. Find $p$ and $q$.

- Total gene copies: $2 \times 1{,}000 = 2{,}000$.
- Copies of $A$: each $AA$ plant has two, each $Aa$ has one: $2(500) + 200 = 1{,}200$.
- $p = \dfrac{1{,}200}{2{,}000} = 0.6$, so $q = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4$.

Check by counting $a$ directly: $200 + 2(300) = 800$, and $800 / 2{,}000 = 0.4$.

## The Hardy-Weinberg principle

In 1908 the mathematician G. H. Hardy and the physician Wilhelm Weinberg independently answered a question people were asking about Mendel's laws: won't dominant alleles automatically take over a population? They showed the answer is no.

Picture gametes as drawn at random from the gene pool. An egg carries $A$ with probability $p$ and $a$ with probability $q$; so does a sperm. By the product rule:

| | Sperm $A$ ($p$) | Sperm $a$ ($q$) |
|---|---|---|
| Egg $A$ ($p$) | $AA$: $p^2$ | $Aa$: $pq$ |
| Egg $a$ ($q$) | $Aa$: $pq$ | $aa$: $q^2$ |

So the next generation's genotype frequencies are

$$p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1,$$

with $p^2$ for $AA$, $2pq$ for $Aa$ (two ways to get it) and $q^2$ for $aa$. Count the alleles in that generation and you get back $p$ and $q$ exactly. Allele frequencies stay put, generation after generation. A population in this steady state is in **[[Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium]]**.

```plot
{"x": [0, 1], "y": [0, 1], "xLabel": "q (frequency of allele a)", "yLabel": "genotype frequency", "functions": [{"f": "(1-x)^2", "label": "AA (p²)"}, {"f": "2*x*(1-x)", "label": "Aa (2pq)", "dashed": true}, {"f": "x^2", "label": "aa (q²)"}], "caption": "Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies. When an allele is rare, most copies of it are in heterozygotes."}
```

Equilibrium holds only under five conditions:

1. no mutation;
2. no migration in or out (no gene flow);
3. a very large population (no genetic drift);
4. random mating;
5. no natural selection (all genotypes survive and reproduce equally).

Real populations never meet all five perfectly, and that is the point. Hardy-Weinberg is a null model, like a control group: it says what happens if nothing is causing evolution. When real data differ from it, something on the list is happening. The diagram shows the reasoning, and Example 3 below works through it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Using Hardy-Weinberg as a null model
  accDescr: Count the genotypes in a sample. Calculate the allele frequencies p and q. Calculate the expected counts p squared times N, 2pq times N and q squared times N. Compare the observed counts with the expected ones. If they are close, there is no evidence of evolution at this gene. If they are far apart, something is acting on the gene: mutation, gene flow, drift, nonrandom mating or selection.
  A["Count genotypes in a sample"] --> B["Calculate p and q"]
  B --> C["Expected counts: p²N, 2pqN, q²N"]
  C --> D["Compare observed with expected counts"]
  D -- close --> E["No evidence of evolution at this gene"]
  D -- far apart --> F["Something is acting: mutation, gene flow, drift, nonrandom mating or selection"]
```

### Example 2

Cystic fibrosis is a recessive disorder. Among people of Northern European ancestry, about 1 in 2,500 babies is born with it. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what fraction of people are carriers?

- Affected people are $aa$, so $q^2 = \dfrac{1}{2{,}500} = 0.0004$.
- $q = \sqrt{0.0004} = 0.02$, and $p = 1 - 0.02 = 0.98$.
- Carriers are $Aa$: $2pq = 2(0.98)(0.02) = 0.0392$, about 4%, or roughly 1 person in 25.

Notice how much more common carriers (about 1 in 25) are than affected people (1 in 2,500). For a rare recessive allele, almost all copies hide in heterozygotes, which is why selection removes harmful recessive alleles so slowly.

Always start from $q^2$, the frequency of the recessive phenotype, because homozygous recessive individuals are the only genotype you can identify by appearance. Dominant-phenotype individuals could be $AA$ or $Aa$.

### Example 3

Is the plant population in Example 1 in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

With $p = 0.6$ and $q = 0.4$, the expected genotype counts out of 1,000 are:

| Genotype | Expected | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| $AA$ | $0.36 \times 1{,}000 = 360$ | 500 |
| $Aa$ | $0.48 \times 1{,}000 = 480$ | 200 |
| $aa$ | $0.16 \times 1{,}000 = 160$ | 300 |

There are far too few heterozygotes and too many of both homozygotes. The population is not in equilibrium. A shortage of heterozygotes is the signature of nonrandom mating, such as self-pollination or mating with relatives, or of a population split into separate groups. (A chi-square test, from lesson 21, can check whether a difference this size could be chance; here $\chi^2$ is over 300, far above the critical value.)

## Mechanisms of evolution

Each broken condition is a way allele frequencies change.

*Mutation* creates new alleles. It is the ultimate source of variation, but any one gene mutates so rarely that mutation alone changes frequencies very slowly.

**[[Gene flow]]** is the movement of alleles between populations when individuals or gametes (such as pollen) migrate. It makes populations more alike and can bring in new alleles.

**[[Genetic drift]]** is random change in allele frequencies from chance events in which individuals happen to reproduce. Flip a coin 10 times and you may easily get 7 heads; flip it 10,000 times and you will be very close to half. In the same way, drift is weak in large populations and strong in small ones, and it can make an allele disappear or become the only one, regardless of whether it is helpful. Two situations make drift especially strong:

- The **[[bottleneck effect]]**: a disaster or overhunting shrinks a population to a few survivors, whose alleles are a random, reduced sample. Northern elephant seals were hunted down to perhaps a few dozen animals by the 1890s. They now number more than 200,000, but have very little genetic variation.
- The **[[founder effect]]**: a few individuals start a new, isolated population, carrying only some of the original alleles. Among the Old Order Amish of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, descended from a small group of founders, a rare recessive form of dwarfism with extra fingers (Ellis–van Creveld syndrome) is far more common than in the general population.

![Two rows of colored marbles, each color an allele. Top row, bottleneck effect: an original population with four colors in about equal numbers passes through a narrow bottle neck as four survivors, three blue and one green, and the recovered population has only blue and green. Bottom row, founder effect: a mainland population with four colors sends four founders to an island, and the island population that grows from them is mostly yellow and red, with a few blue and no green.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In both cases the survivors or founders are a small random sample, so some alleles are lost and others become much more common, by chance alone.

*Nonrandom mating* changes genotype frequencies. Mating with relatives raises homozygotes; mate choice (sexual selection) can also change allele frequencies.

*Natural selection* changes frequencies because genotypes differ in survival and reproduction. Of all five, only selection consistently makes populations better adapted. Drift, gene flow and mutation change populations without regard to fitness.

## Common mistakes

- Taking the frequency of the recessive phenotype as $q$. That frequency is $q^2$; take the square root.
- Thinking dominant alleles are always common. Dominance describes how alleles show up in a heterozygote, not how common they are. The allele for extra fingers in polydactyly is dominant but rare.
- Forgetting the 2 in $2pq$. Heterozygotes arise two ways (egg $A$ with sperm $a$, or egg $a$ with sperm $A$).
- Mixing up $p + q = 1$ (alleles) and $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$ (genotypes).
- Thinking drift is a kind of selection. Drift is random; selection is not.
- Counting individuals instead of gene copies. Each diploid individual carries two copies.

## Key points

- Allele frequencies: $p + q = 1$; count gene copies, two per diploid individual.
- Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: genotype frequencies $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$, steady from generation to generation if there is no mutation, no gene flow, no drift, random mating and no selection.
- To use it, start from the recessive phenotype: $q = \sqrt{\text{frequency of } aa}$; carriers are $2pq$.
- Departures from Hardy-Weinberg show evolution or nonrandom mating at work.
- Mechanisms of evolution: mutation, gene flow, genetic drift (bottleneck and founder effects), nonrandom mating and natural selection; only selection reliably produces adaptation.

lessons.title: Speciation and phylogenetic trees
lessons.body:
The last two lessons explained how allele frequencies change within a population. But evolution has also produced millions of separate species. This lesson asks how one species becomes two, and how biologists draw the resulting family tree of life from evidence.

## What is a species?

The most widely used definition is the biological species concept, proposed by Ernst Mayr in 1942: a species is a group of populations whose members can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring, and that cannot do so with other groups. Horses and donkeys can mate, but their offspring, mules, are almost always sterile, so horses and donkeys are separate species.

The definition has limits. It can't be applied to organisms that reproduce asexually, like bacteria, or to fossils, whose breeding can't be observed. For those, biologists group organisms by shared physical features or DNA sequences. All definitions agree on the central idea: a species is a separate branch of the tree of life, evolving independently of other branches.

**[[Speciation]]** is the process by which one species splits into two or more. The key event is the evolution of reproductive isolation.

## Reproductive isolation

**[[Reproductive isolation]]** is anything that prevents members of two groups from interbreeding or from producing fertile offspring. Once gene flow between two groups stops, mutation, selection and drift act on each separately, and they drift further apart. The barriers fall into two families, sorted by whether they act before or after an egg is fertilized:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Kinds of reproductive isolation
  accDescr: Reproductive isolation splits into prezygotic barriers, which act before fertilization, and postzygotic barriers, which act after it. Prezygotic barriers are habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical and gametic isolation. Postzygotic barriers are hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility and hybrid breakdown.
  A["Reproductive isolation"] --> B["Prezygotic: before fertilization"]
  A --> C["Postzygotic: after fertilization"]
  B --> B1["Habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical and gametic isolation"]
  C --> C1["Hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility and hybrid breakdown"]
```

Barriers that act before fertilization (prezygotic barriers):

- *Habitat isolation:* the groups live in different places within the same area, for example one in water, one on land.
- *Temporal isolation:* they breed at different times of day or year. Where the ranges of the eastern and western spotted skunks meet, in the central United States, the eastern species mates in late winter and the western one in late summer.
- *Behavioral isolation:* courtship signals don't match. Many firefly species differ in their flash patterns, and females answer only their own species' pattern; many birds respond only to their own species' song.
- *Mechanical isolation:* reproductive structures don't fit, as in many insects and in flowers adapted to different pollinators.
- *Gametic isolation:* sperm and egg don't fuse. Sea urchins release gametes into open water, but proteins on the egg surface bind only sperm of the same species.

Barriers that act after fertilization (postzygotic barriers):

- *Hybrid inviability:* hybrid embryos fail to develop or die young.
- *Hybrid sterility:* hybrids survive but can't reproduce. A horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey 62; a mule gets 63, and its chromosomes can't pair properly in meiosis (module 4), so it makes almost no working gametes.
- *Hybrid breakdown:* first-generation hybrids are fertile, but their offspring are weak or sterile.

### Example 1

Two populations of frogs live in the same pond. Population X calls and mates in March; population Y in May. In the lab, if eggs and sperm are combined, hybrid tadpoles develop normally and grow into fertile adults. Are they separate species, and what isolates them?

In nature, they never interbreed because they breed at different times: temporal isolation, a prezygotic barrier. Under the biological species concept they count as separate species, because they don't interbreed *in nature*. The lab result shows that no postzygotic barrier has evolved yet, a sign that the split is recent.

## How new species form

**[[Allopatric speciation]]** ("other homeland") begins when a population is split by a geographic barrier: a new mountain range, a river changing course, a rising sea, or a few individuals reaching an island. Gene flow stops. Each part then evolves on its own, through different mutations, different selection pressures and drift. If the parts later meet again, they may no longer be able to interbreed.

A clear natural test comes from the Isthmus of Panama. When the land bridge between North and South America closed about 3 million years ago, it split marine populations into a Caribbean group and a Pacific group. Snapping shrimp now come in matched pairs of species, one on each side, each pair more similar to each other than to any other species. In the lab, males and females from opposite sides of the isthmus rarely mate successfully.

Speciation can also happen without a geographic barrier, called sympatric speciation ("same homeland"):

- *Polyploidy.* An error in cell division can double a plant's chromosome number. A plant with four sets of chromosomes cannot produce fertile offspring with its two-set parents, so a new species can arise in one generation. Many crops, including wheat, cotton and potatoes, are polyploid.
- *Shifts in habitat or food.* In North America, some apple maggot flies began laying eggs on apples (introduced by European settlers) instead of native hawthorns. Flies mate on their host fruit, and apples ripen earlier than hawthorns, so the two groups are becoming isolated within the same area.

When one ancestral species gives rise to many species, each adapted to a different way of life, the result is called an adaptive radiation. The Galápagos finches, about 15 to 18 species descended from one ancestor that arrived roughly 2 million years ago, are a classic example, with beaks suited to seeds, insects, cactus or even blood.

## Phylogenetic trees

A **[[phylogenetic tree]]** is a diagram of the evolutionary relationships among organisms: a hypothesis about who descended from whom, built from evidence such as anatomy and DNA. To read one:

- The tips are present-day (or fossil) groups.
- Each branch point (node) stands for a common ancestor, and the branches above it are its descendants.
- The root, at the base, is the common ancestor of everything on the tree.
- Relatedness is measured by how recently two groups share a common ancestor, not by how close they sit on the page. Branches can be rotated around a node like a mobile without changing the tree.

![A tree of five species with its parts labeled: the root at the base, the branches as lines through time, the nodes as circles where lines split, and the tips at the species names. A shaded box around species C, D and E and their common ancestor is labeled as a clade.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the figure, species D and E are each other's closest relatives; C is equally related to D and E; and A and B form their own clade.

A **[[clade]]** is an ancestor and all of its descendants: one complete branch. Biologists build trees from shared derived characters, traits that arose in a common ancestor and were passed on to its descendants (fur in mammals, for example). A descendant can later lose such a trait, as snakes lost their legs, which is one reason trees are built from many characters, and today mostly from DNA. Traits shared with distant groups, like a backbone among vertebrates, don't help sort the vertebrates.

### Example 2

Use the character table to build a tree for six vertebrates. (1 = present, 0 = absent.) The lamprey, which has none of the traits, is the outgroup.

| | Jaws | Bony skeleton | Four limbs | Amniotic egg | Hair |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lamprey | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Shark | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Trout | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Frog | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Lizard | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| Human | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

Group by shared traits. Every animal but the lamprey has jaws, so the lamprey branches off first. Among the jawed animals, all but the shark have a bony skeleton, so the shark branches next. Then the trout (no limbs), then the frog (no amniotic egg), leaving lizard and human together. Each trait marks the branch where it first appeared:

```shape
{"width": 520, "segments": [{"from": [5, 0], "to": [5, 1]}, {"from": [5, 0], "to": [6, 0]}, {"from": [5, 1], "to": [6, 1]}, {"from": [4, 0.5], "to": [4, 2]}, {"from": [4, 2], "to": [6, 2]}, {"from": [4, 0.5], "to": [5, 0.5]}, {"from": [3, 1.25], "to": [3, 3]}, {"from": [3, 3], "to": [6, 3]}, {"from": [3, 1.25], "to": [4, 1.25]}, {"from": [2, 2.12], "to": [2, 4]}, {"from": [2, 4], "to": [6, 4]}, {"from": [2, 2.12], "to": [3, 2.12]}, {"from": [1, 3.06], "to": [1, 5]}, {"from": [1, 5], "to": [6, 5]}, {"from": [1, 3.06], "to": [2, 3.06]}, {"from": [0, 4.03], "to": [1, 4.03]}], "labels": [{"at": [6.9, 5], "text": "Lamprey"}, {"at": [6.9, 4], "text": "Shark"}, {"at": [6.9, 3], "text": "Trout"}, {"at": [6.9, 2], "text": "Frog"}, {"at": [6.9, 1], "text": "Lizard"}, {"at": [6.9, 0], "text": "Human"}, {"at": [3.5, 1.55], "text": "limbs"}, {"at": [2.5, 2.42], "text": "bone"}, {"at": [1.5, 3.36], "text": "jaws"}, {"at": [4.5, 0.8], "text": "amniotic egg"}, {"at": [5.5, 0.3], "text": "hair"}], "caption": "Tree built from the character table. Each label marks the branch where that trait arose."}
```

Each nested group is a clade: lizard + human (amniotes), frog + lizard + human (four-limbed animals), and so on.

### Example 3

On that tree, is the lizard more closely related to the frog or to the human?

Find the most recent common ancestor of each pair. Lizard and human share the node at the far right; lizard and frog share only the node before it, further back in time. So the lizard is more closely related to the human, even though lizards and frogs both depend on outside heat and look more alike to us. Looks can mislead; shared ancestry is what counts. This is also why biologists say birds belong in the reptile clade: DNA and fossils show that crocodiles are more closely related to birds than to lizards.

## The tree of all life

The same method scales up to every living thing. In the 1970s Carl Woese compared ribosomal RNA, a molecule every cell carries, and found that cells without a nucleus fall into two deeply separate groups. That work gave the three domains this course uses: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya (the eukaryotes: protists, fungi, plants and animals). All three trace back to one common ancestor of all living cells, at the root of the tree.

Exactly where eukaryotes attach to that tree is still being worked out, and the evidence has shifted. Since 2015, genomes of the Asgard archaea, first found in deep-sea sediment, have turned out to carry many genes once thought to exist only in eukaryotes. Most recent analyses place eukaryotes on a branch that grows out of the archaea, closest to the Asgard group: the first eukaryote seems to have formed when an archaeal cell took in a bacterium that became the mitochondrion (lesson 30). On that view the tree has two primary branches, Bacteria and Archaea, with eukaryotes nested inside the archaeal one. Biologists still use the three domains to sort living things because eukaryotes are so distinctive, and lesson 31 does the same. Either way, a tree is a hypothesis that is revised as evidence comes in.

## Common mistakes

- Reading relatedness from left-to-right order of the tips. Look for the most recent shared node.
- Thinking a tip is the ancestor of the tip next to it. Tips are the groups being compared (usually living ones); ancestors sit at the nodes.
- Thinking a group that branched off early is "less evolved." The lamprey's line has been evolving for exactly as long as ours.
- Calling any two populations that can make a hybrid one species. The test is fertile offspring in nature.
- Thinking speciation always needs a physical barrier. Polyploidy and habitat shifts can split populations that live together.

## Key points

- Biological species concept: populations that interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring.
- Speciation requires reproductive isolation: prezygotic barriers (habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical, gametic) and postzygotic barriers (hybrid inviability, sterility, breakdown).
- Allopatric speciation follows geographic separation; sympatric speciation happens without it, often by polyploidy in plants.
- Phylogenetic trees show common ancestry; relatedness is judged by the most recent common ancestor.
- A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants, identified by shared derived characters.
- All life falls into three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya); current evidence suggests eukaryotes arose from within the archaea.

lessons.title: The history of life on Earth
lessons.body:
The last lesson showed how species split and how trees record those splits. This lesson zooms out to the whole tree over the whole of Earth's history: when life began, how its major groups appeared, and how mass extinctions repeatedly reset the board. The challenge is the scale of time. Human history is a few thousand years; the history of life is billions.

## Deep time and the geologic time scale

Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago, a date measured by radiometric dating (lesson 26) of meteorites and the oldest Earth and Moon rocks. Geologists divide that span into the **[[geologic time scale]]**, a set of named intervals. The largest are eons, divided into eras, which are divided into periods. Many boundaries were drawn in the 1800s, before anyone could date rocks, at places where the fossils change sharply, often because of a mass extinction. Radiometric dating later put numbers on them.

| Eon or era | Time (million years ago) | Highlights |
|---|---|---|
| Hadean eon | 4,540–4,000 | Earth forms; no rock record of life |
| Archean eon | 4,000–2,500 | First prokaryotes; stromatolites |
| Proterozoic eon | 2,500–539 | Oxygen builds up; first eukaryotes; first multicellular life |
| Paleozoic era | 539–252 | Cambrian explosion; fish; plants and animals move onto land |
| Mesozoic era | 252–66 | Age of reptiles: dinosaurs; first mammals, birds and flowering plants |
| Cenozoic era | 66–now | Age of mammals; humans |

The Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic together form the Phanerozoic eon ("visible life"), the time of abundant animal fossils. Everything before it is informally called the Precambrian, nearly 90% of Earth's history. The timeline below draws the eons to scale, then zooms in on the Phanerozoic.

![A timeline bar of Earth's 4,540 million years, split into the Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic eons, with the first fossils, the buildup of oxygen, the first eukaryotes and the Cambrian explosion marked. A second bar zooms into the last 539 million years, split into the Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras, with land plants, the first dinosaurs, the end-Permian and end-Cretaceous extinctions and Homo sapiens marked.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1

Squeeze Earth's 4.54 billion years into one 24-hour day, with Earth forming at midnight. At what time does the Cambrian explosion (539 million years ago) happen? When do modern humans (about 300,000 years ago) appear?

Each hour stands for $4{,}540 \div 24 \approx 189$ million years. The time elapsed before the Cambrian is $4{,}540 - 539 = 4{,}001$ million years, so

$$\text{clock time} = 24 \times \frac{4{,}001}{4{,}540} \approx 21.15 \text{ hours},$$

about 9:09 p.m. Animals with hard parts fill only the last three hours of the day.

Modern humans: $\dfrac{0.3}{4{,}540} \times 24$ hours $\approx 0.0016$ hours $\approx 6$ seconds before midnight.

## How life began

The origin of life is an active research question, and scientists are open about what is still unknown. What is well established:

- Early Earth had almost no free oxygen. In 1953 Stanley Miller and Harold Urey ran electric sparks through a mixture of gases thought to resemble the early atmosphere, with water, and within a week found amino acids. Later experiments under a range of conditions have made sugars, nucleotide bases and other building blocks, showing that the molecules of life can form without life.
- RNA can both store information (like DNA) and act as a catalyst (like an enzyme); the rRNA that links amino acids in your ribosomes (lesson 23) is an example. This supports the RNA world hypothesis: early life may have used RNA for both jobs before DNA and proteins took over.
- Fatty molecules spontaneously form hollow bubbles with membrane-like walls, a possible first step toward cells.

## The first three billion years

The earliest widely accepted fossils are about 3.5 billion years old: microscopic cells and stromatolites, layered mounds built by mats of bacteria. For more than a billion years after that, all life was prokaryotic.

Cyanobacteria evolved oxygen-releasing photosynthesis. Their oxygen at first reacted with dissolved iron, forming rust-red banded rock layers, but by about 2.4 billion years ago it began to build up in the air, the Great Oxidation Event. Oxygen was poisonous to many microbes, but it made aerobic respiration possible, with its much larger ATP yield (module 3).

Eukaryotes appear around 2 billion years ago (estimates range from about 1.6 to 2.1). They arose from a partnership between the two older branches of the tree (lesson 29). The host was most likely an archaeon related to today's Asgard archaea, and it took in an oxygen-using bacterium that became the mitochondrion. Later, one eukaryote lineage that already had mitochondria took in a cyanobacterium, which became the chloroplast of algae and plants. This is the endosymbiotic theory from module 2: mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and bacterial-type ribosomes, and divide by splitting like bacteria. Multicellular algae appear over a billion years ago, and soft-bodied animals by about 575 million years ago.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Endosymbiosis and the origin of eukaryotes
  accDescr: An archaeal host cell took in an oxygen-using bacterium, which became the mitochondrion, giving an early eukaryote with mitochondria. Its descendants include animals, fungi and many protists. Later, one eukaryote lineage that already had mitochondria took in a cyanobacterium, which became the chloroplast, giving algae and plants.
  A["Archaeal host cell"] --> C["Early eukaryote with mitochondria"]
  B["Oxygen-using bacterium"] -- "becomes the mitochondrion" --> C
  C --> E["Animals, fungi and many protists"]
  C --> F["Algae and plants"]
  D["Cyanobacterium"] -- "becomes the chloroplast" --> F
```

Then, starting about 539 million years ago, the Cambrian explosion: within roughly 20 to 25 million years, most of the major animal groups alive today appear in the fossil record, many with shells, skeletons and eyes. Predators and prey drove one another's evolution, and hard parts fossilize well, so the record suddenly becomes rich.

## Life moves onto land

Plants reached land around 470 million years ago, followed by arthropods. Four-limbed vertebrates evolved from lobe-finned fish roughly 390 to 360 million years ago; *Tiktaalik* (lesson 26), about 375 million years old, shows the transition under way. The amniotic egg, which doesn't dry out, freed reptiles from water around 320 million years ago. Dinosaurs appear about 230 million years ago, mammals not long after, birds evolve from small feathered dinosaurs around 150 million years ago, and flowering plants spread from about 130 million years ago.

## Mass extinctions

Species go extinct all the time, at a low background rate. A **[[mass extinction]]** is a geologically brief event in which a large fraction of species dies out worldwide. The fossil record shows five:

| Extinction | About when (million years ago) | Leading explanation |
|---|---|---|
| End-Ordovician | 445 | Glaciation and falling sea level |
| Late Devonian | 372 | Ocean oxygen loss; several pulses |
| End-Permian | 252 | Huge volcanic eruptions in Siberia; warming, acidic, low-oxygen oceans |
| End-Triassic | 201 | Volcanic eruptions as the supercontinent Pangaea split |
| End-Cretaceous | 66 | Asteroid impact at Chicxulub, Mexico, plus volcanic eruptions in India |

The end-Permian was the worst: by most estimates 80 to 90 percent or more of marine species vanished. The end-Cretaceous is the best known. In 1980 Luis and Walter Alvarez reported a thin clay layer at the boundary, worldwide, rich in iridium, a metal rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. A buried crater of the right age, about 180 km across, was later found at Chicxulub. Non-bird dinosaurs, along with many other groups, disappeared.

### Example 2

A cliff shows these layers, from bottom to top: (1) sandstone with trilobite fossils; (2) a volcanic ash layer dated at 260 million years; (3) shale with early dinosaur fossils; (4) an iridium-rich clay layer; (5) rock with fossils of early primates. Put the events in order and estimate their ages.

![A cliff cross-section with five rock layers. From bottom to top: sandstone with trilobite fossils, a thin volcanic ash layer dated at 260 million years, shale with dinosaur bones, a thin clay layer rich in iridium, and rock with early primate teeth. An arrow at the side points up toward younger layers.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- By superposition, lower layers are older: trilobites, then the ash, then dinosaurs, then the iridium layer, then primates.
- The trilobites are older than 260 million years (they lie below the dated ash). That fits the fossil record, since trilobites died out in the end-Permian extinction, 252 million years ago.
- The dinosaurs are younger than 260 million years; the iridium layer matches the end-Cretaceous boundary, 66 million years ago, and the primates come after it.

Two separate tools, rock order and radiometric dates, have to agree, and they do.

Extinctions also open opportunities. After the end-Cretaceous, mammals, which had been mostly small for over 100 million years, diversified rapidly into the empty roles, an adaptive radiation that produced whales, bats, primates and grazers. Many biologists warn that human activity is now driving extinction rates far above the background rate (module 10).

## The tempo of evolution

How fast does change happen? Darwin pictured gradualism: slow, steady change, with species changing little by little. In 1972 Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould pointed out that many fossil species stay nearly unchanged for millions of years, then are replaced fairly quickly (geologically speaking: tens of thousands of years) by related species. They called this pattern **[[punctuated equilibrium]]**. Today both patterns are recognized: some lineages change gradually, others show long stability broken by rapid change, often tied to speciation in small populations or to environmental upheaval.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking humans and dinosaurs lived at the same time. Non-bird dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago; modern humans appeared about 300,000 years ago.
- Assuming life was complex from the start. For more than a billion years after the first fossils, all organisms were single-celled prokaryotes.
- Thinking oxygen was always in the air. It accumulated only after about 2.4 billion years ago, produced by photosynthesis.
- Treating punctuated equilibrium as sudden appearance overnight. "Rapid" here means tens of thousands of years, quick only compared to millions.
- Forgetting that a fossil's age often comes from the volcanic layers around it, so it is a range (older than the layer above, younger than the layer below).

## Key points

- Earth is about 4.54 billion years old; the geologic time scale divides that time into eons, eras and periods, with boundaries often at mass extinctions.
- Experiments show life's building blocks can form without life; the RNA world hypothesis suggests RNA came before DNA and proteins.
- Prokaryotes by 3.5 billion years ago; oxygen buildup about 2.4 billion; eukaryotes about 2 billion (an archaeal host plus a bacterium that became the mitochondrion); the Cambrian explosion about 539 million years ago.
- Five mass extinctions, the worst at the end of the Permian; the end-Cretaceous impact ended the non-bird dinosaurs and opened the way for mammals.
- Evolution can be gradual or follow punctuated equilibrium: long stability broken by relatively rapid change.

lessons.title: Modeling evolution: selection, drift, and testing Hardy-Weinberg
lessons.body:
Lesson 28 set up Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium as a null model and named the forces that push a population away from it. It described those forces in words. This lesson turns two of them, natural selection and genetic drift, into numbers you can calculate with, and then shows how to test real genotype counts against Hardy-Weinberg using the chi-square test from lesson 21. These are the same tools R. A. Fisher, J. B. S. Haldane and Sewall Wright built in the 1920s and 1930s when they joined Mendel's genetics to Darwin's selection, the core of what is called the modern synthesis. You will need the Hardy-Weinberg equations and allele counting from lesson 28.

## Measuring fitness with numbers

Lesson 27 defined fitness as reproductive success. To calculate with it, start from **[[absolute fitness]]**: the average number of offspring that an individual of a given genotype leaves in the next generation (counting only offspring that survive to breed). Absolute numbers depend on how good a year it was, so population geneticists compare genotypes instead. The **[[relative fitness]]** $w$ of a genotype is its absolute fitness divided by the absolute fitness of the best genotype:

$$w = \frac{\text{absolute fitness of the genotype}}{\text{absolute fitness of the fittest genotype}}$$

The fittest genotype has $w = 1$, and every other genotype has $w$ between 0 and 1. The **[[selection coefficient]]** $s = 1 - w$ measures how much worse a genotype does. A genotype with $w = 0.8$ has $s = 0.2$: it leaves 20% fewer offspring than the best genotype.

For example, if $AA$ and $Aa$ plants each leave 50 seeds that grow into adults on average and $aa$ plants leave 30, then $w_{AA} = w_{Aa} = 1$, $w_{aa} = 30/50 = 0.6$, and $s = 0.4$ against $aa$. Because $Aa$ has the same fitness as $AA$, selection here acts only on the recessive phenotype.

## One generation of selection

Selection changes allele frequencies because genotypes contribute unequally to the next generation. The calculation always follows the same steps:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Steps for one generation of selection
  accDescr: Start with zygote genotype frequencies p squared, 2pq and q squared. Multiply each by that genotype's relative fitness. Add the three products to get the mean fitness. Divide each product by the mean fitness to get genotype frequencies among the adults that breed. Count alleles in those adults to get the new allele frequencies p prime and q prime.
  A["Zygotes: p², 2pq, q²"] --> B["Multiply each by its relative fitness w"]
  B --> C["Add the products: mean fitness w̄"]
  C --> D["Divide each product by w̄: frequencies among breeders"]
  D --> E["Count alleles: new p′ and q′"]
```

The sum in the third step is the **[[mean fitness]]** of the population, $\bar w = p^2 w_{AA} + 2pq\,w_{Aa} + q^2 w_{aa}$. Dividing by it rescales the survivors' frequencies so they add up to 1 again. The new frequency of $a$ is the frequency of $aa$ breeders plus half the frequency of $Aa$ breeders:

$$q' = \frac{q^2 w_{aa} + pq\,w_{Aa}}{\bar w}$$

### Example 1

A population starts at $p = q = 0.5$, in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. Fitnesses are $w_{AA} = w_{Aa} = 1$ and $w_{aa} = 0.6$. Find $q$ after one generation of selection.

| | $AA$ | $Aa$ | $aa$ | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zygotes | 0.25 | 0.50 | 0.25 | 1 |
| Times $w$ | $0.25 \times 1 = 0.25$ | $0.50 \times 1 = 0.50$ | $0.25 \times 0.6 = 0.15$ | $\bar w = 0.90$ |
| Breeders (divide by 0.90) | 0.278 | 0.556 | 0.167 | 1 |

New $q' = 0.167 + \tfrac12(0.556) = 0.444$. One generation of fairly strong selection ($s = 0.4$) lowered $q$ from 0.500 to 0.444.

Now repeat with the same fitnesses but starting from $q = 0.1$. Then $q^2 = 0.01$, so very few individuals are $aa$, and $\bar w = 1 - 0.4(0.01) = 0.996$. The new $q' = \dfrac{0.01(0.6) + 0.09}{0.996} = 0.0964$, a drop of only 0.0036. Most copies of a rare recessive allele sit in heterozygotes, where selection cannot see them. The graph shows the change in $q$ per generation for every starting $q$:

```plot
{"x": [0, 1], "y": [-0.08, 0.005], "xLabel": "q (frequency of allele a)", "yLabel": "change in q per generation", "functions": [{"f": "-0.4*x^2*(1-x)/(1-0.4*x^2)"}], "caption": "Selection against aa with s = 0.4. The change is largest near q = 0.7 and nearly zero when q is small."}
```

This is why harmful recessive alleles linger in populations for a very long time, and why selection can almost never remove them completely. New mutations add copies at a low rate, and the two processes can balance.

## Heterozygote advantage

Sometimes the heterozygote is the fittest genotype. This **[[heterozygote advantage]]** keeps both alleles in the population, an example of **[[balancing selection]]**. The best-studied case in humans is sickle-cell hemoglobin. People with two copies of the sickle allele ($SS$) have sickle-cell disease. Carriers ($AS$) have no disease in most conditions and are partly protected against severe malaria, caused by the parasite *Plasmodium falciparum*. People with $AA$ are not protected.

### Example 2

Take illustrative relative fitnesses for a region where malaria is common: $w_{AA} = 0.88$, $w_{AS} = 1$, $w_{SS} = 0.20$. (They are of the size estimated in classic studies; real values vary from place to place and have changed with medical care.) Start with $q = 0.05$ for $S$.

- Zygotes: $AA$ $0.9025$, $AS$ $0.0950$, $SS$ $0.0025$.
- Times $w$: $0.7942$, $0.0950$, $0.0005$; mean fitness $\bar w = 0.8897$.
- New $q' = \dfrac{0.0005 + \tfrac12(0.0950)}{0.8897} = 0.054$.

The $S$ allele rose even though $SS$ has very low fitness, because at this frequency almost every $S$ copy is in a protected carrier. It won't rise forever: as $q$ grows, more $S$ copies end up in $SS$ individuals. Writing $s = 1 - w_{AA} = 0.12$ and $t = 1 - w_{SS} = 0.80$, the frequency stops changing at

$$\hat q = \frac{s}{s + t} = \frac{0.12}{0.92} \approx 0.13.$$

At that point an $S$ allele and an $A$ allele leave, on average, the same number of copies. Frequencies of the sickle allele of roughly 0.1 or more are found in parts of sub-Saharan Africa where malaria has long been common, and the allele is rare where malaria never was. Where malaria disappears, $w_{AA}$ rises to 1, the advantage vanishes, and selection slowly lowers $q$.

## Genetic drift in numbers

Each generation, the $2N$ gene copies passed on by $N$ breeding adults are a random sample of the parents' gene pool. On average the sample keeps the same allele frequency, but it rarely matches exactly. The typical size of the change in one generation is about $\sqrt{pq/2N}$: with $p = 0.5$, that is 0.11 for $N = 10$ but only 0.025 for $N = 200$.

![Two panels of simulated allele frequencies over 60 generations. With 10 individuals the eight lines wander widely, and every one reaches 0 or 1 within about 25 generations. With 200 individuals the lines stay mostly between 0.3 and 0.7.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The figure shows eight simulated populations of each size, all starting at $p = 0.5$ with no selection. In the small populations every line soon hits 0 (the allele is lost) or 1 (it is fixed). **[[Fixation]]** means an allele has reached a frequency of 1, so it is the only allele left at that gene; only a new mutation or gene flow can bring variation back. For a neutral allele, the chance that drift eventually fixes it equals its current frequency: an allele at 0.2 is fixed in about 20% of populations and lost in the other 80%. A brand-new mutation, one copy among $2N$, has only a $\tfrac{1}{2N}$ chance.

Drift also steadily removes genetic variation. In an idealized population of $N$ breeders, the expected heterozygosity $H$ (the fraction of individuals that are heterozygous at a gene) shrinks each generation by a factor of $\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2N}\right)$:

$$H_t = H_0\left(1 - \frac{1}{2N}\right)^t$$

### Example 3
