```mermaid
  accDescr: Opening: blue light activates proton pumps in the guard cell membrane; potassium and chloride ions enter and malate is made; water follows by osmosis; the guard cells swell and bow apart, opening the stoma. Closing: during drought, abscisic acid causes ion channels to release potassium and anions; water leaves the guard cells by osmosis; the guard cells go limp and the stoma closes.
  BL[Blue light] --> H[Proton pumps switched on]
  H --> K["K+ and Cl- enter; malate made"]
  K --> W1[Water enters by osmosis]
  W1 --> O[Guard cells swell and bow apart: stoma opens]
  ABA[Drought: abscisic acid] --> E["K+ and anions leave"]
  E --> W2[Water leaves by osmosis]
  W2 --> C[Guard cells go limp: stoma closes]
```

A typical plant loses several hundred water molecules through its stomata for each carbon dioxide molecule it fixes, which is why the C4 and CAM adaptations of module 3 pay off in hot, dry places.

### Example 3: how hard must a redwood pull?

Holding up a water column of height $h$ takes a pressure difference $\rho g h$, with $\rho = 1000$ kg/m³ and $g = 9.81$ m/s². For a 110 m tree:

$$\rho g h = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 110 = 1.08 \times 10^{6} \text{ Pa} = 1.08 \text{ MPa}$$

That's about 0.01 MPa (0.1 bar) per meter. Friction in the conduits adds more; suppose 0.9 MPa along this path. If the soil water is at $\Psi = -0.3$ MPa, the water at the treetop must be at about

$$-0.3 - 1.08 - 0.9 \approx -2.3 \text{ MPa}.$$

Can water survive that? In 1950 the physicist Lyman Briggs found water in a spinning glass tube held together under nearly 28 MPa (about 280 atmospheres), so cohesion is strong enough; in real xylem, cavitation sets in much sooner. A 2004 study of the tallest redwoods found that the growing water stress near the top (which brings the xylem close to cavitation and limits leaf growth and photosynthesis) would cap tree height at roughly 120–130 m. Meanwhile air at 20 °C and 50% humidity has a water potential near $-93$ MPa (lesson 9), a steep slope that the sun keeps pulling water down.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking auxin always promotes growth. The level that speeds shoot elongation slows root elongation.
- Saying light destroys auxin on the lit side. In coleoptiles, auxin moves to the shaded side.
- Believing short-day plants measure day length. They measure unbroken night; a flash of light resets them.
- Thinking root pressure lifts water to treetops. It's far too weak; transpiration pull does the work.
- Crediting abscisic acid with leaf drop. Ethylene triggers it; ABA closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant.

## Key points

- Auxin was found through coleoptile experiments (Darwins, Boysen-Jensen, Went); it moves by polar transport, loosens walls by acid growth, and drives phototropism, gravitropism and apical dominance, with tissue- and dose-dependent effects.
- Gibberellins lengthen stems and trigger cereal germination; cytokinins promote division and, with auxin, shoot or root formation; ABA closes stomata and holds seeds dormant; ethylene ripens fruit and causes leaf drop.
- Phytochrome switches between Pr and active Pfr with red and far-red light, controlling germination, shade responses and photoperiodism.
- Photoperiodic plants compare night length with a critical value; florigen (FT protein) carries the signal from leaves to the shoot tip.
- Xylem water is under tension of about 0.01 MPa per meter of height plus friction; cavitation limits the pull, and root pressure is too weak to matter in tall trees.

lessons.title: Viruses, bacteria, and antibiotic resistance in depth
lessons.body:
## Small genomes, big consequences

The classification lesson introduced lytic and lysogenic cycles, retroviruses, binary fission and the sideways transfer of genes between bacteria, and lesson 27 showed with replica plating that resistance mutations exist before an antibiotic arrives. This lesson looks inside those processes: how virologists count viruses and measure an infection, how HIV copies itself and why that makes it hard to treat, how viruses evolve, how antibiotics kill bacteria, and how resistance arises and spreads. It ends with the microbes that live on and in us.

## Counting phages and timing an infection

Spread a thin layer of bacteria and a few phages on a nutrient plate. Bacteria grow into a cloudy lawn, but each phage infects a cell, bursts it, and its offspring infect the neighbors, leaving a clear spot called a **[[plaque]]**. Each plaque starts from one phage, so plaques are counted as plaque-forming units (PFU), the same logic as counting bacterial colonies.

In 1939 Emory Ellis and Max Delbrück used plaque counts to follow a single round of infection: they let phages attach to bacteria for a few minutes, then diluted the culture so that newly released phages could not quickly find new hosts. The phage count stayed flat during a latent period of about half an hour while the infected cells built new phages, then jumped and leveled off as the cells burst. The size of the jump, the average number of phages released per infected cell, is the **[[burst size]]**, often around 100.

### Example 1: a burst size

A culture holds $5.0 \times 10^{5}$ infected cells per mL just after infection. After every cell has burst, a sample is diluted to $10^{-5}$ and 0.1 mL is plated with bacteria, giving 62 plaques. Find the burst size.

- Phages per mL $= \dfrac{62}{10^{-5} \times 0.1} = 6.2 \times 10^{7}$ PFU/mL.
- Burst size $= \dfrac{6.2 \times 10^{7}}{5.0 \times 10^{5}} = 124$ phages per infected cell.

### Lysis or lysogeny?

A temperate phage such as lambda chooses between the two cycles you met earlier. In the lysogenic path, its DNA joins the bacterial chromosome as a **[[prophage]]**, and a phage repressor protein keeps the lytic genes switched off. The choice depends on conditions: when several phages infect the same cell, or the host is starving, lysogeny becomes more likely. That makes sense, because those are signs that healthy new hosts are scarce, so riding along inside the current one pays better. When the host's DNA is damaged (by UV light, for example), its emergency repair system destroys the repressor, and the prophage switches to the lytic cycle and escapes a cell that may be dying.

Prophages can change their hosts. In **[[lysogenic conversion]]**, genes carried by a prophage give the bacterium new traits. The genes for cholera toxin, diphtheria toxin and the Shiga toxin of dangerous *E. coli* strains all arrive on phages: *Vibrio cholerae* strains that lack the phage don't cause cholera's deadly diarrhea.

## Retroviruses: copying RNA into DNA

HIV infects helper T cells, the coordinators of the immune response. Its cycle runs as follows.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The HIV replication cycle and where drugs act
  accDescr: HIV's envelope protein binds CD4 and a coreceptor on a helper T cell, and the viral envelope fuses with the cell membrane so the core enters. Reverse transcriptase copies the RNA genome into DNA. Integrase inserts that DNA into a host chromosome, where it is called a provirus. The host's enzymes transcribe viral genes, viral proteins are made and new RNA genomes are packaged, and new virus particles bud from the cell. Viral protease then cuts long polyproteins so the particle matures and becomes infectious. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors, integrase inhibitors and protease inhibitors block the matching steps.
  A[Binds CD4 and a coreceptor; envelope fuses] --> B[Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA]
  B --> C[Integrase inserts the DNA: provirus]
  C --> D[Host enzymes transcribe viral genes]
  D --> E[Viral proteins made; RNA genomes packaged]
  E --> F[New particles bud from the cell]
  F --> G[Protease cuts polyproteins: particle matures]
  X1[Reverse transcriptase inhibitors] -.-> B
  X2[Integrase inhibitors] -.-> C
  X3[Protease inhibitors] -.-> G
```

**[[Reverse transcriptase]]** is the enzyme that copies the viral RNA into DNA. It has no proofreading, and measured error rates are about 3 mistakes per 100,000 bases copied. HIV's genome is about 9,700 bases, so each new copy carries on average about 0.3 new mutations (roughly one new mutation for every three genomes copied). An untreated patient produces billions of new virus particles a day, so every possible single mutation arises over and over, including ones that resist any single drug.

Once integrated, the viral DNA is a **[[provirus]]**, a permanent part of that cell's chromosome. Some infected cells go quiet with the provirus inside, out of reach of drugs that act only on replicating virus. This hidden reservoir is why antiretroviral drugs control HIV but don't cure it. Since 1996, combinations of drugs from different classes have kept the virus suppressed for decades; people whose virus is suppressed to undetectable levels don't transmit it sexually. Example 3 shows the arithmetic behind combination therapy.

Retroviruses have also shaped our own genome. About 8% of human DNA consists of remnants of ancient retroviruses that infected the germ line of our ancestors. Most are broken, but a few have been put to work: a protein our placenta uses to fuse cells comes from an old retroviral envelope gene.

## How viruses evolve

Viruses evolve fast because they have huge populations, generations measured in hours, and, for most RNA viruses, no proofreading. (Coronaviruses are an exception: they have a proofreading enzyme, one reason they mutate more slowly than flu.) Influenza shows two modes of change:

- **[[Antigenic drift]]**: point mutations gradually change the surface proteins hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N), so antibodies from past infections or vaccines fit less well. This is why the flu vaccine is updated every year.
- **[[Antigenic shift]]**: the influenza genome comes in eight separate RNA segments. When two strains, such as a bird strain and a human strain, infect the same cell, segments can be mixed into a new combination with a surface protein few people have met. Shifts produced the 1957 and 1968 pandemics, and the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus was a reassortant of swine, bird and human lineages.

Many new human viruses come from animals. HIV-1, for example, descends from a chimpanzee virus that crossed into people in central Africa in the early twentieth century.

## How antibiotics work

An antibiotic works by hitting something bacteria have and our cells lack, or have in a different form.

| Target | Examples | Why our cells are spared |
|---|---|---|
| Peptidoglycan wall synthesis | Penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin | Human cells have no peptidoglycan |
| Bacterial (70S) ribosomes | Tetracyclines, macrolides, streptomycin | Our cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S) differ |
| DNA gyrase (relieves the twisting of DNA during copying) | Ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones | Our version of the enzyme differs |
| Folate synthesis | Sulfonamides | We get folate from food |

Some antibiotics kill bacteria (bactericidal); others stop growth and leave the immune system to clear the infection (bacteriostatic). The lowest concentration that stops visible growth in a lab test is the **[[minimum inhibitory concentration]]** (MIC), and doctors compare a strain's MIC with the levels a drug reaches in the body to decide whether the strain counts as resistant. Because our mitochondria descend from bacteria, their ribosomes resemble bacterial ones, which explains some side effects of ribosome-targeting drugs.

## How resistance arises

### By mutation

Do bacteria mutate in response to a threat, or do mutations arise at random? In 1943 Salvador Luria and Max Delbrück answered with the fluctuation test, before the Lederbergs' replica plating.

### Example 2: reading a fluctuation test

Ten small cultures were each grown from a few cells, and each whole culture was spread on a plate covered with a phage that kills normal *E. coli*. Separately, ten equal samples were taken from one large culture and plated the same way. Counts of resistant colonies:

| Ten separate cultures | 0, 1, 0, 0, 107, 3, 0, 0, 12, 1 |
|---|---|
| Ten samples of one culture | 14, 15, 9, 13, 17, 11, 12, 16, 10, 13 |

The means are similar (12.4 and 13), but the variances are not: about 1,118 for the separate cultures and about 7 for the samples. If resistance appeared only on contact with the phage, every culture would behave like a sample of the same thing, and counts would scatter narrowly around the mean. Instead most cultures had almost none, and one had 107: a "jackpot" culture in which a mutation happened early, and the mutant then multiplied for many generations before plating. Mutations arise at random during growth; the phage only selects them.

### By gene transfer

Bacteria can also gain resistance genes ready-made, by horizontal gene transfer:

- **[[Conjugation]]**: a cell passes a plasmid through a pilus to a neighbor, even of a different species. Plasmids often carry several resistance genes at once; in the 1950s Japanese doctors found *Shigella* that had picked up resistance to four drugs in one step.
- **[[Transformation]]**: a cell takes up naked DNA released from dead bacteria (as in Griffith's experiment, lesson 22).
- **[[Transduction]]**: a phage accidentally packages bacterial DNA and delivers it to the next host.

Whatever the source, resistance genes work in a few ways: an enzyme destroys the drug (a **[[beta-lactamase]]** breaks the ring in penicillins), the target changes (MRSA has an altered wall-building enzyme that penicillins can't grip), pumps push the drug out, or the outer membrane lets less in.

```plot
{"x": [0, 36], "y": [0, 10], "xLabel": "hours after antibiotic starts", "yLabel": "log₁₀ of cell number", "functions": [{"f": "9 - 0.5*x", "from": 0, "to": 18, "label": "susceptible cells"}, {"f": "min(1 + 0.301*x, 9)", "from": 0, "to": 36, "label": "resistant cells", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Selection in a culture with 10 resistant cells among a billion (illustrative). The drug kills susceptible cells, and the resistant ones, doubling every hour, take over."}
```

### Example 3: why combinations beat single drugs

A tuberculosis lung cavity can hold about $10^{9}$ bacteria. Resistance mutations arise at roughly 1 in $10^{8}$ cells for rifampin and 1 in $10^{6}$ for isoniazid (round numbers).

- Expected rifampin-resistant cells: $10^{9} \times 10^{-8} = 10$. Treat with rifampin alone, and these 10 survive and regrow: the treatment fails.
- Expected isoniazid-resistant cells: $10^{9} \times 10^{-6} = 1000$.
- Resistance to both needs two independent mutations in one cell: $10^{-8} \times 10^{-6} = 10^{-14}$, so the expected number is $10^{9} \times 10^{-14} = 10^{-5}$. Almost certainly none exists, so the drugs together kill every cell.

That's why tuberculosis is treated with several drugs at once, and why HIV is treated with a combination.

## How resistance spreads

Every use of an antibiotic selects for resistance, in the patient's own gut flora as well as in the infection. Unneeded prescriptions (for colds, which are viral), heavy use in livestock, crowded hospitals and international travel all add to the spread. A 2022 global study estimated that bacterial antimicrobial resistance directly caused about 1.27 million deaths in 2019. Resistance often costs bacteria some growth rate, but compensating mutations reduce that cost, so resistance doesn't reliably disappear when a drug is used less. The responses that work are using antibiotics only for bacterial infections, choosing narrow-spectrum drugs, vaccinating to prevent infections, controlling infection in hospitals, and developing new drugs. (The old advice to always finish a course is being revisited: for many infections shorter courses work as well. Follow the prescriber's instructions.)

## The microbiome

Your **[[microbiome]]** is the community of microbes living on and in you, mostly in the large intestine. A 2016 estimate put the bacteria in an adult at about 38 trillion, roughly equal to the body's 30 trillion human cells, and the gut community carries around 150 times as many genes as the human genome. Gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber we can't digest into short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells lining the colon, make vitamin K, train the immune system (germ-free mice have poorly developed immune tissues), and crowd out invaders.

Antibiotics disrupt this community, and the clearest example is *Clostridioides difficile*, which can overgrow after antibiotic treatment and cause severe diarrhea. For repeated *C. difficile* infections, a 2013 trial found that transplanting stool from a healthy donor cured 81% of patients after one treatment, against 31% with the antibiotic vancomycin. Many other reported links, between microbiome makeup and obesity, mood or allergies, are correlations; transfer experiments in mice show the microbiome can cause some of these effects in mice, but in people cause and effect is mostly still unsettled.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking antibiotics cause the mutations that make bacteria resistant. Mutations arise at random; the drug selects them.
- Assuming resistance spreads only from parent to offspring. Plasmids and phages move resistance genes between species.
- Treating a provirus as an active infection that drugs can clear. Integrated, silent provirus is untouched by drugs that block replication.
- Mixing up antigenic drift (gradual point mutations) and antigenic shift (sudden reshuffling of genome segments).
- Reading every microbiome correlation as cause and effect.

## Key points

- Plaque counts measure phages; a one-step growth curve gives the latent period and burst size.
- Temperate phages choose lysogeny when hosts are scarce and leave when the host's DNA is damaged; prophage genes can make bacteria dangerous (lysogenic conversion).
- HIV's error-prone reverse transcriptase and huge population make resistance to single drugs inevitable; combination therapy suppresses it, but the provirus reservoir prevents a cure.
- Flu evolves by antigenic drift and shift.
- Antibiotics target walls, ribosomes, DNA gyrase or folate synthesis. Resistance arises by random mutation (Luria-Delbrück) and spreads by conjugation, transformation and transduction; multi-drug therapy works because double mutants are vanishingly rare.
- The gut microbiome digests fiber, makes vitamins and trains immunity; antibiotics can disrupt it, as *C. difficile* shows.

lessons.title: Homeostasis, nervous and endocrine control
lessons.body:
## Keeping the inside steady

The last module ended with the animal kingdom; this one looks closely at one animal, the human, at the level a biology course expects (it is not medical advice). Your body is a community of tens of trillions of cells, and every one of them needs the same narrow conditions: the right temperature, a steady supply of glucose and oxygen, the right water and salt balance, the right pH. Outside, conditions swing wildly. Homeostasis, the maintenance of a stable internal environment, is what keeps those conditions steady, and every organ system in this module contributes to it. This lesson covers the logic of control and the two systems that carry it out: nerves and hormones.

## Feedback loops

Each regulated variable has a **[[set point]]**, a target value, with a normal range around it. Core body temperature sits near 37 °C; fasting blood glucose stays roughly between 70 and 100 mg/dL. Every control system that holds a set point has the same three parts:

- a sensor (receptor) that detects the current value;
- a control center, often in the brain, that compares the value to the set point;
- an effector, a muscle or gland, that changes the value.

In **[[negative feedback]]**, the response opposes the change: if the value rises, the response pushes it down; if it falls, the response pushes it up. A home thermostat works this way. Almost all homeostasis is negative feedback, because it is self-correcting.

### Example 1: tracing a temperature loop

A runner's core temperature rises to 38.5 °C on a hot day. Trace the negative feedback loop.

1. Stimulus: core temperature rises above the set point.
2. Sensors: temperature-sensitive neurons in the skin and in the hypothalamus, a region at the base of the brain, detect the rise.
3. Control center: the hypothalamus compares the reading to about 37 °C and sends signals through nerves.
4. Effectors: sweat glands release sweat, whose evaporation removes heat; blood vessels in the skin widen (vasodilation), carrying warm blood to the surface to lose heat (that's why the runner's face flushes).
5. Result: temperature falls toward 37 °C, and as it does, the signals weaken. The response shuts itself off.

The diagram shows the same loop. Follow the arrows around: the dashed arrow back to the start is what makes it feedback, because the response removes the stimulus that caused it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Negative feedback loop for body temperature
  accDescr: A rise in core temperature above about 37 degrees C is the stimulus. Temperature sensors in the skin and hypothalamus detect it and signal the hypothalamus, the control center, which compares the reading with the set point. It sends nerve signals to the effectors, sweat glands and skin blood vessels, which respond with sweating and vasodilation. Heat is lost, temperature falls back toward 37 degrees C, and a dashed arrow back to the stimulus shows that the response removes the stimulus, so the signals weaken.
  S["Stimulus: core temperature rises above 37 °C"] --> R["Sensors: temperature-sensitive neurons in skin and hypothalamus"]
  R --> C["Control center: hypothalamus compares with set point"]
  C --> E["Effectors: sweat glands and skin blood vessels"]
  E --> O["Response: sweating and vasodilation, heat lost"]
  O -. "temperature falls, stimulus removed" .-> S
```

In the cold, the same center does the opposite: skin vessels narrow (vasoconstriction) to keep heat in the core, and skeletal muscles shiver, releasing heat.

In **[[positive feedback]]**, the response amplifies the change, pushing the variable further from where it started until some event ends the loop. During childbirth, the baby's head stretches the cervix; stretch receptors signal the brain to release the hormone oxytocin, which strengthens contractions, which stretch the cervix more, and so on until the birth. Blood clotting is another example: activated platelets release chemicals that activate more platelets. Positive feedback is useful for events that must be completed quickly, never for holding a value steady.

## The nervous system: fast, targeted signals

The nervous system has two parts. The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the nerves connecting the CNS to the rest of the body. Its working cells are **[[neurons]]**, cells specialized to carry electrical signals.

A typical neuron has:

- dendrites, short branches that receive signals from other cells;
- a cell body containing the nucleus;
- an axon, a single long extension that carries the signal away, in some cases more than a meter long;
- axon terminals that pass the signal to the next cell.

Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating sheath made by supporting cells, with small gaps between segments. The drawing shows these parts; the impulse always runs from the dendrites and cell body along the axon to the terminals.

![A neuron. Branching dendrites surround a rounded cell body containing a nucleus. A long axon leaves the cell body, wrapped in yellow myelin segments separated by small gaps, and ends in several branched axon terminals. An arrow beneath shows the impulse traveling from the cell body toward the terminals.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The action potential

A resting neuron keeps its inside about 70 millivolts negative relative to the outside. Sodium-potassium pumps spend ATP moving sodium ions out and potassium ions in, building up concentration gradients; potassium then leaks back out through open channels, carrying positive charge out and leaving the inside negative. An **[[action potential]]** is a brief reversal of that voltage: when the membrane is stimulated past a threshold, sodium channels open and sodium ions rush in, making the inside positive; a millisecond later, potassium channels open and potassium ions flow out, restoring the negative inside. That disturbance triggers the next patch of membrane, so the impulse travels along the axon like a falling row of dominoes.

Action potentials are all-or-none: a stimulus either reaches threshold and fires a full-size impulse or does nothing. A stronger stimulus doesn't make a bigger impulse; it makes impulses fire more often. Myelin speeds conduction dramatically, because the impulse jumps from gap to gap. Speeds range from under 1 m/s in thin unmyelinated fibers to over 100 m/s in thick myelinated ones. Much of what we know came from Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley's 1952 experiments on the squid giant axon, about half a millimeter wide and large enough to insert electrodes.

### Example 2: measuring nerve speed

In 1850 Hermann von Helmholtz measured the speed of a nerve impulse using a frog's leg muscle and its nerve. He stimulated the nerve at two points and timed when the muscle twitched. Suppose stimulating 50 mm from the muscle gives a twitch after 3.9 ms, and stimulating 20 mm from it gives a twitch after 2.7 ms. What is the conduction speed?

- The muscle's own delay is the same in both trials, so subtracting cancels it.
- Extra distance: $50 - 20 = 30$ mm. Extra time: $3.9 - 2.7 = 1.2$ ms.
- Speed $= 30 \text{ mm} / 1.2 \text{ ms} = 25$ mm/ms $= 25$ m/s (since 1 mm/ms = 1 m/s).

Before this, many scientists assumed nerve signals were nearly instantaneous. A speed slower than sound showed they were a physical process that could be studied.

### Synapses

Neurons don't touch the next cell. At a **[[synapse]]**, a narrow gap separates the axon terminal from the receiving cell. When an impulse arrives, the terminal releases a **[[neurotransmitter]]**, a chemical messenger, which diffuses across the gap in a fraction of a millisecond and binds receptor proteins on the next cell. Depending on the transmitter and receptor, it can make the receiving cell more likely or less likely to fire. Acetylcholine triggers muscle contraction; dopamine and serotonin act in the brain. The transmitter is then broken down or taken back up, so each signal is brief. Many drugs act at synapses.

Some responses don't wait for the brain. In a reflex, such as pulling a hand off a hot stove, a sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord, where it connects, usually through one or more interneurons (in the knee-jerk reflex, directly), to a motor neuron that makes the muscle contract. The pain registers in the brain a moment after the hand has moved.

## The endocrine system: slower, broadcast signals

A **[[hormone]]** is a chemical messenger secreted by a gland into the blood, which carries it throughout the body. Only target cells with matching receptors respond. Endocrine glands include the pituitary (often called the master gland, controlled by the hypothalamus), thyroid (metabolic rate), adrenal glands (adrenaline for the fight-or-flight response; cortisol), pancreas, and the ovaries and testes (sex hormones).

The first hormone was found in 1902, when William Bayliss and Ernest Starling showed that the intestine still triggered the pancreas to release digestive juice after all the nerves between them were cut. Something in the blood had to carry the message. They extracted it and named it secretin; in 1905 Starling coined the word "hormone" for such blood-borne messengers.

| Feature | Nervous system | Endocrine system |
|---|---|---|
| Signal | Electrical impulse, then neurotransmitter | Hormone in the blood |
| Speed | Milliseconds | Seconds to hours |
| Duration | Brief | Can last hours or longer |
| Reach | Specific cells the neuron connects to | Any cell with the receptor |

### Blood glucose

Blood glucose control is the textbook example of hormonal negative feedback, with two opposing hormones from clusters of cells in the pancreas called islets:

- After a meal, glucose rises. Beta cells release **[[insulin]]**, which makes liver, muscle and fat cells take up glucose and makes the liver store it as glycogen. Glucose falls.
- Between meals, glucose falls. Alpha cells release **[[glucagon]]**, which makes the liver break glycogen down and release glucose. Glucose rises.

The two hormones form two negative feedback loops around one set point, as the diagram shows. Each loop switches itself off as glucose returns to normal.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Insulin and glucagon hold blood glucose near its set point
  accDescr: Blood glucose near its set point, about 90 mg/dL, sits on the left. Upper loop: after a meal glucose rises, beta cells in the pancreas release insulin, body cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen, so glucose falls back to the set point. Lower loop: between meals glucose falls, alpha cells release glucagon, and the liver breaks down glycogen and releases glucose, so glucose rises back to the set point. Both loops are negative feedback.
  N(["Blood glucose near set point, about 90 mg/dL"]) -- "meal: glucose rises" --> B["Beta cells release insulin"]
  B --> U["Cells take up glucose; liver stores glycogen"]
  U -- "glucose falls" --> N
  N -- "fasting: glucose falls" --> A["Alpha cells release glucagon"]
  A --> G["Liver breaks down glycogen, releases glucose"]
  G -- "glucose rises" --> N
```

In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the beta cells, so the body makes little or no insulin; people with it need insulin every day. In type 2 diabetes, about 90–95% of diagnosed cases, cells respond less to insulin (insulin resistance), and the pancreas eventually can't keep up. In both, blood glucose stays high, which over years damages blood vessels and nerves. Insulin was first isolated in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto, and within a year it was saving the lives of children with type 1 diabetes.

```plot
{"x": [0, 240], "y": [0, 320], "xLabel": "time after drinking glucose (min)", "yLabel": "blood glucose (mg/dL)", "functions": [{"f": "90 + 50*(x/30)*exp(1 - x/30)", "label": "typical response"}, {"f": "140 + 160*(x/60)*exp(1 - x/60)", "label": "untreated diabetes", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Glucose tolerance test (illustrative): blood glucose after a standard glucose drink"}
```

### Example 3: reading a glucose tolerance test

Use the graph. For the typical response, find the peak and say what drives the return. Then compare the dashed curve.

The solid curve rises from 90 to a peak of about 140 mg/dL at 30 minutes, as glucose is absorbed. Rising glucose triggers insulin release; cells take up glucose, so the level falls back toward 90 by about two to three hours. The dashed curve starts higher (140, so fasting glucose is already above the normal range), peaks near 300 at about an hour, is still above 200 at three hours, and only gets down to about 170 by four hours. Little effective insulin action means glucose isn't cleared: the negative feedback loop is broken.

## Common mistakes

- Calling any helpful response "positive feedback." Positive feedback amplifies a change; negative feedback reverses it.
- Thinking insulin "is sugar" or raises blood sugar. Insulin lowers it; glucagon raises it.
- Believing a stronger stimulus makes a bigger action potential. It makes more frequent ones.
- Confusing hormones with neurotransmitters: hormones travel in blood; neurotransmitters cross a synapse.

## Key points

- Homeostasis holds variables near a set point using sensors, a control center and effectors.
- Negative feedback reverses changes (temperature, glucose); positive feedback amplifies them to finish an event (childbirth, clotting).
- Neurons carry all-or-none action potentials (sodium in, then potassium out); myelin speeds them; synapses pass signals chemically.
- Hormones travel in the blood to target cells with receptors: slower and longer-lasting than nerve signals.
- Insulin lowers blood glucose, glucagon raises it; diabetes is a failure of this loop.

lessons.title: Circulation, respiration, and excretion
lessons.body:
## Supply and removal

The last lesson described how the body senses and corrects changes. This one covers three systems that do much of the correcting by moving materials. Every cell needs oxygen and glucose delivered and carbon dioxide and nitrogen wastes removed. In a single cell, diffusion handles this, but diffusion is fast only over tiny distances (the surface-area-to-volume problem from the cell module). A large animal solves it with a pump and pipes (the circulatory system), a huge exchange surface for gases (the respiratory system), and a filter that cleans the blood (the excretory system).

## The heart and double circulation

The human heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: two thin-walled atria on top that receive blood, and two thick-walled ventricles below that pump it out. One-way valves between chambers and at the exits keep blood moving forward; their closing makes the "lub-dub" sounds.

In the schematic below, blue marks oxygen-poor blood and red-pink oxygen-rich blood. Diagrams of the heart are drawn as if you were facing the person, so the heart's right side appears on your left.

![Schematic of the human heart seen from the front. On the viewer's left, the right atrium and right ventricle, shaded blue, receive blood from the vena cava and pump it up the pulmonary artery to the lungs. On the viewer's right, the left atrium receives blood from the pulmonary veins and the thick-walled left ventricle, shaded pink, pumps it up the aorta, which arches over to the body. Valves sit between each atrium and ventricle and at the bases of the two arteries; arrows show the direction of flow.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The heart is really two pumps side by side, so blood makes two loops:

- Pulmonary circuit: the right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide, then returns to the left atrium.
- Systemic circuit: the left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood to every other tissue, and it returns oxygen-poor to the right atrium.

Tracing one red blood cell: right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lung capillaries → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body capillaries → veins → back to the right atrium. The left ventricle's wall is the thickest because it pushes blood through the whole body. Keeping the two circuits separate lets the systemic one run at high pressure.

The heartbeat starts in the heart itself: a patch of specialized muscle in the right atrium, the pacemaker (sinoatrial node), fires on its own about 60–100 times a minute at rest. Nerves and hormones such as adrenaline speed it up or slow it down.

## Vessels

| Vessel | Carries blood | Wall | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[Artery]]** | Away from the heart | Thick, muscular, elastic | High pressure; the pulse you feel |
| **[[Capillary]]** | Between arteries and veins | One cell thick | Where exchange with tissues happens |
| **[[Vein]]** | Toward the heart | Thinner, less muscle | Low pressure; valves stop backflow |

Direction, not oxygen, defines the vessel: the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood (away from the heart, to the lungs), and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood. Capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells pass in single file, and so numerous that almost no cell is more than a few cell-widths from one. In the limbs, contracting muscles squeeze the veins, and the valves let blood go only toward the heart.

## Blood

Blood is about 55% plasma (water carrying dissolved nutrients, salts, hormones, proteins and most of the carbon dioxide, as bicarbonate) and 45% cells:

- Red blood cells carry oxygen. Each is packed with roughly 250 million molecules of **[[hemoglobin]]**, an iron-containing protein that binds up to four oxygen molecules. Human red blood cells lose their nucleus as they mature, leaving more room for hemoglobin.
- White blood cells defend the body (lesson 37).
- Platelets, cell fragments, start blood clotting.

## Cardiac output

The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute is the **[[cardiac output]]**:

$$\text{cardiac output} = \text{heart rate} \times \text{stroke volume},$$

where stroke volume is the volume pumped by one ventricle in one beat. At rest, about 70 beats/min $\times$ 70 mL = 4.9 L/min, roughly the body's entire blood volume every minute. During hard exercise, both heart rate and stroke volume rise, and cardiac output can reach about 20 L/min in a healthy young adult and 30 L/min or more in elite endurance athletes.

### Example 1: Harvey's argument

Before 1628, physicians followed Galen, who taught that the liver constantly made new blood from food and that tissues used it up. William Harvey disproved this with an observation and a calculation. Redo it with modern numbers: a resting heart pumps about 70 mL per beat at 72 beats per minute. How much blood does it pump in a day, and what does that imply?

- Per minute: $70 \times 72 = 5040$ mL $\approx 5.0$ L.
- Per day: $5.04 \text{ L/min} \times 1440 \text{ min} \approx 7260$ L.

No one eats or drinks 7,000 liters a day, and the body holds only about 5 L of blood. The same blood must go round and round. Harvey also showed that valves in veins let blood flow only toward the heart. He predicted that tiny connecting vessels must link arteries to veins; Marcello Malpighi saw these capillaries with a microscope in 1661.

## The respiratory system

Air enters through the nose and mouth, passes the pharynx and larynx, and goes down the trachea, which branches into two bronchi, then into thousands of narrower bronchioles, ending in clusters of tiny air sacs called **[[alveoli]]**. The adult lungs hold several hundred million alveoli with a total surface area of very roughly 70 m², about a third of a tennis court, folded into the chest.

Gas exchange is pure diffusion. Alveolar walls and capillary walls are each one thin cell, so air and blood are separated by well under a micrometer. The figure zooms in on that barrier (the layers are drawn much thicker than they really are). Oxygen is more concentrated in alveolar air than in the blood arriving from the body, so it diffuses into the blood and binds hemoglobin; carbon dioxide is more concentrated in that blood, so it diffuses out into the alveoli. In the body's tissues, the gradients run the other way.

![Left: a bronchiole ending in a grape-like cluster of alveoli wrapped in a capillary network. Right: a zoomed-in cross-section of the barrier, with air in the alveolus on top, then the alveolar wall and capillary wall, each one cell thick, then blood plasma with red blood cells. An arrow shows oxygen diffusing down from the air into a red blood cell, and another shows carbon dioxide diffusing up from the blood into the air.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Breathing moves air by changing pressure. To inhale, the diaphragm (a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs) contracts and flattens, and rib muscles lift the rib cage; the chest volume increases, pressure in the lungs drops below air pressure, and air flows in. Quiet exhaling is mostly passive: the muscles relax and the elastic lungs recoil.

The drive to breathe comes mainly from carbon dioxide, not from a lack of oxygen. Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in the blood; sensors in the brainstem (the medulla) and in major arteries detect the resulting drop in pH and increase the breathing rate and depth. That's negative feedback: more breathing removes more carbon dioxide, and pH returns to normal.

### Example 2: ventilation and dead space

A student at rest breathes 12 times a minute, taking in 500 mL per breath (the tidal volume). About 150 mL of each breath only fills the airways (trachea, bronchi), where no gas exchange happens; this is called dead space. Find the total air moved per minute and the air that actually reaches the alveoli.

- Minute ventilation $= 500 \text{ mL} \times 12 = 6000$ mL/min $= 6.0$ L/min.
- Alveolar ventilation $= (500 - 150) \times 12 = 4200$ mL/min $= 4.2$ L/min.

Now suppose the same student breathes shallow and fast: 250 mL at 24 breaths per minute. Minute ventilation is unchanged at 6.0 L/min, but alveolar ventilation falls to $(250 - 150) \times 24 = 2400$ mL/min. Deep, slow breaths ventilate the alveoli far better than shallow, fast ones.

### Oxygen and metabolic rate

Because cells use oxygen to release energy from food (cellular respiration), oxygen consumption measures metabolic rate. About 20 kJ of energy is released for each liter of oxygen used; the exact value (roughly 19 to 21 kJ) depends only a little on whether carbohydrate, fat or protein is being burned. The **[[basal metabolic rate]]** (BMR) is the energy used at complete rest, awake, after fasting. A typical adult at rest uses about 3.5 mL of oxygen per kilogram per minute, about 0.25 L/min for a 70 kg person, which gives $0.25 \times 20 = 5$ kJ per minute, or about 7,200 kJ (about 1,700 kcal) per day just to stay alive. Exercise can raise oxygen use more than tenfold.

## The excretory system

Breaking down amino acids releases nitrogen as ammonia, which is toxic. The liver converts it to urea, which is far less toxic, and the kidneys remove it in urine. The kidneys also regulate water, salts and blood pH, so they are homeostatic organs as much as waste removers.

Each kidney contains about a million **[[nephrons]]**, its filtering units. A nephron works in three steps:

1. Filtration: at the glomerulus, a ball of capillaries, blood pressure pushes water and small molecules (glucose, salts, urea, amino acids) into the nephron. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
2. Reabsorption: as this filtrate flows along the tubule, needed substances (nearly all the glucose and amino acids, most water and salts) are moved back into surrounding capillaries.
3. Secretion: some wastes and excess ions (hydrogen, potassium, some drugs) are moved from the blood into the tubule.

The sketch shows where each step happens. The tubule has named sections: most reabsorption happens in the first, the proximal tubule; the hairpin loop of Henle helps make the tissue around it very salty, so that water can later be drawn out of the collecting duct.

![A nephron. Blood enters a knot of capillaries, the glomerulus, inside a cup-shaped capsule, where filtration pushes fluid into the tubule. The fluid flows through the winding proximal tubule, where arrows show glucose, amino acids, most water and salts being reabsorbed; down and back up the hairpin loop of Henle; through the distal tubule, where an arrow shows hydrogen and potassium ions being secreted; and into the collecting duct, where water is reabsorbed, more when ADH is high. Urine leaves at the bottom toward the ureter.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

What remains drains through collecting ducts to the ureters, bladder and out. The amount of water reabsorbed is set by negative feedback: when the blood becomes too concentrated, the hypothalamus senses it and the pituitary releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water. More water returns to the blood and the urine becomes concentrated and darker. When you drink a lot, ADH falls and you make plenty of dilute urine. The diagram traces the loop.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: ADH controls water reabsorption by negative feedback
  accDescr: Water loss, for example from sweating without drinking, makes the blood too concentrated. The hypothalamus senses this and the pituitary releases more ADH. ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water returns to the blood and a small volume of concentrated urine is made. The blood becomes less concentrated, which turns ADH release back down.
  W["Water lost: blood too concentrated"] --> Hy["Hypothalamus senses it"]
  Hy --> P["Pituitary releases more ADH"]
  P --> K["Collecting ducts let more water back into the blood"]
  K --> R["Blood less concentrated; small volume of dark urine"]
  R -. "ADH release falls" .-> Hy
```

### Example 3: how much is reabsorbed?

The kidneys filter about 180 L of fluid a day but produce only about 1.5 L of urine. What percentage of the filtered water is reabsorbed?

- Reabsorbed $= 180 - 1.5 = 178.5$ L.
- Percentage $= 178.5 / 180 \times 100 \approx 99.2\%$.

Filtering everything small and then taking back what's needed seems wasteful, but it means the kidney doesn't need to recognize every possible waste or toxin. Anything not specifically reclaimed is removed. Glucose normally appears in urine only when blood glucose is so high (as in untreated diabetes) that the carriers reabsorbing it are saturated.

## Common mistakes

- Defining arteries as vessels with oxygen-rich blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content.
- Thinking the left side of the heart pumps to the lungs. The right side does; the left side pumps to the body.
- Saying low oxygen is the main breathing trigger. Rising carbon dioxide (falling pH) is.
- Thinking the lungs actively pull air in. The diaphragm and rib muscles enlarge the chest, and air pressure pushes air in.
- Believing kidneys filter only wastes. They filter almost everything small and reabsorb what the body needs.

## Key points

- Four-chambered heart, double circulation: right side to the lungs, left side to the body.
- Arteries (away, thick), capillaries (exchange, one cell thick), veins (toward, valves).
- Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, about 5 L/min at rest.
- Alveoli give a huge, thin surface for diffusion; carbon dioxide level drives breathing.
- Oxygen use measures metabolic rate: about 20 kJ per liter of oxygen.
- Nephrons filter, reabsorb and secrete; ADH controls water reabsorption by negative feedback.

lessons.title: Digestion, nutrition, and the immune system
lessons.body:
## Getting fuel in and keeping invaders out

The last lesson followed oxygen from the air to the cells. The other raw material of respiration, glucose, and the building blocks for growth come from food, and getting them out of food is the job of the digestive system. The same openings that let food and air in are also doors for bacteria and viruses, so the second half of this lesson covers the immune system, which defends the body against them. As before, this is biology, not medical advice.

## Digestion: from food to molecules

Food arrives as macromolecules (module 1) too large to cross the gut lining. Digestion breaks them into monomers by hydrolysis, each step catalyzed by a specific enzyme:

| Macromolecule | Broken down to | Key enzymes and where they act |
|---|---|---|
| Starch and other carbohydrates | Simple sugars (glucose) | Amylase (mouth, small intestine) |
| Proteins | Amino acids | Pepsin (stomach); trypsin and others (small intestine) |
| Fats | Fatty acids and glycerol (monoglycerides) | Lipase (small intestine) |
| Nucleic acids | Nucleotides | Nucleases (small intestine) |

Digestion is both mechanical (chewing and churning, which make smaller pieces with more surface for enzymes) and chemical (enzymes breaking bonds).

## The path through the gut

1. Mouth: teeth grind food; saliva moistens it and its amylase starts on starch (chew a cracker long enough and it tastes sweet).
2. Esophagus: food is pushed down by **[[peristalsis]]**, waves of muscle contraction that squeeze it along.
3. Stomach: muscular churning plus gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid (pH about 1.5–3.5) and pepsin, which begins protein digestion. The acid also kills many swallowed microbes. A mucus layer protects the stomach wall from its own acid and enzymes.
4. Small intestine: several meters long (about 3 m in a living adult; the often-quoted 6 m is its relaxed length after death) and the site of most digestion and nearly all absorption. The pancreas releases enzymes for every class of macromolecule plus bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid. The liver makes bile, stored in the gallbladder, which emulsifies fats, breaking large droplets into tiny ones so lipase has more surface to work on. Bile contains no enzymes.
5. Large intestine (colon): absorbs water and salts and houses trillions of bacteria that ferment leftover fiber and make some vitamins, such as vitamin K.

The drawing shows the organs in place. Food passes only through the tube (mouth, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestine); the liver, gallbladder and pancreas send their secretions into the small intestine through ducts.

![The human digestive system drawn schematically. A mouth at the top leads to a long esophagus running down to a J-shaped stomach on the body's left. The large liver lies on the body's right, with the small gallbladder beneath it. The pancreas lies in a narrow band under the stomach. The coiled small intestine fills the center of the abdomen, framed on three sides by the wider large intestine, which ends at the bottom.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The inner wall of the small intestine is folded, and the folds are covered with **[[villi]]**, finger-like projections about a millimeter tall, whose cells bear microscopic microvilli. Together these give the small intestine an absorbing surface of very roughly 30 m² (estimates vary with how it's measured). Each villus holds capillaries that absorb sugars and amino acids and a lymph vessel that absorbs fats.

### Example 1: what digestion is chemical?

In the 1770s, Lazzaro Spallanzani tested whether the stomach digests food by grinding or by chemistry. He swallowed small linen bags and perforated wooden tubes holding pieces of meat, recovered them later, and found the meat partly dissolved even though the containers protected it from grinding. He also collected gastric juice and showed that meat placed in it, in a vial kept at body temperature, slowly dissolved, while meat in plain water did not. What does each result show, and what was the control?

- Meat dissolved inside protective containers: grinding isn't required, so something chemical is acting.
- Meat dissolved in gastric juice outside the body: the active agent is in the juice itself, not in the living stomach wall.
- The control: meat in water at the same temperature. Without it, you couldn't rule out that warmth and time alone break meat down.

The active agent was later identified as pepsin, working with stomach acid.

## Nutrition and energy

The body needs carbohydrates, fats and proteins (macronutrients), plus vitamins, minerals, water and fiber. Energy in food is measured in kilocalories (the "Calories" on a food label are kilocalories) or kilojoules (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ). The standard values are:

| Nutrient | Energy |
|---|---|
| Carbohydrate | 4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g) |
| Protein | 4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g) |
| Fat | 9 kcal/g (37 kJ/g) |

Fat is the most energy-dense because its molecules are mostly carbon-hydrogen bonds, with little oxygen; they are less oxidized to start with, so more energy is released when they are fully oxidized in respiration.

### Example 2: reading a label

A granola bar contains 25 g carbohydrate, 4 g protein and 7 g fat. Estimate its energy and the percentage of that energy from fat.

- Carbohydrate: $25 \times 4 = 100$ kcal. Protein: $4 \times 4 = 16$ kcal. Fat: $7 \times 9 = 63$ kcal.
- Total: $100 + 16 + 63 = 179$ kcal.
- From fat: $63 / 179 \times 100 \approx 35.2\%$.

The 7 g of fat is only about 19% of the bar's macronutrient mass but over a third of its energy.

## The immune system, layer by layer

Pathogens (lesson 31) include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists and parasitic worms. The body defends itself in two broad layers.

### Innate immunity

**[[Innate immunity]]** is the defense you're born with. It responds within minutes to hours and in the same way to any invader, recognizing general features shared by many microbes rather than one particular germ.

- Barriers: skin, mucus that traps particles (swept up by cilia in the airways), stomach acid, enzymes in tears and saliva.
- Inflammation: damaged tissue releases chemical signals such as histamine; nearby capillaries widen and leak, causing redness, heat, swelling and pain, and bringing in fluid and white blood cells.
- Phagocytes: white blood cells such as neutrophils and macrophages engulf and digest microbes.
- Natural killer cells destroy virus-infected and cancerous cells; fever raises body temperature in a way that slows some pathogens and speeds immune responses.

### Adaptive immunity

**[[Adaptive immunity]]** is specific: it recognizes one particular pathogen, takes days to build up the first time, and remembers. It depends on recognizing an **[[antigen]]**, any molecule (usually a protein or sugar on a pathogen's surface) that the immune system can identify as foreign. Its cells are lymphocytes, of two kinds:

- **[[B cells]]** make **[[antibodies]]**, Y-shaped proteins whose two tips each bind one specific antigen. Antibodies don't kill directly: they neutralize viruses and toxins, clump microbes together, and mark them for phagocytes.
- **[[T cells]]** come in two main types. Helper T cells coordinate the response, activating B cells and other cells. Cytotoxic (killer) T cells find body cells infected by viruses and destroy them, removing the virus's factories.

Adaptive responses usually begin when phagocytes that have engulfed a pathogen display pieces of its antigens on their surface. Helper T cells that match those antigens are activated and in turn activate the matching B cells and cytotoxic T cells, as the diagram shows.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The adaptive immune response
  accDescr: A pathogen enters the body and phagocytes engulf it and display its antigens. Helper T cells that match the antigen are activated. They activate matching B cells, which multiply and make antibodies that neutralize and mark the pathogen, and matching cytotoxic T cells, which kill infected body cells. Both branches also leave memory cells for a faster response next time.
  P["Pathogen enters"] --> M["Phagocytes engulf it and display its antigens"]
  M --> H["Matching helper T cells activated"]
  H --> B["Matching B cells multiply"]
  H --> C["Matching cytotoxic T cells multiply"]
  B --> A["Antibodies neutralize and mark the pathogen"]
  C --> K["Infected body cells killed"]
  B --> Mem["Memory cells remain"]
  C --> Mem
```

Each lymphocyte carries receptors for just one antigen, and the body makes millions of different lymphocytes before ever meeting an infection. When an antigen appears, only the few cells that match it are activated, and they multiply into a large clone of identical cells, a process called clonal selection. That multiplication is why the first response takes about one to two weeks. Afterwards, most of the clone dies, but long-lived **[[memory cells]]** remain. On a second exposure they respond within days, faster and much more strongly, often clearing the pathogen before you feel sick. That's immunity.

HIV shows how central helper T cells are: the virus infects and destroys them. Without treatment, their numbers fall over years until the adaptive response fails (AIDS), leaving the person open to infections a healthy immune system would control. Antiretroviral therapy does not cure HIV, but it keeps the virus from destroying helper T cells, and people who take it can live long, healthy lives.

```plot
{"x": [0, 60], "y": [0, 110], "xLabel": "days", "yLabel": "antibody level (relative)", "functions": [{"f": "10*(x/12)^3*exp(3 - 3*x/12)", "from": 0, "to": 30, "label": "primary response"}, {"f": "10*(x/12)^3*exp(3 - 3*x/12) + 100*((x - 30)/5)^2*exp(2 - 2*(x - 30)/5)", "from": 30, "to": 60, "label": "secondary response"}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [0, 105], "dashed": true}, {"from": [30, 0], "to": [30, 105], "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [8, 104], "text": "first exposure"}, {"at": [39, 104], "text": "second exposure"}], "caption": "Primary and secondary antibody responses to the same antigen (illustrative)"}
```

### Example 3: reading the response curves

Using the graph, compare the two responses in timing and size, and explain the difference.

After the first exposure on day 0, antibodies stay low for several days, then peak around day 12 at a level of about 10. After the second exposure on day 30, the level climbs within a few days and peaks around day 35 at about 100. The secondary response is faster (about 5 days to peak instead of 12) and roughly ten times larger, because memory cells made in the first response are already waiting and multiply quickly.

## Vaccines

A **[[vaccine]]** exposes the immune system to an antigen from a pathogen without causing the disease, so the body builds memory cells in advance. In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that inoculating a boy with material from cowpox protected him against smallpox. Vaccination later eradicated smallpox worldwide; the World Health Organization declared it gone in 1980.

Vaccines present the antigen in different ways: weakened live pathogens (measles, mumps and rubella), inactivated pathogens (most flu shots), purified proteins or pieces (hepatitis B, HPV), inactivated toxins (tetanus), and mRNA vaccines (several COVID-19 vaccines), which deliver instructions for cells to make one viral protein for a short time. The mRNA never enters the nucleus, can't change a person's DNA, and is broken down within days.

When enough people are immune, a pathogen can't find enough susceptible hosts to keep spreading, which also protects people too young or too ill to be vaccinated. This is **[[herd immunity]]**. If each infected person would infect $R_0$ others in a fully susceptible population, spread stops when the immune fraction exceeds

$$1 - \frac{1}{R_0}.$$

### Example 4: herd immunity threshold

Measles is among the most contagious diseases, with $R_0$ around 12–18. Using $R_0 = 15$, what fraction of the population must be immune, and what vaccination coverage does that need if two doses of vaccine protect about 97% of people?

- Threshold: $1 - \tfrac{1}{15} = \tfrac{14}{15} \approx 0.933$, so about 93% must be immune.
- Coverage needed: $0.933 / 0.97 \approx 0.962$, about 96% of the population vaccinated.

For a disease with $R_0 = 2$, the threshold is only 50%. That's why measles outbreaks start when coverage slips just a few percentage points.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking digestion and absorption both happen mainly in the stomach. The small intestine does most of both.
- Saying bile is an enzyme. It emulsifies fats; lipase digests them.
- Mixing up antigens and antibodies. The antigen is the foreign marker; the antibody is the protein made to bind it.
- Believing antibiotics help against viral infections. They act only on bacteria.
- Thinking vaccines work by treating an infection. They build memory before infection.

## Key points

- Digestion hydrolyzes macromolecules: carbohydrates → sugars, proteins → amino acids, fats → fatty acids and glycerol.
- Mouth → esophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (acid, pepsin) → small intestine (pancreatic enzymes, bile, villi for absorption) → large intestine (water, gut bacteria).
- Energy: 4 kcal/g carbohydrate and protein, 9 kcal/g fat.
- Innate immunity is fast and general (barriers, inflammation, phagocytes); adaptive immunity is specific (B cells and antibodies, T cells) and builds memory.
- Vaccines create memory cells without disease; herd immunity threshold $= 1 - 1/R_0$.

lessons.title: Neurons, action potentials, and synapses
lessons.body:
## Beyond "sodium in, potassium out"

The homeostasis lesson described the action potential in one sentence: sodium rushes in, potassium flows out, and the impulse travels like a row of falling dominoes. That's true, but it leaves the real questions open. Why is a resting neuron negative inside at all? What decides the size of the spike, and why is it all-or-none? Why can't an impulse turn around and run backward? This lesson answers those questions with a little physical chemistry, follows the signal across a synapse, and shows how several well-known drugs and toxins act. It goes a step beyond the core course, to the level of an honors or early AP Biology class.

## Why the inside is negative

Two things set up the resting potential.

First, the **[[sodium-potassium pump]]** (Na⁺/K⁺ pump) in the membrane uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in. Run constantly, it builds steep concentration gradients: inside a typical mammalian neuron, K⁺ is about 140 mM and Na⁺ about 15 mM; outside, K⁺ is about 5 mM and Na⁺ about 145 mM. Keeping these gradients up is expensive. The pump accounts for a large share of the brain's energy use.

Second, the resting membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, because some K⁺ channels are always open. K⁺ ions diffuse out, down their gradient, and each one carries a positive charge with it. The inside becomes negative, and that negative charge starts pulling K⁺ back in. Very quickly the electrical pull inward balances the chemical push outward. The voltage at which the two balance for one ion is its **[[equilibrium potential]]**, given by the **[[Nernst equation]]**. At body temperature (37 °C), for an ion with charge $z$:

$$E_{\text{ion}} = \frac{61.5 \text{ mV}}{z} \log_{10}\frac{[\text{ion}]_{\text{out}}}{[\text{ion}]_{\text{in}}}$$

The 61.5 mV comes from physical constants ($2.303\,RT/F$ at 310 K). Notice that the pump itself contributes only a few millivolts directly (it moves 3 charges out for every 2 in). Its main job is to maintain the gradients; the K⁺ leak turns them into a voltage.

### Example 1: equilibrium potentials

Use the concentrations above to find $E_{\text{K}}$ and $E_{\text{Na}}$.

- Potassium: $E_{\text{K}} = 61.5 \log_{10}(5/140) = 61.5 \times (-1.447) \approx -89$ mV. The inside would have to be 89 mV negative to stop K⁺ leaking out.
- Sodium: $E_{\text{Na}} = 61.5 \log_{10}(145/15) = 61.5 \times 0.985 \approx +61$ mV. Na⁺ would keep flowing in until the inside was about 61 mV positive.

The real resting potential, about −70 mV, lies between the two but much closer to $E_{\text{K}}$, because at rest the membrane is mostly permeable to K⁺ with a small Na⁺ leak. A weighted version of the Nernst equation (the Goldman equation) captures this. If Na⁺ permeability is 4% of K⁺ permeability:

$$V_{\text{rest}} = 61.5 \log_{10}\frac{5 + 0.04(145)}{140 + 0.04(15)} = 61.5 \log_{10}\frac{10.8}{140.6} \approx -68.5 \text{ mV}.$$

That's the key idea of the whole lesson: *the membrane potential moves toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion the membrane is most permeable to at that moment.* Open Na⁺ channels and the voltage heads toward +61 mV; open K⁺ channels and it heads toward −89 mV.

## The action potential, phase by phase

The action potential depends on **[[voltage-gated channels]]**: Na⁺ and K⁺ channels that open or close in response to the membrane voltage itself. The graph shows one action potential recorded at one point on an axon.

![Graph of membrane potential against time for one action potential. The potential rests at about −70 mV, rises after a stimulus to a threshold of about −55 mV, shoots up to a peak of about +35 mV, falls below the resting level to about −80 mV, and slowly returns to −70 mV. Dashed lines mark the sodium equilibrium potential near +60 mV and the potassium equilibrium potential near −90 mV.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. Resting state. Both kinds of voltage-gated channels are closed; leak channels hold the membrane near −70 mV.
2. Depolarization to threshold. A stimulus (or input from other neurons) makes the inside less negative, a **[[depolarization]]**. If it reaches the **[[threshold]]**, about −55 mV, enough voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open to start a chain reaction.
3. Rising phase. Na⁺ rushes in, which depolarizes the membrane further, which opens more Na⁺ channels: a brief positive feedback loop. The potential races toward $E_{\text{Na}}$ and peaks around +30 to +40 mV, short of +61 mV because the next step begins first.
4. Falling phase, or **[[repolarization]]**. Within about a millisecond, Na⁺ channels inactivate: a separate gate plugs them, and they can't reopen until the membrane has been negative again for a moment. Meanwhile the slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, K⁺ flows out, and the potential falls.
5. Undershoot, or **[[hyperpolarization]]**. The K⁺ channels close slowly, so for a few milliseconds the membrane is even more permeable to K⁺ than at rest and dips toward $E_{\text{K}}$, to about −80 mV, before returning to rest.

The positive feedback in step 3 explains the all-or-none rule: below threshold, K⁺ leakage wins and the voltage drifts back; above it, the Na⁺ loop runs to completion, and the peak is set by the channels and the gradients, not by the stimulus. Remarkably few ions move. One action potential changes the concentrations inside a typical neuron by a tiny fraction of a percent, which is why a neuron can keep firing for a while even if its pumps are blocked, though not indefinitely.

Hodgkin and Huxley worked this out in 1952 with the squid giant axon and a voltage clamp, a circuit that holds the membrane at a chosen voltage and measures the current needed to do it. Replacing external Na⁺ with a non-permeating ion abolished the early inward current, proving it was carried by Na⁺. Later, the pufferfish toxin tetrodotoxin (TTX) was found to block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels specifically, and tetraethylammonium to block the K⁺ channels, letting each current be studied alone.

## The refractory period: one-way and rate-limited

During and just after an action potential, the membrane is in a **[[refractory period]]**:

- Absolute refractory period: while the Na⁺ channels are open or inactivated, no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second action potential.
- Relative refractory period: during the undershoot, a second action potential is possible, but only with a stronger than normal stimulus, because the membrane starts farther from threshold and some Na⁺ channels are still inactivated.

This has two consequences. First, an impulse travels only forward: the patch behind it is refractory, so the current spreading backward can't re-excite it. Second, it caps the firing rate. An absolute refractory period of about 1 ms means a neuron can't fire more than about 1,000 times a second, and most fire far less often.

### Example 2: testing the refractory period

An experimenter stimulates an axon twice and varies the gap between the stimuli. The table shows the smallest second stimulus that fires a second action potential, as a multiple of the normal threshold stimulus.

| Gap between stimuli (ms) | 0.5 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 5.0 | 8.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Second stimulus needed (× threshold) | none works | none works | 2.5 | 1.6 | 1.1 | 1.0 |

Interpretation:

- Up to at least 1.0 ms, no stimulus fires a second spike: that's the absolute refractory period (Na⁺ channels inactivated).
- From about 2 to 5 ms, a second spike is possible but needs more than the normal stimulus: the relative refractory period (undershoot plus partial recovery of Na⁺ channels).
- By 8 ms the axon has fully recovered.
- Prediction: the highest steady firing rate is limited by the absolute refractory period, somewhere between about 1 and 2 ms here, so roughly 500 to 1,000 impulses per second at the very most.

## Myelin and saltatory conduction

In an unmyelinated axon, each patch of membrane must fire in turn, so conduction is slow (about 0.5–2 m/s in thin fibers). Making an axon wider speeds conduction, which is why the squid evolved a giant axon. Vertebrates found a better solution: **[[myelin]]**, layers of membrane wrapped around the axon by Schwann cells (in peripheral nerves) or oligodendrocytes (in the brain and spinal cord). Myelin insulates the axon and lowers its capacitance, so current from one active region spreads quickly and with little loss under the myelin to the next gap. The gaps, the **[[nodes of Ranvier]]**, are packed with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, and the action potential is regenerated only there.

![Two axons compared. A myelinated axon has long yellow myelin segments separated by short gaps labeled nodes of Ranvier, with curved arrows jumping from node to node. Below, an unmyelinated axon has many small arrows showing each patch of membrane firing in turn.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This node-to-node regeneration is **[[saltatory conduction]]** (from the Latin for "to leap"). The impulse doesn't literally jump; the current flows continuously, but the slow step, opening channels, only happens at the nodes. Myelinated fibers conduct at up to about 120 m/s while staying thin, which is how a spinal cord can hold millions of fast axons. In multiple sclerosis, the immune system damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord, and conduction slows or fails.

## Synapses in depth

At a chemical synapse, the electrical signal becomes a chemical one and then electrical again.

![A chemical synapse. An axon terminal at the top holds round synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitter; one vesicle is fusing with the membrane and releasing transmitter into the narrow synaptic cleft. Calcium ions enter through a calcium channel. Transmitter binds receptor channels on the postsynaptic cell below, letting sodium ions in, and a reuptake transporter carries transmitter back into the terminal.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. The action potential reaches the axon terminal and opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.
2. Ca²⁺ flows in (it's far more concentrated outside) and triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.
3. The transmitter diffuses across the cleft (about 20–40 nm) and binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell. Many are ligand-gated ion channels, which open when the transmitter binds.
4. The signal is ended by an enzyme that breaks the transmitter down (acetylcholinesterase, for acetylcholine), by **[[reuptake]]** transporters that pump it back into the terminal, or by diffusion away.

The whole sequence takes about half a millisecond, the synaptic delay.

Whether a synapse excites or inhibits depends on the receptor. If the channel lets in Na⁺, the postsynaptic membrane depolarizes a little: an **[[excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)]]**. If it lets in Cl⁻ or lets out K⁺, the membrane is pushed further from threshold: an **[[inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP)]]**. Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter of the brain; GABA is the main inhibitory one. A single EPSP is usually only a millivolt or so, far short of threshold. A neuron fires only when **[[summation]]** of many inputs, arriving close together in time (temporal summation) or at many synapses at once (spatial summation), brings the axon's starting region (the axon hillock) to threshold. Each neuron is a small calculator, adding thousands of plus and minus signals.

### Drugs and toxins at the synapse

Because each step is a distinct protein, each can be blocked or boosted:

| Agent | Target | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) and local anesthetics such as lidocaine | Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels | Action potentials can't fire, so signals (including pain) are blocked |
| Botulinum toxin | Proteins that let vesicles fuse | No acetylcholine release; muscles are paralyzed |
| Curare | Acetylcholine receptors on muscle | Transmitter can't bind; paralysis |
| Organophosphate nerve agents and some insecticides | Acetylcholinesterase | Acetylcholine builds up; muscles are overstimulated |
| SSRIs (such as fluoxetine) | Serotonin reuptake transporter | Serotonin stays in the cleft longer |
| Cocaine | Reuptake transporters for dopamine and related transmitters | Dopamine signaling is prolonged |
| Benzodiazepines | GABA receptors | Inhibitory GABA signals are strengthened |

These are descriptions of mechanism, not medical advice; how a drug affects a whole person depends on far more than one synapse.

### Example 3: reflex timing

A knee-jerk reflex uses a sensory axon and a motor axon, each about 0.9 m long and conducting at 60 m/s, with one synapse in the spinal cord. Estimate the reflex time, taking 0.5 ms per synapse and ignoring the time for the muscle to contract.

- Conduction: total path $= 0.9 + 0.9 = 1.8$ m; time $= 1.8 / 60 = 0.030$ s $= 30$ ms.
- Synapses: one, so 0.5 ms.
- Total: about 30.5 ms.

Now suppose the same path used unmyelinated fibers conducting at 1 m/s: conduction alone would take 1.8 s. Measured knee-jerk latencies are a few tens of milliseconds, which only fast, myelinated fibers can explain. A withdrawal reflex that passes through one or two interneurons adds only a millisecond or so of synaptic delay, so conduction distance and speed dominate.

## Common mistakes

- Saying the Na⁺/K⁺ pump "creates" the resting potential directly. It builds the gradients; the K⁺ leak produces most of the voltage.
- Thinking the spike stops at the peak because Na⁺ has run out. Na⁺ channels inactivate; the gradients barely change.
- Confusing threshold (about −55 mV) with the resting potential (about −70 mV) or with $E_{\text{K}}$ (about −90 mV).
- Believing myelin carries the impulse. Myelin insulates; the action potential is regenerated at the nodes.
- Thinking one EPSP fires a neuron. Firing needs summation of many inputs.
- Mixing up a drug that blocks reuptake (transmitter stays longer) with one that blocks receptors (transmitter can't act).

## Key points

- The pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) maintains the gradients; K⁺ leak makes the resting potential, close to $E_{\text{K}}$.
- Nernst: $E = \dfrac{61.5}{z}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{out}]}{[\text{in}]}$ mV at 37 °C; the membrane moves toward the equilibrium potential of the most permeable ion.
- Action potential: threshold, Na⁺ in (positive feedback), Na⁺ channels inactivate and K⁺ out, undershoot, rest.
- Refractory periods make conduction one-way and limit firing rate.
- Myelin plus nodes of Ranvier give fast saltatory conduction.
- Synapse: Ca²⁺ in, vesicles release transmitter, receptors respond (EPSP or IPSP), signal ended by enzymes or reuptake. Many drugs act on one of these steps.

lessons.title: Immunology in depth
lessons.body:
## How does the immune system know?

The core lesson on digestion and immunity introduced B cells, T cells, antibodies and memory, and the idea that only the lymphocytes matching an antigen multiply. That raises hard questions. How can the body make a matching lymphocyte for a virus it has never met, perhaps one that didn't exist when you were born? How does a T cell "see" a virus hiding inside a cell? Why does a booster shot work better than the first dose? This lesson answers them, with the experiments behind the answers, and ends with the arithmetic of herd immunity. It's biology, not medical advice.

## Clonal selection

In 1957 Frank Macfarlane Burnet proposed the **[[clonal selection]]** theory, now the foundation of immunology. Its claims:

1. Each lymphocyte carries receptors of a single specificity: every receptor on one B cell binds the same antigen.
2. The specificities are generated randomly, before any antigen is encountered. The body doesn't design receptors to fit a pathogen; it makes a huge random library and waits.
3. When an antigen binds a lymphocyte's receptor (with the right extra signals), that cell is selected: it divides repeatedly, forming a clone of identical cells, most of which become effector cells (antibody-secreting plasma cells, or killer T cells), while some become memory cells.
4. Lymphocytes whose receptors bind the body's own molecules are eliminated or silenced while they develop. This tolerance usually prevents autoimmunity; when it fails, diseases such as type 1 diabetes can result.

### Where the diversity comes from

Humans have only about 20,000 protein-coding genes, yet make millions or more different antibodies. In 1976 Susumu Tonegawa showed why: antibody genes are not inherited in working form. In each developing B cell, DNA is cut and rejoined to pick one segment from each of several sets, a process called **[[V(D)J recombination]]**. The heavy-chain gene is assembled from one V (variable), one D (diversity) and one J (joining) segment; the light-chain gene from one V and one J. T-cell receptor genes are assembled the same way. The joints are also imprecise, with nucleotides added or removed, which multiplies the possibilities further.

### Example 1: counting antibodies

Use approximate counts of functional human gene segments: heavy chain 40 V, 23 D and 6 J; kappa light chain 40 V and 5 J; lambda light chain 30 V and 4 J. How many antibodies can be made from segment choices alone?

- Heavy chains: $40 \times 23 \times 6 = 5{,}520$.
- Light chains: kappa $40 \times 5 = 200$, lambda $30 \times 4 = 120$, so $200 + 120 = 320$ (each B cell uses one or the other, so add).
- Pairs: $5{,}520 \times 320 \approx 1.8$ million.

Imprecise joining raises the potential repertoire by many more orders of magnitude (estimates run from about $10^{12}$ to as many as $10^{18}$ possible antibodies), far more than the number of B cells in a body at any one time, so each person carries only a sample of what is possible. Random generation is how a finite genome meets an unlimited variety of antigens.

## Antibody structure and classes

An antibody is four polypeptides: two identical **[[heavy chains]]** and two identical **[[light chains]]**, held together by disulfide bonds into a Y. Each chain has a **[[variable region]]** at the tip of the arm, where its amino acid sequence differs from one antibody to the next, and a **[[constant region]]**, which is the same for all antibodies of a class. The variable regions of one heavy and one light chain fold together into an antigen-binding site, so each Y has two identical binding sites. Rodney Porter and Gerald Edelman worked out this structure in the late 1950s and 1960s by cutting antibodies with enzymes and separating the chains.

![An antibody drawn as a Y. Two long heavy chains form the stem and the inner part of each arm; two shorter light chains lie along the outside of the arms. The tips of all four chains, the variable regions, are shaded differently from the rest, the constant regions. Disulfide bonds link the chains at the hinge. An antigen is bound at the tip of the left arm.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The stem doesn't bind antigen. It's the "handle" other parts of the immune system grab: phagocytes have receptors for it, and it can trigger complement, blood proteins that punch holes in bacteria. That's how antibodies, which can't kill anything themselves, get pathogens destroyed. They neutralize (block a virus or toxin from attaching), clump pathogens together, coat them so phagocytes engulf them more readily (opsonization), and activate complement.

The heavy-chain constant region defines the **[[antibody class]]**:

| Class | Form | Main features |
|---|---|---|
| IgM | Five Y units joined (10 binding sites) | First class made in a primary response; good at clumping and activating complement |
| IgG | Single Y | Most abundant in blood; dominates secondary responses; crosses the placenta to protect a fetus |
| IgA | In secretions, two Y units joined | In mucus, saliva, tears and breast milk; guards the gut and airways |
| IgE | Single Y | Binds mast cells; defends against parasitic worms; triggers allergic reactions |
| IgD | Single Y | Found mainly on the surface of naive B cells; its role is less well understood |

A B cell starts by making IgM.
