Signals from helper T cells can make it switch to IgG, IgA or IgE, swapping the constant region while keeping the same variable region, so the new antibody binds the same antigen but does a different job. This is **[[class switching]]**. During the same response, the variable-region genes mutate rapidly and B cells whose antibodies bind more tightly are preferentially selected, so the antibodies improve over weeks (affinity maturation).

### Example 2: reading an antibody test

Because IgM comes first and IgG later, tests for each class show how recent an infection is. Interpret three people's results for antibodies to the same virus.

| Person | IgM | IgG |
|---|---|---|
| A | positive | negative |
| B | positive | positive |
| C | negative | positive |

- A: IgM only. A very recent primary infection; there hasn't been time to switch to IgG.
- B: both. Infection within the past several weeks; class switching under way.
- C: IgG only. A past infection (or vaccination); IgM has faded but IgG and memory remain.

Real tests need clinical interpretation, but this is why labs measure the classes separately.

## How T cells see antigen: MHC

B-cell receptors and antibodies bind intact antigens floating free. T cells can't. A T-cell receptor recognizes only a short peptide (a fragment of a protein) held in a groove of a cell-surface protein encoded by the **[[major histocompatibility complex (MHC)]]**. In humans they're called HLA, the proteins matched in organ transplants.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Two routes of antigen presentation
  accDescr: Left route: a virus makes proteins inside an infected body cell; the cell cuts some into peptides and displays them on MHC class I, which any nucleated cell has; a cytotoxic T cell with the matching receptor, a CD8 cell, recognizes the complex and kills the infected cell. Right route: an antigen-presenting cell such as a dendritic cell engulfs a microbe; it displays peptides from it on MHC class II; a helper T cell with the matching receptor, a CD4 cell, recognizes the complex and is activated, releasing cytokines that help B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
  V["Virus proteins made inside an infected cell"] --> I["Peptides shown on MHC class I (all nucleated cells)"]
  I --> K["Matching cytotoxic T cell (CD8) kills the cell"]
  E["Microbe engulfed by an antigen-presenting cell"] --> II["Peptides shown on MHC class II (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells)"]
  II --> H["Matching helper T cell (CD4) activated"]
  H --> Cy["Cytokines help B cells and cytotoxic T cells"]
```

- MHC class I is on almost every nucleated cell. It displays peptides from proteins made inside that cell. Normally they're self peptides and are ignored, but in a virus-infected or cancerous cell some are foreign or abnormal, and a **[[cytotoxic T cell]]** (marked by the CD8 protein) with a matching receptor kills the cell. It releases perforin, which makes pores in the target's membrane, and enzymes called granzymes that enter and trigger apoptosis, the cell's own self-destruct program.
- MHC class II is on **[[antigen-presenting cells]]**: dendritic cells (the most important for starting a response), macrophages and B cells. They display peptides from material they've engulfed. A **[[helper T cell]]** (marked by CD4) with a matching receptor is activated and releases **[[cytokines]]**, signaling proteins that switch on B cells, cytotoxic T cells and macrophages.

Dendritic cells carry antigen from tissues to lymph nodes, where the rare matching T cells wait. A B cell is fully activated only when a helper T cell recognizes a peptide from the same antigen on that B cell's class II MHC, a double check that guards against attacking the body's own molecules.

### Example 3: the MHC restriction experiment

In 1974 Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty infected mice of strain A with a virus and collected their cytotoxic T cells. They mixed the T cells with infected or uninfected target cells from different mouse strains and measured how many targets were killed. Results in the pattern they found (illustrative numbers):

| Target cells | Target killed |
|---|---|
| Strain A, infected | 60% |
| Strain A, uninfected | 3% |
| Strain B (different MHC), infected with the same virus | 4% |
| Strain B, uninfected | 3% |

What do the results show?

- Infected strain A cells were killed but uninfected ones weren't: the T cells are specific for the virus.
- Infected strain B cells weren't killed, even though they carried the same virus: the T cells recognize the viral antigen only together with their own strain's MHC.
- Conclusion: T-cell recognition is "MHC restricted": the receptor sees peptide plus self-MHC as one shape. They shared the 1996 Nobel Prize for this.

## Memory and vaccines

After an infection clears, most effector cells die, but memory B and T cells persist for years or decades. They outnumber the naive cells of the same specificity that started the response, respond to less antigen, and (for B cells) have usually already switched class and improved their affinity. That's why a secondary response is faster, larger and mostly IgG. A booster dose works the same way: it triggers a secondary response that expands memory and raises antibody levels.

Vaccine design follows the biology:

- Live attenuated vaccines (measles, mumps and rubella) replicate a little inside cells, so their proteins are shown on class I MHC as well as class II. They tend to produce strong cytotoxic T-cell and antibody responses, often lasting, from one or two doses. They're generally not given to people with weakened immunity.
- Inactivated, subunit and toxoid vaccines (most flu shots, hepatitis B, tetanus) can't replicate. They mainly drive class II presentation and antibodies, and usually need several doses or boosters; subunit and toxoid vaccines usually also contain adjuvants (ingredients that alert innate immunity), though most flu shots do not.
- mRNA and viral-vector vaccines have cells make one viral protein for a short time, so it's presented on both class I and class II.

**[[Passive immunity]]** is protection from antibodies made by someone else: IgG crossing the placenta, IgA in breast milk, or manufactured antibodies given as treatment. It works immediately but fades over weeks to months, because no memory cells are made.

## Herd immunity: the arithmetic

The basic reproduction number $R_0$ is the average number of people one case infects in a population with no immunity. If a fraction $s$ of the population is still susceptible, each case infects on average

$$R_{\text{eff}} = R_0 \times s$$

others, the effective reproduction number. An outbreak grows while $R_{\text{eff}} > 1$ and shrinks when $R_{\text{eff}} < 1$. Setting $R_0 \times s = 1$ gives $s = 1/R_0$, so the immune fraction must exceed $1 - 1/R_0$, the herd immunity threshold from the core lesson. If a vaccine protects a fraction $E$ of those who get it, coverage $V$ gives an immune fraction of $V \times E$, so the needed coverage is $(1 - 1/R_0)/E$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 20], "y": [0, 100], "xLabel": "basic reproduction number R0", "yLabel": "immune share needed (%)", "functions": [{"f": "100*(1 - 1/x)", "from": 1, "to": 20, "label": "threshold 1 − 1/R0"}], "points": [{"at": [2, 50], "label": "R0 = 2: 50%"}, {"at": [4, 75], "label": "R0 = 4: 75%"}, {"at": [15, 93.3], "label": "R0 = 15: 93%"}], "caption": "Herd immunity threshold rises steeply at first, then levels off near 100%"}
```

### Example 4: will an outbreak spread?

A disease has $R_0 = 4$. In one town 70% of people are vaccinated with a vaccine that protects 90% of recipients, and no one else is immune. Ten cases arrive. Will the outbreak grow, and what coverage would stop it?

- Immune fraction: $0.70 \times 0.90 = 0.63$, so $s = 0.37$.
- $R_{\text{eff}} = 4 \times 0.37 = 1.48 > 1$: the outbreak grows. Ten cases become about $10 \times 1.48^3 \approx 32$ after three generations of spread (ignoring chance).
- Needed: $1 - 1/4 = 0.75$ immune, so coverage $= 0.75 / 0.90 \approx 83.3\%$.
- With a vaccine only 70% effective, the needed coverage would be $0.75 / 0.70 \approx 107\%$, impossible: vaccination alone couldn't stop spread, and other measures or a better vaccine would be needed.

These formulas assume everyone mixes evenly and that immunity fully blocks infection and doesn't wane. In real populations, clusters of unvaccinated people can have a local $R_{\text{eff}}$ above 1 even when national coverage looks high, and $R_0$ depends on how people live and gather. The threshold is a guide, not a guarantee. The epidemiology lesson in the honors modules develops these models further.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking antigen "instructs" a lymphocyte to build a matching receptor. Receptors are made randomly first; antigen selects among them.
- Calling the whole antibody "variable." Only the tips of the arms vary; the stem's class decides what the antibody does.
- Saying T cells recognize whole viruses. They recognize peptides presented on MHC.
- Mixing up the classes: class I (all nucleated cells, to CD8 killers) vs class II (antigen-presenting cells, to CD4 helpers).
- Treating passive immunity as long lasting. Without memory cells it fades.
- Forgetting vaccine effectiveness: coverage needed is the threshold divided by effectiveness.

## Key points

- Clonal selection: a random, pre-made library of lymphocytes; antigen selects and expands matching clones; self-reactive cells are removed.
- V(D)J recombination of gene segments, plus imprecise joining, generates enormous receptor diversity.
- Antibodies: two heavy and two light chains; variable regions bind antigen, the constant region sets the class (IgM first, IgG most abundant, IgA in secretions, IgE in allergy and parasites).
- MHC I shows inside proteins to cytotoxic (CD8) T cells; MHC II on antigen-presenting cells shows engulfed material to helper (CD4) T cells, which release cytokines.
- Memory cells make secondary responses fast and large; vaccines and boosters exploit this.
- $R_{\text{eff}} = R_0 s$; herd immunity threshold $1 - 1/R_0$; needed coverage $(1 - 1/R_0)/E$.

lessons.title: Hormones and feedback in depth
lessons.body:
## From "a hormone travels in the blood" to how it works

The homeostasis lesson defined a hormone as a chemical messenger carried in the blood to target cells with matching receptors, and used insulin and glucagon as the classic negative feedback pair. This honors lesson asks what happens at the target cell, how the brain runs a chain of glands, how the pancreas senses glucose, how ADH sets the concentration of urine, and how to read hormone data the way a clinician or researcher does. It's biology, not medical advice.

## Two ways to deliver a message

Hormones fall into two broad groups by how they dissolve.

![Two target cells compared. On the left, a peptide hormone binds a receptor on the cell surface; inside, a second messenger such as cAMP activates an enzyme cascade that changes existing proteins within seconds to minutes. On the right, a steroid hormone diffuses across the membrane, binds a receptor inside the cell, and the hormone-receptor complex enters the nucleus and binds DNA, switching genes on or off so that new proteins are made over hours to days.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- A **[[peptide hormone]]** (insulin, glucagon, ADH, growth hormone) is water-soluble. It travels freely in plasma but can't cross the lipid bilayer, so it binds a receptor on the target cell's surface. The receptor relays the signal inward, often by making a second messenger such as cyclic AMP (cAMP), which activates enzymes that activate more enzymes. Each step multiplies the signal, so a few hormone molecules can change thousands of enzyme molecules within seconds to minutes. Amine hormones such as adrenaline (epinephrine) work the same way.
- A **[[steroid hormone]]** (cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, testosterone) is made from cholesterol and is lipid-soluble. It rides in the blood bound to carrier proteins, slips through the membrane, and binds a receptor inside the cell (in the cytoplasm or the nucleus). The hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, switching particular genes on or off. Effects take hours, because new mRNA and protein must be made, and they can last days. Thyroid hormones, though not steroids, also act through receptors inside the cell.

How long a hormone acts also depends on how fast it is removed. Insulin has a half-life in the blood of only about 5 minutes; cortisol, about an hour or more; the main thyroid hormone T4, about a week. A short half-life lets a level change quickly when secretion changes.

### Example 1: a short half-life

After a meal, a person's insulin level is 80 µU/mL (microunits per milliliter), and then secretion suddenly stops. With a half-life of 5 minutes, what is the level 15 minutes later?

- 15 minutes is $15/5 = 3$ half-lives.
- Level $= 80 \times (1/2)^3 = 80/8 = 10$ µU/mL.

Within a quarter of an hour, almost 90% is gone. Glucose control needs exactly this: the pancreas can raise or drop the signal within minutes.

## The hypothalamus and pituitary

Many glands answer to a two-part control center at the base of the brain. The **[[hypothalamus]]** is brain tissue that senses the blood (temperature, osmolality, hormone levels) and receives input from the rest of the brain. Below it hangs the pituitary, which has two parts with very different origins:

- The **[[posterior pituitary]]** is really an extension of the brain. Hypothalamic neurons make ADH and oxytocin, send them down their axons and release them into the blood there. These are hormones released by neurons.
- The **[[anterior pituitary]]** is a true gland. The hypothalamus controls it with releasing hormones carried a short distance through a private set of portal blood vessels. Each releasing hormone tells the anterior pituitary to secrete a **[[tropic hormone]]**, a hormone whose target is another endocrine gland.

The chains are called axes. The hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis is typical:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis
  accDescr: The hypothalamus releases TRH, which travels through small portal blood vessels to the anterior pituitary. The pituitary releases TSH into the blood, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release the thyroid hormones T4 and T3. These raise metabolic rate in body cells. Dashed arrows show negative feedback: thyroid hormones inhibit both the pituitary and the hypothalamus, so TSH and TRH fall when thyroid hormone is high.
  Hy["Hypothalamus"] -- "TRH" --> P["Anterior pituitary"]
  P -- "TSH" --> Th["Thyroid gland"]
  Th -- "T4 and T3" --> C["Body cells: metabolic rate rises"]
  Th -. "inhibits" .-> P
  Th -. "inhibits" .-> Hy
```

Other axes follow the same pattern: CRH → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol (the stress axis), and GnRH → LH and FSH → ovaries or testes → sex hormones. The final hormone feeds back to inhibit the earlier steps, so the whole chain holds the final hormone near a set point. A chain also amplifies: a tiny amount of releasing hormone leads to much larger amounts of the final hormone.

### Example 2: where is the fault?

Doctors read the axis backward from blood tests. TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) comes from the pituitary; T4 from the thyroid. Using the feedback loop, find the likely site of the problem.

| Patient | TSH | T4 | Reasoning | Likely problem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | High | Low | Little T4, so little feedback; the pituitary shouts louder | Thyroid underactive (primary hypothyroidism) |
| B | Low | High | Plenty of T4 is suppressing the pituitary, yet T4 stays high | Thyroid overactive on its own (primary hyperthyroidism) |
| C | Low | Low | T4 is low but the pituitary isn't responding | Pituitary or hypothalamus failing (secondary) |

Real cases make this concrete. In iodine deficiency, the thyroid can't make enough T4 (each molecule contains four iodine atoms), TSH stays high, and the constant stimulation enlarges the gland into a goiter. In Graves' disease, antibodies bind and switch on the TSH receptor, mimicking TSH, so the thyroid overproduces while real TSH falls to almost nothing: patient B's pattern.

## Glucose regulation in depth

### How a beta cell senses glucose

Beta cells don't have a glucose receptor in the usual sense. They measure glucose by burning it:

1. Glucose enters the beta cell through transporters, in proportion to its blood level.
2. Glycolysis and respiration raise the cell's ATP.
3. ATP closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, so less K⁺ leaks out.
4. The membrane depolarizes, opening voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.
5. Ca²⁺ flows in and triggers exocytosis of insulin granules.

This is the same logic as a neuron (lesson on neurons): a change in K⁺ permeability shifts the voltage, and Ca²⁺ entry triggers release. Sulfonylurea drugs for type 2 diabetes act by closing the same K⁺ channels.

In muscle and fat cells, insulin binds a receptor that is itself an enzyme (a tyrosine kinase), and the signal moves **[[GLUT4]]** glucose transporters from internal vesicles into the plasma membrane, so glucose uptake rises severalfold. In the liver, insulin switches on glycogen and fat synthesis and switches off glucose release. Glucagon, through a surface receptor and cAMP, does the opposite in the liver: it promotes glycogen breakdown and the making of new glucose. Muscle has no glucagon receptors, so muscle glycogen fuels only the muscle itself.

### Diabetes types

- Type 1 (about 5–10% of diagnosed cases): autoimmune destruction of beta cells, so insulin is low or absent.
- Type 2 (about 90–95%): insulin resistance (for example, fewer GLUT4 transporters reach the membrane in response to insulin), at first compensated by extra insulin, until beta cells can no longer keep up.
- Gestational diabetes: high glucose first appearing in pregnancy, as placental hormones increase insulin resistance; it usually resolves after birth but raises later type 2 risk.

When blood glucose exceeds about 180 mg/dL, the kidney's glucose carriers are saturated and glucose spills into urine, pulling water with it: that's why untreated diabetes causes frequent urination and thirst.

### Example 3: reading a glucose tolerance test

Clinical criteria (American Diabetes Association) for an oral glucose tolerance test: fasting glucose under 100 mg/dL is normal, 100–125 is prediabetes, 126 or more suggests diabetes; two hours after a 75 g glucose drink, under 140 is normal, 140–199 is prediabetes, 200 or more suggests diabetes. A diagnosis needs confirmation, usually by a repeat test. Classify these results.

| Person | Fasting glucose | 2-hour glucose | Fasting insulin |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 92 | 118 | normal |
| Q | 112 | 168 | high |
| R | 138 | 245 | very low |
| S | 131 | 226 | high |

- P: both normal.
- Q: prediabetes on both measures; high insulin suggests the body is compensating for insulin resistance.
- R: diabetes range on both, with almost no insulin: the pattern of type 1.
- S: diabetes range, but with plenty of insulin that isn't working: the pattern of type 2.

## ADH and the kidney

**[[Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)]]**, also called vasopressin, is the main control on water. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus track plasma osmolality, the concentration of dissolved particles (normally about 285–295 mOsm/kg). A rise of just 1–2% increases ADH release from the posterior pituitary. ADH binds receptors on collecting-duct cells and, through cAMP, inserts **[[aquaporins]]**, water channel proteins, into their membranes. Water then flows out of the duct into the very salty tissue deep in the kidney, and urine can become as concentrated as about 1,200 mOsm/kg. With no ADH the ducts stay nearly watertight and urine can be as dilute as about 50 mOsm/kg. Alcohol suppresses ADH release, which is why it increases urine output.

In **[[diabetes insipidus]]** ("tasteless" diabetes, unrelated to insulin), the ADH signal fails and large volumes of dilute urine are made. In central diabetes insipidus the pituitary makes too little ADH; in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the kidney doesn't respond to it. Giving a synthetic ADH (desmopressin) tells them apart: urine concentrates in the central form but barely changes in the nephrogenic form. Since 2022, endocrine societies have recommended new names for these two conditions, arginine vasopressin deficiency (central) and arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic), partly to avoid confusion with diabetes mellitus; you will see both sets of names.

### Example 4: the smallest possible urine volume

A person must excrete about 600 mOsm of solutes (urea, salts) a day. If the kidneys can concentrate urine to at most 1,200 mOsm/kg (about 1,200 mOsm per liter), what is the least urine they can make? How much in diabetes insipidus with urine stuck at 150 mOsm/kg?

- Minimum volume $= \dfrac{600 \text{ mOsm}}{1200 \text{ mOsm/L}} = 0.5$ L per day.
- At 150 mOsm/kg: $600/150 = 4$ L per day, eight times as much, and the person must drink to match it.

## Negative and positive feedback in the data

Most axes are negative feedback, but some switch. Estrogen normally inhibits GnRH and LH. Yet when estrogen stays high for a day or two late in the ovarian cycle, it flips to positive feedback and triggers a surge of LH that causes ovulation. Typical values (illustrative):

| Cycle day | 6 | 9 | 11 | 12 | 13 | 14 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Estradiol (pg/mL) | 50 | 100 | 180 | 250 | 300 | 200 | 120 |
| LH (IU/L) | 6 | 6 | 7 | 10 | 45 | 25 | 8 |

Read it the way an endocrinologist would. From day 6 to 11, estradiol more than triples while LH barely moves: negative feedback is holding LH down. Once estradiol has been high (above about 200) for a day or more, LH jumps roughly fourfold in a day: positive feedback. The surge is brief because LH itself changes the follicle, which switches from making mostly estradiol to making progesterone; the stimulus falls away, and ovulation follows about a day and a half after the surge begins. As with oxytocin in childbirth, the event the loop drives is what ends it.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking steroid hormones act through cAMP. Most act on receptors inside the cell and change gene expression.
- Assuming high TSH means an overactive thyroid. High TSH usually means the thyroid is underactive and the pituitary is pushing harder.
- Mixing up diabetes mellitus (glucose, insulin) and diabetes insipidus (water, ADH).
- Saying insulin lets glucose into every cell. It mainly increases uptake in muscle and fat (GLUT4); brain cells take up glucose without it.
- Treating positive feedback as rare or harmful. It's normal for events that must finish: ovulation, birth, clotting.

## Key points

- Peptide hormones bind surface receptors, use second messengers and act fast; steroid hormones bind internal receptors and change gene expression slowly.
- The hypothalamus controls the posterior pituitary through neurons and the anterior pituitary through releasing hormones; axes end in negative feedback.
- Read axis lab tests backward: high TSH with low T4 points to the thyroid; low TSH with low T4 to the pituitary.
- Beta cells sense glucose through ATP closing K⁺ channels; insulin moves GLUT4 to the membrane; type 1 lacks insulin, type 2 resists it.
- ADH inserts aquaporins in collecting ducts; minimum urine volume = solute load ÷ maximum urine concentration.
- Estrogen switches from negative to positive feedback to trigger the LH surge.

lessons.title: Ecosystems and energy flow
lessons.body:
## From one body to a whole ecosystem

The last lesson followed food through a single body: digestion breaks it down, and the energy in it ends up powering cells. Ecology asks the same question at a larger scale. Where did that food's energy come from, where does it go after you use it, and why can a meadow feed thousands of grasshoppers but only a few hawks? This module studies organisms together with their surroundings. This first lesson follows energy through an ecosystem and turns the answers into numbers you can calculate with.

## What an ecosystem is made of

An ecosystem has two kinds of parts. **[[Biotic factors]]** are the living parts and their products: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, fallen leaves, dung. **[[Abiotic factors]]** are the nonliving conditions: sunlight, temperature, water, soil minerals, pH, salinity, wind. The two shape each other. Rainfall decides which plants can grow; the plants then shade the soil, hold water and change the local temperature.

Ecologists group organisms by how they get energy:

- **[[Producers]]** make their own organic molecules, almost always by photosynthesis (plants, algae, cyanobacteria). In deep-sea vents and caves, some bacteria and archaea are producers by chemosynthesis, using energy from chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide.
- Consumers get energy by eating other organisms. Herbivores (primary consumers) eat producers, carnivores eat animals, and omnivores eat both.
- **[[Decomposers]]**, mainly bacteria and fungi, break down dead material and wastes, releasing simple nutrients back to the soil and water. Animals such as earthworms and millipedes that eat dead material help by shredding it.

Each feeding step is a **[[trophic level]]** (from the Greek *trophē*, "nourishment"). Producers are level 1, primary consumers level 2, secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) level 3, and tertiary consumers level 4. A single path such as grass → grasshopper → shrew → owl is a food chain. Real organisms eat many things and are eaten by many things, so ecologists draw a **[[food web]]**: all the feeding links in a community. An omnivore such as a bear can sit at several trophic levels at once, eating berries (level 2) and salmon (level 4 or higher, since salmon themselves eat other animals).

Arrows in food chains and webs point in the direction energy moves: from the food to the eater. "Grass → rabbit" means the rabbit eats the grass.

The food web below is a simplified meadow. Trace any path from a producer to the owl and you have a food chain; the owl sits at level 3 when it eats a mouse but at level 4 when it eats a snake that ate a mouse. Dead remains and wastes from every organism, not just the two shown with dashed arrows, end up with the decomposers.

![A meadow food web. Grass and an oak tree are at the bottom. Grass is eaten by a grasshopper, a rabbit and a mouse; acorns from the oak are eaten by the mouse. The grasshopper is eaten by a shrew; the mouse by a snake, a fox and an owl; the rabbit by the fox; the shrew and the snake by the owl. Dashed arrows lead from the oak tree and the fox to fungi and bacteria, labeled dead remains and wastes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Where the energy comes from: primary productivity

Almost all energy in ecosystems starts as sunlight captured by producers. Only a small fraction of the sunlight reaching a field, typically around 1%, ends up stored in plant molecules; the rest is reflected, passes through, or evaporates water.

The total rate at which producers capture energy is the gross primary productivity (GPP). Producers burn part of that sugar in their own cellular respiration to stay alive and grow. What remains, stored as new tissue that consumers can eat, is the **[[net primary productivity]]** (NPP):

$$\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R_{\text{producers}}$$

NPP is usually reported as energy (kJ per m² per year) or as dry mass (g per m² per year). It is highest in tropical rainforests, coral reefs, estuaries and wetlands, where light, warmth, water and nutrients are all plentiful, and lowest in deserts, tundra and the open ocean. The open ocean still contributes a large share of Earth's total because it is so vast.

### Example 1

A pond's algae capture 25,000 kJ per m² per year (GPP) and use 14,000 kJ per m² per year in respiration. What is the NPP, and what fraction of the captured energy is available to consumers?

1. NPP = GPP − respiration = 25,000 − 14,000 = 11,000 kJ per m² per year.
2. Fraction available: $\tfrac{11{,}000}{25{,}000} = 0.44$, or 44%.

So less than half of what the algae captured is ever on the menu for the pond's animals.

## Why only about 10% passes up each level

When a rabbit eats grass, most of the energy in that grass never becomes rabbit. Three things happen to it:

1. *Not all of it is eaten.* Roots, woody stems and leaves the rabbit never reaches stay behind (and eventually feed decomposers).
2. *Not all that is eaten is absorbed.* Cellulose and other hard-to-digest material leaves as feces.
3. *Most of what is absorbed is used, not stored.* The rabbit spends it on cellular respiration to run its muscles, keep warm and repair cells, and that energy ends as heat that radiates away. Only the remainder builds new rabbit tissue that a fox could eat.

The flowchart follows those three branches.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where the energy in eaten grass goes
  accDescr: The energy stored in grass splits several ways. Parts that are not eaten, such as roots and woody stems, go to decomposers. Of the part a rabbit eats, material it cannot digest leaves as feces and also goes to decomposers. Of the energy the rabbit absorbs, most is used in cellular respiration and leaves the ecosystem as heat. Only a small share builds new rabbit tissue, which is what the next trophic level can eat; overall, roughly 10 percent of the energy in one trophic level ends up in the next.
  G["Energy stored in grass"] --> N["Not eaten: roots, woody stems"]
  G --> E["Eaten by a rabbit"]
  E --> F["Not absorbed: leaves in feces"]
  E --> A["Absorbed into the body"]
  N --> D["Decomposers"]
  F --> D
  A --> R["Used in cellular respiration"]
  R --> H["Lost as heat"]
  A --> T["New rabbit tissue: a small share"]
  T --> X["Food for the next trophic level"]
```

The result is the **[[ten percent rule]]**: on average, about 10% of the energy at one trophic level becomes available at the next. Real values range from under 1% to around 20%. Endotherms such as birds and mammals usually pass on less than ectotherms such as insects and fish, because keeping a body warm costs so much energy.

Two big consequences follow. First, energy flows *one way* through an ecosystem: sunlight in, heat out. It is not recycled, so ecosystems need a constant input of sunlight. Matter is different: carbon, nitrogen and other atoms are recycled again and again, which is the subject of the next lesson. Second, food chains are short. After four or five levels so little energy remains that another level of predators could not find enough to eat.

The classic evidence came from studies that measured every level of a real ecosystem. Raymond Lindeman's study of Cedar Bog Lake in Minnesota (published 1942) first described ecosystems as trophic levels passing energy along with losses at each step. Howard Odum's study of Silver Springs, Florida (1957) measured the energy flow in detail. Rounded, his figures for gross production were:

| Trophic level | Energy (kcal per m² per year) |
|---|---|
| Producers | 20,810 |
| Herbivores | 3,368 |
| Carnivores | 383 |
| Top carnivores | 21 |

From producers to herbivores, $\tfrac{3368}{20{,}810} \approx 16\%$; from herbivores to carnivores, about 11%; from carnivores to top carnivores, about 5.5%. The exact percentage varies, but the steep drop at every step is always there.

## Ecological pyramids

Drawing each trophic level as a bar whose width shows its size gives an ecological pyramid. There are three kinds.

- *Pyramid of energy*: energy flowing through each level per unit area per year. Because energy is lost at every step, this pyramid is *always* upright.
- *Pyramid of biomass*: the **[[biomass]]**, the total dry mass of living organisms, present in each level at one moment (for example, g per m²). Usually upright, but it can be inverted. In the open ocean, the phytoplankton present at any moment can weigh less than the zooplankton eating them, because the phytoplankton reproduce so fast that they are eaten and replaced many times a year.
- *Pyramid of numbers*: how many individuals are in each level. It can be inverted too: a single oak tree supports thousands of caterpillars.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[-5, 0], [5, 0], [5, 1], [-5, 1]]}, {"points": [[-3.75, 1.2], [3.75, 1.2], [3.75, 2.2], [-3.75, 2.2]]}, {"points": [[-2.5, 2.4], [2.5, 2.4], [2.5, 3.4], [-2.5, 3.4]]}, {"points": [[-1.25, 3.6], [1.25, 3.6], [1.25, 4.6], [-1.25, 4.6]]}], "labels": [{"at": [0, 0.5], "text": "Producers: 10,000 kJ"}, {"at": [0, 1.7], "text": "Primary: 1,000 kJ"}, {"at": [0, 2.9], "text": "Secondary: 100 kJ"}, {"at": [0, 4.1], "text": "Tertiary: 10"}], "caption": "Pyramid of energy with 10% transfer (widths not to scale; true widths would shrink tenfold per level)"}
```

### Example 2

The producers in a grassland store 50,000 kJ per m² per year. Using the ten percent rule, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?

Each step up keeps 10%, that is, multiply by 0.1:

1. Primary consumers: $50{,}000 \times 0.1 = 5{,}000$ kJ.
2. Secondary consumers: $5{,}000 \times 0.1 = 500$ kJ.
3. Tertiary consumers: $500 \times 0.1 = 50$ kJ per m² per year.

In one line: $50{,}000 \times 0.1^3 = 50$. Tertiary consumers are three steps above producers, so the exponent is 3, not 4. Counting levels instead of steps is the most common slip.

### Example 3

A farm field produces crops containing 9.0 million kJ of food energy per year. A person needs about 3.0 million kJ per year (roughly 8,200 kJ, or 2,000 Calories, per day). Compare how many people the field can feed if people eat the crops directly versus feeding them to livestock and eating the meat (assume 10% transfer).

1. Eating crops: $\tfrac{9.0 \text{ million}}{3.0 \text{ million}} = 3$ people.
2. Through livestock: the animals keep $9.0 \times 0.1 = 0.90$ million kJ, which feeds $\tfrac{0.90}{3.0} = 0.3$ of a person.

Eating one trophic level lower feeds ten times as many people from the same land. (Real figures differ by animal: chickens convert feed more efficiently than cattle. The direction of the result does not change.)

### Example 4

To estimate the biomass of grass in a 2.0-hectare meadow (1 hectare = 10,000 m²), a student clips all the plants in five 0.25 m² quadrats, dries them in an oven, and weighs them: 60, 75, 70, 55 and 65 g.

1. Mean dry mass per quadrat: $\tfrac{60 + 75 + 70 + 55 + 65}{5} = 65$ g.
2. Biomass per square meter: $\tfrac{65 \text{ g}}{0.25 \text{ m}^2} = 260$ g per m².
3. Meadow area: $2.0 \times 10{,}000 = 20{,}000$ m².
4. Total: $260 \times 20{,}000 = 5{,}200{,}000$ g $=$ 5,200 kg of dry grass.

Biomass is measured as *dry* mass because water content varies so much with weather and time of day.

## Common mistakes

- Drawing food-chain arrows from the eater to the food. The arrow shows energy moving, so it points to the eater.
- Saying energy is recycled. Matter cycles; energy flows through once and leaves as heat.
- Thinking the "lost" 90% is destroyed. It is not destroyed (energy is conserved); most becomes heat from respiration, and the rest goes to decomposers in uneaten parts and feces.
- Using the wrong exponent with the ten percent rule. From level 1 to level 4 is three transfers: multiply by $0.1^3$.
- Assuming every pyramid must be upright. Only the energy pyramid always is.
- Confusing GPP and NPP. Consumers can only eat what is left after the producers' own respiration.

## Key points

- Ecosystems contain biotic and abiotic factors that affect each other.
- Producers capture energy; consumers eat other organisms; decomposers return nutrients from dead material.
- NPP = GPP − producer respiration; it is the energy available to consumers.
- About 10% (roughly 1–20%) of the energy in one trophic level reaches the next; the rest is mostly lost as heat from respiration.
- Energy flows one way through ecosystems; matter cycles.
- Energy pyramids are always upright; biomass and numbers pyramids can be inverted.

lessons.title: Matter cycles and population growth
lessons.body:
## Energy flows, matter cycles

The last lesson ended with a contrast: energy passes through an ecosystem once and leaves as heat, but matter is reused. The carbon atoms in your body have been part of air, plants, dinosaurs and ocean rock. This lesson follows two of those atoms, carbon and nitrogen, around their cycles, then turns to the question of how many organisms an ecosystem can hold: how populations grow, what stops them, and how ecologists count them.

## Biogeochemical cycles

A **[[biogeochemical cycle]]** is the path an element or compound takes as it moves between living things (*bio*), rocks, soil, water and air (*geo*), changing chemical form (*chemical*) along the way. Each cycle has reservoirs, places where the substance is stored, and fluxes, the processes that move it between reservoirs. Some reservoirs turn over quickly (carbon in the air is exchanged with plants within years); others hold material for millions of years (carbon locked in limestone).

The water cycle is the simplest: evaporation and transpiration from plants carry water up, condensation and precipitation bring it down, and runoff and groundwater return it to the oceans. Water also carries dissolved nutrients, linking the other cycles. The sun powers the whole cycle by evaporating water; gravity brings it back down and downhill.

![The water cycle. The sun shines on an ocean at left and land with a tree and a mountain at right. Wavy arrows rise from the ocean to a cloud (evaporation), and an arrow rises from the tree to the cloud (transpiration). Water vapor forms the cloud (condensation) and drifts to a second cloud over the mountain, where rain falls (precipitation). An arrow runs down the land surface into the ocean (runoff), and a dashed arrow underground carries groundwater to the ocean.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The carbon cycle

Carbon is the backbone of every organic molecule. Its main fluxes are two processes you studied in the energy module:

- Photosynthesis takes CO₂ out of the air (or water) and builds it into sugars, the entry point of carbon into food webs.
- Cellular respiration, by producers, consumers and especially decomposers, releases CO₂ back.

Other parts of the cycle:

- The ocean dissolves CO₂ at its surface. Marine organisms build shells of calcium carbonate, and over geologic time these settle and form limestone, a huge slow reservoir.
- Under some conditions dead organisms are buried before they decompose. Over millions of years heat and pressure turn them into coal, oil and natural gas: fossil fuels.
- Combustion of fossil fuels and wood, and volcanic eruptions, return carbon to the air.

The diagram puts these reservoirs and fluxes together. The fast cycle (top) runs through living things in years to centuries; the slow cycle (bottom) runs through fossil fuels and rock over millions of years.

![The carbon cycle. Atmospheric carbon dioxide is at the top. On land, photosynthesis moves carbon into plants; plants are eaten by animals; plants and animals return CO₂ by respiration; their dead matter and wastes go to soil and decomposers, which return CO₂ by decomposition; some dead matter is buried and becomes fossil fuels, which return CO₂ by combustion. In the ocean, CO₂ dissolves into and is released from seawater; marine life takes it up by photosynthesis and returns it by respiration; shells and remains settle into limestone and sediments, which return CO₂ through volcanoes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before industrialization, the fluxes in and out of the atmosphere were nearly balanced. Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from a slow reservoir into the fast cycle. Fossil fuel use released roughly 37 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2024. About half of the CO₂ humans emit stays in the air; the oceans and land plants absorb the rest. As a result, atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million (ppm) before 1750 to about 424 ppm (global average) in 2024. The dissolved CO₂ also makes seawater more acidic, which makes building carbonate shells harder.

The best evidence for the cycle's living side comes from the Keeling curve, the CO₂ record kept at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958. Besides its steady rise, the curve wiggles every year: CO₂ falls during the Northern Hemisphere's spring and summer, when its vast forests photosynthesize, and rises in fall and winter, when respiration and decay dominate. The planet's land plants visibly "breathe."

## The nitrogen cycle

Nitrogen is needed for proteins and nucleic acids. The air is 78% nitrogen gas (N₂), but its triple bond is so strong that plants and animals cannot use it. Nitrogen enters food webs only after it is converted to other forms, almost entirely by bacteria.

1. **[[Nitrogen fixation]]** converts N₂ into ammonia (NH₃) or ammonium (NH₄⁺). Some bacteria do this in soil and water (including cyanobacteria); others, such as *Rhizobium*, live in root nodules of legumes (beans, peas, clover) and trade fixed nitrogen for sugar. Lightning fixes a little. Since the early 1900s, the industrial Haber–Bosch process has fixed nitrogen for fertilizer; it now fixes roughly as much nitrogen as all natural processes on land, or more by some recent estimates.
2. Decomposers release ammonium from dead organisms and wastes (ammonification).
3. Nitrifying bacteria oxidize ammonium to nitrite (NO₂⁻) and then nitrate (NO₃⁻), a process called nitrification.
4. Plants absorb ammonium and nitrate and build them into amino acids and nucleotides; animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
5. **[[Denitrification]]**: in waterlogged, low-oxygen soils, denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back to N₂, closing the cycle.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The nitrogen cycle
  accDescr: Nitrogen gas in the air is converted to ammonium by nitrogen fixation, carried out by bacteria, lightning and the industrial Haber-Bosch process. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate. Plants absorb both ammonium and nitrate; animals get nitrogen by eating plants. Dead matter and wastes from plants and animals are broken down by decomposers, releasing ammonium again, a step called ammonification. In waterlogged, low-oxygen soils, denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, closing the cycle.
  N2["Nitrogen gas N₂ in the air"] -- "nitrogen fixation" --> NH4["Ammonium NH₄⁺"]
  NH4 -- "nitrification" --> NO3["Nitrate NO₃⁻"]
  NH4 -- "absorbed" --> P["Plants"]
  NO3 -- "absorbed" --> P
  P -- "eaten" --> A["Animals"]
  P --> DW["Dead matter and wastes"]
  A --> DW
  DW -- "ammonification" --> NH4
  NO3 -- "denitrification" --> N2
```

Follow the diagram around once: every nitrogen atom in your proteins was fixed from the air by a microbe or a factory, passed through plants, and will eventually return to the air by denitrification.

Excess fertilizer washes into rivers and coasts. The extra nitrate feeds algal blooms; when the algae die, decomposers use up the dissolved oxygen, creating low-oxygen "dead zones" such as the one that forms most summers in the Gulf of Mexico. This process is eutrophication. The phosphorus cycle, by contrast, has no gas stage: phosphorus moves from weathering rock to soil, organisms and sediments, which is why it is often the nutrient in shortest supply in lakes.

## How populations grow

A population changes through four processes: births ($B$), deaths ($D$), immigration ($I$, arrivals) and emigration ($E$, departures):

$$\Delta N = B - D + I - E$$

With plenty of resources and no crowding, each individual adds offspring at the same average rate no matter how many others there are. Growth is then proportional to size, which is **[[exponential growth]]**:

$$\frac{dN}{dt} = rN$$

where $r$ is the per capita growth rate (births minus deaths per individual per unit time). For species that breed once a year it is easier to use the discrete form, where $\lambda$ is the factor the population is multiplied by each year:

$$N_t = N_0\,\lambda^t$$

A population with $\lambda = 1.5$ grows 50% per year. Graphed, exponential growth gives a J-shaped curve: slow at first, then explosive.

### Example 1

Ten rabbits are released on an island with no predators, and the population grows by a factor of $\lambda = 2$ per year. How many rabbits are there after 6 years?

$N_6 = 10 \times 2^6 = 10 \times 64 = 640$ rabbits. After 12 years the same rule would give 40,960, which is why exponential growth never lasts long in nature.

## Carrying capacity and logistic growth

No environment has unlimited food, space, water or nesting sites. The largest population an environment can support over the long term is its **[[carrying capacity]]**, $K$. As a population approaches $K$, birth rates fall and death rates rise. The **[[logistic growth]]** model captures this by multiplying exponential growth by the fraction of $K$ still unused:

$$\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\,\frac{K - N}{K}$$

When $N$ is small, $\frac{K-N}{K}$ is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential. As $N$ approaches $K$, the fraction approaches 0 and growth stops. The graph is S-shaped, and the population grows fastest when $N = K/2$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 20], "y": [0, 1100], "xLabel": "time (generations)", "yLabel": "population size N", "functions": [{"f": "20*exp(0.4*x)", "label": "exponential", "dashed": true}, {"f": "1000/(1 + 49*exp(-0.4*x))", "label": "logistic"}, {"f": "1000", "label": "K = 1000", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Exponential (J-shaped) and logistic (S-shaped) growth from N₀ = 20 with r = 0.4; the logistic curve levels off at K"}
```

The Russian ecologist G. F. Gause tested this in the 1930s by growing *Paramecium* in tubes with a fixed daily food supply. The cultures grew quickly, slowed, and leveled off at a steady size, tracing an S-curve closely matching the logistic model.

### Example 2

A deer population has $r = 0.4$ per year and $K = 800$. Find the growth rate when $N = 200$ and when $N = 600$.

1. $N = 200$: $\frac{dN}{dt} = 0.4 \times 200 \times \frac{800 - 200}{800} = 80 \times 0.75 = 60$ deer per year.
2. $N = 600$: $\frac{dN}{dt} = 0.4 \times 600 \times \frac{200}{800} = 240 \times 0.25 = 60$ deer per year.

Both give 60: the logistic curve is symmetric about $K/2 = 400$, where growth peaks at $0.4 \times 400 \times 0.5 = 80$ deer per year.

## What limits populations

A limiting factor, the same idea you met with photosynthesis rates, is here any resource or condition that keeps a population from growing further. Ecologists sort them by whether their effect depends on crowding.

- **[[Density-dependent factors]]** hit harder as the population becomes denser: competition for food and space, predation, disease and parasites (which spread faster in crowds), and buildup of wastes. They push populations back toward $K$.
- **[[Density-independent factors]]** affect a population the same way whatever its density: a hard freeze, drought, flood, wildfire, or a volcanic eruption.

Populations can overshoot. In 1944, 29 reindeer were released on St. Matthew Island in the Bering Sea, which had abundant lichen and no predators. By 1963 there were about 6,000. They had eaten the slow-growing lichen faster than it could regrow, and after a severe winter the herd crashed to 42 animals in 1966. Food shortage (density-dependent) set up the crash; the harsh winter (density-independent) triggered it.

The human population, about 8.2 billion in 2025, is still growing but more slowly than in the 1960s. United Nations projections (2024) have it peaking at around 10.3 billion in the 2080s.

## Counting a population: mark–recapture

Animals that move cannot simply be counted. The **[[mark–recapture]]** method (the Lincoln–Petersen estimate) works like this: capture $M$ animals, mark them harmlessly, and release them. Later, capture a second sample of $C$ animals and count how many of them, $R$, carry marks. If the marked animals have mixed evenly, the fraction marked in the sample matches the fraction marked in the whole population:

$$\frac{R}{C} = \frac{M}{N} \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = \frac{M \times C}{R}$$

The estimate assumes no births, deaths or migration between samples, that marks are not lost, and that marked animals are no easier or harder to catch than the others.

### Example 3

Ecologists net 40 trout in a pond, tag them, and release them. A week later they net 50 trout, of which 8 are tagged. Estimate the population.

$N = \frac{40 \times 50}{8} = \frac{2000}{8} = 250$ trout. Check: 8 of 50 is 16% marked, and 40 of 250 is also 16%.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the mark–recapture formula upside down. Sanity check: $N$ must be larger than both $M$ and $C$.
- Confusing $r$ and $\lambda$. A population that does not change has $r = 0$ but $\lambda = 1$.
- Thinking logistic growth is fastest near $K$. It is fastest at $K/2$ and nearly zero at $K$.
- Calling nitrogen fixation something plants do. Bacteria (and lightning and factories) fix nitrogen; legumes only host the bacteria.
- Classifying a drought as density-dependent. It kills a fixed fraction whatever the density.

## Key points

- Matter cycles between living things and the environment; energy does not.
- Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration and combustion add it. Fossil fuel burning has raised CO₂ from about 280 to about 424 ppm (2024).
- Bacteria drive the nitrogen cycle: fixation, nitrification, denitrification.
- Exponential growth: $dN/dt = rN$ or $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$ (J-curve).
- Logistic growth: $dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K$ (S-curve), fastest at $K/2$, leveling off at carrying capacity.
- Mark–recapture: $N = MC/R$.

lessons.title: Communities, biomes, biodiversity, and human impact
lessons.body:
## From one population to many

The last lesson treated each population on its own, growing until limiting factors held it near carrying capacity. But many of those limiting factors are other species: the predator that eats you, the competitor that takes your food, the parasite inside you. This lesson looks at how species in a community interact, how communities change over time, how they are spread across Earth's biomes, how biologists measure their diversity, and how human activity is changing all of it.

## Niches and competition

A species' **[[niche]]** is its role in the community: what it eats, where and when it feeds, the temperatures and moisture it tolerates, what eats it. If the habitat is a species' address, the niche is its job.

When two species need the same limited resource, they compete, and both are harmed. In the 1930s G. F. Gause grew two *Paramecium* species separately; each thrived. Grown together on the same food, one always drove the other out. This led to the competitive exclusion principle: two species cannot share exactly the same niche in the same place indefinitely. One will outcompete the other, or the two will evolve to use resources differently.

Robert MacArthur's 1958 study of five warbler species in New England spruce forests showed the second outcome. All five eat insects in the same trees, but each feeds mostly in a different zone: treetops, outer branches, inner branches, lower trunk. Dividing a resource this way is called resource partitioning.

## Predation, herbivory, and symbiosis

In **[[predation]]**, one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey). Herbivory, an animal eating plants, is similar. Predator and prey populations often rise and fall in linked cycles. Fur-trading records of the Hudson's Bay Company, kept for about a century, show snowshoe hare and lynx numbers peaking roughly every 10 years, lynx peaks trailing hare peaks. More hares feed more lynx; more lynx (and over-browsed winter food) then drive hares down; with fewer hares, lynx starve and decline, and the cycle repeats. Field experiments in Yukon later showed that food supply and predators together drive the hare cycle.

```plot
{"x": [0, 30], "y": [0, 120], "xLabel": "time (years)", "yLabel": "relative abundance", "functions": [{"f": "60 + 45*sin(2*pi*x/10)", "label": "prey (hares)"}, {"f": "35 + 20*sin(2*pi*(x - 2)/10)", "label": "predators (lynx)", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Idealized predator–prey cycles: predator peaks lag about 2 years behind prey peaks"}
```

Predators and prey also drive each other's evolution: camouflage, speed, toxins and mimicry are products of this arms race.

Long-term close relationships between species are called symbiosis. There are three main types, classified by who benefits (competition and predation are added to the table for comparison; they are not symbiosis):

| Interaction | Species A | Species B | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[Mutualism]]** | + | + | Rhizobium bacteria fix nitrogen for legumes and get sugar; bees get nectar and pollinate flowers |
| **[[Commensalism]]** | + | 0 | Barnacles riding on a whale get transport to food; the whale is basically unaffected |
| **[[Parasitism]]** | + | − | Tapeworms, ticks and the malaria parasite feed on a host, usually without killing it quickly |
| Competition | − | − | Lions and hyenas competing for the same prey |
| Predation | + | − | A heron eating a frog |

A parasite usually lives on or in its host and feeds on it over a long time; a predator kills its prey outright.

## Keystone species

Some species matter far more than their numbers suggest. In the 1960s Robert Paine repeatedly removed the predatory sea star *Pisaster* from a stretch of rocky shore in Washington State and left a neighboring stretch alone. Without the sea star, mussels it normally ate took over the rock, crowding out other organisms; the number of species in his plot fell from 15 to 8 within a few years. A species like *Pisaster*, whose removal causes a large change in the community, is a **[[keystone species]]**, named after the top stone that holds an arch together. Sea otters, which keep sea urchins from destroying kelp forests, are another well-studied example.

## Ecological succession

Communities change over time in fairly predictable ways after a disturbance. **[[Ecological succession]]** is that gradual replacement of species.

- Primary succession begins where there is no soil: bare rock after a lava flow, or ground exposed by a retreating glacier. Pioneer species such as lichens and mosses colonize first; they break down rock and add organic matter, slowly forming soil that grasses, then shrubs, then trees can use.
- Secondary succession follows a disturbance that leaves soil in place: a wildfire, a hurricane, or an abandoned farm field. It is much faster, because seeds, roots and soil organisms survive. An abandoned field in the eastern United States can pass from weeds to grasses and shrubs to young forest within a few decades.

The flowchart shows both kinds. Secondary succession skips the slow soil-building start.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Primary and secondary succession
  accDescr: Primary succession starts on bare rock with no soil. Pioneer lichens and mosses colonize first and slowly build a thin soil. Grasses and small plants follow, then shrubs, then fast-growing trees, and finally a mature forest. Secondary succession starts after a disturbance such as a fire or an abandoned farm field, where soil is already present, so it skips the pioneer stage and begins with grasses and small plants, which is why it is much faster.
  R["Bare rock, no soil"] --> L["Lichens and mosses: pioneers"]
  L --> G["Grasses and small plants"]
  G --> S["Shrubs"]
  S --> T["Fast-growing trees"]
  T --> F["Mature forest"]
  D["Fire or abandoned field: soil remains"] -. "secondary succession" .-> G
```

Older textbooks described succession ending in a fixed "climax community." Ecologists now see mature communities as dynamic: small disturbances (a fallen tree, a patch fire) keep resetting parts of them.

## Biomes

A **[[biome]]** is a large region with a characteristic climate and the community of organisms adapted to it. Temperature and precipitation are the main factors that decide which biome develops.

| Biome | Climate | Typical life |
|---|---|---|
| Tropical rainforest | Hot all year; over about 200 cm of rain | Tall broadleaf evergreens; the most species of any land biome |
| Savanna | Warm; long dry season | Grasses with scattered trees; large grazers |
| Desert | Under about 25 cm of rain per year | Cacti and other succulents; nocturnal animals |
| Temperate grassland | Cold winters, hot summers; moderate rain; fires | Grasses with deep roots; bison, prairie dogs |
| Temperate deciduous forest | Four seasons; rain spread through the year | Trees that drop leaves in fall (oak, maple) |
| Boreal forest (taiga) | Long, cold winters; short summers | Conifers (spruce, fir); moose, lynx |
| Tundra | Very cold; permafrost; little precipitation | Mosses, lichens, low shrubs; no trees |

Plotting each biome by its average temperature and yearly precipitation shows how climate sorts them. The chart is a simplified sketch: real boundaries blur into one another, and soil, fire and how rain is spread through the year also matter (a savanna and a forest can get similar rainfall, but the savanna has a long dry season and frequent fires).

![A chart with average yearly temperature from minus 15 to 30 degrees Celsius on the horizontal axis and yearly precipitation from 0 to 450 centimeters on the vertical axis, divided into biome regions. Tundra is coldest and dry. Boreal forest is cold with moderate precipitation. Temperate grassland is cool to mild and fairly dry. Desert spans mild to hot temperatures with under 25 centimeters of rain. Temperate deciduous forest is mild and moist. Savanna is hot with moderate rain, and tropical rainforest is hot and very wet.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Aquatic systems are classified by salinity, depth and light instead: freshwater lakes and rivers, wetlands, estuaries where rivers meet the sea, coral reefs, and the open ocean.

## Measuring biodiversity

**[[Biodiversity]]** is the variety of life at three levels: genetic diversity within species, species diversity within communities, and ecosystem diversity across a region. Species diversity has two parts. Richness is the number of species. Evenness is how equally the individuals are spread among them. A forest with five tree species in equal numbers feels more diverse than one that is 96% one species, even though both have five species.

**[[Simpson's diversity index]]** combines both. If a sample has $N$ individuals in total and $n$ of them belong to a given species:

$$D = 1 - \frac{\sum n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}$$

The fraction is the probability that two individuals picked at random (without replacement) are the same species. So $D$ is the probability that they are *different* species. $D$ ranges from 0 (one species only) toward 1 (many, evenly spread species).

### Example 1

Two ponds each contain 30 snails of three species. Pond A has 10, 10 and 10. Pond B has 26, 2 and 2. Compare their diversity.

Both: $N(N-1) = 30 \times 29 = 870$.

1. Pond A: $\sum n(n-1) = 3 \times (10 \times 9) = 270$. $D = 1 - \tfrac{270}{870} = 0.69$.
2. Pond B: $\sum n(n-1) = 26 \times 25 + 2 \times 1 + 2 \times 1 = 654$. $D = 1 - \tfrac{654}{870} = 0.25$.

Same richness, very different diversity: Pond B is dominated by one species, so it scores much lower.

### Example 2

A researcher removes an introduced fish from three lakes and leaves three similar lakes alone. After two years, native frog numbers have risen in the removal lakes and stayed low in the others. The fish eat tadpoles. Which interaction is this, and what does the control show?

1. The fish benefits and the frog is harmed, and the fish kills and eats its victims: predation (+/−).
2. The untouched lakes rule out other explanations, such as a good year for frogs everywhere. Only removing the predator changed frog numbers.

## Human impact

A 2019 global assessment by IPBES (the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services) estimated that about 1 million plant and animal species are at risk of extinction. The IUCN Red List (2026 update) classifies nearly 50,000 of about 176,000 assessed species as threatened. The main drivers:

- *Habitat loss* is the largest. Clearing forests, draining wetlands and converting land to farms and cities removes the places species live and splits what remains into isolated fragments. About 6.7 million hectares of tropical primary forest were lost in 2024, a record year in which fires caused nearly half the loss; the loss fell to about 4.3 million hectares in 2025.
- *Climate change.* Rising greenhouse gases (lesson 39) have warmed Earth: 2024 was the warmest year on record, about 1.5 °C above the late-1800s average, and 2023–2025 were the three warmest years measured. Species ranges are shifting toward the poles and up mountains, spring events are happening earlier, and warmer, more acidic oceans are bleaching coral reefs.
- **[[Invasive species]]**: species introduced to a new region, where they spread and cause harm, often because their natural predators and competitors are missing. Examples include zebra mussels in the Great Lakes, the brown tree snake that wiped out most of Guam's forest birds, and Burmese pythons in the Florida Everglades. A 2023 IPBES report found invasive species played a part in about 60% of recorded extinctions.
- *Pollution and overexploitation.* Some pollutants build up in organisms. Because each predator eats many prey and stores the toxin in its fat, the concentration rises at each trophic level, which is called biomagnification. DDT thinned the eggshells of bald eagles and other birds of prey; after the United States banned it in 1972, eagles recovered and were removed from the endangered list in 2007. Overfishing removes individuals faster than populations can replace them.

Conservation works on the same causes: protected areas and wildlife corridors connecting habitat fragments, restoration of damaged ecosystems, control of invasive species, cleaner energy, and laws such as the US Endangered Species Act (1973).

## Common mistakes

- Swapping commensalism (+/0) and mutualism (+/+). Ask whether the second species gains anything.
- Thinking a keystone species must be common or large. Keystone means large effect, not large numbers.
- Confusing primary and secondary succession. The difference is whether soil is present at the start.
- Treating species richness as the whole of diversity. Evenness matters too, which is what Simpson's index measures.
- Thinking biomagnification means a toxin becomes more toxic. It becomes more concentrated.

## Key points

- Competition (−/−), predation and parasitism (+/−), mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0).
- Two species cannot occupy the same niche indefinitely; resource partitioning lets similar species coexist.
- Keystone species have effects far out of proportion to their abundance.
- Primary succession starts without soil; secondary succession starts with soil.
- Climate (temperature and precipitation) determines biomes.
- Simpson's index $D = 1 - \sum n(n-1)/[N(N-1)]$ measures richness and evenness together.
- Habitat loss, climate change, invasive species, pollution and overexploitation are the main threats to biodiversity.

lessons.title: Life tables, survivorship, and predator-prey models
lessons.body:
## Beyond a single growth rate

Lesson 39 described a population with one growth rate and capped it with a carrying capacity $K$. That model treats every individual alike, but a newly hatched fish and a ten-year-old fish differ in their chance of dying and in how many offspring they have. This lesson builds age-based life tables, uses them to predict growth, looks at how life histories evolve, and then follows two species at once with the Lotka–Volterra models.

## Life tables

A **[[life table]]** summarizes, age by age, how many individuals survive and how many die. The cleanest kind follows a **[[cohort]]**: a group of individuals born at the same time, tracked until the last one dies. (Otherwise ecologists build a "static" table from the ages at death in a sample, assuming conditions stayed constant.)

The standard columns, for age class $x$:

| Symbol | Meaning | How to compute |
|---|---|---|
| $n_x$ | number alive at the start of age $x$ | counted |
| $l_x$ | survivorship: fraction of the cohort still alive at age $x$ | $n_x / n_0$ |
| $d_x$ | number dying during age $x$ | $n_x - n_{x+1}$ |
| $q_x$ | age-specific mortality rate: fraction of those alive at $x$ that die before $x+1$ | $d_x / n_x$ |
| $e_x$ | **[[life expectancy]]**: average further years an individual of age $x$ will live | see Example 2 |

The two "rates" answer different questions. $l_x$ is about the whole cohort since birth; $q_x$ is about the individuals still alive at the start of that year.

### Example 1

A biologist marks 1,000 newly hatched lizards and counts the survivors each year:

| Age $x$ (years) | $n_x$ | $l_x$ | $d_x$ | $q_x$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1,000 | 1.000 | 600 | 0.60 |
| 1 | 400 | 0.400 | 100 | 0.25 |
| 2 | 300 | 0.300 | 120 | 0.40 |
| 3 | 180 | 0.180 | 126 | 0.70 |
| 4 | 54 | 0.054 | 54 | 1.00 |
| 5 | 0 | 0 | — | — |

1. $l_x$: divide each $n_x$ by 1,000. For age 2, $300/1000 = 0.300$.
2. $d_x$: subtract the next row. For age 2, $300 - 180 = 120$.
3. $q_x$: divide deaths by the number alive at the start of that age. For age 2, $120/300 = 0.40$.

Mortality is very high in the first year (60%), lowest for one-year-olds (25%), then climbs with age. Note that $d_3 = 126$ is only a little larger than $d_1 = 100$, yet $q_3 = 0.70$ is almost three times $q_1$, because far fewer lizards are left at age 3. Compare rates, not raw death counts.

### Example 2

Find the life expectancy at birth ($e_0$) and at age 1 ($e_1$) for the same lizards.

1. Estimate the lizard-years lived during each age as the average of the start and end counts, $L_x = (n_x + n_{x+1})/2$: $L_0 = 700$, $L_1 = 350$, $L_2 = 240$, $L_3 = 117$, $L_4 = 27$.
2. Add up all the years still to be lived from age $x$ onward, $T_x = L_x + L_{x+1} + \dots$: $T_0 = 1434$ and $T_1 = 734$.
3. Divide by the number alive: $e_0 = 1434/1000 \approx 1.43$ years and $e_1 = 734/400 \approx 1.84$ years.

A one-year-old lizard can expect to live *longer* (1.84 more years) than a newborn (1.43 years). The newborn still has to survive the deadly first year; the one-year-old already has.

## Survivorship curves

Plotting $n_x$ (survivors out of 1,000) against age gives a **[[survivorship curve]]**. Ecologists plot the vertical axis on a log scale, because then a straight line means a *constant mortality rate*: losing the same fraction each year shows up as equal-sized steps down.

![Graph of survivors per 1,000 on a log scale against age as a percent of maximum life span, with three idealized curves. Type I stays nearly flat until late in life and then drops steeply. Type II is a straight diagonal line. Type III drops steeply at very young ages and then levels off.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Type I*: low mortality until old age, then a steep drop. Humans in countries with good health care, many large mammals.
- *Type II*: roughly constant mortality at every age, a straight line on the log scale. Some songbirds after they leave the nest, many lizards, some rodents.
- *Type III*: enormous mortality among the very young, then a much lower rate for the few survivors. Oysters, most marine fish, many plants that shed thousands of seeds.

These are idealized shapes. Real species mix them: many birds are Type III as eggs and nestlings but Type II as adults. Treat the types as reference points, not boxes.

## Will the population grow? The net reproductive rate

Add a column $m_x$, the **[[fecundity]]**: the average number of female offspring produced by a female of age $x$ (counting only daughters keeps the bookkeeping to one sex). The **[[net reproductive rate]]** is the average number of daughters a newborn female will produce over her whole life:

$$R_0 = \sum l_x m_x$$

Each term is "chance of surviving to age $x$" times "daughters produced at age $x$". If $R_0 > 1$, each generation more than replaces itself and the population grows; if $R_0 = 1$, it holds steady; if $R_0 < 1$, it shrinks.

### Example 3

The lizards above have $m_x = 0, 1.0, 1.5, 1.5, 0.5$ daughters at ages 0 to 4. Is the population growing?

1. Multiply: $l_x m_x = 0,\ 0.400,\ 0.450,\ 0.270,\ 0.027$.
2. Add: $R_0 = 0.400 + 0.450 + 0.270 + 0.027 = 1.147$.

Each female replaces herself with about 1.15 daughters, so the population grows by roughly 15% per generation. (Dividing by the generation time, here about 1.93 years, gives an approximate yearly rate: $r \approx \ln R_0 / T \approx 0.071$.) The table also shows where the leverage is: because so few lizards survive their first year, a small improvement in first-year survival raises every later $l_x$ and has a big effect on $R_0$.

## Life histories: r- and K-selection, with caveats

A species' **[[life history]]** is its schedule of growth, reproduction and survival: when it starts breeding, how many and how large its offspring are, and how long it lives. Energy spent on one part is unavailable for another, so life histories involve trade-offs.

In the 1960s Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson named two extremes after the terms of the logistic equation. **[[r-selected species]]** are favored in unstable or newly opened habitats where populations are usually far below $K$ and the winners are those that multiply fastest: early maturity, many small offspring, little parental care, short lives (dandelions, mosquitoes, mice). **[[K-selected species]]** are favored where populations stay near $K$ and competition is intense: later maturity, fewer and larger offspring, much parental care, long lives (elephants, albatrosses, oaks).

The labels are still useful shorthand, but ecologists have largely moved past the theory behind them, for three reasons:

1. Most species are mixtures (a sea turtle lives a century but lays hundreds of unprotected eggs), so r and K are ends of a continuum at best.
2. The theory says density drives the trade-offs, but experiments show *which ages die* matters more. David Reznick and colleagues studied Trinidad guppies. In streams with fish predators that eat mainly adult guppies, guppies mature earlier and smaller and produce more, smaller young. In 1976 John Endler moved guppies from a high-predation site to an upstream pool whose only predator, a small killifish, eats mainly juveniles. When Reznick's team checked about 11 years later, the transplanted population had evolved later maturity and fewer, larger young. Age-specific mortality, not crowding as such, drove the change.
3. Modern life-history theory works directly from life tables, asking which schedule of $l_x$ and $m_x$ gives the highest fitness.

## Density dependence in the data

The logistic model assumes per capita growth falls in a straight line as $N$ rises: $\dfrac{1}{N}\dfrac{dN}{dt} = r\left(1 - \dfrac{N}{K}\right)$. Field biologists test this by plotting per capita growth (or births per female, or survival) against density. If the points slope downward, the population is regulated by density-dependent factors, and where the line crosses zero is an estimate of $K$.

### Example 4

A bird population's per capita growth rate was 0.30 per year in a year when it numbered 100, and 0.10 per year when it numbered 300. Assuming a straight-line decline, estimate $r$ and $K$.

1. Slope: $\dfrac{0.10 - 0.30}{300 - 100} = -0.001$ per bird.
2. Intercept at $N = 0$: $0.30 + 0.001 \times 100 = 0.40$, so $r \approx 0.40$ per year.
3. The rate reaches zero when $0.40 - 0.001N = 0$, so $K \approx 400$.

Real plots are noisy and often curved, but long-term studies such as those of song sparrows on Mandarte Island, British Columbia, show breeding success falling as density rises.

## Two species at once: the Lotka–Volterra models

In the 1920s Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra independently wrote down the simplest equations for two interacting species. Volterra was prompted by an observation of the biologist Umberto D'Ancona (who married Volterra's daughter): when fishing in the Adriatic was reduced during World War I, predatory fish made up a larger share of the catch.

### Predator and prey

Let $H$ be the number of prey (hares) and $P$ the number of predators (lynx). The **[[Lotka–Volterra model]]** of predation is

$$\frac{dH}{dt} = rH - aHP \qquad \frac{dP}{dt} = b\,aHP - mP$$

- $rH$: prey grow exponentially when there are no predators.
- $aHP$: prey are killed at a rate proportional to how often predators and prey meet; $a$ is the attack rate.
- $b\,aHP$: predators convert prey eaten into new predators with efficiency $b$.
- $mP$: predators die at rate $m$ without food.

Setting each equation to zero shows when each population stops changing. Prey hold steady when $P = r/a$; predators hold steady when $H = m/(ab)$. Away from that balance point the two populations chase each other in cycles, and predator peaks always lag behind prey peaks.

![Line graph of a simulated Lotka–Volterra model over 40 years. The prey population cycles between about 57 and 160 animals and the predator population between about 25 and 60, with a period of about 9 years. Each predator peak comes about 2 years after a prey peak.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 5

For the model in the graph, $r = 0.8$, $a = 0.02$, $b = 0.3$ and $m = 0.6$ (time in years). Find the balance point and predict what happens to it if predators start dying faster.

1. Prey are steady when $P = r/a = 0.8/0.02 = 40$ predators.
2. Predators are steady when $H = m/(ab) = 0.6/(0.02 \times 0.3) = 100$ prey.
3. The cycles in the graph swing around $H = 100$ and $P = 40$.
4. If the predator death rate $m$ rises, $H = m/(ab)$ rises: the model predicts *more* prey on average, while the average number of predators ($r/a$) is unchanged. Each population's average is set by the other species' parameters.

The model is a caricature. Its cycles are "neutral": a small disturbance shifts the system to a different cycle. Real predators get full, and real prey are limited by their own food; adding these gives more realistic models. Laboratory tests showed how fragile simple predator–prey systems are: in Gause's tubes the protist *Didinium* ate every *Paramecium* and then starved, and in Carl Huffaker's 1958 experiments predatory mites wiped out plant-feeding mites on a tray of oranges unless barriers and patchy food let the prey escape and recolonize.

### The hare–lynx story

The best-known data are the Hudson's Bay Company fur records from Canada: about a century of lynx pelts showing peaks every 9 to 11 years, with hare numbers (pieced together from several sources) cycling just ahead. The loop below is the usual reading of those data.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The feedback loop behind the hare and lynx cycle
  accDescr: A loop of five stages. When hares are abundant, lynx are well fed and raise more young, so lynx numbers rise. Heavy predation, together with scarce winter food, then makes the hare population crash. With few hares, lynx go hungry and raise few young, so lynx numbers fall. With predation eased and shrubs regrowing, hares recover and become abundant again. Because each population responds to the other with a delay, lynx peaks follow hare peaks.
  A["Hares abundant"] --> B["Lynx well fed: lynx numbers rise"]
  B --> C["Heavy predation and scarce browse: hares crash"]
  C --> D["Lynx go hungry: lynx numbers fall"]
  D --> E["Predation eases, browse regrows: hares recover"]
  E --> A
```

Read the records with care. Pelt counts measure trappers' catch, which also tracked fur prices and trapping effort, and the hare series mixes regions and methods. Hares also have many other predators (coyotes, owls, goshawks). The decisive test came from experiments at Kluane Lake in the Yukon from 1986 to 1996. On plots about a square kilometer each, where food was added, mammal predators were fenced out, or both, and averaged over the peak and decline years, adding food tripled hare density, excluding mammal predators roughly doubled it, and doing both increased it about elevenfold. Food and predation together (plus the stress of predator threat on breeding hares) drive the cycle: more complicated than the two-species equations, but the same feedback.

### Competition

The Lotka–Volterra competition model adds a second species to the logistic equation:

$$\frac{dN_1}{dt} = r_1 N_1\,\frac{K_1 - N_1 - \alpha_{12}N_2}{K_1}$$

and a matching equation for species 2. The **[[competition coefficient]]** $\alpha_{12}$ measures how much one individual of species 2 uses up species 1's resources, counted in species 1 individuals. If $\alpha_{12} = 0.5$, two individuals of species 2 crowd species 1 as much as one of its own.

The model's main lesson is qualitative. The two species can coexist only if each limits its own growth more than it limits the other's: **[[intraspecific competition]]** (within a species) must be stronger than interspecific competition (between species). In symbols, coexistence needs $\alpha_{12} < K_1/K_2$ and $\alpha_{21} < K_2/K_1$. If the species use resources too similarly, one excludes the other, which is the competitive exclusion seen in Gause's two *Paramecium* species. Resource partitioning, like MacArthur's warblers, lowers the $\alpha$ values and makes coexistence possible.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing $l_x$ with $q_x$. $l_x$ is survival from birth to age $x$; $q_x$ is the death rate *during* age $x$ among those who reached it.
- Comparing ages by $d_x$ instead of $q_x$. More deaths can mean more individuals, not a higher risk.
- Reading a survivorship curve on a linear axis. Only on a log axis does a straight line mean constant mortality.
- Adding $m_x$ without weighting by $l_x$. Daughters a female would have at age 4 count only for the fraction that survive to 4.
- Treating r- and K-selection as a law. They are endpoints of a continuum, and age-specific mortality explains life histories better.

## Key points

- A cohort life table gives $l_x = n_x/n_0$, $d_x = n_x - n_{x+1}$, $q_x = d_x/n_x$ and life expectancy $e_x = T_x/n_x$.
- Survivorship curves are drawn on a log scale; Types I, II and III are idealized patterns.
- $R_0 = \sum l_x m_x$; the population grows if $R_0 > 1$.
- r- and K-selection describe a continuum of life histories; experiments such as Reznick's guppies show age-specific mortality shaping them.
- Lotka–Volterra predation: prey steady at $P = r/a$, predators steady at $H = m/(ab)$; cycles with predator peaks lagging.
- Competition: coexistence requires intraspecific competition to be stronger than interspecific competition.

lessons.title: Productivity, nutrient limits, and global change
lessons.body:
## Measuring a whole ecosystem

Lesson 38 introduced net primary productivity with a simple subtraction, and lesson 39 traced carbon and nitrogen around their cycles. This lesson asks how ecologists actually measure those quantities in a lake or a forest, what limits them, and how the same bookkeeping, scaled up to the whole planet, gives the evidence for human-caused climate change.

## GPP, NPP and the ecosystem's balance

**[[Gross primary productivity]]** (GPP) is the rate at which producers fix carbon (or capture energy) by photosynthesis. Producers immediately respire part of it, a loss called autotrophic respiration ($R_a$). What remains is net primary productivity, $\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R_a$, the new plant and algal tissue available to everything else. Across many ecosystems $R_a$ is roughly half of GPP, so NPP is about half of GPP.

Consumers and decomposers respire too (heterotrophic respiration, $R_h$). Subtracting that gives **[[net ecosystem production]]**:
