## John Snow and the Broad Street pump

In 1854 cholera killed over 500 people within about ten days in the Soho district of London. Most doctors then blamed miasma, foul air from rotting matter. The physician John Snow suspected cholera spread through water contaminated with the waste of sick people. He mapped the deaths and found them clustered around a public pump on Broad Street. The exceptions fit too: workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer and water from the brewery's own well, were spared, and so were most residents of a workhouse with its own well. A woman who lived miles away but had Broad Street water carried to her because she liked its taste died of cholera. On Snow's evidence, the local board removed the pump's handle on September 8. (The outbreak was already declining as people fled, so the handle's removal wasn't proof by itself; the pattern of cases was.)

### Example 3: Snow's "grand experiment"

Two companies supplied water to homes on the same streets of south London. The Southwark and Vauxhall Company drew water from the Thames downstream of sewage outflows; the Lambeth Company had moved its intake upstream in 1852. Snow recorded cholera deaths in the first seven weeks of the 1854 epidemic:

| Water supplier | Houses | Cholera deaths |
|---|---|---|
| Southwark and Vauxhall | 40,046 | 1,263 |
| Lambeth | 26,107 | 98 |

1. Death rates per 10,000 houses: $\dfrac{1{,}263}{40{,}046} \times 10{,}000 \approx 315$ and $\dfrac{98}{26{,}107} \times 10{,}000 \approx 37.5$.
2. Ratio: $315 / 37.5 \approx 8.4$. Homes on the downstream supply had about eight times the death rate.
3. Why it is convincing: households on both supplies lived side by side, rich and poor alike, often without knowing which company served them, so air, wealth and neighborhood were matched. Only the water differed. This is a natural experiment.

Robert Koch identified the cholera bacterium, *Vibrio cholerae*, as the cause in 1883–84, long after Snow had shown how it spread. (The Italian anatomist Filippo Pacini had described it under the microscope in 1854, but his work was largely ignored.)

## Investigating an outbreak

Modern outbreak investigations follow Snow's logic in a standard sequence.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  accTitle: Steps of an outbreak investigation
  accDescr: Investigators first confirm that there is an outbreak and verify the diagnosis, then write a case definition and find cases. They describe the cases by time, place and person, including an epidemic curve, form hypotheses about the source, test them with an analytic study comparing ill and well people, put control measures in place, and communicate the findings. Control measures can start at any point once a likely source is known.
  A["Confirm the outbreak and the diagnosis"] --> B["Write a case definition and find cases"]
  B --> C["Describe by time, place and person"]
  C --> D["Form hypotheses about the source"]
  D --> E["Test with an analytic study"]
  E --> F["Control and prevent"]
  F --> G["Communicate findings"]
```

A **[[case definition]]** sets standard criteria (symptoms, lab results, time and place) for who counts as a case, so cases are counted the same way everywhere. An **[[epidemic curve]]** is a histogram of cases by date of onset. Its shape is a clue: a single sharp peak spanning about one incubation period suggests a point source (one contaminated meal); a plateau suggests a continuing common source (a contaminated water supply); a series of growing peaks spaced about one incubation period apart suggests person-to-person (propagated) spread.

For a food-borne outbreak, investigators compare the **[[attack rate]]** (the fraction of a group who became ill) among people who ate each food with the attack rate among those who didn't. The ratio of the two is the **[[relative risk]]**.

### Example 4: finding the bad dish

After a picnic for 100 people, 46 became ill with vomiting within 12 hours. Interviews give:

| Food | Ate: ill / total | Did not eat: ill / total |
|---|---|---|
| Chicken salad | 42 / 60 | 4 / 40 |
| Bread rolls | 38 / 80 | 8 / 20 |

1. Chicken salad: attack rates $42/60 = 70\%$ and $4/40 = 10\%$. Relative risk $= 70/10 = 7$.
2. Rolls: $38/80 = 47.5\%$ and $8/20 = 40\%$. Relative risk $\approx 1.2$.
3. The chicken salad is the prime suspect: a high attack rate among eaters, a low one among non-eaters, and it accounts for 42 of the 46 cases. The 4 ill people who didn't eat it could be misremembering, unrelated illness, or cross-contamination. The next step is testing leftover food and patients.

## Zoonoses: diseases from animals

A **[[zoonosis]]** is an infectious disease that spreads between animals and people. According to the CDC, more than 6 in 10 known human infectious diseases can be spread from animals, and about three quarters of new or emerging ones come from animals. Examples include rabies, Lyme disease, West Nile virus, avian influenza and Ebola. HIV-1, the virus behind the global AIDS pandemic, began as a related virus of chimpanzees that crossed into people in central Africa in the early twentieth century.

The animal population in which a pathogen normally lives is its **[[reservoir]]**: fruit bats for Nipah virus, white-footed mice and other small animals for the Lyme bacterium. Spillover into people happens at contact points, and often through an intermediate host or a vector such as a tick or mosquito. Clearing forests, hunting and trading wildlife, and crowding livestock all increase contact. Public health agencies therefore watch for unusual illness in wildlife and farm animals as an early warning (the "One Health" approach).

## Antibiotic stewardship

Antibiotics are a shared resource that use itself wears out. Every course of antibiotics selects for resistant bacteria in the patient's body and in the wider community (the mechanisms are in module 8's honors lesson on microbes). Across European countries, those with higher outpatient antibiotic use have higher rates of resistant bacteria. The CDC estimates more than 2.8 million antibiotic-resistant infections and over 35,000 deaths in the United States each year, and a global study estimated about 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019 directly caused by resistant bacterial infections.

**[[Antibiotic stewardship]]** is the coordinated effort to use antibiotics only when they help, choosing the right drug, dose and duration. In practice:

- No antibiotics for viral infections such as colds and most sore throats and bronchitis; US studies estimate about 30% of outpatient prescriptions are unnecessary.
- Narrow-spectrum drugs when the pathogen is known, and tests to identify it.
- Patients take the antibiotic exactly as prescribed and never save or share leftovers. (For many common infections, trials show shorter courses work as well as longer ones, so prescribers are moving to the shortest effective course.)
- Infection prevention and vaccination, so fewer infections need treatment at all.
- Limits in agriculture: since 2017 the US has not allowed medically important antibiotics to be used to promote growth in farm animals.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up incidence (new cases per time) and prevalence (existing cases at a moment).
- Treating $R_0$ as a fixed property of a germ. It depends on contact patterns and changes with behavior; $R_e$ also falls as immunity rises.
- Thinking an epidemic peaks when everyone has been infected. It peaks when $s = 1/R_0$, and then overshoots.
- Comparing the number of ill people instead of attack rates. More ill people ate the rolls than were ill without them, simply because most people ate rolls.

## Key points

- Incidence = new cases per population per time; prevalence = existing cases per population; prevalence ≈ incidence × duration in a steady state.
- $R_0$ is new infections per case in a fully susceptible population; $R_e = R_0 s$; cases grow when $R_e > 1$.
- SIR model: new infections $\beta SI/N$, recoveries $\gamma I$, $R_0 = \beta/\gamma$; infections peak at $s = 1/R_0$, and the herd immunity threshold is $1 - 1/R_0$.
- John Snow linked cholera to water by mapping cases and comparing water suppliers.
- Outbreak investigations use case definitions, epidemic curves, attack rates and relative risk.
- Most emerging diseases are zoonoses; stewardship slows antibiotic resistance by cutting unnecessary use.

lessons.title: Conservation biology
lessons.body:
Lesson 40 listed the main threats to biodiversity: habitat loss, climate change, invasive species, pollution and overexploitation. Conservation biology is the applied science of slowing those losses. It borrows from almost every earlier lesson: population growth and mark–recapture (lesson 39), genetic drift and Hardy-Weinberg (lesson 28), and community ecology (lesson 40). This lesson takes the quantitative tools conservation biologists actually use and ends with cases where conservation worked.

## How fast are species disappearing?

Extinction is normal. Most species that ever lived are extinct, and even outside the five mass extinctions species died out at a slow, steady **[[background extinction rate]]**. To compare rates across groups, biologists count extinctions per million species-years (E/MSY): if you watched a million species for one year, how many would go extinct? Fossil and molecular studies put the background rate at roughly 0.1 E/MSY, though estimates range up to about 1.

Suppose a group of 5,000 well-studied species has 40 documented extinctions in the last 400 years. Its rate is

$$\frac{40}{5{,}000 \times 400} \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 20 \text{ E/MSY},$$

about 200 times a background rate of 0.1. Calculations like this, using real data for birds, mammals and amphibians, give modern rates around 100 E/MSY, on the order of 1,000 times background. The figures are uncertain both ways: some species declared extinct are rediscovered, but many species vanish before anyone describes them, and others are "committed" to extinction by habitat already lost (see extinction debt below).

## Island biogeography

Why do big islands have more species than small ones, and near islands more than remote ones? Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson answered with the theory of **[[island biogeography]]** (1963, 1967). The number of species on an island is a balance between two rates:

- *Immigration* of new species falls as the island fills up, because fewer of the mainland's species are left to arrive. It is lower for islands far from the mainland.
- *Extinction* rises as species accumulate, because more species share the space and each has a smaller population. It is higher on small islands, where populations are small.

The number of species settles at the equilibrium where the curves cross. Species keep arriving and disappearing (turnover), but the count stays roughly constant.

![Graph of rate against the number of species on an island. Two falling immigration curves, one for a near island and one for a far island, and two rising extinction curves, one for a small island and one for a large island. The near, large island reaches equilibrium at the most species; the far, small island at the fewest.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Daniel Simberloff and Wilson tested the theory in the late 1960s. They covered small mangrove islands in the Florida Keys with tents, fumigated them to remove every insect and spider, and recorded recolonization. Within about a year species numbers returned to near their original levels, though the species list was different, and the most distant island recovered most slowly.

The pattern behind the theory is the **[[species-area relationship]]**:

$$S = cA^z$$

where $S$ is the number of species, $A$ the area, and $c$ and $z$ constants fitted to data. For islands, $z$ is usually about 0.2–0.35. With $z \approx 0.3$, ten times the area holds about twice the species ($10^{0.3} \approx 2$).

Nature reserves surrounded by farms and cities are islands too, which is why the theory matters for conservation.

### Example 1: predicting losses from habitat loss

A forest region holds 200 bird species. Logging removes 90% of the forest. Using $z = 0.25$, how many species would eventually remain?

1. Ratio of areas: $A_{\text{new}}/A_{\text{old}} = 0.10$. The constant $c$ cancels: $\dfrac{S_{\text{new}}}{S_{\text{old}}} = \left(\dfrac{A_{\text{new}}}{A_{\text{old}}}\right)^z$.
2. $S_{\text{new}} = 200 \times 0.10^{0.25} = 200 \times 0.562 \approx 112$.
3. Losing 90% of the area loses only about 44% of the species, but that is still about 88 species.

Two cautions. The losses are not immediate: species can persist for decades in remnants too small to support them, an **[[extinction debt]]** that comes due later unless habitat is restored. And species-area predictions are approximate; they depend on how species are spread across the landscape, and some studies argue that this method overestimates losses. Treat such results as estimates with wide uncertainty.

## Fragmentation and edges

Habitat loss rarely removes one neat block. Usually it causes **[[habitat fragmentation]]**: a continuous habitat is broken into smaller, isolated patches separated by farms, roads or towns. Fragments suffer an **[[edge effect]]**: near the boundary, conditions differ from the interior. Edges get more light, wind and drying, more invasive plants, and more nest predators and parasites. In the eastern United States, songbird nests near forest edges are parasitized more often by brown-headed cowbirds, which lay eggs in other birds' nests.

The Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project, started in 1979 near Manaus, Brazil, isolated Amazon forest patches of 1, 10 and 100 hectares and has studied them ever since. Edge effects reached 100 m or more into the forest; large trees died faster near edges, and small fragments lost many understory birds and other species.

![Two ways to protect 100 hectares. Left: one square fragment 1,000 m on a side with a 100 m edge zone around a core of 64 hectares. Right: four separate square fragments 500 m on a side, each with a 100 m edge zone around a core of 9 hectares, 36 hectares of core in all.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: core area

A reserve of 100 ha (1 ha = 10,000 m²) can be one square block or four separate square blocks of 25 ha each. If edge effects reach 100 m, how much interior (core) habitat does each design keep?

1. One block: $\sqrt{1{,}000{,}000 \text{ m}^2} = 1{,}000$ m on a side. The core is $(1{,}000 - 2 \times 100)^2 = 800^2 = 640{,}000$ m², or 64 ha.
2. Four blocks: each is $\sqrt{250{,}000} = 500$ m on a side, with core $(500 - 200)^2 = 300^2 = 90{,}000$ m² = 9 ha. Together: 36 ha.
3. Same total area, but the split design keeps barely more than half as much core habitat. Interior species need the single large block, or strips of habitat that connect the pieces so animals can move between them.

Corridors work: in large field experiments at the Savannah River Site in South Carolina, patches connected by corridors exchanged more pollinators, seeds and animals and kept more plant species than isolated patches.

## Small populations and genetic diversity

How small is too small? A **[[minimum viable population]]** is the smallest population with a high chance (say 95%) of persisting for a set time (say 100 years) despite chance events. Small populations face four kinds of chance: demographic accidents (by chance, all births in a year are males), environmental swings (a drought year), catastrophes (a hurricane), and genetic problems.

The genetic problems come from drift and inbreeding (lesson 28). What matters is not the head count but the **[[effective population size]]** $N_e$: the size of an ideal population that would lose genetic diversity at the same rate. Unequal sex ratios, unequal family sizes and population crashes all make $N_e$ smaller than the census count. For unequal numbers of breeding males $N_m$ and females $N_f$,

$$N_e = \frac{4N_mN_f}{N_m + N_f}$$

and heterozygosity (the proportion of heterozygous genes) falls by a fraction $\tfrac{1}{2N_e}$ each generation:

$$H_t = H_0\left(1 - \frac{1}{2N_e}\right)^t$$

Inbreeding exposes harmful recessive alleles, causing **[[inbreeding depression]]**: lower survival and fertility in offspring of relatives. Low numbers, inbreeding and lost variation then reinforce each other.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The extinction vortex
  accDescr: A cycle that drives small populations toward extinction. A small population has more inbreeding and genetic drift, which cause loss of genetic diversity and inbreeding depression. That lowers survival and reproduction, which makes the population smaller still, and the cycle repeats.
  A["Small population"] --> B["Inbreeding and drift"]
  B --> C["Loss of genetic diversity"]
  C --> D["Lower survival and reproduction"]
  D --> E["Even smaller population"]
  E --> B
```

This feedback loop is the **[[extinction vortex]]**. An old rule of thumb, the "50/500 rule," held that $N_e$ of 50 avoids serious short-term inbreeding and 500 keeps enough variation to adapt; newer analyses suggest at least 100 and 1,000. Many studies put census minimum viable populations in the thousands.

### Example 3: a captive breeding program

A zoo program breeds from 10 males and 40 females. Find $N_e$ and the fraction of heterozygosity left after 20 generations. Compare with 25 males and 25 females.

1. $N_e = \dfrac{4 \times 10 \times 40}{10 + 40} = \dfrac{1{,}600}{50} = 32$, well below the 50 animals counted.
2. $H_{20}/H_0 = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{64}\right)^{20} = 0.984^{20} \approx 0.73$. About 27% of the heterozygosity is lost.
3. With 25 of each sex, $N_e = 50$ and $\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{100}\right)^{20} \approx 0.82$, keeping 82%. Equalizing breeders helps; real programs also pair animals to keep family sizes equal.

The fix for an inbred population is often **[[genetic rescue]]**: bringing in individuals from another population. By the early 1990s only about 20–30 Florida panthers survived, with kinked tails, heart defects and poor sperm quality. Eight female pumas from Texas were released in 1995. Panthers with mixed ancestry had fewer defects and survived better, and the population has grown to an estimated 120–230. Greater prairie chickens in Illinois recovered their egg hatching rates after birds from larger populations in other states were brought in during the 1990s.

## Counting and forecasting populations

Mark–recapture (lesson 39) gives $N = MC/R$. Its assumptions are a closed population (no births, deaths or migration between samples), marks that aren't lost, and every animal equally likely to be caught. If marked animals avoid traps ("trap-shy"), recaptures $R$ are too low and $N$ is overestimated; "trap-happy" animals make it an underestimate. With small samples, ecologists use Chapman's version, $N = \dfrac{(M+1)(C+1)}{R+1} - 1$, which is less biased: for $M = 40$, $C = 50$, $R = 8$ it gives $\tfrac{41 \times 51}{9} - 1 \approx 231$ instead of 250.

**[[Population viability analysis]]** (PVA) uses data on survival, reproduction and their variation to simulate a population's future thousands of times, giving a probability of extinction within, say, 100 years under each management option. One lesson of PVA is that year-to-year variation itself is dangerous.

### Example 4: good years and bad years

A population alternates years of growth $\lambda = 1.5$ and decline $\lambda = 0.6$. The average $\lambda$ is $1.05$. Is it growing?

1. Over two years the population is multiplied by $1.5 \times 0.6 = 0.90$: it shrinks 10% every two years.
2. The long-run growth rate is the geometric mean, $\sqrt{0.90} \approx 0.95$, a 5% decline per year.
3. After ten years, $0.90^5 \approx 0.59$ of the starting population remains. Variable environments can doom a population whose average year looks fine, which is why PVA models variation, not just averages.

## Invasive species

Many introduced species never establish, and only a fraction of those that do become harmful, but the ones that spread can be devastating, often because they escaped the predators, parasites and competitors of their home range. Cane toads, introduced to Queensland in 1935 to control beetles in sugarcane, failed at that job, spread across northern Australia, and poison native predators such as quolls and monitor lizards that eat them. Nile perch introduced to Lake Victoria contributed, along with pollution, to the loss of perhaps 200 or more of its native cichlid fish species. The emerald ash borer, a beetle first found near Detroit in 2002, has killed hundreds of millions of North American ash trees.

Management, from cheapest to most expensive: prevention (inspecting cargo, banning risky imports), early detection and rapid response, eradication, and long-term control. Eradication works best on islands: helicopter baiting from 2011 to 2015 removed rats and mice from the subantarctic island of South Georgia, declared rodent-free in 2018, and its ground-nesting birds are returning. **[[Biological control]]** uses a natural enemy from the invader's home range. In 1888–89 the vedalia beetle from Australia controlled cottony cushion scale, which was destroying California's citrus; the cane toad shows why candidates must now be tested for effects on non-target species first.

## Conservation that worked

- *California condor.* By 1987 all 27 surviving condors were taken into captivity. Captive breeding and releases brought the total to about 600 by 2025, more than half flying free. Lead poisoning from bullet fragments in carcasses remains the main threat.
- *Yellowstone wolves.* Thirty-one wolves from Canada were released in 1995–96, 70 years after wolves were eliminated from the park. Elk numbers and behavior changed. How much this let willows and aspens recover (a trophic cascade) is still debated, because elk also declined for other reasons.
- *Humpback whales.* Commercial hunting of humpbacks was banned worldwide in 1966, and a moratorium on all commercial whaling followed in 1986. Many humpback populations have since recovered strongly.
- *Florida panther* and *South Georgia* (above).

## Common mistakes

- Expecting extinctions to follow habitat loss immediately. Extinction debt means losses can lag by decades.
- Applying the species-area relationship linearly. Losing 90% of the area loses fewer than 90% of species, because $S$ grows as a power of $A$.
- Counting heads instead of effective size. A population of 50 with a skewed sex ratio can behave genetically like one of 32 or fewer.
- Judging growth by the arithmetic mean of $\lambda$. Multiply the yearly factors; the geometric mean decides the long-run trend.
- Assuming a single large reserve always beats several small ones. Large blocks keep more core habitat, but several reserves can spread risk from a single catastrophe; the best design depends on the species.

## Key points

- Background extinction is about 0.1 E/MSY; current rates are estimated near 100 E/MSY.
- Island biogeography: species number is an equilibrium between immigration (lower for far islands) and extinction (higher for small islands); $S = cA^z$ with $z \approx 0.2$–$0.35$.
- Fragmentation shrinks core habitat through edge effects; corridors help connect fragments.
- $N_e = 4N_mN_f/(N_m + N_f)$; heterozygosity falls by $1/(2N_e)$ per generation; small populations can enter an extinction vortex, and genetic rescue can reverse inbreeding depression.
- Mark–recapture estimates depend on its assumptions; population viability analysis forecasts extinction risk, and variable growth lowers long-run growth.
- Prevention is the cheapest invasive-species control; island eradications and careful biological control can succeed; species such as the condor show recovery is possible.

sections.name: The science and chemistry of life
Honors: Development, stem cells, and the genome

questions.stem: A researcher tests whether a soil fungus increases tomato growth. She grows plants with the fungus, plants without it, and a third group given a fertilizer already known to increase growth. What is the third group?
choices: A positive control
A negative control
The experimental group
A confounding variable
questions.explanation: A positive control gets a treatment known to produce the effect, so it shows the method can detect growth increases. The plants without fungus are the negative control; the fungus plants are the experimental group; a confounding variable is an unwanted factor, not a group.

questions.stem: Paper disks soaked in garlic extract, and disks soaked in the solvent alone, are placed on a lawn of bacteria. Clear rings with no bacteria appear around both kinds of disk. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Garlic extract kills bacteria
The solvent itself kills bacteria, so the effect cannot be credited to garlic
The positive control failed, so the plates are faulty
Garlic has no effect on bacteria
questions.explanation: The solvent-only disk is the negative control and should show no effect. A clear ring around it means the solvent kills bacteria, so the rings around the garlic disks could be caused by the solvent. The experiment can neither confirm nor rule out an effect of garlic. (No positive control is described.)

questions.stem: A student puts one tray of 30 seedlings under a red lamp and one tray of 30 seedlings under a blue lamp, then measures all 60 seedlings. How many independent experimental units does each light treatment have?
questions.explanation: The lamp treatment is applied to whole trays, so the tray is the experimental unit: one per treatment. Anything else that differs between the two trays (position, a draft, watering) affects all 30 seedlings in a tray together. Counting the 30 seedlings as replicates is pseudoreplication.

questions.stem: Pilot data show that a measurement has a standard deviation of 12. What is the smallest number of units per group that makes the standard error of a group mean no more than 3?
questions.explanation: SE = SD/√n, so 12/√n ≤ 3 gives √n ≥ 4 and n ≥ 16. (4 is √n, not n; 144 is 12²; 36 would make the SE 2.)

questions.stem: A lab quadruples the number of animals in each group, from 10 to 40. What happens to the standard error of each group mean, assuming the animals vary as before?
choices: It is cut in half
It is cut to one quarter
It doubles
It stays the same
questions.explanation: SE = SD/√n. Multiplying n by 4 multiplies √n by 2, so the SE halves. Uncertainty falls with the square root of sample size, not in proportion to it, which is why precision is expensive.

questions.stem: Why do researchers assign individuals to treatment groups at random?
choices: So that the groups are exactly identical
So that groups differ only by chance, even in factors no one measured
So that the sample represents the whole population
So that the researchers do not know which group is which
questions.explanation: Random assignment cannot make groups identical, but it makes any differences between them a matter of chance, including in unknown factors, and statistics can allow for chance. Representing a population is the job of random sampling; hiding group identity is blinding.

questions.stem: In the randomized 1954 polio vaccine trial, unvaccinated children whose parents refused consent had a lower polio rate (46 per 100,000) than unvaccinated children given the placebo (71 per 100,000). What explains this?
choices: The placebo caused some cases of polio
The vaccine protected children who were not vaccinated
Families who consented differed from those who refused in ways that affected polio risk
The no-consent group was too small to measure accurately
questions.explanation: Neither group received vaccine, so the difference reflects who the families were. Children from better-off, more hygienic homes were both more likely to have consenting parents and more vulnerable to paralytic polio. This is why the fair comparison is vaccine versus placebo among consenting families, assigned at random. The placebo was salt water, and the no-consent group was large (about 350,000).

questions.stem: In a double-blind drug trial,
choices: the participants do not know who gets the drug, but the researchers do
two separate teams test the drug and compare results
every participant receives both the drug and the placebo
neither the participants nor the researchers who treat and assess them know who gets the drug
questions.explanation: Single-blind hides the treatment from participants; double-blind also hides it from the people giving treatment and measuring outcomes, which prevents observer bias. Using two teams is replication, and giving each person both treatments is a crossover design.

questions.stem: Which principle of the Belmont Report requires that the burdens and benefits of research be shared fairly, so that one group is not chosen as subjects just because it is easy to use?
choices: Justice
Respect for persons
Beneficence
Replacement
questions.explanation: The Belmont Report (1979) lists respect for persons (informed consent), beneficence (maximize benefits, minimize harms) and justice (fair selection and sharing of burdens and benefits). Replacement is one of the 3Rs for animal research.

questions.stem: In animal research, the "R" that means using cell cultures, computer models or invertebrates instead of vertebrate animals where possible is ___.
questions.explanation: The 3Rs (Russell and Burch, 1959) are replacement, reduction (using the fewest animals that give a clear answer) and refinement (minimizing pain and distress).

questions.stem: Match each term to an example of it.
choices: Growth is measured as dry mass after 21 days
All the treated plants were kept on the warmer shelf
A sugar pill that looks exactly like the drug
A paper disk soaked in the solvent only
A paper disk soaked in a known antibiotic
questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured. Temperature differing along with treatment is a confounder. A placebo is an inactive look-alike treatment. A solvent-only disk is a negative control; a disk with a known antibiotic would be a positive control.

questions.stem: A student picks the most active-looking water fleas for her caffeine group, then counts heartbeats herself while knowing which dish is which. Which changes would reduce bias in her study? Select all that apply.
choices: Assign animals to groups with a random number generator
Have a classmate label the dishes with codes so the counter does not know the treatments
Test more animals chosen the same way
Count beats for 30 seconds instead of 15
questions.explanation: Random assignment removes the selection bias, and coding the dishes blinds the observer. Testing more animals chosen the same way only gives a more precise biased answer, and counting longer improves precision, not bias.

questions.stem: Put the steps of planning and carrying out an experiment in order.
choices: Ask a question
Write operational definitions and a hypothesis
Get approval from an ethics committee
Randomly assign units to groups
Collect the data blind
Analyze the data
questions.explanation: A question becomes a measurable hypothesis; the design (including controls and sample size) is reviewed for ethics before any subjects are used; units are then randomly assigned, measured without knowledge of their treatment, and the data analyzed.

questions.stem: Treating repeated measurements of the same experimental unit (for example, ten leaves from one plant) as if they were independent replicates is called ___.
questions.explanation: Measurements from one unit share everything that happened to that unit, so they are not independent. Pseudoreplication makes results look far more certain than they are.

questions.stem: Bacterial colonies counted on seven plates: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 47. What is the median?
questions.explanation: In order, the middle (4th) of 7 values is 4. The mean is 70/7 = 10, pulled up by the outlier 47; 3 is the most common value (the mode); 45 is the range.

questions.stem: Most deer in a forest carry a few ticks, but a handful carry hundreds. Which single number best describes the tick load of a typical deer?
choices: The mean
The range
The median
The standard deviation
questions.explanation: The data are strongly skewed, so the few heavily infested deer pull the mean far above what most deer carry. The median resists outliers. The range and SD describe spread, not a typical value.

questions.stem: What is the sample standard deviation of the values 4, 6 and 8?
questions.explanation: The mean is 6; deviations −2, 0, 2; squares sum to 8. Divide by n − 1 = 2 to get 4 (the variance), then take the square root: 2. Dividing by n gives 1.63; 4 forgets the square root; 2.83 is √8, which skips dividing.

questions.stem: The lengths of 36 leaves have a standard deviation of 12 mm. What is the standard error of the mean length?
choices: 2 mm
6 mm
12 mm
questions.explanation: SE = s/√n = 12/√36 = 12/6 = 2 mm. 0.33 is 12/36 (dividing by n instead of √n); 6 is √36; 12 mm is the SD itself.

questions.stem: A researcher keeps adding plants to a sample that started with 10. As the sample grows, what happens to the standard deviation and the standard error of plant height?
choices: Both shrink toward zero
The SD settles near the population's true spread, while the SE keeps shrinking
Both stay the same
The SD shrinks, while the SE stays the same
questions.explanation: The SD describes how much individual plants vary, which doesn't depend on how many you measure. The SE (SD/√n) describes the precision of the mean, which improves as n grows.

questions.stem: A study reports a 95% confidence interval for mean beak depth of 9.2 to 9.8 mm. Which statement is correct?
choices: 95% of the birds have beak depths between 9.2 and 9.8 mm
There is a 95% chance that the next bird measured will fall in this range
If the study were repeated many times, about 95% of intervals made this way would contain the true mean
The sample mean is 95% accurate
questions.explanation: A confidence interval is about the population mean, and the 95% describes how often the method captures it. The range containing about 95% of individual birds would be roughly the mean ± 2 SD, much wider.

questions.stem: Body lengths in a population of fish are roughly normal with mean 50 mm and SD 10 mm. About what percent of fish are between 30 and 70 mm long?
questions.explanation: 30 and 70 are each 2 SD from the mean, and about 95% of normal data lie within 2 SD. 68% would be 40 to 60 mm (1 SD); 99.7% is 3 SD.

questions.stem: A graph shows means with standard error bars for two independent groups of 15 animals. The SE bars overlap. What can you conclude?
choices: The difference is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level
The difference is significant at the 0.05 level
The two groups have the same mean
Nothing, because SE bars cannot be compared
questions.explanation: For independent groups of similar size, overlapping SE bars mean p > 0.05. That is not the same as showing the means are equal: a real difference may exist that the study could not detect.

questions.stem: A sample mean is 120 with a standard error of 4. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval?
questions.explanation: Mean ± 2 SE = 120 ± 8. 116 to 124 uses only 1 SE; 104 to 136 uses 4 SE; 118 to 122 uses half an SE.

questions.stem: A biologist has body mass and resting metabolic rate for 30 mammal species and wants to show how the two are related. Which graph fits best?
choices: A bar graph of the two means
A box plot of metabolic rate
A scatter plot
A pie chart of body mass
questions.explanation: Two measured variables for the same individuals (species) call for a scatter plot, where each point is one species. Bar graphs compare groups; box plots and histograms show one variable's distribution.

questions.stem: This box plot shows tick counts on 15 mice. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A horizontal box plot of ticks per mouse on a scale from 0 to 35, with a box, a line inside it, whiskers on both sides and one separate point far to the right. Five parts are numbered.

choices: Lower quartile
Median
Upper quartile
End of whisker (largest non-outlier)
Outlier
Mean
Standard error
questions.explanation: The box runs from the lower quartile (2) to the upper quartile (11), with the median (5) inside. The right whisker ends at 19, the largest value that is not an outlier; 34 is more than 1.5 box-lengths beyond the box, so it is plotted as an outlier. A box plot does not show the mean or the standard error.

questions.stem: Which statements about the sample standard deviation are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It is in the same units as the data
It measures how much individual values spread around the mean
It shrinks toward zero as the sample size grows
It is always smaller than the standard error
questions.explanation: Taking the square root returns the SD to the data's units, and it describes spread of individuals. It does not shrink with more data (the SE does), and the SE = SD/√n is smaller than the SD whenever n > 1.

questions.stem: Match each kind of error bar to what it shows.
choices: How much individual values vary
How precisely the mean is known (s/√n)
A range of plausible values for the true mean
The difference between the largest and smallest values
questions.explanation: SD bars describe the data; SE bars describe the precision of the mean; a 95% CI (about ±2 SE) gives plausible values for the population mean. The difference between the extremes is the range, which is rarely drawn as an error bar.

questions.stem: Nine plants have a mean height of 12.4 cm and a standard deviation of 3.0 cm. The standard error of the mean is ___ cm.
Put the steps for calculating a sample standard deviation in order.
choices: Find the mean
Subtract the mean from each value
Square each deviation
Add the squared deviations
Divide by n − 1
Take the square root
questions.explanation: s = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)): deviations from the mean, squared so they don't cancel, summed, divided by n − 1, and square-rooted to return to the original units.

questions.stem: A biologist tests whether caffeine changes the heart rate of water fleas. What is the null hypothesis?
choices: Caffeine increases mean heart rate
Caffeine changes mean heart rate
Water fleas in caffeine have a different heart rate
Caffeine has no effect on mean heart rate
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis is the specific "no effect" statement that the test assumes. The other three are versions of the alternative hypothesis.

questions.stem: A test gives p = 0.03. What does this mean?
choices: If the null hypothesis were true, a result at least this extreme would happen about 3% of the time
There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% chance that the treatment works
The treatment changed the outcome by 3%
questions.explanation: A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true, so it cannot be the probability that the null is true or that the treatment works. It also says nothing directly about the size of the effect.

questions.stem: A Type I error is
choices: failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false
rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true
using the wrong statistical test
making a mistake in the arithmetic
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive: concluding there is an effect when there is none. Failing to detect a real effect is a Type II error.

questions.stem: A lab tests 40 genes to see whether each one's activity differs between two groups of mice. In fact none of the genes differ. Testing each at the 0.05 level, about how many "significant" results should the lab expect by chance?
questions.explanation: With a true null, each test has a 5% chance of a false positive: 40 × 0.05 = 2. This is why testing many things and reporting only the hits produces false discoveries.

questions.stem: In a study of 100 seedlings, 60 were treated and 40 untreated; 70 survived and 30 died. If survival is independent of treatment, how many treated seedlings are expected to survive?
questions.explanation: Expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total = 60 × 70 / 100 = 42. Equivalently, 70% of all seedlings survived, so 70% of the 60 treated ones are expected to.

questions.stem: A chi-square test of independence uses a contingency table with 3 rows and 4 columns. How many degrees of freedom does it have?
questions.explanation: df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1) = 2 × 3 = 6. 11 is cells − 1 (the goodness-of-fit rule misapplied); 12 is the number of cells; 7 is rows + columns.

questions.stem: Kettlewell recaptured 27.5% of dark peppered moths and 13.1% of pale ones released in a sooty wood; a chi-square test of independence gave χ² = 11.84 with 1 degree of freedom. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Birds were proven to eat more pale moths
In that wood, recapture rate depended on the moth's form
Moth color and recapture are independent
Dark moths are a different species from pale moths
questions.explanation: Since 11.84 > 3.84, independence is rejected: the forms were recaptured at different rates. The test shows an association, not its cause; bird predation was supported by other evidence, including Majerus's later experiment.

questions.stem: Group 1 has mean 30 (SE 1.5) and group 2 has mean 36 (SE 2.0). What is the t statistic for the difference?
questions.explanation: SE of the difference = √(1.5² + 2.0²) = √6.25 = 2.5, so t = 6/2.5 = 2.4. 1.71 adds the SEs instead of combining their squares; 3.0 uses only one SE; 0.96 divides by 6.25 without taking the square root.

questions.stem: Across 25 populations of a lizard species, altitude and mean body length have a correlation coefficient of r = −0.85. What does this tell you?
choices: High altitude causes lizards to be shorter
There is almost no relationship, since r is negative
85% of lizards are shorter at higher altitude
There is a strong negative straight-line relationship: higher populations tend to have shorter lizards
questions.explanation: An r near −1 means a strong negative linear relationship. The sign gives the direction, not the strength. Correlation alone does not show that altitude causes the difference, and r is not a percentage of individuals.

questions.stem: Countries with higher chocolate consumption per person have won more Nobel prizes per person (r = 0.79). Which is the best interpretation?
choices: A third factor, such as national wealth, could raise both, so the correlation alone shows no cause
Eating chocolate improves the brain, causing more prizes
The correlation is too weak to mean anything
Winning prizes makes people eat more chocolate
questions.explanation: A strong correlation can arise from a confounding variable; wealth plausibly raises both chocolate consumption and research output. Claiming either direction of cause needs other evidence, such as experiments.

questions.stem: For cricket chirp rate, the least-squares line is ŷ = −28.9 + 6.93x, where x is temperature in °C. What chirp rate does it predict at 24 °C?
choices: About 166 chirps per minute
About 137 chirps per minute
About 195 chirps per minute
About 124 chirps per minute
questions.explanation: −28.9 + 6.93 × 24 = −28.9 + 166.3 = 137.4. 166 forgets the intercept; 195 adds 28.9 instead of subtracting it; 124 is the mean chirp rate of the data.

questions.stem: A chi-square test of independence on a 2 × 2 contingency table has ___ degree(s) of freedom.
questions.explanation: df = (2 − 1)(2 − 1) = 1. Once the row and column totals are fixed, choosing one cell determines the other three.

questions.stem: Match each study to the statistical tool that fits it.
left: Comparing F2 phenotype counts with a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio
Asking whether eye color is associated with sex in 200 flies
Comparing mean leaf length of plants in two light treatments
Relating wing length to body mass in 50 birds
choices: Chi-square goodness of fit
Chi-square test of independence
t-test
Correlation and linear regression
questions.explanation: Counts compared with a predicted ratio: goodness of fit. Two categorical variables cross-classified: test of independence. Two group means: t-test. Two measured variables on the same individuals: correlation and regression.

questions.stem: Which statements about p-values are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true
p = 0.04 means there is a 4% chance that the null hypothesis is true
A very small p-value can come from a tiny effect in a very large sample
p > 0.05 proves that the treatment has no effect
questions.explanation: The p-value assumes the null and asks how surprising the data are, so it is not the probability that the null is true. Huge samples can make trivial effects significant, so report effect sizes too. A non-significant result may simply reflect low power.

questions.stem: A regression of y on x has a correlation coefficient of r = 0.90. The line explains ___ percent of the variation in y.
questions.explanation: The coefficient of determination is r² = 0.90² = 0.81, so the line explains 81% of the variation in y.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a chi-square test of independence in order.
choices: State the null and alternative hypotheses
Compute expected counts from the row and column totals
Calculate chi-square from observed and expected counts
Find the degrees of freedom
Compare chi-square with the critical value and decide
questions.explanation: The hypotheses come first; the null (independence) gives the expected counts; χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; df = (r − 1)(c − 1) determines the critical value used to decide.

questions.stem: In which section of a research paper would you look to find the sample sizes, the concentrations used and the statistical tests?
choices: Abstract
Results
Methods
Discussion
questions.explanation: The methods give enough detail for someone else to repeat the study, including organisms, sample sizes, procedures and statistics. The abstract summarizes; results report findings; the discussion interprets them.

questions.stem: What belongs in the results section of a lab report?
choices: An explanation of why the results support the hypothesis
Background on why the question matters
A step-by-step description of the procedure
The findings, with numbers, units, sample sizes and test results, but no interpretation
questions.explanation: Results report what was found. Interpretation goes in the discussion, background in the introduction, and procedures in the methods.

questions.stem: A review article on antibiotic resistance is best described as
choices: a secondary source that summarizes many primary studies
a primary source reporting a new experiment
a preprint that has not been peer reviewed
a news story based on one study
questions.explanation: Review articles survey and summarize the primary literature, usually written by experts and usually peer reviewed. A primary source reports original research by the people who did it.

questions.stem: An abstract says a drug "strongly improved survival." What is the best way to check whether the paper's data support this?
choices: Read the title again
Look at the figures, their legends and the sample sizes
Check how many times the paper has been shared online
Read the introduction
questions.explanation: Figures and legends show the actual evidence: effect size, variation, n and test results. Abstracts sometimes claim more than the data show. Popularity and background say nothing about the data.

questions.stem: Which problem is peer review least able to catch?
choices: A conclusion that goes beyond the data shown
A missing control group
Data that the authors fabricated
An inappropriate statistical test
questions.explanation: Reviewers judge what the authors report: design, controls, statistics and whether conclusions follow. They usually cannot see raw data or lab notebooks, so fabrication rarely shows up. Replication after publication is the deeper check.

questions.stem: A news story reports a "new study" posted on bioRxiv last week. What should a careful reader keep in mind?
choices: It has been peer reviewed, since it is on a science website
It must be false, since it was not published in a journal
It has already been replicated by other labs
It is a preprint, so it has not yet been checked by peer review
questions.explanation: bioRxiv hosts preprints: complete manuscripts posted before or during peer review. They can be valuable and many are later published, but they should be treated as claims not yet checked by reviewers.

questions.stem: A figure shows a control mean of 2.5 units and a treated mean of 3.5 units. What is the percent change from control to treated?
questions.explanation: (3.5 − 2.5)/2.5 × 100% = 40%. 29% divides by the treated value; 1.4 is the fold change (not a percent); 140% confuses the fold change with the percent change.

questions.stem: A gene's activity is 0.80 units in control cells and 0.20 units in treated cells. What is the fold change (treated ÷ control)?
choices: 4, a 300% increase
0.25, a 75% decrease
0.60, a 60% decrease
0.75, a 25% decrease
questions.explanation: 0.20/0.80 = 0.25, so activity fell to a quarter, a 75% decrease. 4 divides the wrong way; 0.60 is the difference, not the ratio; 0.75 is the fraction lost, not the fraction left.

questions.stem: A study finding that a sports drink improves endurance was funded by the drink's maker. What is the best response?
choices: Reject the study, since industry funding makes results false
Accept the study, since funding does not affect science
Examine the methods closely and look for independent studies that test the same claim
Ignore the funding, since it was peer reviewed
questions.explanation: A conflict of interest is a reason for extra scrutiny, not automatic rejection. Funding can influence design, analysis or which results get published, so check the methods and look for independent replication.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this research figure.

image.alt: A two-panel figure. Panel A plots plant dry mass for a control and a nitrogen group as dots with means, error bars and a bracket above; panel B is a scatter plot with a dashed line. Text below the panels describes the figure. Six parts are numbered.

choices: Panel letter
Axis title with units
Individual data point
Error bar
Significance marker
Figure legend
Abstract
Regression line
questions.explanation: The letter A marks the first panel; the y-axis title gives the variable and its units (g); each dot is one plant; the short vertical bar beside each group shows mean ± SE; the asterisk over the bracket marks a significant difference; the text below is the figure legend, which defines all of these. The dashed regression line is in panel B but is not numbered.

questions.stem: Put the parts of a research paper in their usual order.
choices: Abstract
Introduction
Methods
Results
Discussion
References
questions.explanation: Papers follow IMRaD: a summary abstract, then introduction, methods, results and discussion, with references at the end.

questions.stem: A headline says "Coffee drinkers live longer," based on an observational study of 500,000 adults. Which are valid concerns about the headline? Select all that apply.
choices: Coffee drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in other ways that affect lifespan
An observational study cannot by itself show that coffee causes longer life
With 500,000 people, the association must be due to chance
Because the study was large, confounding is ruled out
questions.explanation: Large size makes chance an unlikely explanation and gives precise estimates, but it does nothing about confounding: coffee drinkers might differ in income, health or habits. Only randomized experiments, or many studies with different weaknesses agreeing, can support a causal claim.

questions.stem: Match each sentence from a lab report to the section where it belongs.
left: Caffeine stimulates the human heart, but its effect on invertebrate hearts is less studied.
Eight water fleas per group were randomly assigned to 2 mg/mL caffeine or pond water.
Mean heart rate was 245 bpm in caffeine and 213 bpm in pond water (t = 6.0, p < 0.001).
These results support the hypothesis that caffeine stimulates the water flea heart.
choices: Introduction
Methods
Results
Discussion
questions.explanation: Background goes in the introduction, procedures in the methods, numbers and test results in the results, and interpretation in the discussion.

questions.stem: When a journal formally withdraws a published paper because its findings are seriously flawed or the result of misconduct, the paper is said to have received a ___.
questions.explanation: A retraction removes a paper from the scientific record. The 1998 paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was retracted in 2010.

questions.stem: Within seconds of the first sperm fusing with a sea urchin egg, other sperm can no longer fuse with it. What causes this fast block to polyspermy?
choices: The egg's membrane voltage jumps from negative to positive.
The fertilization envelope lifts away from the egg surface.
The sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus.
The egg begins its first cleavage division.
questions.explanation: Sperm entry opens ion channels, and the membrane potential rises from about −70 mV to positive values within seconds; sperm cannot fuse with a positively charged sea urchin egg membrane. The fertilization envelope is the slow block, which takes about a minute. Fusion of the nuclei and cleavage come much later and do not block other sperm.

questions.stem: A researcher injects a sea urchin egg with a chemical that traps calcium ions so their concentration cannot rise. A sperm then fertilizes the egg. What is the most likely result?
choices: A normal fertilization envelope forms, but cleavage is faster than usual.
The acrosome reaction fails, so the sperm cannot reach the egg membrane.
No cortical reaction occurs, so no fertilization envelope forms and the egg stays poorly activated.
The egg depolarizes permanently and never needs a slow block.
questions.explanation: The calcium wave set off by sperm entry triggers the cortical granules to release their contents, building the fertilization envelope, and also switches on the egg's metabolism. Without a calcium rise, neither happens. The acrosome reaction occurs in the sperm, before contact with the egg membrane, so trapping calcium inside the egg does not stop it. The fast electrical block is temporary, which is why the slow block is needed.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes what happens during cleavage?
choices: Cells divide and grow, so the embryo doubles in size with each division.
The embryo grows but the number of cells stays the same.
Cells move inward to form three germ layers.
Cells divide rapidly without growing, so they get smaller while the embryo stays about the same size.
questions.explanation: Cleavage divisions skip most of the growth phases (G1 and G2), so the egg's cytoplasm is divided into more and smaller cells while the whole embryo stays about the same size. Assuming growth between divisions is the usual mistake. Forming germ layers is gastrulation, which comes later.

questions.stem: Why does only a small disc of cytoplasm on top of a chick egg divide during cleavage?
choices: Chick eggs are fertilized by several sperm, and only one region receives a sperm nucleus.
The huge mass of yolk cannot be cut by cleavage furrows, so only the yolk-free cap divides.
Birds have no maternal mRNA, so most of the egg is inactive.
The shell prevents the rest of the egg from dividing.
questions.explanation: Yolk gets in the way of the cleavage furrow. The chick egg cell is mostly yolk, so cleavage is partial (meroblastic): only the thin disc of cytoplasm on top divides. Sea urchin and human eggs, with little yolk, cleave completely; frogs, with moderate yolk, cleave completely but unequally. The shell has nothing to do with it.

questions.stem: Frog embryos begin transcribing their own genes after about 12 cleavages. When extra DNA was injected into fertilized eggs, this midblastula transition came earlier. What does this result support?
choices: The transition is triggered when the ratio of DNA to cytoplasm reaches a threshold.
The transition is timed by a clock that counts hours since fertilization.
The transition begins when the embryo has used up its yolk.
Injected DNA codes for a protein that starts transcription.
questions.explanation: Each cleavage doubles the amount of DNA without adding cytoplasm, so the DNA-to-cytoplasm ratio climbs. Adding DNA reached the threshold sooner, and so did the transition, which fits the ratio hypothesis (Newport and Kirschner, 1982). A clock counting hours would not be affected by extra DNA, and the result held for DNA that did not code for anything special.

questions.stem: The cells lining the air sacs and airways of the lungs come from which germ layer?
choices: Endoderm
Mesoderm
Ectoderm
Neural crest
questions.explanation: The lungs begin as an outgrowth of the embryonic gut, so their lining comes from endoderm, like the lining of the gut, liver and pancreas. Their surrounding muscle, cartilage and blood vessels come from mesoderm. Thinking "deep inside the body" means mesoderm is a common slip.

questions.stem: A human blastocyst has an outer layer of cells and a small cluster of cells inside. Which part develops into the body of the fetus?
choices: The trophoblast
The zona pellucida
The blastocoel
The inner cell mass
questions.explanation: Only the inner cell mass becomes the embryo itself (and is the source of embryonic stem cells). The trophoblast forms the embryo's part of the placenta, the blastocoel is the fluid-filled cavity, and the zona pellucida is the protein coat around the egg, which the blastocyst hatches out of.

questions.stem: Which of these structures develop from ectoderm? Select all that apply.
choices: Epidermis of the skin
Brain and spinal cord
Kidneys
Lens of the eye
Lining of the liver and gut
questions.explanation: Ectoderm forms the epidermis, the whole nervous system (via the neural tube and neural crest) and the lens of the eye. Kidneys come from mesoderm, and the lining of the gut and liver comes from endoderm.

questions.stem: In vertebrates, a stiff rod of mesoderm along the back, the ___, signals the ectoderm above it to form the neural plate.
questions.explanation: The notochord, the rod that gives chordates their name, induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube.

questions.stem: A zygote undergoes 9 synchronous cleavage divisions with no cell death. How many cells does the embryo have? ___
questions.explanation: Each division doubles the number of cells, so after $n$ divisions there are $2^n$ cells: $2^9 = 512$.

questions.stem: Put these stages of vertebrate development in order, earliest first.
choices: Fertilization
Cleavage
Blastula
Gastrulation
Neurulation
questions.explanation: Fertilization forms the zygote; cleavage divides it into many cells; the cells form a hollow blastula; gastrulation moves cells into three germ layers; then the notochord induces neurulation, the folding of the neural tube.

questions.stem: This is a cut-open sea urchin gastrula. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A cut-open sea urchin embryo during gastrulation: an outer ring of cells, a tube folding inward from an opening at the bottom, a few loose cells with projections floating in the fluid-filled space, and the space itself. Six points are numbered.

choices: Ectoderm
Endoderm
Archenteron
Blastopore
Mesenchyme (mesoderm)
Blastocoel
Notochord
Neural tube
questions.explanation: 1 The outer layer is ectoderm. 2 The wall of the infolding tube is endoderm. 3 The tube's inside is the archenteron, the primitive gut. 4 Its opening is the blastopore, which becomes the anus in sea urchins and other deuterostomes. 5 The loose cells in the cavity are mesenchyme, mesoderm cells that will build the skeleton. 6 The remaining fluid-filled space is the blastocoel. A notochord and neural tube are vertebrate (chordate) structures that form later.

questions.stem: Match each animal to its pattern of cleavage.
choices: Complete and equal: a hollow ball of equal cells
Complete but unequal: small cells on top, large yolky cells below
Partial: only a disc of cells on top of the yolk divides
Complete and slow, forming a morula and then a blastocyst
questions.explanation: The amount and position of yolk set the pattern. Sea urchin eggs have little, evenly spread yolk; frog yolk is concentrated in the lower half; the chick egg is almost all yolk; mammal eggs have very little yolk and cleave slowly while traveling down the oviduct.

questions.stem: A frog egg is 1.2 mm across. After 6 synchronous cleavage divisions with no growth, about what is the average diameter of a cell?
choices: 0.2 mm
0.6 mm
0.3 mm
questions.explanation: Six divisions give $2^6 = 64$ cells, each with $\tfrac{1}{64}$ of the volume. Diameter scales as the cube root of volume: $64^{1/3} = 4$, so $d = 1.2 \div 4 = 0.3$ mm. Dividing the diameter by 64 (0.019 mm) forgets the cube root; dividing by 2 or by 6 treats the cell count or the number of divisions as if it scaled the diameter directly.

questions.stem: Spemann swapped presumptive neural tissue and presumptive epidermis between newt embryos. At the early gastrula stage each piece developed according to its new location; at the late gastrula stage the presumptive neural tissue formed neural tissue in the belly. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Presumptive neural tissue becomes determined between the early and late gastrula stages.
Presumptive neural tissue is already differentiated at the early gastrula stage.
Cells lose the genes for other fates during gastrulation.
The belly region induces neural tissue at the late gastrula stage.
questions.explanation: A transplant tests determination: an undetermined tissue follows its new position, a determined one keeps its old fate. The fate of the future neural tissue was fixed by the late gastrula, though it did not yet look different (so it was not differentiated). Gurdon-type experiments show genes are not lost, and the belly did not make neural tissue in the early transplants, so it is not an inducer of neural fate.

questions.stem: In the Spemann–Mangold experiment, dorsal lip tissue from a light-colored newt embryo was grafted onto the belly side of a dark-colored embryo, and a second body axis formed. Most of the second neural tube was dark. What does this show?
choices: The graft divided rapidly and built the whole second embryo itself.
The host's cells were already determined to form a second nervous system.
The graft induced host cells that would have formed belly tissue to form a neural tube.
Pigment cells migrated from the graft into the host.
questions.explanation: Dark cells came from the host. The graft itself formed mostly notochord, and it changed the fate of host belly cells, organizing them into a neural tube and other axial tissues. That is induction, and the dorsal lip was named the organizer. If the graft had built everything, the second neural tube would be light.

questions.stem: The organizer secretes proteins such as chordin and noggin. How do they cause nearby ectoderm to become neural tissue?
choices: They enter the nucleus and act as transcription factors for neural genes.
They bind BMP4 and prevent it from signaling, so the ectoderm is not told to become epidermis.
They kill the epidermal cells by triggering apoptosis.
They are morphogens whose high concentration directly switches on epidermal genes.
questions.explanation: BMP4 signals ectoderm to become epidermis. Chordin and noggin bind BMP4 outside the cells and block it, so ectoderm near the organizer takes a neural fate. They are secreted proteins acting outside the cell, not transcription factors, and they block an epidermal signal rather than activating epidermal genes.

questions.stem: A morphogen forms the gradient $C(x) = C_0 e^{-x/\lambda}$ with $\lambda = 100$ µm. A target gene turns on wherever $C \ge 0.2\,C_0$. About how far from the source is the boundary of its expression?
choices: 20 µm
69 µm
230 µm
161 µm
questions.explanation: Solve $C_0 e^{-x/\lambda} = 0.2\,C_0$: $x = \lambda \ln(1/0.2) = 100 \ln 5 \approx 161$ µm. 20 µm comes from multiplying $\lambda$ by 0.2; 230 µm is the boundary for a threshold of $0.1\,C_0$; 69 µm is $\lambda \ln 2$, the shift from doubling the dose.

questions.stem: A female fruit fly has no working copies of the bicoid gene. What do the embryos she produces look like, whatever the father's genotype?
choices: They lack head and thorax structures and have rear-end structures at both ends.
They have two heads and no abdomen.
They develop normally, because each embryo makes its own Bicoid after fertilization.
They develop legs in place of antennae.
questions.explanation: bicoid is a maternal effect gene: the mother places its mRNA at the front of every egg. With none, the embryos have no Bicoid gradient, so no head or thorax forms and posterior structures develop at both ends. The father's alleles arrive too late to help. Legs in place of antennae is the Antennapedia homeotic mutation.

questions.stem: When the single gene MyoD was expressed in cultured fibroblasts, the cells began making muscle proteins and fused into muscle fibers. What does this show?
choices: Fibroblasts had lost their muscle genes and MyoD replaced them.
MyoD is a structural protein that forms muscle fibers.
Muscle cells are made by fusing fibroblasts with existing muscle cells.
A single master transcription factor can switch on the gene program of a cell type.
questions.explanation: MyoD codes for a transcription factor that turns on muscle genes (and its own gene), so it can switch a cell into the muscle program. The fibroblasts already had the muscle genes; they were simply not expressed. MyoD is not a structural protein, and no existing muscle cells were involved.

questions.stem: Which observations support the idea that Bicoid acts as a morphogen whose concentration specifies position? Select all that apply.
choices: Injecting bicoid mRNA into the rear of an egg makes head structures form there.
Extra copies of bicoid in the mother shift body boundaries toward the rear.
Bicoid protein is present at equal levels in every nucleus.
Embryos from mothers lacking bicoid lack head and thorax.
questions.explanation: A morphogen should be necessary (loss removes anterior structures), sufficient where added (ectopic mRNA makes a head), and dose-dependent (more Bicoid moves boundaries back). Equal levels everywhere would give no positional information; in fact Bicoid forms a front-to-back gradient.

questions.stem: Hox genes share a 180-base-pair DNA sequence that codes for a DNA-binding region of the protein. This sequence is called the ___.
questions.explanation: The homeobox codes for the 60-amino-acid homeodomain, which lets Hox proteins bind DNA and act as transcription factors. Finding it in fly genes led quickly to the Hox genes of vertebrates.

questions.stem: Match each mutation or experiment to its result.
left: Dorsal lip grafted to the belly side
choices: Legs grow in place of antennae
A fly with four wings instead of two wings and two halteres
Embryos lack head and thorax
A second body axis forms
Every segment of the embryo is missing
questions.explanation: Antennapedia and Ultrabithorax mutations are homeotic: one body part develops as another (antenna as leg; third thoracic segment as a copy of the second). Losing maternal Bicoid removes anterior structures. The dorsal lip graft is the Spemann–Mangold organizer experiment. No single listed mutation removes every segment.

questions.stem: Put the levels of the fruit fly segmentation cascade in order, from the first to act to the last.
choices: Maternal genes such as bicoid
Gap genes
Pair-rule genes
Segment polarity genes
questions.explanation: The mother's bicoid mRNA sets up a gradient; gap genes respond with broad blocks of expression; pair-rule genes make seven stripes; segment polarity genes mark the front and back of all 14 segments. Each level reads the one above it, and the pattern gets finer at every step. Hox genes then give each segment its identity.

questions.stem: A female fly homozygous for a loss-of-function bicoid allele ($bcd/bcd$) was herself born from a $bcd/+$ mother. She mates with a $+/+$ male. What happens to her embryos?
choices: All develop normally, because they are all $bcd/+$.
Half develop normally.
All lack head and thorax.
She is abnormal herself and cannot lay eggs.
questions.explanation: For a maternal effect gene, the mother's genotype decides. She makes no Bicoid mRNA, so every egg lacks it, even though every embryo is $bcd/+$. She herself developed normally because her own mother ($bcd/+$) supplied Bicoid. Reasoning from the embryos' own genotypes gives the wrong answer here.

questions.stem: What does "colinearity" mean for Hox genes?
choices: All Hox genes are expressed in every segment at the same level.
The order of the genes on the chromosome matches the front-to-back order of the body regions where they act.
Each Hox gene is located on a different chromosome.
Hox genes are transcribed together as one long mRNA.
questions.explanation: In flies and vertebrates, genes at one end of a Hox cluster act in the head and front of the body and genes at the other end act toward the rear, in the same order. Hox genes in a cluster sit next to each other on one chromosome and are expressed in different regions, each from its own promoter.

questions.stem: Only cells that have the right receptors and transcription factors can respond to an inducing signal. This ability to respond is called ___.
questions.explanation: Induction needs both a signal and competent responding cells. The same signal can therefore have different effects, or none, in different tissues.

questions.stem: A blood stem cell in bone marrow can produce red blood cells, all kinds of white blood cells and platelets, but not neurons or liver cells. Which term describes its potency?
choices: Totipotent
Pluripotent
Unipotent
Multipotent
questions.explanation: Making several cell types of one family (the blood cells) is multipotency. Pluripotent cells can make every cell type of the body, totipotent cells also the placenta, and unipotent cells only one type.

questions.stem: What can a totipotent cell do that a pluripotent cell cannot?
choices: Divide indefinitely in culture
Form tissues of all three germ layers
Produce the placenta and other supporting tissues as well as the body
Self-renew
questions.explanation: Pluripotent cells (inner cell mass, embryonic stem cells, iPSCs) can make all three germ layers and can self-renew, and embryonic stem cells divide indefinitely in culture. Only totipotent cells, the zygote and the earliest blastomeres, can also make the trophoblast that forms the placenta.

questions.stem: Till and McCulloch found that the number of spleen colonies in irradiated mice rose in direct proportion to the number of bone marrow cells injected. Why was this proportionality important?
choices: It showed that each colony grows from a single cell.
It showed that radiation had no effect on the spleen.
It showed that every marrow cell is a stem cell.
It showed that colonies form only when many cells cooperate.
questions.explanation: If one cell can start a colony, colonies should scale linearly with cells injected. If several cells had to cooperate, the count would rise faster than linearly at higher doses. Marker studies later confirmed each colony is a clone. Only about 1 in 10,000 injected cells made a colony, so most marrow cells are not stem cells.

questions.stem: Irradiated mice injected with 300,000 marrow cells develop an average of 24 spleen colonies. If only 20% of injected colony-forming cells lodge in the spleen, what is the estimated true number of colony-forming cells per 100,000 marrow cells?
questions.explanation: Detected frequency: $24 \div 3 = 8$ colonies per 100,000 cells. Each detected colony represents $1 \div 0.2 = 5$ injected colony-forming cells, so the true frequency is $8 \times 5 = 40$ per 100,000. 8 forgets the correction; 1.6 multiplies by 0.2 instead of dividing; 160 divides by 0.05.

questions.stem: In the experiment that produced Dolly, 277 eggs were fused with udder cells, 29 embryos were transferred to surrogates, and 1 lamb was born. What is the best explanation for the low success rate?
choices: Udder cells lack many of the genes needed to build a sheep.
The egg cytoplasm only partly erases the donor nucleus's epigenetic marks, so development often goes wrong.
Surrogate ewes reject cloned embryos as foreign.
Udder cells contain only half the chromosomes of a zygote.
questions.explanation: Dolly herself shows the udder-cell nucleus had a complete genome. Failures happen at every stage, before and after transfer, because reprogramming of the donor nucleus's epigenetic marks is incomplete. Udder cells are diploid body cells, and rejection by surrogates does not explain the many failures before transfer.

questions.stem: Takahashi and Yamanaka started with 24 candidate genes that together reprogrammed fibroblasts. How did they find which genes were needed?
choices: They tested each of the 24 genes alone and kept the one that worked best.
They sequenced the fibroblasts' genomes to find missing genes.
They used CRISPR to delete genes from embryonic stem cells.
They removed one gene at a time from the mixture and saw which removals stopped colonies from forming.
questions.explanation: Leaving out one factor at a time revealed which were essential: if colonies disappeared without a gene, that gene was needed. This narrowed the list to four (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc). Single genes alone did not reprogram cells, and the fibroblasts were not missing any genes.

questions.stem: Cells injected under the skin of an immune-deficient mouse form a tumor containing gut-like tissue, cartilage, muscle and nerve tissue. What does this teratoma show about the injected cells?
choices: They are pluripotent, able to form tissues of all three germ layers.
They are unipotent.
They are totipotent, because the tumor contains placenta.
They came from adult bone marrow.
questions.explanation: Gut lining is endoderm, cartilage and muscle are mesoderm, and nerve tissue is ectoderm. Forming all three is the teratoma test for pluripotency. Nothing in the tumor is placenta, and bone marrow stem cells are multipotent and do not form teratomas.

questions.stem: Which statements about induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are true? Select all that apply.
choices: They can be made from a patient's own skin or blood cells.
Making them does not require destroying an embryo.
They are totipotent and can form a placenta.
Leftover undifferentiated iPSCs in a transplant could form tumors.
They raise no ethical questions at all.
questions.explanation: iPSCs are reprogrammed body cells, so no embryo is used and they can be matched to a patient. Like embryonic stem cells they are pluripotent, not totipotent, and can form teratomas, a safety concern for therapies. They still raise questions about donor consent, genetic privacy and the possibility of making gametes or embryo-like structures.

questions.stem: After a salamander loses a limb, cells near the wound gather into a growing bud that rebuilds the missing part. This bud is called a ___.
questions.explanation: The blastema forms from cells that dedifferentiate near the wound. Tracking labeled cells shows they mostly keep a memory of their tissue of origin, so the blastema is a mix of restricted progenitors rather than pluripotent cells.

questions.stem: Match each researcher or team to their discovery.
choices: Spleen colonies proving blood stem cells exist
First nuclear transfers producing frog tadpoles
Dolly the sheep cloned from an adult cell
Reprogramming body cells with four transcription factors
Discovery of the organizer in newt embryos
questions.explanation: Till and McCulloch's spleen colonies (1961), Briggs and King's frog nuclear transfers (1952), Wilmut and Campbell's Dolly (born 1996) and Yamanaka's iPSCs (2006) are the milestones of this lesson. The organizer was discovered by Spemann and Mangold (lesson 46).

questions.stem: Planarians were irradiated to kill all their dividing cells, and a single neoblast from another strain was transplanted into each. In some worms, the descendants of that one cell replaced every tissue. What does this show?
choices: Planarian neurons can divide after irradiation.
Every planarian cell is a stem cell.
At least some adult planarian neoblasts are pluripotent.
Regeneration in planarians does not require cell division.
questions.explanation: One cell that rebuilds all tissue types must be able to make every cell type: pluripotency, here in an adult animal. The host's own dividing cells were dead, so the new tissue came from the transplant and did require division. Only some neoblasts behave this way, so not every cell is a stem cell.

questions.stem: Researchers label the cartilage cells in an axolotl's arm with a fluorescent marker, then amputate the arm. In the regrown arm, where would you expect to find most of the labeled cells?
choices: Spread evenly through muscle, skin, nerve and cartilage
Mostly in the new skin
Nowhere, because the labeled cells die at the wound
Mostly in the new cartilage
questions.explanation: Lineage tracing in axolotls (2009) showed blastema cells mostly keep a memory of their origin: cartilage-derived cells make cartilage, muscle-derived cells make muscle. An even spread would be expected only if the blastema were pluripotent, which it is not. The labeled cells survive and divide in the blastema, so they do appear in the new limb, but not in the skin, which regrows from epidermis.

questions.stem: Put the steps of reproductive cloning by somatic cell nuclear transfer in order.
choices: Remove the chromosomes from an unfertilized egg
Fuse the egg with a body cell from the animal to be cloned
Stimulate the reconstructed egg to start dividing
Grow it to an early embryo in culture
Transfer the embryo into a surrogate mother
questions.explanation: The egg's own chromosomes are removed first, so the body cell's nucleus supplies all the nuclear DNA. After fusion an electric pulse or chemicals start development, the embryo is cultured for a few days, and then it is transferred to a surrogate. Stopping at the cultured embryo to harvest stem cells would be therapeutic cloning.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is a value claim rather than an empirical claim?
choices: Human embryos should not be used in research after day 14.
Most cloned embryos fail to develop to birth.
iPSCs made with c-Myc can form tumors in mice.
Human embryonic stem cells were first grown in 1998.
questions.explanation: "Should not" states what ought to be done, so it is a value claim; evidence about development informs it but cannot settle it alone. The other three can be checked with data or records.

questions.stem: What is the C-value paradox?
choices: Genome size varies enormously among eukaryotes and does not track how complex organisms are.
Organisms with more genes always have smaller genomes.
Haploid cells have twice as much DNA as diploid cells.
Bacteria have larger genomes than most animals.
questions.explanation: An onion has about five times as much DNA as a human, and a fern about 50 times, with no corresponding difference in complexity or gene number.
