The explanation is mostly noncoding DNA, especially transposable elements. Bacteria have small genomes, and diploid cells have twice the haploid amount, not half.

questions.stem: Baker's yeast has about 6,000 protein-coding genes in a 12-million-bp genome. About how many genes per million base pairs is that?
questions.explanation: $6{,}000 \div 12 = 500$ genes per million bp, about one gene every 2,000 bp. That is about half the density of E. coli (about 935 per Mb) and nearly 80 times that of humans (about 6.5 per Mb). 50 and 5,000 are decimal-place slips; 2,000 is the number of base pairs per gene, not genes per million base pairs.

questions.stem: How do retrotransposons such as LINE-1 and Alu spread through a genome?
choices: They cut themselves out of one site and paste themselves into another using transposase.
They are transcribed into RNA, and reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy that inserts at a new site.
They are copied only when the whole genome duplicates.
They enter cells from outside as viruses in every generation.
questions.explanation: Retrotransposons "copy and paste" through an RNA intermediate, so each round adds a copy; this is how Alu reached about a million copies. Cut-and-paste with transposase describes DNA transposons, which move without multiplying as fast. Retrotransposons are inherited within the genome, not reinfecting from outside.

questions.stem: A transposable element about 300 bp long makes up 12% of a 3.0-billion-bp genome. About how many copies are there?
choices: 1.2 million
360 million
questions.explanation: Total element DNA: $0.12 \times 3.0 \times 10^9 = 3.6 \times 10^8$ bp. Copies: $3.6 \times 10^8 \div 300 = 1.2 \times 10^6$. The smaller answers drop powers of ten, and 360 million is the number of base pairs of element DNA, not the number of copies.

questions.stem: A copy of a gene that has been disabled by mutations, so it no longer makes a working product, is called a ___.
questions.explanation: After duplication, the most common fate of an extra copy is to collect disabling mutations and become a pseudogene. Humans have over 10,000 of them, including many in the smell-receptor and globin families.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Genes related by duplication within a lineage
Genes in different species descended from one ancestral gene by speciation
One duplicate gains a new function
Duplicates divide the original gene's jobs between them
A gene moved by a virus between species
questions.explanation: Human α- and β-globin are paralogs; human and mouse β-globin are orthologs. Red and green opsins in primates are an example of neofunctionalization; duplicates expressed at different stages or in different tissues often show subfunctionalization. Gene transfer between species by a virus is horizontal transfer, not one of these terms.

questions.stem: Which pair of genes are paralogs?
choices: Human β-globin and chimpanzee β-globin
Human α-globin and human β-globin
Mouse Pax6 and fly eyeless
Human β-globin and mouse β-globin
questions.explanation: α- and β-globin arose by a duplication within the vertebrate lineage and now sit side by side in the same genome: paralogs. The other pairs are genes in different species descended from one ancestral gene through speciation: orthologs.

questions.stem: Duplications in the β-globin gene cluster produced chains used at different stages of life. What is the advantage of fetal hemoglobin?
choices: It carries carbon dioxide instead of oxygen.
It binds oxygen more tightly than adult hemoglobin, so the fetus can take oxygen from the mother's blood.
It binds oxygen less tightly, so it releases oxygen to the mother.
It does not need iron.
questions.explanation: Higher oxygen affinity lets fetal blood pull oxygen across the placenta from maternal blood. Lower affinity would send oxygen the wrong way. Fetal hemoglobin carries oxygen with iron-containing heme like adult hemoglobin. Expressing different duplicates at different stages is an example of how gene copies divide up roles.

questions.stem: When the mouse Pax6 gene was switched on in the leg tissue of a fruit fly, extra eyes grew on the leg. What kind of eyes were they, and what does this show?
choices: Mouse camera eyes, showing the mouse gene carries instructions for building a vertebrate eye.
Fly compound eyes, showing the mouse gene switched on the fly's own eye-building program (deep homology).
Fly compound eyes, showing that fly and mouse eyes are homologous structures.
No real eyes, only pigment, showing the genes are unrelated.
questions.explanation: The mouse protein acted as a master switch for the fly's own eye genes, so the eyes were fly compound eyes. Different eye structures built under the control of genes inherited from a common ancestor is deep homology. The eyes themselves are not considered homologous structures; their shared control gene is.

questions.stem: Many lake populations of three-spined sticklebacks have lost their pelvic spines. What did researchers find about the Pitx1 gene in these fish?
choices: The Pitx1 gene has been deleted from the genome.
The Pitx1 protein has a nonsense mutation.
The Pitx1 protein is unchanged, but the gene is no longer expressed in the developing pelvis.
Pitx1 is expressed at higher levels in every tissue.
questions.explanation: Lake fish make normal Pitx1 protein in the jaw, pituitary and other tissues; only pelvic expression is missing, because a pelvic enhancer was deleted. Losing the whole gene or protein would also disrupt its other jobs, which in mice is lethal.

questions.stem: Which findings support the conclusion that pelvic loss in lake sticklebacks was caused by a cis-regulatory change? Select all that apply.
choices: Independent lake populations carry deletions of a Pitx1 enhancer.
Adding back a working pelvic enhancer restored pelvic structures in lake fish.
Lake fish have no Pitx1 gene at all.
Pitx1 expression in the jaw and pituitary is normal in lake fish.
questions.explanation: The gene and protein are intact and still used elsewhere; what is missing is one tissue-specific switch on the same DNA. Deletions of that switch, and rescue by restoring it, point directly to a cis-regulatory change. The statement that lake fish lack the gene is false.

questions.stem: In a hybrid between an ocean and a lake stickleback, only the ocean allele of Pitx1 is expressed in the pelvic region. What does this suggest?
choices: The difference lies in a regulatory protein encoded by another gene.
The lake allele's protein-coding sequence is broken.
The hybrid lost the lake allele during development.
The difference lies in DNA linked to the lake allele itself, such as its enhancer.
questions.explanation: In a hybrid both alleles share the same cell and the same regulatory proteins. If the difference were in a separate (trans) regulator, the ocean version would switch on both alleles. Expression from only one allele means the difference travels with that allele: a cis change. Whether a protein works does not determine whether its mRNA is made.

questions.stem: Put these genomes in order of size, smallest first.
choices: E. coli
Baker's yeast
Human
Onion
Fork fern Tmesipteris
questions.explanation: About 4.6 million bp for E. coli, 12 million for yeast, 3.1 billion for humans, 16 billion for onion and about 160 billion for the fern. The onion and fern placements are the C-value paradox in action.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects current evidence about the noncoding DNA in the human genome?
choices: All of it is functional, because about 80% shows some biochemical activity.
None of it has a function; only protein-coding genes matter.
More is functional than the 1.5% that codes for protein, but evolutionary conservation suggests much of it is not under selection.
It is made entirely of active transposons.
questions.explanation: Regulatory elements, RNA genes and other noncoding sequences clearly have functions, but only about 10% of the genome appears to be conserved by selection. Biochemical activity (as reported by ENCODE) is not the same as function. Transposable-element-derived DNA is about 45% of the genome, and almost all copies are inactive.

questions.stem: Which statement gives an ultimate explanation for why male field crickets chirp?
choices: A neural circuit in the thorax fires rhythmically and drives the wings
Chirping speeds up as the temperature rises
Males that chirp attract more females and leave more offspring than silent males
Young males copy the chirps of older males nearby
questions.explanation: An ultimate explanation says how the behavior affects fitness and why it evolved, so the mate-attraction answer is ultimate. The neural circuit and the temperature effect are proximate (mechanism). Copying older males would be a proximate developmental claim, and cricket song is in fact largely unlearned.

questions.stem: A nesting greylag goose starts rolling an egg back into her nest. Partway through, a researcher removes the egg. What does the goose do, and what does that show?
choices: She finishes the rolling movement anyway, so the behavior is a fixed action pattern
She stops at once, so the behavior is controlled by constant feedback from the egg
She searches for the egg, so the behavior is learned by trial and error
She abandons the nest, so the behavior is a habituated response
questions.explanation: Lorenz and Tinbergen saw the goose complete the tucking motion with no egg there. Running to completion once triggered is the mark of a fixed action pattern. Stopping or searching would point to feedback control or learning, which is not what happens; habituation is a fading response to a repeated harmless stimulus.

questions.stem: Male sticklebacks in breeding season attacked crude models with red undersides but mostly ignored a realistic fish model with no red. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Sticklebacks cannot see shapes, only colors
Male sticklebacks learn to attack red objects by trial and error
Realistic models frighten male sticklebacks away
A red underside is the sign stimulus that triggers the attack
questions.explanation: The one feature that predicted attack was red underneath, regardless of how fish-like the model was, so red is the sign stimulus. The experiment doesn't show that shape is invisible (only that it doesn't trigger attack), says nothing about learning, and the realistic model was ignored rather than fled from.

questions.stem: Which of these are examples of learning? Select all that apply.
choices: Birds that at first fled a new scarecrow stop fleeing after days of it never moving
A goose rolls a golf ball into her nest the first time she sees one nearby
Ducklings follow the first moving object they see after hatching
A toad that was stung while trying to eat a bee stops striking at bees
questions.explanation: Ignoring a harmless scarecrow is habituation, following the first moving object is imprinting (learning in a sensitive period), and the toad shows operant conditioning. Rolling a golf ball is a fixed action pattern triggered by a rounded object: unlearned.

questions.stem: Match each type of learning to an example.
choices: Sea anemones stop retracting when touched again and again by harmless water currents
A dog salivates at the sound of a can opener that always comes before its food
A rat presses a lever more often after each press delivers a food pellet
A newly hatched gosling bonds with the first moving object it sees
A spider builds a perfect web without ever having seen one
questions.explanation: Habituation is a fading response to a harmless repeated stimulus. Classical conditioning links two stimuli (sound and food). Operant conditioning links the animal's own action to a consequence. Imprinting happens in a sensitive period early in life. The spider's web is unlearned, so it matches none of them.

questions.stem: Tinbergen placed a ring of pine cones around a digger wasp's nest entrance, and after she left, moved the ring a short distance away. Where did returning wasps search, and what does that show?
choices: At the real entrance, showing they navigate by the smell of the nest
In the center of the moved ring, showing they learned landmarks around the nest
Randomly, showing the cones confused their sun compass
At the real entrance, showing they ignore landmarks entirely
questions.explanation: Wasps searched inside the displaced ring, so they had learned the landmarks around the nest (spatial learning). If they used smell, or ignored landmarks, they would have gone to the real entrance. Random search would not single out the ring's center.

questions.stem: A forager's waggle runs point 30° to the left of straight up and last 1.5 s. The sun is at a compass bearing of 200°, and in this colony 1 s of waggling stands for about 1,000 m. Where is the food?
choices: At a bearing of 230°, about 1.5 km away
At a bearing of 330°, about 1.5 km away
At a bearing of 170°, about 1.0 km away
At a bearing of 170°, about 1.5 km away
questions.explanation: Up stands for the sun (200°); left of up means counterclockwise from the sun: $200° - 30° = 170°$. Distance: $1.5 \times 1{,}000 = 1{,}500$ m. 230° turns the wrong way; 330° measures the angle from north instead of from the sun; 1.0 km ignores the extra half second.

questions.stem: In the honeybee waggle dance, the angle of the waggle run measured from straight up on the comb equals the angle between the direction of the food and the direction of the ___.
questions.explanation: Straight up on the vertical comb stands for the sun's direction (its compass bearing). A dance 40° right of vertical means food 40° clockwise from the sun, so the same food gets a different dance angle as the sun moves across the sky.

questions.stem: Stephen Emlen raised indigo buntings in a planetarium whose sky rotated around the bright star Betelgeuse instead of the North Star. In migration season the birds oriented as if Betelgeuse were north. What does this show?
choices: Buntings are born knowing the shape of the northern constellations
Buntings navigate by Earth's magnetic field, not by stars
Young buntings learn north as the point the night sky rotates around
Buntings cannot orient at all without seeing the sun
questions.explanation: The birds took whatever point the sky turned around as north, so they learn the center of rotation rather than inheriting a star map. A built-in map would point them to the real North Star. Magnetic cues were the same in either sky, so they can't explain the shift, and the birds clearly oriented at night without the sun.

questions.stem: Pigeons are kept on a light schedule that sets their internal clock 6 hours behind real time. They are released at noon in the Northern Hemisphere, south of their loft, so home is north. If they rely on a time-compensated sun compass, which way should they head (use the simple model of 15° of sun movement per hour)?
choices: East, about 90° clockwise from home
North, because the sun compass corrects itself
West, about 90° counterclockwise from home
South, about 180° away from home
questions.explanation: The birds think it is 6 am, when the sun should be in the east. To fly north with the sun in the east, they keep the sun on their right. The real sun is in the south, and keeping the south on your right means facing east: a 90° clockwise error. West is the answer for a clock shifted 6 hours ahead. A correct northward flight would mean they weren't using the sun compass.

questions.stem: A bird can eat three kinds of prey. A: 400 J, 50 s to handle. B: 900 J, 150 s. C: 150 J, 25 s. Which does optimal foraging theory predict it should prefer?
choices: A, because it gives the most energy per second of handling
B, because it holds the most energy
C, because it takes the least time to handle
All three equally, because each is worth eating
questions.explanation: Profitability = energy ÷ handling time: A $400/50 = 8$ J/s, B $900/150 = 6$ J/s, C $150/25 = 6$ J/s. A is best. Choosing B looks only at energy and C only at time; the theory compares their ratio.

questions.stem: Put the steps of Tinbergen's digger wasp experiment in order.
choices: The wasp is inside her nest
A ring of pine cones is placed around the entrance
The wasp flies over the nest on an orientation flight and leaves to hunt
The ring is moved a short distance away
The returning wasp searches in the center of the moved ring
questions.explanation: The cones must be in place before the wasp's orientation flight so she can learn them; they are moved only after she leaves, and her return tests what she learned.

questions.stem: Herring gull chicks pecked more at a thin red rod with white bands than at a realistic model of a parent's head. An exaggerated cue that draws a stronger response than the natural one is called a ___ stimulus.
questions.explanation: The chicks' pecking is triggered by a red spot on the parent's bill. The banded red rod exaggerated that cue, making it a supernormal stimulus.

questions.stem: Researchers played recordings of vervet monkey alarm calls with no predator present. Monkeys ran into trees at "leopard" calls, looked up or dived into bushes at "eagle" calls, and scanned the ground at "snake" calls. What do these playback results show?
choices: Vervets only respond to alarm calls when they can see the predator
The calls carry specific information about the type of predator
Vervets give one general alarm call for all predators
The responses are fixed action patterns triggered by any loud sound
questions.explanation: Different recorded calls produced different, fitting escapes with no predator in view, so the calls themselves carry information about predator type. That rules out needing to see the predator and rules out a single general call; a response to any loud sound would be the same for every call.

questions.stem: Which behavior is altruism in the evolutionary sense?
choices: A mother bear feeding her own cubs
A worker honeybee stinging an intruder and dying as a result
A cleaner fish eating parasites off a larger fish
A lion taking a kill from a group of hyenas
questions.explanation: The stinging worker gives up her life (and any chance of reproducing) to benefit the colony: a cost to the actor and a benefit to others. Feeding one's own young raises the parent's own reproductive success. The cleaner fish is mutualism (both gain), and the lion gains at the hyenas' expense.

questions.stem: Two half siblings share a mother but have different fathers. What is their coefficient of relatedness?
choices: $\tfrac12$
$\tfrac18$
$\tfrac14$
$\tfrac34$
questions.explanation: There is one path through the shared mother, with 2 steps: $(\tfrac12)^2 = \tfrac14$. $\tfrac12$ is full siblings (two such paths). $\tfrac18$ is first cousins, and $\tfrac34$ is haplodiploid full sisters.

questions.stem: Using the path method, what is the coefficient of relatedness $r$ between first cousins? (Give a fraction or decimal.)
questions.explanation: First cousins share two grandparents. Each path (cousin → parent → grandparent → aunt or uncle → cousin) has 4 steps: $(\tfrac12)^4 = \tfrac{1}{16}$. Two paths: $\tfrac{1}{16} + \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac18$.

questions.stem: Helping a half sibling costs an animal 1 offspring of its own. What is the smallest whole number of extra offspring the half sibling must gain for Hamilton's rule to favor helping?
questions.explanation: Need $rB > C$ with $r = \tfrac14$ and $C = 1$: $\tfrac14 B > 1$, so $B > 4$. The smallest whole number is 5. $B = 4$ gives $rB = 1$, which only ties. 2 uses $r = \tfrac12$ (full sibling) and only ties too.

questions.stem: Which observation from Belding's ground squirrels best supports the idea that their alarm calls evolved by kin selection?
choices: Females living near close relatives call more often than males, which move away from their birth area
Callers are stalked and caught by predators more often than non-callers
Squirrels call more often when hawks are overhead than when no predator is present
Squirrels that hear a call run to their burrows
questions.explanation: Kin selection predicts that costly help is aimed at relatives. Calls come mostly from females surrounded by kin, while dispersing males call less. That callers are caught more shows the call is costly (the puzzle), not why it persists. Calling at predators and responding to calls are true but say nothing about relatedness.

questions.stem: In ants, bees and wasps, why are two full sisters related by $r = \tfrac34$ when their mother mated only once?
choices: Each sister gets three quarters of her genes from her mother
Sisters develop from unfertilized eggs and are haploid
The queen is haploid, so all her eggs are identical
Their haploid father gives every daughter the same genes, and their mother's half is shared with probability one half
questions.explanation: Half of each sister's genome comes from the father and is identical (shared with probability 1); the other half comes from the diploid mother and is shared with probability $\tfrac12$: $\tfrac12(1) + \tfrac12(\tfrac12) = \tfrac34$. Females come from fertilized eggs and are diploid; males are the haploid ones, and the queen is diploid.

questions.stem: Which findings weaken the idea that haplodiploidy by itself explains the evolution of eusociality? Select all that apply.
choices: Termites are fully diploid yet eusocial
Honeybee queens typically mate with a dozen or more males
A worker's relatedness to her brothers is only $\tfrac14$
Workers are more related to full sisters than to their own daughters
questions.explanation: Diploid eusocial termites show haplodiploidy isn't necessary. Multiple mating makes most workers half sisters ($r = \tfrac14$), removing the advantage. Low relatedness to brothers cancels the sister advantage unless workers bias investment toward sisters. The last statement (sisters at $\tfrac34$ versus daughters at $\tfrac12$) is the basis of the hypothesis, so it supports rather than weakens it.

questions.stem: A queen mates with 2 males, each fathering half her daughters. What is the average coefficient of relatedness between two of her worker daughters? (Give a fraction or decimal.)
questions.explanation: With $n$ fathers, $\bar r = \tfrac14 + \tfrac{1}{2n}$. For $n = 2$: $\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$. Equivalently, half the pairs are full sisters ($\tfrac34$) and half are half sisters ($\tfrac14$), averaging $\tfrac12$: no more than a worker's relatedness to her own daughter.

questions.stem: In which situation is reciprocal altruism most likely to evolve?
choices: Short-lived animals that meet strangers once and never again
Animals that cannot tell one individual from another
Long-lived animals in stable groups that recognize each other and meet often
Animals that always help any individual, whether or not it helped them before
questions.explanation: Reciprocity needs repeated meetings, recognition of partners and the ability to stop helping cheaters. One-time meetings and no recognition let cheaters win, and helping everyone unconditionally gives cheaters a free ride.

questions.stem: Match each mating system to an example.
choices: A bull elephant seal controls a beach with dozens of females
A female jacana defends a territory holding several males that incubate her eggs
A pair of songbirds raises chicks together through the season
Chimpanzees of both sexes mate with several partners without lasting bonds
A worker ant helps raise her mother's eggs
questions.explanation: Polygyny is one male with several females; polyandry is one female with several males; social monogamy is one pair raising young together (even if some chicks have other fathers); promiscuity has no lasting bonds. A worker ant helping is eusocial cooperation, not a mating system.

questions.stem: Malte Andersson cut the tails of some male long-tailed widowbirds and glued the pieces onto others. Males with lengthened tails attracted more females than males with normal or shortened tails. What does this show?
choices: Intrasexual selection: long tails help males win fights
Intersexual selection: females prefer males with long tails
Natural selection: long tails help males escape predators
Kin selection: females prefer related males
questions.explanation: The tail length was changed experimentally and female settlement followed it, so females choose on tail length: intersexual selection (mate choice). The study didn't test fighting or predation, and nothing about relatedness was involved.

questions.stem: In a group of four females and four males, the females have 2, 2, 2 and 2 offspring and the males have 8, 0, 0 and 0. Which statement is correct?
choices: The sexes have the same mean but males vary far more, so sexual selection is stronger on males
Males have a higher mean number of offspring than females
Females vary more, so sexual selection is stronger on females
The data are impossible, because each male must have 2 offspring
questions.explanation: Both means are 2: every offspring has one mother and one father, and the sexes are equal in number. But males range from 0 to 8 while every female has 2, so male success varies much more, which means stronger sexual selection on males. The data are possible; one male simply fathered all the offspring.

questions.stem: In some pipefish species, males carry the eggs in a brood pouch and so invest more in each offspring than females do. What does parental investment theory predict for these species?
choices: Males compete for females and are the more ornamented sex
Neither sex is choosy, because both invest heavily
Females compete for males and may be the more ornamented sex
Females stop producing eggs until a male is found
questions.explanation: The sex that invests more becomes the limiting resource and the choosier sex, so the roles flip: females compete for males, and in several pipefish species females are the brighter sex. Predicting male competition ignores the reversal of investment.

questions.stem: Put these relatives of a diploid animal in order from most to least closely related to it.
choices: Identical twin
Full sibling
Half sibling
First cousin
questions.explanation: Identical twin $r = 1$; full sibling $\tfrac12$; half sibling $\tfrac14$; first cousin $\tfrac18$.

questions.stem: A new drug keeps people with an incurable chronic disease alive much longer but does not cure them or prevent new cases. What happens over the following years?
choices: Incidence falls and prevalence falls
Incidence stays the same and prevalence rises
Incidence rises and prevalence stays the same
Incidence stays the same and prevalence falls
questions.explanation: New cases (incidence) are unaffected, but each case lasts longer, so more people are living with the disease at any time: prevalence ≈ incidence × duration rises. The drug prevents nothing, so incidence doesn't fall; people aren't removed from the sick pool faster, so prevalence doesn't fall.

questions.stem: A town of 40,000 people records 80 new cases of a disease in one year. What is the incidence?
choices: 200 per 100,000 per year
80 per 100,000 per year
0.2 per 100,000 per year
2,000 per 100,000 per year
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{80}{40{,}000} = 0.002$ per year; $0.002 \times 100{,}000 = 200$ per 100,000 per year. 80 forgets to scale to 100,000, 0.2 is per 100 people, and 2,000 slips a decimal place.

questions.stem: A disease is in a steady state with a prevalence of 0.02 and an incidence of 0.004 per year. About how many years does a case last on average? (Give a number.)
questions.explanation: Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration, so duration ≈ $\dfrac{0.02}{0.004 \text{ per year}} = 5$ years.

questions.stem: A disease has $R_0 = 4$. In a well-mixed population where 60% of people are immune, what is $R_e$, and what happens to the number of cases?
choices: $R_e = 2.4$; cases grow
$R_e = 1.6$; cases grow
$R_e = 0.6$; cases shrink
$R_e = 4$; cases grow
questions.explanation: $R_e = R_0 \times s = 4 \times 0.40 = 1.6$, above 1, so cases grow. 2.4 multiplies by the immune fraction instead of the susceptible fraction; 0.6 forgets $R_0$; 4 ignores immunity.

questions.stem: An SIR model has $N = 5{,}000$, $S = 4{,}000$, $I = 500$, $\beta = 0.5$ per day and $\gamma = 0.25$ per day. What is $I$ one day later?
questions.explanation: New infections $= \dfrac{0.5 \times 4{,}000 \times 500}{5{,}000} = 200$; recoveries $= 0.25 \times 500 = 125$. $I = 500 + 200 - 125 = 575$. 700 forgets recoveries; 625 uses $S/N = 1$ (250 new) and then subtracts recoveries; 375 subtracts the recoveries but leaves out the new infections.

questions.stem: These curves come from an SIR model of one epidemic. Name the compartment each numbered curve shows.

image.alt: A graph of fraction of the population against time in days for an epidemic model, with three numbered curves: one starts near 100% and falls in an S-shape, one rises to a peak and falls back to zero, and a dashed one rises in an S-shape and levels off near the top.

choices: Susceptible
Infectious
Removed
Exposed
questions.explanation: Almost everyone starts susceptible, so curve 1 falls from near 100%. The infectious fraction (2) rises, peaks when the susceptible fraction reaches $1/R_0$, and dies away. The removed fraction (3) only ever grows. The basic SIR model has no exposed compartment (that would be SEIR).

questions.stem: In a simple SIR epidemic with $R_0 = 4$, at what susceptible fraction does the number of infectious people peak?
choices: 0%, when everyone has been infected
questions.explanation: Infections peak when $R_e = R_0 s = 1$, so $s = 1/R_0 = \tfrac14 = 25\%$. 75% is the herd immunity threshold ($1 - 1/R_0$), which is the immune fraction, not the susceptible one. The epidemic peaks long before everyone is infected.

questions.stem: Which are assumptions of the basic SIR model? Select all that apply.
choices: Everyone mixes at random with everyone else
Recovered people stay immune
People with symptoms reduce their contacts
The transmission rate $\beta$ stays constant
questions.explanation: The basic model assumes random mixing, permanent immunity in the removed group and fixed rates $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Changing behavior during an outbreak is exactly what the basic model leaves out; adding it requires a more complex model.

questions.stem: Why was John Snow's comparison of the two south London water companies such strong evidence that cholera spread through water?
choices: Homes on the two supplies were mixed together on the same streets, so they differed mainly in their water
Snow identified the cholera bacterium in the Southwark and Vauxhall water under a microscope
The Lambeth Company served only wealthy districts, so its customers were healthier
Snow randomly assigned households to each water company
questions.explanation: Because pipes of both companies ran down the same streets, wealth, air and neighborhood were matched; only the water differed, a natural experiment with an 8-fold difference in death rates. Snow never saw the bacterium (Koch identified it in 1883–84), the supplies were not split by wealth, and Snow did not assign households: the arrangement already existed.

questions.stem: At a wedding, 30 of the 40 guests who ate the crab cakes became ill, and 3 of the 20 who didn't eat them became ill. What is the relative risk for eating the crab cakes?
questions.explanation: Attack rates: $30/40 = 75\%$ and $3/20 = 15\%$. Relative risk $= 75/15 = 5$. 10 compares the numbers of ill people (30 ÷ 3) instead of rates; 0.2 is the ratio upside down.

questions.stem: Match each epidemic curve shape to the kind of outbreak it suggests.
left: One sharp peak lasting about one incubation period
Cases rise and stay at a plateau for weeks
A series of growing peaks about one incubation period apart
choices: A point source, such as one contaminated meal
A continuing common source, such as a contaminated water supply
Person-to-person (propagated) spread
A disease with no infectious cause
questions.explanation: A single exposure makes cases cluster within one incubation period. A source that keeps exposing people keeps cases coming at a steady level. Each generation of person-to-person cases infects the next one incubation period later, giving successive waves.

questions.stem: Put these steps of an outbreak investigation in order.
choices: Confirm that there is an outbreak and verify the diagnosis
Write a case definition and find cases
Describe the cases by time, place and person
Form hypotheses about the source
Test the hypotheses with an analytic study
questions.explanation: You need to know there is a real outbreak before defining cases; you need cases before you can describe them; the description (including the epidemic curve) suggests hypotheses; and an analytic study comparing ill and well people tests them. Control measures can start as soon as a likely source is known.

questions.stem: The Lyme disease bacterium normally lives in white-footed mice and other small animals and reaches people through tick bites. In this system, the mice are the
choices: vector
reservoir
intermediate host that must be eaten
case definition
questions.explanation: A reservoir is the population in which a pathogen normally lives and multiplies. The tick is the vector that carries it to people. Nothing here is passed by being eaten, and a case definition is a set of criteria for counting cases.

questions.stem: Which action is an example of good antibiotic stewardship?
choices: Giving antibiotics for a cold just in case
Using a broad-spectrum antibiotic when a test shows a narrow-spectrum one will work
Keeping leftover antibiotics to take at the next sign of illness
Not prescribing antibiotics for a viral sore throat
questions.explanation: Antibiotics don't work on viruses, so withholding them for a viral infection avoids needless selection for resistance. Prescribing "just in case," choosing broad-spectrum drugs when a narrow one will do, and self-treating with leftovers all add use without benefit.

questions.stem: A group of 2,000 species has 30 documented extinctions in the last 500 years. What is its extinction rate in extinctions per million species-years (E/MSY)?
choices: 3 E/MSY
30 E/MSY
300 E/MSY
0.03 E/MSY
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{30}{2{,}000 \times 500} \times 1{,}000{,}000 = \dfrac{30}{1{,}000{,}000} \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 30$ E/MSY, about 300 times a background rate of 0.1. 300 is that ratio, not the rate; 3 and 0.03 come from slipping powers of ten.

questions.stem: According to the theory of island biogeography, which island should hold the most species at equilibrium?
choices: A small island far from the mainland
A small island near the mainland
A large island far from the mainland
A large island near the mainland
questions.explanation: Nearness raises the immigration rate, and large size lowers the extinction rate (bigger populations), so the curves cross at the highest species number for a large, near island. A small, far island has the fewest.

questions.stem: This graph shows the MacArthur–Wilson model. Identify each numbered curve.

image.alt: A graph of rate against number of species on an island, from 0 to P. Two falling curves start on the rate axis, one high and solid and one lower and dashed. Two rising curves start at zero, one steep and solid and one shallow and dashed. Each curve has a numbered marker.

choices: Immigration, near island
Immigration, far island
Extinction, small island
Extinction, large island
Speciation, large island
questions.explanation: Immigration falls as an island fills (fewer new species left to arrive), and it is higher for near islands, so 1 is near and 2 is far. Extinction rises with the number of species and is higher on small islands with small populations, so 3 is small and 4 is large.

questions.stem: A forest holds 100 species of birds. Clearing leaves 10% of its area. Using $S = cA^z$ with $z = 0.3$, about how many species should eventually remain?
questions.explanation: $S_{\text{new}} = 100 \times 0.1^{0.3} = 100 \times 0.50 \approx 50$. 10 assumes species fall in proportion to area; 90 subtracts 10% instead of keeping 10% of the area; 70 uses half the exponent ($0.1^{0.15}$). The power law means a 90% habitat loss costs about half the species here, eventually.

questions.stem: With $z = 0.3$ in the species-area relationship $S = cA^z$, an area 10 times larger holds about ___ times as many species. (Give a whole number.)
questions.explanation: $10^{0.3} \approx 1.995$, so about 2 times as many species.

questions.stem: A square forest fragment measures 400 m by 400 m (16 ha). If edge effects reach 100 m in from every side, how much core habitat is left?
choices: 4 ha
9 ha
12 ha
1 ha
questions.explanation: The core is $(400 - 2 \times 100)^2 = 200^2 = 40{,}000$ m² $= 4$ ha, only a quarter of the fragment. 9 ha subtracts the edge from one side only ($300^2$). 12 ha subtracts an edge area as if it were a single 100 m strip; 1 ha subtracts 300 m.

questions.stem: A captive population breeds from 5 males and 45 females. What is its effective population size?
questions.explanation: $N_e = \dfrac{4N_mN_f}{N_m + N_f} = \dfrac{4 \times 5 \times 45}{50} = 18$. 50 is the census count; 25 is the average of the two sexes; 9 forgets the factor of 4 and uses 2. The few males limit genetic diversity.

questions.stem: A population has $N_e = 25$. Using $H_t = H_0\left(1 - \frac{1}{2N_e}\right)^t$, about what fraction of its heterozygosity remains after 10 generations?
questions.explanation: $\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{50}\right)^{10} = 0.98^{10} \approx 0.82$. 98% is one generation only. 60% subtracts $10 \times 4\%$, using $1/N_e$ instead of $1/(2N_e)$; 67% compounds that same wrong rate ($0.96^{10}$).

questions.stem: Put the stages of the extinction vortex in order, starting from a small population.
choices: A population becomes small
Inbreeding and genetic drift increase
Genetic diversity is lost and inbreeding depression appears
Survival and reproduction fall
The population becomes smaller still
questions.explanation: Small size increases inbreeding and drift, which strip out genetic variation and expose harmful recessive alleles; lower survival and reproduction then shrink the population further, which restarts the loop.

questions.stem: Which are edge effects in a forest fragment? Select all that apply.
choices: More light, wind and drying near the boundary
More nest parasitism by cowbirds near the boundary
More invasive plants spreading in from the boundary
More interior-dwelling species near the boundary
questions.explanation: Edges are brighter, windier and drier, and they let in invasive plants, nest predators and nest parasites such as brown-headed cowbirds. Interior species are those that avoid edges, so they are found farther in, not near the boundary.

questions.stem: A population alternates years of growth $\lambda = 1.2$ and decline $\lambda = 0.8$. What is its long-run trend?
choices: Stable, because the average $\lambda$ is exactly 1
Slowly growing, because good years come first
Rapidly crashing, because half the years are bad
Slowly declining, by about 4% every two years
questions.explanation: Over two years the population is multiplied by $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$, a 4% loss every two years (geometric mean $\sqrt{0.96} \approx 0.98$ per year). The arithmetic mean of 1 is misleading; the order of years doesn't change the product; and the decline is slow, not a crash.

questions.stem: In a mark–recapture study, animals that have been caught once learn to avoid the traps. How does this bias the Lincoln–Petersen estimate $N = MC/R$?
choices: It has no effect, because the marks stay on
It underestimates the population, because $R$ is too high
It overestimates the population, because $R$ is too low
It overestimates the population, because $M$ is too high
questions.explanation: Trap-shy marked animals are under-represented in the second sample, so recaptures $R$ are too low, and dividing by a too-small $R$ inflates $N$. Trap-happy animals would cause the opposite bias. $M$ is just the number marked, which is known exactly.

questions.stem: Match each case to the approach to invasive species it illustrates.
left: Helicopter baiting removes all rats and mice from South Georgia
Vedalia beetles from Australia control cottony cushion scale on California citrus
Inspectors check incoming cargo for hitchhiking insects
Cane toads released to eat sugarcane beetles spread and poison native predators
choices: Eradication
Biological control
Prevention
A failed biological control introduction
Genetic rescue
questions.explanation: Island baiting removes the invader completely (eradication). The vedalia beetle is a classic biological control success, while the cane toad is a classic failure that became an invader itself. Cargo inspection stops invaders arriving (prevention), the cheapest option. Genetic rescue is about inbred populations, not invaders.

questions.stem: By the early 1990s only about 20–30 Florida panthers remained, many with heart defects and kinked tails. Which result best shows that the 1995 release of eight Texas pumas worked as genetic rescue?
choices: Panthers with Texas ancestry had fewer defects and survived better, and the population grew
The Texas pumas stayed in a separate area and did not breed with the panthers
Panther numbers kept falling after 1995
The released pumas were all males
questions.explanation: Genetic rescue works by mixing new alleles into an inbred population; fewer defects and better survival among mixed-ancestry panthers, followed by population growth to an estimated 120–230, show that happened. Pumas that didn't breed couldn't rescue anything, falling numbers would show failure, and the release was of eight females.

questions.stem: A crystal of salt grows larger when left in a saturated salt solution. Why is it not considered alive?
choices: It has no cells, no metabolism and no genetic information; growth alone does not make something alive
It does not grow fast enough to count as growth
It is alive, because growth is the defining feature of life
It cannot be alive because it contains sodium, which living things lack
questions.explanation: Life is defined by a set of characteristics, not by any single one. The crystal grows by adding ions to its surface, but it has no cells, metabolism, homeostasis or DNA. Treating growth as the definition is the misconception behind calling it alive; and living things certainly contain sodium.

questions.stem: A mule is the sterile offspring of a horse and a donkey. Which statement is correct?
choices: A mule is not alive, because it cannot reproduce
A mule is alive; reproduction is a characteristic of species and lineages, not a requirement for every individual
A mule is alive only while it is growing
A mule is alive only because it evolves during its lifetime
questions.explanation: The mule has cells, metabolism, homeostasis and DNA, and it was produced by reproduction. Sterile individuals (mules, worker bees) are alive. Individuals also do not evolve during their lifetimes; populations evolve over generations.

questions.stem: Your body temperature stays near 37 °C whether you are outside in winter or in a hot room. This is an example of
choices: metabolism
evolution
homeostasis
development
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is keeping internal conditions stable despite outside changes. Metabolism is the set of chemical reactions in the body; evolution is change in populations over generations; development is the change in form as an organism matures.

questions.stem: Which statement about evolution as a characteristic of life is correct?
choices: Each organism evolves new inherited traits as it grows older
Only organisms that reproduce asexually evolve
Evolution happens to individuals but not to populations
Populations evolve over many generations; an individual's inherited traits do not change during its life
questions.explanation: Evolution is a change in the inherited traits of a population across generations. A common misconception is that individuals evolve, for example a giraffe stretching its neck and passing on a longer neck. Both sexually and asexually reproducing species evolve.

questions.stem: The sum of all the chemical reactions that take place in an organism is called its
choices: homeostasis
metabolism
stimulus
emergent property
questions.explanation: Metabolism includes every reaction that breaks molecules down to release energy and builds the molecules the organism needs. Homeostasis is maintaining stable conditions; a stimulus is a change the organism detects; an emergent property is a new ability that appears at a higher level of organization.

questions.stem: Which list is in order from smallest to largest level of organization?
choices: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
tissue, cell, organ, organism, organ system
cell, organ, tissue, organ system, organism
organism, organ system, organ, tissue, cell
questions.explanation: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and organ systems make up an organism. One distractor swaps cell and tissue, another swaps organ and tissue, and one runs from largest to smallest.

questions.stem: All of the gray squirrels living in one city park make up a
choices: community
ecosystem
population
biosphere
questions.explanation: A population is all the members of one species in one area. A community would include every species in the park; an ecosystem adds the nonliving parts such as soil and water; the biosphere is all life on Earth.

questions.stem: Which of these is part of an ecosystem but NOT part of a community?
choices: the frogs in the pond
the bacteria in the pond mud
the algae on the pond surface
the water in a pond
questions.explanation: A community is all the living populations in an area. An ecosystem is the community plus its nonliving (abiotic) surroundings, such as water, sunlight and minerals. Frogs, bacteria and algae are all living, so they belong to the community.

questions.stem: A single heart muscle cell can contract, but only a whole heart can pump blood through the body. This illustrates
choices: an emergent property
homeostasis
a population
a controlled variable
questions.explanation: An emergent property is an ability that appears from the way parts are arranged and interact at a higher level, and that the parts alone do not have. Pumping requires chambers and valves built from several tissues.

questions.stem: During a long run on a hot day, a runner's body temperature rises from 37.0 °C to 37.8 °C in the first 15 minutes, then stays near 37.8 °C for the next 30 minutes while her sweat rate rises and levels off. What best explains why her temperature stopped rising?
choices: Her muscles stopped producing heat after 15 minutes
Her metabolism stopped while she was running
Body temperature cannot rise above 37.8 °C under any conditions
Increased sweating raised heat loss until it balanced the extra heat from her muscles
questions.explanation: This is negative feedback: the rise in temperature triggers more sweating, and evaporation carries heat away until heat loss matches heat production. Her muscles keep producing heat the whole time, and body temperature can rise much higher, as in heat stroke, if sweating fails.

questions.stem: Viruses contain genetic material and evolve. Why do most biologists not classify them as living organisms?
choices: They are too small to be seen with a light microscope
They contain no proteins
They are not made of cells and cannot carry out metabolism or reproduce on their own
They never change over time
questions.explanation: A virus has no cells and no metabolism of its own; it reproduces only by taking over a host cell. Size is not a criterion for life (many bacteria are tiny too), viruses do have protein coats, and they evolve rapidly.

questions.stem: A student tests whether the amount of light affects how fast duckweed plants reproduce. She grows identical pots of duckweed under lamps at different distances and counts new plants after 2 weeks. What is the dependent variable?
choices: the distance of the lamp
the number of new duckweed plants
the type of duckweed
the length of the experiment
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured to see the effect: the number of new plants. The lamp distance is the independent variable (what she changes). The type of duckweed and the 2-week length are controlled variables.

questions.stem: In the duckweed experiment, the student changes how far each lamp is from its pot. This lamp distance is the
choices: dependent variable
controlled variable
independent variable
control group
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the factor the experimenter deliberately changes. The dependent variable is the measured outcome (number of plants), controlled variables are held constant, and the control group is a set of subjects used as a baseline.

questions.stem: In Redi's 1668 experiment, why did he cover some jars of meat with gauze instead of sealing them completely?
choices: So that flies could still reach the meat in every jar
So that the meat would rot more slowly in the covered jars
So that the covered jars would be the control group
So that air could still reach the meat and only the flies' access differed between the groups
questions.explanation: Critics argued that sealed jars lacked fresh air needed for spontaneous generation. Gauze let air in but kept flies out, so the only difference between groups was whether flies could reach the meat. The open jars were the baseline (control) group.

questions.stem: A student plays music to bean plants on a sunny windowsill and keeps a second group, without music, in a dim closet. The music group grows taller. What is the main problem with this experiment?
choices: Two variables differ between the groups, so the effect cannot be blamed on music
The dependent variable should have been the type of music
There is no independent variable
Plants cannot respond to any stimulus
questions.explanation: Light and music both differ between the groups. Light is known to affect growth, so it could explain the result by itself. A fair test changes only the independent variable (music) and keeps light, water and soil the same.

questions.stem: Why do scientists use many plants in each group instead of just one?
choices: Using more plants guarantees that the hypothesis is proven
Individuals vary naturally, so more subjects make it less likely that a difference is due to chance
More plants make the independent variable larger
One plant would make the experiment have no dependent variable
questions.explanation: Replication and larger samples reduce the effect of natural variation between individuals. No sample size proves a hypothesis; data can only support or fail to support it.

questions.stem: Five pea plants grew 12, 15, 9, 14 and 10 cm. What is their mean height?
choices: 15 cm
12 cm
60 cm
11 cm
questions.explanation: Mean = sum / count = (12 + 15 + 9 + 14 + 10) / 5 = 60 / 5 = 12 cm. 60 cm is the sum before dividing, 15 cm is the largest value, and 11 cm is not the mean of these values.

questions.stem: A bacterial culture had 400 colonies before treatment and 300 colonies after. What is the percent change?
questions.explanation: Percent change = (new − original) / original × 100% = (300 − 400) / 400 × 100% = −25%. Dividing by the new value (300) gives −33%; dropping the sign gives +25%; −100% is the raw difference written as a percent.

questions.stem: Which statement is a testable scientific hypothesis?
choices: If tomato plants receive more nitrogen fertilizer, then they will produce more fruit
Tomatoes taste better than cucumbers
Plants grow because of an invisible force that cannot be measured
Tomato plants are the most beautiful garden plants
questions.explanation: A hypothesis must be testable and falsifiable: some possible result could show it wrong. Fruit number can be measured under different fertilizer levels. Taste and beauty claims are opinions, and an unmeasurable force cannot be tested.

questions.stem: In science, the word theory means
choices: a guess that has not yet been tested
a hypothesis that has become a law after enough experiments
a broad explanation supported by a large body of evidence that has survived repeated testing
a description of a pattern without any explanation
questions.explanation: A scientific theory, such as cell theory or the theory of evolution, is a well-tested explanation tying together many observations. The everyday meaning of guess is the misconception. Theories do not turn into laws: laws describe patterns, theories explain them.

questions.stem: A study finds that towns with more storks also have more human births. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Storks cause human births to increase
Human births cause stork numbers to increase
The data prove there is no relationship between the two
The two are correlated, but a third factor such as town size could explain both
questions.explanation: Correlation does not show causation. Bigger towns have more people (so more births) and more roofs and land for storks to nest on, so a hidden variable, town size, can produce the pattern. Only a controlled experiment, where one factor is changed, can show cause and effect.

questions.stem: A student tests whether a new plant food increases the number of tomatoes per plant. Which group is the control group?
choices: Plants given twice the recommended plant food
Plants given the same water, soil and light but no plant food
All the conditions that are kept the same in both groups
The number of tomatoes counted on each plant
questions.explanation: The control group is the set of subjects that does not get the treatment and serves as a baseline. The conditions kept the same are controlled variables (a frequent mix-up), and the number of tomatoes is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: Water is a polar molecule because
choices: it has a full positive charge on one end and a full negative charge on the other
its atoms are held together by ionic bonds
oxygen pulls the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, leaving oxygen slightly negative and the hydrogens slightly positive
it is a straight molecule with hydrogens on opposite sides of the oxygen
questions.explanation: The O–H bonds are covalent, but the sharing is unequal, so the oxygen end is partly negative (δ−) and the hydrogen ends partly positive (δ+). The charges are partial, not full ions. Water is bent; if it were straight, the partial charges would cancel.

questions.stem: Hydrogen bonds in water form between
choices: a hydrogen atom of one water molecule and the oxygen atom of a neighboring molecule
the two hydrogen atoms within one water molecule
the oxygen and a hydrogen within the same water molecule
two oxygen atoms that share electrons
questions.explanation: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules: the δ+ hydrogen of one water molecule and the δ− oxygen of another. The bonds within one water molecule are covalent bonds, which are much stronger.

questions.stem: Water rises in the thin xylem tubes of a tall tree as a continuous column pulled up from the leaves. Which property of water holds the column together?
choices: high specific heat
cohesion
low density of ice
ability to dissolve salts
questions.explanation: Cohesion, the hydrogen-bond attraction between water molecules, keeps the column from breaking as evaporation from leaves pulls it upward. Adhesion to the tube walls helps too. Specific heat, ice density and solvent power do not hold the column together.

questions.stem: Cities on the coast have milder winters and cooler summers than cities far inland at the same latitude. Which property of water explains this?
choices: high specific heat
cohesion
adhesion
polarity of the solute
questions.explanation: Water absorbs and releases a lot of energy for each degree of temperature change, so oceans change temperature slowly and moderate nearby air. Cohesion and adhesion concern attraction between molecules, not heat storage.

questions.stem: Why does ice float on liquid water?
choices: Ice contains trapped air from the atmosphere
Ice molecules are lighter than liquid water molecules
Hydrogen bonds lock frozen water into an open lattice that is less dense than the liquid
Freezing breaks the covalent bonds inside water molecules
questions.explanation: In ice, each molecule is held by hydrogen bonds at fixed distances, making a spread-out lattice about 8% less dense than liquid water (it takes up about 9% more space). The molecules are identical in mass; freezing changes hydrogen bonds between molecules, not the covalent bonds within them.

questions.stem: Solution A has a pH of 3 and solution B has a pH of 6. How does the hydrogen ion concentration of A compare with B?
choices: A has 3 times more H⁺
A has 2 times more H⁺
A has 1000 times less H⁺
A has 1000 times more H⁺
questions.explanation: Each pH unit is a tenfold change, and A is 3 units lower, so it has $10^3 = 1000$ times more H⁺. Treating the scale as linear gives 3 times; dividing 6 by 3 gives 2 times; getting the direction backward gives 1000 times less (lower pH means more H⁺).

questions.stem: What is the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution with pH 5?
choices: $5$ mol/L
questions.explanation: $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-5}$ mol/L. Forgetting the negative sign gives $10^5$; $10^{-9}$ is the OH⁻ concentration at 25 °C, since the two exponents add to −14.

questions.stem: Which pH describes a basic (alkaline) solution?
questions.explanation: Solutions above pH 7 are basic, pH 7 is neutral, and below 7 is acidic. So 9.5 is basic, 7.0 neutral, and 4.2 and 1.8 are acidic.

questions.stem: A student adds 20 drops of acid to pure water and to a buffer solution. The pH of the water falls from 7.0 to 2.6; the pH of the buffer falls from 7.0 to 6.7. What do the results show?
choices: The buffer released extra H⁺ when acid was added
The buffer kept its pH exactly constant no matter how much acid was added
The buffer took up most of the added H⁺ and resisted the change in pH
Pure water is a better buffer than the buffer solution
questions.explanation: A buffer absorbs added H⁺, so its pH changed only 0.3 units while unbuffered water changed by more than 4 units. The buffer's pH did change slightly, and a buffer's capacity is limited, so it does not hold pH exactly constant.

questions.stem: Which six elements make up about 98% of the mass of living things?
choices: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, sulfur
carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, sodium, potassium, calcium
carbon, helium, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, iron
hydrogen, oxygen, iron, calcium, chlorine, sulfur
questions.explanation: The CHNOPS elements make up nearly all living matter. Sodium, potassium, calcium and iron are essential but present in much smaller amounts, and helium is not used by living things at all.

questions.stem: Table salt dissolves easily in water but vegetable oil does not. The best explanation is that
choices: salt is nonpolar and oil is polar
water is polar, so it attracts charged and polar substances but not nonpolar ones such as oil
oil molecules are too large to fit between water molecules
water forms covalent bonds with salt but not with oil
questions.explanation: The partial charges on water molecules surround and pull apart ions such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Oil is nonpolar (hydrophobic), so water molecules attract each other rather than the oil. Dissolving does not involve forming covalent bonds with the solute.

questions.stem: How many water molecules are released when 12 glucose molecules are joined into a single straight chain by dehydration synthesis?
questions.explanation: A chain of $n$ monomers has $n - 1$ bonds, and each bond releases one water molecule: $12 - 1 = 11$. Answering 12 counts one water per monomer instead of one per bond.

questions.stem: Glucose has a molar mass of 180 g/mol and water 18 g/mol. What is the molar mass of a chain of 3 glucose units joined by dehydration synthesis?
choices: 540 g/mol
486 g/mol
522 g/mol
504 g/mol
questions.explanation: Three units form 2 bonds and release 2 water molecules: $3(180) - 2(18) = 540 - 36 = 504$ g/mol. 540 forgets the water; 486 subtracts 3 waters; 522 subtracts only one.

questions.stem: When you digest a protein into amino acids, the bonds between amino acids are broken by
choices: hydrolysis, which adds water across each bond
dehydration synthesis, which removes water
denaturation, which removes the R groups
ionic bonding with stomach acid
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis splits a polymer by adding a water molecule across each bond. Dehydration synthesis is the reverse, building polymers. Denaturation unfolds a protein but leaves its peptide bonds intact.

questions.stem: A molecule contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus. Hydrolysis breaks it into many monomers of four kinds, each with a sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogen base. The molecule is
choices: a protein
a polysaccharide
a triglyceride
a nucleic acid
questions.explanation: Monomers with a sugar, phosphate and base are nucleotides, and four kinds suggests DNA or RNA. Proteins are made of 20 kinds of amino acids and usually lack phosphorus; typical polysaccharides contain only C, H and O; triglycerides are glycerol plus fatty acids.

questions.stem: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose. Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?
choices: The glucose units in cellulose are linked in a different orientation that human enzymes cannot break
Cellulose is made of fructose instead of glucose
Cellulose is a protein and starch is a carbohydrate
Starch contains nitrogen that human enzymes recognize
questions.explanation: Both are made only of glucose; the difference is the linkage between units. Human enzymes fit the starch linkage but not the cellulose linkage. Cows digest cellulose only with help from gut microbes that make the right enzymes.

questions.stem: Butter is solid at room temperature while olive oil is liquid. What is the main reason?
choices: Olive oil has more saturated fatty acids, which are straight
Butter is a carbohydrate and olive oil is a lipid
Butter has more saturated fatty acids, whose straight chains pack tightly together
Olive oil contains more phosphorus
questions.explanation: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds, so their chains are straight and pack closely, forming a solid. The double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids put kinks in the chains, keeping oils liquid. Both are lipids.

questions.stem: A food sample turns iodine solution blue-black, but Benedict's solution stays blue after heating and biuret stays blue. The sample contains
choices: glucose
starch
protein
lipid
questions.explanation: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. Benedict's would turn orange or brick-red with simple sugars such as glucose, and biuret would turn violet with protein; both stayed blue, so those are absent. Lipids are detected by a translucent spot on paper.

questions.stem: Which molecule is the main long-term energy store in animals and provides about 9 kcal per gram?
choices: fat (triglyceride)
glucose
protein
DNA
questions.explanation: Fats store about 9 kcal/g, roughly twice the 4 kcal/g of carbohydrates and proteins, so they are a compact long-term store. Glucose is the quick energy source; proteins mainly do jobs; DNA stores information.

questions.stem: In the late 1950s, Anfinsen unfolded the enzyme ribonuclease with chemicals; when the chemicals were removed, it refolded and regained its activity. What did this show?
choices: Proteins can work without having any particular shape
Enzymes are made of nucleic acids, not amino acids
The amino acid sequence contains all the information needed for the protein to fold into its working shape
Once a protein unfolds, it can never regain its activity
questions.explanation: Nothing but the chain itself was present, yet it folded back into the active shape, so the primary structure (sequence) determines the 3-D structure. Activity disappeared when it was unfolded, showing that shape matters for function.

questions.stem: Which comparison of DNA and RNA is correct?
choices: DNA has ribose and uracil; RNA has deoxyribose and thymine
DNA has deoxyribose and thymine; RNA has ribose and uracil
Both have deoxyribose, but only RNA has thymine
DNA is made of amino acids and RNA is made of nucleotides
questions.explanation: DNA's sugar is deoxyribose and its bases are A, T, G, C. RNA's sugar is ribose and it uses uracil in place of thymine. Both are polymers of nucleotides.

questions.stem: The function of a protein depends most directly on
choices: the number of phosphate groups it contains
how many glucose units it is built from
whether its fatty acids are saturated
its three-dimensional shape, which is determined by its amino acid sequence
questions.explanation: Proteins are chains of amino acids that fold into specific shapes, and the shape determines what the protein can bind and do. Proteins are not built from glucose or fatty acids, and phosphate groups are characteristic of nucleotides.

questions.stem: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions by
choices: adding energy to the reactants
increasing the total energy released by the reaction
being used up as they react with the substrate
lowering the activation energy of the reaction
questions.explanation: An enzyme provides an easier pathway with a lower activation energy. It does not supply energy or change the overall energy difference between reactants and products, and it comes out of the reaction unchanged, ready to be reused.

questions.stem: The enzyme lactase breaks down lactose but has no effect on sucrose. The best explanation is that
choices: lactose fits the shape and chemistry of lactase's active site, but sucrose does not
sucrose denatures lactase
lactase is used up after breaking down lactose
sucrose is not a carbohydrate
questions.explanation: Enzyme specificity comes from the active site, which matches the shape and chemical properties of its substrate. Sucrose is a carbohydrate too, but it does not fit lactase's active site. Enzymes are not used up.

questions.stem: Catalase produces 0 mL of oxygen at 0 s and 12 mL at 15 s. What is the initial rate of reaction?
choices: 12 mL/s
0.8 mL/s
180 mL/s
questions.explanation: Rate = change in amount / change in time = 12 mL / 15 s = 0.8 mL/s. Dividing time by volume gives 1.25; 12 mL/s ignores the time; 180 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: In a catalase experiment, oxygen is produced quickly at first, but the rate slows and finally stops after a few minutes. The most likely reason is that
choices: the catalase is being used up in the reaction
the hydrogen peroxide substrate is being used up
the catalase has evolved to stop working
the oxygen produced denatures the enzyme immediately
questions.explanation: Enzymes are reused, but the substrate is consumed. As hydrogen peroxide runs out, fewer substrate molecules collide with active sites. Adding more peroxide would restart the reaction, which would not happen if the enzyme had been used up.

questions.stem: A human digestive enzyme is tested at different temperatures. Its activity rises from 10 °C to 37 °C and then falls steeply, reaching almost zero at 55 °C. Why does activity fall above 37 °C?
choices: The molecules move too slowly to collide
The enzyme is killed because it is a living organism
The substrate becomes a different molecule at high temperature
The enzyme denatures: heat breaks the weak bonds holding its active site in shape
questions.explanation: High temperatures disrupt hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions, so the active site loses its shape. Molecules move faster, not slower, at high temperature. Enzymes are molecules, not living things, so they denature rather than die.

questions.stem: An enzyme sample is kept at 4 °C overnight, where it shows very little activity. Then it is warmed to its optimum of 37 °C. Predict what happens.
choices: Its activity returns, because cold slows enzymes without denaturing them
It stays inactive, because cold permanently denatures enzymes
It becomes more active than an enzyme that was never chilled
It changes its optimum temperature to 4 °C
questions.explanation: Low temperature slows molecular motion and collisions, but the enzyme keeps its shape. Warming restores normal activity. Heat and extreme pH, not cold, cause denaturation.

questions.stem: Pepsin works in the stomach and trypsin works in the small intestine. Which prediction about their optimum pH is correct?
choices: Both have an optimum near pH 7
Pepsin has an optimum near pH 2 and trypsin near pH 8
Pepsin has an optimum near pH 8 and trypsin near pH 2
Both have an optimum near pH 2
questions.explanation: Each enzyme's optimum matches the environment where it works: the stomach is strongly acidic (about pH 2) and the small intestine slightly basic (about pH 8). Assuming all enzymes share one optimum is a common error.

questions.stem: With a fixed amount of enzyme, the reaction rate rises as substrate concentration increases, then levels off. Why does it level off?
choices: The enzyme has been denatured by the substrate
The substrate is used up at high concentrations
All the active sites are occupied, so the enzyme is working at its maximum rate
Extra substrate acts as a competitive inhibitor
questions.explanation: At high substrate concentration every active site is busy all the time (the enzyme is saturated). Only adding more enzyme would raise the rate further. The substrate is plentiful, not used up, and it does not denature or inhibit the enzyme.

questions.stem: A drug slows an enzyme at low substrate concentration, but at very high substrate concentration the rate with the drug is nearly the same as without it. The drug is most likely
choices: a noncompetitive inhibitor
a cofactor
a denaturing agent
a competitive inhibitor
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site, so flooding the reaction with substrate outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor changes the enzyme's shape from another site, so extra substrate would not restore the rate. A denaturing agent would not be overcome by substrate either, and a cofactor helps an enzyme work.

questions.stem: A student boils a slice of liver, cools it, and adds it to hydrogen peroxide. Almost no bubbles form. A fresh slice bubbles vigorously. What conclusion is supported?
choices: Boiling used up all the hydrogen peroxide
Cooling the liver denatured the catalase
Boiling denatured the catalase in the liver, and cooling did not restore it
Liver does not contain catalase
questions.explanation: The fresh slice is the control: it shows the liver has active catalase and the peroxide works. The only difference is boiling, which denatures the enzyme permanently. The peroxide was not boiled, and cooling only slows enzymes.

questions.stem: In 1897 Buchner showed that juice from ground yeast, filtered so that no living cells remained, could still ferment sugar into alcohol. What did this demonstrate?
choices: Fermentation requires living yeast cells
Fermentation is carried out by chemicals (enzymes) that can work outside living cells
Enzymes are made of DNA
Sugar can turn into alcohol with no catalyst at all
questions.explanation: With no living cells present, the reaction still happened, so molecules in the juice, now called enzymes, were doing the chemistry. This overturned the idea that a vital force of life was required. Later work showed most enzymes are proteins.

questions.stem: In feedback inhibition, the end product of a series of reactions
choices: inhibits an enzyme early in the series, so the cell stops making the product when it has enough
activates the first enzyme so that more product is made
denatures every enzyme in the series
becomes the substrate for the first enzyme
questions.explanation: The end product binds an early enzyme and slows it, turning down the whole pathway when the product builds up. This is how cells avoid wasting materials. It is regulation, not denaturation.

questions.stem: Why can a polypeptide chain twist at the bonds next to each alpha carbon but not around the peptide bond itself?
choices: The peptide bond is an ionic bond, and ionic bonds cannot rotate
The peptide bond has partial double-bond character, which holds the atoms around it flat
R groups sit on both sides of the peptide bond and block it
The peptide bond is a hydrogen bond that breaks whenever it rotates
questions.explanation: Electrons are shared partly across the C=O and C–N bonds, so the C–N peptide bond behaves partly like a double bond and does not rotate; the six atoms around it lie in one plane. Rotation happens only at the single bonds on either side of each alpha carbon. The peptide bond is covalent, not ionic or a hydrogen bond, and R groups hang off the alpha carbons, not the peptide bond.

questions.stem: What holds an α helix in its coiled shape?
choices: Disulfide bonds between neighboring cysteines
Ionic bonds between charged R groups on opposite sides of the coil
Hydrogen bonds between the backbone C=O of one amino acid and the backbone N–H of the amino acid four positions along
Hydrogen bonds between the R groups of neighboring strands lying side by side
questions.explanation: Secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms, which is why any sequence can in principle form it. In the α helix each C=O pairs with the N–H four amino acids further on. Side-by-side strands describe a β sheet (and even there the hydrogen bonds are between backbone atoms); disulfide and ionic bonds between R groups belong to tertiary structure.

questions.stem: What is the main driving force that makes a soluble protein fold into a compact shape with an oily core?
choices: The hydrophobic effect: burying nonpolar R groups frees the ordered water around them
Disulfide bonds, which form between every pair of amino acids in the core
Peptide bonds forming between distant parts of the chain
Chaperones, which carry a template of the final shape
questions.explanation: Nonpolar R groups force nearby water into ordered arrangements; clustering them in the interior releases that water, which is favorable. Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bonds then refine the shape. Disulfides form only between cysteines, peptide bonds join neighbors in the chain only, and chaperones prevent wrong interactions but hold no template.

questions.stem: Anfinsen let ribonuclease (8 cysteines, 4 disulfide bonds) re-form its disulfide bonds while urea kept the chain unfolded. Only about 1% of the activity returned. Which explanation fits the data best?
choices: Urea had broken the peptide bonds, so most of the chains were destroyed
The enzyme needs a chaperone, so it can never refold in a test tube
Only 1% of the cysteines formed disulfide bonds at all
The bonds paired at random: 8 cysteines can pair 105 ways, and only 1 way is native, about 1%
questions.explanation: With the chain unfolded, nothing guided which cysteines met, so pairings were random. The number of ways is $7 \times 5 \times 3 \times 1 = 105$ and $1/105 \approx 0.95\%$, matching the data. Urea breaks weak interactions, not peptide bonds; and the same enzyme refolded fully without chaperones when urea was removed first.

questions.stem: Levinthal calculated that a 100-amino-acid chain trying shapes at random would need far longer than the age of the universe to find its fold, yet real proteins fold in seconds or less. What does this show?
choices: Proteins never reach their native shape inside cells
Folding is not a random search: local structures form fast and are kept, narrowing the options like a funnel
Each amino acid can take only one position, so there is just one possible shape
Proteins fold only after they reach their final location in the cell
questions.explanation: The paradox disappears if folding is guided: helices and turns form within microseconds and are kept because they lower the energy, and hydrophobic collapse limits the remaining options. Proteins do reach native shapes; each amino acid does have several possible positions, which is what makes a random search impossible.

questions.stem: In sickle cell hemoglobin, a glutamate on the surface of the β chain is replaced by valine. Why does this one change cause disease?
choices: The chain can no longer form any α helices
Valine breaks the peptide bonds near the heme groups
The nonpolar valine creates a sticky patch that binds a neighboring hemoglobin, so molecules link into long fibers
Valine is charged, so it pulls the iron out of the heme group
questions.explanation: Glutamate is charged and sits happily in water; valine is nonpolar. On the surface of deoxygenated hemoglobin the valine fits into a hydrophobic pocket on another molecule, so molecules join into fibers that deform red blood cells. Each molecule still folds normally, and valine is nonpolar, not charged.

questions.stem: The oily core of a cell membrane is about 3.0 nm thick. An α helix rises 0.15 nm per amino acid (0.54 nm per turn). About how many amino acids must a helix have to span the core?
choices: about 6
about 9
about 200
about 20
questions.explanation: Amino acids needed $= 3.0 \div 0.15 = 20$, which matches the roughly 20-amino-acid nonpolar helices that cross real membranes. Dividing by 0.54 nm gives about 6, the number of turns, not amino acids. About 9 comes from using the β strand rise of 0.34 nm.

questions.stem: A proline is placed in the middle of a sequence that would otherwise form a long α helix. What is the most likely result?
choices: The helix is broken or kinked, because proline's ring locks its rotation and it lacks the backbone N–H the helix needs
The helix becomes longer, because proline is nonpolar
A disulfide bond forms at the proline
Nothing changes, because secondary structure depends only on the backbone
questions.explanation: Proline's R group bonds back to its own backbone nitrogen, so it has no N–H to donate a hydrogen bond and its swivel is locked; prolines usually break or kink helices. Disulfide bonds need cysteine. Secondary structure is held by the backbone, but which pattern forms depends on the R groups.

questions.stem: How do molecular chaperones such as Hsp70 help proteins fold in the cell?
choices: They carry instructions for the final shape of each protein
They add disulfide bonds to every new protein in the cytoplasm
They bind exposed hydrophobic stretches, preventing wrong interactions and aggregation, and release the chain to try again
They cut misfolded chains into individual amino acids
questions.explanation: Chaperones shield hydrophobic patches, especially on chains still coming off the ribosome, so they don't stick to other chains. The shape information is still in the sequence, as Anfinsen showed. Breaking down misfolded chains is the job of the proteasome, and the cytoplasm rarely forms disulfide bonds.

questions.stem: What makes a prion different from a virus or bacterium as an infectious agent?
choices: It is a short RNA molecule that codes for a toxic protein
It is a misfolded protein with no DNA or RNA, and it converts normal copies of the protein into its misfolded form
It is a bacterium that lives inside brain cells
It is a normal protein that has lost all of its amino acids
questions.explanation: A prion is a misfolded, β-sheet-rich form of a normal protein (PrP). Contact with it converts normally folded PrP into the misfolded form, so the misfolding spreads without any genetic material. This is why prion diseases such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease were so puzzling.
