questions.explanation: $f = \dfrac{[L]}{[L] + K_d} = \dfrac{12}{12 + 4} = 0.75$. 25% is $K_d/([L] + K_d)$, the unoccupied fraction; 33% is $K_d/[L]$; 67% is $([L] - K_d)/[L]$.

questions.stem: One activated receptor switches on 20 G proteins, each activating one adenylyl cyclase that makes 50 cAMP. Every 2 cAMP free one active protein kinase A subunit, and each subunit activates 10 target enzymes. How many target enzymes are activated?
questions.explanation: cAMP $= 20 \times 50 = 1000$; active PKA subunits $= 1000 / 2 = 500$; target enzymes $= 500 \times 10 = 5000$. 10,000 forgets that 2 cAMP are needed per subunit; 500 stops one step early; 82 adds the numbers instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Epinephrine makes liver cells release glucose but makes heart muscle cells beat faster and harder. What best explains the different responses?
choices: The heart receives a different form of epinephrine
Only liver cells have receptors for epinephrine
The two cell types have different receptors, relay proteins or target proteins
Epinephrine enters heart cells but not liver cells
questions.explanation: Both cell types respond, so both have receptors, and the hormone is the same molecule in the same blood. What differs is the equipment inside each cell: the receptor subtypes, relay proteins and targets that turn the signal into a response. Epinephrine acts at the surface of both.

questions.stem: What happens first after a growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase?
choices: The receptor enters the nucleus and binds DNA
A G protein swaps GDP for GTP
Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP
Two receptor molecules pair up and add phosphates to tyrosines on each other
questions.explanation: Ligand binding brings two receptor molecules together, and each kinase phosphorylates its partner's tyrosines, creating docking sites for relay proteins. G protein activation and cAMP are features of GPCR pathways, and a membrane RTK does not enter the nucleus.

questions.stem: A mutation leaves Ras unable to break down its GTP. What is the most likely effect on the cell?
choices: Ras can no longer be activated, so the cell stops dividing
Ras stays active, sending a divide signal even without growth factor
The receptor tyrosine kinase is destroyed
cAMP levels fall to zero
questions.explanation: Like other G proteins, Ras is on with GTP and switches itself off by hydrolyzing it. If it cannot, it stays on and keeps the MAP kinase cascade running, which is why such mutations are common in cancers. The receptor is unaffected, and Ras is not part of the cAMP pathway.

questions.stem: A drug blocks phosphodiesterase in liver cells responding to epinephrine. What happens to the response?
choices: cAMP stays high longer, so the response is stronger and lasts longer
cAMP cannot be made, so there is no response
The receptor can no longer bind epinephrine
Nothing changes, because phosphodiesterase acts only in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down and is one of the off switches. Blocking it lets cAMP build up and persist, prolonging PKA activity. cAMP is still made by adenylyl cyclase, the receptor is unaffected, and phosphodiesterase works in the cytosol.

questions.stem: Small molecules or ions such as cAMP and calcium ions, which spread a signal through the cell after a receptor is activated, are called ___ messengers.
questions.explanation: They are second messengers: the hormone or other ligand is the first messenger, which brings the message to the receptor, and the second messenger carries it on inside the cell.

questions.stem: Match each receptor type to an example.
choices: Epinephrine receptor that activates adenylyl cyclase
Insulin receptor
Acetylcholine receptor on muscle cells
Estrogen receptor that binds DNA
Aquaporin
questions.explanation: The epinephrine receptor works through a G protein; the insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase; the acetylcholine receptor opens an ion pore when acetylcholine binds; and steroid hormones such as estrogen bind receptors inside the cell that act on genes. An aquaporin is a water channel, not a receptor.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a GPCR–cAMP pathway in order.
choices: The ligand binds the G protein-coupled receptor
The receptor changes shape and the G protein swaps GDP for GTP
The G protein's α subunit activates adenylyl cyclase
Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cAMP
cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates target proteins
questions.explanation: Reception (ligand binding) changes the receptor, which activates the G protein by GDP–GTP exchange; the α subunit switches on adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP from ATP; cAMP activates PKA, whose phosphorylations produce the response.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this signaling pathway.

image.alt: A signaling pathway across a membrane. Numbered parts: a protein crossing the membrane seven times with a signal molecule bound on its outer side; a three-part protein on the inner surface next to it; a large enzyme spanning the membrane; a cluster of small six-sided molecules in the cytoplasm; and an oval protein that the small molecules activate.

choices: G protein-coupled receptor
G protein
Adenylyl cyclase
cAMP (second messenger)
Protein kinase A
Receptor tyrosine kinase
Ligand-gated ion channel
questions.explanation: The seven-pass receptor (1) binds the signal and activates the three-subunit G protein (2), whose α subunit switches on adenylyl cyclase (3). The cyclase makes cAMP (4) from ATP, and cAMP activates protein kinase A (5). A receptor tyrosine kinase passes the membrane once and works as a pair; an ion channel would form a pore.

questions.stem: Which of these help switch off a GPCR–cAMP signal? Select all that apply.
choices: The G protein's α subunit hydrolyzes its GTP to GDP
Phosphodiesterase converts cAMP to AMP
Protein phosphatases remove phosphates from target proteins
More adenylyl cyclase is made
Receptors are taken into the cell by endocytosis
questions.explanation: GTP hydrolysis turns off the G protein, phosphodiesterase destroys cAMP, phosphatases undo the kinases' work, and removing receptors from the surface makes the cell less sensitive. Making more adenylyl cyclase would strengthen the signal, not end it.

questions.stem: A student writes, "Plants create energy from sunlight." Which statement best corrects the student?
choices: Plants create energy only during the day, not at night.
Plants get their energy from minerals in the soil, not sunlight.
Plants destroy light energy and replace it with chemical energy.
Plants convert light energy into chemical energy; energy is never created.
questions.explanation: The first law of thermodynamics says energy is converted, never created or destroyed. Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in sugar. Saying light is "destroyed" breaks the same law, and soil supplies minerals, not energy.

questions.stem: Your cells capture roughly a third of the energy in glucose as ATP. What happens to most of the rest?
choices: It is destroyed by the chemical reactions.
It is stored in the carbon dioxide you exhale.
It is released as heat.
It is turned back into new glucose.
questions.explanation: The second law of thermodynamics: every energy conversion loses some energy as heat that can no longer do work. That heat keeps birds and mammals warm. Energy cannot be destroyed (first law), CO₂ is a low-energy waste product, and remaking glucose would cost energy, not save it.

questions.stem: Which of these is an anabolic process?
choices: Joining amino acids into a protein
Breaking glucose down to carbon dioxide and water
Digesting starch into glucose
Breaking down stored fat to release energy
questions.explanation: Anabolism builds large molecules from small ones and requires energy, as in protein synthesis. The other three break molecules down and release (or at least do not require) energy, so they are catabolic.

questions.stem: The products of a reaction hold less free energy than its reactants. This reaction is
choices: endergonic, so it needs energy from ATP to proceed
exergonic, so it can proceed without an energy input
anabolic, because it builds a larger molecule
impossible, because energy cannot be lost
questions.explanation: Releasing free energy (products lower than reactants) is the definition of exergonic, and such reactions can proceed on their own (an enzyme may still be needed to make them fast). Endergonic is the opposite. The energy is not lost; it is released, often as heat.

questions.stem: Which parts make up a molecule of ATP?
choices: Adenine, deoxyribose, and three phosphate groups
Adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups
Adenine, ribose, and two phosphate groups
Adenine, glucose, and three phosphate groups
questions.explanation: ATP is adenosine (adenine + the sugar ribose) triphosphate (three phosphates). Deoxyribose is the sugar in DNA, and two phosphates describes ADP.

questions.stem: When a cell hydrolyzes ATP to power a process, what are the products?
choices: AMP and a second molecule of ATP
ADP and a molecule of glucose
ADP and an inorganic phosphate group
Adenine and three free phosphate groups
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis removes the last phosphate: ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ + energy. The cell later recharges ADP back to ATP. Glucose is not made from ATP, and only one phosphate is removed in the usual reaction.

questions.stem: A reaction needs 18 kJ/mol to proceed. It is coupled to the hydrolysis of one ATP, which releases 30.5 kJ/mol. What is the overall energy change, and can the coupled process proceed?
choices: −12.5 kJ/mol; yes, it can proceed
+12.5 kJ/mol; no, it cannot proceed
+48.5 kJ/mol; no, it cannot proceed
−48.5 kJ/mol; yes, it can proceed
questions.explanation: Add the two steps: −30.5 + 18 = −12.5 kJ/mol. A negative total means energy is released overall, so the coupled process can go. +12.5 reverses the signs; ±48.5 adds the sizes instead of combining a release with a requirement.

questions.stem: An endergonic step requires 70 kJ/mol. If each ATP hydrolysis releases 30.5 kJ/mol, what is the smallest number of ATP that must be coupled to it?
questions.explanation: Two ATP release 61 kJ/mol, which is less than 70, so the total would still be uphill (+9 kJ/mol). Three ATP release 91.5 kJ/mol, giving −21.5 kJ/mol overall. Four would work but is not the smallest number.

questions.stem: Your body holds only about 50 g of ATP at any moment, yet it uses roughly its own body mass of ATP every day. Which explains this?
choices: Most ATP is stored in fat cells and released when needed.
ATP is constantly regenerated from ADP and phosphate.
ATP is absorbed directly from food in large amounts.
Each ATP molecule can be hydrolyzed many times without changing.
questions.explanation: ATP is a currency, not a store. Each molecule is hydrolyzed to ADP and recharged over and over, many times a day. Long-term energy is stored as fat and glycogen, not ATP. Once hydrolyzed, ATP is ADP until it is recharged.

questions.stem: In the reaction NAD⁺ + 2 electrons + H⁺ → NADH, the NAD⁺ is
choices: oxidized, because it gains electrons
reduced, because it loses electrons
oxidized, because it loses electrons
reduced, because it gains electrons
questions.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain). NAD⁺ picks up two electrons and becomes NADH, the reduced, electron-carrying form. The molecule that gave up the electrons was oxidized.

questions.stem: Why do cells break glucose down in many small steps instead of one big reaction?
choices: So energy is released in small amounts that can be captured as ATP instead of lost as heat
Because a one-step reaction would release less total energy
Because a one-step reaction would create energy and break the first law
So that glucose can be broken down without any enzymes
questions.explanation: The total energy released is the same either way (a flame releases the same amount). Small steps let the cell trap the energy in usable packets (ATP, NADH) rather than releasing it all at once as heat. Each step needs its own enzyme, and no reaction creates energy.

questions.stem: Which are the raw materials (reactants) of photosynthesis?
choices: Glucose and oxygen
Oxygen and water
Carbon dioxide and water
Carbon dioxide and glucose
questions.explanation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Glucose and oxygen are the products; they are the reactants of cellular respiration, which is why the two processes are often called reverses of each other.

questions.stem: Algae are given water whose oxygen atoms are the heavy isotope ¹⁸O, with ordinary CO₂. The O₂ gas they release contains ¹⁸O. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The oxygen gas released in photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide.
The oxygen gas comes equally from water and carbon dioxide.
The oxygen in glucose comes from water.
The oxygen gas released in photosynthesis comes from water.
questions.explanation: Only the water was labeled, and the label showed up in the O₂, so the O₂ comes from splitting water (Ruben and Kamen, 1941). The reverse experiment, labeling CO₂, gave unlabeled O₂. This experiment says nothing about glucose, whose oxygen actually comes from CO₂.

questions.stem: Van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds in five years while the soil lost only about 2 ounces. Where did most of the tree's added dry mass actually come from?
choices: Water absorbed by the roots
Carbon dioxide taken from the air
Minerals absorbed from the soil
Sunlight converted into matter
questions.explanation: Most of a plant's dry mass is carbon compounds built from CO₂ fixed in the Calvin cycle. Van Helmont credited the water, because he never measured the air. The soil loss shows minerals contribute very little, and light supplies energy, not matter.

questions.stem: In Priestley's experiments, a mouse in a sealed jar with a sprig of mint in the light survived much longer than a mouse in a sealed jar alone. The best explanation is that the mint
choices: released oxygen that the mouse used
absorbed oxygen that would have harmed the mouse
released carbon dioxide that the mouse needed
absorbed heat from the mouse's body
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis releases O₂, which the mouse uses in cellular respiration, and also takes up the CO₂ the mouse exhales. The mouse needs oxygen, not carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Most leaves look green because chlorophyll
choices: absorbs green light more strongly than any other color
gives off green light when it is struck by sunlight
absorbs little green light and reflects it
absorbs green light and uses it most efficiently
questions.explanation: The color you see is the light that is not absorbed. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light, so green is reflected and transmitted to your eye.

questions.stem: Engelmann lit a strand of alga with a spectrum of colors. Oxygen-seeking bacteria gathered mostly along the parts lit by blue and red light. What did this show?
choices: Photosynthesis releases oxygen fastest in blue and red light.
The bacteria are attracted to blue and red light.
Green light drives photosynthesis fastest.
The alga has chlorophyll only in the blue- and red-lit sections.
questions.explanation: The bacteria were an oxygen detector: they crowded where O₂ was being released, so the rate of photosynthesis (the action spectrum) peaks in blue and red, matching chlorophyll's absorption. The bacteria respond to oxygen, not light, and chlorophyll runs along the whole strand.

questions.stem: Where in a chloroplast do the light-dependent reactions take place?
choices: In the stroma
In the outer chloroplast membrane
In the cytoplasm outside the chloroplast
In the thylakoid membranes
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll, the photosystems, the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are all in the thylakoid membranes. The stroma is where the Calvin cycle runs.

questions.stem: Which products of the light-dependent reactions are used to power the Calvin cycle?
choices: Oxygen and glucose
Carbon dioxide and water
ATP and NADPH
ADP and NADP⁺
questions.explanation: The light reactions charge up ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle spends them to reduce CO₂ to sugar and returns ADP and NADP⁺ to be recharged. O₂ is a by-product that leaves the leaf.

questions.stem: To make 2 molecules of glucose, how many CO₂, ATP, and NADPH does the Calvin cycle use?
choices: 6 CO₂, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH
12 CO₂, 36 ATP, 24 NADPH
12 CO₂, 24 ATP, 36 NADPH
2 CO₂, 6 ATP, 4 NADPH
questions.explanation: One glucose (6 carbons) needs 6 CO₂, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH, so two glucose need 12 CO₂, 36 ATP and 24 NADPH. The first choice is the amount for one glucose; the third swaps ATP and NADPH.

questions.stem: An Elodea sprig releases 36 bubbles of oxygen in 3 minutes. What is the rate of photosynthesis?
choices: 108 bubbles per minute
12 bubbles per minute
33 bubbles per minute
3 bubbles per minute
questions.explanation: Rate = bubbles ÷ time = 36 ÷ 3 = 12 bubbles per minute. Multiplying gives 108, subtracting gives 33.

questions.stem: A plant's rate of photosynthesis rises with light intensity and then levels off at a plateau. On the plateau, which change is most likely to increase the rate?
choices: Raising the light intensity further
Lowering the temperature to 5 °C
Removing some of the plant's leaves
Raising the carbon dioxide concentration
questions.explanation: On the plateau, light is no longer the limiting factor, so more light does nothing. Some other factor, often CO₂, is now limiting; raising it raises the plateau. Cold slows the Calvin cycle enzymes, and fewer leaves means less photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A plant is moved from bright light into darkness. Within seconds, the Calvin cycle slows to a stop. Why?
choices: Calvin cycle enzymes need to absorb light directly.
Carbon dioxide cannot enter leaves in the dark.
It runs out of the ATP and NADPH made by the light reactions.
Rubisco is destroyed as soon as light is removed.
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle does not use light itself, but it depends on the ATP and NADPH that only the light reactions make. Once those run out, it stops. This is why "light-independent" is more accurate than "dark reactions."

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic cell, where do glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain take place, in that order?
choices: Cytoplasm; mitochondrial matrix; inner mitochondrial membrane
Mitochondrial matrix; cytoplasm; outer mitochondrial membrane
Cytoplasm; inner mitochondrial membrane; mitochondrial matrix
Inner mitochondrial membrane; mitochondrial matrix; cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, before pyruvate enters the mitochondrion. The Krebs cycle runs in the matrix, and the electron transport chain is built into the folded inner membrane (cristae), where the H⁺ gradient forms.

questions.stem: What is the net yield of glycolysis from one molecule of glucose?
choices: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate
4 ATP, 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate
2 ATP, 6 CO₂, and 2 pyruvate
30 ATP, 10 NADH, and 2 pyruvate
questions.explanation: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2 in its investment phase, so the net is 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate. No CO₂ is released in glycolysis; that happens in the mitochondrion. About 30 ATP is the total for all of respiration.

questions.stem: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration?
choices: It combines with carbon from glucose to form carbon dioxide.
It splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in glycolysis.
It becomes part of the ATP molecules made by ATP synthase.
It accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain, forming water.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; it combines with electrons and H⁺ to make water, keeping the chain flowing. The CO₂ comes from the carbon in glucose during pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, and glycolysis needs no oxygen at all.

questions.stem: A person breathes oxygen gas labeled with the isotope ¹⁸O. In which product of respiration does the label appear?
choices: Carbon dioxide
Water
Glucose
ATP
questions.explanation: Inhaled O₂ accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain and becomes water. The oxygen atoms in exhaled CO₂ come from glucose and water, not from the O₂ you breathe, a common misconception.

questions.stem: Cyanide blocks the last protein of the electron transport chain, so electrons cannot be passed to oxygen. What is the most direct effect?
choices: Glycolysis stops immediately because it requires oxygen.
The Krebs cycle speeds up and makes extra ATP to compensate.
Oxygen use and ATP production by chemiosmosis both stop.
The cell starts producing more carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: With the chain blocked, no H⁺ is pumped and no O₂ is used, so oxidative phosphorylation stops, and the cell loses most of its ATP supply. Glycolysis does not need oxygen, and the Krebs cycle soon stops too, because NADH cannot unload and NAD⁺ runs out.

questions.stem: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂, how many ATP are made from 10 NADH, 2 FADH₂, and 4 ATP made directly?
questions.explanation: 10 × 2.5 = 25, 2 × 1.5 = 3, and 25 + 3 + 4 = 32. Using the older values of 3 and 2 gives 30 + 4 + 4 = 38; 25 counts only the NADH; 29 forgets the 3 ATP from FADH₂.

questions.stem: Older textbooks say one glucose yields 36 to 38 ATP; current estimates are about 30 to 32. Why the difference?
choices: Cells today make less ATP than cells did when the books were written.
Older figures forgot to count the ATP made in glycolysis.
Older figures assumed 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH₂; measurements show fewer.
Older figures included ATP made by photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: The difference comes from the conversion factors. The link between electron transport and ATP synthase is an H⁺ gradient, and measurements give about 2.5 and 1.5 ATP per NADH and FADH₂, not 3 and 2. Including glycolysis was never the issue, and cells have not changed.

questions.stem: What is the main function of fermentation?
choices: To regenerate NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue making ATP
To make about 30 extra ATP when oxygen is absent
To produce oxygen for the electron transport chain
To turn lactate into glucose for the Krebs cycle
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, NADH cannot unload in the electron transport chain and NAD⁺ runs out, which would stop glycolysis. Fermentation passes NADH's electrons to pyruvate, regenerating NAD⁺. It makes no ATP itself; all 2 ATP per glucose come from glycolysis.

questions.stem: Bread dough rises because the yeast in it
choices: release oxygen during photosynthesis
release carbon dioxide during alcoholic fermentation
release lactic acid gas during lactic acid fermentation
release water vapor during the Krebs cycle
questions.explanation: Alcoholic fermentation converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂; the CO₂ bubbles make the dough rise (the ethanol evaporates during baking). Yeast are fungi and cannot photosynthesize, and lactate is not a gas.

questions.stem: A culture of cells needs 300 ATP. Without oxygen (2 ATP per glucose), how many glucose molecules must it use?
questions.explanation: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 glucose. With oxygen, about 300 ÷ 30 = 10 would be enough. 600 multiplies instead of dividing; 15 is the ratio between the two methods.

questions.stem: How many grams of CO₂ are produced when 90 g of glucose is completely oxidized? (Glucose = 180 g/mol; CO₂ = 44 g/mol.)
questions.explanation: 90 g is 0.5 mol of glucose. Each mole makes 6 mol CO₂, so 3 mol × 44 g/mol = 132 g. 264 g is the amount from a full mole (180 g); 44 g is the mass of just one mole of CO₂; 90 g assumes the CO₂ weighs the same as the glucose.

questions.stem: A potted plant is kept in a sealed, dark container. The CO₂ level inside steadily rises. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Plants photosynthesize faster in the dark.
Plants respire only when they cannot photosynthesize.
Plant cells carry out cellular respiration.
The plant is fixing CO₂ through the Calvin cycle.
questions.explanation: Rising CO₂ in the dark means the plant is releasing it by respiration. Plant cells respire all the time, day and night; in light, photosynthesis usually outpaces respiration so the plant takes up CO₂ overall. The data cannot show respiration stops in light, and fixing CO₂ would lower the level.

questions.stem: A day or two after a hard workout, your muscles ache. What is the best current explanation?
choices: Tiny injuries to muscle fibers and the repair process that follows
Lactic acid that stays in the muscles for several days
Muscles running out of ATP until the next meal
Muscle cells switching to alcoholic fermentation
questions.explanation: Lactate made during hard exercise is cleared from muscle within about an hour, so it cannot explain soreness days later. Delayed soreness comes from small injuries to muscle fibers and inflammation during repair. Human muscle cells use lactic acid fermentation, never alcoholic fermentation.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this molecule of ATP.

image.alt: A chain of three circles marked P, joined to a five-sided ring containing an O, which is joined to a fused pair of rings made of a six-sided and a five-sided ring. Three parts are numbered.

choices: Adenine
Ribose
Phosphate group removed when ATP becomes ADP
Deoxyribose
Glucose
Thymine
questions.explanation: ATP is adenosine (the base adenine, 1, joined to the sugar ribose, 2) plus a chain of three phosphate groups. Hydrolysis removes the phosphate at the far end of the chain, 3, leaving ADP. Deoxyribose is the sugar of DNA, and thymine is a DNA base, not part of ATP.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Breaks large molecules down and releases energy
Builds large molecules and requires energy
Its products hold less free energy than its reactants
Its products hold more free energy than its reactants
Speeds up a reaction without being used up
questions.explanation: Catabolism (such as respiration) breaks down and releases energy; anabolism (such as protein synthesis) builds up and costs energy. Exergonic reactions go downhill in free energy and endergonic ones go uphill. "Speeds up a reaction without being used up" describes an enzyme (a catalyst).

questions.stem: When a molecule loses electrons, the process is called ___; when a molecule gains electrons, it is called ___.
questions.explanation: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain (of electrons). When NAD⁺ picks up electrons to become NADH, it is reduced, and the molecule that gave up the electrons is oxidized.

questions.stem: Which of these processes are endergonic, so that a cell must couple them to an energy source such as ATP hydrolysis? Select all that apply.
choices: Joining amino acids into a protein
Pumping Na⁺ out of a cell against its concentration gradient
Hydrolyzing ATP to ADP and phosphate
Breaking glucose down to CO₂ and water
questions.explanation: Building a protein (anabolism) and moving ions against their gradient (active transport) both need an energy input, and ATP supplies it. ATP hydrolysis and the breakdown of glucose are exergonic: they release energy rather than needing it.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the ATP cycle in order, starting with the breakdown of food.
choices: Glucose is broken down by cellular respiration
The energy released joins ADP and phosphate into ATP
ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP and phosphate to power cellular work
ADP returns to be recharged into ATP again
questions.explanation: Catabolism (breaking down glucose) releases energy that recharges ADP into ATP. ATP is then spent on work, such as pumping ions or building molecules, becoming ADP and phosphate again, which are recycled. A cell repeats this cycle constantly because it holds only a small amount of ATP at any moment.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this chloroplast.

image.alt: An oval organelle with two membranes around it. Inside, four stacks of flat discs sit in a fluid, joined by thin links. Four places are numbered.

choices: Outer membrane
Inner membrane
Granum (stack of thylakoids)
Stroma
Crista
Matrix
questions.explanation: A chloroplast has two surrounding membranes, an outer one (1) and an inner one (2). Inside, thylakoids are stacked into grana (3); the light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes. The fluid around them is the stroma (4), where the Calvin cycle runs. Cristae and the matrix are parts of a mitochondrion.

questions.stem: Put these steps of the Calvin cycle in order, starting with carbon fixation.
choices: Rubisco attaches CO₂ to RuBP
ATP and NADPH convert the products into G3P
One G3P leaves the cycle to be made into sugar
The remaining G3P are rearranged, using ATP, to rebuild RuBP
questions.explanation: Fixation comes first: rubisco joins CO₂ to the five-carbon RuBP. Reduction follows: ATP and NADPH from the light reactions turn the products into G3P. For every three CO₂ fixed, one G3P leaves as product, and the other five are used, with more ATP, to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can start again.

questions.stem: In photosynthesis, the O₂ released comes from splitting ___, and the carbon atoms in sugar come from ___.
questions.explanation: Ruben and Kamen's ¹⁸O experiment showed the oxygen gas comes from water, split at photosystem II. The carbon comes from CO₂, fixed by rubisco in the Calvin cycle.

questions.stem: Which of these happen in the stroma of a chloroplast? Select all that apply.
choices: Rubisco attaches CO₂ to RuBP
G3P is made
Water is split and O₂ is released
Light is absorbed by chlorophyll
ATP is spent to power reactions
questions.explanation: The stroma is the site of the Calvin cycle: carbon fixation by rubisco, reduction to G3P, and regeneration of RuBP, all of which spend ATP (and NADPH). Water splitting and light absorption by chlorophyll happen in the thylakoid membranes.

questions.stem: Match each scientist to the finding about photosynthesis.
choices: Most of a growing tree's mass does not come from the soil
A plant restores air that a candle or a mouse has used up
Plants restore air only in light, through their green parts
The O₂ released comes from water, not CO₂
Sugar is made inside the thylakoid space
questions.explanation: Van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds while the soil lost about 2 ounces. Priestley's mint sprig revived the air in a sealed jar; Ingenhousz showed this needs light and green tissue. Ruben and Kamen used ¹⁸O to trace O₂ to water. Sugar is made in the stroma, not the thylakoid space.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this mitochondrion.

image.alt: An oval organelle with a smooth outer membrane and an inner membrane folded into many finger-like folds. Four places are numbered.

choices: Outer membrane
Intermembrane space
Crista (fold of the inner membrane)
Matrix
Thylakoid
Stroma
questions.explanation: The smooth outer membrane (1) surrounds the narrow intermembrane space (2), where H⁺ ions pile up during electron transport. The inner membrane folds into cristae (3), which carry the electron transport chain and ATP synthase. The matrix (4) inside holds the enzymes of pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle. Thylakoids and stroma belong to chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Put the stages of aerobic respiration in the order a glucose molecule goes through them.
choices: Glycolysis
Pyruvate oxidation
Krebs cycle
Electron transport chain and chemiosmosis
questions.explanation: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm splits glucose into 2 pyruvate. In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate oxidation turns each pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle. The NADH and FADH₂ from these stages feed the electron transport chain on the inner membrane, where chemiosmosis makes most of the ATP.

questions.stem: In aerobic respiration, the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain is ___.
questions.explanation: Oxygen takes the electrons from the last protein of the chain and combines with H⁺ to form water. Without it, the chain backs up and stops, which is why you need to breathe.

questions.stem: Which of these steps release CO₂? Select all that apply.
choices: Glycolysis
Pyruvate oxidation
Krebs cycle
Lactic acid fermentation
Alcoholic fermentation
questions.explanation: Pyruvate oxidation releases 2 CO₂ and the Krebs cycle 4 CO₂ per glucose; together they release all six carbons of glucose. In alcoholic fermentation, yeast remove CO₂ from pyruvate before making ethanol. Glycolysis splits glucose without losing any carbon, and lactic acid fermentation turns pyruvate straight into lactate with no CO₂.

questions.stem: Match each molecule or protein to its role in breaking down glucose.
choices: Picks up electrons in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle
Accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain
Uses the flow of H⁺ to make ATP
Three-carbon product of glycolysis, reduced in fermentation
Fixes CO₂ into a five-carbon sugar
questions.explanation: NAD⁺ is the electron carrier that becomes NADH; fermentation exists to regenerate it. O₂ is the final electron acceptor. ATP synthase makes ATP by chemiosmosis. Pyruvate is glycolysis's product; fermentation reduces it to lactate (or, after removing CO₂, to ethanol). Fixing CO₂ into sugar is rubisco's job in photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A reaction releases heat ($\Delta H < 0$) and increases entropy ($\Delta S > 0$). Using $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, what can you conclude?
choices: $\Delta G$ is negative at every temperature, so the reaction can always proceed
$\Delta G$ is positive at every temperature, so the reaction never proceeds
The reaction can proceed only at high temperatures
The reaction can proceed only at low temperatures
questions.explanation: With $\Delta H$ negative and $\Delta S$ positive, $-T\Delta S$ is also negative (T is always positive in kelvins), so $\Delta G$ is negative at any temperature. Temperature matters only when the two terms have opposite signs.

questions.stem: A mixture of reactants has $\Delta G = -40$ kJ/mol for its reaction, yet no measurable product forms in a day. What is the best explanation?
choices: The reaction is actually endergonic under these conditions
The mixture must already be at equilibrium
The activation energy is high, so the reaction is very slow without a catalyst
A negative $\Delta G$ means the reverse reaction is favored
questions.explanation: $\Delta G$ tells whether a reaction can proceed, not how fast. A large activation energy can make a favorable reaction extremely slow, which is why cells need enzymes. A negative $\Delta G$ means the forward reaction is favored and the mixture is not at equilibrium ($\Delta G = 0$ there).

questions.stem: A reaction has $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -11.4$ kJ/mol at 25 °C, where each 5.7 kJ/mol corresponds to a factor of 10 in $K'$. What is its equilibrium constant $K'$, approximately?
questions.explanation: $-11.4$ kJ/mol is two steps of 5.7 kJ/mol, so $K' = 10^2 = 100$. Check: $K' = e^{11.4/2.48} = e^{4.6} \approx 100$. A negative $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ means $K' > 1$, which rules out 0.01 (that would be for $+11.4$).

questions.stem: A pathway step has $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = +5.0$ kJ/mol. In a cell at 37 °C ($RT = 2.58$ kJ/mol), the ratio of product to reactant is kept at $Q = 0.010$. What is the actual $\Delta G$?
choices: $+5.0$ kJ/mol
$-6.9$ kJ/mol
questions.explanation: $\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ\prime} + RT\ln Q = 5.0 + 2.58 \times \ln 0.010 = 5.0 + 2.58 \times (-4.61) = 5.0 - 11.9 = -6.9$ kJ/mol, so the step runs forward. $+16.9$ adds the terms with the wrong sign, $-11.9$ forgets $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$, and $+5.0$ ignores the concentrations.

questions.stem: Hexokinase couples glucose phosphorylation ($\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = +13.8$ kJ/mol) to ATP hydrolysis ($-30.5$ kJ/mol). Coupling changes the equilibrium constant of the glucose reaction by a factor of about
choices: 30.5 (the kJ/mol released by ATP)
2 (one reaction added to another)
16.7 (the new free energy change)
$2 \times 10^{5}$ (the equilibrium constant of ATP hydrolysis)
questions.explanation: Free energies of coupled reactions add, so equilibrium constants multiply: $K'_{\text{coupled}} = K'_{\text{glucose}} \times K'_{\text{ATP}}$. $K'$ for ATP hydrolysis is $e^{30.5/2.48} \approx 2 \times 10^{5}$, taking $K'$ from about 0.0038 to about 840.

questions.stem: Standard free energies of hydrolysis (kJ/mol): PEP −61.9, phosphocreatine −43.0, ATP −30.5, glucose-6-phosphate −13.8, glycerol-3-phosphate −9.2. Which phosphate transfer can proceed under standard conditions?
choices: PEP + ADP → pyruvate + ATP
Glucose-6-phosphate + ADP → glucose + ATP
Glycerol-3-phosphate + ADP → glycerol + ATP
ATP + creatine → ADP + phosphocreatine
questions.explanation: A phosphate moves spontaneously from a donor higher in the table to an acceptor lower down. PEP to ADP: $-61.9 + 30.5 = -31.4$ kJ/mol, favorable; this is substrate-level phosphorylation at the end of glycolysis. Glucose-6-phosphate ($-13.8 + 30.5 = +16.7$) and glycerol-3-phosphate ($+21.3$) cannot make ATP, and ATP cannot make phosphocreatine under standard conditions ($-30.5 + 43.0 = +12.5$).

questions.stem: Electrons flow spontaneously between redox pairs
choices: from a pair with a more positive $E^{\circ\prime}$ to one with a more negative $E^{\circ\prime}$
only between pairs with the same $E^{\circ\prime}$
from a pair with a more negative $E^{\circ\prime}$ to one with a more positive $E^{\circ\prime}$
in whichever direction makes $\Delta E^{\circ\prime}$ negative
questions.explanation: The more positive the reduction potential, the more strongly the oxidized form attracts electrons. Electrons therefore fall from negative to positive (NADH at −0.32 V toward O₂ at +0.82 V), making $\Delta E^{\circ\prime}$ positive and $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -nF\Delta E^{\circ\prime}$ negative.

questions.stem: NADH ($E^{\circ\prime} = -0.32$ V) passes two electrons to ubiquinone ($E^{\circ\prime} = +0.05$ V). With $F = 96.5$ kJ/(mol·V), what is $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$?
choices: $-36$ kJ/mol
$-71$ kJ/mol
$+71$ kJ/mol
$-52$ kJ/mol
questions.explanation: $\Delta E^{\circ\prime} = 0.05 - (-0.32) = 0.37$ V, so $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -2 \times 96.5 \times 0.37 = -71$ kJ/mol. $-36$ forgets that two electrons move ($n = 2$), $+71$ has the sign backward, and $-52$ comes from subtracting 0.05 from 0.32 instead of adding.

questions.stem: ATP hydrolysis releases 30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions but about 50 kJ/mol inside a typical cell. Why?
choices: Body temperature is much higher than 25 °C
Cells keep ATP far above its equilibrium level, with ADP and phosphate low
Enzymes add extra energy to each ATP molecule
The phosphate bonds in ATP are stronger inside cells
questions.explanation: $\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ\prime} + RT\ln Q$, and in cells $Q = [\text{ADP}][\text{P}_i]/[\text{ATP}]$ is tiny (around $10^{-4}$), making $RT\ln Q$ about $-20$ kJ/mol. The temperature difference changes $RT$ by only about 4%. Enzymes never change $\Delta G$.

questions.stem: Using $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -RT\ln K'$: a reaction with $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = 0$ has an equilibrium constant $K'$ equal to ___.
questions.explanation: If $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = 0$ then $\ln K' = 0$, so $K' = 1$: at equilibrium, products and reactants are balanced (at standard concentrations). Negative $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ gives $K' > 1$, positive gives $K' < 1$.

questions.stem: Match each symbol to what it measures.
choices: Change in heat content (enthalpy)
Change in entropy (disorder)
Free energy change with everything at 1 M and pH 7
Ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium
Voltage difference between two redox pairs
questions.explanation: $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ combine in $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ is the standard reference value, related to the equilibrium constant $K'$ by $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -RT\ln K'$. The voltage difference between redox pairs is $\Delta E^{\circ\prime}$.

questions.stem: Which changes would make $\Delta G$ for ATP hydrolysis inside a cell more negative (so each ATP releases more energy)? Select all that apply.
choices: Raising the concentration of ATP
Lowering the concentration of ADP
Lowering the concentration of phosphate
Adding more of an ATP-hydrolyzing enzyme
Raising the concentration of ADP
questions.explanation: $Q = [\text{ADP}][\text{P}_i]/[\text{ATP}]$. More ATP or less ADP or phosphate makes $Q$ smaller, so $RT\ln Q$ is more negative and so is $\Delta G$. More ADP does the opposite. An enzyme changes the rate, never $\Delta G$.

questions.stem: Put these redox pairs in the order electrons pass through them in the mitochondrial respiratory chain, from the strongest electron donor to the strongest acceptor.
choices: NAD⁺ / NADH
Ubiquinone / ubiquinol (Q / QH₂)
Cytochrome c (Fe³⁺ / Fe²⁺)
½O₂ / H₂O
questions.explanation: Electrons flow toward more positive reduction potentials: NADH (−0.32 V), ubiquinone (+0.05 V), cytochrome c (+0.25 V), oxygen (+0.82 V). Each step releases part of the roughly 220 kJ/mol available from NADH to oxygen.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

image.alt: A membrane drawn across the middle, with the intermembrane space above and the matrix below. Several protein complexes and two small carriers sit in or on the membrane; electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass along them to oxygen, and hydrogen ions are pumped upward and flow back down through a protein with a knob in the matrix. Five parts are numbered.

choices: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)
Ubiquinone (Q)
Cytochrome c
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)
ATP synthase
Photosystem II
Plastocyanin
questions.explanation: NADH gives its electrons to complex I (1), which passes them to ubiquinone (2), the mobile carrier inside the membrane. Complex III passes them to cytochrome c (3) on the outer face, which carries them to complex IV (4), where oxygen is reduced to water. Protons flow back through ATP synthase (5), whose knob in the matrix makes ATP. Photosystem II and plastocyanin are parts of the thylakoid chain.

questions.stem: How many H⁺ ions are moved across the inner mitochondrial membrane for each pair of electrons that NADH sends to oxygen?
questions.explanation: Complex I moves 4, complex III 4 and complex IV 2: $4 + 4 + 2 = 10$. Six is the count for electrons from succinate (FADH₂), which skip complex I; 4 is complex I or III alone.

questions.stem: Why does FADH₂ (from succinate) yield fewer ATP than NADH?
choices: Its electrons enter at ubiquinone, bypassing the proton pumping of complex I
It carries only one electron instead of two
It is made in the cytoplasm and must be shuttled into the mitochondrion
It passes its electrons straight to oxygen
questions.explanation: Complex II hands succinate's electrons, through bound FAD, to ubiquinone, so they pass only complexes III and IV (6 H⁺ instead of 10). FADH₂ carries two electrons like NADH, is made in the matrix by the Krebs cycle, and its electrons still go through complexes III and IV before reaching oxygen.

questions.stem: A mitochondrion has a membrane potential of 150 mV and a pH difference of 0.8 units across its inner membrane, both pushing protons inward. Using $\Delta p = \Delta\psi + 61.5 \text{ mV} \times \Delta\text{pH}$, what is the proton-motive force?
choices: About 151 mV
About 101 mV
About 199 mV
About 49 mV
questions.explanation: $\Delta p = 150 + 61.5 \times 0.8 = 150 + 49.2 = 199$ mV. 151 mV adds the pH difference without converting it to millivolts, 101 mV subtracts the two parts although both push the same way, and 49 mV is the pH part alone.

questions.stem: An ATP synthase has a ring of 12 c subunits and makes 3 ATP per full turn. How many H⁺ pass through it per ATP made?
questions.explanation: One full turn of the ring carries 12 H⁺ (one per c subunit) and makes 3 ATP (one per β subunit), so $12 \div 3 = 4$ H⁺ per ATP. 12 is the number per turn, not per ATP.

questions.stem: In the Jagendorf–Uribe experiment, thylakoids soaked at pH 4 and then moved to pH 8 with ADP and phosphate made ATP in complete darkness. What did this show?
choices: ATP synthase needs light to change shape
A proton gradient alone, without light or electron transport, can drive ATP synthesis
ATP is made from a high-energy chemical intermediate stored in the dark
Chloroplasts make ATP only when the stroma is acidic
questions.explanation: No light meant no electron transport, so the only energy source was the imposed pH difference, with the inside of the thylakoids acidic and the outside basic. The ATP made far exceeded what any stored intermediate could explain, and uncouplers abolished it, supporting Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis.

questions.stem: Isolated mitochondria with plenty of ADP and substrate are given the uncoupler DNP. What happens?
choices: Oxygen use and ATP synthesis both fall
Oxygen use and ATP synthesis both rise
Oxygen use falls while ATP synthesis rises
Oxygen use rises while ATP synthesis falls
questions.explanation: DNP carries protons back into the matrix, collapsing the gradient. With no gradient holding it back, electron transport (and so oxygen use) speeds up, but protons no longer pass through ATP synthase, so ATP synthesis falls and the energy becomes heat.

questions.stem: Why was the Racker–Stoeckenius vesicle experiment (1974) strong evidence for chemiosmosis?
choices: The vesicles had no electron transport chain, yet a light-driven proton pump plus ATP synthase made ATP
It showed that ATP synthase can make ATP without any membrane
It isolated the high-energy chemical intermediate of oxidative phosphorylation
It showed that bacteriorhodopsin carries electrons to ATP synthase
questions.explanation: The only link between the light-driven pump (bacteriorhodopsin, which moves protons, not electrons) and ATP synthase was the proton gradient across the sealed vesicle membrane. ATP was made anyway, so a gradient is enough. A sealed membrane was essential, and no chemical intermediate was ever found.

questions.stem: Chloroplasts run cyclic electron flow, which makes ATP but no NADPH, in addition to linear electron flow. Why?
choices: Linear flow alone makes too little ATP for each NADPH compared with what the Calvin cycle uses
Linear flow alone makes too much ATP, which must be balanced
Cyclic flow splits extra water to release more O₂
Cyclic flow is the only way to reduce NADP⁺
questions.explanation: Linear flow moves about 12 H⁺ per 2 NADPH; with 14 c subunits (4.67 H⁺ per ATP) that is about 2.6 ATP, or 1.29 ATP per NADPH. The Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP per 2 NADPH (1.5). Cyclic flow pumps extra protons without making NADPH or splitting water, closing the gap.

questions.stem: Brown fat helps newborns and hibernating mammals stay warm. Its mitochondria contain uncoupling protein 1 (thermogenin), which
choices: blocks complex IV so that electrons cannot reach oxygen
speeds up ATP synthase so more ATP is made
pumps extra protons out of the matrix
lets protons leak back into the matrix, so the energy is released as heat
questions.explanation: Thermogenin is a natural uncoupler: protons flow back through it instead of through ATP synthase. Electron transport runs fast, little ATP is made, and the energy of the gradient becomes heat. Blocking complex IV would stop respiration altogether, as cyanide does.

questions.stem: The combined electrical and pH gradient of protons across a membrane, which drives ATP synthase, is called the ___.
questions.explanation: The proton-motive force, $\Delta p$, has an electrical part (membrane potential) and a chemical part (pH difference). In mitochondria it is about 200 mV, mostly electrical.

questions.stem: Match each substance to how it affects mitochondria.
choices: Blocks complex I
Blocks complex IV
Blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase
Carries protons across the membrane (an uncoupler)
Blocks photosystem II
questions.explanation: Rotenone stops electrons entering from NADH at complex I. Cyanide (and carbon monoxide) stop electrons reaching oxygen at complex IV. Oligomycin plugs ATP synthase, which also slows electron transport through respiratory control. DNP shuttles protons across the membrane, uncoupling electron transport from ATP synthesis.

questions.stem: Put the carriers in the order electrons pass through them in linear electron flow in the thylakoid membrane.
choices: Water
Photosystem II
Plastoquinone
Cytochrome b₆f complex
Plastocyanin
Photosystem I
NADP⁺
questions.explanation: Photosystem II takes electrons from water (releasing O₂), and plastoquinone carries them to the cytochrome b₆f complex, which pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space. Plastocyanin carries them to photosystem I, where light boosts them again, and ferredoxin and FNR pass them to NADP⁺, making NADPH.

questions.stem: Which statements about ATP synthase are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: It is driven by H⁺ flowing down its concentration and electrical gradient
Its central stalk rotates as protons pass through
Each full turn makes 3 ATP
It pumps electrons across the membrane
It is found only in mitochondria
questions.explanation: Protons flowing through the c-ring turn it and the attached central stalk, which drives each of the three β subunits through the binding-change cycle, making 3 ATP per turn. ATP synthase moves protons, not electrons, and it is also found in chloroplasts and bacterial plasma membranes.

questions.stem: In three turns of the Calvin cycle, rubisco combines 3 RuBP (five carbons each) with 3 CO₂. How many molecules of 3-PGA (three carbons each) are formed?
questions.explanation: Carbon count: $3 \times 5 + 3 = 18$ carbons, and $18 \div 3 = 6$ molecules of 3-PGA. Each six-carbon intermediate splits into two 3-PGA. 18 is the number of carbons, not molecules.

questions.stem: Algae photosynthesizing in bright light with plenty of CO₂ are suddenly put in the dark. What happens to the amounts of 3-PGA and RuBP over the next minute?
choices: RuBP rises and 3-PGA falls
Both rise
3-PGA rises and RuBP falls
Both stay the same
questions.explanation: In the dark, ATP and NADPH run out, so 3-PGA can no longer be reduced and piles up. Rubisco briefly keeps using RuBP to fix CO₂, but RuBP cannot be regenerated without ATP, so it falls. Cutting off CO₂ instead gives the opposite pattern.

questions.stem: Which step of the Calvin cycle uses NADPH?
choices: Fixation of CO₂ onto RuBP
Regeneration of RuBP from G3P
Export of G3P to make sucrose
Reduction of 3-PGA to G3P
questions.explanation: NADPH supplies the electrons that reduce phosphorylated 3-PGA to the sugar G3P, using 6 NADPH (and 6 ATP) per three turns. Fixation needs no ATP or NADPH, and regeneration uses only ATP (3 per three turns).

questions.stem: Rubisco in a leaf carries out 500 carboxylations per second and 100 oxygenations per second. Photorespiration releases 1 CO₂ per 2 oxygenations. What is the net CO₂ fixed per second?
questions.explanation: The 100 oxygenations release $100 \div 2 = 50$ CO₂ in the salvage pathway, so net fixation is $500 - 50 = 450$ per second. 400 subtracts every oxygenation as if each lost a CO₂, and 500 ignores photorespiration.

questions.stem: Why does photorespiration in C3 plants increase on hot, dry days?
choices: Stomata close, so CO₂ in the leaf falls and O₂ builds up, and rubisco favors CO₂ less as temperature rises
The light reactions stop, so rubisco has no ATP
PEP carboxylase begins to react with O₂ instead of CO₂
Heat makes the leaf's mitochondria fix CO₂
questions.explanation: Closing stomata to save water cuts off fresh CO₂ while the light reactions keep releasing O₂, raising the O₂ : CO₂ ratio at rubisco. Warmth also lowers CO₂'s solubility relative to O₂ and weakens rubisco's preference for CO₂. PEP carboxylase does not react with O₂ at all.

questions.stem: Sugarcane leaves given ¹⁴CO₂ for a few seconds have most of the label in malate and aspartate, not 3-PGA. This shows that sugarcane
choices: lacks rubisco and the Calvin cycle
first fixes CO₂ into four-carbon acids before the Calvin cycle
makes sugar directly from malate without rubisco
carries out photorespiration instead of photosynthesis
questions.explanation: This was the key observation of Kortschak and of Hatch and Slack in the 1960s. The first stable products are four-carbon acids made by PEP carboxylase; the CO₂ is released again in bundle-sheath cells and fixed by rubisco in the Calvin cycle, which C4 plants still use.

questions.stem: Ignoring photorespiration, how many ATP and NADPH does a C4 plant (5 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂) use to make one glucose?
choices: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH
30 ATP and 12 NADPH
30 ATP and 18 NADPH
24 ATP and 12 NADPH
questions.explanation: One glucose needs 6 CO₂: $6 \times 5 = 30$ ATP and $6 \times 2 = 12$ NADPH. 18 ATP is the C3 cost. The C4 pump adds ATP (to regenerate PEP) but no NADPH.

questions.stem: In a C4 leaf, where are rubisco and the Calvin cycle found?
choices: In bundle-sheath cells around the veins
In the outer mesophyll cells
In the guard cells of the stomata
In the epidermis
questions.explanation: Kranz anatomy puts PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells and rubisco in bundle-sheath cells, where CO₂ released from malate is concentrated. Keeping rubisco away from the leaf's air spaces and in high CO₂ is what suppresses photorespiration.

questions.stem: The acidity of a CAM plant's leaf sap is measured at dawn and at dusk. What would you expect?
choices: Most acidic at dusk, least acidic at dawn
The same at dawn and dusk
Most acidic at dawn, least acidic at dusk
Acidic only on cloudy days
questions.explanation: CAM plants fix CO₂ at night into malic acid stored in the vacuole, so acid builds up overnight and peaks at dawn. During the day the malic acid is broken down to supply CO₂ to the Calvin cycle, so the sap is least acidic by dusk.

questions.stem: Match each plant to the type of photosynthesis it uses.
choices: C4
CAM
C3
questions.explanation: Corn and sugarcane are C4 grasses. Pineapple, like cacti and agaves, uses CAM. Wheat, rice, soybeans and most trees are C3 plants, fixing CO₂ directly with rubisco.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the C4 pathway in order.
choices: CO₂ (as bicarbonate) is attached to PEP in a mesophyll cell
The oxaloacetate formed is converted to malate
Malate moves into a bundle-sheath cell
Malate releases CO₂ near rubisco
Rubisco fixes the CO₂ in the Calvin cycle
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into four-carbon oxaloacetate in the mesophyll; it becomes malate, which moves to a bundle-sheath cell and releases CO₂ there. The concentrated CO₂ is fixed by rubisco into the Calvin cycle, and the leftover pyruvate returns to the mesophyll to be turned back into PEP using ATP.

questions.stem: In C4 and CAM plants, the enzyme ___ carries out the first fixation of CO₂, producing a four-carbon acid.
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase attaches CO₂ (as bicarbonate) to PEP, making oxaloacetate. Unlike rubisco it does not react with O₂, which is why it can be used to gather and concentrate CO₂.

questions.stem: Which are advantages of C4 photosynthesis over C3 photosynthesis in hot, sunny, dry conditions? Select all that apply.
choices: Much less photorespiration
Less water lost per CO₂ fixed
Less rubisco needed, saving nitrogen
Fewer ATP used per CO₂ fixed
CO₂ is taken in only at night
questions.explanation: Concentrating CO₂ around rubisco suppresses photorespiration, lets the plant keep its stomata less open (saving water), and means less rubisco is needed. C4 costs more ATP per CO₂ (about 5 versus 3), and taking in CO₂ only at night is CAM, not C4.

questions.stem: During which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA replicated?
choices: Prophase
G1 phase
Anaphase
S phase
questions.explanation: DNA is copied in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, before mitosis begins. By prophase the chromosomes already consist of two sister chromatids. G1 is growth before copying; anaphase is when the copies separate.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes interphase?
choices: The cell rests and carries out almost no activity until it divides.
The nucleus divides and the chromosomes separate.
The cell grows, carries out its normal functions, and replicates its DNA.
The cytoplasm divides to form two daughter cells.
questions.explanation: Interphase (G1, S, G2) is the busiest part of the cycle: growth, normal work, and DNA replication. Calling it a resting phase is a common misconception. Dividing the nucleus is mitosis, and dividing the cytoplasm is cytokinesis.

questions.stem: A cell has 12 chromosomes in G1. How many chromosomes and chromatids does it have in G2?
choices: 24 chromosomes and 24 chromatids
12 chromosomes and 24 chromatids
12 chromosomes and 12 chromatids
6 chromosomes and 12 chromatids
questions.explanation: After S phase each chromosome has two sister chromatids joined at one centromere. It is still one chromosome, so the count stays 12, with 24 chromatids. Counting chromatids as chromosomes gives 24; halving is what meiosis does, not interphase.

questions.stem: A human body cell (46 chromosomes) is in anaphase of mitosis. How many chromosomes are in the whole cell at this moment?
questions.explanation: In anaphase the 46 pairs of sister chromatids separate, and each chromatid now counts as a chromosome: 92 in the cell, 46 moving to each pole. After cytokinesis each daughter cell has 46.

questions.stem: Chromosomes are lined up along the middle of the cell, each attached to spindle fibers from both poles. Which stage is this?
choices: Prophase
Anaphase
Telophase
Metaphase
questions.explanation: Lining up at the middle (the metaphase plate) defines metaphase. In prophase the chromosomes are still condensing, in anaphase the chromatids are moving apart, and in telophase they have reached the poles.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the stages of mitosis in order?
choices: Metaphase, prophase, anaphase, telophase
Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
Prophase, anaphase, metaphase, telophase
Interphase, prophase, telophase, anaphase
questions.explanation: Chromosomes condense (prophase), line up (metaphase), separate (anaphase), and arrive at the poles as new nuclei form (telophase). Interphase is not part of mitosis.

questions.stem: Why do plant cells form a cell plate during cytokinesis instead of a cleavage furrow?
choices: Plant cells do not have a cell membrane to pinch.
Plant cells divide only by binary fission.
Their rigid cell wall prevents the cell from pinching in two.
The cell plate is needed to separate the sister chromatids.
questions.explanation: A plant cell is enclosed by a stiff wall, so it builds a new wall from the middle outward instead of pinching. Plant cells do have membranes, binary fission is the prokaryote process, and the chromatids are already separated in anaphase.

questions.stem: In a root tip sample of 300 cells, 24 are in some stage of mitosis. What is the mitotic index?
questions.explanation: Mitotic index = 24 ÷ 300 × 100% = 8%. Dividing by the 276 non-dividing cells gives 8.7%; 92% is the share in interphase; 24% treats the count as a percent.

questions.stem: In an unsynchronized sample of 400 cells, 20 are in metaphase. The full cell cycle takes 20 hours. About how long does metaphase last?
choices: 20 minutes
5 minutes
60 minutes
6 hours
questions.explanation: The fraction of cells in a stage equals the fraction of time spent in it: 20 ÷ 400 = 0.05, and 0.05 × 20 h = 1 h = 60 minutes.

questions.stem: Compared with the parent cell, the two daughter cells produced by mitosis are
choices: genetically identical, with the same number of chromosomes
genetically identical, with half the number of chromosomes
genetically different, with the same number of chromosomes
genetically different, with half the number of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Mitosis gives each daughter cell one copy of every chromosome, so they match the parent in number and genes (apart from rare copying errors). Halving the number and creating genetic differences are features of meiosis.

questions.stem: A graph of DNA content per cell shows the amount rising steadily from 1 unit to 2 units over several hours, then staying at 2 until it suddenly drops back to 1. The rising section corresponds to
choices: G1 phase
S phase
Anaphase
Cytokinesis
questions.explanation: DNA content doubles gradually as it is replicated in S phase. G1 holds steady at 1 unit, and the sudden drop back to 1 is cell division (cytokinesis), when the DNA is split between two cells.

questions.stem: In onion roots, the mitotic index is 15% in the region just behind the tip and 2% in a region farther back. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Cells near the tip spend more time in interphase.
Cells farther back have more chromosomes.
Mitosis takes longer in cells farther back.
Cells near the tip are dividing much more actively.
questions.explanation: A higher mitotic index means a larger share of cells are dividing, as expected in the growth zone near a root tip. More time in interphase would lower the index. The index says nothing about chromosome number, and a slower mitosis would raise the index, not lower it.

questions.stem: What does the spindle (metaphase) checkpoint check before allowing anaphase to begin?
choices: That the cell has grown large enough to divide
That the DNA has been replicated
That every chromosome is attached to spindle fibers from both poles
That growth factors are present outside the cell
questions.explanation: The spindle checkpoint delays anaphase until all chromosomes are correctly attached, so each daughter gets one copy of each. Cell size and growth factors are checked at G1, and completion of DNA replication at G2.

questions.stem: When a cell in S phase was fused with a cell in G1, the G1 nucleus began replicating its DNA early. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: DNA can be copied only when two nuclei share one cell.
The cytoplasm of the S-phase cell contains signals that trigger DNA replication.
The G1 nucleus had already finished G1 before the fusion.
Cell fusion damages DNA, which triggers replication.
questions.explanation: The G1 nucleus was pushed into S phase ahead of schedule by something in the S-phase cell, pointing to chemical signals in the cytoplasm (later identified as cyclin–CDK complexes). Single-nucleus cells copy DNA normally, and damage halts the cycle rather than speeding it up.

questions.stem: How do cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) behave during the cell cycle?
choices: CDK levels rise and fall; cyclins stay constant and are always active.
Both are made only during mitosis and destroyed during interphase.
Cyclins are made once in the life of a cell and never broken down.
Cyclin levels rise and fall; CDKs stay fairly constant but are active only when bound to cyclin.
questions.explanation: Cyclins are made and destroyed each cycle (hence the name). CDKs are present all the time but act only when a cyclin binds; destroying the cyclin switches the CDK off. This rise and fall times the transitions of the cycle.

questions.stem: A mutation leaves the RAS protein, which relays "divide" signals from growth factors, permanently switched on. This mutation has changed
choices: a proto-oncogene into an oncogene
a tumor suppressor gene into an oncogene
an oncogene into a proto-oncogene
a proto-oncogene into a tumor suppressor gene
questions.explanation: RAS is a normal gas-pedal gene (a proto-oncogene). An overactive, stuck-on version is an oncogene, and one mutated copy is enough. Tumor suppressor genes are brakes, and cancer involves their loss, not their creation.

questions.stem: Cells that have lost both working copies of the p53 gene are exposed to DNA-damaging radiation. What is the most likely result, compared with normal cells?
choices: The cells repair their DNA faster than normal cells.
The cells stop dividing permanently and enter G0.
Damaged cells keep dividing and pass on mutations instead of stopping or undergoing apoptosis.
The cells are unaffected because p53 only works during mitosis.
questions.explanation: p53 halts the cycle at G1 when DNA is damaged and triggers apoptosis if repair fails. Without it, damaged cells keep dividing and mutations accumulate, which is why p53 is mutated in about half of human cancers.

questions.stem: Children with inherited retinoblastoma often develop tumors in both eyes at a young age. Knudson's two-hit explanation is that these children
choices: inherit one damaged copy of a tumor suppressor gene, so a single new mutation in a cell is enough
inherit two damaged copies of an oncogene, so no new mutations are needed
inherit an oncogene that only becomes active in the eyes
are exposed to more ultraviolet light than other children
questions.explanation: Both copies of the RB tumor suppressor gene must be lost. Inherited cases start with one bad copy in every cell, so one more hit in any retinal cell is enough, making tumors earlier and more numerous. Non-inherited cases need two hits in the same cell.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a malignant tumor from a benign tumor?
choices: Its cells divide more than normal cells.
It forms a mass of abnormal cells.
It begins from a single abnormal cell.
Its cells can invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body.
questions.explanation: Both kinds of tumor are masses of abnormally dividing cells that started from one cell. Only malignant tumors invade and metastasize, and metastasis causes most cancer deaths.

questions.stem: Starting from one cell, about how many cells are there after 20 doublings?
choices: About 1 million
About 1 billion
questions.explanation: 2²⁰ = 1,048,576, about a million. Since 2¹⁰ ≈ 1000, 20 doublings give about 1000 × 1000. 40 is 2 × 20 (adding instead of multiplying), and about a billion takes 30 doublings.

questions.stem: Tumor cells in a dish increase from 500 to 8,000 in 48 hours. What is their doubling time?
choices: 12 hours
16 hours
3 hours
6 hours
questions.explanation: 8000 ÷ 500 = 16 = 2⁴, so there were 4 doublings, and 48 ÷ 4 = 12 hours. Using 16 as the number of doublings gives 3 hours; 16 hours assumes 3 doublings.

questions.stem: Why does the risk of most cancers increase with age?
choices: Older cells stop having checkpoints entirely.
Cancer is caused by a single mutation that appears at a set age.
Several mutations must build up in the same cell line, and that takes time.
Older people have more cells, so each cell divides faster.
questions.explanation: Most cancers need multiple mutations in proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, so the chance that one cell has collected enough rises the longer we live. A single mutation is almost never enough, and checkpoints do not simply switch off with age.

questions.stem: Which statement about stem cells is correct?
choices: Adult stem cells are pluripotent, while embryonic stem cells are multipotent.
Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, while most adult stem cells are multipotent.
Stem cells cannot divide; they only differentiate.
Induced pluripotent stem cells are taken directly from early embryos.
questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells can become any body cell type (pluripotent); adult stem cells, such as blood stem cells, make a limited range (multipotent). Stem cells self-renew by dividing. iPSCs are reprogrammed body cells, such as skin cells, which is why they avoid using embryos.

questions.stem: Chemotherapy often causes hair loss and damage to the lining of the gut. Why?
choices: Cancer cells move into the hair follicles and gut during treatment.
The drugs act only on cells in G0.
Hair and gut cells are the source of most cancers.
Many chemotherapy drugs target rapidly dividing cells, including normal ones.
questions.explanation: Hair follicles and the gut lining divide rapidly, like cancer cells, so drugs that attack dividing cells harm them too. Cells in G0 are not dividing, so they are largely spared.

questions.stem: Mature nerve cells in the brain almost never divide. In which part of the cell cycle do they remain?
choices: S phase
G2
G0
Metaphase
questions.explanation: Cells that leave the cycle after G1 and stop dividing are in G0. They are fully active, just not dividing. S, G2 and metaphase are all stages on the way to division.

questions.stem: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a normal human egg cell have?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid: n = 23, one from each homologous pair. Fertilization restores 2n = 46. 22 is the number of autosomes in a gamete, leaving out the sex chromosome.

questions.stem: How do homologous chromosomes differ from sister chromatids?
choices: Homologs are identical copies; sister chromatids come from different parents.
Homologs carry different genes; sister chromatids carry the same genes.
There is no difference; the terms mean the same thing.
Homologs come from different parents and may carry different versions of genes; sister chromatids are identical copies.
questions.explanation: One homolog came from each parent; they carry the same genes in the same order but possibly different versions. Sister chromatids are made by copying one chromosome in S phase, so they are identical (before crossing over).

questions.stem: What separates during anaphase I of meiosis?
choices: Sister chromatids, while homologous chromosomes stay together
Homologous chromosomes, while sister chromatids stay together
Both homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids
Nothing; the cell divides without separating chromosomes
questions.explanation: Anaphase I pulls homologs to opposite poles; sister chromatids stay joined until anaphase II. This is what halves the chromosome number, and it is the key difference from mitosis, where sister chromatids separate.

questions.stem: During which stage does crossing over occur?
choices: Prophase I
Metaphase II
Anaphase I
Telophase II
questions.explanation: Crossing over happens when homologs are paired closely along their length, which is in prophase I. By anaphase I they are already separating, and in meiosis II homologs are no longer together.

questions.stem: A species has 2n = 10. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment produce?
questions.explanation: There are n = 5 pairs, each able to line up 2 ways: 2⁵ = 32. 10 is 2 × 5 (multiplying instead of raising 2 to the 5th power); 25 is 5²; 1024 is 2¹⁰, using 2n instead of n.

questions.stem: A fruit fly has 2n = 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations are possible in a zygote produced by two flies?
questions.explanation: Each parent can make 2⁴ = 16 kinds of gametes, and any egg can meet any sperm: 16 × 16 = 256. 16 counts gametes from one parent only; 64 is 8 × 8 (using 2n = 8 as the number of gamete types), and 32 adds 16 + 16 instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 20 completes meiosis I. What does each resulting cell contain?
choices: 10 chromosomes, each made of 1 chromatid
10 chromosomes, each made of 2 chromatids
20 chromosomes, each made of 2 chromatids
20 chromosomes, each made of 1 chromatid
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologs, halving the number to 10, but the sister chromatids stay together until meiosis II. There is no DNA replication between the two divisions, so the gametes end up with 10 single-chromatid chromosomes.

questions.stem: One homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I, but meiosis II is normal. What are the four gametes?
choices: Two with an extra chromosome (n + 1) and two missing one (n − 1)
Two normal, one n + 1, and one n − 1
All four normal
Four with an extra chromosome (n + 1)
questions.explanation: Both homologs go to one cell in meiosis I, so that cell's two products each get an extra copy and the other cell's two products each lack it. Nondisjunction in meiosis II instead gives two normal gametes, one n + 1 and one n − 1.

questions.stem: Which is true of meiosis but not of mitosis?
choices: Sister chromatids separate at an anaphase.
The DNA is replicated beforehand, during S phase.
A spindle moves the chromosomes.
Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments.
questions.explanation: Pairing of homologs (synapsis) and crossing over happen only in prophase I of meiosis. Sister chromatids separate in mitosis and in meiosis II, DNA replicates before both, and both use a spindle.

questions.stem: Van Beneden found that in a roundworm, the egg nucleus and sperm nucleus each contributed 2 chromosomes and the fertilized egg had 4. What did this support?
choices: Sperm contribute more chromosomes than eggs.
Chromosome number doubles in every generation.
Gametes carry half the chromosome number of body cells.
Only the egg passes chromosomes to the offspring.
questions.explanation: Each gamete brought half of the zygote's number, and the two halves added up to the body-cell number. This pointed to a reduction division (meiosis) that keeps the chromosome number constant across generations.

questions.stem: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) usually results from
choices: crossing over between chromosome 21 and its homolog
nondisjunction, producing a gamete with an extra chromosome 21
a mutation in a single gene on chromosome 21
a gamete that is missing chromosome 21
questions.explanation: If chromosome 21 fails to separate in meiosis, a gamete gets two copies; after fertilization the zygote has three (47 chromosomes). Crossing over is normal and does not change chromosome number, and a missing chromosome would give 45, not 47.

questions.stem: How does meiosis in females differ from meiosis in males?
choices: Females make four eggs per meiosis; males make one sperm.
Females skip meiosis II, so eggs are diploid.
Only males use crossing over during meiosis.
Females make one egg and small polar bodies per meiosis; males make four sperm.
questions.explanation: Unequal division of the cytoplasm gives one large egg (keeping stored nutrients) plus polar bodies that break down, while each male meiosis gives four sperm. Both sexes complete both divisions, and crossing over happens in both.

questions.stem: Each numbered animal cell is at a different stage of mitosis. Name the stage of each cell.

image.alt: Four animal cells, each with four chromosomes, at different stages of division, shown in mixed order. Cell 1 is long with single chromatids near both ends; cell 2 has condensed chromosomes inside a dashed nuclear outline; cell 3 is pinching in two with a nucleus in each half; cell 4 has chromosomes in a column at its middle with spindle fibers from both ends.

choices: Anaphase
Prophase
Telophase
Metaphase
Interphase
questions.explanation: Cell 1: single chromatids are being pulled toward opposite poles, so the sisters have separated: anaphase. Cell 2: the chromosomes are condensed and doubled, the nuclear envelope (dashed) is breaking down, and the spindle poles are just moving apart: prophase. Cell 3: two new nuclei with uncoiling chromosomes in a cell that is pinching in two: telophase with cytokinesis. Cell 4: duplicated chromosomes lined up at the middle, attached to fibers from both poles: metaphase. Interphase cells show no condensed chromosomes at all.

questions.stem: Starting just after a cell forms, put these parts of the cell cycle in order.
choices: G1
S phase
G2
Prophase
Metaphase
Anaphase
Telophase
questions.explanation: Interphase comes first: G1 (growth), S (DNA copied), G2 (preparation). Then mitosis: prophase (condense, spindle forms), metaphase (line up), anaphase (chromatids separate), telophase (nuclei re-form), with cytokinesis overlapping telophase.

questions.stem: After S phase, each chromosome consists of two identical ___ joined at a constricted region called the ___.
questions.explanation: Copying the DNA in S phase turns each chromosome into two identical sister chromatids, held together most tightly at the centromere. It still counts as one chromosome until the chromatids separate in anaphase.

questions.stem: Which of these happen during interphase? Select all that apply.
choices: The DNA is replicated.
The cell grows and makes proteins and organelles.
Sister chromatids separate.
The cell makes proteins it will need for the spindle.
The nuclear envelope breaks down.
questions.explanation: Interphase includes G1 (growth), S (DNA replication) and G2 (making proteins for division, such as spindle components). Sister chromatids separate in anaphase and the nuclear envelope breaks down in prophase, both during mitosis.

questions.stem: Match each stage to what happens in it.
choices: Chromosomes condense and the spindle forms
Chromosomes line up at the middle of the cell
Sister chromatids move to opposite poles
Nuclear envelopes re-form around two sets of chromosomes
The cytoplasm divides into two cells
The DNA is copied
questions.explanation: The four stages of mitosis divide the nucleus: condense (prophase), line up (metaphase), separate (anaphase), re-form nuclei (telophase). Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm. DNA copying belongs to S phase of interphase, not to any stage of mitosis.

questions.stem: The drawing shows a layer of tissue, a blood vessel and a distant organ. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A cross-section of tissue: a single layer of cells on a thin membrane, a dome of extra cells in the middle of the layer, a cluster of irregular cells on the right breaking through the membrane into the tissue below, a blood vessel with one irregular cell inside it, and a separate organ containing a small cluster of irregular cells.

choices: Normal tissue
Benign tumor
Cancer cells invading nearby tissue
Cancer cell traveling in the blood
Secondary tumor (metastasis)
Stem cells repairing the tissue
questions.explanation: 1 is the orderly normal layer. 2 is a mass of extra cells that stays above the basement membrane: a benign tumor. 3 shows malignant cells that have broken through the membrane and are invading the tissue below. 4 is a cancer cell carried in the blood, and 5 is a new tumor it seeded in a distant organ, which is metastasis.

questions.stem: Match each checkpoint to what it checks.
choices: Cell size, growth signals and DNA damage
DNA copied completely and correctly
Every chromosome attached to fibers from both poles
Nuclear envelopes re-formed around both sets
questions.explanation: The G1 checkpoint decides whether to divide at all (size, nutrients, growth factors, DNA damage). The G2 checkpoint makes sure replication is complete and correct before mitosis. The spindle checkpoint holds anaphase until every chromosome is attached to both poles. No checkpoint waits on nuclear envelopes re-forming.

questions.stem: Which statements describe tumor suppressor genes? Select all that apply.
choices: Their normal proteins slow division, repair DNA or trigger apoptosis.
p53 and RB are examples.
One overactive mutant copy is enough to push a cell toward cancer.
Inheriting one faulty copy can raise a person's cancer risk.
They are genes that viruses insert into cells.
questions.explanation: Tumor suppressors are the brakes (p53, RB). Usually both copies must be lost in a cell, but inheriting one faulty copy means only one more hit is needed, as in inherited retinoblastoma. A single overactive copy describes an oncogene, and tumor suppressors are normal cell genes, not viral ones.

questions.stem: Orderly, programmed cell death that removes damaged or unneeded cells without causing inflammation is called ___.
