questions.explanation: Apoptosis is a tidy self-destruction: the cell dismantles itself and is eaten by neighbors. It removes cells with unrepairable DNA damage and sculpts the body during development, such as removing the webbing between fingers.

questions.stem: Match each cell to its potency. (Answers can be used more than once.)
left: Blood stem cell in bone marrow
choices: Totipotent
Pluripotent
Multipotent
Unable to divide
questions.explanation: The zygote can make every cell type including the placenta (totipotent). Embryonic stem cells and iPSCs can make every body cell type (pluripotent). Blood stem cells make only the related blood cell types (multipotent). All of these can divide.

questions.stem: All four cells come from an organism with 2n = 4. Red marks chromosomes from the mother and blue from the father. Name the stage of each numbered cell.

image.alt: Four dividing cells. Cell 1 is small with two duplicated chromosomes, one long and one short, lined up singly at its middle. Cell 2 has four duplicated chromosomes lined up singly in a column at its middle. Cell 3 has duplicated chromosomes, still with both chromatids, being pulled toward the two poles, two to each side. Cell 4 has duplicated chromosomes lined up at the middle in side-by-side pairs, a red and a blue chromosome of the same size in each pair.

choices: Metaphase II
Metaphase of mitosis
Anaphase I
Metaphase I
Anaphase II
questions.explanation: Cell 4 has homologs lined up as pairs, which happens only in metaphase I. Cell 3 shows whole duplicated chromosomes (two chromatids still joined) moving apart: homologs separating in anaphase I. Cell 2 has all four chromosomes in a single column with homologs not paired: metaphase of mitosis. Cell 1 has only two chromosomes, one of each size, so it is haploid, and they line up singly: metaphase II. In anaphase II, single chromatids would be moving apart.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happen, from before meiosis to the end.
choices: DNA is replicated in S phase
Homologous chromosomes pair and cross over
Homologous pairs line up at the middle of the cell
Homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles
Chromosomes line up singly in two haploid cells
Sister chromatids move to opposite poles
Four haploid cells form
questions.explanation: DNA is copied once, before meiosis. Meiosis I: prophase I (pairing and crossing over), metaphase I (pairs line up), anaphase I (homologs separate). Meiosis II, with no new replication: metaphase II (chromosomes line up singly), anaphase II (sister chromatids separate), then telophase II and cytokinesis give four haploid cells.

questions.stem: In humans, body cells are diploid with 2n = ___, and gametes are haploid with n = ___.
questions.explanation: Human body cells have 23 pairs, 46 chromosomes. Meiosis puts one chromosome of each pair into a gamete, 23 in all, and fertilization restores 46.

questions.stem: A cell from a species with 2n = 4 completes meiosis normally. Which statements about the four cells it produces are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Each is haploid.
Each has 2 chromosomes.
They are genetically identical to one another.
Each chromosome consists of a single chromatid.
Each has the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the number (n = 2) and ends with sister chromatids separated, so each cell has 2 single-chromatid chromosomes. Crossing over and independent assortment make the four cells genetically different, and their chromosome number is half the parent's, not equal to it.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: One from each parent; same genes, possibly different versions
Identical copies made in S phase and joined at a centromere
A haploid egg or sperm
The diploid cell formed when an egg and sperm join
A cell with three complete sets of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Homologs pair up in meiosis I and carry the same genes but can differ in versions; sister chromatids are exact copies. Gametes are haploid, and fertilization joins two of them into a diploid zygote. A cell with three sets is a triploid, which is not one of these terms.

questions.stem: Cytoplasm from a mature frog egg, injected into an immature oocyte that received no hormone, made the oocyte's nucleus break down and its chromosomes condense. Cytoplasm from an immature oocyte had no effect. What does this show?
choices: The hormone that triggers maturation is stored in the nucleus.
The cytoplasm of a cell in M phase contains a factor that can drive another cell into M phase.
Injecting any cytoplasm damages the oocyte and breaks down its nucleus.
Immature oocytes lack chromosomes until they are injected.
questions.explanation: Only cytoplasm from an M-phase cell had the effect, so the injection itself is not the cause (the control rules that out). Something in that cytoplasm, named maturation-promoting factor (MPF), triggers M phase. The oocyte already has chromosomes; they were simply not condensed.

questions.stem: MPF activity could be passed from oocyte to oocyte through many serial injections without diluting away, even when protein synthesis was blocked. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Each oocyte makes new MPF protein from mRNA after injection.
MPF is a mutation that copies itself into each oocyte's DNA.
The injected MPF is too stable to be diluted.
Oocytes store inactive MPF, and a little active MPF switches the stored MPF on.
questions.explanation: With protein synthesis blocked, no new MPF can be made, yet activity rises in each recipient. The oocyte must hold MPF in an inactive form that injected active MPF converts, through positive feedback (active CDK1 activates Cdc25 and inhibits Wee1). Simple stability could not prevent dilution over many transfers, and MPF is a protein complex, not a mutation.

questions.stem: When MPF was purified and identified, it turned out to be
choices: cyclin B bound to the kinase CDK1
the tumor suppressor p53 bound to MDM2
cyclin D bound to the kinase CDK4
a caspase bound to cytochrome c
questions.explanation: MPF is cyclin B with CDK1 (the product of the yeast gene cdc2). Cyclin D–CDK4 acts in G1 on Rb, p53–MDM2 is the damage-response pair, and caspases with cytochrome c belong to apoptosis.

questions.stem: Yeast cells lacking the kinase Wee1 enter mitosis early and divide at about half the normal size. Why?
choices: Without Wee1, cyclin B cannot be destroyed, so cells stay in mitosis.
Wee1 is the cyclin that activates CDK1.
Without Wee1 adding inhibitory phosphates, cyclin B–CDK1 becomes active before the cell has grown to its usual size.
Wee1 removes the activating phosphate from CDK1, so its loss blocks mitosis.
questions.explanation: Wee1 adds inhibitory phosphates that hold cyclin B–CDK1 off during G2 while the cell grows. Without it, the complex switches on early, so the cell divides when smaller. Cyclin destruction is the APC/C's job, Wee1 is a kinase not a cyclin, and its loss speeds mitosis rather than blocking it.

questions.stem: A modified cyclin B that the APC/C cannot tag with ubiquitin is added to a cycling frog egg extract. What happens?
choices: The extract cycles faster than normal.
MPF stays active and the extract is stuck in M phase.
MPF never becomes active, so the extract stays in interphase.
DNA replication repeats many times without mitosis.
questions.explanation: MPF switches on as usual, but leaving mitosis requires destroying cyclin B. A cyclin that cannot be tagged is never sent to the proteasome, so CDK1 stays active and the extract stays in M phase. This experiment showed cyclin destruction is needed to exit mitosis.

questions.stem: A mutant Rb protein cannot bind E2F at all. How would cells carrying only this mutant Rb most likely behave?
choices: They enter S phase without needing growth factors, because E2F is always free.
They can never enter S phase, because E2F is permanently blocked.
They stop at the spindle checkpoint.
They undergo apoptosis as soon as they reach G1.
questions.explanation: Rb's job is to hold E2F until cyclin–CDKs phosphorylate it. If Rb cannot bind E2F, E2F is free all the time and switches on S-phase genes without any growth-factor signal, the same effect as losing Rb. That is why RB is a tumor suppressor.

questions.stem: Some tumors keep normal p53 genes but make far too much MDM2. What is the likely effect?
choices: p53 levels rise, so the cells arrest permanently.
MDM2 repairs DNA damage in place of p53.
The cells become more sensitive to DNA damage and die by apoptosis.
p53 is destroyed even after DNA damage, so the cells behave as if p53 were missing.
questions.explanation: MDM2 tags p53 for destruction. With excess MDM2, p53 cannot build up after damage, so p21 is not made, damaged cells keep dividing, and apoptosis is not triggered. Overactive MDM2 therefore acts much like losing p53. MDM2 is not a repair enzyme.

questions.stem: In a model of an inherited tumor-suppressor mutation, the number of tumors per carrier is a Poisson count with a mean of 2. What fraction of carriers develop no tumor?
questions.explanation: For a Poisson count, $P(0) = e^{-m} = e^{-2} = 0.135$, so 13.5% get no tumor. 86.5% is the fraction with at least one tumor ($1 - e^{-2}$); 27.1% is the chance of exactly one ($2e^{-2}$).

questions.stem: In a flow cytometer, an unsynchronized culture with a 24-hour cycle shows 60% of cells with 2C DNA, 25% between 2C and 4C, and 15% with 4C. About how long is S phase?
choices: 14.4 hours
6 hours
3.6 hours
25 hours
questions.explanation: Cells between 2C and 4C are replicating, so they are in S. Time in S is about $0.25 \times 24 = 6$ hours. 14.4 h is G1 (the 2C cells) and 3.6 h is G2 + M (the 4C cells); 25 treats the percent as hours.

questions.stem: A pathologist sees cells that have shrunk, with condensed chromatin, membrane blebs, and DNA cut into fragments in multiples of about 180 base pairs, and no inflammation nearby. What is happening?
choices: Apoptosis
Necrosis
Mitosis
Metastasis
questions.explanation: Shrinkage, chromatin condensation, blebbing and a DNA ladder (cuts between nucleosomes) with no inflammation are the signs of apoptosis. Necrosis makes cells swell and burst and triggers inflammation. Mitosis does not fragment DNA, and metastasis is the spread of cancer.

questions.stem: In most follicular lymphomas, a translocation makes B cells produce far too much Bcl-2. Why does this contribute to cancer?
choices: Bcl-2 is a cyclin that drives cells through G1.
Bcl-2 cuts cohesin and causes nondisjunction.
Bcl-2 activates executioner caspases.
Bcl-2 blocks the release of cytochrome c, so cells that should die by apoptosis survive.
questions.explanation: Bcl-2 keeps the mitochondrial pores closed, preventing cytochrome c release and the caspase cascade of the intrinsic pathway. Too much Bcl-2 lets damaged or unneeded B cells survive and accumulate. It is not a cyclin, does not cut cohesin, and blocks rather than activates caspases.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis in order.
choices: DNA damage stabilizes p53
BAX opens pores in the outer membrane of mitochondria
Cytochrome c leaks into the cytoplasm
The apoptosome activates caspase 9
Executioner caspases cut hundreds of cell proteins
Phagocytes engulf the cell's fragments
questions.explanation: Damage stabilizes p53, which switches on pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX. BAX pores release cytochrome c, which joins Apaf-1 in the apoptosome to activate the initiator caspase 9. Caspase 9 activates executioner caspases (3 and 7), which dismantle the cell, and phagocytes clear the fragments without inflammation.

questions.stem: Match each protein to its role.
choices: Adds inhibitory phosphates to CDK1
Removes inhibitory phosphates from CDK1
Tags cyclin B and securin for destruction
Cuts cohesin so sister chromatids separate
Blocks cyclin–CDK complexes after DNA damage
Releases cytochrome c from mitochondria
questions.explanation: Wee1 and Cdc25 set the timing of CDK1 activation from opposite sides. The APC/C ends mitosis and starts anaphase by tagging cyclin B and securin, which frees separase to cut cohesin. p21 is the CDK inhibitor that p53 switches on. Cytochrome c release is done by BAX pores in apoptosis.

questions.stem: Which changes can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene? Select all that apply.
choices: A point mutation that locks its protein in the active state
Amplification of the gene into many copies
A translocation that fuses it to another gene
Loss of both copies of the gene
A mutation that destroys the protein's function
questions.explanation: Oncogenes arise by gain of function: a stuck-on protein (RAS), too much protein (HER2 amplification), or a new fusion protein (BCR-ABL). Losing both copies or destroying function is the loss-of-function route that inactivates tumor suppressor genes.

questions.stem: The protein-cutting enzymes that carry out apoptosis, made as inactive precursors and activated in a cascade, are called ___.
questions.explanation: Caspases are cysteine proteases that cut just after aspartate. Initiator caspases (8 and 9) activate executioner caspases (3 and 7), which dismantle the cell.

questions.stem: A tumor from a person who inherited one faulty copy of a tumor suppressor gene has lost the good copy by deletion. This kind of second hit is called loss of ___.
questions.explanation: The person was heterozygous (one good, one faulty copy). Losing the good copy by deletion, chromosome loss or mitotic recombination leaves only faulty copies: loss of heterozygosity, a common second hit.

questions.stem: What is the main job of chiasmata during meiosis I?
choices: They attach chromosomes to the nuclear envelope.
They copy the DNA a second time before meiosis II.
They hold each homologous pair together so the spindle can pull the two homologs to opposite poles.
They keep sister chromatids together until anaphase II.
questions.explanation: Because chromatid arms have been swapped at a chiasma, cohesion along the arms ties the homologs together until anaphase I, letting them attach to opposite poles under tension. Pairs with no crossover are prone to nondisjunction. Keeping sisters together until anaphase II is the job of centromere cohesin protected by shugoshin.

questions.stem: In a mutant lacking shugoshin, all cohesin is cut at anaphase I. What is the most likely result?
choices: Sister chromatids separate too early, so they segregate randomly in meiosis II and many gametes are aneuploid.
Homologs never separate, so all gametes are diploid.
Crossing over cannot occur.
Meiosis proceeds normally because shugoshin acts only in mitosis.
questions.explanation: Shugoshin protects centromere cohesin during anaphase I so sisters stay joined until anaphase II. Without it, sisters come apart early and can no longer be pulled evenly to opposite poles in meiosis II, giving gametes with extra or missing chromosomes. Crossing over happens earlier, in prophase I, and homologs still separate.

questions.stem: A cell heterozygous AB/ab undergoes meiosis with one crossover between the two genes. Classify each numbered product chromatid as parental or recombinant.

image.alt: On the left, a homologous pair in prophase I: two red chromatids carrying A and B and two blue chromatids carrying a and b, with the two inner chromatids crossing between the genes. On the right, four separate chromatids, numbered 1 to 4, carrying A and B, A and b, a and B, and a and b.

choices: Parental
Recombinant
questions.explanation: The crossover involved only the two inner chromatids, swapping the parts beyond the crossover point. Chromatids 2 (A b) and 3 (a B) carry new combinations, so they are recombinant. Chromatids 1 (A B) and 4 (a b) were not involved and keep the parental combinations. One crossover between two genes therefore gives 2 recombinant and 2 parental chromatids.

questions.stem: At a marker near the centromere of chromosome 21, a mother has M1 and M2 and the father has P1 and P2. A child with trisomy 21 has M2, M2 and P1. Where did the error most likely happen?
choices: Maternal meiosis I
Maternal meiosis II
Paternal meiosis I
Paternal meiosis II
questions.explanation: The extra copy came from the mother (two maternal markers). They are identical (M2 and M2), so they are sister chromatids that failed to separate: maternal meiosis II. A maternal meiosis I error would give two different homologs, M1 and M2.

questions.stem: Using the same family (mother M1/M2, father P1/P2), a child with trisomy 21 has M1, P1 and P2. Where did the error most likely happen?
choices: Maternal meiosis I
Maternal meiosis II
Paternal meiosis I
Paternal meiosis II
questions.explanation: Two markers come from the father, and they are different (P1 and P2), so both of his homologs went into one sperm: paternal meiosis I. Paternal meiosis II would give two identical markers, such as P1 and P1.

questions.stem: A person has the karyotype 47,XYY. In which parent and division did nondisjunction most likely occur?
choices: Father, meiosis II
Mother, meiosis I
Father, meiosis I
Mother, meiosis II
questions.explanation: Only the father can supply a Y, so the sperm was YY. Two Y chromosomes in one sperm must be sister chromatids that failed to separate, which happens in meiosis II. A father's meiosis I error would give an XY sperm instead.

questions.stem: A child has three copies of chromosome 21 in about 30% of blood cells and two copies in the rest. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Nondisjunction in maternal meiosis I
Crossing over between chromosome 21 and its homolog
Polyploidy in all of the child's cells
Nondisjunction in a mitotic division of the early embryo, producing mosaicism
questions.explanation: A meiotic error alone would put the extra chromosome in the zygote and so in every cell. A mix of normal and trisomic cells means a mitotic error after fertilization created two cell lines: mosaicism. (Sometimes a trisomic zygote loses the extra copy in one early mitosis, which also gives a mosaic; either way the mix comes from a mitotic error.) Crossing over does not change chromosome number, and polyploidy would add whole sets.

questions.stem: An organism with 2n = 8 is heterozygous for two genes on every chromosome pair. Suppose crossovers occur between the two genes in 2 of the 4 pairs and never in the other 2. How many kinds of gamete are possible?
questions.explanation: Each pair with a crossover between the genes can contribute 4 kinds of chromatid; each pair without one, 2. So $4^2 \times 2^2 = 16 \times 4 = 64$. 16 ignores crossing over ($2^4$), 256 assumes crossovers in all four pairs ($4^4$), and 32 counts only one crossover pair.

questions.stem: A triploid plant has a basic set of x = 7 chromosomes. If each set of three homologs splits 1 and 2 at random, independently, what fraction of its gametes is balanced (exactly one or exactly two of every chromosome)?
questions.explanation: All-one-copy has probability $\left(\tfrac12\right)^7 = \tfrac1{128}$, and all-two-copies the same, so the total is $2 \times \tfrac1{128} = \tfrac1{64}$. 1/128 counts only one of the two balanced outcomes.

questions.stem: Species A (2n = 14) and species B (2n = 20) form a sterile hybrid. Later, the hybrid's chromosome number doubles, giving a fertile allopolyploid. How many chromosomes does the fertile plant have?
questions.explanation: The hybrid gets a gamete from each parent: $7 + 10 = 17$ chromosomes, with no partners to pair with, so it is sterile. Doubling gives $2 \times 17 = 34$, in which every chromosome has an identical partner. 68 doubles twice; 24 adds the wrong numbers.

questions.stem: Bread wheat is hexaploid, 2n = 6x = 42. How many chromosomes are in a normal wheat gamete, and how many in one basic set (x)?
choices: 42 in a gamete, 7 in a set
21 in a gamete, 14 in a set
7 in a gamete, 21 in a set
21 in a gamete, 7 in a set
questions.explanation: A gamete has half the body-cell number: $n = 42 \div 2 = 21$, which is three basic sets. One basic set is $x = 42 \div 6 = 7$. Wheat is an allopolyploid of three ancestral grass genomes, each with 7 chromosomes.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happen in normal meiosis.
choices: Homologs pair and the synaptonemal complex forms
Crossovers form between non-sister chromatids
The synaptonemal complex comes apart; homologs stay joined at chiasmata
Homologs attach to opposite poles under tension
Arm cohesin is cut and homologs separate
Centromere cohesin is cut and sister chromatids separate
questions.explanation: Prophase I: synapsis, crossing over, then disassembly of the synaptonemal complex leaving chiasmata. Metaphase I: homologs attach to opposite poles, held under tension by the chiasmata. Anaphase I: arm cohesin is cut, releasing homologs, while shugoshin protects centromere cohesin. Anaphase II: centromere cohesin is cut and sisters separate.

questions.stem: Match each finding to where the chromosome error most likely happened.
left: Trisomy with two different maternal markers near the centromere
Trisomy with two identical maternal markers near the centromere
A mix of cells with 46 and 47 chromosomes
choices: Paternal meiosis II
Maternal meiosis I
Maternal meiosis II
A mitotic division after fertilization
Paternal meiosis I
questions.explanation: YY sperm come only from sister chromatids failing to separate in the father's meiosis II. Two different homologs from one parent mean meiosis I; two identical copies mean sister chromatids, meiosis II. A mixture of cell lines (mosaicism) means the error happened in a mitosis after the zygote formed.

questions.stem: Which statements about polyploidy are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Colchicine can double the chromosome number by blocking spindle formation.
An allopolyploid combines chromosome sets from two different species.
Triploid plants usually make mostly balanced gametes.
Polyploidy can produce a new plant species in a single step.
Polyploidy means having one extra chromosome.
questions.explanation: Colchicine stops the spindle so chromosomes double without division. Allopolyploids join genomes from two species, and because they cannot breed successfully with either parent they can be new species at once (Karpechenko's radish-cabbage). Triploids make very few balanced gametes, and one extra chromosome is aneuploidy, not polyploidy.

questions.stem: After crossing over, homologs stay joined at X-shaped points, each called a ___.
questions.explanation: A chiasma (plural chiasmata) is the visible sign of a crossover. Together with cohesion along the chromatid arms, it holds the homologs together until anaphase I.

questions.stem: A fertile plant whose chromosomes come from two different species, formed by hybridization followed by chromosome doubling, is called an ___.
questions.explanation: An allopolyploid carries full chromosome sets from two (or more) species. Doubling gives every chromosome a partner, which restores fertility, as in Karpechenko's radish-cabbage and in bread wheat.

questions.stem: Mendel crossed true-breeding purple-flowered peas with true-breeding white-flowered peas. Every F1 plant was purple, yet about one quarter of the F2 plants were white. What best explains this?
choices: The F1 plants carried the white allele, but it was masked by the dominant purple allele
The white allele was destroyed in the F1 and re-created by mutation in the F2
The purple and white factors blended in the F1 and separated again in the F2
Environmental conditions in the F2 year turned some purple plants white
questions.explanation: The F1 plants were Pp: the p allele was present but hidden because P is dominant. When two Pp plants were crossed, pp offspring appeared in about 1/4 of the F2. Mutation is far too rare to give a steady 1/4. Blending would make the F1 an intermediate color and could not bring back pure white.

questions.stem: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p). Two Pp plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to have white flowers?
questions.explanation: Each parent gives p with probability 1/2, and a white plant (pp) needs p from both: $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. 3/4 is the purple fraction; 1/2 is the heterozygous fraction; 1/16 belongs to a two-gene cross.

questions.stem: What is the expected genotype ratio among the offspring of Aa × Aa?
choices: 3 AA : 1 aa
1 AA : 1 aa
1 AA : 1 Aa : 2 aa
1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa
questions.explanation: The Punnett square has four equal boxes: AA, Aa, aA and aa, so 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. The 3 : 1 ratio is the phenotype ratio (AA and Aa look the same), not the genotype ratio.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant (T is dominant to t for dwarf) is crossed with a dwarf plant. Of 60 offspring, 31 are tall and 29 are dwarf. What is the genotype of the tall parent?
choices: TT
tt
Tt
It cannot be determined from a test cross
questions.explanation: This is a test cross: the dwarf parent (tt) gives only t. Dwarf offspring (tt) must have received t from the tall parent as well, so it is Tt, and Tt × tt predicts 1 tall : 1 dwarf, matching 31 : 29. A TT parent would give only tall offspring; a tt parent would not be tall.

questions.stem: What kinds of gametes does an Aa individual produce?
choices: Every gamete carries both A and a
Half carry AA and half carry aa
Half carry A and half carry a
All carry A, because A is dominant
questions.explanation: By the law of segregation, the two alleles separate into different gametes, each gamete gets one allele, and the two types are equally common. A gamete never carries two alleles of the same gene. Dominance affects the phenotype, not which allele gets into a gamete.

questions.stem: Which pair of pea plants have the same phenotype but different genotypes? (Purple, P, is dominant to white, p.)
choices: PP and pp
Pp and pp
pp and pp
PP and Pp
questions.explanation: PP and Pp both have purple flowers because one P allele is enough. PP and pp, and Pp and pp, differ in phenotype (purple vs white). Two pp plants have the same genotype.

questions.stem: Which statement about dominant alleles is correct?
choices: A dominant allele is always the most common allele in a population
A dominant allele shows its effect even in a heterozygote
A dominant allele is always better for survival
A dominant allele is passed to offspring more often than a recessive one
questions.explanation: Dominant only describes how alleles interact in a heterozygote. It says nothing about frequency (the dominant allele for Huntington's disease is rare), benefit, or how often it is inherited: a heterozygote passes each allele with probability 1/2.

questions.stem: What event in meiosis is the physical basis of Mendel's law of segregation?
choices: Homologous chromosomes separating in anaphase I
DNA replicating during the S phase
Sister chromatids separating in mitosis
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I
questions.explanation: The two alleles of a gene sit on the two homologous chromosomes, and homologs go to opposite poles in anaphase I, so each gamete gets one allele. Replication copies alleles rather than separating them, mitosis doesn't make gametes, and crossing over swaps segments between homologs but doesn't separate the allele pair.

questions.stem: Mendel's F2 plants for stem length were 787 tall and 277 dwarf. What does this result suggest about the F1 plants that were crossed to produce them?
choices: They were TT × tt
Both were heterozygous, Tt × Tt
They were Tt × tt
They were TT × Tt
questions.explanation: 787/277 is about 2.84 : 1, close to the 3 : 1 expected from Tt × Tt. Tt × tt gives 1 : 1, TT × tt and TT × Tt give only tall offspring.

questions.stem: In the offspring of Pp × Pp, what fraction of the purple-flowered plants are heterozygous?
questions.explanation: Purple plants fill 3 of the 4 Punnett boxes (PP, Pp, Pp), and 2 of those 3 are Pp, so 2/3. The answer 1/2 is the fraction of all offspring that are Pp; here the white plants are excluded.

questions.stem: Two Aa parents have three children, all with the dominant phenotype. What is the probability that their fourth child has the recessive phenotype?
questions.explanation: Each fertilization is independent, so the earlier children don't change the odds: P(aa) = 1/4 for every child. Expecting the recessive child to be "due" is the gambler's fallacy; 1/256 is the chance that all four children are aa.

questions.stem: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white (b). A Bb guinea pig is crossed with a bb guinea pig, and 120 offspring are produced over several litters. About how many are expected to be white?
questions.explanation: Bb × bb gives 1/2 Bb (black) and 1/2 bb (white), so expect $\tfrac12 \times 120 = 60$ white. 30 uses 1/4 (as if it were Bb × Bb); 90 is the 3/4 dominant fraction of that cross.

questions.stem: Which gametes can an AaBb individual produce, assuming the two genes assort independently?
choices: Aa and Bb, each 1/2 of the gametes
Only AB and ab, each 1/2 of the gametes
AA, BB, aa and bb, each 1/4 of the gametes
AB, Ab, aB and ab, each 1/4 of the gametes
questions.explanation: Each gamete gets one allele of each gene. A or a (1/2 each) combines independently with B or b (1/2 each), giving four types at $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. Aa or AA would put two alleles of one gene in a gamete; only AB and ab would mean the genes are completely linked.

questions.stem: Round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) is dominant to green (y). In the cross RrYy × RrYy, what fraction of offspring have round, green seeds?
questions.explanation: Gene by gene: P(round) = 3/4 from Rr × Rr, P(green) = 1/4 from Yy × Yy. Product rule: $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{3}{16}$. 9/16 is round and yellow; 1/16 is wrinkled and green.

questions.stem: Mendel's RrYy × RrYy cross gave 315 round-yellow, 108 round-green, 101 wrinkled-yellow and 32 wrinkled-green seeds. Which conclusion do these data support?
choices: The two genes are always inherited together as a unit
The seed-shape and seed-color genes assort independently
The traits blend together in the offspring
Alleles of the seed-color gene do not segregate
questions.explanation: All four combinations appear, close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, including the new combinations round-green and wrinkled-yellow. If the genes traveled together, only the parental types would appear (3 : 1). The traits come back in pure form, so there is no blending, and each gene alone still shows 3 : 1, so segregation holds.

questions.stem: In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three unlinked genes), what is the probability of an aabbcc offspring?
questions.explanation: Each gene gives the homozygous recessive genotype with probability 1/4, and the genes are independent, so $\left(\tfrac14\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{64}$. 1/8 uses 1/2 per gene (the chance of one recessive allele from one parent).

questions.stem: An RrYy plant is test-crossed with an rryy plant. What phenotype ratio is expected in the offspring?
questions.explanation: RrYy makes RY, Ry, rY and ry gametes equally; rryy adds only ry. Each gamete type from the heterozygote therefore produces its own phenotype, in equal numbers: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is for two double heterozygotes.

questions.stem: What is the probability that an offspring of Aa × Aa is homozygous (either AA or aa)?
questions.explanation: AA and aa are mutually exclusive outcomes, so use the sum rule: $\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$. Multiplying them (1/16) is the product-rule mistake; "either … or" adds.

questions.stem: How many genetically different kinds of gametes can an individual with genotype AaBBCcDd produce, if all four genes are unlinked?
questions.explanation: Only heterozygous genes double the number of gamete types: A/a, C/c and D/d are heterozygous and BB always gives B, so $2^3 = 8$. 16 would treat BB as heterozygous.

questions.stem: Two parents are carriers (Aa) of a recessive condition. If they have two children, what is the probability that exactly one child has the condition?
questions.explanation: Affected then unaffected: $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac34 = \tfrac{3}{16}$. Unaffected then affected: also 3/16. These orders are mutually exclusive, so add: $\tfrac{6}{16} = \tfrac38$. Stopping at 3/16 counts only one order.

questions.stem: In the cross AaBbCc × aabbCc (unlinked genes, complete dominance), what fraction of offspring show the dominant phenotype for all three genes?
questions.explanation: Aa × aa: dominant phenotype 1/2. Bb × bb: 1/2. Cc × Cc: 3/4. Product: $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac34 = \tfrac{3}{16}$. 27/64 would be correct for AaBbCc × AaBbCc, not for this cross.

questions.stem: Which event in meiosis explains Mendel's law of independent assortment?
choices: Sister chromatids separate at anaphase II
DNA is copied before meiosis begins
Each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up at metaphase I independently of the other pairs
The cytoplasm divides at the end of telophase II
questions.explanation: Whether the chromosome with R goes to the same pole as the chromosome with Y or the one with y depends on how the two pairs happen to orient at metaphase I, and each pair orients at random. The other events occur in meiosis but don't determine which alleles of different genes end up together.

questions.stem: A test cross AaBb × aabb gives mostly AaBb and aabb offspring and only a few Aabb and aaBb offspring. What is the best explanation?
choices: Genes A and B are close together on the same chromosome
A and B show incomplete dominance
The genes assort independently
Nondisjunction occurred in every meiosis
questions.explanation: Independent assortment predicts 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. An excess of the parental combinations means the alleles A and B (and a and b) tend to stay together: the genes are linked. The rare recombinant offspring come from crossing over between them. Incomplete dominance changes phenotypes, not how alleles are packaged.

questions.stem: Round (R) is dominant to wrinkled and yellow (Y) is dominant to green. In the cross RrYy × Rryy, what fraction of offspring have round, yellow seeds?
questions.explanation: Rr × Rr gives round 3/4; Yy × yy gives yellow 1/2. Product: $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac38$. 9/16 assumes a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 cross, but one parent is yy.

questions.stem: Red snapdragons crossed with white snapdragons give all pink offspring. If two of the pink plants are crossed, what phenotype ratio is expected?
choices: 3 pink : 1 white
All pink
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
3 red : 1 white
questions.explanation: Pink is the heterozygote $C^RC^W$. Crossing two heterozygotes gives 1 $C^RC^R$ : 2 $C^RC^W$ : 1 $C^WC^W$, and with incomplete dominance each genotype has its own color. 3 : 1 would apply only if one allele were fully dominant; all pink is what blending would predict.

questions.stem: A red bull and a white cow produce a roan calf whose coat is a mixture of individual red hairs and individual white hairs. This is an example of
choices: codominance
incomplete dominance
epistasis
polygenic inheritance
questions.explanation: Both alleles are fully expressed side by side: each hair is pure red or pure white. Incomplete dominance would give hairs of an intermediate color. Epistasis involves two genes, and polygenic traits vary continuously.

questions.stem: A woman with type A blood and a man with type B blood have a child with type O blood. What are the parents' genotypes?
choices: Mother $I^AI^A$, father $I^BI^B$
Mother $I^Ai$, father $I^Bi$
Mother $I^Ai$, father $I^BI^B$
Mother $ii$, father $ii$
questions.explanation: A type O child is $ii$ and must have received $i$ from each parent, so both parents carry $i$: $I^Ai$ and $I^Bi$. Parents who are $ii$ would themselves be type O.

questions.stem: A parent with type AB blood ($I^AI^B$) and a parent with type O blood ($ii$) have children. Which blood types are possible among their children?
choices: AB and O only
A, B, AB and O
A, B and O
A and B only
questions.explanation: The AB parent gives $I^A$ or $I^B$; the O parent gives only $i$. Children are $I^Ai$ (type A) or $I^Bi$ (type B), each with probability 1/2. Neither AB (needs both $I^A$ and $I^B$) nor O (needs two $i$ alleles) is possible.

questions.stem: With the three ABO alleles $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$, how many different genotypes are possible?
questions.explanation: Three homozygotes ($I^AI^A$, $I^BI^B$, $ii$) plus three heterozygotes ($I^AI^B$, $I^Ai$, $I^Bi$) make 6. Four is the number of blood types (phenotypes), because $I^AI^A$ and $I^Ai$ both give type A and $I^BI^B$ and $I^Bi$ both give type B.

questions.stem: Why can type O red blood cells be transfused into a patient with type A blood?
choices: Type O blood contains no antibodies at all
Type O red cells carry the A antigen, which matches the patient
Type O red cells carry neither the A nor the B antigen, so the patient's anti-B antibodies have nothing to attack
The $i$ allele is dominant to $I^A$
questions.explanation: The danger in a transfusion is the patient's antibodies attacking antigens on donor red cells. A type A patient has anti-B antibodies, and type O cells have no A or B antigen. Type O plasma actually contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, and $i$ is recessive.

questions.stem: A child has type O blood and the mother has type A. Which man could NOT be the child's biological father, judging by ABO type alone?
choices: A man with type AB
A man with type A
A man with type B
A man with type O
questions.explanation: The child is $ii$ and needs an $i$ allele from the father. A type AB man is $I^AI^B$ and has no $i$ to give. Men with type A or B may be $I^Ai$ or $I^Bi$, and a type O man is $ii$. Blood type can exclude a man but never prove he is the father.

questions.stem: Human adult height varies continuously and forms a bell-shaped distribution. What is the best explanation?
choices: One gene with two alleles shows complete dominance
One gene with many alleles is codominant
Height is determined by the environment alone
Many genes each add a small effect, and the environment adds further variation
questions.explanation: Height is polygenic: many genes with small additive effects produce many genotype classes, and nutrition and health blur them into a smooth curve. A single gene with complete dominance would give two distinct classes.

questions.stem: In a model where three unlinked genes each have an additive allele (A, B, C), what fraction of the offspring of AaBbCc × AaBbCc carry exactly three additive alleles?
questions.explanation: The six allele positions each get an additive allele with probability 1/2, so the count follows the 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1 pattern out of 64. Exactly three: $\tfrac{20}{64} = \tfrac{5}{16}$. 1/64 is the fraction with all six (or none).

questions.stem: A single allele causes sickle-shaped red blood cells, anemia, episodes of pain and organ damage, and in carriers some resistance to malaria. One gene affecting many traits is called
choices: epistasis
codominance
polygenic inheritance
pleiotropy
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy means one gene influences several traits. Epistasis is one gene masking another gene; polygenic inheritance is the opposite situation, many genes affecting one trait.

questions.stem: In Labrador retrievers, B (black) is dominant to b (chocolate), but any dog that is ee is yellow regardless of its B gene. Two BbEe dogs are mated. What fraction of their puppies are expected to be yellow?
questions.explanation: A puppy is yellow whenever it is ee, which has probability 1/4 from Ee × Ee, whatever the B genotype. The full ratio is 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow. 3/16 is the chocolate fraction ($\tfrac14$ bb × $\tfrac34$ not ee).

questions.stem: Himalayan rabbits are white with dark ears, nose and paws. If a patch of white back fur is shaved and the skin kept cold with an ice pack, the fur grows back dark. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Cold temperatures cause a mutation in the fur-color gene
The pigment enzyme works only at low temperature, so the environment affects the phenotype
Dark fur is a polygenic trait
The dark allele is dominant only on the ears and paws
questions.explanation: The rabbit's genotype didn't change; the same genes produced dark fur where the skin was cooler. This shows an environmental effect on gene expression. A mutation would not appear reliably wherever cold is applied.

questions.stem: Why are X-linked recessive conditions such as hemophilia A much more common in males than in females?
choices: The Y chromosome carries a dominant allele that causes the condition
Males inherit their X chromosome from their father
Recessive alleles are dominant in males
Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
questions.explanation: A male has only one copy of each X-linked gene, so whatever allele it carries shows. A female needs a recessive allele on both X chromosomes. Males inherit their X from their mother, and the Y carries no allele for these genes.

questions.stem: A woman who is a carrier for hemophilia A ($X^HX^h$) and a man without hemophilia ($X^HY$) have a son. What is the probability that the son has hemophilia?
questions.explanation: A son gets Y from his father and one of his mother's X chromosomes, $X^H$ or $X^h$, with equal probability, so 1/2. The answer 1/4 is the probability that a child of unknown sex is an affected son.

questions.stem: A color-blind man ($X^bY$) and a woman who is homozygous for normal vision ($X^BX^B$) have children. Which describes their daughters?
choices: All are carriers with normal vision
All are color-blind
Half are color-blind and half are carriers
Half are carriers and half are $X^BX^B$
questions.explanation: Every daughter receives her father's only X, $X^b$, and an $X^B$ from her mother, so all are $X^BX^b$: normal vision, carriers. None can be color-blind, because the mother has no $X^b$ to give.

questions.stem: A man with an X-linked recessive condition has a son. Why can't the son inherit the condition from his father?
choices: The allele is recessive, so it is masked in all sons
A father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to every son
X-linked alleles are passed only to daughters by mothers
Sons inherit both sex chromosomes from their mother
questions.explanation: A child is male because he got his father's Y, so his single X came from his mother. The father's X goes to every daughter instead. Sons get only one sex chromosome from their mother, not both.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two parents who do not have a condition have a daughter who does. Which inheritance pattern fits?
choices: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Y-linked
questions.explanation: A dominant condition would require an affected parent. An X-linked recessive daughter needs an $X^a$ from her father, who would then be affected. Y-linked traits never appear in daughters. So both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive allele.

questions.stem: Two unaffected carrier parents (Aa × Aa) have a child with an autosomal recessive condition and also an unaffected son. What is the probability that this unaffected son is a carrier?
questions.explanation: The son is not aa, so only three Punnett boxes remain possible: AA, Aa, aA. Two of the three are carriers: 2/3. The value 1/2 is the carrier probability for a child whose phenotype is not yet known.

questions.stem: In a standard pedigree, what does a filled-in square represent?
choices: A female who has the trait
A male who is a carrier
A male who does not have the trait
A male who has the trait
questions.explanation: Squares are males and circles females; a filled symbol means the person has the trait. Carriers, when shown, are marked with a dot or a half-filled symbol, and an open square is an unaffected male.

questions.stem: Morgan crossed a white-eyed male fruit fly with a red-eyed female. The F1 were all red-eyed, and in the F2 every white-eyed fly was male. What did he conclude?
choices: The eye-color gene is on the X chromosome
White eyes are dominant in males
The eye-color gene is on the Y chromosome
Eye color is a polygenic trait
questions.explanation: F2 sons get their only X from their carrier mother, so half are white-eyed, while daughters all get the father's red-eye X. A Y-linked gene would pass from father to all sons and appear in the F1 males. The all-red F1 shows white is recessive.

questions.stem: A color-blind woman ($X^bX^b$) and a man with normal vision ($X^BY$) have a son. What is the probability that he is color-blind?
questions.explanation: A son's X comes from his mother, and every X she has carries $b$. So every son is $X^bY$ and color-blind. (Every daughter is an $X^BX^b$ carrier.)

questions.stem: In a family, two parents who both have a condition have a child who does not. Which inheritance pattern is consistent with this?
choices: Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Y-linked
Autosomal dominant
questions.explanation: Two affected parents can each be Aa for a dominant condition and have an aa child. For an autosomal recessive condition, two aa parents can only have aa children; for X-linked recessive, an affected mother and father give only affected children. A Y-linked trait can't affect the mother.

questions.stem: About 8% of men in a population are red-green color-blind. If the same fraction of X chromosomes carry the allele, about what percentage of women would you expect to be color-blind?
questions.explanation: A man is affected if his one X carries the allele (probability 0.08). A woman needs it on both X chromosomes: $0.08 \times 0.08 = 0.0064 = 0.64\%$. That is why the condition is much rarer in women.

questions.stem: How many autosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.explanation: A typical body cell has 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes (44) and one pair of sex chromosomes. 46 counts the sex chromosomes too; 22 is the number of autosomal pairs; 23 is the number in a gamete.

questions.stem: If nondisjunction of one chromosome pair occurs in meiosis I, what are the four gametes like?
choices: All four are normal
Two have an extra chromosome and two are missing one
Two are normal, one has an extra chromosome and one is missing one
All four have an extra chromosome
questions.explanation: In meiosis I both homologs go to one cell, so that cell's two products are n + 1 and the other cell's two products are n − 1. Two normal gametes plus one n + 1 and one n − 1 is the result of nondisjunction in meiosis II.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes are in the body cells of a person with Down syndrome caused by trisomy 21?
questions.explanation: Trisomy means three copies of one chromosome instead of two, so 46 + 1 = 47. 45 would be a monosomy (as in 45,X); 69 would be a whole extra set of chromosomes (triploidy).

questions.stem: A sperm that carries both an X and a Y chromosome, after nondisjunction in meiosis I, fertilizes a normal egg. What is the karyotype of the zygote?
choices: 47,XXY
47,XYY
46,XY
questions.explanation: The egg adds 23 chromosomes including an X; the sperm has 24 including X and Y. Total: 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome). 45,X comes from a gamete with no sex chromosome; 47,XYY would need two Y chromosomes from the father (nondisjunction in meiosis II).

questions.stem: Which condition could NOT be detected from a standard karyotype?
choices: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
Turner syndrome (45,X)
Cystic fibrosis, caused by a recessive allele of a single gene
A large deletion on chromosome 5
questions.explanation: A karyotype shows chromosome number and large structural changes. A cystic fibrosis allele is a small change within one gene that leaves the chromosome looking normal; it needs DNA testing.

questions.stem: A segment of chromosome 9 breaks off and becomes attached to chromosome 22. This structural change is
choices: a deletion
an inversion
a duplication
a translocation
questions.explanation: A translocation moves a segment to a non-homologous chromosome. A deletion loses a segment, an inversion flips one in place, and a duplication repeats one.

questions.stem: A chi-square test compares observed counts in four phenotype classes with a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 prediction. How many degrees of freedom are there?
questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom = number of categories − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3. Using the number of categories (4) is the common mistake; 15 is 16 − 1, the ratio total minus one.

questions.stem: A cross is expected to give 3 : 1. Of 120 offspring, 84 show the dominant trait and 36 the recessive trait. What is $\chi^2$?
questions.explanation: Expected: 90 and 30. $\chi^2 = \dfrac{(84-90)^2}{90} + \dfrac{(36-30)^2}{30} = 0.40 + 1.20 = 1.60$. Dividing by the observed counts instead gives 1.43; 0.40 is only the first term; 3.84 is the critical value, not the statistic.

questions.stem: A test cross expected to give 1 : 1 yields $\chi^2 = 5.2$. Using $p = 0.05$, what should you conclude?
choices: Fail to reject, because 5.2 is less than the critical value 5.99
Reject the 1 : 1 hypothesis, because 5.2 is greater than the critical value 3.84 for df = 1
The data prove the 1 : 1 hypothesis is true
Fail to reject, because $\chi^2$ is positive
questions.explanation: Two categories give df = 1, critical value 3.84. Since $5.2 \ge 3.84$, a deviation this large would happen by chance less than 5% of the time, so reject. 5.99 is the critical value for df = 2. A chi-square test never proves a hypothesis.

questions.stem: Why must a chi-square test use raw counts rather than percentages?
choices: Percentages can't be squared
Percentages always add to 100, which makes $\chi^2$ zero
The test depends on sample size, and percentages hide how many individuals were counted
Expected values can only be whole numbers
questions.explanation: A 55% : 45% split is unremarkable among 20 offspring but very unlikely by chance among 2000. Counts carry that sample-size information; percentages discard it. Expected counts can be non-integers (e.g. 312.75).

questions.stem: The risk of trisomy 21 rises with the age of the egg-producing parent. What is the main reason?
choices: Egg cells stay paused partway through meiosis I for years or decades, which raises the chance of nondisjunction
Older parents produce more eggs per cycle
Chromosome 21 is copied more often in older people
Sperm cells cannot undergo nondisjunction
questions.explanation: Human oocytes begin meiosis I before birth and pause until ovulation, so an egg released at 40 has been paused for about 40 years; errors in separating chromosomes become more likely. Nondisjunction also occurs in sperm formation, but it accounts for a smaller share of trisomy 21.

questions.stem: This picture follows Mendel's flower-color experiment. Name each numbered generation.

image.alt: Three rows of pea flowers joined by arrows. Row 1: a purple PP flower crossed with a white pp flower. Row 2, reached by crossing: four purple Pp flowers. Row 3, reached by self-pollination: three purple flowers (PP, Pp, Pp) and one white flower (pp).

choices: P generation
F1 generation
F2 generation
F3 generation
Test-cross offspring
questions.explanation: Row 1 is the parental (P) generation: two true-breeding plants, PP and pp. Their offspring are the first filial generation, F1, all Pp and purple. Letting the F1 self-pollinate gives the F2, with 3 purple : 1 white. No row is a test cross, which would need a cross with a homozygous recessive (pp) plant.

questions.stem: A pea plant with two identical alleles for a gene, such as PP, is ___ for that gene; a plant with two different alleles, Pp, is ___.
questions.explanation: "Homo-" means same and "hetero-" means different. PP and pp are homozygous; Pp is heterozygous. PP and Pp plants look alike (purple), which is why a genotype can't be read from the phenotype alone.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: A stretch of DNA that affects a trait
One version of a gene
The pair of alleles an individual carries
The trait you can observe
The cell formed when two gametes fuse
questions.explanation: A gene (such as the flower-color gene) comes in alleles (P and p). The genotype is the allele pair (PP, Pp or pp); the phenotype is what shows (purple or white). The cell formed by fertilization is a zygote, which isn't one of these terms.

questions.stem: Purple (P) is dominant to white (p). Which statements about the cross Pp × Pp are true? Select all that apply.
choices: About 3/4 of the offspring are expected to be purple
The expected genotype ratio is 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp
About half of the offspring are expected to be PP
Each gamete carries exactly one allele of the flower-color gene
questions.explanation: The Punnett square has four equally likely boxes, PP, Pp, Pp and pp: genotypes 1 : 2 : 1 and phenotypes 3 purple : 1 white. Every gamete carries one allele (the law of segregation). PP is only 1/4 of the offspring; half are Pp, not PP.

questions.stem: The offspring of a cross come out 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp. Type each parent's genotype, using P and p: ___ and ___.
questions.explanation: PP offspring need a P from each parent, and pp offspring need a p from each parent, so both parents carry both alleles: Pp × Pp. That cross gives exactly 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp. (Capital letters matter: P is the dominant allele and p the recessive one.)

questions.stem: The probability that two independent events both happen is found by multiplying their probabilities. This is called the ___ rule.
questions.explanation: The product rule: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$ for independent events. The sum rule is for "or" with mutually exclusive outcomes.

questions.stem: Put these events in order, from just before meiosis in an RrYy plant to its gametes.
choices: DNA replicates, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids
Homologous pairs line up at the metaphase plate, each pair oriented at random
Homologs separate in anaphase I
Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II
Four haploid cells form, each carrying one allele of each gene (RY, Ry, rY or ry)
questions.explanation: DNA is copied before meiosis begins (interphase). In metaphase I the R/r pair and the Y/y pair line up independently, which is the source of independent assortment. Anaphase I separates homologs, meiosis II separates sister chromatids, and the result is four haploid cells. Across many meioses, RY, Ry, rY and ry each make up 1/4.

questions.stem: In the cross RrYy × RrYy (round and yellow dominant, genes unlinked), match each phenotype to its probability.
questions.explanation: Gene by gene: round 3/4, wrinkled 1/4; yellow 3/4, green 1/4. Round and yellow $= \tfrac34 \times \tfrac34 = \tfrac{9}{16}$; round and green $= \tfrac34 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{3}{16}$; wrinkled and green $= \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{16}$. "Wrinkled, any color" ignores the color gene, so it is just $\tfrac14$ (equal to $\tfrac{3}{16} + \tfrac{1}{16}$).

questions.stem: Which of these calculations for the offspring of Aa × Aa are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: P(two children, both aa) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16
questions.explanation: AA and aa are mutually exclusive, so add: 1/2. Two children are independent, so multiply: 1/16. "Not aa" is the complement of aa: 3/4. The Aa calculation is wrong: Aa can form two ways (A from the mother and a from the father, or the reverse), so $P(\text{Aa}) = \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$, not $\tfrac14$.

questions.stem: A branch diagram is drawn for AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three unlinked genes, complete dominance), splitting each branch into "dominant" and "recessive" for each gene in turn. How many end branches (phenotype classes) does it have?
questions.explanation: Each gene doubles the number of branches (dominant or recessive phenotype): $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ phenotype classes, in a 27 : 9 : 9 : 9 : 3 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. 27 is the number of genotypes (3 per gene, $3^3$) and also the size of the largest class out of 64; 6 adds instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Each red blood cell carries the antigens shown by the key. Name the ABO blood type of each numbered cell.

image.alt: Four red blood cells. Cell 1 has both triangle and circle antigens on its surface, cell 2 has none, cell 3 has only triangles, and cell 4 has only circles. A key shows that triangles are A antigens and circles are B antigens.

choices: Type AB
Type O
Type A
Type B
questions.explanation: Blood type is named for the antigens on the red cells: A antigens only, type A (cell 3); B only, type B (cell 4); both, type AB (cell 1, from codominant $I^A$ and $I^B$); neither, type O (cell 2, genotype $ii$).

questions.stem: Match each example to the kind of inheritance it shows.
left: Red × white snapdragons give pink offspring
Roan cattle have separate red hairs and white hairs
A person with $I^AI^B$ has both A and B antigens
Adult height varies continuously in a bell curve
Any ee Labrador is yellow, whatever its B gene
choices: Incomplete dominance
Codominance
Polygenic inheritance
Epistasis
Sex linkage
questions.explanation: Pink is an intermediate heterozygote (incomplete dominance). Roan coats and AB blood show both alleles fully (codominance). Continuous variation comes from many genes with small effects (polygenic). The E gene masking the B gene is epistasis. None of these genes is on the X chromosome.

questions.stem: Using the ABO allele symbols, a person with type O blood has the genotype ___ (type the two lower-case letters).
questions.explanation: Type O needs two copies of the recessive $i$ allele, so the genotype is $ii$. Any $I^A$ or $I^B$ allele would add an A or B antigen.

questions.stem: Considering ABO type only, which donors could give red blood cells to a patient with type B blood? Select all that apply.
choices: A type O donor
A type B donor
A type A donor
A type AB donor
questions.explanation: A type B patient has anti-A antibodies in their plasma, which attack red cells carrying the A antigen. Type O cells (no A or B antigen) and type B cells (B antigen only) are safe. Type A and type AB cells carry the A antigen and would be attacked.

questions.stem: Cuttings from one hydrangea plant are planted in two gardens. In acidic soil they bloom blue; in more alkaline soil they bloom pink. What does this show?
choices: The two gardens selected plants with different flower-color alleles
Flower color in hydrangeas shows incomplete dominance
Soil pH causes mutations in the flower-color genes
Phenotype depends on the environment as well as the genotype
questions.explanation: Cuttings of one plant are genetically identical, so the different colors come from the environment acting on the same genotype. No selection or mutation happened between cuttings, and incomplete dominance is about heterozygotes, not about the same genotype in different conditions.

questions.stem: Name each numbered pedigree symbol or line.

image.alt: A row of five pedigree symbols: a circle with a dot in it, an open square, a filled circle, an open circle and a filled square. Below, a small family: a square and a circle joined by a horizontal line, with a line leading down to a son (filled square) and a daughter (open circle).

choices: Carrier female
Unaffected male
Affected female
Unaffected female
Affected male
Mating line joining two parents
Line to their children
questions.explanation: Squares are males and circles females; filled means affected, open means unaffected, and a dot marks a known carrier. Marker 6 sits on the horizontal line joining a man and a woman, which shows a mating; the line that drops from it leads to their children.

questions.stem: This pedigree shows a rare condition, so assume people who marry into the family don't carry the allele. Which inheritance pattern fits best?

image.alt: Three generations. Generation I: an affected man (I-1) and an unaffected woman (I-2). Generation II: their affected son II-2, who has children with unaffected II-1; an unaffected daughter II-3; and an affected daughter II-4, who has children with unaffected II-5. Generation III: II-1 and II-2 have an affected daughter and an unaffected son; II-4 and II-5 have an affected son and an unaffected daughter.

choices: Autosomal recessive
Autosomal dominant
X-linked recessive
Y-linked
questions.explanation: Every affected person has an affected parent, and the trait appears in every generation, in both sexes. Autosomal recessive would need each unaffected spouse to be a carrier, which is unlikely for a rare allele. X-linked recessive is ruled out because I-1 passes the condition to his son II-2 (fathers give sons a Y, not an X) and because an affected father with a non-carrier wife would have no affected children. Y-linked is ruled out by the affected daughters.

questions.stem: A son always receives his X chromosome from his ___.
questions.explanation: A son is XY: his Y must come from his father, so his only X comes from his mother. That is why an X-linked trait in a son traces back through his mother, and why fathers never pass X-linked alleles to sons.

questions.stem: This pedigree shows an X-linked recessive trait. Which people must carry at least one copy of the recessive allele? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Generation I: an affected man (I-1) and an unaffected woman (I-2). Generation II: their unaffected son II-1 and two carrier daughters, II-2 and II-3; II-3 has children with an unaffected man, II-4. Generation III: an affected son III-1, an unaffected daughter III-2 and an unaffected son III-3.

choices: II-1
II-2
III-2
questions.explanation: I-1 is affected, so he carries the allele on his X. Every daughter gets her father's only X, so II-2 must be a carrier. II-1 is an unaffected male: with only one X, any recessive allele would show, so he has none. III-2's mother is a carrier and her father is unaffected, so she has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier; she doesn't have to be one.

questions.stem: Match each inheritance pattern to a pedigree clue that points to it.
choices: Two unaffected parents have an affected daughter
Every affected person has an affected parent, and two affected parents have an unaffected child
Mostly affected males, with unaffected mothers, and never passed from father to son
Only females are ever affected
questions.explanation: An affected daughter of unaffected parents rules out dominance and X-linked recessive, leaving autosomal recessive. Two affected parents with an unaffected child means both are heterozygous for a dominant allele. Mostly affected males with carrier mothers and no father-to-son transmission is the X-linked recessive signature. No pattern in this lesson affects only females.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this replicated chromosome, as it appears in a karyotype.

image.alt: A replicated chromosome: two identical side-by-side strands joined at a narrow point, with a short section above the narrow point and a long section below. Dark stripes cross both strands. Brackets mark the upper section, the lower section and the pair of strands.

choices: Centromere
Band
Short arm (p)
Long arm (q)
Sister chromatids
Homologous chromosome
questions.explanation: The narrow point is the centromere, which joins the two sister chromatids (identical copies made in S phase). It divides the chromosome into a short arm, p, and a long arm, q. Dark stripes are stained bands, used to identify each chromosome. A homologous chromosome would be a second, separate chromosome, the matching one from the other parent.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a chi-square test in order.
choices: State the hypothesis and the ratio it predicts
Calculate the expected count in each category
Compute (O − E)²/E for each category and add them up
Compare chi-square with the critical value for df = categories − 1 and decide whether to reject
questions.explanation: The hypothesis comes first, because it fixes the expected counts. The expected counts are needed to compute $\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E$, and the finished $\chi^2$ is then compared with the critical value at $p = 0.05$ for df = categories − 1.

questions.stem: Having an abnormal number of one or more chromosomes, as in trisomy 21 or 45,X, is called ___.
questions.explanation: Aneuploidy means a number of chromosomes that isn't an exact multiple of the haploid set: one extra (trisomy) or one missing (monosomy). Whole extra sets are polyploidy instead.

questions.stem: Using the figure, which statements about nondisjunction are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Two diagrams following one chromosome pair through meiosis. Left, nondisjunction in meiosis I: the four gametes are n + 1, n + 1, n − 1 and n − 1. Right, nondisjunction in meiosis II in one of the two cells: the gametes are n + 1, n − 1, n and n.

choices: When nondisjunction happens in meiosis I, all four gametes are abnormal
When nondisjunction happens in meiosis II, half of the gametes can be normal
An n + 1 gamete fertilized by a normal gamete gives a trisomic zygote
Nondisjunction in meiosis II produces two n + 1 gametes
questions.explanation: In meiosis I both homologs go to one cell, so its two gametes are n + 1 and the other cell's two are n − 1. In meiosis II only one cell's chromatids fail to separate: one n + 1, one n − 1, and two normal gametes, so there is only one n + 1 gamete, not two. An n + 1 gamete plus a normal n gamete gives three copies of that chromosome, a trisomy.

questions.stem: Match each karyotype to the condition it describes.
choices: Down syndrome
Turner syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome
Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
Cri-du-chat syndrome
questions.explanation: +21 means an extra chromosome 21 (Down syndrome); 45,X is one X and no second sex chromosome (Turner); 47,XXY is an extra X in a male (Klinefelter); +18 is trisomy 18 (Edwards). Cri-du-chat is a deletion on chromosome 5, which changes structure rather than the number of chromosomes.

questions.stem: Fruit fly geneticists measuring linkage test-cross a heterozygous female, not a heterozygous male. Why?
choices: Male fruit flies have no crossing over in meiosis, so a heterozygous male would give no recombinant offspring
Males carry only one copy of every gene, so they cannot be heterozygous
Females produce more offspring, which is the only reason
Recombinant offspring of males do not survive
questions.explanation: In Drosophila, meiosis in males lacks crossing over, so a doubly heterozygous male passes on only his two parental chromosomes. Males do have two copies of autosomal genes (only X-linked genes are single-copy). Offspring numbers and survival are not the reason.

questions.stem: A dihybrid test cross gives 412 AaBb, 398 aabb, 96 Aabb and 94 aaBb offspring. What is the recombination frequency between A and B?
questions.explanation: The two large classes (AaBb, aabb) are parental; the two small ones are recombinant. $\dfrac{96 + 94}{1000} = 0.19$, or 19% (19 map units). 9.5% counts only one recombinant class; 23.5% divides by the parental total (810) instead of all offspring; 38% doubles the right answer.

questions.stem: Recombination frequencies among three linked genes are: A–B 12%, B–C 7%, A–C 19%. What is the gene order?
choices: The order can't be found without a three-point cross
C is in the middle: A–C–B
A is in the middle: B–A–C
B is in the middle: A–B–C
questions.explanation: The largest distance (A–C, 19) spans the two outer genes, so B is between them; check $12 + 7 = 19$. The order is A–B–C (equivalently C–B–A). The other orders would need A–C to be one of the smaller distances, and pairwise distances are enough to order three genes; a three-point cross only refines the distances.

questions.stem: Why does the recombination frequency between two genes on the same chromosome never meaningfully exceed 50%, however far apart they are?
choices: Genes more than 50 map units apart move to different chromosomes
Each crossover involves only two of the four chromatids, and multiple crossovers between distant genes randomize the alleles
Crossing over happens in only half of all meioses
Recombinant gametes are less likely than parental gametes to be used in fertilization
questions.explanation: Crossing over happens at the four-chromatid stage. Even if every meiosis has a crossover between the genes, only two of four chromatids are recombinant, and with several crossovers some swap the alleles back. The result approaches the 50% of independent assortment. Genes don't move between chromosomes; crossovers aren't limited to half of meioses; gametes aren't chosen by type.

questions.stem: In a three-point test cross, the parental classes are D E F and d e f, and the two rarest classes are D e F and d E f. Which gene is in the middle?
choices: D
F
It cannot be told without the map distances
E
questions.explanation: A double crossover swaps only the middle gene relative to the two outer genes. Comparing D E F with D e F, only E has changed, so E is in the middle (order D–E–F). The map distances aren't needed to find the order.

questions.stem: Genes A and B are 10 map units apart. A plant that is Ab / aB is test-crossed with ab / ab and produces 1000 offspring. About how many offspring are expected to be AaBb (from AB gametes)?
questions.explanation: In this plant the parental gametes are Ab and aB (repulsion). AB is a recombinant gamete: recombinants make up 10%, split equally between AB and ab, so AB is 5%, and $0.05 \times 1000 = 50$. 100 is all recombinants together; 450 is one parental class; 250 assumes no linkage.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say two genes are 25 map units apart?
choices: They are 25,000 base pairs apart
They are on chromosomes 25 positions apart in the karyotype
About 25% of gametes are recombinant for the two genes
They have a 25% chance of being on different chromosomes
questions.explanation: One map unit (centimorgan) is defined as 1% recombination, so 25 map units means about 25% recombinant gametes. Map units measure crossover frequency, not physical length, and have nothing to do with karyotype position.

questions.stem: In a three-point cross, 20 double-crossover offspring are expected if crossovers in the two intervals are independent, but only 12 are observed. What is the interference?
questions.explanation: Coefficient of coincidence = observed ÷ expected $= 12/20 = 0.6$. Interference $= 1 - 0.6 = 0.4$. 0.6 is the coefficient of coincidence itself; 1.67 divides the wrong way; 0.12 has no meaning here.

questions.stem: Two genes show a recombination frequency of 50% in a test cross. What can you conclude?
choices: They are certainly on different chromosomes
They are certainly on the same chromosome, very close together
The test cross must have been done wrong
They are either on different chromosomes or far apart on the same chromosome
questions.explanation: 50% recombination is what independent assortment gives, and genes far apart on one chromosome also approach 50% because of multiple crossovers. The test can't tell the two cases apart; mapping intermediate genes can. Close genes would show low recombination.

questions.stem: Three linked genes have these recombination frequencies: R–S 22%, S–T 9%, R–T 13%. On the map, which gene is at each numbered position?

image.alt: A horizontal chromosome with three numbered gene positions: position 1 at the left end, position 2 thirteen map units to its right, and position 3 nine map units beyond position 2.

choices: Gene R
Gene T
Gene S
questions.explanation: The largest frequency, R–S (22), spans the outer genes, so T is in the middle ($13 + 9 = 22$). The left interval is 13 units, which matches R–T, and the right interval is 9, matching T–S. So position 1 is R, position 2 is T and position 3 is S.

questions.stem: One map unit, a recombination frequency of 1%, is also called a ___.
questions.explanation: The centimorgan (cM) is named after Thomas Hunt Morgan, whose fly lab discovered linkage; his student Alfred Sturtevant built the first map.

questions.stem: Put the steps of analyzing a three-point test cross in order.
choices: Identify the parental classes (the two most common) and the double-crossover classes (the two rarest)
Find the middle gene by comparing the parental and double-crossover classes
Calculate each interval's distance, counting the double crossovers in both intervals
Compare observed and expected double crossovers to find the interference
questions.explanation: You need the parental and double-crossover classes to find the gene order; you need the order to know which single-crossover classes belong to which interval; and you need both interval distances to compute the expected number of double crossovers for the interference.

questions.stem: Which results show that genes A and B are linked? Select all that apply.
choices: In an AaBb × aabb test cross, two classes far outnumber the other two
The recombination frequency between A and B is 8%
An AaBb × aabb test cross gives about 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
An AaBb × AaBb cross gives about 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
questions.explanation: Linkage shows up as an excess of parental classes, which means a recombination frequency well below 50% (8% here). A 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 test cross and a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 F2 are what independent assortment predicts, so they give no evidence of linkage.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: Offspring with an allele combination found on one of the heterozygous parent's chromosomes
Offspring with a new allele combination made by crossing over
A recombination frequency of 1%
One crossover making another nearby less likely
A physical length of 1,000 base pairs
questions.explanation: Parental and recombinant types are defined by allele combinations relative to the heterozygote's chromosomes. A map unit is 1% recombination, a measure of crossover frequency rather than a physical length. Interference is the shortfall of double crossovers below the product-rule expectation.

questions.stem: Two true-breeding white-flowered lines are crossed. The F1 are all purple, and the F2 has about 9 purple : 7 white. What is the best explanation?
choices: Two genes are involved, and a plant needs a dominant allele at both to make purple pigment
One gene with incomplete dominance controls flower color
Purple is a new mutation that arose in the F1
One gene is involved, and white is dominant to purple
questions.explanation: A ratio in sixteenths points to two genes and a doubly heterozygous F1. Only C_P_ (9/16) is purple; the other 7/16 lack one of the two enzymes. Each white parent supplied the working allele the other lacked, which is why the F1 is purple (complementation). One gene can't give 9 : 7, and a mutation wouldn't appear in every F1 plant.

questions.stem: In summer squash, W_ fruit are white; ww fruit are yellow if Y_ and green if yy. A WwYy plant is test-crossed with a wwyy plant. What phenotype ratio is expected?
choices: 12 white : 3 yellow : 1 green
2 white : 1 yellow : 1 green
1 white : 1 yellow : 1 green
1 white : 2 yellow : 1 green
questions.explanation: Ww × ww gives W_ (white) 1/2 and ww 1/2. Among the ww half, Yy × yy gives yellow 1/2 and green 1/2, so yellow 1/4 and green 1/4. Result: 1/2 white : 1/4 yellow : 1/4 green = 2 : 1 : 1. The 12 : 3 : 1 ratio belongs to WwYy × WwYy, not a test cross.

questions.stem: An F2 of shepherd's purse has 151 plants with triangular seed capsules and 9 with oval capsules. Which explanation fits these data?
choices: One gene, with triangular dominant (3 : 1)
Two complementary genes (9 : 7)
Two duplicate genes, where a dominant allele at either gene gives a triangular capsule (15 : 1)
Two genes with recessive epistasis (9 : 3 : 4)
questions.explanation: For 15 : 1 the expected counts out of 160 are 150 and 10, very close to 151 and 9 ($\chi^2 \approx 0.11$). A 3 : 1 ratio predicts 120 : 40, far off; 9 : 7 predicts 90 : 70; 9 : 3 : 4 would need three classes.

questions.stem: Two yellow mice ($A^YA$) are mated repeatedly and have 90 surviving pups. $A^YA^Y$ embryos die before birth. About how many of the 90 pups are expected to be yellow?
questions.explanation: The cross gives 1/4 $A^YA^Y$ (dies) : 1/2 $A^YA$ (yellow) : 1/4 $AA$ (agouti). Among survivors, yellow is $\dfrac{1/2}{3/4} = \dfrac23$, and $\tfrac23 \times 90 = 60$. 67.5 uses the 3 : 1 ratio, forgetting the lethal class; 30 is the agouti count.

questions.stem: Two true-breeding fruit fly lines both have the same recessive eye-color mutation phenotype. When they are crossed, all the F1 have that mutant eye color. What does this complementation test show?
choices: The two mutations are in the same gene
The two mutations are in different genes
The mutations are dominant
The mutations are linked but in different genes
questions.explanation: If the mutations were in different genes, each parent would supply a working copy of the gene the other lacks, and the F1 would be normal. A mutant F1 means neither parent has a working copy of that gene, so both mutations are in the same gene. The parents are true-breeding for a recessive phenotype, so the mutations aren't dominant.

questions.stem: Two true-breeding wheat lines differ in kernel color. In the F2, about 1 in 64 kernels is as pale as the pale parent. Assuming equal, additive genes, how many genes differ between the lines?
questions.explanation: Each F2 extreme needs homozygous recessive at every gene: $\left(\tfrac14\right)^n = \tfrac{1}{64}$, so $n = 3$. (6 is the number of alleles involved, $2n$; 64 is the denominator, not the number of genes.)

questions.stem: In one population, the heritability of adult height is estimated at 0.8. Which statement is correct?
choices: 80% of each person's height is caused by genes
Height in this population cannot be changed by diet
About 80% of the variation in height among people in this population is associated with genetic differences
Any height difference between this population and another must be genetic
questions.explanation: Heritability is a ratio of variances in a particular population: $V_G/V_P$. It says nothing about the share of one person's height due to genes, doesn't mean a trait is fixed (average heights rose with better nutrition), and can't explain differences between populations, which may be environmental.

questions.stem: A flock has a mean egg mass of 50 g. Hens averaging 58 g are chosen as parents. If the narrow-sense heritability is 0.25, what mean egg mass is predicted for their daughters?
questions.explanation: Selection differential $S = 58 - 50 = 8$ g. Response $R = h^2 S = 0.25 \times 8 = 2$ g, so the daughters' mean is about $50 + 2 = 52$ g. 58 g would require $h^2 = 1$; 54 g uses $h^2 = 0.5$.

questions.stem: Genetically uniform inbred lines of a plant have a variance in height of 3 cm². A genetically varied population grown in the same conditions has a variance of 12 cm². What is the broad-sense heritability of height in that population?
questions.explanation: In the uniform lines all variance is environmental, so $V_E = 3$. Then $V_G = 12 - 3 = 9$ and $H^2 = 9/12 = 0.75$. 0.25 is $V_E/V_P$; 0.33 is $V_E/V_G$; 4 is $V_P/V_E$, and heritability can't exceed 1.

questions.stem: Each numbered row shows the 16 F2 outcomes of AaBb × AaBb, with same-colored boxes having the same phenotype. The top row (9 : 3 : 3 : 1) is for comparison. Name the kind of gene interaction in each numbered row.

image.alt: A reference row of 16 boxes in four colors grouped 9 A_B_, 3 A_bb, 3 aaB_ and 1 aabb, labeled 9:3:3:1 no interaction. Below are four numbered rows. Row 1: A_B_ and A_bb share one color, aaB_ a second and aabb a third. Row 2: A_B_ one color, A_bb a second, and aaB_ and aabb share a third. Row 3: all boxes share one color except aabb. Row 4: all A_B_ boxes share one color, and all the other boxes share a second.

choices: Dominant epistasis (12 : 3 : 1)
Recessive epistasis (9 : 3 : 4)
Duplicate dominant genes (15 : 1)
