Complementary genes (9 : 7)
questions.explanation: Row 1 merges A_B_ with A_bb (12), so one dominant allele, A, hides the B gene: dominant epistasis. Row 2 merges aaB_ with aabb (4), so aa hides the B gene: recessive epistasis. Row 3 has 15 alike and only aabb different: one dominant allele at either gene is enough. Row 4 has only A_B_ (9) different from the other 7: both dominant alleles are needed, as with complementary genes.

questions.stem: Match each F2 ratio to the example that produces it.
choices: Mouse coat color: agouti, black and albino
Sweet pea flowers from two different white lines
Summer squash fruit: white, yellow and green
Shepherd's purse seed capsules: triangular and oval
Snapdragon flowers: red, pink and white
questions.explanation: cc albino mice hide the agouti gene (9 : 3 : 4). Sweet pea purple needs C_P_ (9 : 7). Dominant W makes squash white (12 : 3 : 1). Either dominant allele makes a triangular capsule (15 : 1). Snapdragon color is one gene with incomplete dominance, 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.stem: The range of phenotypes that a single genotype produces across different environments is called its ___.
questions.explanation: A norm of reaction can be drawn as a line of phenotype against environment for each genotype, as for the cloned yarrow plants grown at different elevations. Lines that cross show a genotype-by-environment interaction.

questions.stem: Which statements about heritability are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: It describes a particular population in a particular environment
A trait with high heritability can still change when the environment changes
A heritability of 0.8 for height means 80% of each person's height comes from genes
Making the environment more uniform tends to raise heritability
questions.explanation: $H^2 = V_G/V_P$ is measured in one population and environment. A more uniform environment shrinks $V_E$, so the ratio rises. High heritability doesn't stop environmental change from shifting the trait (heights rose with nutrition). Heritability is about variation among people, not the makeup of one person's trait.

questions.stem: In the sweet pea pigment pathway, put the substances in the order they are made.
choices: Colorless precursor
Colorless intermediate, made by the enzyme from gene C
Purple pigment, made by the enzyme from gene P
questions.explanation: The enzyme encoded by C converts the precursor to the intermediate, and the enzyme encoded by P converts the intermediate to purple pigment. A cc plant stops at the precursor and a pp plant at the intermediate; both are white, which is why only C_P_ plants are purple.

questions.stem: In the Avery, MacLeod and McCarty experiment, extract from heat-killed S bacteria was treated with different enzymes before being mixed with live R bacteria. Which result identified DNA as the transforming principle?
choices: Transformation stopped after protease treatment but still happened after DNase treatment.
Transformation happened with every enzyme treatment.
Transformation still happened after protease or RNase treatment, but not after DNase treatment.
Transformation stopped after every enzyme treatment.
questions.explanation: Destroying a molecule that is needed should stop transformation. Only DNase (which destroys DNA) stopped it, so DNA is required; protein and RNA are not. If transformation stopped with every enzyme, or with none, no single molecule could be singled out.

questions.stem: Hershey and Chase labeled one batch of bacteriophages with radioactive sulfur and another with radioactive phosphorus. Why these two elements?
choices: Sulfur is found in DNA but not protein, and phosphorus is found in protein but not DNA.
Sulfur is found in protein but not DNA, and phosphorus is found in DNA but hardly at all in protein.
Both elements are found only in DNA, so they label it twice.
Both elements are found only in the bacterial cell, not in the virus.
questions.explanation: The point was to label the two candidate molecules separately. Proteins contain sulfur (in some amino acids) and almost no phosphorus; DNA has phosphorus in every nucleotide's phosphate group and no sulfur. Swapping them reverses the chemistry.

questions.stem: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, after infection and blending, where was most of the radioactive phosphorus found, and what did that show?
choices: In the empty phage coats, showing that protein carries the genetic instructions
Inside the bacteria, showing that phage protein enters the cell
Inside the bacteria, showing that phage DNA enters the cell and carries the genetic instructions
Spread evenly between the coats and the bacteria, showing that both molecules are genetic material
questions.explanation: Phosphorus labels DNA. It went into the bacteria, while the sulfur-labeled protein stayed outside with the coats. The material that enters and directs new phages is DNA.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 18% cytosine. What percentage is adenine?
questions.explanation: C pairs with G, so G = 18% and G + C = 36%. That leaves 100 − 36 = 64% for A + T, and A = T, so A = 32%. 18% wrongly assumes A equals C; 64% forgets to split A + T in half; 82% is just 100 − 18.

questions.stem: One strand of a DNA molecule is 5′-GGATCA-3′. What is the complementary strand, written with its ends labeled?
choices: 3′-CCTAGT-5′
5′-CCTAGT-3′
3′-GGATCA-5′
3′-CCUAGU-5′
questions.explanation: Pair each base (G–C, A–T): C C T A G T. The strands are antiparallel, so the partner written under the original runs 3′ to 5′. Labeling it 5′ to 3′ ignores antiparallel orientation; repeating the original bases is not complementary; U appears only in RNA.

questions.stem: Why is the DNA double helix the same width (about 2 nm) along its whole length?
choices: Every base pair joins a two-ring purine with a one-ring pyrimidine.
Every base pair joins two purines.
Hydrogen bonds pull the backbones to a fixed distance regardless of the bases.
The sugar–phosphate backbone is on the inside of the helix.
questions.explanation: A–T and G–C each pair a double-ring base (A or G) with a single-ring base (T or C), so every rung is the same length. Two purines would make a wider rung. The backbones are on the outside, and hydrogen bonds alone don't fix the width.

questions.stem: Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria on heavy nitrogen (15N), then moved them to light nitrogen (14N). After one generation all the DNA formed a single band of intermediate density. Which model did this result rule out?
choices: Semiconservative replication
Dispersive replication
Conservative replication
No model; the result fits all three
questions.explanation: Conservative replication would keep the original heavy helix intact and make a separate all-light helix: two bands, heavy and light. A single hybrid band rules it out. Both semiconservative and dispersive replication predict one intermediate band after one generation; the second generation (half hybrid, half light) ruled out dispersive.

questions.stem: In the Meselson–Stahl experiment, what fraction of the DNA is hybrid (one heavy, one light strand) after 3 generations in light nitrogen?
questions.explanation: After $n$ generations there are $2^n$ helices from each original one, and the two original heavy strands sit in exactly two of them. With $n = 3$: $2/8 = 1/4$ hybrid, $3/4$ light. 1/2 is the answer after 2 generations; 3/4 is the light fraction.

questions.stem: Why is the lagging strand made in short Okazaki fragments?
choices: The lagging strand is copied by RNA polymerase, which makes only short pieces.
Helicase can unwind only short stretches of the lagging strand.
The lagging strand is built 3′ to 5′, which is slower.
DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only to a 3′ end, so the strand that runs the other way must be built in pieces away from the fork.
questions.explanation: All new DNA grows 5′ to 3′. The two template strands are antiparallel, so on one of them the new strand must grow away from the fork; it is made in fragments as the fork opens and later joined by ligase. No strand is built 3′ to 5′, and DNA polymerase, not RNA polymerase, does the copying.

questions.stem: Match the enzyme to its job in replication: which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments into one continuous strand?
choices: Helicase
Primase
DNA polymerase
DNA ligase
questions.explanation: Ligase seals the gaps in the backbone between fragments. Helicase unwinds the helix, primase makes the RNA primers, and DNA polymerase adds the nucleotides.

questions.stem: A student says Chargaff's rules mean that a single DNA strand must have equal amounts of A and T. Why is this wrong?
choices: The rules apply only to RNA.
The rules describe double-stranded DNA: each A on one strand is matched by a T on the other strand, not on the same strand.
The rules say A equals G, not A equals T.
The rules apply only to human DNA.
questions.explanation: A = T holds for the double helix because of base pairing between strands. One strand can be rich in A as long as its partner is equally rich in T. Chargaff found the rules in many species; they don't apply to RNA, which is usually single-stranded.

questions.stem: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACGGT-5′. What mRNA is transcribed from it?
choices: 5′-AUGCCA-3′
5′-ATGCCA-3′
5′-UACGGU-3′
5′-ACCGUA-3′
questions.explanation: Pair each template base with an RNA base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, T→A, giving AUGCCA. ATGCCA is the DNA complement (RNA uses U, not T). UACGGU copies the template with U for T. ACCGUA reverses the correct sequence.

questions.stem: Where does RNA polymerase first bind to begin transcribing a gene?
choices: The promoter
The start codon
The operator
The ribosome
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase binds the promoter, a DNA sequence just upstream of the gene. The start codon (AUG) is where translation starts, on the mRNA. The operator is a repressor-binding site in bacterial operons.

questions.stem: A eukaryotic pre-mRNA has four exons and three introns. What happens to it before it leaves the nucleus?
choices: The introns are removed, the exons are joined, and a cap and a tail are added.
The exons are removed and the introns are joined.
Nothing; mRNA is translated inside the nucleus.
The introns are translated into a separate protein.
questions.explanation: Introns are cut out and exons are spliced together (exons are the parts that are expressed). The 5′ cap and 3′ tail protect the mRNA. Translation happens in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: Translate the mRNA 5′-CCAUGGCUUGGUAGCA-3′ using the codon table, starting at the first AUG.
choices: Pro–Trp–Leu–Gly–Ser
Met–Ala–Trp–Stop–Gln
Tyr–Arg–Thr
Met–Ala–Trp
questions.explanation: The first AUG follows CC. Read from there: AUG (Met), GCU (Ala), UGG (Trp), UAG (Stop). The stop codon ends translation and adds nothing, so the chain is Met–Ala–Trp. Reading from the first base gives a different frame; Tyr–Arg–Thr comes from looking up the complementary triplets instead of the codons.

questions.stem: Why must codons be at least three bases long?
choices: Two-base codons give only 16 combinations, too few for 20 amino acids; three bases give 64.
Ribosomes are exactly three bases wide.
There are three kinds of RNA.
Each amino acid contains three nitrogen atoms.
questions.explanation: With four bases, $4^2 = 16$ two-letter words can't name 20 amino acids, but $4^3 = 64$ three-letter words can, with extras (which is why the code is redundant).

questions.stem: A tRNA has the anticodon 3′-UAC-5′. Which codon does it pair with, and which amino acid does it carry?
choices: AUG, methionine
UAC, tyrosine
AUG, tyrosine
CAU, histidine
questions.explanation: The anticodon pairs with the codon: U–A, A–U, C–G gives 5′-AUG-3′, which codes for Met. Looking up UAC in the table is the classic error (the table lists codons, not anticodons). CAU is the anticodon read 5′ to 3′ and then looked up as if it were a codon.

questions.stem: The mRNA coding region of a gene, from the start codon through the stop codon, is 900 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
questions.explanation: 900 ÷ 3 = 300 codons, one of which is the stop codon, which codes for no amino acid. So 299 amino acids. 300 counts the stop codon; 900 treats each nucleotide as an amino acid.

questions.stem: What ends translation when a ribosome reaches a stop codon?
choices: A tRNA carrying a stop amino acid pairs with the codon.
RNA polymerase falls off the mRNA.
The ribosome runs out of ATP.
A release factor protein binds the stop codon and frees the polypeptide.
questions.explanation: No tRNA matches UAA, UAG or UGA. A release factor binds instead, the chain is released, and the ribosome comes apart. RNA polymerase works in transcription, not translation.

questions.stem: A human insulin gene placed in bacteria makes working human insulin. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?
choices: It is redundant.
It is nearly universal.
It has three stop codons.
It is read in overlapping triplets.
questions.explanation: Bacteria read codons the same way human cells do, so a human gene's codons specify the same amino acids. Redundancy (several codons per amino acid) is true but doesn't explain it. The code is not read in overlapping triplets.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares RNA with DNA?
choices: RNA contains deoxyribose and thymine and is usually double-stranded.
RNA contains ribose and thymine and is usually double-stranded.
RNA contains ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded.
RNA contains deoxyribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded.
questions.explanation: RNA's sugar is ribose (DNA's is deoxyribose), uracil replaces thymine, and most RNA molecules are a single strand.

questions.stem: Which molecule actually catalyzes the peptide bonds between amino acids in a ribosome?
choices: mRNA
tRNA
rRNA
DNA polymerase
questions.explanation: The core of the ribosome is ribosomal RNA, and the rRNA itself forms peptide bonds. mRNA carries the code and tRNA delivers amino acids; DNA polymerase copies DNA.

questions.stem: In the lac operon of E. coli, what happens when lactose is present?
choices: Lactose binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.
Lactose binds the promoter and attracts the repressor.
The repressor binds lactose and stays on the operator more tightly.
Lactose binds the repressor, which changes shape and releases the operator, so the genes are transcribed.
questions.explanation: The repressor normally sits on the operator and blocks transcription. A form of lactose binds the repressor, changing its shape so it lets go of the DNA. Lactose never binds the DNA itself.

questions.stem: A mutant E. coli strain makes a repressor that cannot bind to the operator. How are its lac genes expressed?
choices: Off, whether or not lactose is present
On, whether or not lactose is present
On only when lactose is present, as normal
On only when lactose is absent
questions.explanation: With no working repressor on the operator, nothing blocks RNA polymerase, so transcription runs all the time. A repressor that cannot release (for example, one that can't bind lactose) would instead keep the genes off.

questions.stem: A nerve cell and a skin cell from the same person make very different proteins. What is the best explanation?
choices: They contain different genes.
Nerve cells have lost the genes for skin proteins.
They express different genes from the same DNA, controlled by different transcription factors.
Skin cells have extra chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Nearly all body cells carry the same genome. Cell types differ in which genes are switched on, set largely by combinations of transcription factors and by how tightly DNA is packed.

questions.stem: Which describes an epigenetic change?
choices: A base substitution changes a codon.
A chromosome segment is deleted.
A plasmid carrying a new gene enters a bacterium.
Methyl groups added to DNA silence a gene, and the pattern is copied when the cell divides.
questions.explanation: Epigenetic changes alter gene activity without changing the DNA sequence, through tags such as DNA methylation or histone modification that can be passed to daughter cells. The other choices all change the DNA sequence or add new DNA.

questions.stem: A codon in an mRNA changes from GAA to GAG. What type of mutation is this?
choices: Missense
Silent
Nonsense
Frameshift
questions.explanation: GAA and GAG both code for glutamic acid (Glu), so the protein is unchanged: silent. A missense mutation would change the amino acid, a nonsense mutation would create a stop codon, and a frameshift needs an insertion or deletion.

questions.stem: The mRNA 5′-AUG GCA UGG AAA UAA-3′ codes for Met–Ala–Trp–Lys. A mutation changes UGG to UGA. What is the result?
choices: A nonsense mutation: the protein is Met–Ala only.
A missense mutation: Trp is replaced by Arg.
A silent mutation: the protein is unchanged.
A frameshift: every amino acid after Ala changes.
questions.explanation: UGA is a stop codon, so translation ends after Ala and the protein is cut short: a nonsense mutation. One base was substituted, not inserted or deleted, so the frame is unchanged.

questions.stem: One base is deleted near the start of a gene's coding region. Why is this usually more harmful than a single-base substitution?
choices: It always creates a stop codon at the site of the deletion.
It removes exactly one amino acid.
It changes the DNA in every cell of the body.
It shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it and often creating an early stop codon.
questions.explanation: Codons are read in fixed groups of three from AUG, so losing one base regroups every later base. A substitution affects at most one codon. Removing exactly one amino acid requires deleting three bases.

questions.stem: The most common cystic fibrosis mutation deletes three bases from the gene. What effect does this have on the reading frame?
choices: It shifts the frame, changing every amino acid after the deletion.
It changes one amino acid to a stop codon.
None; one amino acid is missing but the rest of the sequence is read in the normal frame.
It doubles the length of the protein.
questions.explanation: Three bases are one codon, so the frame is kept. The protein lacks one phenylalanine but is otherwise normal in sequence (though it misfolds). Only insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three cause frameshifts.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a skin cell on a man's arm after years of sun exposure. Can it be passed to his children?
choices: Yes, because all mutations are inherited.
No, because it is a somatic mutation, not in a cell that makes sperm.
Yes, but only to his sons.
No, because ultraviolet light cannot cause mutations.
questions.explanation: Only germline mutations (in cells that make eggs or sperm) reach the next generation. A somatic mutation is passed only to that cell's descendants in the body, though it may contribute to skin cancer. UV light is a well-known mutagen.

questions.stem: Sickle cell disease results from codon 6 of a hemoglobin gene changing from GAG to GUG. Using the codon table, what kind of mutation is this?
choices: Silent: both codons code for Glu
Missense: Glu is replaced by Val
Nonsense: GUG is a stop codon
Frameshift: a base was inserted
questions.explanation: GAG codes for Glu and GUG for Val, so one amino acid changes: missense. GUG is not a stop codon, and the change is a substitution (one base swapped), not an insertion.

questions.stem: A PCR reaction starts with 10 copies of a target sequence. Assuming perfect doubling, how many copies are present after 10 cycles?
questions.explanation: $N = N_0 \times 2^n = 10 \times 2^{10} = 10 \times 1024 = 10{,}240$. 200 uses $N_0 \times 2n$ (adding instead of doubling); 1,024 forgets the starting 10 copies; 100 is $10 \times 10$.

questions.stem: Why does PCR use a DNA polymerase from bacteria that live in hot springs?
choices: Hot-spring polymerase copies RNA instead of DNA.
It works only at room temperature, which keeps the primers attached.
Each cycle heats the mixture to about 95 °C to separate the strands, which would destroy most enzymes.
It needs no primers.
questions.explanation: The denaturing step near 95 °C would ruin an ordinary enzyme every cycle. Taq polymerase survives it, so it can be added once. It still needs primers and copies DNA.

questions.stem: Put the three temperature steps of one PCR cycle in order.
choices: Anneal primers, denature, extend
Extend, denature, anneal primers
Denature, extend, anneal primers
Denature (about 95 °C), anneal primers (about 50–65 °C), extend (about 72 °C)
questions.explanation: The strands must first separate (denature) so the primers can bind (anneal) to single strands; only then can the polymerase extend from the primers.

questions.stem: DNA fragments of 300, 1,200 and 5,000 base pairs are run on the same gel. Which travels farthest from the well, and toward which electrode?
choices: The 5,000 bp fragment, toward the positive electrode
The 300 bp fragment, toward the negative electrode
The 300 bp fragment, toward the positive electrode
The 5,000 bp fragment, toward the negative electrode
questions.explanation: DNA's phosphate backbone is negatively charged, so it moves toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments slip through the gel more easily and travel farthest.

questions.stem: On a gel, ladder bands of 2,000 bp and 1,000 bp are 44 mm and 50 mm from the wells. An unknown band is at 47 mm. Which estimate is best?
choices: Exactly 1,500 bp
About 2,500 bp
About 1,400 bp
About 700 bp
questions.explanation: The band lies between the 1,000 and 2,000 bp bands, so its size is between them. Distance is linear in the logarithm of size, so halfway in distance is the geometric middle, $\sqrt{1000 \times 2000} \approx 1{,}414$ bp, not the arithmetic middle of 1,500. 2,500 and 700 lie outside the bracketing bands.

questions.stem: A linear DNA molecule 8,000 bp long has restriction sites at positions 2,000 and 5,000. What fragment sizes are produced?
questions.explanation: Two cuts in a linear molecule make three pieces: 0 to 2,000 (2,000 bp), 2,000 to 5,000 (3,000 bp), and 5,000 to 8,000 (3,000 bp). They add up to 8,000. Listing the cut positions as sizes is the usual error; two pieces would come from a circle.

questions.stem: To make human insulin in bacteria, why are the plasmid and the insulin gene cut with the same restriction enzyme?
choices: So the bacteria will be killed by the antibiotic
So the insulin gene is copied by PCR
So the plasmid becomes linear and stays that way
So their sticky ends are complementary and can pair before ligase seals them
questions.explanation: The same enzyme leaves matching single-stranded tails on both pieces. They base-pair, and DNA ligase joins the backbones to make recombinant DNA. The antibiotic step selects bacteria that took up a plasmid; it is meant to kill those that didn't.

questions.stem: Bacteria are mixed with recombinant plasmids carrying an antibiotic-resistance gene and then grown on a plate containing that antibiotic. What grows?
choices: Only bacteria that did not take up a plasmid
Only bacteria that took up a plasmid
All the bacteria
No bacteria
questions.explanation: The resistance gene travels on the plasmid, so only bacteria carrying a plasmid survive the antibiotic. This step selects the transformed cells from the many that took up nothing.

questions.stem: At one STR region, crime-scene DNA has alleles with 8 and 11 repeats. Suspect 1 has 8 and 11; suspect 2 has 8 and 10. What can be concluded from this region alone?
choices: Suspect 1 is definitely the source.
Suspect 2 is excluded; suspect 1 is not excluded but is not identified by one region.
Both suspects are excluded.
Neither suspect can be excluded.
questions.explanation: Suspect 2 has a 10-repeat allele that is not in the evidence, so suspect 2 cannot be the source. Suspect 1 matches, but many people share any one pair of alleles; labs compare about 20 regions before calling a match.

questions.stem: How does CRISPR-Cas9 find the gene it cuts?
choices: A guide RNA designed to match the target sequence base-pairs with it.
Cas9 recognizes a fixed six-base palindrome, like a restriction enzyme.
It cuts at random and the right cuts are selected later.
It binds the gene's promoter by recognizing RNA polymerase.
questions.explanation: The guide RNA is the targeting part: change its sequence and Cas9 cuts a different gene. A restriction enzyme, by contrast, always cuts the same fixed site.

questions.stem: This is the untwisted section of DNA from the lesson, with its labels removed. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A double helix beside an untwisted ladder of four base pairs (A–T, G–C, T–A, C–G). Each side of the ladder alternates circles and pentagons, rectangles for the bases reach toward the middle, and the bases meet across dashed lines. 5′ and 3′ ends are marked.

choices: Phosphate group
Deoxyribose sugar
Nitrogen base
Hydrogen bonds
Ribose sugar
Peptide bond
questions.explanation: 1: the circles in the backbone are phosphate groups. 2: the pentagons are the five-carbon sugar deoxyribose (ribose is the sugar in RNA). 3: the rectangles are the nitrogen bases, here adenine. 4: the dashed lines between paired bases are hydrogen bonds, three for this G–C pair. Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins, not nucleotides.

questions.stem: In double-stranded DNA, adenine always pairs with ___ and guanine always pairs with ___.
questions.explanation: Each base pair is one purine with one pyrimidine: A–T (two hydrogen bonds) and G–C (three hydrogen bonds). Uracil replaces thymine only in RNA.

questions.stem: Put these events at a replication fork in the order they happen for one Okazaki fragment.
choices: Helicase unwinds the double helix
Primase lays down a short RNA primer
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the primer's 3′ end
The RNA primer is replaced with DNA
DNA ligase seals the gap between fragments
questions.explanation: The strands must be separated first. Polymerase can't start a strand from nothing, so a primer comes next; polymerase extends it 5′ → 3′. Later the RNA primer is swapped for DNA, and ligase joins the finished fragment to its neighbor.

questions.stem: Which statements describe the lagging strand? Select all that apply.
choices: It is made as a series of Okazaki fragments.
It needs many RNA primers, one for each fragment.
It is built in the 3′ → 5′ direction.
It is built continuously toward the replication fork.
questions.explanation: The lagging strand is built in pieces (Okazaki fragments), each started from its own primer. Like every new strand it grows 5′ → 3′; that rule is exactly why it must be made in fragments working away from the fork. The strand built continuously toward the fork is the leading strand.

questions.stem: Match each experiment to what it showed.
choices: Something from dead S bacteria permanently changed live R bacteria
Only destroying DNA stopped transformation
Phage DNA, not protein, enters the bacterium
Each new DNA helix keeps one old strand
In DNA, A equals T and G equals C
questions.explanation: Griffith discovered transformation without knowing its cause; Avery's enzyme tests pinned it on DNA; Hershey and Chase's ³²P and ³⁵S labels showed DNA enters the cell; Meselson and Stahl's density bands showed semiconservative replication. The leftover statement is Chargaff's rule.

questions.stem: The picture shows translation in progress. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A large oval above and a smaller oval below clamp around a strand with boxed triplets reading AUG, UUU, GGC, AAA, UGA. Two adapter molecules stand on the strand, one carrying a chain of Met and Phe and one carrying Gly, each with three letters at its base. A third, empty adapter drifts away on the left.

choices: Ribosome
mRNA
tRNA
Anticodon
RNA polymerase
Promoter
questions.explanation: 1: the two-part structure clamped around the message is the ribosome (this marker is on its large subunit). 2: the strand of codons is the mRNA. 3: the adapters that carry amino acids are tRNAs. 4: the three bases at the bottom of a tRNA, pairing with a codon, are its anticodon. RNA polymerase and promoters belong to transcription.

questions.stem: A tRNA has the anticodon 3′-GGU-5′. The mRNA codon it pairs with is 5′-___-3′.
questions.explanation: Pair each anticodon base with its RNA partner, keeping the strands antiparallel: G–C, G–C, U–A gives the codon 5′-CCA-3′ (which codes for Pro). Writing CCT would use DNA's T, and ACC reads the codon backwards.

questions.stem: Put the steps in making a protein from a eukaryotic gene in order.
choices: RNA polymerase binds the promoter
The gene is transcribed into pre-mRNA
The RNA is capped, tailed and spliced
The mRNA leaves the nucleus
A ribosome finds the AUG start codon
tRNAs deliver amino acids and peptide bonds form
A release factor binds the stop codon and the chain is released
questions.explanation: Transcription (binding, then elongation) and processing happen in the nucleus. The finished mRNA moves to the cytoplasm, where translation starts at AUG, elongates codon by codon, and ends when a release factor recognizes the stop codon.

questions.stem: Which features are found in RNA but not in DNA? Select all that apply.
choices: The base uracil
The sugar ribose
Usually a single strand
A sugar–phosphate backbone
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, has ribose instead of deoxyribose, and is usually single-stranded. Both nucleic acids have a sugar–phosphate backbone, so that one is not a difference.

questions.stem: Match each kind of RNA to its job in protein synthesis.
choices: Carries the gene's codons from DNA to the ribosome
Brings a specific amino acid and pairs with a codon
Forms the ribosome's core and joins amino acids
Unwinds DNA at the replication fork
Seals gaps between Okazaki fragments
questions.explanation: mRNA is the message, tRNA is the adapter with an anticodon, and rRNA is the ribosome's structural and catalytic core. Unwinding DNA is helicase's job and sealing fragments is ligase's; both are proteins.

questions.stem: The picture shows the lac operon when no lactose is present, with labels removed. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A strand of DNA with a separate gene box on the far left, then a short box, a second short box, and three long gene boxes. An oval protein sits above the first short box, and a second, arch-shaped protein sits on the second short box.

choices: Promoter
Operator
Repressor
RNA polymerase
Gene for a lactose-using enzyme
Enhancer
Ribosome
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase (4) binds the promoter (1). The repressor (3) sits on the operator (2), which overlaps the start of transcription, so the polymerase can't move into the genes (5). Enhancers are eukaryotic control regions, and ribosomes translate mRNA rather than binding DNA.

questions.stem: In the lac operon, lactose turns the genes on by binding the ___, which then lets go of the ___.
questions.explanation: Lactose (as allolactose) binds the repressor and changes its shape, so it releases the operator and RNA polymerase can transcribe the genes. Lactose does not bind the DNA itself.

questions.stem: Match each change in an mRNA's coding region to its type of mutation. Use the codon table.
choices: Silent
Nonsense
Missense
Frameshift
In-frame deletion
questions.explanation: UAU and UAC both code for Tyr (silent). UGG (Trp) becoming UGA (stop) cuts the protein short (nonsense). AAA (Lys) becoming AGA (Arg) changes one amino acid (missense). Losing one base shifts every later codon (frameshift). An in-frame deletion would remove a multiple of three bases.

questions.stem: Which are ways that eukaryotic cells control which genes are expressed? Select all that apply.
choices: Transcription factors binding enhancers
Packing DNA tightly around histones, helped by methyl tags
MicroRNAs that block translation of an mRNA
Rewriting the gene's DNA sequence differently in each cell type
questions.explanation: Transcription factors, chromatin packing with epigenetic tags, and microRNAs are all real control points. Cell types differ in which genes they express, not in their DNA sequence, so rewriting genes is not how cells specialize.

questions.stem: Lactose becomes available to E. coli that has no glucose. Put the events in order.
choices: Lactose enters the cell
Lactose binds the repressor
The repressor changes shape and leaves the operator
RNA polymerase transcribes the lac genes
The enzymes break down the lactose
With lactose gone, the repressor binds the operator again
questions.explanation: Lactose must reach the repressor before the repressor can release the operator; only then is transcription possible. The enzymes made use up the lactose, and the free repressor rebinds, switching the genes off: negative feedback.

questions.stem: The picture shows a gel with its labels removed. The first lane is a ladder. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A rectangular gel between a dark bar at the top and a red bar at the bottom. Four lanes each begin at a small rectangular slot near the top. The first lane has eight evenly spaced bands; the other lanes have two bands each.

choices: Well
Negative electrode
Positive electrode
Longest fragment in the ladder
Shortest fragment in the ladder
Primer
Promoter
questions.explanation: Samples are loaded into wells (1) at the end nearest the negative electrode (2). DNA is negatively charged, so it moves away from there toward the positive electrode (3). Long fragments move slowest and stay nearest the wells (4); the shortest travel farthest (5).

questions.stem: A PCR tube starts with 3 copies of a target sequence. Assuming perfect doubling, after 5 cycles there are ___ copies.
questions.explanation: $N = N_0 \times 2^n = 3 \times 2^5 = 3 \times 32 = 96$. Using $2n$ instead of $2^n$ would give 30, the usual mistake.

questions.stem: Put the steps for making a protein such as human insulin in bacteria in order.
choices: Cut the plasmid and the gene with the same restriction enzyme
Mix them so their sticky ends pair
Seal the joints with DNA ligase
Put the recombinant plasmids into bacteria
Grow the bacteria on the antibiotic to keep only those with a plasmid
Grow the selected bacteria in large tanks and collect the protein
questions.explanation: Matching sticky ends come from cutting both with the same enzyme; they pair and ligase seals them. The plasmids are then put into bacteria, the antibiotic selects cells that took one up, and those cells are grown to make the protein.

questions.stem: Which must be in a PCR tube to copy a target sequence? Select all that apply.
choices: Template DNA containing the target
Two primers matching the ends of the target
A heat-resistant DNA polymerase
Free DNA nucleotides
A restriction enzyme
Ribosomes
questions.explanation: PCR needs the template, primers to start each new strand, a polymerase that survives 95 °C (such as Taq), and nucleotides to build with. Restriction enzymes cut DNA and ribosomes make proteins; neither is part of PCR.

questions.stem: Match each tool to its job.
choices: Cuts DNA at one specific short sequence
Joins DNA fragments together
Sorts DNA fragments by size
Makes many copies of a chosen stretch of DNA
Cuts a sequence chosen by a guide RNA
Reads mRNA codons to build a protein
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes cut fixed sites, ligase seals, gels separate by size, PCR copies, and Cas9 cuts wherever its guide RNA matches. Reading codons to build a protein is the ribosome's job.

questions.stem: Tryptophan is plentiful in an E. coli cell. What happens at the trp operon?
choices: Tryptophan binds the operator directly and blocks RNA polymerase.
Tryptophan pulls the repressor off the operator, so the genes are transcribed.
Tryptophan binds the repressor, which can then bind the operator and block transcription.
Tryptophan binds CAP, which activates the trp genes.
questions.explanation: Tryptophan is a corepressor: the trp repressor is inactive alone and binds the operator only with tryptophan attached. That shuts off the genes for making more tryptophan. Pulling a repressor off the operator is how an inducer works (lac), and CAP is part of lac control, not trp.

questions.stem: Which match of pathway and operon type is expected, and why?
choices: A pathway that breaks down a sugar is repressible, because the sugar shuts it off.
A pathway that breaks down a sugar is inducible, because its enzymes are needed only when the sugar is present.
A pathway that builds an amino acid is inducible, because the amino acid turns it on.
A pathway that builds an amino acid is always on, because amino acids are always needed.
questions.explanation: Breakdown (catabolic) pathways should run when their food is around, so the food acts as inducer (lac). Building (anabolic) pathways should stop when their product is plentiful, so the product acts as corepressor (trp). Running a pathway nonstop wastes energy.

questions.stem: E. coli is grown with both glucose and lactose available. Which describes the lac operon?
choices: Repressor off the operator, CAP–cAMP bound: high transcription
Repressor on the operator, CAP–cAMP not bound: no transcription
Repressor on the operator, CAP–cAMP bound: low transcription
Repressor off the operator, CAP–cAMP not bound: low transcription
questions.explanation: Lactose releases the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP can't bind and boost the promoter. The operon is only weakly transcribed. High transcription needs lactose present and glucose absent.

questions.stem: A partial diploid has the genotype $I^S O^+ Z^+$ / $I^+ O^C Z^+$. With no glucose, when is β-galactosidase made?
choices: Both with and without lactose
Only when lactose is present
Never
Only when lactose is absent
questions.explanation: The $I^S$ repressor can't bind inducer, so it stays on any normal operator: the first copy is off for good. But no repressor can bind $O^C$, so the second copy, which has a working $Z$, is transcribed all the time. Enzyme is made with and without lactose. Answering never forgets that $O^C$ is immune to every repressor.

questions.stem: A reporter assay tests DNA upstream of a muscle gene in muscle cells (relative light output): −4,000 to 0: 80; −2,500 to 0: 82; −1,500 to 0: 79; −500 to 0: 6; core promoter only (−100 to 0): 5. Where is the element needed for high expression in muscle?
choices: Between −4,000 and −2,500
Between −1,500 and −500
Between −2,500 and −1,500
In the core promoter, −100 to 0
questions.explanation: Activity stays high until the −1,500 to −500 piece is removed, then drops to about the core promoter's basal level (79 → 6). Removing the farther pieces changed nothing. The core promoter gives only basal activity (5), so it isn't the source of the high expression.

questions.stem: A 300-base-pair DNA piece raises transcription of a reporter about 30-fold whether it is placed 5,000 bases upstream, flipped in reverse orientation, or placed downstream of the gene. What is it most likely to be?
choices: A promoter
An operator
An enhancer
An intron splice site
questions.explanation: Working at a distance, in either orientation and on either side of the gene is the signature of an enhancer. A promoter must sit at the start of the gene in the right orientation; operators are bacterial repressor sites next to the promoter; splice sites act on RNA, not on how much is transcribed.

questions.stem: Gene X is transcribed only when activators P and Q are both bound at its enhancer. Cell type 1 makes P and R, type 2 makes P and Q, and type 3 makes Q and R. Where is gene X on?
choices: In type 2 only
In types 1 and 2
In types 2 and 3
In all three types
questions.explanation: Only type 2 has both required activators. Types 1 and 3 each lack one of them. This is combinatorial control: the same few factors in different combinations switch different gene sets on in different cell types.

questions.stem: How is a cell's DNA methylation pattern passed on when it divides?
choices: DNA polymerase builds the new strand with methylated cytosines wherever the template has them.
The methyl groups are copied into the mRNA and then back into the DNA.
All methylation is erased at each division and added back at random.
After replication, each CpG site is methylated only on the old strand, and a maintenance enzyme methylates the new strand to match.
questions.explanation: Because CpG pairs with CpG on the other strand, both strands carry the mark. Replication leaves half-methylated sites, which the maintenance enzyme recognizes and completes. Polymerase uses ordinary nucleotides, information doesn't flow from RNA back to DNA this way, and random re-marking couldn't keep cell types stable.

questions.stem: Cells are treated with a drug that blocks histone deacetylases, the enzymes that remove acetyl groups from histones. What is the most likely effect on a gene silenced by tightly packed chromatin?
choices: Its histones lose more acetyl groups and the chromatin packs tighter.
The gene's DNA sequence changes.
The gene's promoter becomes more heavily methylated.
Its histones stay acetylated, the chromatin loosens, and the gene may become active.
questions.explanation: Blocking removal leaves acetyl groups on, which weakens the histones' grip on DNA and attracts activators, so silenced genes can turn on. Packing tighter is the opposite effect. The drug changes chromatin, not the base sequence, and it doesn't add DNA methyl groups.

questions.stem: A mutation destroys the site in an mRNA's 3′ untranslated region that pairs with a microRNA's seed. What happens to the protein the mRNA encodes?
choices: Its amino acid sequence changes.
Its level rises, because the microRNA no longer reduces translation and stability of the mRNA.
Its level falls, because the microRNA can no longer help ribosomes bind.
Nothing changes, because microRNAs act on DNA rather than mRNA.
questions.explanation: The microRNA was turning this mRNA down; without the pairing site the mRNA escapes, so more protein is made. The 3′ untranslated region isn't translated, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged. MicroRNAs pair with mRNAs, not DNA, and they reduce translation rather than help it.

questions.stem: Which are examples of epigenetic regulation? Select all that apply.
choices: One X chromosome being silenced in each cell of a female mammal, with the same X silent in the cell's descendants
Only the father's copy of the IGF2 gene being expressed
A nonsense mutation that shortens a protein
A promoter methylated in liver cells and kept silent in their daughter cells
questions.explanation: X inactivation, imprinting and inherited promoter methylation all change gene activity through cell divisions without changing the DNA sequence. A nonsense mutation is a change in the sequence itself, so it is genetic, not epigenetic.

questions.stem: In lac operon partial diploids, which of these act in trans, so that they can affect the operon on the other DNA molecule? Select all that apply.
choices: The lac repressor protein
The operator
The promoter
The CAP protein
questions.explanation: Proteins diffuse, so the repressor and CAP can bind either copy of the operon. The operator and promoter are DNA sites that control only the genes beside them on the same molecule (cis-acting).

questions.stem: Match each molecule to its role in gene regulation.
choices: Inducer that inactivates the lac repressor
Corepressor that activates its own repressor
Signal of low glucose that lets CAP bind DNA
Protein complex linking activators to RNA polymerase II
Cuts microRNA hairpins in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Allolactose turns lac on by releasing the repressor; tryptophan turns trp off by activating its repressor; cAMP rises when glucose is low and switches on CAP; Mediator bridges enhancer-bound activators and the polymerase. Cutting microRNA hairpins in the cytoplasm is Dicer's job.

questions.stem: A gene has three clusters of mutually exclusive exons, with 4, 6 and 5 alternatives. Every mRNA uses exactly one exon from each cluster. The number of different mRNAs possible is ___.
questions.explanation: Independent choices multiply: $4 \times 6 \times 5 = 120$. Adding them (15) would count each exon, not each combination.

questions.stem: The picture shows how a distant control region turns on a eukaryotic gene. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A DNA molecule bent into a loop. A box on the upper arm has a protein hanging from it; below that protein is a large rounded complex, which rests on an oval protein sitting on a box on the lower arm, next to a long gene box. A smaller protein sits beside the oval. An arrow under the gene points right.

choices: Enhancer
Activator
Mediator
RNA polymerase II
Promoter
Operator
Repressor
questions.explanation: The activator (2) binds the enhancer (1), far along the DNA. The DNA loops so the activator touches Mediator (3), which contacts RNA polymerase II (4) sitting with the general transcription factors at the promoter (5). Operators and the lac-style repressor belong to bacterial operons.

questions.stem: Put the steps by which a microRNA silences a target gene in order.
choices: The microRNA gene is transcribed into a long RNA that folds into a hairpin
Drosha cuts out a short hairpin, which is exported from the nucleus
Dicer cuts the hairpin into a double-stranded RNA about 22 bases long
One strand is loaded into an Argonaute protein
The seed region pairs with a site in the target mRNA's 3′ untranslated region
Translation of the target falls and the mRNA is broken down faster
questions.explanation: The microRNA is made like other RNA, trimmed twice (Drosha in the nucleus, Dicer in the cytoplasm), loaded as a single strand into Argonaute, and then guided by its seed to target mRNAs, which are translated less and decay faster.

questions.stem: Why does adding a dideoxynucleotide (ddNTP) stop DNA synthesis in Sanger sequencing?
choices: It lacks the 3′-OH group needed to attach the next nucleotide.
It lacks a nitrogen base, so it can't pair with the template.
It is too large to fit in DNA polymerase.
It always pairs with the wrong base, so polymerase removes it.
questions.explanation: Polymerase joins each new nucleotide to the 3′-OH of the last one. A ddNTP has its base, so it is added normally, but it has no 3′-OH, so nothing can follow it.

questions.stem: A Sanger run uses a 20-base primer. The fragments and their colored terminal bases are: 23 T, 21 G, 24 A, 22 C, 25 C. What is the template strand, written 5′ to 3′?
choices: 5′-GCTAC-3′
5′-GTAGC-3′
5′-CGATG-3′
5′-CATCG-3′
questions.explanation: Sorted by length (21 to 25) the terminal bases spell the new strand 5′-GCTAC-3′. The template is its antiparallel complement, 3′-CGATG-5′, which reads 5′-GTAGC-3′. GCTAC is the new strand itself, CGATG is the complement written with the wrong ends, and CATCG is the new strand reversed.

questions.stem: A 4.6-million-base bacterial genome is sequenced with 2 million reads, each 150 bases long. What is the average coverage?
choices: About 6.5×
About 650×
About 65×
About 0.65×
questions.explanation: $C = \dfrac{N \times L}{G} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^6 \times 150}{4.6 \times 10^6} \approx 65$. The other choices are off by powers of ten, usually from dropping the millions in only one place.

questions.stem: Why are genomes sequenced to about 30× coverage instead of 1×?
choices: At 1× every base is read exactly once, which takes too long.
Higher coverage makes each read longer.
The genome is copied 30 times in each cell, so 30 reads are needed per base.
At 1× random reads leave about 37% of bases unread, and each base is read only once, so errors and heterozygous sites can't be checked.
questions.explanation: Reads land at random, so at an average of 1× about $e^{-1} \approx 37\%$ of bases get no read at all, and the rest are read once with no check. At 30× almost nothing is missed and each base is seen many times. Coverage doesn't change read length, and cells hold two copies of each chromosome, not 30.

questions.stem: A chromosome region contains a 12,000-base sequence repeated four times in a row. Why are long reads better than 150-base reads for sequencing it?
choices: Long reads are more accurate per base than short reads.
Short reads can't read DNA rich in A and T.
A long read can span a whole repeat copy plus unique DNA on either side, so the copies can be placed and counted.
Long reads need no DNA polymerase or other enzymes.
questions.explanation: Short reads from inside a repeat look identical wherever they came from, so the assembly can't tell how many copies there are or where each read belongs. Long reads anchor in unique sequence. Long reads are not more accurate per base; their advantage is length.

questions.stem: Two sequences are aligned over 50 positions. There are 3 mismatches and 2 gap positions; every other position is identical. What is the percent identity?
questions.explanation: Identical positions: $50 - 3 - 2 = 45$, and $45 / 50 = 90\%$. 94% subtracts only the mismatches (47 of 50), 96% subtracts only the gaps (48 of 50), and 10% is the fraction that differs.

questions.stem: A guide RNA perfectly matches a 20-base site in a gene, but the site is not followed by an NGG sequence. What does the common Cas9 do there?
choices: It cuts both strands as usual.
It cuts only the strand that pairs with the guide.
It cuts the guide RNA instead of the DNA.
It doesn't cut, because it must first find a PAM next to the target.
questions.explanation: Cas9 opens DNA only next to a PAM (5′-NGG-3′ for the common Cas9), and only then tests the guide match. Without a PAM it moves on, which is also how bacteria avoid cutting the matching sequences stored in their own CRISPR arrays.

questions.stem: A researcher wants Cas9 to change one specific base in a gene to a chosen new base. What else must be supplied?
choices: Nothing; end joining will insert the chosen base
A repair template carrying the new base, for homology-directed repair
A second PAM on the other strand
A restriction enzyme to trim the cut ends
questions.explanation: Cas9 only cuts. End joining glues the ends back, often with random small insertions or deletions, which is useful for knocking a gene out, not for a chosen change. A precise change needs a template the cell can copy.

questions.stem: Casgevy, approved in 2023, treats sickle cell disease by editing a patient's blood stem cells outside the body. What does the edit do?
choices: It breaks an enhancer of BCL11A, so the cells' red-cell descendants make fetal hemoglobin again.
It replaces the sickle allele with the normal allele in every cell of the body.
It inserts a new hemoglobin gene into the patient's eggs or sperm.
It deletes the beta-globin gene entirely.
questions.explanation: BCL11A switches off fetal hemoglobin after birth. Disrupting its red-cell enhancer leaves fetal hemoglobin on, which makes up for the faulty adult form. Only the treated blood stem cells are changed, not every cell and not eggs or sperm, so the change isn't inherited.

questions.stem: Which of these genetic changes could be passed on to a patient's children?
choices: Editing blood stem cells outside the body and returning them
Delivering a working gene to cells of the retina with a virus
Editing an early embryo before it is implanted
Silencing a liver gene with a small-RNA drug
questions.explanation: Edits in an early embryo reach every cell, including future eggs or sperm, so they are germline changes. The other three change only somatic cells of the patient, and a small-RNA drug changes no DNA at all.

questions.stem: Which statements about the human genome are supported by genome sequencing? Select all that apply.
choices: About 1.5% of it codes for protein.
It has roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.
Two unrelated people differ at about half of their bases.
It has far more genes than any other animal.
questions.explanation: Only about 1.5% codes for protein, in about 20,000 genes, about as many as a roundworm. Unrelated people differ at about 1 base in 1,000 (0.1%), not half.

questions.stem: Match each method to its description.
choices: Fragments stopped by colored terminators; reads about 1,000 bases
Billions of reads about 150 bases long, read in parallel
Single long molecules read by changes in an electric current
Lines up two sequences to count matches, mismatches and gaps
Copies one stretch of DNA by repeated heating and cooling
questions.explanation: Sanger uses chain-terminating ddNTPs; short-read machines read clusters in parallel; nanopores read single molecules by current; alignment is a computer comparison. Copying a stretch by temperature cycles is PCR.

questions.stem: A 5,000,000-base genome is sequenced with 2,000,000 reads, each 150 bases long. The average coverage is ___×.
The commonly used Cas9 cuts only next to the PAM sequence 5′-___-3′, where N stands for any base.
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9, the usual editing enzyme, needs 5′-NGG-3′ just past the 20-base target on the non-target strand. Other Cas proteins recognize different PAMs.

questions.stem: The picture shows Cas9 bound to its target. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A large oval protein holds a stretch of DNA whose two strands are pulled apart. A red RNA strand pairs with the lower DNA strand and then loops inside the protein. A small box sits on the upper strand just past the paired region, and a dashed line with arrowheads crosses both strands a short distance from that box.

choices: Cas9
PAM
Cut site
Guide RNA
Target DNA strand
Primer
Promoter
questions.explanation: Cas9 (1) holds everything. It first recognizes the PAM (2), then the guide RNA (4) pairs with the target DNA strand (5). Both strands are cut (3) a few bases from the PAM. Primers belong to PCR and sequencing, and promoters to transcription.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a Cas9 edit in order.
choices: Cas9 binds a guide RNA
The complex scans the DNA for a PAM
At a PAM, Cas9 unwinds the neighboring DNA
The guide RNA pairs with the target strand
Cas9 cuts both DNA strands near the PAM
The cell repairs the break, creating the edit
questions.explanation: Cas9 needs its guide first; it then checks for a PAM, opens the DNA beside it and tests the guide match. A full match triggers both cuts, and the cell's repair (end joining or template repair) makes the actual change.

questions.stem: A bone sample contains 1/16 of the carbon-14 found in living tissue. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. About how old is the bone?
choices: 91,680 years
22,920 years
45,840 years
11,460 years
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{1}{16} = \left(\tfrac12\right)^4$, so 4 half-lives have passed: $4 \times 5{,}730 = 22{,}920$ years. 91,680 multiplies by 16 instead of using 4 half-lives; 45,840 uses 8 half-lives (taking 1/16 as 16 ÷ 2); 11,460 is 2 half-lives.

questions.stem: Why can't carbon-14 be used to date a 70-million-year-old dinosaur fossil?
choices: Dinosaurs did not contain carbon.
After so many half-lives, essentially no carbon-14 would be left to measure.
Carbon-14 decays faster in older rocks.
Carbon-14 is only found in volcanic rock.
questions.explanation: 70 million years is over 12,000 half-lives of carbon-14, so the amount left would be immeasurably small; carbon-14 works to about 50,000 years. Dinosaur fossils are dated with long-lived isotopes in nearby volcanic layers. Decay rates don't depend on the age of the rock.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of a human, a bat, a whale and a cat have the same set of bones arranged in the same pattern, though they are used for different tasks. These are
choices: analogous structures, evidence of a common ancestor
homologous structures, evidence of a common ancestor
vestigial structures with no function
analogous structures that evolved separately
questions.explanation: Same underlying structure, different jobs: that is homology, explained by inheritance from a shared ancestor. Analogous structures do similar jobs with different structures. These limbs are fully functional, so they are not vestigial.

questions.stem: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing both allow flight, but one is a modified forelimb with bones and the other is a thin outgrowth of the body wall. What are they an example of?
choices: Analogous structures produced by convergent evolution
Homologous structures inherited from a winged ancestor
Vestigial structures
Transitional fossils
questions.explanation: Similar function but different structure and origin means analogous. The common ancestor of birds and insects had no wings; flight evolved separately in each line.

questions.stem: Some whales have small hip bones embedded in their bodies, not attached to any legs. What is the best description?
choices: Vestigial structures inherited from four-legged ancestors
Analogous structures
Structures that the whale grew because it needed them
Evidence that whales are fish
questions.explanation: Reduced remnants of structures that were functional in ancestors are vestigial. Fossil whales show a series from four-legged land mammals to fully aquatic forms, consistent with these bones being leftovers.

questions.stem: Before 2004, fish fossils were known from rocks about 385 million years old and four-legged animals from rocks about 365 million years old. Where were researchers most likely to find a fish–tetrapod transitional fossil?
choices: In deep-ocean rocks about 500 million years old
In any rock younger than 300 million years
In shallow freshwater rocks about 375 million years old
In rocks older than 400 million years
questions.explanation: A transition should lie between the ages of the two groups and in the environment where early tetrapods lived. That prediction led to Tiktaalik, found in about 375-million-year-old rocks on Ellesmere Island. Rocks much older or younger would be the wrong time.

questions.stem: Cytochrome c differs from the human version by 0 amino acids in chimpanzees, 13 in chickens and 21 in tuna. Which conclusion do these data support?
choices: Tuna evolved from chickens.
Humans share a more recent common ancestor with chickens than with tuna.
Chimpanzees and humans are the same species.
Cytochrome c has not changed since the first cells.
questions.explanation: Fewer differences mean less time since two lines split. Chickens differ by fewer amino acids than tuna, so the human–chicken split is more recent. Identical cytochrome c doesn't make two species the same (they differ in many other genes), and no living species evolved from another living species.

questions.stem: Species on the Galápagos Islands most closely resemble species from which place?
choices: Islands with a similar climate on the other side of the world
The nearby South American mainland
Africa
Europe, where Darwin lived
questions.explanation: Biogeography shows island species resemble those on the nearest mainland, the source of their ancestors, not species in similar climates far away. That pattern makes sense if species descend from colonists.

questions.stem: A volcanic ash layer contains 1/4 of its original potassium-40 (half-life 1.25 billion years). A fossil lies in the rock layer directly below the ash. What can be said about the fossil's age?
choices: It is at least 2.5 billion years old.
It is at most 2.5 billion years old.
It is exactly 1.25 billion years old.
It is about 5 billion years old.
questions.explanation: 1/4 remaining means 2 half-lives: $2 \times 1.25 = 2.5$ billion years. Lower layers are older, so the fossil is at least that old. 1.25 billion is one half-life (1/2 remaining); 5 billion uses 4 half-lives.

questions.stem: Which statement about humans and chimpanzees is accurate?
choices: Humans evolved from modern chimpanzees.
They share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 8 million years ago.
Chimpanzees evolved from humans.
They have no ancestors in common.
questions.explanation: Both are living species that descend from a shared ancestor; neither evolved from the other. Both lines have been evolving for the same length of time since the split.

questions.stem: Why is the near-universal genetic code considered evidence for evolution?
choices: It shows that all organisms have the same genes.
It proves that the code can never change.
It is most simply explained if all life inherited the code from a common ancestor.
It shows that bacteria evolved from humans.
questions.explanation: Many different codes would work chemically, yet almost all life uses the same one, which points to a single origin. Organisms share the code, not all their genes, and minor variant codes do exist.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions is enough for natural selection to change a population?
choices: Variation in a trait, inheritance of that trait, and differences in reproductive success linked to it
A changing environment and individuals that try to adapt
A large population with no variation
Variation caused only by the environment, such as muscles built by exercise
questions.explanation: Selection needs heritable variation that affects survival or reproduction. Effort doesn't change genes, a population with no variation has nothing to select, and traits acquired during life (like gym muscles) aren't inherited.

questions.stem: In evolutionary terms, which individual has the highest fitness?
choices: A small, weak bird that raises 8 offspring that survive to breed
A large, strong bird that lives 15 years but raises 2 offspring
The fastest bird, which raises no offspring
A bird that lives longest without breeding
questions.explanation: Fitness is reproductive success relative to others: the number of offspring contributed to the next generation. Size, strength, speed and lifespan matter only if they lead to more offspring.

questions.stem: In the Lederbergs' replica-plating experiment, colonies that grew on antibiotic plates were traced back to the original plate, which had never been exposed to the antibiotic. Those original colonies were already resistant. What does this show?
choices: The antibiotic caused the resistance mutations.
Bacteria become resistant because they need to survive.
Resistance is not inherited.
Resistance mutations arose randomly before exposure; the antibiotic selected them.
questions.explanation: The original colonies were resistant without ever meeting the antibiotic, so the mutations came first and the antibiotic only revealed and favored them. Mutation is random with respect to need.

questions.stem: A moth population has 500 light and 500 dark moths. On sooty bark, 30% of light moths and 60% of dark moths survive. What percent of the survivors are dark?
choices: About 66.7%
questions.explanation: Survivors: light $500 \times 0.30 = 150$, dark $500 \times 0.60 = 300$. Dark fraction $= 300/450 \approx 66.7\%$. 50% is the starting share; 60% is the dark survival rate, not the share of survivors; 90% adds the two rates.

questions.stem: During the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, mostly large, hard seeds remained. Medium ground finch survivors had deeper beaks than those that died. What happened to the next generation?
choices: Its average beak depth was unchanged, because selection acts only on individuals.
Its average beak depth was larger, because beak depth is heritable.
Its beaks were smaller, because birds ate less.
Every bird developed a deeper beak by cracking hard seeds.
questions.explanation: Deeper-beaked birds survived and bred, and beak depth is inherited, so the average in the offspring generation rose. Individual birds didn't change their beaks by use; the population's makeup changed.

questions.stem: Human birth weight historically had the highest survival near the average, with lower survival for very small and very large babies. What type of selection is this?
choices: Directional selection
Disruptive selection
Stabilizing selection
Artificial selection
questions.explanation: Favoring the middle and removing both extremes is stabilizing selection: the average stays and the spread narrows. Directional selection would shift the average; disruptive would favor both extremes.

questions.stem: In a finch population, birds with small bills eat soft seeds well and birds with large bills crack hard seeds well, but intermediate bills do neither well. Over time, what pattern of selection is expected?
choices: Disruptive selection, favoring both extremes
Stabilizing selection, favoring intermediate bills
Directional selection toward small bills
No selection, because all bills are used
questions.explanation: When both extremes do better than the middle, selection is disruptive and can split the distribution into two peaks, as in the black-bellied seedcracker.

questions.stem: Cabbage, broccoli, kale and Brussels sprouts were all bred from one species of wild cabbage. This is an example of
choices: natural selection
genetic drift
artificial selection
convergent evolution
questions.explanation: People chose which plants to breed for leaves, buds, flowers or stems: artificial selection. In natural selection, the environment does the choosing through survival and reproduction.

questions.stem: Lamarck proposed that giraffes got long necks by stretching to reach leaves and passing the longer necks to their young. Why is this rejected?
choices: Changes acquired during an animal's life are not written into its DNA, so they are not inherited.
Giraffes do not eat leaves.
Neck length is not variable in giraffes.
Natural selection cannot act on body size.
questions.explanation: Stretching doesn't change the genes in eggs or sperm. The accepted explanation is that giraffes with heritably longer necks left more offspring.

questions.stem: Which statement about natural selection is correct?
choices: Individuals evolve during their lifetimes to fit the environment.
Selection produces the mutations a population needs.
Selection plans ahead for future environments.
Individuals are selected, but populations evolve.
questions.explanation: Selection acts on individuals (who survives and reproduces), and the result is a change in the population over generations. It has no foresight and doesn't create mutations; it sorts existing variation.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of individuals show a recessive trait. What is the frequency of heterozygous carriers?
A population of 500 has 180 AA, 240 Aa and 80 aa individuals. What is the frequency of allele A?
questions.explanation: Gene copies: $2 \times 500 = 1{,}000$. Copies of A: $2(180) + 240 = 600$. $p = 600/1000 = 0.6$. 0.36 is the AA genotype frequency; 0.48 is the Aa frequency; 0.4 is $q$.

questions.stem: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 people. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, about what fraction of people are carriers?
choices: About 1 in 100
About 1 in 5,000
About 1 in 50
About 1 in 10,000
questions.explanation: $q^2 = 1/10{,}000$, so $q = 1/100 = 0.01$ and $p = 0.99$. $2pq = 2(0.99)(0.01) \approx 0.02$, about 1 in 50. 1 in 100 is $q$, not $2pq$. Carriers are far more common than affected people.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
choices: No natural selection
Random mating
The dominant allele must be more common than the recessive allele.
A very large population
questions.explanation: The conditions are no mutation, no gene flow, a very large population (no drift), random mating and no selection. Allele frequencies can be anything; equilibrium says they stay constant, not that dominant alleles are common.

questions.stem: With $p = 0.6$ and $q = 0.4$, a population of 1,000 is expected to have 480 heterozygotes under Hardy-Weinberg. A survey finds only 200. Which explanation best fits this shortage?
choices: Inbreeding or self-fertilization (nonrandom mating)
Random mating in a very large population
Gene flow that adds heterozygotes
A counting method that only finds homozygotes for A
questions.explanation: Too few heterozygotes and too many homozygotes is the signature of mating with relatives or self-fertilization. Random mating in a large population is the equilibrium case and would give about 480.

questions.stem: Northern elephant seals were hunted to a few dozen animals in the 1890s. Today there are over 200,000, but they have very little genetic variation. What explains the low variation?
choices: Gene flow from other seal species
Stabilizing selection on body size
The bottleneck effect
A high mutation rate
questions.explanation: The few survivors carried only a small, random sample of the original alleles, and the population regrew from them: a bottleneck, a form of genetic drift. Gene flow and mutation would add variation, not remove it.

questions.stem: A rare recessive form of dwarfism is much more common among the Old Order Amish of Lancaster County than in the general population. The best explanation is
choices: the founder effect
natural selection favoring the allele
gene flow into the community
a high mutation rate in the community
questions.explanation: The community descends from a small number of founders, at least one of whom happened to carry the allele, so it became more common by chance: the founder effect. Nothing suggests the allele is favored.

questions.stem: Why does genetic drift have a much larger effect in small populations than in large ones?
choices: Chance deviations from expected numbers are proportionally larger in small samples.
Small populations have higher mutation rates.
Natural selection is stronger in small populations.
Large populations have no random events.
questions.explanation: Like coin flips: 10 tosses can easily give 70% heads, but 10,000 tosses will be very close to 50%. Each generation is a sample of the parents' alleles, and small samples wander more.

questions.stem: Pollen carried by wind from one population of pines to another, distant population is an example of
choices: genetic drift
gene flow
mutation
the founder effect
questions.explanation: Moving alleles between populations (through migrating individuals or their gametes) is gene flow. It tends to make populations more alike.

questions.stem: Which mechanism of evolution consistently makes a population better adapted to its environment?
choices: Genetic drift
Gene flow
Natural selection
Mutation
questions.explanation: Only selection favors alleles because they improve survival and reproduction. Drift is random, gene flow depends on who migrates, and mutation is random with respect to need, though it supplies the raw variation.

questions.stem: Polydactyly (extra fingers) is caused by a dominant allele, yet it is rare. How can this be?
choices: Dominant alleles always become more common, so it must not really be dominant.
Dominance describes how an allele shows up in heterozygotes, not how common it is.
The allele is recessive in most people.
Hardy-Weinberg does not apply to humans.
questions.explanation: An allele can be dominant and still have a low frequency $p$. Hardy and Weinberg showed that dominant alleles do not automatically spread; frequencies stay constant unless something like selection or drift changes them.

questions.stem: Horses and donkeys can mate and produce mules, but mules are almost always sterile. Under the biological species concept, horses and donkeys are
choices: the same species, because they can mate
separate species, isolated by mechanical isolation
separate species, isolated by hybrid sterility
the same species, because mules are healthy
questions.explanation: The test is fertile offspring. Mules are sterile, a postzygotic barrier, so horses and donkeys are separate species. Mating can happen, so it is not mechanical isolation.

questions.stem: Two species of frogs live in the same ponds; one breeds in early spring and the other in early summer. What kind of barrier keeps them apart?
choices: Habitat isolation (prezygotic)
Hybrid inviability (postzygotic)
Gametic isolation (prezygotic)
Temporal isolation (prezygotic)
questions.explanation: Breeding at different times is temporal isolation, which acts before fertilization. They share a habitat, so it isn't habitat isolation, and no hybrids form, so postzygotic barriers don't come into play.

questions.stem: Sea urchins of two species release eggs and sperm into the same water, but sperm of one species can't bind to the other species' eggs. This is
choices: behavioral isolation
hybrid sterility
temporal isolation
gametic isolation
questions.explanation: Egg-surface proteins bind only sperm of the same species, so fertilization fails: gametic isolation, a prezygotic barrier. Behavior and timing are not the issue here.

questions.stem: When the Isthmus of Panama formed about 3 million years ago, populations of snapping shrimp were split into Caribbean and Pacific groups that have since become separate species. This is an example of
choices: sympatric speciation by polyploidy
gene flow
convergent evolution
allopatric speciation
questions.explanation: A geographic barrier split the populations and stopped gene flow; each side then evolved separately. That is allopatric speciation. Sympatric speciation happens without geographic separation.

questions.stem: An error in cell division doubles a plant's chromosome number. The new plant can't produce fertile offspring with its parent species but can reproduce with itself or other plants like it. What has happened?
choices: Allopatric speciation
Sympatric speciation by polyploidy
A bottleneck
Directional selection
questions.explanation: The polyploid is reproductively isolated from its parents in a single generation, in the same place. This is a common route to new plant species, with no geographic barrier needed.

questions.stem: Why is the biological species concept hard to apply to bacteria?
choices: Bacteria have no DNA.
Bacteria never evolve.
Bacteria reproduce asexually, so interbreeding can't be the test.
Bacteria all belong to one species.
questions.explanation: The concept is defined by interbreeding. Organisms that reproduce asexually, and fossils, are grouped instead by shared features or DNA sequences.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, how do you tell which of two species is more closely related to a third?
choices: Choose the species printed next to it at the tips.
Find which pair shares the most recent common ancestor (the node closest to the tips).
Choose the species that looks most similar.
Count how many tips separate them on the page.
questions.explanation: Relatedness is about the most recent shared ancestor. Tip order can change by rotating branches around nodes without changing the tree, and similar appearance can come from convergent evolution.

questions.stem: Using the vertebrate tree from the lesson (lamprey, shark, trout, frog, lizard, human), which group is a clade?
choices: Shark and frog
Frog, lizard and human
Trout and lizard
Lamprey, frog and human
questions.explanation: A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. Frog, lizard and human are all the descendants of the four-limbed ancestor. The other groups each leave out some descendants of their common ancestor.

questions.stem: In a character table, which trait would help show which two of these three animals (frog, lizard and human) are most closely related?
choices: An amniotic egg, present in lizards and humans but not frogs
A backbone, which all three have
Four limbs, which all three have
Body size, which varies within each group
questions.explanation: A shared derived trait groups the species that inherited it from a common ancestor. The amniotic egg is shared by lizards and humans, marking them as a clade (the amniotes) that excludes frogs. A backbone and four limbs are shared by all three, so they can't separate them, and body size varies too much and can evolve repeatedly. A trait found in only one of the three, like hair in humans, marks that line but can't show which two are closest.

questions.stem: A student says the lamprey, which branches off first on a vertebrate tree, is "less evolved" than humans. What is wrong with this?
choices: Lampreys are actually the ancestors of humans.
Lampreys appeared after humans.
Nothing; early branches are less evolved.
The lamprey's lineage has been evolving for exactly as long as ours since the two split.
questions.explanation: All living groups at the tips have had the same amount of time to evolve since their common ancestor. Living lampreys are not our ancestors; ancestors sit at the nodes, not the tips.

questions.stem: About 15 to 18 species of Galápagos finches, with beaks suited to seeds, insects or cactus, descend from one ancestral species. This pattern is called
choices: a bottleneck
stabilizing selection
an adaptive radiation
gene flow
questions.explanation: One ancestor diversifying into many species, each adapted to a different way of life, is an adaptive radiation.

questions.stem: Genome studies of the Asgard archaea have changed how biologists picture the base of the tree of life. What do most recent analyses suggest?
choices: Eukaryotes descend from bacteria, and archaea branched off from eukaryotes later.
Archaea are eukaryotes that lost their nucleus.
Viruses form a fourth domain at the root of the tree.
Eukaryotes arose from within the archaea, from an archaeal cell that took in a bacterium.
questions.explanation: Asgard archaea carry many genes once thought unique to eukaryotes, and most analyses place eukaryotes on a branch growing out of the archaea, with the mitochondrion coming from an engulfed bacterium. Archaea have no nucleus and never did, archaea are not descended from eukaryotes, and viruses are not cells, so they are not placed in any domain.

questions.stem: If Earth's 4.54 billion years were compressed into 24 hours, about when would the Cambrian explosion (539 million years ago) occur?
choices: About 3 a.m.
About noon
About 11:59 p.m.
About 9 p.m.
questions.explanation: The time elapsed before the Cambrian is $4{,}540 - 539 = 4{,}001$ million years, and $24 \times 4001/4540 \approx 21.2$ hours, about 9 p.m. 3 a.m. comes from using 539/4540 of the day from midnight instead of time remaining.

questions.stem: In the Miller–Urey experiment, electric sparks passed through a mixture of gases and water produced amino acids. What did this show?
choices: Life arose from sparks in a single week.
The first cells contained DNA.
Oxygen was necessary for life to begin.
Some building blocks of life can form from simple chemicals without living things.
questions.explanation: The experiment made molecules, not cells, so it shows only that life's building blocks can form without life. Early Earth had almost no free oxygen; the experiment used no oxygen gas.

questions.stem: Why is the ability of RNA to act as a catalyst important for ideas about the origin of life?
choices: It proves that proteins came before nucleic acids.
RNA can store information and speed up reactions, so early life may have used RNA for both before DNA and proteins.
It shows that DNA is unnecessary in modern cells.
It means RNA can make energy from sunlight.
questions.explanation: The RNA world hypothesis rests on RNA doing both jobs (as rRNA still does when forming peptide bonds). It doesn't make DNA unnecessary today, and it suggests nucleic acids, not proteins, came first.

questions.stem: Put these events in order from oldest to most recent: (1) Great Oxidation Event, (2) first eukaryotes, (3) earliest widely accepted fossils of prokaryotes, (4) Cambrian explosion.
questions.explanation: Prokaryote fossils about 3.5 billion years ago; oxygen buildup about 2.4 billion; eukaryotes about 2 billion; Cambrian explosion about 539 million years ago.

questions.stem: Which observation supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria?
