choices: Mitochondria are found only in plant cells.
Mitochondria are made by the Golgi apparatus.
Mitochondria contain no ribosomes.
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and divide by splitting, like bacteria.
questions.explanation: Their own circular DNA, bacterial-type ribosomes and division by splitting all point to descent from engulfed bacteria. Mitochondria are found in nearly all eukaryotes, including animals.

questions.stem: Which mass extinction was the largest, wiping out by most estimates 80 to 90 percent or more of marine species?
choices: End-Permian, about 252 million years ago
End-Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago
End-Ordovician, about 445 million years ago
End-Triassic, about 201 million years ago
questions.explanation: The end-Permian extinction, linked to massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia, was the worst. The end-Cretaceous, which ended the non-bird dinosaurs, is the best known but was smaller.

questions.stem: A thin clay layer rich in iridium is found worldwide at the boundary between rocks of the Cretaceous and the following period. What does it most strongly support?
choices: A large asteroid impact about 66 million years ago
A slow decline in sea level over millions of years
The first appearance of flowering plants
A global ice age 252 million years ago
questions.explanation: Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. A worldwide layer at that boundary, plus the Chicxulub crater of the right age, points to an impact. The 252-million-year date belongs to the end-Permian.

questions.stem: Layers in a cliff, bottom to top: sandstone with trilobites, volcanic ash dated at 300 million years, shale with dinosaur bones. What can be said about the trilobite fossils?
choices: They are younger than 300 million years.
They are older than 300 million years.
They are exactly 300 million years old.
They are younger than the dinosaurs.
questions.explanation: By superposition, lower layers are older, so the trilobites predate the ash, and the dinosaurs postdate it. A fossil's age is usually a range bracketed by dated layers.

questions.stem: After the end-Cretaceous extinction, mammals diversified rapidly into many new forms, including whales, bats and grazers. This is best described as
choices: a mass extinction of mammals
a population bottleneck in dinosaurs
stabilizing selection on mammal size
an adaptive radiation into roles left empty
questions.explanation: Extinctions open ecological roles; surviving groups then diversify to fill them. Mammals had been mostly small for over 100 million years before this radiation.

questions.stem: Fossils of a snail lineage show almost no change for 3 million years, then a fairly quick shift (over tens of thousands of years) to a new form that stays stable again. Which model does this pattern match?
choices: Gradualism
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
Punctuated equilibrium
Endosymbiosis
questions.explanation: Long stability broken by relatively rapid change is punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge and Gould, 1972). Gradualism predicts slow, steady change throughout.

questions.stem: Why did oxygen-releasing photosynthesis by cyanobacteria matter so much for later life?
choices: It removed all carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
It produced the first amino acids.
It caused the end-Cretaceous extinction.
The oxygen it built up made aerobic respiration possible, which yields much more ATP.
questions.explanation: Oxygen accumulated from about 2.4 billion years ago. Aerobic respiration gives about 30 ATP per glucose versus 2 from fermentation, which supports larger, more active organisms.

questions.stem: The picture shows the bones of a human arm, from shoulder (top) to fingertips. Name the numbered parts. The same parts appear in a cat's foreleg, a whale's flipper and a bat's wing.

image.alt: The bones of a human arm drawn from the shoulder at the top down to the fingertips, with five numbered markers from top to bottom.

choices: Upper arm bone (humerus)
Forearm bones (radius and ulna)
Wrist bones (carpals)
Palm bones (metacarpals)
Finger bones (phalanges)
questions.explanation: From the shoulder down: one upper-arm bone, two forearm bones side by side, a cluster of small wrist bones, the palm bones, then the finger bones. A cat, whale and bat have the same parts in the same order, only resized and reshaped, which is why these forelimbs are homologous.

questions.stem: Body parts that share the same underlying structure because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even if they now do different jobs, are called ___ structures.
questions.explanation: Homologous structures, such as the human arm and the bat wing, share a parts list inherited from a common ancestor. Structures that do the same job but are built differently are analogous.

questions.stem: Sort each pair or structure into the kind of evidence it shows.
left: A bat's wing and a whale's flipper
A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing
Tiny hip bones inside some whales
A human arm and a cat's foreleg
choices: Homologous
Analogous
Vestigial
questions.explanation: Bat wings, whale flippers, human arms and cat forelegs share the same bones from a common ancestor: homologous. Bird and butterfly wings do the same job but are built differently and evolved separately: analogous. Whale hip bones and the human tailbone are reduced remnants of structures that were larger in ancestors: vestigial.

questions.stem: Which observations are evidence that the organisms involved share a common ancestor? Select all that apply.
choices: Human arms and bat wings have the same set of bones in the same order.
Humans and monkeys carry the same broken vitamin C gene, with some of the same disabling mutations.
Birds and butterflies both have wings that they use to fly.
Nearly all organisms use the same genetic code.
questions.explanation: Shared bone patterns, a shared broken gene and a shared genetic code are all most simply explained by inheritance from a common ancestor. Bird and butterfly wings are analogous: they evolved separately, so they show similar selection pressures, not shared ancestry.

questions.stem: A piece of wood has 1/32 as much carbon-14 as living wood. ___ half-lives of carbon-14 have passed since the tree died.
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{1}{32} = \left(\tfrac12\right)^5$, so 5 half-lives have passed, about $5 \times 5{,}730 = 28{,}650$ years.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the Lederbergs' replica-plating experiment in order.
choices: Grow many colonies on a master plate with no antibiotic.
Press a velvet pad onto the master plate to pick up cells from every colony.
Press the same pad onto a plate that contains the antibiotic.
Note the positions of the few colonies that grow on the antibiotic plate.
Test colonies from the same positions on the master plate for resistance.
questions.explanation: The pad copies the pattern of colonies onto the antibiotic plate, so the colonies that grow there can be matched to colonies on the master plate. Those master-plate colonies turn out to be resistant even though they never met the antibiotic: the mutations came first and the antibiotic only selected them.

questions.stem: In evolutionary biology, an individual's reproductive success compared with others in its population is called its ___.
questions.explanation: Fitness is measured by offspring contributed to the next generation, not by strength, speed or how long the individual lives.

questions.stem: Match each example to the kind of selection it shows.
left: In a drought, finches with deeper beaks survive better and the average beak deepens.
Babies of average birth weight historically survived best.
Seedcrackers with small or large bills do well and those with medium bills do poorly.
Farmers bred kale and broccoli from wild cabbage.
choices: Directional selection
Stabilizing selection
Disruptive selection
Artificial selection
Genetic drift
questions.explanation: Directional selection moves the average toward one extreme (deeper beaks). Stabilizing selection favors the middle (average birth weight). Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the middle (small and large bills). Artificial selection is breeding chosen by people. None of these is genetic drift, which is change by chance.

questions.stem: The figure shows the Lederbergs' replica-plating experiment. Which conclusions does it support? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Replica plating: a master plate without antibiotic, a velvet pad, and an antibiotic plate where only two colonies grow; the matching positions are circled on both plates.

choices: Some cells were resistant before they ever met the antibiotic.
The antibiotic selected resistant cells that were already present.
The antibiotic caused the mutations that made cells resistant.
Resistance appeared only after the cells were exposed to the antibiotic.
questions.explanation: The colonies at the circled positions on the master plate were resistant although they had never touched the antibiotic, so the resistance mutations arose first, by chance. The antibiotic only revealed and favored them; it did not cause them.

questions.stem: A moth population has 300 light and 200 dark moths. On sooty bark, 50% of light moths and 80% of dark moths survive. To the nearest whole percent, ___% of the survivors are dark.
questions.explanation: Light survivors: $300 \times 0.50 = 150$. Dark survivors: $200 \times 0.80 = 160$. Dark share: $\dfrac{160}{150 + 160} = \dfrac{160}{310} \approx 0.516$, about 52%, up from 40% before selection.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of allele a is $q = 0.3$. The expected frequency of heterozygotes ($2pq$), as a decimal, is ___.
Match each mechanism of evolution to an example of it.
choices: Wind carries pollen from one pine population to another.
By chance a few individuals happen to leave most of the offspring in a small population.
A copying error in DNA creates a new allele.
Insects with a resistance allele survive spraying and leave more offspring.
Self-pollinating plants produce more homozygotes than expected.
questions.explanation: Gene flow moves alleles between populations; drift changes frequencies by chance; mutation creates new alleles; selection changes frequencies because genotypes differ in survival and reproduction; nonrandom mating (here self-fertilization) changes genotype frequencies, raising homozygotes.

questions.stem: The figure shows the bottleneck effect with colored marbles standing for alleles. Which statements about a bottleneck are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Colored marbles show the bottleneck effect, where a few survivors regrow a population with fewer colors, and the founder effect, where a few founders start an island population with different color proportions.

choices: The survivors are a random sample of the original alleles.
The recovered population can lack alleles that the original population had.
The alleles that pass through the bottleneck are always the best-adapted ones.
Once the population regrows to its old size, its lost alleles return.
questions.explanation: A bottleneck is a form of genetic drift: which alleles survive is a matter of chance, not fitness, so some alleles are lost. Regrowing the population does not bring them back; only mutation or gene flow can, which is why northern elephant seals still have very little variation.

questions.stem: Put the steps for checking whether a population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium at one gene in order.
choices: Count the individuals of each genotype.
Calculate the allele frequencies p and q from the counts.
Calculate the expected genotype frequencies p², 2pq and q².
Multiply by the population size to get expected counts.
Compare the observed counts with the expected counts.
questions.explanation: Allele frequencies come from the observed counts first; the Hardy-Weinberg equations then predict genotype frequencies, which become expected counts. A large gap between observed and expected counts means something is acting on the gene.

questions.stem: When a few individuals start a new, isolated population that carries only some of the original population's alleles, the resulting genetic drift is called the ___ effect.
questions.explanation: The founder effect: the founders are a small random sample, so rare alleles they happen to carry can become common, as with Ellis–van Creveld syndrome among the Old Order Amish.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this phylogenetic tree.

image.alt: A phylogenetic tree of five species, A to E, with time running left to right and four numbered markers on different parts of the tree.

choices: Root
Node (a common ancestor)
Branch (a lineage through time)
Tip (a group being compared)
Character
Population
questions.explanation: The root (1) is the base of the tree, the ancestor of everything on it. A node (2) is a branch point, standing for the common ancestor of the groups above it, here species D and E. A branch (3) is a line between nodes, a lineage evolving through time. A tip (4) is the end of a branch, one of the groups being compared.

questions.stem: Sort each barrier as prezygotic (acts before fertilization) or postzygotic (acts after fertilization).
left: Two frog species breed in different months.
Females answer only their own species' flash pattern.
Sperm cannot bind to another species' eggs.
choices: Postzygotic
Prezygotic
questions.explanation: Timing (temporal), courtship signals (behavioral) and sperm–egg binding (gametic) all stop fertilization from happening: prezygotic. Hybrid sterility and hybrid inviability act on a zygote that has already formed: postzygotic.

questions.stem: Which of these can lead to sympatric speciation, without any geographic barrier? Select all that apply.
choices: A plant's chromosome number doubles, so it can't make fertile offspring with its parent species.
Some flies switch to laying eggs on a new host fruit that ripens at a different time.
A new mountain range splits a population in two.
A river changes course and isolates part of a population.
questions.explanation: Polyploidy and a host shift (as in apple maggot flies) can isolate groups living in the same place: sympatric speciation. Mountains and rivers are geographic barriers, the start of allopatric speciation.

questions.stem: An ancestor and all of its descendants, one complete branch of a phylogenetic tree, is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A clade includes a common ancestor and every one of its descendants. Clades are identified by shared derived characters, such as the amniotic egg for lizards and humans.

questions.stem: Using the vertebrate tree from the lesson, put these animals in order from most closely related to humans to least closely related.
choices: Lizard
Frog
Trout
Shark
Lamprey
questions.explanation: Relatedness follows how recently each animal shares a common ancestor with humans. Lizards share the amniote ancestor, frogs the four-limbed ancestor, trout the bony-skeleton ancestor, sharks the jawed ancestor, and lampreys only the oldest node on the tree.

questions.stem: The top bar shows Earth's whole history split into four eons; the bottom bar zooms into the most recent eon, split into three eras. Numbers are millions of years ago. Name the numbered intervals.

image.alt: Two unlabeled timeline bars. The top bar runs from 4,540 million years ago to now, with boundaries at 4,000, 2,500 and 539. The bottom bar zooms into the last 539 million years, with boundaries at 252 and 66.

choices: Hadean
Archean
Proterozoic
Paleozoic
Mesozoic
Cenozoic
questions.explanation: Eons: Hadean (4,540–4,000), Archean (4,000–2,500), Proterozoic (2,500–539), then the Phanerozoic. The Phanerozoic splits into the Paleozoic (539–252), Mesozoic (252–66) and Cenozoic (66–now) eras. The two big extinctions mark the era boundaries: end-Permian at 252, end-Cretaceous at 66.

questions.stem: Put these events in the history of life in order, from oldest to most recent.
choices: Earliest widely accepted fossils of prokaryotes
Oxygen builds up in the atmosphere
First eukaryotes
Cambrian explosion
Plants reach land
End-Cretaceous extinction
questions.explanation: About 3.5 billion years ago, 2.4 billion, about 2 billion, 539 million, about 470 million, and 66 million years ago.

questions.stem: Match each mass extinction to its leading explanation.
choices: Glaciation and falling sea level
Loss of oxygen in the oceans
Huge volcanic eruptions in Siberia
Volcanic eruptions as Pangaea split apart
Asteroid impact at Chicxulub
questions.explanation: These are the leading explanations from the lesson's table. The end-Permian (about 252 million years ago) was the largest; the end-Cretaceous (66 million years ago) ended the non-bird dinosaurs, with volcanic eruptions in India also contributing.

questions.stem: Use the cliff in the figure. Which conclusions are supported? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Five rock layers in a cliff, from bottom to top: sandstone with trilobites, volcanic ash dated at 260 million years, shale with dinosaur bones, an iridium-rich clay layer, and rock with early primate fossils.

choices: The trilobites are older than 260 million years.
The dinosaur bones are younger than 260 million years.
The primate fossils are younger than the iridium layer.
The trilobites are younger than the dinosaur bones.
questions.explanation: By superposition, lower layers are older. The trilobites lie below the dated ash, so they are older than 260 million years; the dinosaur bones lie above it, so they are younger. The primates lie above the iridium layer, which matches the 66-million-year end-Cretaceous boundary. The trilobites are the oldest fossils in the cliff, not younger than the dinosaurs.

questions.stem: The pattern in which species change little for long periods and then change relatively quickly, often around speciation, is called ___.
questions.explanation: Punctuated equilibrium, named by Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould in 1972. "Relatively quickly" still means tens of thousands of years. The contrasting pattern of slow, steady change is gradualism.

questions.stem: In a plant population, AA plants leave an average of 4.0 offspring, Aa plants 5.0 and aa plants 2.5. What is the relative fitness of AA?
questions.explanation: Divide by the fittest genotype, Aa: $w_{AA} = 4.0/5.0 = 0.8$. 1.25 divides the wrong way; 0.2 is the selection coefficient $s = 1 - w$; 1.0 would be right only if AA were the fittest genotype.

questions.stem: A population starts in Hardy-Weinberg proportions with $p = q = 0.5$. Relative fitnesses are $w_{AA} = w_{Aa} = 1$ and $w_{aa} = 0.5$. What is $q$ among the adults after one generation of selection?
questions.explanation: Zygotes 0.25, 0.50, 0.25; times $w$: 0.25, 0.50, 0.125; mean fitness $\bar w = 0.875$. $q' = \dfrac{0.125 + \tfrac12(0.50)}{0.875} = \dfrac{0.375}{0.875} \approx 0.43$. 0.375 forgets to divide by $\bar w$; 0.25 is $q^2$; 0.5 assumes nothing changes.

questions.stem: Selection against a recessive phenotype ($aa$) lowers $q$ quickly when $q$ is large, but very slowly once $q$ is small. Why?
choices: Rare alleles mutate back into the dominant allele.
Selection stops acting once an allele falls below 10%.
When $q$ is small, most copies of $a$ are in heterozygotes, which have normal fitness.
Heterozygotes have lower fitness than $aa$ individuals.
questions.explanation: Only $aa$ individuals are selected against. When $q = 0.1$, just 1% of individuals are $aa$ but 18% are carriers, so about 90% of $a$ copies are hidden in heterozygotes. Selection keeps acting at every frequency; it simply has little to act on.

questions.stem: At a gene with heterozygote advantage, $w_{AA} = 0.9$, $w_{Aa} = 1$ and $w_{aa} = 0.6$. At what frequency $q$ of allele $a$ does selection stop changing the population?
questions.explanation: $s = 1 - w_{AA} = 0.1$ and $t = 1 - w_{aa} = 0.4$, so $\hat q = \dfrac{s}{s + t} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.5} = 0.2$. 0.8 is the equilibrium $p$, not $q$; 0.25 is $s/t$; 0.1 is $s$ alone.

questions.stem: A neutral allele has a frequency of 0.15 in a small population with no selection, mutation or gene flow. What is the probability that drift eventually fixes it?
questions.explanation: For a neutral allele, the chance of eventual fixation equals its current frequency, 0.15; it is lost the other 85% of the time. 0.5 assumes every allele has an even chance; 0.0225 is $0.15^2$.

questions.stem: In an idealized population of 50 breeders with no mutation, gene flow or selection, about what fraction of the starting heterozygosity remains after 100 generations?
questions.explanation: $H_t / H_0 = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2N}\right)^t = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{100}\right)^{100} \approx 0.37$. 0.13 uses $1 - \tfrac1N$ instead of $1 - \tfrac{1}{2N}$ (forgetting that diploids carry $2N$ gene copies).

questions.stem: Over four generations a population has 500, 20, 500 and 500 breeding adults. What is its effective population size over this stretch?
choices: About 71
questions.explanation: Use the harmonic mean: $N_e = \dfrac{4}{\tfrac{1}{500} + \tfrac{1}{20} + \tfrac{1}{500} + \tfrac{1}{500}} = \dfrac{4}{0.056} \approx 71$. 380 is the ordinary average, which hides the bottleneck; the single generation of 20 dominates, but the other generations still count.

questions.stem: When you test genotype counts at one gene with two alleles against Hardy-Weinberg using chi-square, how many degrees of freedom do you use?
choices: 2, because there are three genotype categories
3, one for each genotype
0, because the expected counts come from the data
1: three categories minus 1, minus 1 more because p was estimated from the same data
questions.explanation: Three genotype categories give $3 - 1 = 2$, and estimating $p$ from the same counts uses up one more, leaving df = 1 (critical value 3.84 at the 0.05 significance level). Using 2 is the usual mistake; it makes the test too lenient.

questions.stem: A sample of 100 individuals has 40 $AA$, 20 $Aa$ and 40 $aa$. Test for Hardy-Weinberg proportions (critical value 3.84). What do you find?
choices: $\chi^2 = 36$; fail to reject, since chance can explain the gap.
$\chi^2 = 0$; the data fit perfectly because $p = 0.5$.
$\chi^2 = 36$; reject, with too few heterozygotes, as inbreeding would cause.
$\chi^2 = 3.6$; fail to reject.
questions.explanation: $p = \dfrac{2(40) + 20}{200} = 0.5$, so expected counts are 25, 50, 25. $\chi^2 = \dfrac{15^2}{25} + \dfrac{30^2}{50} + \dfrac{15^2}{25} = 9 + 18 + 9 = 36 > 3.84$: reject. Getting $p = 0.5$ says nothing about genotype proportions, and 3.6 comes from a slip in the arithmetic.

questions.stem: A captive population has 10 breeding males and 40 breeding females. Using $N_e = \dfrac{4N_m N_f}{N_m + N_f}$, its effective population size is ___.
questions.explanation: $N_e = \dfrac{4(10)(40)}{10 + 40} = \dfrac{1600}{50} = 32$, well below the 50 adults counted. The scarcer sex limits how many lineages are passed on.

questions.stem: The selection coefficient of a genotype is $s = 1 - w$, where $w$ is the genotype's ___ fitness.
questions.explanation: Relative fitness: the genotype's average offspring number divided by that of the fittest genotype. A genotype with $w = 0.75$ has $s = 0.25$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for calculating one generation of selection in order.
choices: Write the zygote genotype frequencies p², 2pq and q².
Multiply each genotype frequency by its relative fitness.
Add the three products to get the mean fitness.
Divide each product by the mean fitness.
Count alleles among the breeders to get the new p and q.
questions.explanation: Selection acts on genotypes, so start from Hardy-Weinberg zygotes, weight each genotype by its fitness, rescale by the mean fitness so the frequencies add to 1, and only then count alleles.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: An allele reaches a frequency of 1 and is the only one left.
The size of an idealized population that would lose variation by drift at the same rate.
The heterozygote has higher fitness than either homozygote.
How much lower a genotype's fitness is than the fittest genotype's.
The average relative fitness of the population.
Movement of alleles between populations.
questions.explanation: Movement of alleles between populations is gene flow, which is not one of these terms.

questions.stem: Which of these make a population's effective size smaller than its census size? Select all that apply.
choices: Many more breeding females than breeding males
A crash to a few individuals some generations ago
A constant size, equal numbers of each sex, and every adult equally likely to breed
A few adults producing most of the offspring
questions.explanation: Unequal sex ratios, past bottlenecks (through the harmonic mean) and unequal family sizes all mean fewer lineages are passed on, so drift acts as in a smaller population. A constant size with equal sexes and equal chances to breed is the idealized case, where $N_e$ equals the census size.

questions.stem: In a study of vertebrates (fish, frogs, lizards, mammals), which character is a shared derived character that marks the mammals as a clade?
choices: A backbone
Four limbs
Lungs
Hair
questions.explanation: Hair arose in the common ancestor of mammals and is found in no other vertebrates. A backbone, four limbs and lungs are shared with other vertebrates, so for mammals they are shared ancestral characters and can't define the group.

questions.stem: Why do biologists include an outgroup when building a phylogenetic tree?
choices: It shows which character states are ancestral and where to root the tree.
It is the most advanced species in the study.
It is the ancestor of all the species in the ingroup.
It is the species with the most derived characters.
questions.explanation: A state found in the outgroup, which branched off earlier, is taken as ancestral, and the root goes on the branch leading to it. An outgroup is a living relative, not the ancestor, and no living species is "more advanced".

questions.stem: The figure shows Trees 1 and 2 from the lesson's six-character table. How many changes would Tree 3, in which species B and C are closest, require?

image.alt: Two trees of species A, B and C plus an outgroup, with numbered bars for character changes: Tree 1 (A and B closest) has 7, Tree 2 (A and C closest) has 9.
image.caption: Character states, outgroup all 0. A: 1 1 1 1 1 0. B: 1 1 1 0 1 1. C: 0 0 0 1 1 0.

questions.explanation: On Tree 3, characters 1, 2 and 3 (shared by A and B) each need 2 changes: 6. Character 4 (shared by A and C) needs 2. Characters 5 and 6 need 1 each. Total $6 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 10$, the worst of the three trees; Tree 1, with 7, is the most parsimonious.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of homoplasy?
choices: Hair in mice and in humans
A backbone in trout and in frogs
Wings in bats and in birds, considered as wings
An amniotic egg in lizards and in humans
questions.explanation: Bats and birds evolved flight separately; their common ancestor had no wings, so wings are a similarity not inherited from a common ancestor: homoplasy by convergence. (Their forelimb bones are homologous; the wings built from them are not.) The other traits were inherited from a common ancestor.

questions.stem: How many different rooted trees, with two branches at every node, are possible for 5 species?
questions.explanation: $1 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 105$ (the product of odd numbers up to $2n - 3 = 7$). 15 is the number for 4 species; 120 is $5!$; 25 is $5^2$.

questions.stem: Fossils date the split between two lineages to 30 million years ago, and a gene differs between them at 9% of sites. Two other species in the group differ at 3%. About how long ago did they split?
choices: 10 million years
20 million years
5 million years
90 million years
questions.explanation: The two lineages diverge at $9\% / 30 = 0.30\%$ per million years ($r = 0.15\%$ per lineage), so $T = \dfrac{3}{2 \times 0.15} = 10$ million years. 20 divides by $r$ instead of $2r$; 5 divides by 2 twice; 90 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: For splits hundreds of millions of years old, a fast-changing gene tends to make the split look more recent than it is. Why?
choices: Fossils of old splits are always dated wrongly.
Sites that change more than once hide earlier changes, so differences stop growing in step with time.
Mutation rates were much higher in the distant past.
Older species have fewer genes to compare.
questions.explanation: This is saturation: once a site has changed, a later change at the same site may hide the first or even restore the original base, so the count of differences underestimates the changes that happened. Slower genes, many genes and models of multiple changes are used for old splits.

questions.stem: A tree built from one antibiotic-resistance gene places two distantly related bacteria side by side, but trees built from 100 other genes place them far apart. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The trees from the 100 other genes are all wrong.
The two bacteria are really the same species.
The resistance gene moved between their lineages by horizontal gene transfer.
Resistance genes never change, so they cannot be used.
questions.explanation: When one gene disagrees with the species tree supported by many others, transfer of that gene between lineages is the usual explanation, and resistance genes often travel on plasmids. The single gene's tree is real; it just records the gene's history, not the species'.

questions.stem: The traditional group "reptiles" includes turtles, lizards, snakes and crocodiles but not birds. Why is that group not a clade?
choices: Turtles are not really reptiles.
It leaves out birds, which descend from the same common ancestor.
Lizards and snakes are not closely related.
The animals in it have no shared derived characters at all.
questions.explanation: Crocodiles share a more recent common ancestor with birds than with lizards, so a group with crocodiles but without birds leaves out some descendants: a paraphyletic group. Adding birds makes the reptiles a clade. Snakes are in fact closely related to lizards.

questions.stem: A species known to have branched off before the group being studied, used to decide which character states are ancestral, is called an ___.
questions.explanation: The outgroup also roots the tree. It should be close enough to the ingroup that its states still reflect the ingroup's ancestor.

questions.stem: A gene changes at 0.4% per million years in each lineage. Two species differ in this gene at 4.8% of sites. They split about ___ million years ago.
questions.explanation: $T = \dfrac{d}{2r} = \dfrac{4.8}{2 \times 0.4} = 6$ million years. Dividing by $r$ alone would give 12, forgetting that both lineages changed.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: A trait state that arose in a group's common ancestor and marks the group
A trait state inherited from an older ancestor and found outside the group too
A similarity not inherited from a common ancestor
Choosing the tree that needs the fewest changes
Movement of genes between organisms other than from parent to offspring
questions.explanation: Shared derived characters define clades; shared ancestral characters don't. Homoplasy (convergence or reversal) is what makes characters conflict, parsimony is one way to choose among the resulting trees, and horizontal transfer can give a gene a different history from its species.

questions.stem: Put the steps for dating a split with a molecular clock in order.
choices: Find a split dated independently by fossils or geology.
Measure the gene difference across that dated split.
Divide that difference by twice the known time to get the rate per lineage.
Divide the difference between the two species of interest by twice that rate.
questions.explanation: The clock has to be calibrated with a known date before it can be used: rate = difference ÷ (2 × known time), then time = difference ÷ (2 × rate). Each step needs the result of the one before it.

questions.stem: Which of these are ways bacteria transfer genes horizontally? Select all that apply.
choices: Transformation: taking up DNA released by other cells
Transduction: receiving DNA carried by a virus
Conjugation: passing a plasmid through direct contact
Binary fission: dividing into two daughter cells
questions.explanation: Transformation, transduction and conjugation move DNA between cells that are not parent and offspring. Binary fission is ordinary reproduction, passing genes vertically from a parent cell to its daughters.

questions.stem: Which way of writing the scientific name of humans follows the capitalization rules of binomial nomenclature?
choices: Homo Sapiens
homo sapiens
HOMO sapiens
Homo sapiens
questions.explanation: The genus is capitalized and the specific epithet is always lowercase: Homo sapiens (italicized in print). Capitalizing the epithet is the most common slip; the genus is never lowercase or written in all capitals.

questions.stem: A wolf and a coyote are in the same genus, Canis. Which statement must be true?
choices: They are also the same species.
They are also in the same family, order, class, phylum, kingdom and domain.
They share no ranks above genus.
They must be able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
questions.explanation: Ranks are nested, so sharing a genus means sharing every rank above it (family Canidae, order Carnivora, and so on). It does not mean sharing the species rank below it, and interbreeding is not guaranteed by being in the same genus.

questions.stem: What evidence led Carl Woese to propose that archaea form a domain separate from bacteria?
choices: Differences in cell shape seen under a light microscope
Results of the Gram stain
Comparisons of ribosomal RNA sequences
Whether or not the cells have a nucleus
questions.explanation: Woese compared sequences of ribosomal RNA, a molecule all cells have. Archaea and bacteria both lack a nucleus and look alike under a microscope, which is exactly why they had been lumped together; the Gram stain separates groups of bacteria, not domains.

questions.stem: Which statement about archaea is supported by current evidence?
choices: They are a kind of bacteria that lives only in extreme environments.
They have a nucleus but no mitochondria.
In the machinery they use to copy DNA and make proteins, they resemble eukaryotes more than bacteria.
Many species cause disease in humans.
questions.explanation: Archaea are a separate domain whose RNA polymerase and other gene-expression machinery are eukaryote-like. They also live in soil, oceans and the human gut, not only in extreme places; they have no nucleus; and no archaea are known to cause human disease.

questions.stem: A culture starts with 500 bacteria that divide every 30 minutes. Assuming exponential growth, how many cells are there after 3 hours?
questions.explanation: 3 hours = 180 min, so $n = 180/30 = 6$ generations, and $N = 500 \times 2^{6} = 500 \times 64 = 32\,000$. Multiplying by 6 gives 3,000 (generations are doublings, not multiples); using 3 generations (the hours) gives 4,000; multiplying by 12 gives 6,000.

questions.stem: A bacterial population grows from 100 cells to 1,600 cells in 2 hours of exponential growth. What is its generation time?
choices: 7.5 minutes
30 minutes
20 minutes
60 minutes
questions.explanation: $1600/100 = 16 = 2^{4}$, so there were 4 generations in 120 minutes: $120/4 = 30$ minutes each. Dividing 120 by 16 (the fold increase) gives 7.5 minutes, which confuses the number of doublings with the fold change.

questions.stem: A water sample is diluted to $10^{-5}$, and 0.1 mL of the dilution is spread on a plate. 84 colonies grow. What was the concentration in the original sample?
choices: $8.4 \times 10^{7}$ CFU/mL
$8.4 \times 10^{6}$ CFU/mL
$8.4 \times 10^{2}$ CFU/mL
$8.4 \times 10^{-5}$ CFU/mL
questions.explanation: CFU/mL $= \dfrac{84}{10^{-5} \times 0.1} = 84 \times 10^{6} = 8.4 \times 10^{7}$. Forgetting that only 0.1 mL was plated gives $8.4 \times 10^{6}$; forgetting the dilution gives 840; multiplying by the dilution instead of dividing gives a tiny, impossible number.

questions.stem: A bacterial culture infected with a phage keeps growing normally for several days. After a dose of UV light, the cells burst within an hour. What best explains this?
choices: The phage was in the lysogenic cycle, and UV damage switched it into the lytic cycle.
The phage was in the lytic cycle the whole time, and UV light sped it up.
UV light killed the phage, so the bacteria burst from lack of nutrients.
The bacteria were resistant to the phage until UV light mutated them.
questions.explanation: Normal growth after infection means the viral DNA was integrated and copied along with the host chromosome (lysogenic). DNA damage from UV is a classic trigger that switches it to the lytic cycle, so new phages were made and the cells lysed. A lytic infection would have destroyed the culture within hours, not days.

questions.stem: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as the flu?
choices: Viruses are too small for antibiotic molecules to reach.
Viruses hide inside the nucleus, where antibiotics cannot enter.
Every virus is already resistant to every antibiotic.
Viruses lack the cell walls, ribosomes and metabolism that antibiotics target.
questions.explanation: Antibiotics attack structures specific to bacteria, such as peptidoglycan walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses have none of these; they use the host cell's machinery. Resistance is not the reason, and size is not the problem.

questions.stem: A particular virus infects human liver cells but not skin cells. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Skin cells have cell walls that block viruses.
Liver cells lack DNA, so the virus can insert its own.
Viruses can only infect cells that are dividing rapidly.
Liver cells have surface receptor molecules that the virus can attach to, and skin cells do not.
questions.explanation: A virus attaches to specific receptor molecules on its host cell, so it infects only cell types that display them. Human cells have no cell walls, all of them contain DNA, and many viruses infect cells that are not dividing.

questions.stem: Bacteria in a flask grow exponentially for a while, then the population stops increasing. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The bacteria have reached their maximum generation time.
Binary fission can only happen a fixed number of times.
The bacteria have switched to sexual reproduction.
Nutrients are running out and waste products are building up.
questions.explanation: A closed flask has limited food, and wastes accumulate, so division slows until births balance deaths (the stationary phase). There's no built-in limit on the number of fissions, and bacteria don't reproduce sexually.

questions.stem: A textbook sorts life into three domains, but a recent research paper draws a tree with only two primary branches, Bacteria and Archaea. How can both be reasonable?
choices: The paper counts eukaryotes as bacteria because they have mitochondria.
Archaea have recently been shown to be a kind of bacteria.
The paper leaves out eukaryotes because many of them are multicellular.
On that tree eukaryotes sit inside the archaeal branch, but they are distinctive enough to keep as a domain.
questions.explanation: Genome studies place eukaryotes within the archaea (closest to the Asgard archaea), so a tree of descent has two primary branches; the three-domain system remains a useful classification because eukaryotes differ so much from both. Mitochondria came from a bacterium but the host was archaeal, archaea are not bacteria, and no tree of life leaves out eukaryotes.

questions.stem: Why do biologists say that protists are not a natural evolutionary group?
choices: Protists do not have a nucleus.
All protists are single-celled, unlike other eukaryotes.
Some protists are more closely related to plants, animals or fungi than to other protists.
Protists are not made of cells.
questions.explanation: A natural group contains an ancestor and all its descendants. DNA shows protists scattered across the eukaryote tree, with some closer to plants and others closer to animals and fungi, so the group is defined only by what it isn't. Protists are eukaryotes with nuclei, and some, like kelp, are multicellular.

questions.stem: A single-celled protist is covered in thousands of short, hair-like structures that beat in waves to move it. These structures are
choices: pseudopods
flagella
hyphae
cilia
questions.explanation: Many short, coordinated hair-like structures are cilia, as in Paramecium. Pseudopods are flowing extensions of cytoplasm (amoebas), flagella are few and long and whip-like, and hyphae are fungal filaments.

questions.stem: Malaria is caused by
choices: a virus carried by mosquitoes
a bacterium in contaminated water
a single-celled protist carried by mosquitoes
a fungus that grows in the lungs
questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protist parasite spread by Anopheles mosquitoes. It multiplies in the liver and then in red blood cells. It is not a virus or a bacterium, though mosquitoes do carry some viral diseases.

questions.stem: The organism that caused the Irish potato famine grows in threads like a fungus, but it is classified as a protist. Which evidence supports that classification?
choices: Its cell walls contain cellulose rather than chitin, and its DNA groups it with diatoms and brown algae.
It grows in thread-like filaments.
It feeds by absorbing nutrients from its host.
It reproduces with spores.
questions.explanation: Phytophthora's cellulose walls and its DNA place it among protists. Threads, absorptive feeding and spores are exactly the features it shares with true fungi, so they can't separate it from them.

questions.stem: A student covers half of each of four dishes of Euglena with foil. After 30 minutes she counts cells in samples from each half: lit halves 410, 395, 430, 402; dark halves 90, 110, 85, 98. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Euglena move toward light.
Light makes Euglena reproduce faster.
Euglena die in the dark.
Foil attracts Euglena.
questions.explanation: In every replicate, many more cells are in the lit half after only 30 minutes, too short for large changes from reproduction or death; the simplest explanation is movement toward light. Cells were counted in the covered half too, so foil did not attract them.

questions.stem: Roughly what share of all photosynthesis on Earth is carried out by phytoplankton in the oceans?
choices: About 1%
About 10%
Nearly all of it
About half
questions.explanation: Ocean phytoplankton (photosynthetic protists such as diatoms, plus cyanobacteria) do roughly half of global photosynthesis. Land plants do most of the rest, so 'nearly all' is wrong, and 1% or 10% badly underestimates the oceans.

questions.stem: Which set of features shows that a mushroom is not a plant?
choices: It grows from the ground and does not move.
It cannot photosynthesize, its cell walls contain chitin, and it stores glycogen.
Its cells have cell walls.
It reproduces by releasing spores.
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophs with chitin walls that store glycogen, like animals. Growing in soil, staying put and having cell walls are shared with plants, and ferns and mosses also release spores, so those features can't distinguish them.

questions.stem: How does a fungus growing on rotting fruit get its food?
choices: It engulfs pieces of fruit into a gut and digests them.
It photosynthesizes using light passing through the fruit.
It absorbs whole proteins and starch without breaking them down.
It releases digestive enzymes into the fruit and absorbs the small molecules produced.
questions.explanation: Fungi digest outside their bodies: hyphae secrete enzymes and absorb the resulting sugars and amino acids. They have no gut and never photosynthesize, and large molecules must be broken down before they can be absorbed.

questions.stem: A mushroom popping up from a lawn is best described as
choices: the short-lived spore-producing structure of a much larger underground mycelium
the entire body of the fungus
a seed of the fungus
a single giant hypha
questions.explanation: The mushroom is a fruiting body. Most of the fungus is the mycelium of branching hyphae spreading through the soil. Fungi have spores, not seeds.

questions.stem: Pine seedlings grown in sterilized soil (no fungi) are smaller and contain less phosphorus than seedlings grown in soil with mycorrhizal fungi. What best explains the difference?
choices: Fungal hyphae extend the root system's reach and deliver minerals such as phosphate in exchange for sugars.
The fungi photosynthesize and give the seedlings extra sugar.
Sterilizing soil adds phosphorus that harms seedlings.
The fungi are parasites that make the seedlings grow faster to escape them.
questions.explanation: In a mycorrhizal partnership, the huge surface of the hyphae absorbs water and minerals such as phosphate for the plant, which pays in sugars. Fungi can't photosynthesize, and the result shows the fungi helping rather than harming.

questions.stem: On Fleming's 1928 plate, bacteria grew everywhere except in a clear zone around a Penicillium mold. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The mold eats bacteria by engulfing them.
A substance spreading out from the mold kills or stops the growth of these bacteria.
The bacteria could not grow because the mold used up all the light.
The mold and bacteria are mutualists.
questions.explanation: The clear zone extends beyond the mold itself, so something diffusing out of the mold, not contact or engulfing, inhibited the bacteria. That substance was penicillin. Bacteria on a plate don't need light, and inhibiting one's partner is not mutualism.

questions.stem: Lichens are often the first organisms to grow on bare rock. A lichen is
choices: a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium
a type of moss
a single species of photosynthetic fungus
a colony of protists
questions.explanation: A lichen combines a fungus, which provides structure and absorbs minerals, with an alga or cyanobacterium that photosynthesizes. It is not a moss (a plant), and no fungus photosynthesizes.

questions.stem: Which group of plants has vascular tissue but does not produce seeds?
choices: Ferns
Mosses
Pine trees
Flowering plants
questions.explanation: Ferns have xylem and phloem but reproduce with spores. Mosses lack vascular tissue; pines (gymnosperms) and flowering plants (angiosperms) make seeds.

questions.stem: Why do mosses stay only a few centimeters tall?
choices: Their leaves cannot photosynthesize.
They cannot make seeds.
They lack vascular tissue, so water moves through them only by slow diffusion and capillary action.
Their cells have no cell walls.
questions.explanation: Without xylem, water can't be moved far, so mosses stay short and live in damp places. Mosses do photosynthesize and have cellulose walls; lacking seeds affects reproduction, not height (ferns lack seeds and grow tall).

questions.stem: In a fern, the large leafy plant you see in the forest is the
choices: haploid gametophyte
diploid sporophyte
haploid sporophyte
diploid gametophyte
questions.explanation: In ferns and seed plants the sporophyte, which is diploid and makes spores by meiosis, is the dominant stage. The gametophyte is haploid; in mosses it's the familiar green plant, but in ferns it's a tiny separate structure.

questions.stem: A strip of bark, including the phloem, is cut away in a ring around a tree trunk, leaving the xylem intact. What is the most likely long-term result?
choices: Water can no longer reach the leaves, so they wilt within hours.
Sugars build up above the cut and the roots eventually starve.
The roots fill with excess sugar.
Nothing, because sugars travel in the xylem.
questions.explanation: Phloem carries sugars from leaves (sources) down to roots (sinks). With the phloem ring gone, sugar collects above the cut and the roots slowly starve. The xylem is intact, so water still reaches the leaves.

questions.stem: In a potometer, the air bubble moves 36 mm in 4 minutes along a capillary with a cross-section of 0.50 mm². What is the rate of water uptake?
choices: 9.0 mm³/min
72 mm³/min
18 mm³/min
4.5 mm³/min
questions.explanation: Volume $= 0.50 \times 36 = 18$ mm³, so the rate is $18/4 = 4.5$ mm³/min. Using the distance alone gives 9.0 (forgot the area); 18 is the total volume, not a rate; 72 multiplies by the time instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Under which conditions would a well-watered plant transpire fastest?
choices: Cool, humid, still and bright
Warm, dry, windy and bright
Warm, humid, still and dark
Cool, dry, still and dark
questions.explanation: Transpiration is evaporation: heat, dry air and wind all speed it, and light opens the stomata. Humid, still air slows evaporation, and darkness closes stomata.

questions.stem: What supplies the energy that lifts water from the roots to the top of a tall tree?
choices: ATP spent by root cells pumping water upward
Contractions of the xylem walls
Evaporation of water from the leaves, driven by the sun
Sugar flowing down through the phloem
questions.explanation: In the cohesion-tension mechanism, evaporation (transpiration) pulls on continuous water columns held together by hydrogen bonds. The plant spends no ATP lifting water; xylem cells are dead and can't contract; phloem moves sugar, not the water column.

questions.stem: A leaf imprint is viewed at a magnification where the field of view is 0.50 mm in diameter. There are 39 stomata in the field. What is the stomatal density?
choices: About 199 per mm²
About 50 per mm²
About 78 per mm²
About 156 per mm²
questions.explanation: Area $= \pi r^2 = \pi(0.25)^2 \approx 0.196$ mm², so density $= 39/0.196 \approx 199$ per mm². Using 0.50 mm as the radius gives about 50; dividing by the diameter gives 78; dividing by the radius gives 156.

questions.stem: Darwin found that grass seedlings lit from one side bent toward the light, but not when their tips were covered with an opaque cap. They still bent when the cap was transparent. What does this show?
choices: Light acts directly on the cells that bend.
The tip detects the light, even though the bending happens lower down.
The cap blocked the hormone from entering the seedling.
Seedlings bend toward heat rather than light.
questions.explanation: The transparent cap is the control: covering the tip by itself doesn't stop bending; blocking light to the tip does. So the tip senses light and signals the region below, where bending happens. Shading only the lower part did not stop bending, which rules out light acting directly on the bending cells.

questions.stem: Frits Went placed agar blocks that had held seedling tips off-center on cut seedlings kept in the dark. The seedlings bent away from the side with the block. What did this show?
choices: Light is needed for seedlings to bend.
The signal from the tip is a chemical that can diffuse into agar and makes cells on that side grow more.
Agar itself is a plant hormone.
Cells under the block stopped growing.
questions.explanation: The tips' signal moved into the agar, so it must be a chemical (later named auxin). More auxin on one side made that side elongate more, bending the seedling away from it, even in darkness. A control block that never touched tips would rule out agar itself.

questions.stem: A tomato is botanically a fruit because it
choices: develops from the ovary of a flower and contains seeds
tastes sweet
develops from the anther
grows on a vine
questions.explanation: A fruit is a ripened ovary holding seeds; the ovules inside become the seeds. The anther makes pollen. Sweetness and growth habit have nothing to do with the botanical definition.

questions.stem: During a drought, a plant closes its stomata. What is the main cost of this response?
choices: The plant loses more water.
Less carbon dioxide enters the leaf, so photosynthesis slows.
The roots can no longer absorb minerals by diffusion.
Oxygen builds up and poisons the cells.
questions.explanation: Stomata let carbon dioxide in and water vapor out at the same time, so closing them saves water at the expense of carbon uptake and photosynthesis. Closing them reduces water loss rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: Which characteristic separates animals from fungi?
choices: Animals digest food inside their bodies and their cells lack walls.
Animals are heterotrophs.
Animals are eukaryotes.
Animals store energy as glycogen.
questions.explanation: Both animals and fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that store glycogen. Fungi digest food outside the body and have chitin cell walls; animals digest internally and have no cell walls.

questions.stem: Roughly what fraction of described animal species are invertebrates?
choices: About 5%
About 25%
About 50%
About 95%
questions.explanation: Invertebrates, dominated by insects and other arthropods, make up about 95% of described animal species. Vertebrates, though familiar, are a small minority.

questions.stem: Bilateral symmetry is closely linked to cephalization. Why?
choices: Bilateral animals cannot move, so they need a brain to catch food.
Radial animals have more sense organs than bilateral ones.
An animal that moves head-first benefits from sense organs and nerve cells concentrated at the front end.
Cephalization requires a shell to protect it.
questions.explanation: A bilateral body has a front end that meets new surroundings first, so concentrating senses and nerve cells there (cephalization) pays off. Radial animals such as jellyfish meet the world from all sides and lack a head.

questions.stem: Which animal has bilateral symmetry but no body cavity of any kind?
choices: An earthworm
A jellyfish
A flatworm
A crab
questions.explanation: Flatworms are bilateral with no body cavity between gut and body wall. Earthworms and crabs have a true coelom, and jellyfish are radially symmetric.

questions.stem: Which feature do all chordates have at some stage of their lives?
choices: A backbone
Four limbs
A notochord
Lungs
questions.explanation: All chordates have a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and post-anal tail at some stage. Lancelets and sea squirts are chordates with no backbone, and fish have neither four limbs nor (in most) lungs.

questions.stem: Why was the evolution of the amniotic egg important?
choices: It allowed fish to breathe air.
It made animals endothermic.
It let vertebrates reproduce on land without needing water for their eggs.
It allowed fertilization to occur outside the body.
questions.explanation: The amnion and other membranes surround the embryo with its own fluid and handle gas exchange and wastes, so reptiles (including birds) and mammals could reproduce away from water. It is unrelated to air breathing and endothermy, and amniotic eggs are fertilized internally.

questions.stem: As a room is cooled from 25 °C to 5 °C, an animal's oxygen consumption at rest rises steadily. The animal is most likely
choices: an ectotherm whose metabolism speeds up in the cold
an ectotherm becoming more active to find warmth
an endotherm whose body temperature is falling with the air
an endotherm burning more fuel to hold its body temperature
questions.explanation: An endotherm keeps its body near a constant temperature, so in colder air it loses heat faster and must raise its metabolism, using more oxygen. An ectotherm's metabolism slows in the cold, and an endotherm's body temperature stays nearly constant.

questions.stem: Key: 1a. Jointed legs: go to 2. 1b. No jointed legs: go to 3. 2a. Eight legs: spider. 2b. Six legs: insect. 3a. Segmented body: earthworm. 3b. Unsegmented soft body with a shell: snail. An animal has no jointed legs and a soft, unsegmented body with a coiled shell. What is it?
choices: Earthworm
Snail
Insect
Spider
questions.explanation: Step 1b (no jointed legs) leads to 3, and 3b (unsegmented, shell) gives snail. Each step of a dichotomous key offers two mutually exclusive choices based on observable features.

questions.stem: A marine animal has tube feet and is radially symmetric as an adult, but its larvae are bilateral. In its embryo, the first opening becomes the anus. To which phylum does it belong?
choices: Cnidaria
Echinodermata
Mollusca
Arthropoda
questions.explanation: Tube feet, adult radial symmetry with bilateral larvae, and deuterostome development identify an echinoderm (like a sea star). Cnidarians are radial throughout and have no tube feet; mollusks and arthropods are protostomes.

questions.stem: Why are sea stars considered closer relatives of humans than insects are?
choices: Sea stars have a backbone.
Sea stars and humans both have radial symmetry as adults.
Sea stars and chordates are both deuterostomes, sharing a pattern of embryo development and DNA evidence of common ancestry.
Insects have no body cavity.
questions.explanation: Echinoderms and chordates are deuterostomes, a lineage confirmed by DNA. Sea stars have no backbone, humans are bilateral, and insects do have a coelom.

questions.stem: Where do birds fit on the vertebrate evolutionary tree?
choices: Within the reptiles, as descendants of feathered dinosaurs
On a separate branch closer to mammals than to reptiles
Within the amphibians
As the ancestors of all reptiles
questions.explanation: Birds descend from feathered theropod dinosaurs, so they sit inside the reptile branch; crocodiles are their closest living relatives. Birds and mammals are both endothermic, but they evolved it separately.

questions.stem: Why must a growing grasshopper molt?
choices: Its skin dries out every few days.
Molting removes parasites from its coelom.
Molting is how it reproduces asexually.
Its exoskeleton cannot grow, so it must be shed and replaced with a larger one.
questions.explanation: An arthropod's chitin exoskeleton is rigid and non-living, so it must be shed periodically for the animal to grow. Molting is not a form of reproduction.

questions.stem: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya are the three ___ of life, a system proposed by Carl ___ after comparing ribosomal RNA sequences.
questions.explanation: The three domains are the broadest rank of classification. Carl Woese (with George Fox) found in 1977 that ribosomal RNA splits prokaryotes into two groups as different from each other as either is from eukaryotes, and the three-domain system was formalized in 1990.

questions.stem: Put these taxonomic ranks in order from the broadest (most inclusive) to the narrowest.
choices: Domain
Kingdom
Phylum
Class
Order
Family
Genus
questions.explanation: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus (and then species): "Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup." Each rank sits inside the one before it, so organisms that share a genus also share every rank above it.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this bacterium.

image.alt: A rod-shaped bacterium with an outer layer, a wall, a membrane, a tangled loop of DNA in the middle, small dots and a small ring in the cytoplasm, short hair-like projections, and a long whip-like tail.

choices: Capsule
Cell wall
Nucleoid (DNA)
Flagellum
Pilus
Nucleus
Mitochondrion
questions.explanation: 1 is the sticky outer capsule; 2 is the cell wall just inside it (peptidoglycan in most bacteria); 3 is the nucleoid, where the circular chromosome lies with no membrane around it; 4 is the flagellum, which spins to move the cell; 5 is a pilus, used for attachment. Bacteria have no nucleus and no mitochondria.

questions.stem: Which statements are true of all viruses? Select all that apply.
choices: They contain genetic material, either DNA or RNA.
Their genetic material is enclosed in a protein coat.
They have their own ribosomes.
They can reproduce only inside a host cell.
They are wrapped in a membrane envelope.
questions.explanation: Every virus has DNA or RNA inside a protein capsid and can multiply only by using a host cell's machinery. No virus has ribosomes. Only some viruses, such as influenza and HIV, have an envelope; bacteriophages and many others do not.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Viral genes take over at once and the cell bursts
Viral DNA is copied along with the host chromosome
A prokaryote copies its chromosome and splits in two
A small extra circle of DNA in a bacterium
A membrane that surrounds the bacterial chromosome
questions.explanation: Lytic infections kill the host quickly; lysogenic ones hide in its chromosome until triggered. Binary fission is how prokaryotes divide, without mitosis. Plasmids are small DNA circles that often carry genes such as antibiotic resistance. Bacteria have no membrane around their chromosome.

questions.stem: A fungus is built from thread-like filaments called ___; the branching mass they form is called a ___.
questions.explanation: Hyphae are the threads (one is a hypha); together they form the mycelium, the main body of the fungus. A mushroom is only the fruiting body the mycelium sends up.

questions.stem: Match each protist to the way it moves.
choices: Pseudopods
Cilia
Flagellum
Hyphae
questions.explanation: An amoeba flows into extensions of its cytoplasm (pseudopods); a Paramecium is covered with short beating cilia; Euglena swims with a long whip-like flagellum. Hyphae are fungal filaments, not a way of moving.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this fungus.

image.alt: A mushroom growing from soil, with tiny particles falling from the underside of its top, and a network of threads spreading through the soil below.

choices: Cap
Gills
Spores
Stalk
Mycelium
Root
Seed
questions.explanation: The cap and stalk hold up the gills, where spores form and fall. The cap, gills and stalk together are the fruiting body; most of the fungus is the mycelium of hyphae in the soil. Fungi have no roots and make spores, not seeds.

questions.stem: Which features do fungi share with animals but not with plants? Select all that apply.
choices: They are heterotrophs.
They store food as glycogen.
Their cells have cell walls.
They make food by photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Fungi and animals both get food from other organisms and store it as glycogen, clues to their close relationship. Plants also have cell walls (cellulose rather than chitin), and fungi never photosynthesize.

questions.stem: Put these stages of the malaria parasite's life cycle in order, starting with the mosquito bite.
choices: A mosquito injects parasites into a person
Parasites multiply in the liver
Parasites invade and burst red blood cells
Some parasites become sexual forms
A feeding mosquito takes up the sexual forms
questions.explanation: Plasmodium multiplies first in the liver, then in repeated rounds inside red blood cells (the bursting causes the fevers). Sexual forms in the blood are swallowed by a biting mosquito, where they fuse and develop, ready for the next bite.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this flower, shown cut in half lengthwise.

image.alt: A flower cut lengthwise: petals on each side, two stalks ending in oval heads, a central column rising from a swollen base that holds small oval bodies, and green structures under the flower on top of a stem.

choices: Anther
Filament
Stigma
Style
Ovary
Petal
Sepal
Receptacle
questions.explanation: The stamen is an anther (1, makes pollen) on a filament (2). The carpel is a sticky stigma (3) that catches pollen, a style (4), and an ovary (5) that holds the ovules and later becomes the fruit. Petals (6) often attract animals. Sepals are the green leaf-like parts below the petals.

questions.stem: Name the numbered tissues and cells in this leaf cross-section.

image.alt: A leaf cross-section: a thin waxy layer and a row of clear cells on top, a row of tall green cells, loosely packed round green cells with air spaces, a vein in the middle with large and small cells, and a bottom row of cells with a pore between two small cells.

choices: Upper epidermis
Palisade mesophyll
Spongy mesophyll
Xylem
Phloem
Guard cell
Root hair
Cuticle
questions.explanation: The clear upper epidermis (1) lies under the waxy cuticle. Tall palisade cells (2) hold most chloroplasts; loose spongy cells (3) leave air spaces for gas exchange. In the vein, xylem (4, larger cells, upper side) brings water and phloem (5, smaller cells, lower side) carries sugar away. Guard cells (6) open and close each stoma. The cuticle is the thin top layer, not a numbered part, and root hairs are on roots.

questions.stem: Put the stages of alternation of generations in order, starting with the sporophyte.
choices: The diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis
A haploid spore grows into a gametophyte
The gametophyte makes eggs and sperm by mitosis
An egg and sperm fuse at fertilization
The diploid zygote grows into a new sporophyte
questions.explanation: Meiosis in the sporophyte makes haploid spores; a spore grows by mitosis into a haploid gametophyte, which makes gametes by mitosis; fertilization restores the diploid number in the zygote, which grows into the next sporophyte.

questions.stem: Water and minerals travel up from the roots in the ___, while sugars travel from sources to sinks in the ___.
questions.explanation: Xylem (dead, lignin-walled tubes) carries water up, pulled by transpiration. Phloem (living sieve tubes) carries sugar from where it is made or stored to where it is used, up or down.

questions.stem: Which changes would increase the transpiration rate of a well-watered plant? Select all that apply.
choices: A fan blowing across the leaves
Higher humidity around the leaves
A rise in air temperature
Moving the plant into darkness
Brighter light on the leaves
questions.explanation: Wind sweeps away humid air, warmth speeds evaporation, and bright light opens stomata, so all three raise transpiration. Humid air slows evaporation, and darkness closes stomata.

questions.stem: This simplified lancelet shows the features that define chordates. Name the numbered structures.

image.alt: A simplified fish-shaped animal with two long rods running along its back, a block of vertical slits behind the mouth, a tube running from there to an opening on the underside, and a tapering rear end.

choices: Dorsal hollow nerve cord
Notochord
Pharyngeal slits
Post-anal tail
Gut
Vertebral column
Heart
questions.explanation: The hollow nerve cord (1) runs along the back above the notochord (2), the flexible supporting rod. Pharyngeal slits (3) open from the throat. The gut (5) leads to the anus, and the tail (4) continues past it. A lancelet has no vertebral column; that is why it counts as an invertebrate chordate.

questions.stem: Match each phylum to an example animal.
choices: Jellyfish
Octopus
Earthworm
Crab
Sea urchin
Sponge
questions.explanation: Jellyfish are cnidarians (stinging cells, radial symmetry); octopuses are mollusks (as are snails and clams); earthworms are segmented annelids; crabs are arthropods with jointed legs; sea urchins are echinoderms. Sponges belong to a different phylum, Porifera.

questions.stem: An animal that keeps a nearly constant body temperature using heat from its own metabolism, such as a bird or a mammal, is called an ___.
questions.explanation: Endotherms generate most of their body heat internally. Ectotherms, such as lizards, get most of their heat from their surroundings, though behavior like basking can make them warm.

questions.stem: Which of these animals are deuterostomes? Select all that apply.
choices: Sea star
Human
Earthworm
Shark
Snail
questions.explanation: Deuterostomes are the echinoderms (sea star) and the chordates (human, shark). Earthworms (annelids) and snails (mollusks) are protostomes, whose first embryonic opening becomes the mouth.

questions.stem: Put these features in the order they first appeared in the evolution of the lineage leading to reptiles and mammals.
choices: Notochord
Jaws
Four limbs
Amniotic egg
questions.explanation: The notochord is a chordate feature, older than vertebrates. Jaws evolved in fish, four limbs in the first tetrapods (with amphibians as living descendants), and the amniotic egg in the ancestors of reptiles, birds and mammals, freeing reproduction from water.

questions.stem: Boysen-Jensen cut off coleoptile tips, placed a thin layer of gelatin between each tip and its stump, and lit the seedlings from one side. They still bent toward the light. What does this show?
choices: The signal from the tip can cross a nonliving gap, so it is probably a chemical.
The signal travels as an electrical impulse along living cells.
The gelatin itself causes bending.
The stump, not the tip, senses the light.
questions.explanation: An electrical or cell-to-cell signal could not pass through gelatin, but a dissolved chemical can diffuse across it. Gelatin alone without a tip causes no bending, and earlier work had already shown that the tip senses light.

questions.stem: Coleoptile tips are placed on agar blocks and the auxin collected is measured. A tip in darkness yields 30 units. A tip lit from one side yields 30 units. A tip lit from one side, with a barrier in only its lower part separating two blocks, yields 10 units on the lit side and 20 on the shaded side. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Light destroys auxin on the lit side.
Light makes the tip produce extra auxin on the shaded side.
Light causes auxin to move toward the shaded side, with no change in the total.
Light causes auxin to move toward the lit side.
questions.explanation: The total is 30 in every case ($10 + 20 = 30$), so auxin is neither destroyed nor newly made; it is redistributed toward the shade, as the Cholodny-Went hypothesis predicts. More ends up on the shaded side, not the lit side.

questions.stem: A seedling root is laid horizontally, and auxin collects on its lower side. Why does the root curve downward?
choices: Auxin makes the lower cells elongate faster, pushing the tip down.
Root cells are very sensitive to auxin, so the extra auxin slows elongation on the lower side and the upper side outgrows it.
Gravity pulls the root tip down because it is heavier than the rest of the root.
Auxin dissolves the cell walls on the lower side.
questions.explanation: In roots, the auxin increase that would speed shoot cells inhibits elongation. The upper side grows faster, so the root bends down. In a shoot the same redistribution speeds the lower side, so the shoot bends up. Gravity is sensed by settling starch grains; it doesn't pull the root into shape.

questions.stem: Auxin applied to the end of a stem segment that was nearer the shoot tip moves through to the other end, even when the segment is turned upside down. Auxin applied to the other end barely moves. What explains this?
choices: Auxin is heavier than water and sinks.
Auxin diffuses equally in both directions.
Transpiration carries auxin upward in the xylem.
Carrier proteins that export auxin sit at the lower (basal) end of each cell, so transport runs one way.
questions.explanation: This is polar auxin transport. PIN carrier proteins concentrated at the basal end of cells pass auxin from cell to cell toward the base, regardless of orientation, so gravity and simple diffusion can't explain it. The xylem carries water upward, the opposite direction.

questions.stem: According to the acid growth hypothesis, what would a drug that blocks the plasma membrane proton pumps do to stem segments treated with auxin?
choices: Prevent the rapid auxin-induced elongation, because the cell walls would not be acidified and loosened
Make the segments elongate faster, because more protons stay inside the cells
Have no effect, because auxin acts only by changing gene expression
Make the segments bend toward light
questions.explanation: Auxin activates proton pumps; the acidified wall activates expansins that loosen it, and turgor stretches the cell. Blocking the pumps blocks the fast response. Auxin also changes gene expression, but over hours, not minutes.

questions.stem: Pieces of tobacco tissue are grown on a medium with a high ratio of cytokinin to auxin. What will they most likely form?
choices: Roots
An undifferentiated mass of dividing cells
Shoots
Flowers
questions.explanation: Skoog and Miller found that a high cytokinin-to-auxin ratio gives shoots, a high auxin-to-cytokinin ratio gives roots, and an intermediate ratio gives a mass of dividing cells. Flowering depends on other signals.

questions.stem: A corn mutant cannot make abscisic acid. What would you expect to see?
choices: Fruits that never ripen
Kernels that sprout while still on the cob
Stems that grow extremely tall
Leaves that never fall off
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid keeps seeds dormant, so mutants lacking it germinate on the cob. Ripening and leaf drop are mainly ethylene's job, and tall stems point to gibberellin.

questions.stem: A short-day plant with a critical night length of 10 hours is grown with 9 hours of light and 15 hours of darkness, but a brief flash of red light is given 7 hours into each night. Predict the result.
choices: It does not flower, because the longest unbroken dark period is only 8 hours.
It flowers, because the total darkness is 15 hours.
It flowers, because the day is shorter than 12 hours.
It does not flower, because red light destroys florigen.
questions.explanation: The flash splits the night into 7 and 8 hours, both shorter than the 10-hour critical night, so the plant behaves as if nights were short. What counts is unbroken darkness, not total darkness or day length. The flash acts through phytochrome, not by destroying florigen.

questions.stem: Ignoring friction, what pressure difference is needed just to hold up a column of water in the xylem of an 80 m tree? (Use $\rho = 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.81$ m/s².)
choices: 7.8 MPa
78 MPa
0.78 MPa
questions.explanation: $\rho g h = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 80 = 784\,800$ Pa $\approx 0.78$ MPa, about 0.01 MPa per meter. The other choices are off by powers of ten, the usual slip when converting pascals to megapascals ($1 \text{ MPa} = 10^{6}$ Pa).

questions.stem: A suction pump at the top of a pipe cannot raise water more than about 10 m, yet trees move water over 100 m up. What does this imply about the water in their xylem?
choices: It is pushed up by root pressure of more than 10 MPa.
It is under tension (negative pressure), held together by cohesion between water molecules.
It moves up as water vapor rather than liquid.
It is pumped by living xylem cells that contract.
questions.explanation: Suction can only lower pressure toward zero, which atmospheric pressure turns into about 10 m of lift. Higher columns must be pulled from above, putting the water under negative pressure that cohesion withstands. Root pressure is at most a few tenths of a megapascal, water moves as liquid in the xylem, and xylem conduits are dead.

questions.stem: The plant pigment that is converted to its active form by red light and back to its inactive form by far-red light is called ___.
questions.explanation: Phytochrome switches between Pr (absorbs red, about 660 nm) and the active Pfr (absorbs far-red, about 730 nm). The blue-light receptors behind phototropism are different proteins, the phototropins.

questions.stem: Match each plant hormone to one of its main effects.
choices: Elongation of shoot cells on the shaded side
Stem lengthening and cereal seed germination
Cell division and delaying leaf aging
Closing stomata during drought
Fruit ripening and leaf drop
questions.explanation: Auxin drives phototropism by elongating shaded-side cells; gibberellins lengthen stems and trigger amylase in germinating grain; cytokinins promote division and delay leaf aging; abscisic acid closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant; ethylene, a gas, ripens fruit and causes leaves to drop.

questions.stem: Put the steps of stomatal opening in order, starting with the light signal.
choices: Blue light switches on proton pumps in the guard cells
Potassium and chloride ions enter the guard cells
Water enters the guard cells by osmosis
The swollen guard cells bow apart and the pore opens
questions.explanation: Proton pumping drives ion uptake; the extra solute lowers the guard cells' water potential so water flows in; the hoop-reinforced walls make the swelling cells bow apart. Abscisic acid reverses the sequence by letting ions out.

questions.stem: Which observations support the cohesion-tension mechanism? Select all that apply.
choices: When a transpiring twig is cut, the sap snaps back from the cut surface.
In a pressure chamber, pressure must be applied to push sap back to the cut end of a shoot.
Droplets appear at leaf edges on humid mornings.
Xylem conduits are living cells that squeeze water upward.
Water in narrow tubes can hold together under tensions of tens of megapascals.
questions.explanation: Sap snapping back and the pressure chamber both show the xylem water was under tension, and the measured strength of water shows a stretched column can survive. Guttation droplets come from root pressure, a push from below, and xylem conduits are dead at maturity.

questions.stem: A long-day plant has a critical night length of 11 hours. Under which 24-hour schedules will it flower? Select all that apply.
choices: 16 hours light, 8 hours dark
8 hours light, 16 hours dark
8 hours light, 16 hours dark, with a red flash in the middle of the night
8 hours light, 16 hours dark, with a red flash followed at once by a far-red flash in the middle of the night
12 hours light, 12 hours dark
questions.explanation: A long-day plant needs nights shorter than 11 hours. The 8-hour night qualifies, and a red flash splits a 16-hour night into two 8-hour pieces. Far-red right after red cancels the flash, so that night counts as 16 hours, and a 12-hour night is still too long.

questions.stem: Why can the number of plaques on a plate be used to count the phages that were spread on it?
choices: Each plaque is a colony of phages growing on the agar.
Plaques form only where two phages land together.
Each plaque starts from one phage infecting one cell, whose offspring then kill the cells around it.
Each plaque is one bacterium that resisted infection.
questions.explanation: One phage infects a cell, bursts it, and the released phages infect the neighbors, clearing a spot in the bacterial lawn. One plaque, one starting phage. Phages can't grow on agar by themselves, and a plaque is where bacteria died, not where they survived.

questions.stem: A culture has $4.0 \times 10^{5}$ infected cells per mL. After every cell has burst, a sample is diluted to $10^{-4}$, and 0.1 mL is plated with bacteria, giving 96 plaques. What is the burst size?
choices: 2.4 phages per cell
96 phages per cell
240 phages per cell
24 phages per cell
questions.explanation: Phages per mL $= \dfrac{96}{10^{-4} \times 0.1} = 9.6 \times 10^{6}$ PFU/mL. Burst size $= \dfrac{9.6 \times 10^{6}}{4.0 \times 10^{5}} = 24$. Forgetting the 0.1 mL gives 2.4; using one extra factor of ten in the dilution gives 240; 96 is just the plaque count.

questions.stem: When many lambda phages infect each cell in a culture, more of the infections become lysogenic. Why is this a sensible strategy for the phage?
choices: Many phages per cell signals that uninfected hosts are scarce, so staying inside the current host pays better than bursting it.
Many phages per cell provide enough DNA to fill the bacterial chromosome.
The bacteria kill phages faster when many attack at once.
Lysogeny produces more new phages per cell than lysis does.
