questions.explanation: Lysogeny is a bet on the host's future. If few fresh hosts remain, offspring released by lysis would find nothing to infect, so riding along as a prophage is better. Lysogeny releases no phages until induction, and it isn't about filling the chromosome.

questions.stem: A harmless strain of a bacterium becomes toxin-producing after it is infected by a particular temperate phage. What best explains this?
choices: The phage mutated the bacterium's own genes into toxin genes.
The phage carries the toxin gene, which is expressed from the prophage in the host chromosome.
The infection weakened the bacterium, releasing toxins it had stored.
Toxins are made only by phages, never by bacteria.
questions.explanation: This is lysogenic conversion. The toxin genes for cholera, diphtheria and Shiga toxin all travel on phages and are made by the bacterium once the prophage is in place. The phage doesn't invent new genes from the host's, and the toxin is made by the bacterial cell.

questions.stem: HIV reverse transcriptase makes about $3 \times 10^{-5}$ errors per base copied, and the genome is about 9,700 bases long. About how many new mutations does each new copy of the genome carry on average?
choices: About 3
About 30
About 0.3, roughly one new mutation per three genomes copied
About 0.003
questions.explanation: $9700 \times 3 \times 10^{-5} \approx 0.29$. With billions of copies made each day, every possible single mutation appears many times, which is why one drug alone soon fails. The other choices misplace the decimal point.

questions.stem: Antiretroviral drugs can suppress HIV to undetectable levels for decades, yet stopping treatment lets the virus return. Why?
choices: The drugs stop working after a few years.
Integrated provirus in resting cells is not touched by drugs that block replication, and it can restart production later.
HIV hides inside red blood cells.
The drugs only slow the virus and never stop it multiplying.
questions.explanation: Drugs block steps such as reverse transcription, integration and maturation, but a provirus already integrated into a quiet cell's chromosome isn't replicating. When treatment stops, such cells can produce virus again. Red blood cells have no nucleus and aren't HIV targets.

questions.stem: What two conditions make antigenic shift possible in influenza?
choices: A proofreading polymerase and a DNA genome
Infection of red blood cells and a lysogenic cycle
A single long RNA genome and a very slow mutation rate
A genome in separate segments, and two different strains infecting the same cell
questions.explanation: When two strains infect one cell, their eight RNA segments can be packaged in new combinations, producing a virus with surface proteins few people have immunity to. Gradual point mutations cause antigenic drift instead. Influenza has an RNA genome without proofreading.

questions.stem: An infection contains $10^{10}$ bacteria. Resistance to drug A arises in 1 cell in $10^{7}$ and resistance to drug B in 1 cell in $10^{6}$, independently. About how many cells are expected to resist both drugs before treatment starts?
choices: $10^{-3}$, so almost certainly none
questions.explanation: Double resistance needs both mutations in one cell: $10^{-7} \times 10^{-6} = 10^{-13}$ per cell, so $10^{10} \times 10^{-13} = 10^{-3}$ cells. That is why combination therapy works. $10^{3}$ and $10^{4}$ are the counts resistant to drug A or drug B alone; $10^{-13}$ is the per-cell probability, not the expected number.

questions.stem: In a fluctuation test, separate cultures had resistant-colony counts of 0, 0, 2, 0, 85, 1, 0, 4, 0, 0, while samples from a single culture gave counts close to their mean. What does the huge spread among separate cultures show?
choices: The phage induced resistance in a random fraction of cells.
The plates were contaminated unevenly.
Resistance mutations arose at random times during growth, before the cells met the phage.
Resistance is inherited only by some daughter cells.
questions.explanation: If resistance were induced on contact, every culture would give similar counts, like the samples from one culture. A culture where a mutation happened early grows a "jackpot" of resistant descendants, while most cultures have none, exactly as seen. The phage selects resistance; it doesn't create it.

questions.stem: A study finds that people with a certain illness have less diverse gut bacteria than healthy people. Which conclusion is justified by this finding alone?
choices: Low diversity causes the illness.
The illness causes low diversity.
Probiotics would cure the illness.
The two are associated, but the study can't show which causes which, or whether something else causes both.
questions.explanation: An observational comparison shows a correlation. The illness, its treatment, diet or another factor could change the microbiome, or the microbiome could contribute to illness. Experiments, such as transferring microbes into germ-free mice, are needed to test causation.

questions.stem: The HIV enzyme that copies the viral RNA genome into DNA is called ___.
questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template, the reverse of transcription. Integrase then inserts the DNA into a host chromosome. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as AZT were the first HIV drugs.

questions.stem: Match each kind of horizontal gene transfer to what happens.
choices: A plasmid passes from one cell to another through a pilus
A cell takes up naked DNA from its surroundings
A phage carries bacterial DNA to a new host cell
A cell splits into two identical daughter cells
questions.explanation: All three move genes between existing cells, often between species, which is how resistance genes spread quickly. Splitting into two identical cells is binary fission, which passes genes only from parent to offspring.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the HIV replication cycle in order.
choices: The virus binds CD4 and a coreceptor, and its envelope fuses with the cell membrane
Reverse transcriptase copies the RNA genome into DNA
Integrase inserts the DNA into a host chromosome
Host enzymes transcribe viral genes and viral proteins are made
New particles bud from the cell
Protease cuts the viral polyproteins and the particle matures
questions.explanation: Entry, reverse transcription, integration (the provirus), expression of viral genes, budding, then maturation by protease. Drug classes block entry, reverse transcription, integration or maturation.

questions.stem: Which of these are ways bacteria resist antibiotics? Select all that apply.
choices: Making an enzyme that destroys the drug
Pumping the drug out of the cell
Altering the drug's target so it binds poorly
Waiting for the antibiotic to cause the needed mutation
Moving the target into the nucleus, where the drug cannot reach
questions.explanation: Beta-lactamases destroy penicillins, efflux pumps push drugs out, and altered targets (such as MRSA's wall-building enzyme) resist binding. Antibiotics select existing mutations rather than causing the needed ones, and bacteria have no nucleus.

questions.stem: Which of these are well-established roles of human gut bacteria? Select all that apply.
choices: Fermenting dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids
Making vitamin K
Producing the body's insulin
Helping the immune system develop
Crowding out disease-causing microbes
questions.explanation: Gut bacteria ferment fiber we can't digest, make vitamin K, shape immune development (germ-free mice have underdeveloped immune tissues) and resist invaders such as C. difficile. Insulin is made by the pancreas, not by gut bacteria.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of negative feedback?
choices: Oxytocin strengthening contractions that release more oxytocin during childbirth
Activated platelets releasing chemicals that activate more platelets
Sweating when body temperature rises, which cools the body back toward 37 °C
Ripening fruit releasing ethylene that makes nearby fruit ripen and release more ethylene
questions.explanation: In negative feedback, the response reverses the change: sweating lowers a temperature that rose. The other three are positive feedback, where the response amplifies the change until an event (birth, a sealed wound, ripe fruit) ends it.

questions.stem: Why does the body rely on negative feedback, rather than positive feedback, to hold variables such as temperature steady?
choices: Negative feedback opposes any change, so it is self-correcting; positive feedback would push the variable further from its set point.
Positive feedback is too slow to respond to changes.
Negative feedback needs no sensors or effectors.
Positive feedback only works through hormones.
questions.explanation: Holding a set point requires a response that reverses deviations. Positive feedback amplifies them, which suits events that must be completed (childbirth, clotting) but would make a variable run away. Both kinds use sensors and effectors, and positive feedback can involve nerves as well as hormones.

questions.stem: A person steps out into freezing wind. Which pair of responses does the hypothalamus trigger to keep the core warm?
choices: Widening of skin blood vessels and sweating
Narrowing of skin blood vessels and shivering
Widening of skin blood vessels and shivering
Narrowing of skin blood vessels and sweating
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction keeps warm blood away from the cold skin, reducing heat loss, and shivering muscles release heat. Vasodilation and sweating are the responses to overheating; mixing them with cold responses would work against each other.

questions.stem: After a meal, blood glucose is 150 mg/dL; the set point is 90 mg/dL. Suppose insulin action removes half of the excess above the set point every 30 minutes. What is the glucose level 1 hour later?
choices: 120 mg/dL
105 mg/dL
90 mg/dL
75 mg/dL
questions.explanation: The excess is $150 - 90 = 60$. After 30 min it is 30, after 60 min it is 15, so glucose is $90 + 15 = 105$ mg/dL. 120 is the value after only one interval; 90 assumes the excess disappears completely; 75 halves the whole glucose level instead of the excess.

questions.stem: A sensory neuron is stimulated first weakly (but above threshold) and then much more strongly. How do its action potentials differ?
choices: They are larger with the stronger stimulus.
They are the same size, but they fire more often with the stronger stimulus.
They travel faster with the stronger stimulus.
Only the weak stimulus produces action potentials.
questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, each impulse has the same size and speed. Stimulus strength is coded by how frequently they fire.

questions.stem: Repeating Helmholtz's experiment, a nerve is stimulated 60 mm from a muscle (twitch after 3.0 ms) and 15 mm from it (twitch after 1.5 ms). What is the conduction speed?
choices: 20 m/s
30 m/s
10 m/s
40 m/s
questions.explanation: Subtracting cancels the muscle's own delay: $\dfrac{60 - 15}{3.0 - 1.5} = \dfrac{45 \text{ mm}}{1.5 \text{ ms}} = 30$ mm/ms $= 30$ m/s. Using one trial alone (60/3.0 or 15/1.5) includes the muscle delay and gives 20 or 10; 60/1.5 mixes the trials.

questions.stem: Diseases that damage myelin slow nerve signals. Why does myelin normally speed conduction?
choices: It produces extra neurotransmitter.
It makes action potentials larger.
It pumps sodium ions into the axon.
It insulates the axon so the impulse jumps from gap to gap instead of traveling continuously.
questions.explanation: Myelin is a fatty insulating sheath with gaps; the action potential is regenerated only at the gaps, so it effectively jumps along the axon. It doesn't change the size of the impulse or release transmitters, and the ion pumps are in the neuron's own membrane.

questions.stem: What makes the inside of a neuron become positive during the rising phase of an action potential?
choices: Potassium ions rushing in through opened channels
Sodium ions being pumped out by the sodium-potassium pump
Sodium ions rushing in through opened channels
Neurotransmitter molecules entering the axon
questions.explanation: At threshold, sodium channels open and positive sodium ions flood in. Potassium then flows out (not in) to restore the negative inside. The pump maintains the resting gradients but is too slow to produce the spike.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine at the synapses between nerves and muscles. What would you predict?
choices: Acetylcholine stays in the synapse and keeps stimulating the muscle, causing prolonged contraction.
The muscle can no longer receive any signal.
Nerve impulses stop traveling along the axon.
The muscle relaxes permanently because acetylcholine is used up.
questions.explanation: Normally the transmitter is broken down so each signal is brief. If it isn't removed, it keeps binding receptors and the muscle keeps being stimulated. Conduction along the axon itself is unaffected.

questions.stem: Bayliss and Starling cut all the nerves between the intestine and the pancreas, yet acid entering the intestine still made the pancreas release digestive juice. What did they conclude?
choices: The pancreas works without any signal at all.
The nerves had grown back during the experiment.
Acid travels from the intestine directly into the pancreas.
A chemical messenger carried in the blood links the two organs.
questions.explanation: With the nerves cut, the signal had to travel another way: through the blood. They extracted the messenger (secretin), the first hormone discovered. The response was triggered by acid in the intestine, so it wasn't spontaneous.

questions.stem: Several hours after a meal, blood glucose drops below the set point. Which response restores it?
choices: The pancreas releases glucagon, and the liver breaks down glycogen and releases glucose.
The pancreas releases insulin, and cells take up more glucose.
The pancreas releases glucagon, and muscle cells take up glucose from the blood.
The liver stores more glucose as glycogen.
questions.explanation: Low glucose triggers glucagon from the alpha cells, which makes the liver release glucose from its glycogen stores. Insulin and glycogen storage lower blood glucose, which would make the problem worse.

questions.stem: What is the underlying problem in type 1 diabetes?
choices: Cells stop responding to insulin even though plenty is made.
The pancreas makes too much glucagon.
The kidneys fail to remove glucose from the blood.
The immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells, so little insulin is produced.
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune: beta cells are destroyed, so the body makes little or no insulin. Insulin resistance describes type 2 diabetes. Kidneys normally reabsorb glucose rather than remove it.

questions.stem: Blood leaving the right ventricle goes next to the
choices: body, through the aorta
left atrium, through a valve
lungs, through the pulmonary vein
lungs, through the pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: The right side of the heart pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery. The aorta leaves the left ventricle; the pulmonary veins bring blood back from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries oxygen-rich blood?
choices: The pulmonary vein
The pulmonary artery
The vena cava
A vein returning blood from the leg
questions.explanation: The pulmonary veins carry freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Vessels are named for direction (arteries away from the heart, veins toward it), not oxygen content, so the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood.

questions.stem: During exercise, a student's heart rate is 80 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 75 mL. What is the cardiac output?
choices: 0.6 L/min
60 L/min
155 mL/min
6.0 L/min
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume $= 80 \times 75 = 6000$ mL/min $= 6.0$ L/min. 0.6 and 60 are unit-conversion slips (1000 mL = 1 L); 155 adds the two numbers instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: William Harvey calculated that the heart pumps far more blood in a day than a person eats and drinks, or than the whole body contains. What did this show?
choices: The liver makes new blood very quickly.
Blood is mostly water absorbed from the air.
The same blood must circulate repeatedly instead of being made from food and used up.
Arteries and veins are not connected.
questions.explanation: Thousands of liters a day can't be made from food or held in the body, so the same blood must loop round. That contradicted Galen's idea of constant production and consumption, and it predicted connections between arteries and veins (capillaries), found later.

questions.stem: Why does exchange of oxygen and nutrients with tissues happen in capillaries rather than in arteries?
choices: Capillary walls are one cell thick, so substances diffuse across them quickly.
Capillaries have valves that push substances out.
Blood in capillaries is under the highest pressure.
Capillaries carry blood directly from the heart.
questions.explanation: Diffusion is fast only across short distances, and capillary walls are a single thin cell layer. Arteries have thick, muscular walls; valves are found in veins; pressure is highest in the large arteries.

questions.stem: What is the main signal that makes you breathe faster during exercise?
choices: Falling oxygen in the blood
Rising blood glucose
Falling body temperature
Rising carbon dioxide, which lowers blood pH
questions.explanation: Brainstem sensors respond mainly to carbon dioxide, which forms carbonic acid and lowers pH. Faster breathing removes it: negative feedback. Low oxygen matters only when it gets quite low.

questions.stem: What happens as you inhale?
choices: The lungs expand on their own, pulling the diaphragm upward.
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, chest volume increases, pressure in the lungs falls, and air flows in.
The diaphragm relaxes, increasing pressure in the lungs and drawing air in.
Air pressure in the lungs rises above outside air pressure.
questions.explanation: Contracting the diaphragm and rib muscles enlarges the chest; lower pressure inside means outside air pushes in. Lungs have no muscle of their own; a relaxing diaphragm and higher lung pressure push air out.

questions.stem: A person breathes 15 times per minute with a tidal volume of 600 mL. Dead space is 150 mL per breath. What is the alveolar ventilation?
choices: 9.0 L/min
2.25 L/min
6.75 L/min
0.45 L/min
questions.explanation: Alveolar ventilation $= (600 - 150) \times 15 = 6750$ mL/min $= 6.75$ L/min. 9.0 L/min is total minute ventilation (ignores dead space), 2.25 L/min is the dead-space ventilation, and 0.45 L is the useful air in a single breath, not per minute.

questions.stem: A resting person uses 0.30 L of oxygen per minute. About 20 kJ of energy is released per liter of oxygen. How much energy does the person use per hour?
choices: 360 kJ
6 kJ
18 kJ
questions.explanation: Per minute: $0.30 \times 20 = 6$ kJ. Per hour: $6 \times 60 = 360$ kJ. 6 kJ is per minute, 18 kJ multiplies 0.30 by 60 without the energy factor, and 8,640 kJ is the total for a whole day.

questions.stem: The kidneys of a person filter 170 L of fluid in a day and produce 1.7 L of urine. What percentage of the filtered water is reabsorbed?
questions.explanation: Reabsorbed $= 170 - 1.7 = 168.3$ L, and $168.3/170 = 0.99$, so 99%. 1% is the fraction that becomes urine; 90% and 10% are off by a factor of ten in the urine fraction.

questions.stem: Glucose is found in the fluid entering a nephron's tubule, but healthy urine contains almost no glucose. Why?
choices: Glucose is too large to be filtered.
Glucose is filtered at the glomerulus and then almost entirely reabsorbed into the blood along the tubule.
The bladder absorbs glucose from urine.
Glucose is converted to urea in the kidney.
questions.explanation: Filtration is nonselective for small molecules, so glucose enters the filtrate; carriers in the tubule then reclaim nearly all of it. Glucose is small enough to pass the filter, which is why it's in the filtrate. Urea comes from amino acids, not glucose.

questions.stem: After hours of hiking without water, a person's blood becomes more concentrated. What happens next?
choices: ADH release falls, and a large volume of dilute urine is made.
The kidneys stop filtering blood until the person drinks.
The pituitary releases more ADH, more water is reabsorbed, and a small volume of concentrated urine is made.
More water is secreted into the tubules to flush out salt.
questions.explanation: Concentrated blood is sensed by the hypothalamus; ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so water returns to the blood: negative feedback. Less ADH is the response to drinking a lot. Filtration continues all the time.

questions.stem: Where does most chemical digestion and nearly all absorption of nutrients take place?
choices: The stomach
The large intestine
The esophagus
The small intestine
questions.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes and bile act in the small intestine, and its villi absorb the products. The stomach starts protein digestion but absorbs little; the large intestine mainly absorbs water; the esophagus only moves food.

questions.stem: What does bile do?
choices: It is an enzyme that digests fats into fatty acids.
It digests proteins in the stomach.
It breaks large fat droplets into tiny ones, giving lipase more surface to work on.
It neutralizes all the acid in the large intestine.
questions.explanation: Bile, made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, emulsifies fat; it contains no enzymes. Lipase does the chemical digestion. Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach, and bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes acid in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Proteins in food are absorbed mainly in the form of
choices: fatty acids
amino acids
simple sugars
nucleotides
questions.explanation: Digestion hydrolyzes proteins (starting with pepsin in the stomach) into amino acids, which are absorbed in the small intestine. Fatty acids come from fats, sugars from carbohydrates, nucleotides from nucleic acids.

questions.stem: In celiac disease, an immune reaction to gluten flattens the villi of the small intestine. What would you predict?
choices: Faster absorption, because food passes more easily
No change in absorption, because villi only produce mucus
Less acid production in the stomach
Reduced absorption of nutrients, because the absorbing surface area is much smaller
questions.explanation: Villi multiply the surface area for absorption, so flattening them reduces nutrient uptake. They are absorbing structures, not mucus producers, and the stomach is unaffected.

questions.stem: A snack contains 30 g of carbohydrate, 10 g of protein and 12 g of fat. Using 4, 4 and 9 kcal per gram, what is its energy content?
choices: 268 kcal
208 kcal
468 kcal
52 kcal
questions.explanation: $30 \times 4 + 10 \times 4 + 12 \times 9 = 120 + 40 + 108 = 268$ kcal. Using 4 kcal/g for fat gives 208; using 9 kcal/g for everything gives 468; 52 is just the total mass in grams.

questions.stem: Spallanzani put meat in gastric juice at body temperature and saw it dissolve. Which control was needed to conclude that the juice itself digested the meat?
choices: Meat in gastric juice at a colder temperature
Gastric juice with no meat added
Meat in plain water at the same temperature for the same time
A larger piece of meat in gastric juice
questions.explanation: Only the juice should differ between the groups. Meat in water under identical conditions shows whether warmth and time alone break meat down. The other setups change different variables or have no meat to observe.

questions.stem: Which of these is part of adaptive immunity?
choices: Stomach acid killing swallowed bacteria
Antibodies made against one particular strain of virus
Inflammation around a splinter
Neutrophils engulfing any bacteria they meet
questions.explanation: Adaptive immunity is specific to one antigen and builds memory; antibodies are its hallmark. Stomach acid, inflammation and general phagocytes act against any invader and belong to innate immunity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an antigen from an antibody?
choices: An antigen is made by B cells; an antibody is found on the surface of bacteria.
Antigens and antibodies are two names for the same molecule.
An antigen is a foreign molecule the immune system recognizes; an antibody is a protein made by B cells that binds it.
An antigen is a type of white blood cell; an antibody is a type of virus.
questions.explanation: The antigen is the marker (often a surface protein of a pathogen); the antibody is the Y-shaped protein the body makes to bind that marker. Swapping the two (saying B cells make antigens) is a common mix-up.

questions.stem: A person's second exposure to an antigen produces antibodies within a few days at about ten times the level of the first exposure, which took about two weeks to peak. What explains this?
choices: Memory cells formed during the first response multiply quickly when the antigen returns.
Antibodies from the first exposure have been circulating at a high level ever since.
The antigen is weaker the second time.
Innate immunity learns to recognize the antigen.
questions.explanation: The first exposure leaves long-lived memory B and T cells, so the secondary response is faster and larger. Antibody levels fall after the primary response, the antigen hasn't changed, and memory is a feature of adaptive, not innate, immunity.

questions.stem: What does an mRNA vaccine deliver?
choices: A weakened form of the whole virus that multiplies slowly
Ready-made antibodies against the virus
Instructions that cells use for a short time to make one protein of the pathogen, which the immune system learns to recognize
Genes that become permanently part of the person's DNA
questions.explanation: The mRNA is translated in the cytoplasm into one viral protein (the antigen), then broken down within days; it never enters the nucleus and can't change DNA. Ready-made antibodies give short-term passive protection, not vaccination; live attenuated vaccines are a different type.

questions.stem: A disease has $R_0 = 5$. What fraction of the population must be immune to reach the herd immunity threshold?
questions.explanation: Threshold $= 1 - \tfrac{1}{R_0} = 1 - \tfrac15 = 0.80$, or 80%. 20% is $1/R_0$ itself; 95% is the kind of value needed for measles, whose $R_0$ is much higher.

questions.stem: HIV infects and destroys helper T cells. Why does this weaken the immune system so broadly?
choices: Helper T cells activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so both antibody and cell-killing responses fail.
Helper T cells are the only cells that make antibodies.
Helper T cells form the skin barrier.
Helper T cells are the main phagocytes.
questions.explanation: Helper T cells coordinate the adaptive response. Without them, B cells (which make antibodies) and cytotoxic T cells are poorly activated, leaving the body open to infections. Antibodies come from B cells, and phagocytes are innate cells.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this neuron.

image.alt: A neuron with six numbered parts: branches on the left, a rounded body with a smaller circle inside it, segments wrapped around a long fiber, the fiber itself, and branched endings on the right.

choices: Dendrites
Nucleus
Cell body
Myelin sheath
Axon
Axon terminals
Synapse
Villus
questions.explanation: Dendrites (1) are the short branches that receive signals; the cell body (3) holds the nucleus (2). The axon (5) carries the impulse away, wrapped in segments of myelin sheath (4) with small gaps between them, and ends in axon terminals (6), which release neurotransmitter. A synapse is the gap between a terminal and the next cell, not part of the neuron itself.

questions.stem: A runner overheats. Put the steps of the negative feedback loop in order.
choices: Core temperature rises above the set point
Temperature sensors in the skin and hypothalamus detect the rise
The hypothalamus compares the reading with the set point
Sweat glands and skin blood vessels respond
Temperature falls back toward 37 °C and the signals weaken
questions.explanation: Every control loop runs stimulus, sensor, control center, effector, response. The last step is what makes it negative feedback: the response removes the stimulus, so the loop switches itself off.

questions.stem: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the ___ cells of the pancreas, so the body makes little ___.
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune: the insulin-making beta cells in the pancreatic islets are destroyed, so little or no insulin is produced. (Alpha cells, which make glucagon, are not the target.)

questions.stem: Which of these are examples of positive feedback? Select all that apply.
choices: Oxytocin release that strengthens contractions during childbirth
Activated platelets releasing chemicals that activate more platelets
Shivering when body temperature falls
Insulin release after a meal raises blood glucose
questions.explanation: In childbirth and clotting, the response amplifies the change until an event (birth, a sealed wound) ends the loop. Shivering reverses a fall in temperature, which is negative feedback. Insulin lowers glucose, it doesn't raise it, and its release is also negative feedback.

questions.stem: Match each feature to the control system it describes.
left: Signal carried in the blood to any cell with the receptor
choices: Endocrine system
Nervous system
questions.explanation: Nerve signals are electrical along the axon and chemical across a synapse, fast and brief, and reach only the cells the neuron connects to. Hormones travel in the blood, act on any cell with a matching receptor, and are slower but longer lasting.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this heart, drawn as seen from the front (the heart's right side is on your left).

image.alt: A schematic heart seen from the front with four chambers and the large vessels attached. Numbered markers sit in each of the four chambers, on the arched vessel leaving the thick-walled lower chamber, and on the vessel leading to the lungs.

choices: Right atrium
Right ventricle
Left atrium
Left ventricle
Aorta
Pulmonary artery
Vena cava
Pulmonary vein
questions.explanation: Seen from the front, the right atrium (1) and right ventricle (2) are on your left; they handle oxygen-poor blood and send it up the pulmonary artery (6) to the lungs. Blood returns to the left atrium (3), and the thick-walled left ventricle (4) pumps it into the aorta (5), which arches over to the body. The vena cava brings blood into the right atrium and the pulmonary veins enter the left atrium; neither is marked.

questions.stem: Put the stops of a red blood cell in order, starting in the right atrium.
choices: Right atrium
Right ventricle
Pulmonary artery
Lung capillaries
Pulmonary vein
Left atrium
Left ventricle
questions.explanation: The right side pumps blood to the lungs (pulmonary circuit) and it comes back to the left side, which pumps it to the body through the aorta. Atrium always comes before ventricle on each side.

questions.stem: The kidney's filtering units are called ___. In each one, blood pressure pushes fluid out of a ball of capillaries called the ___.
questions.explanation: About a million nephrons in each kidney filter blood at the glomerulus, then reabsorb what the body needs and secrete some wastes along the tubule.

questions.stem: Which features make the alveoli efficient at gas exchange? Select all that apply.
choices: Walls only one thin cell thick
A huge total surface area
A dense network of surrounding capillaries
Muscular walls that pump air in and out
questions.explanation: Diffusion is fast over short distances and large areas, and capillaries keep carrying oxygen away and bringing carbon dioxide, so the gradients stay steep. Alveoli have no muscle of their own; the diaphragm and rib muscles move air.

questions.stem: Match each event in urine formation to where it happens.
left: Blood pressure pushes water and small molecules out of the blood
Nearly all glucose and amino acids are reclaimed
Water reabsorption is adjusted by ADH
choices: Glomerulus and capsule
Proximal tubule
Collecting duct
Bladder
questions.explanation: Filtration happens at the glomerulus; the proximal tubule reabsorbs most of what the body needs, including nearly all glucose; ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water. The bladder only stores urine.

questions.stem: Name the numbered organs of the digestive system.

image.alt: A schematic digestive system with six numbered organs: a tube running down from the mouth, a large organ on the body's right, a J-shaped sac, a narrow organ beneath it, a long coiled tube in the center, and a wider tube framing it.

choices: Esophagus
Liver
Stomach
Pancreas
Small intestine
Large intestine
Gallbladder
Kidney
questions.explanation: Food goes down the esophagus (1) to the stomach (3), then through the long, coiled small intestine (5), framed by the wider large intestine (6). The liver (2) makes bile and the pancreas (4) makes digestive enzymes; both send them into the small intestine. The gallbladder, the small sac under the liver, isn't marked.

questions.stem: Put the parts of the digestive tract in the order food passes through them.
choices: Mouth
Esophagus
Stomach
Small intestine
Large intestine
questions.explanation: Mouth (chewing, amylase), esophagus (peristalsis), stomach (acid and pepsin), small intestine (most digestion and absorption), large intestine (water and salts). The liver and pancreas aren't on the path; their secretions enter through ducts.

questions.stem: Match each digestive secretion to what it does.
choices: Breaks starch into sugars
Begins protein digestion in the stomach
Breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Breaks fat into tiny droplets without digesting it
Absorbs water in the colon
questions.explanation: Each enzyme acts on one class of macromolecule: amylase on starch, pepsin (and later trypsin) on proteins, lipase on fats. Bile has no enzymes; it emulsifies fat so lipase has more surface. Water absorption in the colon isn't done by a secretion.

questions.stem: Antibodies are made by ___ cells. After an infection, long-lived ___ cells allow a faster, stronger response to the same antigen.
questions.explanation: B cells (as antibody-secreting plasma cells) make antibodies. Memory B and T cells remain after the first response, which is why a second exposure, or a vaccine booster, produces a faster and larger response.

questions.stem: Which of these belong to innate immunity? Select all that apply.
choices: Stomach acid killing swallowed microbes
Inflammation around a cut
Antibodies against one strain of flu
Phagocytes engulfing any bacteria they meet
Memory cells from a past infection
questions.explanation: Innate defenses are present from birth and act the same way against any invader: barriers such as stomach acid, inflammation and general phagocytes. Antibodies and memory cells are specific to one antigen, so they belong to adaptive immunity.

questions.stem: A cell has K⁺ at 4 mM outside and 160 mM inside. Using $E = 61.5 \log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{out}]}{[\text{in}]}$ mV, what is the K⁺ equilibrium potential?
questions.explanation: $\log_{10}(4/160) = \log_{10}(0.025) = -1.602$, and $61.5 \times (-1.602) \approx -98.5$ mV. $+98.5$ comes from flipping the ratio (in/out); $-226.9$ uses the natural log instead of $\log_{10}$; $-61.5$ is just the constant. K⁺ tends to leak out, so the inside must be negative to hold it in.

questions.stem: The resting potential (about −70 mV) lies between $E_{\text{K}}$ (about −90 mV) and $E_{\text{Na}}$ (about +60 mV), but much closer to $E_{\text{K}}$. Why?
choices: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺.
There is more K⁺ than Na⁺ outside the cell.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves K⁺ out of the cell.
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are open at rest.
questions.explanation: The membrane potential moves toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion the membrane is most permeable to. At rest, leak channels make it mostly permeable to K⁺, with a small Na⁺ leak pulling it a little positive of $E_{\text{K}}$. Outside, Na⁺ is far more concentrated than K⁺; the pump moves K⁺ in, not out; voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are closed at rest.

questions.stem: If the K⁺ concentration in the fluid around neurons rises well above normal, what happens to their resting potential?
choices: It becomes more negative, because more K⁺ leaks out.
It doesn't change, because the pump keeps the gradient constant.
It reverses to about +60 mV.
It becomes less negative (depolarized), because $E_{\text{K}}$ becomes less negative.
questions.explanation: More K⁺ outside brings the ratio out/in closer to 1, so its logarithm, and $E_{\text{K}} = 61.5\log_{10}([\text{K}]_{\text{out}}/[\text{K}]_{\text{in}})$, is less negative, and the K⁺-dominated resting potential follows it toward threshold. (Doubling outside K⁺ from 5 to 10 mM moves $E_{\text{K}}$ from about −89 to about −70 mV.) This is why blood K⁺ is tightly regulated, especially for heart cells.

questions.stem: Why does the action potential peak near +35 mV and then fall, instead of staying positive?
choices: The cell runs out of Na⁺ ions.
Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ flows out.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump suddenly speeds up and pumps the Na⁺ back out.
Neurotransmitter is released and pulls the voltage down.
questions.explanation: Within about a millisecond, an inactivation gate plugs the Na⁺ channels while the slower K⁺ channels open; the membrane becomes mostly permeable to K⁺ and the voltage heads back toward $E_{\text{K}}$. Very few ions move in one spike, so Na⁺ doesn't run out, and the pump is far too slow to shape a single spike.

questions.stem: Tetrodotoxin (TTX) blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. What would you expect in an axon treated with TTX?
choices: Action potentials fire more often.
The resting potential becomes strongly positive.
No action potentials can fire, but the resting potential barely changes.
Action potentials fire but travel backward.
questions.explanation: The rising phase depends on voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so no spike can start. The resting potential is set mainly by K⁺ leak channels and the gradients, which TTX doesn't touch, so it stays close to normal. That's why TTX was so useful for separating the Na⁺ current from the others.

questions.stem: An axon is stimulated twice. With 0.8 ms between stimuli, even a very strong second stimulus fails to fire. With 1.5 ms, a second spike fires only if the stimulus is 3 times the normal threshold strength. With 6 ms, a normal stimulus works. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: The absolute refractory period lasts at least 0.8 ms, and the relative refractory period covers at least part of the time from 1.5 ms to 6 ms.
The absolute refractory period lasts at least 6 ms.
The axon has no refractory period; the stimulator was faulty at 0.8 ms.
The relative refractory period comes before the absolute refractory period.
questions.explanation: No stimulus at all works during the absolute refractory period (Na⁺ channels inactivated), so it lasts at least 0.8 ms. A spike that needs a stronger stimulus marks the relative refractory period, which follows the absolute one. By 6 ms the axon has recovered, so the absolute period can't be that long.

questions.stem: In a myelinated axon, why are voltage-gated Na⁺ channels concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier?
choices: Myelin itself conducts the action potential, so channels are only needed at the ends.
The nodes are where neurotransmitter is released.
Na⁺ channels at the nodes pump Na⁺ out to keep the axon at rest.
The action potential is regenerated only at the nodes; under the myelin, current spreads passively and quickly to the next node.
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon so current from one node spreads quickly to the next with little loss; the slow step, opening channels, happens only at the nodes. That's saltatory conduction. Myelin doesn't carry the impulse, transmitter release happens at the axon terminals, and pumps are not channels.

questions.stem: An SSRI blocks the serotonin reuptake transporter. What is its direct effect at the synapse?
choices: Less serotonin is released from the vesicles.
Serotonin stays in the synaptic cleft longer, prolonging its action on the receptors.
The serotonin receptors on the next cell are blocked.
Serotonin is broken down faster by enzymes.
questions.explanation: Reuptake is one way a transmitter's signal is ended. Blocking the transporter leaves serotonin in the cleft longer. A receptor blocker would stop the transmitter acting at all, and release isn't directly changed. This describes the mechanism only; the drug's effects on a person are far more complex.

questions.stem: A reflex uses a sensory axon and a motor axon, each 0.75 m long and conducting at 50 m/s, with two synapses of 0.5 ms each. Ignoring muscle contraction, what is the reflex time?
choices: 16 ms
30 ms
31 ms
3.1 ms
questions.explanation: Path $= 2 \times 0.75 = 1.5$ m, so conduction takes $1.5/50 = 0.030$ s $= 30$ ms. Two synapses add $2 \times 0.5 = 1$ ms: total 31 ms. 30 ms leaves out the synapses; 16 ms counts only one axon; 3.1 ms is a unit slip.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this action potential recording.

image.alt: A graph of membrane potential in millivolts against time in milliseconds for one action potential, with a dashed horizontal line at about −55 mV. Five numbered markers sit at different points on the curve, from the flat start through the spike to the dip afterward.

choices: Resting potential
Threshold
Depolarization (rising phase)
Repolarization (falling phase)
Hyperpolarization (undershoot)
Synaptic delay
Equilibrium potential of Na⁺
questions.explanation: The flat line at about −70 mV is the resting potential (1). At about −55 mV, threshold (2), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open in a rush, and Na⁺ entry drives the rising phase (3). Na⁺ channels then inactivate and K⁺ channels open: the falling phase (4). Slow-closing K⁺ channels carry the potential below rest, toward $E_{\text{K}}$: the undershoot (5). $E_{\text{Na}}$ (about +60 mV) is above the peak and isn't marked.

questions.stem: Put the events of chemical synaptic transmission in order.
choices: An action potential reaches the axon terminal
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ flows in
Vesicles fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter
Neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors
Ligand-gated channels open in the postsynaptic membrane
Neurotransmitter is removed by an enzyme or by reuptake
questions.explanation: Electrical signal, then Ca²⁺ entry (the trigger for release), exocytosis, diffusion and binding, the postsynaptic response, and finally removal so that each signal is brief. The whole sequence takes about half a millisecond.

questions.stem: The gaps in the myelin sheath, where action potentials are regenerated, are called nodes of ___. Conduction that skips from gap to gap is called ___ conduction.
questions.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are packed with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; between them, myelin insulates the axon. Saltatory (from the Latin for "to leap") conduction is much faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon of the same width.

questions.stem: Match each toxin or drug to its target.
choices: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Release of acetylcholine from vesicles
Acetylcholine receptors on muscle
Acetylcholinesterase
Serotonin reuptake transporter
questions.explanation: TTX blocks the channels that make the rising phase. Botulinum toxin prevents vesicles fusing, so no acetylcholine is released. Curare sits on the muscle's receptors so acetylcholine can't bind. Organophosphates inhibit the enzyme that breaks acetylcholine down, so it builds up. The serotonin transporter is the target of SSRIs.

questions.stem: Which of these make a postsynaptic neuron more likely to fire an action potential? Select all that apply.
choices: A transmitter opening Na⁺ channels in its membrane
Many EPSPs arriving close together in time
A transmitter opening Cl⁻ channels that let Cl⁻ in
Extra GABA binding its receptors
questions.explanation: Na⁺ entry depolarizes the membrane (an EPSP), and EPSPs arriving close together add up (temporal summation) toward threshold. Cl⁻ entry pushes the inside more negative, an IPSP; GABA, the main inhibitory transmitter, typically works this way.

questions.stem: According to the clonal selection theory, when does a B cell acquire its ability to bind one particular antigen?
choices: Before it ever meets that antigen, through random rearrangement of its antibody genes
When the antigen binds and reshapes its receptor to fit
When a helper T cell tells it which antibody to make
After it has divided into plasma cells
questions.explanation: Specificity is generated randomly while the B cell develops (V(D)J recombination), before any antigen arrives. Antigen only selects the cells that already fit and makes them multiply. The idea that antigen instructs or molds the receptor was the older, disproved "instructive" theory; helper T cells activate B cells but don't choose their specificity.

questions.stem: A species has 50 V, 20 D and 5 J heavy-chain segments, 35 V and 5 J kappa segments, and 25 V and 4 J lambda segments. Counting segment choices only, how many heavy-light chain pairs are possible?
questions.explanation: Heavy chains: $50 \times 20 \times 5 = 5{,}000$. Light chains: $35 \times 5 + 25 \times 4 = 175 + 100 = 275$ (a cell uses kappa or lambda, so add). Pairs: $5{,}000 \times 275 = 1{,}375{,}000$. 875,000 forgets the lambda chains; 5,275 adds heavy and light instead of multiplying; 75 adds the heavy segments.

questions.stem: What determines whether an antibody is IgG, IgM, IgA or IgE?
choices: The variable regions of the light chains
The constant region of the heavy chains
Which antigen the antibody binds
Whether the antibody was made by a T cell or a B cell
questions.explanation: The heavy-chain constant region defines the class and decides what the antibody does (cross the placenta, enter secretions, bind mast cells). In class switching, the constant region changes while the variable regions, and so the antigen bound, stay the same. Antibodies are made only by B cells.

questions.stem: A patient's blood has IgM antibodies against a virus but no IgG against it. What is the most likely interpretation?
choices: The patient was vaccinated against the virus years ago.
The patient is immune and has memory cells from a past infection.
The patient has a recent, first infection with the virus.
The patient cannot make antibodies.
questions.explanation: IgM is the first class made in a primary response; switching to IgG takes longer. IgM without IgG points to a recent first exposure. A past infection or vaccination would show IgG (with IgM gone), and the patient is clearly making antibodies.

questions.stem: Which statement about MHC class I is correct?
choices: It is on nearly all nucleated cells and displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell to cytotoxic (CD8) T cells.
It is found only on antigen-presenting cells and displays engulfed material to helper T cells.
It is an antibody that circulates in the blood.
It displays whole, unbroken viruses on the cell surface.
questions.explanation: Class I lets any infected or cancerous cell show what it is making, so cytotoxic T cells can find and kill it. The description of antigen-presenting cells and helper T cells is MHC class II. MHC proteins are membrane proteins, not antibodies, and they hold short peptides, not whole viruses.

questions.stem: Cytotoxic T cells from virus-infected mice of strain A killed infected strain A cells but not strain B cells infected with the same virus. What does this show?
choices: Strain B cells can't be infected by the virus.
The T cells recognize uninfected strain A cells as foreign.
Cytotoxic T cells kill any cell carrying the virus, regardless of strain.
The T cells recognize the viral antigen only when it is presented on their own strain's MHC.
questions.explanation: This is MHC restriction (Zinkernagel and Doherty, 1974): the T-cell receptor sees viral peptide and self-MHC together. Strain B cells carried the virus, so infection wasn't the issue, and uninfected strain A cells weren't killed, so the T cells weren't attacking self.

questions.stem: A disease has $R_0 = 5$. In a community, 80% of people are vaccinated with a vaccine that protects 90% of recipients, and no one else is immune. What is $R_{\text{eff}}$?
questions.explanation: Immune fraction $= 0.80 \times 0.90 = 0.72$, so susceptible $= 0.28$ and $R_{\text{eff}} = 5 \times 0.28 = 1.40$, above 1, so an outbreak could grow. 1.00 ignores vaccine effectiveness ($5 \times 0.20$); 3.60 multiplies by the immune fraction instead of the susceptible one; 0.28 is the susceptible fraction itself.

questions.stem: A disease has $R_0 = 6$ and a vaccine is 95% effective. What vaccination coverage is needed to reach the herd immunity threshold?
questions.explanation: Threshold $= 1 - \tfrac16 = 0.833$ immune. Since only 95% of the vaccinated become immune, coverage $= 0.833 / 0.95 \approx 0.877$, or 87.7%. 83.3% forgets effectiveness; 79.2% multiplies by 0.95 instead of dividing; 17.5% starts from $1/R_0$.

questions.stem: A newborn is protected by IgG antibodies that crossed the placenta, but the protection fades over a few months. Why?
choices: The baby's immune system destroys the mother's antibodies as foreign.
IgG can only work inside the mother's body.
The antibodies switch class to IgM after birth.
This is passive immunity, so no memory cells were made and the borrowed antibodies are gradually broken down.
questions.explanation: Antibodies received from someone else protect at once, but nothing replaces them as they're cleared, because the baby's own B cells never responded. Only active immunity (infection or vaccination) makes memory cells. Maternal IgG works in the baby; it isn't treated as foreign, and class switching happens in B cells, not in circulating antibodies.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this antibody and what it is binding.

image.alt: A Y-shaped antibody made of four chains, with a small irregular shape bound at the tip of the left arm. Numbered markers sit on the bound shape, the stem, the outer chain of the right arm, and the very tip of the right arm.

choices: Antigen
Heavy chain
Light chain
Antigen-binding site
MHC protein
T-cell receptor
questions.explanation: The antigen (1) binds at the tip of an arm. The two long heavy chains (2) form the stem and the inner part of each arm; the shorter light chains (3) lie along the outside of the arms. At the tip of each arm, the variable regions of one heavy and one light chain fold together into an antigen-binding site (4), here empty on the right arm. MHC proteins and T-cell receptors are different molecules on cell surfaces.

questions.stem: Put the events of a B-cell response in order.
choices: Gene rearrangement gives a developing B cell one receptor specificity
Antigen binds the receptors of the matching B cell
A helper T cell recognizing the same antigen activates the B cell
The B cell divides repeatedly into a clone
Clone members become antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells
questions.explanation: Specificity comes first, before any antigen; antigen then selects the matching cell, a helper T cell gives the second signal, the cell multiplies, and the clone produces both effectors (plasma cells) and memory cells. That's clonal selection.

questions.stem: Match each antibody class to its key feature.
choices: First class made in a primary response
Crosses the placenta to protect a fetus
Guards mucous membranes and is in breast milk
Binds mast cells and triggers allergic reactions
Presents peptides to T cells
questions.explanation: IgM (five Y units) comes first; IgG is the most abundant in blood, dominates secondary responses and crosses the placenta; IgA is secreted in mucus, saliva, tears and milk; IgE binds mast cells. Presenting peptides to T cells is the job of MHC proteins, not antibodies.

questions.stem: Helper T cells recognize peptides displayed on MHC class ___, and they carry the marker protein CD___.
questions.explanation: Helper T cells are CD4 cells that recognize peptides on MHC class II, found on antigen-presenting cells. Cytotoxic T cells are CD8 cells that recognize MHC class I.

questions.stem: Which changes would raise the vaccination coverage needed to reach herd immunity? Select all that apply.
choices: A pathogen with a higher $R_0$
A vaccine that protects a smaller share of recipients
A pathogen with a lower $R_0$
A vaccine that protects a larger share of recipients
questions.explanation: Coverage needed $= (1 - 1/R_0)/E$. A higher $R_0$ raises the numerator, and a lower effectiveness $E$ shrinks the denominator; both push the needed coverage up. A lower $R_0$ or a more effective vaccine lowers it.

questions.stem: Why do the effects of a steroid hormone such as cortisol usually take hours to appear?
choices: Steroids travel very slowly in the blood.
The hormone-receptor complex changes gene expression, so new mRNA and proteins must be made.
Steroid hormones must first be converted into peptide hormones.
Steroid receptors are on the cell surface and must be carried inside.
questions.explanation: Steroids cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell; the complex acts as a transcription factor, so the response waits on transcription and translation. Blood carries hormones around the body in about a minute, steroids aren't converted into peptides, and their receptors are inside the cell.

questions.stem: Glucagon is a peptide hormone. Where are its receptors, and why?
choices: On the target cell's surface, because a water-soluble peptide can't cross the lipid bilayer
In the nucleus, because glucagon acts directly on DNA
In the cytoplasm, because glucagon dissolves in the membrane
In the blood, bound to carrier proteins
questions.explanation: Peptide hormones are water-soluble and can't diffuse through the hydrophobic core of the membrane, so they bind surface receptors and act through second messengers such as cAMP. Internal receptors are for lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid hormone); carrier proteins in blood transport steroids but are not receptors.

questions.stem: A hormone is at 120 units when its secretion stops. Its half-life in the blood is 10 minutes. What is its level 30 minutes later?
choices: 60 units
40 units
30 units
15 units
questions.explanation: 30 minutes is 3 half-lives: $120 \to 60 \to 30 \to 15$. 60 is one half-life; 30 is two; 40 divides by 3 instead of halving three times.

questions.stem: A patient has high TSH and low T4. Where is the problem most likely to be?
choices: The pituitary is making too little TSH.
The thyroid is overactive.
The thyroid is underactive, and the pituitary is responding to the lack of feedback.
The hypothalamus is making too little TRH.
questions.explanation: Low T4 removes negative feedback, so a healthy pituitary releases more TSH. High TSH with low T4 means the thyroid isn't responding: primary hypothyroidism. A failing pituitary or hypothalamus would give low TSH with low T4; an overactive thyroid gives high T4 and low TSH.

questions.stem: Why does long-term iodine deficiency cause the thyroid to enlarge into a goiter?
choices: Iodine normally shrinks the thyroid directly.
Without iodine, little T4 is made, feedback weakens, and constant high TSH stimulates the gland to grow.
The body stores unused iodine in the thyroid, which swells.
High T4 levels overstimulate the thyroid.
questions.explanation: T4 contains iodine, so without it T4 falls. Less T4 means less negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, TSH stays high, and the continuous stimulation enlarges the gland. T4 is low, not high, and there's no excess iodine to store.

questions.stem: Using the criteria in the lesson (fasting: under 100 normal, 100–125 prediabetes, 126 or more diabetes; 2 hours: under 140 normal, 140–199 prediabetes, 200 or more diabetes), how would you classify a fasting glucose of 108 mg/dL and a 2-hour value of 185 mg/dL?
choices: Prediabetes range on both measures
Normal
Diabetes range on both measures
Diabetes range on the 2-hour value only
questions.explanation: 108 is in the 100–125 band and 185 is in the 140–199 band, so both are in the prediabetes range. Neither reaches the diabetes cutoffs (126 fasting, 200 at 2 hours), and both are above normal. A real diagnosis is confirmed by repeat testing.

questions.stem: A person has high fasting blood glucose and also high fasting insulin. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Type 1 diabetes, because the beta cells have been destroyed
Too much glucagon and no insulin
Normal glucose regulation
{'Insulin resistance, as in type 2 diabetes': 'insulin is present but cells respond poorly'}
questions.explanation: Plenty of insulin that fails to lower glucose means the target cells aren't responding: insulin resistance, the hallmark of type 2 diabetes. Type 1 would show low insulin; "no insulin" contradicts the data; high fasting glucose isn't normal.

questions.stem: A patient makes large volumes of dilute urine. After an injection of desmopressin (synthetic ADH), the urine stays dilute. What is the most likely cause?
choices: {'Central diabetes insipidus': 'the pituitary releases too little ADH.'}
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
{'Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus': "the kidney doesn't respond to ADH."}
Drinking too little water
questions.explanation: If the problem were missing ADH (central), supplying it would concentrate the urine. No response means the collecting ducts can't respond to ADH: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Diabetes mellitus involves glucose and insulin, and drinking too little would give concentrated urine.

questions.stem: A person must excrete 720 mOsm of solutes a day, and their kidneys can concentrate urine to at most 1,200 mOsm per liter. What is the smallest daily urine volume possible?
questions.explanation: Volume $=$ solutes $\div$ concentration $= 720 / 1200 = 0.6$ L. 1.67 L divides the wrong way round ($1200/720$); 6.0 L and 0.06 L are decimal slips.

questions.stem: Put the steps of insulin release from a beta cell in order.
choices: Glucose enters the beta cell
Respiration of glucose raises the cell's ATP
ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels close
The membrane depolarizes and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open
Ca²⁺ enters and triggers exocytosis of insulin
questions.explanation: The beta cell measures glucose by burning it: more ATP closes K⁺ channels, the reduced K⁺ leak depolarizes the membrane, Ca²⁺ channels open, and Ca²⁺ triggers release, the same logic as transmitter release at a synapse.

questions.stem: Match each hormone to where it comes from.
choices: Made by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary
Anterior pituitary
Beta cells of the pancreas
Adrenal cortex
Thyroid gland
questions.explanation: ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. TSH is a tropic hormone from the anterior pituitary. Insulin comes from pancreatic beta cells, cortisol from the adrenal cortex (at the end of the CRH, ACTH axis). The thyroid makes T4 and T3, not any of these.

questions.stem: ADH makes collecting-duct cells insert water channel proteins called ___ into their membranes.
questions.explanation: Through cAMP, ADH moves aquaporins into the collecting-duct membrane, so water can flow out into the salty tissue around the duct and return to the blood.

questions.stem: Which hormones act mainly by binding receptors inside their target cells? Select all that apply.
choices: Cortisol
Estrogen
Insulin
Glucagon
Thyroid hormone (T3)
questions.explanation: Cortisol and estrogen are lipid-soluble steroids, and thyroid hormone, though not a steroid, also crosses the membrane; all three bind receptors inside the cell and change gene expression. Insulin and glucagon are peptides that bind surface receptors.

questions.stem: In the cycle data from the lesson, estradiol rose from 50 to 180 pg/mL between days 6 and 11 while LH stayed near 6–7 IU/L; on day 13, after estradiol had been above 200 for about a day, LH jumped to 45 IU/L. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Estradiol has no effect on LH.
Estradiol first restrains LH (negative feedback), then, once high for long enough, triggers an LH surge (positive feedback).
LH controls estradiol only by negative feedback.
The LH surge causes estradiol to rise from day 6 to day 11.
questions.explanation: A large rise in estradiol with flat LH shows LH being held down; the sudden LH surge after sustained high estradiol shows the switch to positive feedback. The surge came after the estradiol rise, so it can't have caused it, and the jump rules out "no effect".

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, what do the arrows show?
choices: The direction energy moves, from the food to the organism that eats it
Which organism hunts which, pointing from predator to prey
The order in which the organisms evolved
The direction in which matter is lost from the ecosystem
questions.explanation: Food-chain arrows point from the food to the eater, because they show energy (and matter) moving into the consumer. Reading them as "hunts" reverses them, the most common error. They say nothing about evolutionary order, and matter is recycled rather than lost.

questions.stem: The producers in a prairie store 80,000 kJ of energy per square meter per year. Using the ten percent rule, about how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
choices: 800 kJ
80 kJ
8 kJ
questions.explanation: Secondary consumers are two transfers above producers: $80{,}000 \times 0.1 \times 0.1 = 800$ kJ. 8,000 kJ stops after one transfer (that is the primary consumers). 80 kJ takes three transfers, which counts levels instead of steps, and 8 kJ takes four.

questions.stem: A forest's plants capture 30,000 kJ per m² per year (gross primary productivity) and use 18,000 kJ per m² per year in their own cellular respiration. What is the net primary productivity?
choices: 48,000 kJ per m² per year
18,000 kJ per m² per year
12,000 kJ per m² per year
3,000 kJ per m² per year
questions.explanation: NPP = GPP − producer respiration = 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000 kJ per m² per year. Adding gives 48,000, but respiration is a loss. 18,000 is the respiration itself. 3,000 is 10% of GPP, which confuses NPP with the ten percent rule between trophic levels.

questions.stem: Which ecological pyramid can never be inverted (wider at the top than at the bottom)?
choices: Pyramid of numbers
Pyramid of biomass
All three can be inverted in some ecosystems
Pyramid of energy
questions.explanation: Each trophic level gets its energy from the level below and loses some as heat, so a higher level can never carry more energy flow than the one feeding it. Numbers pyramids invert easily (one tree, thousands of caterpillars), and biomass pyramids can invert in the open ocean.

questions.stem: In some parts of the open ocean, the zooplankton present at a given moment weigh more than the phytoplankton they eat. How is this possible?
choices: Phytoplankton reproduce so quickly that they are eaten and replaced many times a year
Zooplankton are producers that make their own food
Energy flows from zooplankton back to phytoplankton
Zooplankton get most of their energy directly from sunlight
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid is a snapshot of what is present at one moment. Fast-reproducing phytoplankton have a small standing biomass but a large total production over the year, enough to feed a larger standing mass of zooplankton. Zooplankton are consumers, and energy never flows back down the food chain.

questions.stem: A rabbit eats 1,000 kJ of grass, but only about 100 kJ ends up as new rabbit tissue. Where does most of the rest go?
choices: It is destroyed during digestion
It is released as heat from the rabbit's cellular respiration, with some leaving in feces
It is stored as fat for the fox
It is returned to the grass as sunlight
questions.explanation: Most absorbed energy powers the rabbit's activity and body heat through cellular respiration and leaves as heat; undigested material leaves in feces and feeds decomposers. Energy is conserved, never destroyed. Fat is part of the 100 kJ of tissue, and energy does not return to plants as sunlight.

questions.stem: Which of these is an abiotic factor in a forest ecosystem?
choices: A fungus decomposing a log
The deer that browse on shrubs
The pH of the soil
Fallen leaves on the forest floor
questions.explanation: Soil pH is a nonliving physical and chemical condition. The fungus and deer are living. Fallen leaves are dead but came from living things, so they count as biotic material.

questions.stem: In Odum's Silver Springs study, the producers' gross production was about 20,810 kcal per m² per year and the herbivores' was about 3,368. About what percent of the producers' energy reached the herbivores?
questions.explanation: $3368 \div 20{,}810 \approx 0.16$, or about 16%, a bit above the typical 10%. 84% is the share that was not transferred. 6.2% comes from dividing the wrong way ($20{,}810 \div 3368 \approx 6.2$). 11% is the herbivore-to-carnivore transfer in the same study.

questions.stem: A grizzly bear eats berries in late summer and salmon (which eat smaller fish) in the fall. Which statement about the bear is correct?
choices: It feeds at more than one trophic level
It is a producer because it eats plants
It is only a primary consumer
It is a decomposer because it eats dead fish
questions.explanation: Eating berries makes the bear a primary consumer (level 2); eating salmon that eat other fish puts it at level 4 or higher. Omnivores often occupy several levels. Eating plants makes it a consumer, not a producer, and catching live fish is predation, not decomposition.

questions.stem: If all decomposers were removed from an ecosystem, what would happen over time?
choices: Producers would get more energy, because decomposers no longer take any
Nutrients would stay locked in dead material, and producers would run short of them
Nothing important, because decomposers are at the top of the food chain
Energy would begin to cycle instead of flowing through
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes and release nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus for plants to reuse. Without them, nutrients pile up in dead material and plant growth would eventually stall. Producers get their energy from sunlight, not from decomposers, and energy never cycles.

questions.stem: A student clips, dries and weighs all plants in four 0.50 m² quadrats and gets a mean dry mass of 120 g per quadrat. What is the estimated biomass density?
choices: 60 g per m²
120 g per m²
240 g per m²
480 g per m²
questions.explanation: Divide the mean mass by the quadrat area: $120 \text{ g} \div 0.50 \text{ m}^2 = 240$ g per m². 60 multiplies by 0.50 instead of dividing. 120 ignores the quadrat size. 480 adds up all four quadrats without dividing by the area they cover (2.0 m²).

questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and moves its carbon into food webs?
choices: Cellular respiration
Combustion of fossil fuels
Decomposition
Photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis builds CO₂ into sugars, the entry point of carbon into living things. Respiration, decomposition (which is respiration by decomposers) and combustion all release CO₂ to the air.

questions.stem: The Mauna Loa CO₂ record rises every year but also dips each Northern Hemisphere spring and summer. What best explains the summer dips?
choices: Photosynthesis by the large area of northern land plants increases during their growing season
People burn less fossil fuel in summer
Warm oceans absorb more CO₂ in summer
Volcanoes are less active in summer
questions.explanation: The Northern Hemisphere has most of the world's land plants. In its growing season, photosynthesis outpaces respiration and draws CO₂ down; in fall and winter, decay and respiration dominate. Fuel use does not fall enough to explain it, warm water actually holds less dissolved gas, and volcanoes have no seasons.

questions.stem: What happens in nitrogen fixation?
choices: Plants absorb nitrate from the soil through their roots
Bacteria convert nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia or ammonium
Bacteria convert nitrate back into nitrogen gas
Animals excrete nitrogen in urea
questions.explanation: Fixation turns unusable N₂ into ammonia/ammonium, mostly by bacteria (some in legume root nodules), plus lightning and the industrial Haber–Bosch process. Absorbing nitrate is assimilation, converting nitrate to N₂ is denitrification, and urea excretion is part of returning nitrogen through wastes.

questions.stem: Where is denitrification most likely to happen?
choices: In legume root nodules
In lightning strikes
In waterlogged, low-oxygen soil
In the leaves of plants during photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in place of oxygen, so they are most active where oxygen is scarce, such as soggy soils and wetland sediments, releasing N₂ back to the air. Root nodules and lightning are sites of nitrogen fixation, the opposite process.

questions.stem: Fertilizer runoff reaches a bay, and fish later die in a large low-oxygen dead zone. What is the most direct cause of the low oxygen?
choices: Nitrate is poisonous to fish
Fertilizer reacts with oxygen in the water
Algae use up oxygen by photosynthesis
Decomposers breaking down the dead algae from blooms use up the oxygen
questions.explanation: Extra nitrogen fuels algal blooms. When the algae die, decomposers respire as they break them down and consume the dissolved oxygen. This is eutrophication. Photosynthesis releases oxygen rather than using it, and the fertilizer does not react with oxygen directly.

questions.stem: A population of 50 frogs grows by a factor of $\lambda = 1.2$ each year. Using $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$, about how many frogs are there after 3 years?
questions.explanation: $N_3 = 50 \times 1.2^3 = 50 \times 1.728 = 86.4 \approx 86$. 80 adds 20% of the original 50 each year (linear growth, $50 + 3 \times 10$). 180 multiplies by $1.2 \times 3$. 104 uses 4 years ($50 \times 1.2^4$).

questions.stem: A population follows logistic growth with $r = 0.5$ per year and $K = 1000$. How fast is it growing when $N = 250$?
choices: 125 individuals per year
About 94 individuals per year
About 31 individuals per year
375 individuals per year
questions.explanation: $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\frac{K-N}{K} = 0.5 \times 250 \times \frac{750}{1000} = 93.75 \approx 94$. 125 is $rN$, the exponential rate that ignores $K$. 31 uses $N/K$ instead of $(K-N)/K$. 375 divides by $N$ instead of $K$, which leaves just $r(K-N)$.

questions.stem: For a population growing logistically toward carrying capacity $K$, at what population size is the number of individuals added per year greatest?
choices: Very small $N$, near 0
Just below $K$
Above $K$
questions.explanation: $dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K$ is a product of $N$ (small when the population is small) and $(K-N)$ (small near $K$); it peaks halfway, at $N = K/2$, the steepest part of the S-curve. Above $K$ the growth rate is negative.

questions.stem: Which of these is a density-independent factor?
choices: A disease that spreads faster when animals are crowded
Competition for nesting sites
Predators that focus on the most common prey
An early frost that kills 40% of the insects in an area whatever their number
questions.explanation: A frost kills the same fraction whether the population is large or small, so its effect does not depend on density. Disease, competition and predation all hit harder as density rises, so they are density-dependent.

questions.stem: Biologists catch and band 60 birds, then release them. A week later they catch 45 birds, and 9 have bands. What is the Lincoln–Petersen estimate of the population?
questions.explanation: $N = \frac{MC}{R} = \frac{60 \times 45}{9} = 300$. Check: 9 of 45 (20%) are banded, and 60 is 20% of 300. 2,700 forgets to divide by $R$. 405 is $45 \times 9$, and 7 inverts the formula; a population smaller than the 60 birds already banded is impossible.

questions.stem: Reindeer introduced to St. Matthew Island grew from 29 (1944) to about 6,000 (1963), overgrazed the slow-growing lichen, and crashed to 42 (1966) after a severe winter. Which conclusion do these data best support?
choices: Reindeer populations are limited only by predators
The population overshot the island's carrying capacity and damaged its own food supply
The population was growing logistically and stayed near $K$
Density-independent factors had no role in the crash
questions.explanation: The herd grew almost exponentially past what the lichen could sustain, then crashed, a classic overshoot. There were no predators, so predation cannot be the limit. A population that stays near $K$ does not crash by 99%. The severe winter (density-independent) triggered the crash after food shortage (density-dependent) set it up.

questions.stem: Barnacles attach to a whale's skin and filter food as the whale swims; the whale is neither helped nor harmed. What kind of interaction is this?
choices: Mutualism
Parasitism
Commensalism
Competition
questions.explanation: One species benefits and the other is unaffected (+/0): commensalism. Mutualism needs both to benefit, parasitism needs the host to be harmed, and competition harms both.

questions.stem: A sample contains 20 beetles: 5 each of four species. What is Simpson's diversity index, $D = 1 - \frac{\sum n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}$?
questions.explanation: $\sum n(n-1) = 4 \times (5 \times 4) = 80$ and $N(N-1) = 20 \times 19 = 380$, so $D = 1 - \frac{80}{380} = 0.79$. 0.21 forgets to subtract from 1. 0.75 uses $n^2/N^2$ (sampling with replacement) instead of the formula given, and 0.25 is just $1/4$.

questions.stem: Forest X has 100 trees: 25 each of four species. Forest Y has 100 trees: 85 of one species and 5 each of three others. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both have the same species richness, but X is more diverse because it is more even
Y is more diverse because it has more trees of its main species
They are equally diverse because both have four species
X is less diverse because no species dominates
questions.explanation: Both forests have four species (equal richness), but X spreads its trees evenly while Y is dominated by one species. Diversity indexes such as Simpson's count evenness as well as richness, so X scores higher. Treating richness as the whole of diversity is the mistake behind the third choice.

questions.stem: When Robert Paine removed the sea star Pisaster from a rocky shore, mussels took over and the number of species fell from 15 to 8. What does this show?
choices: Sea stars compete with mussels for sunlight
Pisaster is a keystone species that maintains diversity by keeping a dominant competitor in check
Mussels are parasites of other shore organisms
Removing a predator always increases diversity
questions.explanation: The predator kept mussels from monopolizing space, so its removal caused a large drop in species: the definition of a keystone species. Sea stars are predators of mussels, not competitors for light. The mussels outcompeted the others rather than parasitizing them, and the result shows the opposite of "removing a predator increases diversity."

questions.stem: A farm field is abandoned. Weeds appear the first year, then grasses and shrubs, then young pine trees after about 15 years. What is this?
choices: Primary succession, because the community is starting over
Competitive exclusion
Secondary succession, because soil was already present
Biomagnification
questions.explanation: Succession that begins where soil remains (after farming, fire or storms) is secondary succession, and it is fast because seeds and soil organisms are already there. Primary succession starts on bare rock or new ground with no soil.

questions.stem: A biome has very cold temperatures most of the year, permanently frozen ground below the surface, and low-growing mosses, lichens and shrubs but no trees. Which biome is it?
choices: Boreal forest
Desert
Temperate grassland
Tundra
questions.explanation: Permafrost and a treeless landscape of mosses, lichens and low shrubs define the tundra. The boreal forest is also cold but has dense conifers. Deserts are defined by low precipitation, and temperate grasslands have deep soils and warm summers.

questions.stem: Gause grew two Paramecium species separately and each thrived. Grown together on the same limited food, one species always died out. Which idea does this support?
choices: The competitive exclusion principle
Mutualism between the two species
The ten percent rule
Primary succession
questions.explanation: Two species using the same limited resource in the same place cannot coexist indefinitely; one outcompetes the other. That is competitive exclusion. Mutualism would help both species, and the ten percent rule and succession concern energy flow and community change over time.

questions.stem: According to the 2019 IPBES global assessment, what is the largest single driver of biodiversity loss on land?
choices: Invasive species
Habitat loss from changes in land use
Light pollution
Natural volcanic eruptions
questions.explanation: Converting forests, grasslands and wetlands to farms, cities and roads is the leading driver. Invasive species, climate change, pollution and overexploitation matter too, but rank behind land-use change on land. Volcanoes are natural and not a major cause of current losses.

questions.stem: In a lake, DDT measures 0.04 ppm in zooplankton and 10 ppm in fish-eating birds. By what factor is DDT more concentrated in the birds?
questions.explanation: $10 \div 0.04 = 250$. This is biomagnification: each predator eats many prey and stores the fat-soluble toxin. 0.004 divides the wrong way, and 25 and 2,500 are decimal-place slips.

questions.stem: Why do invasive species often spread so rapidly after being introduced to a new region?
choices: They have higher mutation rates than native species
They are always larger than native species
They are producers, which grow faster than consumers
They often lack the predators, parasites and competitors that limited them in their native range
questions.explanation: Freed from the enemies that kept them in check at home, introduced species can grow nearly exponentially, as the brown tree snake did on Guam. Invasives include animals and plants of every size, and nothing makes their mutation rates special.

questions.stem: Long-term fur records show snowshoe hare and lynx numbers both cycling about every 10 years. How do the peaks typically line up?
choices: Lynx peaks come shortly after hare peaks
Lynx peaks come shortly before hare peaks
The peaks happen in exactly the same year
The two cycles are unrelated
questions.explanation: Abundant hares feed more lynx, so lynx numbers rise after hares do; when hares crash, lynx follow. Predators cannot peak before their food supply has grown. Field experiments show food supply and predation together drive the hare cycle.

questions.stem: In this meadow food web, name the role of each numbered organism.
