image.alt: A meadow food web with grass and an oak tree at the bottom, a grasshopper, rabbit and mouse above them, a shrew, snake and fox above those, an owl at the top, and fungi and bacteria at the side receiving dead remains. Arrows point from food to eater. Four organisms are numbered.

choices: Producer
Primary consumer
Secondary consumer
Decomposer
Abiotic factor
Tertiary consumer
questions.explanation: 1 Grass makes its own food by photosynthesis: a producer. 2 The rabbit eats only grass: a primary consumer (level 2). 3 The snake eats the mouse, a primary consumer, so it is a secondary consumer (level 3). 4 Fungi and bacteria break down dead remains and wastes: decomposers. Nothing here is abiotic, and none of the numbered organisms eats a secondary consumer, so none is a tertiary consumer (the owl can be, when it eats a snake).

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → mouse → snake → owl, the owl is at trophic level ___. (Type a number.)

image.alt: A meadow food web in which grass is eaten by a mouse, the mouse by a snake, and the snake by an owl, among other feeding links.

questions.explanation: Count the levels from the producer: grass is level 1, the mouse (primary consumer) level 2, the snake (secondary consumer) level 3, and the owl level 4, a tertiary consumer. When the owl eats a mouse directly it is at level 3, so in the whole web the owl feeds at more than one level.

questions.stem: In the chain grass → grasshopper → shrew → owl, put the organisms in order from the trophic level with the MOST energy available per year to the level with the LEAST.
choices: Grass
Grasshopper
Shrew
Owl
questions.explanation: Energy is lost at every transfer, mostly as heat from respiration, so each level up has roughly a tenth of the energy of the one below it. Grass (producers) has the most, then grasshoppers, then shrews, and the owl at the top has the least. This is why the energy pyramid is always upright.

questions.stem: Which statements about energy in ecosystems are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Most energy an animal absorbs is used in cellular respiration and leaves as heat
Decomposers recycle energy back to the producers
Uneaten plant parts and feces pass energy to decomposers
A pyramid of energy can be inverted in the open ocean
Food chains rarely have more than four or five levels because so little energy reaches the top
questions.explanation: True: respiration uses most absorbed energy and releases it as heat; uneaten parts and feces feed decomposers; and with about 10% passed on per step, little energy is left after four or five levels. False: decomposers recycle nutrients, not energy (energy flows one way and leaves as heat). It is the biomass pyramid, not the energy pyramid, that can be inverted in the open ocean.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: Energy producers store as new tissue after their own respiration
Total dry mass of living organisms in an area
One feeding step in a food chain
About a tenth of the energy at one level reaches the next
Energy recycled by decomposers each year
questions.explanation: NPP is GPP minus producer respiration, the energy available to consumers. Biomass is measured as dry mass because water content varies. A trophic level is a feeding step (producers are level 1). The ten percent rule describes the average transfer between levels. The distractor describes something that does not happen: energy is not recycled.

questions.stem: Name the process shown at each numbered point of the water cycle.

image.alt: A water cycle diagram without process labels: the sun over an ocean, arrows rising from the ocean and from a tree toward a cloud, a second cloud with rain over a mountain, an arrow running down the land into the ocean, and groundwater flowing underground. Five points are numbered.

choices: Evaporation
Condensation
Precipitation
Transpiration
Runoff
Nitrogen fixation
Combustion
questions.explanation: 1 Water evaporates from the ocean surface, powered by the sun. 2 Water vapor cools and condenses into the droplets that make a cloud. 3 Water falls from clouds as precipitation. 4 Plants release water vapor from their leaves: transpiration. 5 Water flowing over the land surface back to the ocean is runoff. Nitrogen fixation belongs to the nitrogen cycle and combustion to the carbon cycle.

questions.stem: Put these steps in the order a nitrogen atom could follow, starting from the air.
choices: Soil bacteria convert N₂ gas to ammonium
Nitrifying bacteria convert the ammonium to nitrate
A bean plant absorbs the nitrate and builds it into protein
A rabbit eats the bean plant
Decomposers release ammonium from the rabbit's wastes
questions.explanation: Nitrogen enters living things only after fixation (N₂ to ammonium). Nitrification then turns ammonium into nitrate, which plants absorb and build into amino acids and proteins. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants, and decomposers return it to the soil as ammonium (ammonification), ready to be nitrified, absorbed or denitrified again.

questions.stem: The largest population an environment can support over the long term is its ___, written $K$.
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity ($K$) is set by limiting resources such as food, water and space. In logistic growth, the population's growth slows as $N$ approaches $K$ and stops when $N = K$.

questions.stem: Which processes add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere? Select all that apply.

image.alt: The carbon cycle, showing atmospheric CO₂ exchanged with land plants, animals, soil and decomposers, fossil fuels, the ocean, marine life and limestone.

choices: Cellular respiration
Photosynthesis
Burning fossil fuels
Decomposition
CO₂ dissolving into the ocean
Volcanic eruptions
questions.explanation: Respiration, decomposition (respiration by decomposers), combustion of fossil fuels and volcanoes all release CO₂ to the air. Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air, and so does CO₂ dissolving into seawater (the ocean is a carbon sink).

questions.stem: Classify each factor limiting a deer population.
left: A disease that spreads faster in crowded herds
More wolves hunting where deer are plentiful
choices: Density-dependent
Density-independent
questions.explanation: Density-dependent factors hit harder when the population is denser: disease spreads faster in crowds, competition for food intensifies, and predators concentrate where prey are plentiful. Density-independent factors such as a freeze or a wildfire kill about the same fraction whatever the density.

questions.stem: The chart plots biomes by average yearly temperature and yearly precipitation. Name the biome at each numbered region.

image.alt: A chart with average yearly temperature from minus 15 to 30 degrees Celsius across the bottom and yearly precipitation from 0 to 450 centimeters up the side, divided into seven unlabeled biome regions. Five regions are numbered.

choices: Tundra
Boreal forest
Desert
Savanna
Tropical rainforest
Temperate grassland
Temperate deciduous forest
questions.explanation: 1 The coldest, dry corner (below about −5 °C) is tundra. 2 Cold but wetter (about −5 to 5 °C) is boreal forest. 3 Under about 25 cm of rain a year, whatever the temperature range, is desert. 4 Hot with moderate rain and a long dry season is savanna. 5 Hot and very wet (over about 200 cm) is tropical rainforest. Temperate grassland and temperate deciduous forest are the two unnumbered regions in the middle temperatures.

questions.stem: Put the stages of primary succession on a new lava flow in order.
choices: Bare rock with no soil
Lichens and mosses colonize
Grasses and small plants grow in thin soil
Shrubs move in
Trees form a forest
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts without soil. Pioneer lichens and mosses break down rock and add organic matter, slowly building soil. Grasses and small plants follow, then shrubs, then trees. Secondary succession (after a fire or on an abandoned field) skips the pioneer stage because soil is already there.

questions.stem: Match each interaction to its effect on the two species (+ helped, − harmed, 0 unaffected).
questions.explanation: In mutualism both partners gain (legumes and Rhizobium). In commensalism one gains and the other is unaffected (barnacles on a whale). In parasitism one gains at the other's expense, usually over a long time (a tick on a deer). In competition both are harmed because they use the same limited resource.

questions.stem: Which changes to a community would increase its Simpson's diversity index $D = 1 - \frac{\sum n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}$? Select all that apply.
choices: A new species arrives and becomes moderately common
The species' numbers become more even
One species grows until it makes up most of the individuals
The rarest species, represented by a single individual, disappears
questions.explanation: Simpson's index rises with richness (more species) and with evenness (individuals spread more equally). A new, moderately common species adds richness; more even numbers add evenness. One species taking over lowers evenness, so $D$ falls. Losing a species with a single individual leaves $\sum n(n-1)$ unchanged but shrinks $N(N-1)$, so the fraction grows and $D$ falls.

questions.stem: A species whose removal causes a large change in its community, like the sea star Pisaster on rocky shores, is called a ___ species.
questions.explanation: Keystone species have effects far out of proportion to their abundance. When Robert Paine removed Pisaster, mussels took over and the number of species fell from 15 to 8. Sea otters, which keep sea urchins from destroying kelp forests, are another example.

questions.stem: In a cohort of 1,000 beetles, 300 are alive at the start of age 2 and 180 at the start of age 3. What is the age-specific mortality rate $q_2$?
questions.explanation: $d_2 = 300 - 180 = 120$ beetles die during age 2, and $q_2 = d_2/n_2 = 120/300 = 0.40$. 0.60 is the fraction that survive ($180/300$). 0.12 divides the deaths by an original cohort of 1,000, which is $d_x/n_0$, not a rate for those alive at age 2. 120 is the number of deaths, $d_2$, not a rate.

questions.stem: In a lizard life table, life expectancy at birth is $e_0 = 1.4$ years but at age 1 it is $e_1 = 1.8$ years. What best explains this?
choices: The table must contain an arithmetic error, because life expectancy always falls with age
Many lizards die in their first year; a one-year-old has already survived that risky period
Older lizards have lower mortality at every age than younger ones
Life expectancy counts only the years an animal spends reproducing
questions.explanation: $e_0$ averages over all newborns, including the 60% that die in their first year. A lizard that reaches age 1 has escaped that high early mortality, so its expected remaining life can be longer. This happens whenever first-year mortality is very high. Life expectancy does not always fall with age, mortality in this table later rises again with age, and $e_x$ counts all remaining years, not just breeding years.

questions.stem: Survivors per 1,000 are plotted on a log scale against age. Identify each numbered survivorship curve.

image.alt: Graph of survivors per 1,000 on a log scale against age as a percent of maximum life span, with three unlabeled curves that all start at 1,000. One stays high until late life and then plunges, one is a straight diagonal line, and one plunges at very young ages and then levels off. Each curve is numbered.

choices: Type I
Type II
Type III
Logistic curve
questions.explanation: 1 High survival until old age, then a steep drop: Type I (humans, large mammals). 2 A straight line on a log scale means the same fraction dies every year: Type II (many lizards, some adult birds). 3 Very high mortality among the young and then low mortality for survivors: Type III (oysters, most marine fish). A logistic curve shows population size over time, not survival with age.

questions.stem: On a survivorship graph with a log-scale vertical axis, a population's curve is a straight line sloping down. What does this tell you?
choices: The same number of individuals dies each year
Most individuals die in old age
The same fraction of the survivors dies each year
Most individuals die soon after birth
questions.explanation: On a log scale, equal vertical steps are equal ratios, so a straight line means a constant proportion of survivors dies each age interval: a Type II curve. A constant number of deaths per year would be a straight line on a linear axis instead. Death mostly in old age is Type I, and death mostly soon after birth is Type III.

questions.stem: A fish population has survivorship $l_x$ = 1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.05 at ages 0 to 3 and fecundity $m_x$ = 0, 2, 4, 2 daughters per female. What is the net reproductive rate $R_0$, and what will the population do?
choices: $R_0 = 8$; it grows
$R_0 = 0.475$; it shrinks
$R_0 = 1.8$; it grows
$R_0 = 1.9$; it grows
questions.explanation: $R_0 = \sum l_x m_x = 1(0) + 0.5(2) + 0.2(4) + 0.05(2) = 0 + 1.0 + 0.8 + 0.1 = 1.9$. Each female leaves 1.9 daughters, so the population grows. 8 adds the $m_x$ values without weighting by survival. 1.8 leaves out the age-3 term. 0.475 averages the four products instead of adding them; $R_0$ is a lifetime total.

questions.stem: Which traits are traditionally associated with r-selected species? Select all that apply.
choices: Many small offspring
Early maturity
Extensive parental care
Long life span
Populations that boom and crash far below carrying capacity
questions.explanation: r-selected species are favored where populations are usually below $K$ and fast multiplication pays: early maturity, many small offspring, and boom-and-bust numbers. Extensive parental care and long lives are K-selected traits. Remember the caveat: real species are mixtures, and age-specific mortality explains life histories better than the r/K labels.

questions.stem: Guppies moved from a stream where predators eat mainly adults to one where the only predator eats mainly juveniles evolved, within about 11 years, later maturity and fewer, larger offspring. Which conclusion do these results best support?
choices: Which ages suffer the most mortality can drive the evolution of life-history traits
Guppies changed their traits by choice to avoid the new predator
Population density alone determines life-history traits
Life-history traits cannot evolve in fewer than a thousand generations
questions.explanation: When adults face high mortality, breeding early and often is favored; when juveniles are the ones eaten, it pays to mature later and invest in fewer, larger young that grow past the danger. The change was evolution by natural selection, not choice, and it happened in about 30–60 generations. The experiment changed the pattern of mortality by age, which is why it challenges the density-based r/K explanation.

questions.stem: A population's per capita growth rate was 0.30 per year when it numbered 100 and 0.10 per year when it numbered 300. Assuming per capita growth falls in a straight line with density, estimate the carrying capacity $K$.
questions.explanation: Slope: $(0.10 - 0.30)/(300 - 100) = -0.001$ per individual. At $N = 0$ the rate is $0.30 + 0.001 \times 100 = 0.40$, so $r = 0.40$. The rate reaches zero when $0.40 - 0.001N = 0$, at $N = 400$. 300 is the last data point, not where growth stops; 500 and 200 come from slips in the slope or intercept.

questions.stem: In the Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model, predators hold steady when the prey number is $H = m/(ab)$. If the predator death rate is $m = 0.5$, the attack rate is $a = 0.01$ and the conversion efficiency is $b = 0.2$, the prey number at which predators hold steady is ___.
questions.explanation: $H = \dfrac{m}{ab} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.01 \times 0.2} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.002} = 250$ prey. Below 250 prey, predators decline; above it, they increase.

questions.stem: In both the Lotka–Volterra model and the hare–lynx records, why do predator peaks come after prey peaks?
choices: Predators reproduce faster than prey
Predators switch to other prey when hares are common
Predator numbers grow only after abundant prey has let them raise more young, and keep rising until prey become scarce
Prey numbers are set by weather, which changes after predator numbers
questions.explanation: Predators respond to food with a delay: abundant prey must first be eaten and turned into new predators. Predators keep increasing while prey are plentiful, and their numbers peak just as heavy predation drives prey down. Predators such as lynx actually reproduce more slowly than hares, switching prey would weaken the cycle, and weather does not explain the regular lag.

questions.stem: At Kluane Lake, averaged over the peak and decline years, adding food tripled hare density, excluding mammal predators roughly doubled it, and doing both increased it about elevenfold. What do these results show?
choices: Food alone drives the hare cycle
Predators alone drive the hare cycle
Neither food nor predators matter to hares
Food and predation act together, and their combined effect is larger than either alone
questions.explanation: Each treatment alone had an effect, so neither factor can be ignored, and the combined effect (11×) was much more than either (3× or 2×) and more than the 6× expected if the effects simply multiplied. The cycle is driven by food and predation interacting, along with predator-caused stress on breeding.

questions.stem: In the predator–prey model $\frac{dH}{dt} = rH - aHP$ and $\frac{dP}{dt} = baHP - mP$, match each term to what it represents.
choices: Prey births minus deaths with no predators
Prey killed by predators
New predators produced from prey eaten
Predator deaths
Prey carrying capacity
questions.explanation: $rH$ is exponential prey growth. $aHP$ removes prey in proportion to how often predators meet prey. $baHP$ converts a fraction $b$ of prey eaten into new predators. $mP$ is predator mortality. The basic model has no carrying capacity for prey, one of the reasons it is unrealistic.

questions.stem: Starting from a hare peak, put these events in a predator–prey cycle in order.
choices: Hare numbers peak
Lynx numbers peak
Hare numbers reach their low
Lynx numbers reach their low
questions.explanation: Abundant hares feed lynx, so lynx peak a little after hares. Heavy predation then drives hares to their low, and with little food the lynx decline to their own low afterward. With predation eased, hares recover and the cycle repeats.

questions.stem: In the Lotka–Volterra competition model, species 1 has $K_1 = 600$ and species 2 has $K_2 = 500$. Each species-2 individual affects species 1 like 0.4 of its own ($\alpha_{12} = 0.4$), but each species-1 individual affects species 2 like 1.5 of its own ($\alpha_{21} = 1.5$). Coexistence requires $\alpha_{12} < K_1/K_2$ and $\alpha_{21} < K_2/K_1$. What does the model predict?
choices: Species 1 excludes species 2
Species 2 excludes species 1
The two species coexist
Both species go extinct
questions.explanation: $K_1/K_2 = 1.2$ and $\alpha_{12} = 0.4 < 1.2$, so species 2 cannot exclude species 1. But $K_2/K_1 \approx 0.83$ and $\alpha_{21} = 1.5 > 0.83$: species 1 suppresses species 2 more than species 2 limits itself. Species 1 wins. Coexistence would need both conditions to hold, and the model never drives both species extinct.

questions.stem: Which is the most important caution when treating Hudson's Bay Company pelt records as counts of lynx populations?
choices: Lynx pelts cannot be told apart from hare pelts
The number of pelts also depended on trapping effort and fur prices, not only on how many lynx were alive
Lynx do not eat hares
The records cover too few years to show any cycle
questions.explanation: Pelt counts measure the catch, which rises and falls with how hard trappers worked and how much fur paid, as well as with lynx numbers. That is why ecologists confirmed the cycle with field studies and experiments. The records span about a century and show many cycles, lynx do eat mostly hares, and the pelts are easy to distinguish.

questions.stem: Lake water starts with 7.0 mg O₂/L. After 4 hours the light bottle reads 8.1 mg/L and the dark bottle 6.4 mg/L. What is the gross primary productivity over the 4 hours?

image.alt: An initial bottle of lake water with algae, a clear light bottle and a dark bottle wrapped to block light, suspended in the lake.

choices: 1.1 mg O₂/L
0.6 mg O₂/L
1.7 mg O₂/L
0.5 mg O₂/L
questions.explanation: GPP = light − dark = $8.1 - 6.4 = 1.7$ mg O₂/L. Equivalently, net production ($8.1 - 7.0 = 1.1$) plus respiration ($7.0 - 6.4 = 0.6$) = 1.7. 1.1 is net production only, 0.6 is respiration only, and 0.5 subtracts respiration from net production instead of adding it.

questions.stem: In a light and dark bottle experiment, the initial oxygen is 7.6 mg/L, the light bottle ends at 8.5 mg/L and the dark bottle at 7.0 mg/L. Gross primary productivity is ___ mg O₂ per liter for the run.
questions.explanation: GPP = light − dark = $8.5 - 7.0 = 1.5$ mg O₂/L. Check: net production $8.5 - 7.6 = 0.9$ plus respiration $7.6 - 7.0 = 0.6$ gives 1.5.

questions.stem: Why does the light and dark bottle method need the dark bottle?
choices: To measure how much light reaches the depth where the bottles hang
To prevent the algae from photosynthesizing too fast
To provide a bottle in which algae cannot grow at all
To measure respiration, which goes on in the light bottle too and hides part of the oxygen produced
questions.explanation: In the light bottle, respiration uses up some of the oxygen photosynthesis makes, so its oxygen gain shows only net production. The dark bottle, where only respiration occurs, measures that loss so it can be added back: GPP = light − dark. The dark bottle does not measure light, and it does not merely stop growth: it is a measurement of respiration.

questions.stem: Tower measurements show that a forest's net ecosystem production (NEP) averaged +2 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year over a decade. What does this mean?
choices: The forest took in more carbon by photosynthesis than plants, animals and decomposers released by respiration, so it stored carbon
The forest's plants did no respiration
The forest released 2 tonnes more carbon than it absorbed
The forest's net primary productivity was zero
questions.explanation: NEP = GPP − plant respiration − heterotrophic respiration. A positive value means more carbon was fixed than respired, so the forest acted as a carbon sink, storing carbon in wood and soil. A net release would make NEP negative. Plants still respire, and NPP must be greater than NEP whenever consumers and decomposers respire.

questions.stem: In the Lake 226 experiment, one basin received carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus and developed a dense algal bloom; the other received the same carbon and nitrogen but no phosphorus and stayed clear. What does this show?
choices: Nitrogen was the limiting nutrient
Phosphorus was the limiting nutrient
Carbon was the limiting nutrient
Algae need no nutrients besides light
questions.explanation: The only difference between the basins was phosphorus, and only the phosphorus basin bloomed, so phosphorus limited algal growth. Both basins got nitrogen and carbon, so neither of those can explain the difference. The result helped lead to limits on phosphate detergents.

questions.stem: Some regions of the open ocean have plenty of nitrate and phosphate but few phytoplankton. When iron was added to a patch of the equatorial Pacific in 1995, a large bloom followed. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Nitrate was limiting there
Light was limiting there
Iron was limiting there
Adding iron is a proven way to stop climate change
questions.explanation: Adding iron, and nothing else, produced the bloom, so iron was the limiting nutrient in that patch; nitrate and phosphate were already plentiful, and light was unchanged. Whether iron fertilization would store carbon for long is a separate, unresolved question, so the experiment does not show it can stop climate change.

questions.stem: Which processes return nitrogen to the atmosphere as N₂ gas? Select all that apply.
choices: Denitrification
Nitrification
Anammox
Nitrogen fixation
Ammonification
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria reduce nitrate step by step to N₂, and anammox bacteria combine ammonium with nitrite to make N₂; both happen where oxygen is low. Nitrification turns ammonium into nitrite and nitrate, fixation does the opposite of returning N₂ (it removes N₂ from the air), and ammonification releases ammonium from dead matter.

questions.stem: Ammonium in a farm field is nitrified, and the nitrate later washes into a waterlogged wetland and is denitrified. Put the forms of nitrogen in the order they appear.
choices: Ammonium (NH₄⁺)
Nitrite (NO₂⁻)
Nitrate (NO₃⁻)
Nitrous oxide (N₂O)
Nitrogen gas (N₂)
questions.explanation: Nitrification needs oxygen: ammonia oxidizers make nitrite, then nitrite oxidizers make nitrate. In the low-oxygen wetland, denitrifiers reduce nitrate (through nitrite and nitric oxide) to nitrous oxide and finally N₂. If denitrification stops partway, N₂O, a strong greenhouse gas, escapes.

questions.stem: In 2023, human activities emitted about 11.1 billion tonnes of carbon (GtC) as CO₂, and the atmosphere gained about 5.9 GtC. What was the airborne fraction?
choices: About 47%
About 1.9%
About 188%
About 53%
questions.explanation: Airborne fraction = $5.9/11.1 \approx 0.53$, about 53%. The other 47% (5.2 GtC) went into the ocean and land sinks, so 47% is the sink share, not the airborne fraction. 188% divides the wrong way, and 1.9% is not a ratio of these two numbers at all.

questions.stem: One part per million (ppm) of atmospheric CO₂ contains about 2.12 GtC. If the atmosphere gains 5.3 GtC in a year, CO₂ rises by about ___ ppm. (Give one decimal place.)
questions.explanation: $5.3 \div 2.12 = 2.5$ ppm. Multiplying instead of dividing would give about 11, far more than any year on record.

questions.stem: As CO₂ has risen, the fraction of carbon-13 and carbon-14 in atmospheric CO₂ has fallen. Why does this point to fossil fuels as the source?
choices: Fossil fuels formed from ancient plants, which are low in carbon-13, and are so old that their carbon-14 has decayed away
Volcanoes release CO₂ that is rich in carbon-14
The ocean releases CO₂ with no carbon-13
Carbon-14 is destroyed by rising temperature
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis favors carbon-12, so plant-derived carbon is low in carbon-13; fossil fuels are millions of years old, far longer than carbon-14's half-life of about 5,700 years, so they contain none. Adding such carbon dilutes both isotopes in the air, exactly as observed. Volcanic carbon has no carbon-14 either but is not depleted in carbon-13 the same way, ocean carbon is not carbon-13-free, and temperature does not destroy carbon-14.

questions.stem: Match each line of evidence to what it shows.
left: Yearly wiggle in the Keeling curve
choices: CO₂ today is higher than at any time in 800,000 years
Northern Hemisphere land plants take up CO₂ in summer
The added CO₂ comes from burning fuel
Seawater is absorbing CO₂
The Sun has grown much brighter since 1950
questions.explanation: Ice cores preserve ancient air, showing CO₂ between about 180 and 300 ppm for 800,000 years. The seasonal Keeling wiggle tracks northern photosynthesis and decay. Combustion uses oxygen as it makes CO₂, so falling O₂ fingerprints burning. Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering pH. The distractor is false: solar output has not risen enough to explain recent warming.

questions.stem: Ocean producers are well under 1% of Earth's producer biomass, yet they account for about half of global net primary productivity. How is that possible?
choices: Ocean producers are larger than land plants
Phytoplankton grow and are eaten so quickly that a small standing biomass is replaced many times a year
Ocean producers do not respire
Ocean producers photosynthesize at night as well as during the day
questions.explanation: Productivity is a rate, and biomass is a stock. Phytoplankton divide every few days and are grazed almost as fast, so a tiny standing stock produces a huge flow, the same reason open-ocean biomass pyramids can be inverted. Phytoplankton are microscopic, they do respire, and photosynthesis needs light.

questions.stem: Pond-water flasks are given nutrients for a week. Final chlorophyll (µg/L): control 6, nitrogen added 22, phosphorus added 7, both added 45. What do the results show?
choices: Phosphorus is the primary limiting nutrient
Neither nutrient limits the algae
Nitrogen is the primary limiting nutrient, and phosphorus becomes limiting once nitrogen is added
Both nutrients are toxic to the algae
questions.explanation: Adding nitrogen alone nearly quadruples growth (6 to 22), while phosphorus alone does almost nothing (6 to 7), so nitrogen is the first limit. With nitrogen supplied, adding phosphorus too doubles growth again (22 to 45): the algae are co-limited, with nitrogen first. Both additions raised growth, so neither is toxic.

cards.back: Exactly how a variable is measured or applied, e.g. "growth = dry mass after 21 days". Makes a study repeatable.
Positive: a treatment known to give the effect (shows the method works). Negative: everything but the tested factor, expected to show no effect (e.g. solvent only).
A factor that changes along with the treatment and also affects the outcome, e.g. all treated plants on the warmer shelf.
The unit is what independently gets the treatment (pot, cage, dish). Counting many measurements of one unit as replicates is pseudoreplication.

cards.front: Sample size needed for a target SE
cards.back: $n \ge (\text{SD}/\text{SE}_{\text{target}})^2$, rounded up. Halving the SE takes 4 times the sample.
The chance a study detects a real effect of a given size. Small studies have low power, so "no significant difference" from them means little.
Random assignment: chance decides who gets which treatment, so groups differ only by chance. Blinding: people don't know who got what, preventing observer bias.
Single-blind: subjects don't know their treatment. Double-blind: neither subjects nor the researchers treating and measuring them know.

cards.front: Why more data don't fix bias
cards.back: Bias is systematic: a bigger biased sample just gives a more precise wrong answer. Fix the design (randomize, blind, sample fairly).
Respect for persons (informed consent), beneficence (maximize benefits, minimize harms), justice (share burdens and benefits fairly). An IRB reviews studies on people.
Replace animals where possible, reduce the number used, refine procedures to minimize pain and distress (Russell and Burch, 1959).
Randomized placebo trial: 28 vs 71 cases per 100,000. Comparing volunteers with non-volunteers was biased, because consenting families differed in polio risk.
Mean = sum/n, pulled by outliers. Median = middle value, resists outliers. Use the median for skewed data such as parasite counts.
$s = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}$: deviations from the mean, squared, summed, divided by $n - 1$, square-rooted.
About 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean and about 95% within 2 SD (1.96 exactly).
$\text{SE} = s/\sqrt{n}$. Measures how precisely the mean is known; shrinks as $n$ grows.
SD: spread of individuals; settles near the true spread with more data. SE: precision of the mean; keeps shrinking with more data.
$\bar{x} \pm 2\,\text{SE}$. Small samples need a larger multiplier from the t distribution (2.36 for n = 8).
About 95% of intervals made this way, in repeated studies, would contain the true mean. Not "95% of the data lie inside."
Check the legend first. Overlapping SE bars: not significant. Non-overlapping 95% CIs: significant (p < 0.05). Slightly overlapping CIs can still be significant.
Groups: dot plot with mean and error bars. Change over time or dose: line graph. Two measured variables: scatter plot. One distribution: histogram or box plot.
Box from lower to upper quartile, line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme non-outliers, outliers (beyond 1.5 box-lengths) as points.
The probability, if the null hypothesis is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. Reject $H_0$ when $p \le \alpha$ (usually 0.05).
Not the chance $H_0$ is true; not the size or importance of the effect; p > 0.05 is not proof of no effect.

cards.front: Type I vs Type II error
cards.back: Type I: rejecting a true $H_0$ (false positive, rate $\alpha$). Type II: failing to reject a false $H_0$ (missing a real effect).
Expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total; $\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E$; df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).
$t = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\text{SE}_1^2 + \text{SE}_2^2}}$, df = $n_1 + n_2 - 2$. For moderate samples, $|t| >$ about 2 is significant.
Counts vs a predicted ratio: chi-square goodness of fit. Two categorical variables: chi-square independence. Two means: t-test. Two measured variables: correlation and regression.
From −1 to 1: sign gives direction, size gives strength of a straight-line relationship. Correlation can come from a confounder, reverse cause or chance.
$\hat{y} = a + bx$ with $b = \dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y})}{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}$ and $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$; $r^2$ = fraction of variation explained. Don't extrapolate.
Introduction (why), Methods (what was done), Results (what was found), Discussion (what it means); after the title and abstract.

cards.front: How to read a paper efficiently
cards.back: Abstract, then figures and legends, then discussion, then methods to judge whether the evidence can be trusted.

cards.front: Peer review: what it can and can't do
cards.back: Experts check design, statistics and conclusions before publication. It can't usually see raw data or detect fraud; replication is the real test.
A manuscript posted publicly (bioRxiv, medRxiv) before peer review. Fast and open, but not yet checked: treat as a claim.
Where is it from? Who did it and who paid? What kind of evidence (experiment or observation; cells, mice or people; n)? Does the claim match the data? Do other studies agree?
Percent change = (new − old)/old × 100%. Fold change = new/old. A fold change of 1.5 is a 50% increase; 0.25 is a 75% decrease.
Results: numbers, units, n, variation and test results, no interpretation. Discussion: whether the hypothesis is supported, comparison with other work, limitations, next steps.
A financial or personal stake in a study's outcome (e.g. a company funding a test of its own product). A reason to look harder and seek independent replication, not to reject outright.
Primary: original research reported by those who did it. Review: a secondary source summarizing many primary studies.

cards.front: Stages of early animal development, in order
cards.back: Fertilization → cleavage → blastula (blastocyst in mammals) → gastrulation (three germ layers) → neurulation (neural tube) → organ formation.

cards.front: Fast block vs slow block to polyspermy (sea urchin)
cards.back: Fast: membrane voltage jumps positive within seconds (temporary). Slow: calcium wave triggers the cortical reaction, which lifts a fertilization envelope (permanent).
Rapid divisions without growth (G1 and G2 mostly skipped): cell number doubles each round, cells get smaller, the embryo stays the same size. After n divisions: 2ⁿ cells.
Little yolk (sea urchin, mammal): complete, equal. Moderate yolk in the lower half (frog): complete but unequal. Huge yolk (chick): partial, only a disc on top divides.
Volume ÷ 2ⁿ, so diameter ÷ 2^(n/3): every 3 divisions halve the diameter.
In frogs at about the 12th cleavage (about 4,000 cells): divisions slow and the embryo starts transcribing its own genes. Triggered by the DNA-to-cytoplasm ratio (adding DNA makes it come earlier).
Blastula: ball of cells around a blastocoel. Blastocyst (mammals): trophoblast (→ placenta) around a cavity plus an inner cell mass (→ the embryo itself).
Ectoderm: epidermis, nervous system, lens, neural crest. Mesoderm: notochord, muscle, bone, blood, heart, kidneys, gonads. Endoderm: lining of gut and lungs, liver, pancreas.

cards.front: Gastrulation in sea urchin vs frog vs chick and human
cards.back: Sea urchin: vegetal sheet buckles in to form the archenteron. Frog: cells roll in over the dorsal lip of the blastopore. Chick and human: cells move in through the primitive streak of a flat disc.

Notochord induces the ectoderm above it to form the neural plate; its edges fold up and fuse into the neural tube (brain and spinal cord). Neural crest cells break away and migrate; somites form beside the tube.

cards.front: Neural tube closure and folic acid
cards.back: The human neural tube closes by about day 28 after fertilization, often before pregnancy is known; 400 µg of folic acid daily lowers the risk of spina bifida and anencephaly.
Determination: fate fixed (tested by transplant), no visible change yet. Differentiation: the cell actually specializes in structure and function.

cards.front: Spemann's early vs late gastrula transplants
cards.back: Early gastrula: transplanted tissue follows its new position (not determined). Late gastrula: presumptive neural tissue makes neural tissue anywhere (determined).
Determinants: molecules unevenly placed in the egg and inherited by some cells. Induction: signals from neighboring cells change a group's fate (responding cells must be competent).
Dorsal lip from a light newt gastrula grafted to the belly side of a dark one: a second body axis formed, its neural tube mostly from dark host cells. The graft induced its neighbors.

cards.front: How the organizer makes neural tissue
cards.back: It secretes BMP blockers (chordin, noggin). BMP4 tells ectoderm to become epidermis; shielded ectoderm becomes neural.
For C(x) = C₀e^(−x/λ), the boundary at threshold T is x = λ ln(C₀/T). Doubling the dose shifts it by λ ln 2 ≈ 0.69λ.

cards.front: Evidence that Bicoid is a morphogen
cards.back: No maternal Bicoid: no head or thorax. Bicoid mRNA injected elsewhere: head forms there. Extra gene copies: head region enlarges and boundaries shift back.
The embryo's phenotype follows the mother's genotype (she loads the mRNA into the egg). A bcd/bcd female is normal, but all her embryos lack head and thorax.
Maternal genes (bicoid gradient) → gap genes (blocks) → pair-rule genes (7 stripes) → segment polarity genes (14 segments); Hox genes give each segment its identity.
Antennapedia: legs in place of antennae. Ultrabithorax-region mutations: third thoracic segment becomes a second one, giving four wings.
Homeobox (180 bp) codes for a DNA-binding homeodomain; genes are colinear (chromosome order = body order); flies have 8 in one split cluster, mammals 39 in four clusters.
Totipotent (zygote; also placenta) → pluripotent (inner cell mass, ES cells, iPSCs; whole body) → multipotent (blood stem cells; one family) → unipotent (one cell type).

Irradiated mice given marrow cells grew spleen colonies with several blood cell types; colony number was proportional to cells injected and each colony was a clone: the first proof of blood stem cells.

cards.front: Stem cell frequency from colony counts
cards.back: Detected frequency = colonies ÷ cells injected. True frequency = detected ÷ fraction of stem cells that reach the spleen.
Pluripotent cells from the inner cell mass, grown indefinitely in culture (mouse 1981, human 1998). Tested by teratoma formation. Taking them destroys the embryo.
Cells injected into an immune-deficient mouse form a tumor with tissues of all three germ layers if they are pluripotent; also shows the tumor risk of leftover undifferentiated cells.
Briggs and King 1952 (frog blastula nuclei), Gurdon 1962 (tadpole intestine nuclei), Dolly 1996 (adult sheep udder cell). Success falls as donor cells become more specialized.
277 eggs fused with udder cells → 29 embryos transferred → 1 lamb (about 0.36% per fused egg). Low success reflects incomplete epigenetic reprogramming.
Reproductive: nuclear transfer embryo grown into a whole organism. Therapeutic: nuclear transfer embryo used only to derive patient-matched embryonic stem cells.
Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc. Found (2006) by starting with 24 candidates and removing one at a time; together they reprogram fibroblasts into iPSCs.
Driven by neoblasts, dividing adult stem cells; a single transplanted neoblast can rebuild all tissues of an irradiated worm, so some neoblasts are pluripotent.
Wound cells dedifferentiate into a blastema that regrows the limb; it needs nerves, and its cells mostly keep a memory of their origin (cartilage → cartilage).

cards.front: Empirical vs value claims in stem cell ethics
cards.back: Empirical: testable with evidence (e.g. iPSCs can form tumors). Value: about what we ought to do (e.g. embryo research should stop at day 14).
Genome size varies over 10,000-fold among eukaryotes (onion about 5× human, a fern about 50×) while gene number varies only a few-fold; the difference is mostly noncoding DNA.
Genes ÷ genome size. E. coli about 935 per Mb (about 88% coding); human about 6.5 per Mb (about 1–1.5% coding).
About 1.5% protein-coding, about 45% derived from transposable elements, introns a quarter or more; about 10% appears conserved by selection.
DNA transposons: cut and paste with transposase. Retrotransposons: copy and paste through RNA and reverse transcriptase (LINE-1 about 17%, Alu about 10% of the human genome).
Unequal crossing over, retrotransposition of an mRNA (intron-less copy), and whole-genome duplication (two rounds early in vertebrates: 1 Hox cluster in lancelets, 4 in mammals).
Paralogs: related by duplication within a lineage (human α- and β-globin). Orthologs: separated by speciation (human and mouse β-globin).
Pseudogene (most common: disabled and decays), neofunctionalization (one copy gains a new job), subfunctionalization (copies split the old jobs).
Mouse Pax6 switched on in fly legs makes extra fly compound eyes: the same ancestral control gene directs non-homologous eyes.
Lake sticklebacks lost a pelvic enhancer of Pitx1 in independent populations; the protein and its other jobs (jaw, pituitary) are intact. Restoring the enhancer restores the pelvis.

cards.front: Why form often evolves by cis-regulatory change
cards.back: Toolkit genes have many jobs; changing the protein affects all of them, while changing one tissue-specific enhancer changes only one. In a hybrid, a cis change affects only its own allele.

cards.front: Proximate vs ultimate causes of behavior
cards.back: Proximate: how it works (stimuli, nerves, hormones, development). Ultimate: why it evolved (effect on fitness, evolutionary history). Both explain the same behavior at different levels.
Mechanism and development (proximate); function and evolutionary history (ultimate).
An unlearned behavior sequence triggered by a sign stimulus that runs to completion once started, e.g. a greylag goose rolling an egg (or a doorknob) back into the nest.
Learning during a sensitive period early in life that is hard to reverse; Lorenz's goslings followed him. The capacity is built in; what is learned depends on experience.
Imprinting, habituation, classical conditioning (stimulus–stimulus), operant conditioning (action–consequence), spatial learning, social learning.
He ringed a nest with pine cones, then moved the ring; returning wasps searched in the moved ring, showing they navigate by learned landmarks.
Angle of the waggle run from straight up = angle of the food from the sun's direction. Longer waggle run = farther food (calibration varies by colony).
Piloting (landmarks), compass orientation (sun, stars, magnetic field), true navigation (map plus compass from unfamiliar places).
Shifting a pigeon's internal clock by 6 h shifts its sun-compass heading by about 90° (15° per hour in the simple model), evidence for a time-compensated sun compass.
Energy gained ÷ handling time. Optimal foraging theory predicts animals prefer the most profitable prey, which is not always the largest.
Helping is favored when $rB > C$ ($r$ = relatedness of actor to recipient, $B$ = recipient's extra offspring, $C$ = actor's lost offspring).
Parent–child $\tfrac12$; full siblings $\tfrac12$; half siblings, grandparent, aunt or uncle $\tfrac14$; first cousins $\tfrac18$. Add $(\tfrac12)^L$ over all paths.
Own reproduction plus the extra reproduction of relatives one causes, weighted by relatedness. Kin selection acts on it.
Worker to full sister $\tfrac34$; to brother $\tfrac14$; to her own offspring $\tfrac12$.

Brothers are only $\tfrac14$ related; many queens mate multiply (average $r = \tfrac14 + \tfrac{1}{2n}$); termites and naked mole-rats are diploid yet eusocial; most haplodiploid species aren't eusocial; ecology matters.
Repeated meetings between the same individuals, recognition of partners, and the ability to stop helping cheaters (e.g. vampire bats sharing blood).
The sex that invests more per offspring (usually females) tends to be choosier; the other sex competes. In role-reversed species such as some pipefish and jacanas, females compete.
Intrasexual: competition within a sex (elephant seal fights). Intersexual: mate choice by the other sex (widowbird females prefer long tails).
Monogamy (1 male, 1 female), polygyny (1 male, several females), polyandry (1 female, several males), promiscuity (no lasting bonds).
Incidence: new cases per population per time. Prevalence: existing cases per population at one time. Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration (steady state).
$R_0$: infections per case in a fully susceptible population. $R_e = R_0 \times s$: infections per case now. Cases grow if $R_e > 1$, shrink if $R_e < 1$.
New infections $= \beta SI/N$; recoveries $= \gamma I$; $S$ falls by new infections, $I$ rises by new infections minus recoveries, $R$ rises by recoveries. $R_0 = \beta/\gamma$.

cards.front: When does an SIR epidemic peak?
cards.back: When the susceptible fraction falls to $1/R_0$ (so $R_e = 1$). The epidemic then overshoots: about 94% are eventually infected when $R_0 = 3$.
Set $R_0 s = 1$: an infection can't grow once more than $1 - 1/R_0$ of the population is immune.

1854: deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump, with telling exceptions; homes supplied by the downstream Southwark and Vauxhall Company had about 8 times the cholera death rate of Lambeth homes.
One sharp peak: point source. Plateau: continuing common source. Successive growing peaks one incubation period apart: person-to-person spread.
Attack rate = ill ÷ exposed in a group. Relative risk = attack rate among exposed ÷ attack rate among unexposed.
Diseases spread between animals and people (rabies, Lyme, avian flu, Ebola). More than 6 in 10 known human infectious diseases and about 3 in 4 emerging ones come from animals.
Antibiotics only when needed (not for viruses), the right narrow-spectrum drug, dose and duration; prevent infections; limit farm use. Every use selects for resistance.
Background about 0.1 extinctions per million species-years (E/MSY); current estimates near 100 E/MSY, about 1,000 times higher.
Species number is an equilibrium of immigration (falls with distance from the mainland) and extinction (higher on small islands). Large, near islands hold the most species.
$S = cA^z$, with $z \approx 0.2$–$0.35$ on islands. Ratio form: $S_2/S_1 = (A_2/A_1)^z$. With $z = 0.3$, 10 times the area holds about twice the species.

Edges are lighter, windier, drier and have more invaders and nest predators. A square of side $L$ with edge depth $d$ keeps core $(L - 2d)^2$; one large block keeps more core than several small ones of the same total area.
$N_e = \dfrac{4N_mN_f}{N_m + N_f}$. 10 males and 40 females give $N_e = 32$, not 50.
$H_t = H_0\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2N_e}\right)^t$: a fraction $1/(2N_e)$ is lost each generation.
Small population → inbreeding and drift → lost diversity and inbreeding depression → lower survival and reproduction → smaller population.
Florida panthers (about 20–30 left, with heart defects and kinked tails) received 8 female Texas pumas in 1995; defects fell and numbers grew to an estimated 120–230.
The long-run growth rate is the geometric mean of yearly $\lambda$ values: alternating 1.5 and 0.6 averages 1.05 but gives $\sqrt{0.9} \approx 0.95$, a decline.
Trap-shy marked animals → too few recaptures → overestimate. Trap-happy → underestimate. Chapman: $N = \dfrac{(M+1)(C+1)}{R+1} - 1$.
Prevention, early detection and rapid response, eradication (works best on islands, e.g. South Georgia rats), then long-term control, including tested biological control.
California condor (27 birds in 1987, about 600 by 2025), Yellowstone wolves (reintroduced 1995–96), humpback whales after hunting bans (1966, 1986), Florida panther genetic rescue.
Made of cells; metabolism (uses energy); homeostasis; responds to stimuli; grows and develops; reproduces; heritable DNA; populations evolve.

cards.front: Why is a flame or a growing crystal not alive?
cards.back: It shows one or two features (growth, energy release) but has no cells, metabolism, homeostasis or DNA. Life needs the whole set.
Keeping internal conditions stable despite outside changes, usually by negative feedback (e.g. sweating when hot).

cards.front: Levels of organization, smallest to largest
cards.back: atom → molecule → organelle → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere
Population: one species in an area. Community: all species in an area. Ecosystem: the community plus nonliving surroundings.
A new ability that arises from how parts interact at a higher level, e.g. a heart pumps but a single muscle cell cannot.
Independent: the one factor you change (x-axis). Dependent: what you measure (y-axis).
Control group: subjects without the treatment, used as a baseline. Controlled variables: conditions kept the same in all groups.
Individuals vary; more subjects and repeated trials make it less likely a difference is due to chance.
$\dfrac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%$ (negative = decrease)
Hypothesis: testable explanation of one observation. Theory: broad, well-tested explanation. Law: describes a pattern without explaining it.
Two variables changing together does not show one causes the other; a third variable may drive both. Controlled experiments test causation.
Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, sulfur: about 98% of living mass.
Oxygen pulls shared electrons harder than hydrogen, and the molecule is bent: O end δ−, H ends δ+.

cards.front: Properties of water caused by hydrogen bonds
cards.back: Cohesion and surface tension, adhesion and capillary action, high specific heat, ice floats, excellent solvent for polar and ionic substances.
Cohesion: water attracted to water. Adhesion: water attracted to other substances.
$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, so $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$ mol/L

cards.front: A difference of 3 pH units means…
cards.back: A $10^3 = 1000$-fold difference in H⁺ concentration; the lower pH has more H⁺.
Resists pH change by taking up or releasing H⁺; blood is buffered near pH 7.4 by bicarbonate/carbonic acid.
Dehydration synthesis joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis splits polymers and uses water.

cards.front: Water released when $n$ monomers form one chain
cards.back: $n - 1$ molecules (one per bond)

cards.front: Four classes of macromolecules and their monomers
cards.back: Carbohydrates: monosaccharides. Proteins: amino acids. Nucleic acids: nucleotides. Lipids: no true monomer (fats are glycerol + 3 fatty acids).
All glucose polymers. Starch: plant energy store. Glycogen: animal energy store. Cellulose: plant cell walls (different linkage, indigestible to humans).
Saturated: no C=C double bonds, straight chains, solid (butter). Unsaturated: double bonds kink the chains, liquid (oils).
Benedict's (heated): simple sugars → orange/brick-red. Iodine: starch → blue-black. Biuret: protein → violet. Paper spot or Sudan III: lipid.
Primary: amino acid sequence. Secondary: helices and sheets. Tertiary: 3-D fold of one chain. Quaternary: several chains together.
DNA: deoxyribose, A T G C, double-stranded, stores information. RNA: ribose, A U G C, usually single-stranded, helps make proteins.
They lower the activation energy; they are not used up and do not change the overall energy of the reaction.

cards.front: Effect of temperature on enzyme activity
cards.back: Rises to an optimum (≈37 °C for human enzymes), then falls steeply as the enzyme denatures. Cold slows enzymes but does not denature them.
Competitive: binds the active site; overcome by more substrate. Noncompetitive: binds elsewhere and changes shape; extra substrate does not help.

cards.front: Why the peptide bond does not rotate
cards.back: Partial double-bond character (shared electrons) holds its six atoms flat; the chain twists only at the bonds on either side of each alpha carbon.
3.6 amino acids per turn; 0.15 nm rise per amino acid (0.54 nm per turn); C=O of amino acid n hydrogen bonds to N–H of n + 4.
Helix: one coiled segment, H-bonds within it. Sheet: extended strands (≈0.34 nm per amino acid) side by side, H-bonds between strands. Both are backbone hydrogen bonds.

cards.front: Main driving force of protein folding
cards.back: The hydrophobic effect: burying nonpolar R groups in the core releases ordered water. H-bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals contacts and disulfides refine the fold.
Glycine: tiny, flexible, common in turns. Proline: rigid ring, no N–H, breaks helices. Cysteine: forms S–S disulfide bonds.
8 cysteines can pair 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105 ways; random pairing gives the native set 1/105 ≈ 1% of the time.
A random search of 3^100 shapes would take ~10^27 years, yet proteins fold in seconds or less; folding follows an energy funnel, not a random search.
Bind exposed hydrophobic stretches (Hsp70) or give a sheltered chamber (GroEL/GroES) so chains don't aggregate; they hold no shape information.

cards.front: Sickle cell at the molecular level
cards.back: β-globin glutamate 6 → valine on the surface; the nonpolar patch sticks to neighboring deoxyhemoglobin, forming fibers that sickle red cells.
A misfolded, β-rich form of the protein PrP that converts normal PrP to the misfolded form; infectious with no DNA or RNA.
$v = \dfrac{V_{\max}[\text{S}]}{K_m + [\text{S}]}$; at $[\text{S}] = K_m$, $v = V_{\max}/2$
$k_{\text{cat}} = V_{\max}/[\text{E}]_{\text{total}}$ (per second). Efficiency $k_{\text{cat}}/K_m$, capped by diffusion near $10^8$–$10^9$ M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
$1/v$ vs $1/[\text{S}]$: slope $K_m/V_{\max}$, y-intercept $1/V_{\max}$, x-intercept $-1/K_m$.
Competitive: Km up, Vmax same. Pure noncompetitive: Vmax down, Km same. Uncompetitive: both down. Irreversible: covalent, permanent.
$K_m^{\text{app}} = K_m(1 + [\text{I}]/K_i)$; $V_{\max}$ unchanged
Several subunits bind substrate cooperatively → S-shaped curve. Activators shift it left, inhibitors right. Example: ATCase (CTP inhibits, ATP activates).
In E. coli, isoleucine allosterically inhibits threonine deaminase, the first of five enzymes in its own pathway.
Inactive precursor activated by cutting, e.g. trypsinogen → trypsin by enteropeptidase in the small intestine; protects the cells that make it.
Biotic: living parts of an ecosystem (organisms, dead leaves, dung). Abiotic: nonliving conditions (light, temperature, water, pH, minerals).
Producers make their own food (photosynthesis or chemosynthesis). Consumers eat other organisms. Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and return nutrients.

cards.front: Which way do food-chain arrows point?
cards.back: From the food to the eater: the direction energy moves (grass → rabbit means the rabbit eats the grass).
A food chain is one feeding path; a food web shows all the interlinked feeding relationships in a community.
NPP = GPP − producer respiration: the energy producers store as new biomass, available to consumers.
About 10% (roughly 1–20%) of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next. Energy at level $n$ above producers $= E_0 \times 0.1^n$.

cards.front: Why is so little energy passed up a trophic level?
cards.back: Not everything is eaten, not everything eaten is absorbed (feces), and most absorbed energy is used in cellular respiration and lost as heat.
Energy flows one way (sunlight in, heat out). Matter (carbon, nitrogen, water) cycles and is reused.

cards.front: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
cards.back: The pyramid of energy. Pyramids of numbers (one tree, many insects) and biomass (open-ocean plankton) can be inverted.

cards.front: Why measure biomass as dry mass?
cards.back: Water content varies with weather and time of day, so drying gives a consistent measure of living material.

cards.front: Carbon cycle: processes that add vs remove atmospheric CO₂
cards.back: Remove: photosynthesis, dissolving in the ocean. Add: cellular respiration, decomposition, combustion of fuels, volcanoes.
About 280 ppm before 1750; about 424 ppm in 2024, mainly from burning fossil fuels.
N₂ → (fixation by bacteria) ammonium → (nitrification) nitrite → nitrate → absorbed by plants → animals → (decomposers) ammonium; denitrification returns nitrate to N₂.
Excess nutrients (fertilizer runoff) cause algal blooms; decomposers breaking down dead algae use up dissolved oxygen, creating dead zones.
$\Delta N = B - D + I - E$ (births − deaths + immigration − emigration).
Continuous: $dN/dt = rN$. Discrete (yearly): $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$. J-shaped curve.
$dN/dt = rN\dfrac{K-N}{K}$. S-shaped curve; fastest at $N = K/2$; levels off at $K$.
Dependent (stronger when crowded): competition, predation, disease, parasites. Independent (same regardless of density): frost, drought, flood, fire.
$N = \dfrac{M \times C}{R}$: $M$ marked first, $C$ caught second, $R$ marked in the second catch.
Marked animals mix evenly, marks are not lost, marking does not change catchability, and no births, deaths or migration between samples.
Mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/−. (Predation is +/−, competition −/−.)
Two species cannot share the same niche in the same place indefinitely; one wins, or they partition resources (MacArthur's warblers).
A species with an effect far larger than its abundance. Paine removed the sea star Pisaster and species on the shore fell from 15 to 8.
Primary: starts with no soil (lava, retreating glacier), pioneers are lichens and mosses. Secondary: soil remains (after fire or farming), faster.

cards.front: What mainly determines which biome develops?
cards.back: Climate: temperature and precipitation.

cards.front: Tundra vs boreal forest vs desert
cards.back: Tundra: very cold, permafrost, no trees. Boreal forest: cold winters, conifers. Desert: under about 25 cm of rain a year.
$D = 1 - \dfrac{\sum n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}$. Near 0: one species dominates. Near 1: many evenly represented species.
Richness: number of species. Evenness: how equally individuals are spread among them. Diversity indexes combine both.
Habitat loss (largest), climate change, invasive species, pollution, overexploitation.
A persistent, fat-soluble toxin (such as DDT) becomes more concentrated at each higher trophic level.
$l_x = n_x/n_0$ (survivorship), $d_x = n_x - n_{x+1}$ (deaths), $q_x = d_x/n_x$ (mortality rate), $e_x = T_x/n_x$ (life expectancy).
$l_x$: fraction of the cohort surviving from birth to age $x$. $q_x$: fraction of those alive at age $x$ that die before $x+1$.
When first-year mortality is high, an individual that survives its first year has escaped that risk and can expect to live longer than a newborn.
Type I: most die old (humans, large mammals). Type II: constant fraction dies each age, straight line on a log scale (many lizards). Type III: most die young (oysters, most fish).
$R_0 = \sum l_x m_x$, daughters per female per lifetime. $R_0 > 1$: grows; $= 1$: steady; $< 1$: shrinks.
r: early maturity, many small offspring, little care, short life. K: late maturity, few large offspring, much care, long life. A continuum; age-specific mortality explains life histories better.
Guppies moved to a stream where predators eat mainly juveniles evolved later maturity and fewer, larger young in about 11 years: mortality by age shapes life histories.
$dH/dt = rH - aHP$; $dP/dt = baHP - mP$. Prey steady at $P = r/a$; predators steady at $H = m/(ab)$. Cycles with predator peaks lagging.
Averaged over peak and decline: food added 3×, predators excluded 2×, both about 11× hare density. Food and predation interact.
When each limits itself more than it limits the other: $\alpha_{12} < K_1/K_2$ and $\alpha_{21} < K_2/K_1$. Otherwise one excludes the other.
Plot per capita growth against $N$; fit a line $r(1 - N/K)$. The intercept is $r$, and where the line hits zero is $K$.
NPP = GPP − producer respiration. NEP = NPP − consumer and decomposer respiration. NEP > 0 means the ecosystem stores carbon.
Respiration = initial − dark. Net production = light − initial. GPP = light − dark.
One O₂ released per CO₂ fixed, so mg C = mg O₂ × 12/32 = mg O₂ × 0.375 (approximate).
Lake 226 (1973): phosphorus limits lakes. Ryther and Dunstan (1971): nitrogen limits coastal seas. IronEx II (1995): iron limits parts of the open ocean.
C : N : P ≈ 106 : 16 : 1 in ocean plankton. N:P well below 16 suggests N limitation; well above suggests P limitation.
About half of global NPP (a total of roughly 105 GtC per year) is in the ocean, though phytoplankton are under 1% of producer biomass: they turn over in days.
Fixers (nitrogenase, N₂ → NH₄⁺); nitrifiers (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻, need O₂); denitrifiers (NO₃⁻ → N₂O → N₂, low O₂); anammox (NH₄⁺ + NO₂⁻ → N₂).
Emitted 11.1 GtC (fossil 10.1, land use 1.0). Atmosphere +5.9, ocean 2.9, land 2.3. Airborne fraction about 53%. 2.12 GtC ≈ 1 ppm.

cards.front: Evidence that rising CO₂ comes from fossil fuels
cards.back: Falling carbon-13 and carbon-14 fractions in air CO₂, falling atmospheric O₂, and emissions inventories that match the rise.
For 800,000 years CO₂ stayed between about 180 and 300 ppm; today it is about 424 ppm (2024).

cards.front: The three parts of the cell theory
cards.back: All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; all cells come from preexisting cells.

cards.front: Who contributed what to cell theory
cards.back: Hooke (1665) named cells; Leeuwenhoek saw microbes; Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) are made of cells; Virchow: every cell from a cell.
Boiled broth open to air via an S-shaped neck stayed sterile; breaking the neck let dust and microbes in. Microbes come from microbes, not spontaneous generation.
Ocular × objective (e.g. 10× × 40× = 400×)
Actual size = image size ÷ magnification (convert mm to µm: × 1000)

cards.front: Field of view at higher power
cards.back: Shrinks in proportion: new diameter = old diameter × (low mag ÷ high mag). Cell size ≈ field diameter ÷ number of cells across.
Magnification: how much bigger the image is. Resolution: smallest separation still seen as two points (≈ 0.2 µm light, ≈ 1 nm or better electron).
Light: living cells, color, ≈ 1000×. Electron: far higher resolution, but dead specimens in a vacuum. TEM: thin slices; SEM: surfaces.
Plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, ribosomes
Prokaryote: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, DNA in nucleoid, 1–5 µm (bacteria, archaea). Eukaryote: nucleus and organelles, 10–100 µm (animals, plants, fungi, protists).
Bacteria, Archaea (both prokaryotic) and Eukarya; found by comparing ribosomal RNA (Woese, 1977; domains formally proposed 1990).
Virus: not a cell, DNA or RNA in a capsid, 20–300 nm, no ribosomes or metabolism, reproduces only in a host, not affected by antibiotics. Bacterium: a living cell, 1–5 µm.

cards.front: Why antibiotics don't treat viral infections
cards.back: They target bacterial structures (peptidoglycan walls, bacterial ribosomes) that viruses don't have.
Holds DNA; double envelope with pores; nucleolus makes ribosome parts.
Rough ER: ribosomes, makes proteins for export and membranes. Smooth ER: makes lipids, detoxifies (liver), stores calcium (muscle).
Ribosome on rough ER → ER → vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → exocytosis (shown by Palade's pulse–chase experiments).
Membrane sac of digestive enzymes, acidic inside (≈ pH 5); digests food particles, bacteria and worn-out organelles.
Mitochondrion: cellular respiration, makes ATP (plants and animals). Chloroplast: photosynthesis, makes sugar (plants and algae).

cards.front: Plant cells have, animal cells lack
cards.back: Cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts, large central vacuole
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have double membranes, their own circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes, divide by splitting, and have DNA most similar to particular bacteria.
Membrane = fluid phospholipid bilayer with a mosaic of proteins that move sideways (Frye–Edidin cell fusion experiment).
Small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂). Water slowly (fast via aquaporins). Ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.
Passive (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis): down the gradient, no energy. Active: against the gradient, needs ATP and a pump.
Water moves toward the higher solute concentration ("water follows solute").
Hypertonic: cell loses water (shrinks, plasmolysis). Hypotonic: cell gains water (animal cell may burst, plant cell turgid). Isotonic: no net change.
$\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p$, with $\Psi_s = -iCRT$; water moves from higher to lower $\Psi$.
Active transport: each ATP moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.

cards.front: SA:V of a cube of side $s$
cards.back: SA $= 6s^2$, $V = s^3$, so SA:V $= 6/s$; it falls as the cube grows.
Needs grow with volume but supply through the membrane grows only with surface area; diffusion is only fast over short distances.
A cell specializes by switching genes on and off; nearly all body cells have the same DNA (Gurdon's frog nuclear transfer).

Proteins carry built-in address labels. A signal sequence at the start of a protein is bound by SRP, which brings the ribosome to the ER; the chain is threaded into the ER through a translocon (Blobel).

cards.front: Sorting signals in the endomembrane system
cards.back: Signal sequence only → secreted (default); + KDEL → returned to and kept in the ER; + mannose-6-phosphate → lysosome. No signal sequence → stays in the cytosol.

cards.front: COPII vs COPI vs clathrin coats
cards.back: COPII: ER → Golgi. COPI: Golgi → ER and between Golgi sacs. Clathrin: from the trans-Golgi network and the plasma membrane (endocytosis).

cards.front: How a vesicle fuses with the right membrane
cards.back: Rab proteins help it dock; SNAREs on the vesicle and target wind together and pull the membranes into fusion. Botulinum and tetanus toxins cut SNAREs.
Lysosomal enzymes are never tagged with mannose-6-phosphate, so they are secreted into the blood instead of reaching lysosomes, which fill with undigested material.
LDL binds receptors in clathrin-coated pits → coated vesicle → endosome (acid releases LDL) → receptors recycled, LDL to lysosome. Too few receptors: familial hypercholesterolemia.
Cargo stops at the first block it meets, so a double mutant looks like the single mutant whose step comes earlier (Schekman's yeast sec mutants).

cards.front: Microtubule vs intermediate filament vs microfilament
cards.back: Microtubule: hollow, 25 nm, tubulin; tracks, spindle, cilia. Intermediate filament: 8–12 nm ropes (keratin, lamins); strength. Microfilament: 7 nm, actin; shape, crawling, contraction.
Kinesin: along microtubules, mostly toward plus ends (outward). Dynein: toward minus ends (inward); also bends cilia and flagella. Myosin: along actin.
8 nm per step, one ATP per step; 1 m of axon takes $1.25 \times 10^8$ steps.
Colchicine stops microtubules growing; paclitaxel stops them shrinking. Both wreck the spindle and stall mitosis.
Reception (ligand binds receptor) → transduction (relay proteins, second messengers) → response (enzyme, channel or gene activity changes).
G protein-coupled receptor; receptor tyrosine kinase; ligand-gated ion channel (surface); intracellular receptor for steroids and other signals that get inside.
Ligand binds GPCR → G protein swaps GDP for GTP → α subunit activates adenylyl cyclase → ATP → cAMP → protein kinase A → response.
Growth factor → two receptors pair up → cross-phosphorylate tyrosines → relay proteins activate Ras → MAP kinase cascade → transcription factors → cell division genes.
Epinephrine plus liver membranes made a heat-stable small molecule (cAMP) that activated phosphorylase in the cytosol: the second messenger.
Ligand leaves the receptor; Gα hydrolyzes GTP; phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP; phosphatases remove phosphates; receptors are taken inside.
Locks the Gα that activates adenylyl cyclase in its GTP form → cAMP stays high → chloride and water pour into the gut → severe diarrhea.

Each enzyme in a cascade activates many molecules of the next, so multiply the factors: in the lesson's illustrative liver-cell example, one hormone molecule releases about a million glucose units per second.
Energy is converted from one form to another, never created or destroyed.
Every energy conversion loses some energy as unusable heat, so entropy increases; living things need a constant energy input.
Catabolism breaks molecules down and releases energy (respiration). Anabolism builds molecules and requires energy (protein synthesis, Calvin cycle).
Exergonic reactions release free energy and can proceed on their own; endergonic reactions absorb free energy and need an input, usually from ATP.
Adenine + ribose + three phosphate groups (adenosine triphosphate).
ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ + energy (about 30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions).
Using ATP hydrolysis to drive an endergonic process, usually by transferring a phosphate group to another molecule; works if the total energy change is negative.
Catabolism recharges ADP + Pᵢ into ATP; cellular work spends ATP back to ADP. A cell holds little ATP and remakes it constantly.
Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain. NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
NADH and FADH₂ carry electrons in respiration; NADPH carries them in photosynthesis.
6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Autotrophs make their own food from inorganic materials (plants, algae). Heterotrophs eat other organisms (animals, fungi).
Water, split by photosystem II (shown with ¹⁸O by Ruben and Kamen, 1941).
Van Helmont (mass not from soil) → Priestley (plants restore air) → Ingenhousz (only in light) → Engelmann (action spectrum) → Ruben and Kamen (O₂ from water) → Calvin (carbon path, ¹⁴C).
Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light and reflects green.
Absorption: how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength. Action: how fast photosynthesis runs at each wavelength.
Thylakoid membranes. In: light, H₂O, ADP, NADP⁺. Out: O₂, ATP, NADPH.
Stroma. Rubisco fixes CO₂; ATP and NADPH reduce it to G3P. Per glucose: 6 CO₂, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH.
Light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature; the scarcest one sets the rate.
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (about 30–32 ATP)

cards.front: Stages of aerobic respiration, in order
cards.back: Glycolysis (cytoplasm) → pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) → electron transport chain and chemiosmosis (inner membrane).
Glucose → 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP and 2 NADH; no O₂ needed.
With pyruvate oxidation: 6 CO₂, 8 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP.
Final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain; forms water.
About 30–32 (2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, 4 direct). Older books: 36–38, using 3 and 2.
H⁺ pumped across a membrane by an electron transport chain flows back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. Used in both mitochondria and chloroplasts.
Regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep making 2 ATP per glucose without oxygen.
Lactic acid: pyruvate → lactate (muscle, yogurt bacteria). Alcoholic: pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂ (yeast).
Aerobic: needs O₂, about 30 ATP per glucose, CO₂ + H₂O. Fermentation: no O₂, 2 ATP, lactate or ethanol + CO₂.
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. Negative $\Delta G$: can proceed on its own; positive: needs an energy input; zero: equilibrium.

cards.front: Actual vs standard free energy change
cards.back: $\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ\prime} + RT\ln Q$. $RT \approx 2.58$ kJ/mol at 37 °C. Small $Q$ (products scarce) pushes a reaction forward.

cards.front: Free energy and the equilibrium constant
cards.back: $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -RT\ln K^{\prime}$. At 25 °C, every 5.7 kJ/mol is a factor of 10 in $K^{\prime}$; $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = 0$ means $K^{\prime} = 1$.

cards.front: ATP hydrolysis in a cell vs standard
cards.back: About −30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions but about −50 kJ/mol in cells, because ATP is kept far above equilibrium relative to ADP and phosphate.
Glucose + Pᵢ → glucose-6-P: +13.8 kJ/mol. Coupled to ATP hydrolysis (−30.5): −16.7 kJ/mol. Free energies add; equilibrium constants multiply.
PEP (−61.9) > 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (−49.3) > phosphocreatine (−43.0) > ATP (−30.5) > glucose-6-P (−13.8) kJ/mol. ATP in the middle can be made from those above and phosphorylate those below.
$\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -nF\Delta E^{\circ\prime}$, with $\Delta E^{\circ\prime} = E^{\circ\prime}_{\text{acceptor}} - E^{\circ\prime}_{\text{donor}}$ and $F = 96.5$ kJ/(mol·V).

cards.front: Reduction potentials along the respiratory chain
cards.back: NAD⁺/NADH −0.32 V; Q/QH₂ +0.05 V; cytochrome c +0.25 V; ½O₂/H₂O +0.82 V. Electrons flow toward more positive values.
$\Delta E^{\circ\prime} = 1.14$ V, so $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -2 \times 96.5 \times 1.14 \approx -220$ kJ/mol, released in steps along the chain.
NADH → complex I → ubiquinone (Q) → complex III → cytochrome c → complex IV → O₂. Succinate enters at complex II → Q.

cards.front: Protons pumped per pair of electrons
cards.back: Complex I: 4, complex III: 4, complex IV: 2, complex II: 0. NADH gives 10 H⁺; succinate (FADH₂) gives 6.
$\Delta p = \Delta\psi + 61.5 \text{ mV} \times \Delta\text{pH}$ (37 °C). About 200 mV in mitochondria, mostly membrane potential; thylakoids store more as a pH difference.

cards.front: ATP synthase as a rotary motor
cards.back: Protons turn the c-ring (F₀) and central stalk; each β subunit of F₁ binds ADP + Pᵢ, makes ATP, releases it (binding-change mechanism). 3 ATP per turn; H⁺ per ATP = c subunits ÷ 3.
With about 4 H⁺ per ATP (3 through the synthase + 1 for transport): NADH 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ATP; FADH₂ 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 ATP. Approximate, not whole numbers.
H₂O → photosystem II → plastoquinone → cytochrome b₆f → plastocyanin → photosystem I → ferredoxin → FNR → NADPH.

cards.front: Why chloroplasts need cyclic electron flow
cards.back: Linear flow gives about 12 H⁺ per 2 NADPH; with 14 c subunits that is about 1.29 ATP per NADPH, short of the 1.5 the Calvin cycle uses. Cyclic flow makes ATP without NADPH.
Thylakoids soaked at pH 4, then moved to pH 8 with ADP + Pᵢ in the dark, made ATP: a proton gradient alone drives ATP synthesis.
Both stop ATP synthesis. Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase, so O₂ use slows (respiratory control). DNP is an uncoupler, so O₂ use speeds up and the energy becomes heat.
3 RuBP (15 C) + 3 CO₂ → 6 3-PGA (18 C) → 6 G3P (6 ATP, 6 NADPH) → 1 G3P out; 5 G3P + 3 ATP → 3 RuBP. Total 9 ATP + 6 NADPH per G3P.

cards.front: Light-to-dark transient in the Calvin cycle
cards.back: Light off: 3-PGA rises, RuBP falls (no ATP/NADPH for reduction or regeneration). CO₂ cut off: RuBP rises, 3-PGA falls.
Rubisco adds O₂ to RuBP → 3-PGA + 2-phosphoglycolate. Salvage through chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion releases 1 CO₂ per 2 oxygenations and costs ATP. Worse when hot and when stomata close.
C3: rubisco fixes CO₂ directly. C4: PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ in mesophyll, rubisco in bundle sheath (separated in space). CAM: PEP carboxylase at night, Calvin cycle by day (separated in time).
About 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂ (2 extra ATP to regenerate PEP) vs 3 ATP + 2 NADPH for C3. Per glucose: 30 vs 18 ATP. Pays off in hot, bright, dry conditions.
PEP carboxylase: fixes HCO₃⁻ onto PEP, no reaction with O₂, used to concentrate CO₂ in C4 and CAM plants. Rubisco: fixes CO₂ onto RuBP, also reacts with O₂.
C4 leaf structure: bundle-sheath cells (rubisco, Calvin cycle) packed around each vein, surrounded by mesophyll cells (PEP carboxylase).
C3: wheat, rice, soybeans, trees. C4: corn, sugarcane, sorghum, millets. CAM: cacti, agaves, pineapple, jade plant, many orchids.

cards.front: Water lost per CO₂ fixed (rough figures)
cards.back: About 500 water molecules per CO₂ for C3, about 250 for C4, about 50 for CAM; varies widely with conditions.
Interphase: G1 (growth) → S (DNA replication) → G2 (preparation); then M phase: mitosis and cytokinesis.
G1 about 11 h, S about 8 h, G2 about 4 h, M about 1 h.
After S phase a chromosome has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere; it is still one chromosome. Count centromeres to count chromosomes.
Prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase (then cytokinesis).
Chromosomes condense; spindle forms; nuclear envelope breaks down.
Chromosomes line up at the middle of the cell, attached to spindle fibers from both poles.
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles; chromosome count in the cell briefly doubles.
Chromosomes reach the poles; nuclear envelopes re-form; chromosomes uncoil.

cards.front: Cytokinesis in animal vs plant cells
cards.back: Animal: cleavage furrow pinches the cell. Plant: a cell plate forms and becomes a new wall.
(cells in mitosis ÷ total cells) × 100%

cards.front: Time in a stage from a snapshot
cards.back: Time in stage = (cells in stage ÷ total cells) × length of the cell cycle.
G1: size, nutrients, growth factors, DNA damage. G2: DNA fully and correctly copied. Spindle (metaphase): all chromosomes attached.
A non-dividing state outside the cycle (mature nerve and heart muscle cells); cells are active but not dividing.
Cyclin levels rise and fall each cycle; a CDK is active only when bound to its cyclin and then phosphorylates targets to drive the next phase.
Programmed cell death that removes damaged or unneeded cells without inflammation.
Proto-oncogene = gas pedal (RAS); overactive mutation → oncogene, one copy enough. Tumor suppressor = brake (p53, RB); usually both copies must be lost.
Tumor suppressor that halts the cycle when DNA is damaged and triggers apoptosis if repair fails; mutated in about half of human cancers.
Benign stays in place. Malignant invades nearby tissue and can metastasize (spread through blood or lymph).
N = N₀ × 2ⁿ; 10 doublings ≈ ×1,000; 30 doublings ≈ ×1 billion.
Totipotent: every cell type including placenta (zygote). Pluripotent: every body cell type (embryonic stem cells, iPSCs). Multipotent: several related types (blood stem cells).
Body cells reprogrammed by adding four genes to act like embryonic stem cells (Yamanaka: mouse fibroblasts 2006, human skin cells 2007).
Diploid (2n): two sets of chromosomes, as in body cells (human 46). Haploid (n): one set, as in gametes (human 23).
Homologs: one from each parent, same genes, possibly different versions. Sister chromatids: identical copies made in S phase.
Meiosis I separates homologs (2n → n, reduction). Meiosis II separates sister chromatids (like mitosis).
Mitosis: 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 genetically different haploid cells; homologs pair and cross over.

cards.front: Three sources of genetic variation in sexual reproduction
cards.back: Crossing over (prophase I), independent assortment (metaphase I), random fertilization.
2ⁿ, where n = number of homologous pairs; humans 2²³ = 8,388,608.

cards.front: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs II
