cards.back: Meiosis I: all four gametes abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1). Meiosis II: two normal, one n + 1, one n − 1.
Each female meiosis gives one egg plus polar bodies; each male meiosis gives four sperm.
Cyclin B bound to CDK1. Found by injecting mature frog egg cytoplasm into immature oocytes (Masui and Markert, 1971); drives cells into M phase.

cards.front: Three conditions for an active CDK
cards.back: Cyclin bound; activating phosphate added; inhibitory phosphates (added by Wee1) removed by Cdc25.

cards.front: Why entry into mitosis is switch-like
cards.back: Positive feedback: active cyclin B–CDK1 activates Cdc25 and inhibits Wee1, freeing more CDK1.
Tags cyclin B and securin with ubiquitin for destruction; freed separase cuts cohesin to start anaphase; held back by unattached kinetochores.
Cyclin D–CDK4/6 (G1), cyclin E–CDK2 (G1/S), cyclin A–CDK2 (S), cyclin B–CDK1 (G2/M).
Unphosphorylated Rb holds E2F. Cyclin D–CDK4/6 then cyclin E–CDK2 phosphorylate Rb, freeing E2F to switch on S-phase genes: the restriction point.
MDM2 normally destroys p53. DNA damage (via ATM/ATR) stabilizes p53, which switches on p21 (G1 arrest), repair genes and apoptosis genes such as BAX.
Intrinsic: BAX pores release cytochrome c → apoptosome → caspase 9 (blocked by Bcl-2). Extrinsic: Fas ligand binds Fas death receptor → caspase 8. Both activate caspases 3 and 7.
Apoptosis: shrinks, DNA ladder, blebs, eaten by phagocytes, no inflammation. Necrosis: swells and bursts, inflammation.
131 of 1,090 somatic cells die. ced-3 = caspase, ced-4 = Apaf-1 relative, ced-9 = Bcl-2 relative (protects).
Gain of function: activating point mutation (RAS), amplification (HER2), translocation or fusion (BCR-ABL). Dominant in the cell.

cards.front: Two-hit model with a Poisson count
cards.back: Carrier tumors ~ Poisson with mean m: P(no tumor) = e^(−m). Knudson: m ≈ 3, so about 95% of carriers get a tumor.
2C = G1; between 2C and 4C = S; 4C = G2 or M. Fraction of cells in each estimates fraction of cycle time.
Crossovers plus arm cohesion tie homologs together so they attach to opposite poles under tension; pairs with no crossover risk nondisjunction.
Protects centromere cohesin at anaphase I so sister chromatids stay together until anaphase II.
Involves 2 of the 4 chromatids: 2 recombinant and 2 parental products, so recombinant gametes are at most about 50%.

cards.front: Telling meiosis I from meiosis II errors
cards.back: Markers near the centromere: two different homologs from one parent = meiosis I; two identical copies = meiosis II.
About 90% maternal (roughly 70% of all cases maternal meiosis I, 20% maternal meiosis II), about 5% paternal, a few percent mitotic (mosaic).
Usually paternal meiosis II: a YY sperm from sister chromatids that failed to separate (less often, a mitotic error after fertilization).
4^c × 2^(n−c) for n pairs each heterozygous for two genes, with c pairs having a crossover between them.
Number of chromosomes from one grandparent is binomial: P(k) = C(n, k)/2^n; humans average 11.5 of 23.
Auto: extra sets from its own species (unreduced gametes, colchicine). Allo: sets from two species, hybrid plus doubling (Karpechenko radish-cabbage, bread wheat 6x = 42).
Sets of three cannot split evenly; a balanced gamete needs all sets to go the same way: probability 2 × (1/2)^x (bananas, seedless watermelons, x = 11: about 1/1024).
A gene is a unit of inheritance (a stretch of DNA affecting a trait). Alleles are the different versions of one gene, such as P (purple) and p (white).
Genotype: the alleles an individual has (PP, Pp, pp). Phenotype: the observable trait (purple or white).
Homozygous: two identical alleles (PP or pp). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Pp).
A dominant allele shows its effect with one copy (in a heterozygote). A recessive allele shows only when there are two copies. Dominant does not mean common or beneficial.
The two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes, each gamete getting one, with equal probability. Physical basis: homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I.

cards.front: Aa × Aa: genotype and phenotype ratios
cards.back: Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
Cross a dominant-phenotype individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive. All dominant offspring suggests AA; any recessive offspring proves Aa (expected 1 : 1).

cards.front: Of the dominant-phenotype offspring of Aa × Aa, what fraction are heterozygous?
cards.back: 2/3 (two Aa boxes out of three non-aa boxes).

Alleles of different (unlinked) genes go into gametes independently. Physical basis for genes on different chromosomes: each homologous pair orients at random at metaphase I. Genes close together on one chromosome travel together unless crossing over separates them.
9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (two dominant : first dominant only : second dominant only : both recessive), out of 16.
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Example: P(aabbcc) from AaBbCc × AaBbCc = (1/4)³ = 1/64.
For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Example: P(AA or aa) from Aa × Aa = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

cards.front: Number of gamete types from n heterozygous unlinked genes
cards.back: $2^n$. AaBbCc makes 8; homozygous genes add no variety.

cards.front: Probability that exactly k of n children are affected (probability p each)
cards.back: $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. For two carrier parents and 2 children, exactly one affected = 2 × (1/4)(3/4) = 3/8.
Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is intermediate (pink from red × white). Codominance: heterozygote shows both traits fully (AB blood, roan cattle).
1 : 2 : 1 for both genotypes and phenotypes (red : pink : white), since each genotype has its own phenotype.
A: $I^AI^A$ or $I^Ai$. B: $I^BI^B$ or $I^Bi$. AB: $I^AI^B$. O: $ii$. $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant; both dominant to $i$.
A: A antigen, anti-B antibodies. B: B antigen, anti-A. AB: both antigens, no antibodies. O: no antigens, both antibodies.
A trait controlled by many genes with small additive effects (height, skin color); gives continuous, bell-shaped variation.
Pleiotropy: one gene affects many traits (sickle-cell allele). Epistasis: one gene masks another (ee Labradors are yellow; 9 : 3 : 4).

cards.front: Why X-linked recessive traits are more common in males
cards.back: Males have one X, so one recessive allele is expressed. Females need two copies.
Sons: 1/2 affected. Daughters: none affected, 1/2 carriers. Any child: 1/4 is an affected son.

cards.front: Affected father × homozygous normal mother (X-linked recessive)
cards.back: All daughters are carriers; no sons are affected (sons get the father's Y).
Square = male, circle = female, filled = affected, dot or half-filled = carrier, horizontal line = mating, Roman numerals = generations.

cards.front: Pedigree clues: autosomal recessive vs dominant vs X-linked recessive
cards.back: Autosomal recessive: unaffected parents can have an affected child. Autosomal dominant: affected people have an affected parent; affected parents can have an unaffected child. X-linked recessive: mostly males, never father to son.

cards.front: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs meiosis II
cards.back: Meiosis I: all four gametes abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1). Meiosis II: two normal, one n + 1, one n − 1.
Down syndrome: 47,+21 (trisomy 21). Turner syndrome: 45,X. Klinefelter syndrome: 47,XXY.
Deletion (segment lost), duplication (repeated), inversion (flipped), translocation (moved to a non-homologous chromosome).

cards.front: Chi-square formula and degrees of freedom
cards.back: $\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ using counts; df = number of categories − 1.
df 1: 3.84; df 2: 5.99; df 3: 7.81; df 4: 9.49. Below the value: fail to reject. At or above: reject.
Genes close together on one chromosome; they are inherited together more often than independent assortment predicts, unless a crossover falls between them.
Parental: allele combinations already on the heterozygote's chromosomes, the two most common classes. Recombinant: new combinations from crossing over, the two least common classes.
Recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring × 100%. Example: 450 recombinants of 2500 = 18%.

cards.front: Why use heterozygous female fruit flies for mapping
cards.back: Male Drosophila have no crossing over in meiosis, so a heterozygous male gives no recombinants.
1 map unit = 1 cM = 1% recombination frequency. Measures crossover frequency, not physical length.

cards.front: Ordering three genes from pairwise distances
cards.back: The largest distance spans the two outer genes; the third gene is in the middle. Short distances roughly add up.
One crossover affects only 2 of the 4 chromatids, and multiple crossovers between distant genes cancel out, randomizing the alleles as independent assortment would.

cards.front: Three-point cross: finding the middle gene
cards.back: Parental classes = most common; double crossovers = rarest. The gene that differs between them is in the middle.
For each interval, (single crossovers in that interval + all double crossovers) ÷ total × 100.
Coefficient of coincidence = observed ÷ expected double crossovers (expected = RF1 × RF2 × total). Interference = 1 − coefficient of coincidence.
Coupling: AB / ab (dominant alleles on one chromosome). Repulsion: Ab / aB. In a test cross the parental (common) classes differ accordingly.
9 : 3 : 4 recessive epistasis (mouse albino); 9 : 7 complementary genes (sweet pea); 12 : 3 : 1 dominant epistasis (squash); 15 : 1 duplicate genes (shepherd's purse).

cards.front: Clue that an F2 involves two genes
cards.back: Classes come out in sixteenths (9 : 7, 12 : 3 : 1, 15 : 1, 9 : 3 : 4), from a doubly heterozygous F1.
Cross two true-breeding recessive mutants with the same phenotype. Normal F1: mutations in different genes. Mutant F1: same gene.
Two heterozygotes give 1 : 2 : 1, but the homozygous lethal class dies, leaving 2 : 1 among survivors (yellow mice: 2 yellow : 1 agouti).

cards.front: Number of genes from F2 extremes
cards.back: With n equal additive genes, each F2 extreme is (1/4)^n and there are 2n + 1 phenotype classes. 1/64 means 3 genes; 1/256 means 4.
The range of phenotypes one genotype produces across environments (cloned yarrow grown at different elevations).
$H^2 = V_G/V_P$ (all genetic variance). $h^2 = V_A/V_P$ (additive variance only); $h^2$ predicts response to selection.
$R = h^2 S$. Example: mean 120 cm, selected parents 130 cm, $h^2 = 0.4$: R = 4 cm, offspring mean 124 cm.
Not the share of one person's trait due to genes; not a sign the trait can't change; not an explanation of differences between groups. It applies to one population in one environment.

cards.front: Griffith, Avery, Hershey–Chase: what did each show?
cards.back: Griffith (1928): something from dead S bacteria transforms R bacteria. Avery (1944): only destroying DNA stops transformation, so the transforming principle is DNA. Hershey–Chase (1952): phage DNA (³²P), not protein (³⁵S), enters bacteria.
A phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) and a nitrogen base.
DNA: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds), G–C (3 hydrogen bonds). RNA: A–U, G–C. Each pair is one purine (A, G) with one pyrimidine (T, C, U).
In double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C, so %A + %G = 50%. Example: 22% G gives 22% C and 28% each of A and T.
The two DNA strands run in opposite directions: under 5′-ATG-3′ lies 3′-TAC-5′.
Generation 0: one heavy band. Generation 1: one hybrid band (rules out conservative). Generation 2: half hybrid, half light (rules out dispersive). Replication is semiconservative.
Helicase unwinds → primase lays RNA primers → DNA polymerase builds 5′ → 3′ (leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments) → primers replaced → ligase joins fragments.
Leading: built continuously toward the replication fork. Lagging: built in Okazaki fragments away from the fork, because polymerase adds only to 3′ ends.
DNA → RNA → protein. Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation makes protein from mRNA.
DNA: deoxyribose, thymine, usually double-stranded. RNA: ribose, uracil, usually single-stranded.
mRNA carries the codons; tRNA brings amino acids and has the anticodon; rRNA forms the ribosome core and makes peptide bonds.
Initiation (RNA polymerase binds the promoter) → elongation (RNA built 5′ → 3′, complementary to the template strand) → termination. In eukaryotes: add cap and tail, splice out introns.
The template strand is read by RNA polymerase. The coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA, with T in place of U.
64 triplet codons; AUG = start (Met); UAA, UAG, UGA = stop; redundant (several codons per amino acid), unambiguous, nearly universal.
Find the first AUG from the 5′ end, read non-overlapping triplets, look each codon up in the table, stop at the first stop codon (which adds no amino acid).

cards.front: Codons vs amino acids in a coding region
cards.back: A coding region of $n$ codons (start through stop) makes $n - 1$ amino acids; it has $3n$ nucleotides.

Initiation (small subunit finds AUG, Met-tRNA pairs, large subunit joins) → elongation (tRNAs match codons, peptide bonds form, ribosome moves one codon) → termination (release factor at the stop codon).
No lactose: repressor binds the operator, genes off. Lactose present: lactose binds the repressor, which leaves the operator, genes on.
RNA polymerase binds the promoter; the repressor binds the operator, blocking polymerase.
Transcription factors and enhancers, DNA packing and epigenetic tags (DNA methylation, histone changes), RNA splicing, mRNA lifespan, microRNAs, and protein activation or breakdown.
Silent: codon changes, same amino acid. Missense: different amino acid (sickle cell GAG → GUG, Glu → Val). Nonsense: becomes a stop codon, protein cut short.

Insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three; every codon after it changes and an early stop often appears. Deleting exactly 3 bases removes one amino acid and keeps the frame.
Somatic: in body cells, not inherited (may contribute to cancer). Germline: in cells that make eggs or sperm, can be passed to offspring.
Denature (~95 °C) → anneal primers (~50–65 °C) → extend (~72 °C). Copies after $n$ cycles: $N = N_0 \times 2^n$.
DNA is negative and moves toward the positive electrode. Small fragments move farthest. Distance is roughly linear in log(size), so estimate sizes from a ladder on a log scale.
$n$ cuts give $n + 1$ fragments of a linear DNA molecule but $n$ fragments of a circular one (such as a plasmid).
Cut plasmid and gene with the same restriction enzyme → sticky ends pair → ligase seals → put into bacteria → select with antibiotic → bacteria express the gene (for example, human insulin).

cards.front: How DNA profiling excludes or matches
cards.back: Compare STR lengths at about 20 regions. One mismatch excludes a person; a match at every region is strong evidence (identical twins share a profile).
Inducible (lac): normally off; an inducer inactivates the repressor to turn genes on. Repressible (trp): normally on; a corepressor activates the repressor to turn genes off.

cards.front: Which pathways are inducible and which repressible?
cards.back: Breakdown (catabolic) pathways are usually inducible: run only when the food is present. Building (anabolic) pathways are usually repressible: shut off by their own product.

cards.front: The trp operon with high tryptophan
cards.back: Tryptophan (corepressor) binds the trp repressor, which then binds the operator and blocks transcription of the five tryptophan-making genes.
High transcription only with lactose present (repressor released) and glucose absent (cAMP high, CAP–cAMP bound). Glucose + lactose: low. No lactose: essentially none.
Cis: a DNA site (operator, promoter, enhancer) that controls only genes on its own molecule. Trans: a diffusible product (repressor, CAP, transcription factor) that can act on any copy.

$I^-$ (no repressor): recessive, since normal repressor acts in trans. $O^C$ (operator can't bind repressor): constitutive for genes on the same molecule only (cis). $I^S$ (repressor can't bind inducer): dominant, uninducible.

Activators bind the enhancer, which can be far away and in either orientation; the DNA loops, and Mediator links the activators to RNA polymerase II and the general transcription factors at the promoter.

Join candidate control DNA to an easily measured reporter gene (such as luciferase), remove or move pieces, and see which pieces change output. A piece that works far away and backwards is an enhancer.
Acetyl groups on histone tails loosen chromatin and usually activate genes. Methyl groups on CpG cytosines in promoters usually silence genes.

cards.front: How a methylation pattern is copied
cards.back: CpG pairs with CpG, so both strands are marked. After replication each site is half-methylated; a maintenance enzyme methylates the new strand to match.
X inactivation in female mammals (calico cats), genomic imprinting (only the father's IGF2 copy is active), and cell types keeping their identity through divisions.
Mutually exclusive clusters multiply: Dscam has $12 \times 48 \times 33 \times 2 = 38{,}016$ possible mRNAs. Each optional cassette exon doubles the count ($2^n$ for $n$ of them).

Transcribed as a hairpin, cut by Drosha and Dicer to about 22 bases, loaded into Argonaute; its seed (bases 2–8) pairs with sites in target mRNA 3′ untranslated regions, reducing translation and speeding decay.
A little of each fluorescent ddNTP stops new strands at every position; capillary electrophoresis sorts them by length, and the color of each end, read shortest first, spells the new strand 5′ → 3′.
$C = NL/G$ (reads × read length ÷ genome size). The fraction of bases missed by chance is about $e^{-C}$: 37% at 1×, essentially none at 30×.
Short reads (about 150 bases): cheap, accurate, billions per run, but can't place long repeats. Long reads (thousands of bases or more, e.g. nanopore): span repeats and structural changes.
About 3.1 billion bp per set; about 20,000 protein-coding genes; about 1.5% codes for protein; about half derived from transposable elements; unrelated people differ at about 1 base in 1,000.
Identical positions ÷ aligned positions (gaps included) × 100. Silent third-codon-position differences are usually the most common.

cards.front: How Cas9 finds and cuts its target
cards.back: Scans for a PAM (5′-NGG-3′) → unwinds the DNA beside it → the 20-base guide pairs with the target strand → both strands are cut about 3 bases from the PAM.
Find NGG; take the 20 bases just 5′ of it; the guide spacer has that sequence with U for T. The cut falls 3 bases from the PAM.

cards.front: End joining vs template repair after a Cas9 cut
cards.back: Nonhomologous end joining: frequent, leaves small insertions or deletions, used to knock genes out. Homology-directed repair: needs a supplied template, less frequent, makes precise edits.

Somatic: changes only the patient's body cells (e.g. Casgevy, edited blood stem cells); not inherited. Germline: changes embryos, eggs or sperm, so the change passes to future generations; widely considered unacceptable for now.

Fossil record (order, transitional fossils), radiometric dating, homologous and vestigial structures, embryos, molecular similarities, biogeography, and evolution observed directly (antibiotic resistance).
Fraction left after $h$ half-lives $= \left(\tfrac12\right)^h$; age $= h \times$ half-life. Carbon-14: 5,730 years (up to ~50,000 years). Potassium-40: 1.25 billion years.
Homologous: same structure from a common ancestor, possibly different jobs (human arm, bat wing). Analogous: same job, different structure and origin (bird wing, insect wing).
Hip bones in whales and some snakes, the human tailbone, small human ear muscles: reduced remnants of ancestral structures.
A fish with neck, lungs and limb-like fin bones (~375 million years old), found by predicting the age and type of rock where a fish–tetrapod transition should be.
More differences in a gene or protein (like cytochrome c) between two species means a longer time since their common ancestor.
Variation + inheritance + overproduction + differential reproductive success → heritable traits that help become more common over generations.
Reproductive success relative to others in the population, not strength or speed.
Resistant colonies existed on a plate never exposed to the antibiotic: mutations arise randomly before selection; the environment selects, it does not create them.
Drought left large, hard seeds; deeper-beaked medium ground finches survived; the next generation had deeper beaks on average. Wet years later reversed the direction.
Multiply each group by its survival rate, then divide: dark share $= \dfrac{n_D s_D}{n_L s_L + n_D s_D}$.

cards.front: Directional vs stabilizing vs disruptive selection
cards.back: Directional: one extreme favored, average shifts. Stabilizing: average favored, spread narrows. Disruptive: both extremes favored, middle declines.
Artificial: people choose which individuals breed (dogs, cabbage and broccoli). Natural: the environment determines who survives and reproduces.
Change individuals (populations evolve), plan ahead, create needed mutations, or pass on traits acquired during life.
$p + q = 1$ (alleles); $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$ (genotypes $AA$, $Aa$, $aa$).
No mutation, no gene flow, very large population (no drift), random mating, no natural selection.
$q = \sqrt{\text{frequency of } aa}$, $p = 1 - q$, carriers $= 2pq$. Example: 1 in 2,500 affected → $q = 0.02$, carriers ≈ 0.039 (about 1 in 25).
$p = \dfrac{2(\text{number } AA) + (\text{number } Aa)}{2N}$, because each individual carries two copies.
Mutation, gene flow, genetic drift (bottleneck and founder effects), nonrandom mating, natural selection. Only selection consistently produces adaptation.
Bottleneck: a population crashes and regrows from few survivors (northern elephant seals). Founder: a few individuals start a new population (Ellis–van Creveld syndrome among the Old Order Amish).
Populations that can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring, isolated from other such groups. Does not work for asexual organisms or fossils.
Prezygotic (before fertilization): habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical, gametic. Postzygotic: hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility (mules), hybrid breakdown.
Allopatric: a geographic barrier splits the population (snapping shrimp across the Isthmus of Panama). Sympatric: no barrier, for example polyploidy in plants or a host shift in apple maggot flies.
Nodes are common ancestors; tips are the groups compared (usually living ones). Two groups are most closely related if they share the most recent node. Rotating branches changes nothing.
A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. Clades are identified by shared derived traits that arose in their common ancestor (hair for mammals).
Paleozoic 539–252 million years ago, Mesozoic 252–66, Cenozoic 66–present. Everything before 539 is the Precambrian, nearly 90% of Earth's history.

cards.front: Key dates in the history of life
cards.back: Earth 4.54 billion years ago; first fossils ~3.5 billion; oxygen builds up ~2.4 billion; eukaryotes ~2 billion; Cambrian explosion ~539 million; Homo sapiens ~300,000 years.
End-Ordovician (~445), Late Devonian (~372), End-Permian (~252, the largest), End-Triassic (~201), End-Cretaceous (66, asteroid impact). Dates in millions of years ago.
Gradualism: slow, steady change. Punctuated equilibrium: long stability broken by relatively rapid change (Eldredge and Gould, 1972). Both occur.

An archaeal host cell, related to today's Asgard archaea, took in an oxygen-using bacterium that became the mitochondrion; later one eukaryote lineage took in a cyanobacterium that became the chloroplast. So many trees show eukaryotes branching from within the archaea.
$w$ = genotype's offspring number ÷ fittest genotype's, so the fittest has $w = 1$. Selection coefficient $s = 1 - w$.
Zygotes $p^2, 2pq, q^2$ → multiply each by its $w$ → add to get $\bar w$ → divide each by $\bar w$ → count alleles: $q' = (q^2 w_{aa} + pq\,w_{Aa})/\bar w$.
When $q$ is small, almost every copy is in a heterozygote with normal fitness, so selection against $aa$ lowers $q$ very slowly.
With $w_{AA} = 1 - s$, $w_{Aa} = 1$, $w_{aa} = 1 - t$: both alleles stay, at $\hat q = s/(s + t)$. Example: sickle-cell hemoglobin where malaria is common.
Estimate $p$ from the counts; expected $p^2N$, $2pqN$, $q^2N$; $\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E$; df = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1, critical value 3.84.
A neutral allele is eventually fixed with probability equal to its current frequency; a new mutation (one copy of $2N$) with probability $1/(2N)$.
$H_t = H_0\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2N}\right)^t$. With $N = 25$, about 64% is lost in 50 generations; with $N = 500$, about 5%.
Unequal sexes: $N_e = 4N_mN_f/(N_m + N_f)$. Changing size over $t$ generations: harmonic mean, $N_e = t / \sum (1/N_i)$, dominated by the smallest generation.
Roughly, when $s$ is smaller than about $1/(2N_e)$, an allele behaves as if neutral; in small populations even harmful alleles can be fixed.
You must count $AA$, $Aa$ and $aa$ separately, so use codominant traits (MN blood group) or DNA typing. Failing to reject doesn't prove no evolution.

cards.front: Shared derived vs shared ancestral character
cards.back: Derived: arose in the group's common ancestor (hair for mammals), defines a clade. Ancestral: inherited from an older ancestor and found outside the group too (backbone for mammals).
Clade: an ancestor and all its descendants. Paraphyletic: an ancestor and only some descendants, like reptiles without birds.
A relative that branched off earlier: its states are taken as ancestral, and the root goes on its branch.
Similarity not from common ancestry: convergence (bat and bird wings, as wings) or reversal (snakes losing legs). On a tree it appears as the same change happening more than once.
Count the changes each tree needs and choose the fewest. Only states shared by some but not all ingroup species are informative.
$1 \times 3 \times 5 \times \cdots \times (2n - 3)$: 3 for 3 species, 15 for 4, 105 for 5, about 34 million for 10.
Difference between two species $d = 2rT$ ($r$ per lineage), so $T = d/(2r)$. Calibrate $r$ from a split dated by fossils or geology.
Rates differ among genes and lineages; old splits saturate (repeated changes at a site hide earlier ones), making them look too young. Use many genes, several calibrations and relaxed clocks.
Transformation (taking up DNA), transduction (DNA carried by a virus), conjugation (plasmids passed by contact). Spreads antibiotic resistance between species.
One gene's history can differ from the species' history, for example after horizontal transfer, so species trees are built from many genes.
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species ("Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup").

cards.front: Rules for writing a binomial name
cards.back: Genus capitalized, species epithet lowercase, both italicized (or underlined): Homo sapiens. Genus may be abbreviated after first use: E. coli.
Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya (Woese, from ribosomal RNA comparisons). Current evidence suggests eukaryotes arose from within the archaea, closest to the Asgard archaea.
Groups should reflect ancestry: each group contains an ancestor and all its descendants. Classifications change as DNA evidence comes in.
A series of paired, mutually exclusive choices about observable features that leads step by step to an identification.
Both lack a nucleus. Bacteria: peptidoglycan walls, ester-linked lipids, many pathogens. Archaea: no peptidoglycan, ether-linked lipids, eukaryote-like gene machinery, no known human pathogens.
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan wall, stains purple. Gram-negative: thin wall plus outer membrane, stains pink.
$N = N_0 \times 2^{n}$, where $n$ = elapsed time $\div$ generation time.

cards.front: Phases of a bacterial growth curve
cards.back: Lag, exponential (log), stationary, death.
$\text{CFU/mL} = \dfrac{\text{colonies}}{\text{dilution} \times \text{volume plated}}$; count plates with 30–300 colonies.
Lytic: virus replicates at once and bursts the cell. Lysogenic: viral DNA joins the host chromosome and is copied silently until a trigger switches it to lytic.

cards.front: Why antibiotics don't work on viruses
cards.back: Viruses have no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own for antibiotics to target.
An RNA virus whose reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host genome.
Any eukaryote that is not a plant, animal or fungus; not a natural evolutionary group.
Pseudopods (amoeba), cilia (Paramecium), flagella (Euglena).
Caused by the protist Plasmodium, spread by Anopheles mosquitoes; multiplies in liver and red blood cells.
Fungi: heterotrophs, chitin walls, store glycogen, digest externally and absorb. Plants: photosynthesize, cellulose walls, store starch.
A hypha is one thread-like filament; a mycelium is the whole branching network of hyphae.
Mycorrhiza: fungus + plant roots (minerals for sugar). Lichen: fungus + alga or cyanobacterium.

cards.front: Four plant groups and their innovations
cards.back: Mosses (no vascular tissue), ferns (vascular tissue), gymnosperms (seeds on cones, pollen), angiosperms (flowers and fruit).
Haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis; zygote grows into diploid sporophyte, which makes spores by meiosis. Sporophyte dominant in ferns and seed plants.
Xylem: dead tubes, water and minerals up from roots. Phloem: living sieve tubes, sugars from source to sink (up or down).
Transpiration pulls water out of leaves; cohesion (hydrogen bonds) transmits the pull down unbroken xylem columns; adhesion helps; roots take in water by osmosis. Powered by the sun.
Volume = tube cross-section area × distance bubble moves; rate = volume ÷ time.
Stamen = anther + filament (male). Carpel/pistil = stigma + style + ovary with ovules (female). Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.
Darwin: the seedling tip senses light. Went: the signal is a chemical that diffuses into agar (auxin), which makes the shaded side elongate.
Radial: many planes through a central axis (jellyfish). Bilateral: one plane, left and right halves, front end with cephalization.
Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail (at some stage).
Protostome: first embryo opening becomes mouth (mollusks, annelids, arthropods). Deuterostome: it becomes the anus (echinoderms, chordates).
Endotherm: heat from metabolism, constant body temperature, high food cost (birds, mammals). Ectotherm: heat from environment, body temperature tracks surroundings.
Gelatin between tip and stump still allowed bending (the signal is a diffusible chemical); mica on the shaded side blocked it (the signal travels down the shaded side).
Agar that held coleoptile tips, set off-center on a cut seedling in the dark, made it bend away from the block; bending grew with the number of tips. The chemical was later identified as auxin (IAA).
One-sided light moves auxin laterally to the shaded side (rather than destroying it), so shaded cells elongate more and the shoot bends toward light.
Auxin moves one way, tip to base, cell by cell, because auxin-exporting PIN proteins sit at the lower end of each cell; it works even upside down.
Auxin → proton pumps → acidified wall → expansins loosen it → turgor stretches the cell.
Auxin collects on the lower side of both. Shoots: it speeds elongation, so they curve up. Roots (more sensitive): it slows elongation, so they curve down.

cards.front: Five classic plant hormones and a main effect
cards.back: Auxin: elongation, tropisms. Gibberellins: stem growth, germination. Cytokinins: cell division. Abscisic acid: stomatal closing, seed dormancy. Ethylene: ripening, leaf drop.
High auxin:cytokinin → roots; low → shoots; intermediate → undifferentiated callus (Skoog and Miller).
Pr absorbs red (about 660 nm) and becomes active Pfr; Pfr absorbs far-red (about 730 nm) and returns to Pr. The last flash in a red/far-red series decides the response.

Both measure unbroken night. Short-day (long-night) plants flower when night > critical night length; long-day plants when night < theirs. A red flash mid-night breaks the night; far-red after it cancels the break.
Flowering signal made in leaves, carried in phloem to the shoot tip; identified as the FT protein (2007).

cards.front: Pressure to hold up a water column
cards.back: $\rho g h$: about 0.01 MPa per meter (1.08 MPa for 110 m), plus friction. Suction alone can lift water only about 10.3 m.
Root pressure: a push from ions pumped into xylem, at most a few tenths of a MPa, causes guttation. Transpiration pull: tension from evaporation, lifts water up tall trees.
Phages spread on a bacterial lawn each make one clear plaque; PFU/mL = plaques ÷ (dilution × volume plated).
After a short infection and dilution, phage count stays flat during the latent period, then jumps as cells burst. Burst size = phages released ÷ infected cells.
When many phages infect each cell or hosts are starving (fresh hosts scarce). DNA damage destroys the repressor and induces the lytic cycle.
Prophage genes give the host new traits; cholera, diphtheria and Shiga toxin genes arrive on phages.
Bind CD4 + coreceptor and fuse → reverse transcription → integration (provirus) → transcription and translation → budding → maturation by protease.

cards.front: Why HIV is controlled but not cured
cards.back: Error-prone reverse transcriptase (about 0.3 new mutations per genome copy) makes single drugs fail, so combinations are used; silent provirus in resting cells survives treatment.
Drift: gradual point mutations in surface proteins (yearly vaccine updates). Shift: two strains in one cell swap genome segments, making a new subtype (pandemics).
Peptidoglycan wall synthesis (penicillins), 70S ribosomes (tetracyclines, macrolides), DNA gyrase (fluoroquinolones), folate synthesis (sulfonamides).
Destroy the drug (beta-lactamase), alter the target (MRSA), pump the drug out (efflux), keep it out (fewer membrane pores).
Separate cultures varied wildly in resistant mutants ("jackpots"), samples of one culture did not: mutations arise at random before exposure, and the agent only selects.
Conjugation: plasmid through a pilus. Transformation: uptake of naked DNA. Transduction: a phage carries bacterial DNA.
Probabilities multiply: with rates $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-6}$, a double mutant arises in 1 cell in $10^{14}$, far more than the $10^{9}$ cells in an infection.
Ferments fiber to short-chain fatty acids, makes vitamin K, trains the immune system, crowds out pathogens; antibiotics can disrupt it (C. difficile).

cards.front: Three parts of a homeostatic control loop
cards.back: Sensor (receptor), control center (often the brain), effector (muscle or gland).
Negative: response opposes the change (temperature, glucose). Positive: response amplifies the change until an event ends it (childbirth, clotting).
Sweating and vasodilation of skin vessels, triggered by the hypothalamus.
Vasoconstriction of skin vessels and shivering.
Dendrites (receive), cell body (nucleus), axon (carries impulse away, often myelinated), axon terminals (release neurotransmitter).
Rest at about −70 mV; threshold reached; sodium channels open, Na⁺ in (inside becomes positive); potassium channels open, K⁺ out (restores negative).
Every action potential has the same size; stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency.
Stimulate at two distances; speed = difference in distance ÷ difference in time (mm/ms = m/s).
Impulse arrives; neurotransmitter released; diffuses across gap; binds receptors on next cell; then broken down or taken back up.
Nervous: electrical plus neurotransmitter, milliseconds, brief, targeted. Endocrine: hormones in blood, seconds to hours, longer lasting, any cell with the receptor.
Insulin (beta cells): lowers blood glucose; cells take up glucose, liver stores glycogen. Glucagon (alpha cells): raises it; liver breaks down glycogen.
Type 1: autoimmune destruction of beta cells, little insulin. Type 2: cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance).

cards.front: Path of blood through the heart
cards.back: Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body → veins → right atrium.
Artery: away from heart, thick elastic wall. Vein: toward heart, thin wall, valves. Capillary: one cell thick, exchange.
Heart rate × stroke volume; about 70 × 70 mL ≈ 5 L/min at rest.
Volume at end of filling − volume left after contraction.
The heart pumps thousands of liters a day, far more than is eaten or contained in the body, so blood must circulate.

cards.front: Path of air into the lungs
cards.back: Nose/mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Diaphragm contracts and flattens, ribs lift, chest volume up, lung pressure down, air flows in.
Rising carbon dioxide, which lowers blood pH, detected in the medulla.
Minute = tidal volume × rate. Alveolar = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate.
About 20 kJ per liter of oxygen; resting use about 3.5 mL O₂ per kg per minute.
Filtration (glomerulus), reabsorption (tubule back to blood), secretion (blood into tubule).
Released when blood is too concentrated; makes collecting ducts reabsorb more water, giving concentrated urine (negative feedback).
Carbohydrates → simple sugars; proteins → amino acids; fats → fatty acids and glycerol; nucleic acids → nucleotides.

cards.front: Roles of stomach, small intestine, large intestine
cards.back: Stomach: acid, pepsin, churning. Small intestine: most digestion and nearly all absorption (villi). Large intestine: water absorption, gut bacteria.
Carbohydrate 4 kcal, protein 4 kcal, fat 9 kcal (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ).
Innate: fast, general, from birth (barriers, inflammation, phagocytes). Adaptive: slower first time, specific, memory (B cells, antibodies, T cells).
Primary: about 1–2 weeks to peak, smaller. Secondary: within days, much larger, because of memory cells.
$1 - \dfrac{1}{R_0}$; e.g. $R_0 = 15$ gives about 93%.
3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP. It maintains the gradients; the K⁺ leak makes most of the resting voltage.
$E = \dfrac{61.5}{z}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{out}]}{[\text{in}]}$ mV. Typical $E_{\text{K}} \approx -90$ mV, $E_{\text{Na}} \approx +60$ mV.
It moves toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion the membrane is most permeable to at that moment.
Rest (−70 mV); depolarization to threshold (−55); rising phase (Na⁺ in, positive feedback); falling phase (Na⁺ channels inactivate, K⁺ out); undershoot toward $E_{\text{K}}$; rest.
Absolute: no second spike possible (Na⁺ channels inactivated). Relative: a spike needs a stronger stimulus (undershoot). Makes conduction one-way and caps firing rate.
Myelin insulates the axon; the action potential is regenerated only at nodes of Ranvier, giving speeds up to about 120 m/s.
AP reaches terminal; Ca²⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ in; vesicles release transmitter; it binds receptors; postsynaptic channels open; transmitter removed by enzyme or reuptake.
EPSP: small depolarization (e.g. Na⁺ in, glutamate). IPSP: small hyperpolarization (e.g. Cl⁻ in, GABA). A neuron fires when summed inputs reach threshold.
TTX and lidocaine: Na⁺ channels. Botulinum: ACh release. Curare: ACh receptors. Organophosphates: acetylcholinesterase. SSRIs: serotonin reuptake. Benzodiazepines: GABA receptors.
Each lymphocyte has one random, pre-made specificity; antigen selects matching cells, which multiply into effector and memory clones; self-reactive cells are removed.
Heavy chains = V × D × J; light chains = V × J (kappa plus lambda); pairs = heavy × light; imprecise joining adds much more.
Two heavy and two light chains joined by disulfide bonds; variable regions at the arm tips form two identical antigen-binding sites; the heavy-chain constant region sets the class.
IgM: first made, pentamer. IgG: most abundant, crosses placenta. IgA: secretions and milk. IgE: mast cells, allergy, worms. IgD: on naive B cells.

cards.front: MHC class I vs class II
cards.back: Class I: nearly all nucleated cells, inside proteins, to CD8 cytotoxic T cells. Class II: antigen-presenting cells, engulfed material, to CD4 helper T cells.

cards.front: IgM vs IgG in a blood test
cards.back: IgM only: recent first infection. IgM and IgG: within weeks. IgG only: past infection or vaccination.
$R_{\text{eff}} = R_0 \times$ susceptible fraction; outbreak grows if above 1. Coverage needed $= (1 - 1/R_0)/E$ for a vaccine of effectiveness $E$.
Active (infection, vaccine): own B and T cells respond, memory forms, long lasting. Passive (maternal IgG, milk IgA, antibody treatment): immediate but fades, no memory.
Peptide: water-soluble, surface receptor, second messenger (cAMP), fast. Steroid: lipid-soluble, internal receptor, changes gene expression, slow and lasting.
Posterior: releases ADH and oxytocin made by hypothalamic neurons. Anterior: gland controlled by hypothalamic releasing hormones via portal vessels; makes tropic hormones.
TRH → TSH → thyroid → T4/T3; T4/T3 inhibit the pituitary and hypothalamus (negative feedback).
High TSH, low T4: thyroid underactive. Low TSH, high T4: thyroid overactive. Low TSH, low T4: pituitary or hypothalamus problem.

cards.front: How a beta cell releases insulin
cards.back: Glucose in → ATP rises → K_ATP channels close → depolarization → Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ triggers insulin exocytosis.
Fasting: under 100 normal, 100–125 prediabetes, 126+ diabetes. 2 hours: under 140 normal, 140–199 prediabetes, 200+ diabetes. Confirm by repeat testing.
High plasma osmolality → more ADH → cAMP in collecting-duct cells → aquaporins inserted → water reabsorbed → concentrated urine (up to about 1,200 mOsm/kg).
Central: too little ADH; urine concentrates after desmopressin. Nephrogenic: kidney unresponsive; little change after desmopressin.
Solute load ÷ maximum urine concentration, e.g. 600 mOsm ÷ 1,200 mOsm/L = 0.5 L/day.
Estrogen normally inhibits LH (negative feedback); sustained high estrogen late in the cycle triggers an LH surge (positive feedback) and ovulation follows.

glossary.definition: A statement of exactly how a variable will be measured or manipulated in a study (for example, "growth" as dry mass after 21 days), so others can repeat it.
A factor that differs between groups along with the treatment and also affects the outcome, so its effect cannot be separated from the treatment's.
A group given a treatment already known to produce the effect, showing that the method can detect an effect when one exists.
A group treated exactly like the experimental group except for the factor being tested, expected to show no effect (for example, solvent only).
The smallest unit that independently receives a treatment (a pot, a cage, a culture, a person); replication must happen at this level.
Treating repeated measurements of the same experimental unit (many leaves from one plant, many cells from one dish) as if they were independent replicates, which overstates certainty.
The number of independent experimental units in a group, written $n$. Uncertainty in a mean falls in proportion to $1/\sqrt{n}$.
The probability that a study detects a real effect of a given size; it rises with sample size and effect size. Many studies aim for 80%.
Using a chance process to decide which experimental unit gets which treatment, so groups differ only by chance, even in factors nobody measured.
Keeping people from knowing which treatment each unit received. Single-blind: the subjects don't know. Double-blind: neither subjects nor the researchers treating and measuring them know.
An inactive treatment made to look identical to the real one, given to a control group so that the effect of simply being treated is the same in both groups.
A systematic error that pushes results in one direction; unlike chance error, it does not average out with more data.
Bias that arises when the individuals studied do not represent the population the conclusion is about.
Bias that arises when an observer's expectations influence what is measured or recorded; prevented by blinding.
A study in which researchers measure what already happens instead of assigning treatments; it can show associations but cannot by itself rule out confounding.
A person's voluntary agreement to take part in research after being told its purpose, procedures, risks and benefits in plain language, with the right to quit at any time.
An independent committee that must review and approve research on people before it begins, weighing risks against benefits and checking consent procedures.
Principles for animal research (Russell and Burch, 1959): replace animals with other methods where possible, reduce the number used, and refine procedures to minimize pain and distress.
The sum of the values divided by how many there are, written $\bar{x}$; sensitive to outliers.
The middle value when data are put in order (or the mean of the two middle values); resists outliers, so it suits skewed data.
A value far from the rest of the data. It may be an error or a real extreme; it should be checked, not deleted just because it is inconvenient.
The largest value minus the smallest; a simple measure of spread that depends on only two values.
Roughly the typical distance of values from the mean: $s = \sqrt{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2/(n - 1)}$. It describes how much individuals vary.
A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution in which about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean and about 95% within 2 SD.
A measure of how precisely a sample mean estimates the population mean: $\text{SE} = s/\sqrt{n}$. It shrinks as the sample grows.
A range of plausible values for a population mean; a 95% confidence interval is about $\bar{x} \pm 2\,\text{SE}$ (a little wider for small samples).
A line drawn above and below a mean on a graph showing the SD, the SE or a confidence interval; the figure legend must say which.
A graph of a distribution: a box from the lower to the upper quartile with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme non-outlier values, and outliers as separate points.
The specific "no effect" or "no difference" statement that a statistical test assumes in order to calculate how surprising the data are.
The statement accepted if the null hypothesis is rejected, such as "the treatment changes the mean."
The probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
The threshold ($\alpha$, usually 0.05) chosen in advance: if $p \le \alpha$, the null hypothesis is rejected and the result is called statistically significant.
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true (a false positive); it happens with probability $\alpha$ when the null is true.
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false (missing a real effect); power is the probability of avoiding it.
A chi-square test comparing observed counts in categories with the counts a model predicts (such as a 3 : 1 ratio); df = categories − 1.
A chi-square test of whether two categorical variables in a contingency table are associated; expected count = row total × column total ÷ grand total, df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).
A table of counts that cross-classifies individuals by two categorical variables, one in the rows and one in the columns.
The number of values free to vary once the totals or estimates are fixed; it selects which critical value a test uses.
A test comparing two means: $t$ = difference in means ÷ standard error of the difference; with two independent groups, df = $n_1 + n_2 - 2$.
A tendency for two measured variables to rise and fall together (positive) or in opposite directions (negative); by itself it does not show causation.
A number $r$ from −1 to 1 measuring the strength and direction of a straight-line relationship between two variables.
Fitting the straight line $\hat{y} = a + bx$ that minimizes the sum of squared vertical distances from the points; used to predict $y$ from $x$ within the range of the data.
The square of the correlation coefficient, $r^2$: the fraction of the variation in $y$ explained by the regression line.
A report of original research by the people who did it, with their methods, data and conclusions.
A secondary source that summarizes and evaluates many primary studies on a topic.
The standard structure of a research paper: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion (after the title and abstract).
A one-paragraph summary at the start of a paper giving the question, methods, main results and conclusion.
The text with a figure that says what is plotted, the sample size, what the error bars show and which statistical test was used.
Evaluation of a manuscript by independent experts before publication; it catches many problems but cannot guarantee a result is correct or detect most fraud.
A complete manuscript posted publicly (for example on bioRxiv or medRxiv) before or during peer review; a claim not yet checked by reviewers.
The formal withdrawal of a published paper by a journal because it is seriously flawed or the result of misconduct.
A financial or personal stake that an author or funder has in a study's outcome; a reason for extra scrutiny, not automatic rejection.
Fusion of a sperm and an egg into one diploid cell, the zygote; it also blocks entry by other sperm and activates the egg.
The single diploid cell formed by fertilization; the first cell of a new organism, and totipotent.
Release of enzymes from the vesicle at the tip of a sperm when it meets the egg's outer coat, clearing a path and exposing species-specific binding proteins.
Calcium-triggered release of cortical granule contents just after fertilization, which forms or modifies the egg's outer layer so no more sperm can enter (the slow block to polyspermy).
The rapid mitotic divisions of the early embryo, without growth, that divide the egg's cytoplasm into many smaller cells.
One of the cells produced by cleavage of the zygote.
The early embryo at the end of cleavage: a ball of cells surrounding a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoel.
The fluid-filled cavity inside a blastula (or blastocyst).

The point in early development (about the 12th cleavage in frogs) when divisions slow and lose synchrony and the embryo begins transcribing its own genes; triggered by the rising ratio of DNA to cytoplasm.
The mammalian version of the blastula (about day 5 in humans): an outer trophoblast around a cavity, with an inner cell mass on one side.
The outer cell layer of a blastocyst; it forms the embryo's part of the placenta, not the body.
The cluster of pluripotent cells inside a blastocyst that develops into the embryo itself; the source of embryonic stem cells.
The period of coordinated cell movements that turns the blastula into an embryo with three germ layers and sets up the body axes.
One of the three cell layers formed at gastrulation (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), each giving rise to particular tissues.
The outer germ layer; forms the epidermis, the nervous system, the lens of the eye and the neural crest.
The middle germ layer; forms the notochord, muscle, bone and cartilage, dermis, heart, blood and vessels, kidneys and gonads.
The inner germ layer; forms the lining of the gut and its glands, the liver and pancreas, and the lining of the lungs and airways.
The primitive gut formed when cells fold inward during gastrulation; its opening is the blastopore.
The opening where cells move inside during gastrulation; it becomes the anus in deuterostomes (including vertebrates) and usually the mouth in protostomes.
A groove along the midline of a flat embryonic disc (as in birds and mammals) through which cells move inward to form mesoderm and endoderm; it appears around day 14–15 in humans.
A stiff rod of mesoderm along the back of a chordate embryo; it signals the ectoderm above it to form the neural plate.
Formation of the neural tube: the neural plate's edges rise into folds that meet and fuse beneath the surface ectoderm.
The hollow tube formed by neurulation that becomes the brain and spinal cord; in humans it closes by about day 28 after fertilization.
One of the paired blocks of mesoderm beside the neural tube; they form the vertebrae, back and limb muscles, and dermis.
Cells that break away from the edges of the closing neural tube and migrate widely, forming pigment cells, peripheral neurons and glia, and much of the facial skeleton.
Commitment of a cell to a particular fate before it looks specialized; a determined cell keeps that fate even when transplanted to a new place.
A molecule (often an mRNA or protein) placed unevenly in the egg, so that the cells inheriting it after cleavage take a particular fate.
In development, a change in the fate of one group of cells caused by signals from a neighboring group.
The ability of a cell or tissue to respond to an inducing signal, which depends on having the right receptors and transcription factors.
The dorsal lip of the amphibian blastopore; grafted to another embryo it induces a second body axis. It works partly by secreting proteins that block BMP signaling.
A substance that spreads from a source to form a concentration gradient; cells adopt different fates depending on whether the local concentration is above or below thresholds.
Information about where a cell is in the embryo, often read from the concentration of a morphogen, that helps decide its fate.
A fruit fly transcription factor made from maternal mRNA anchored at the front of the egg; its front-to-back gradient specifies head and thorax.
A gene whose product the mother puts into the egg, so the embryo's phenotype depends on the mother's genotype rather than its own.
A family of homeobox-containing genes for transcription factors that give each region along the head-to-tail axis its identity; found in nearly all animals, often in clusters.
A mutation that makes one body part develop as if it were another, such as legs in place of antennae in Antennapedia flies.
A 180-base-pair DNA sequence, shared by Hox and many other developmental genes, that codes for a 60-amino-acid DNA-binding region (the homeodomain).
The match between the order of Hox genes along the chromosome and the front-to-back order of the body regions where they act.
The ability of a stem cell to divide while keeping at least one daughter as a stem cell, maintaining the stem cell supply.
A division that produces two different daughters, such as one stem cell and one cell that will differentiate.
The microenvironment around stem cells whose signals keep them in the stem state; daughters that leave it begin to differentiate.
Able to give rise to every cell type, including the placenta and other supporting tissues; true only of the zygote and the earliest blastomeres.
Able to give rise to several cell types of one family, such as a blood stem cell making all blood cell types.
Able to give rise to only one cell type, as muscle satellite cells make only skeletal muscle.
The multipotent stem cell of the bone marrow that produces all blood cell types; first shown to exist by Till and McCulloch's spleen colony experiments.
A stem cell in a mature tissue (bone marrow, gut lining, skin, muscle) that replaces worn-out cells; usually multipotent or unipotent.
A pluripotent cell taken from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst and grown in culture, where it can divide indefinitely.
A disorganized tumor containing tissues from all three germ layers; forming one in a mouse is a standard test of pluripotency.
Putting the nucleus of a body cell into an egg whose own chromosomes were removed, so the egg develops using the donor's genome; the method used to clone Dolly.
Resetting a specialized cell's pattern of gene expression and epigenetic marks to an embryonic-like state, by nuclear transfer or by transcription factors.
Using nuclear transfer to produce a whole organism genetically identical (in nuclear DNA) to the donor.
Using nuclear transfer only to make an early embryo as a source of embryonic stem cells genetically matched to a patient.
The four transcription factors Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc, which together reprogram body cells into induced pluripotent stem cells.
A dividing adult stem cell of planarian flatworms; at least some are pluripotent and can rebuild a whole worm.
Loss of a cell's specialized features so that it can divide and help rebuild tissue, as in salamander limb regeneration.
A bud of dividing, partly dedifferentiated cells that forms at a wound and regrows a lost part, such as a salamander limb.
The amount of DNA in one haploid genome, measured in picograms or base pairs (1 pg is about 978 million bp).
The observation that genome size varies enormously among eukaryotes and does not track organismal complexity or gene number, explained mostly by differences in noncoding DNA.
DNA that does not code for protein: introns, regulatory sequences, RNA genes, repeats, pseudogenes and transposable-element-derived sequence; about 98–99% of the human genome.
A DNA sequence that can move or copy itself to new positions in the genome; discovered by Barbara McClintock in maize.
A transposable element that copies itself through an RNA intermediate and reverse transcriptase ("copy and paste"); LINE-1 and Alu elements are examples.
Doubling of an entire chromosome set at once (polyploidy); two rounds are thought to have occurred early in vertebrate evolution.
A group of genes descended by duplication from one ancestral gene, such as the globin genes.
One of two or more genes related by a duplication event within a lineage, such as human α-globin and β-globin.
One of two or more genes in different species descended from a single gene in their common ancestor, separated by speciation.
A copy of a gene disabled by mutations so it no longer makes a working product; often the fate of a duplicated gene.
Evolution of a new function in one copy of a duplicated gene while the other copy keeps the original function.
Division of an ancestral gene's functions between its duplicate copies, for example by expression in different tissues or at different times.
Evolutionary developmental biology: the study of how changes in developmental genes and their regulation produce evolutionary change in form.
Shared ancestry of the genes that control the development of structures that are not themselves homologous, such as Pax6 controlling both insect and vertebrate eyes.
A regulatory DNA sequence, such as an enhancer, on the same DNA molecule as the gene it controls; changes in it can alter where or when a gene is expressed without changing the protein.
The immediate "how" of a behavior: the stimuli, nerves, hormones and genes that produce it, and how it develops during the animal's life.
The evolutionary "why" of a behavior: how it affects survival and reproduction, and how it arose in the species' ancestors.
An unlearned sequence of actions that, once triggered by a sign stimulus, usually runs to completion, such as a goose rolling an egg back into her nest.
A specific feature of the environment that triggers a fixed action pattern, such as the red belly that triggers attack in male sticklebacks.
Learning that happens only during a limited sensitive period early in life and is hard to reverse, such as goslings bonding with the first moving object they see.
The limited window in an animal's development during which a particular kind of learning, such as imprinting, can take place.
A simple form of learning in which an animal stops responding to a repeated stimulus that brings neither reward nor harm.
Learning to link a neutral stimulus with a stimulus that already causes a response, so the neutral stimulus alone comes to cause it (Pavlov's dogs salivating at a sound).
Learning to link one's own behavior with a reward or punishment, so the behavior becomes more or less frequent.
Learning and remembering the layout of the surroundings, such as landmarks around a nest.
Learning by watching or interacting with other individuals, such as young chimpanzees learning to fish for termites.
A chemical signal released by an animal that affects the behavior or physiology of other members of the same species.
The honeybee forager's dance on the vertical comb: the angle of the waggle run from straight up gives the food's direction relative to the sun, and its duration gives the distance.
Regular, usually seasonal, long-distance movement of animals between regions, such as between breeding and wintering grounds.
The idea that natural selection favors feeding behavior that maximizes net energy gained per unit time (or another fitness currency), within the animal's constraints such as predation risk.
In evolutionary biology, behavior that lowers the actor's own reproductive success and raises another individual's.
Natural selection acting through the reproductive success of relatives, which share some of an individual's alleles; it explains much altruism toward kin.

The probability $r$ that an allele in one individual is present in another because both inherited it from a common ancestor: $\tfrac12$ for parent and child or full siblings, $\tfrac14$ for half siblings, $\tfrac18$ for first cousins.
Helping a relative is favored by selection when $rB > C$: relatedness times the benefit to the recipient exceeds the cost to the actor, both measured in offspring.
An individual's own reproductive success plus its effect on the reproduction of relatives, weighted by relatedness.

The most extreme social organization: overlapping generations, cooperative care of young, and a reproductive division of labor with sterile or nonbreeding workers (ants, many bees and wasps, termites, naked mole-rats).

A sex-determination system in which males develop from unfertilized eggs and are haploid, while females are diploid; found in ants, bees and wasps. Full sisters (same mother and father) share $r = \tfrac34$.
Helping a non-relative with the expectation of help in return later; it can evolve when individuals meet repeatedly, recognize each other and stop helping cheaters.
Anything a parent spends on one offspring (eggs, pregnancy, feeding, guarding) that reduces what it can spend on others; the sex that invests more is usually the choosier one.
Selection on traits that increase mating success, through competition within one sex (intrasexual) or mate choice by the other sex (intersexual).
The study of how diseases are distributed in populations and what causes them, used to control health problems.
The rate of new cases of a disease: new cases divided by the population at risk, per unit time (for example, per 100,000 people per year).
The proportion of a population that has a disease at a given time, counting both new and existing cases. In a steady state, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration.
The average number of people one infected person infects in a fully susceptible population, written $R_0$; in the SIR model $R_0 = \beta/\gamma$.

The average number of new infections caused by each case at a given time, $R_e = R_0 \times s$ (fraction susceptible) in a well-mixed population. Cases grow when it is above 1 and shrink when it is below 1.
An epidemic model with susceptible, infectious and removed (recovered or dead) compartments; new infections are $\beta SI/N$ per day and recoveries $\gamma I$ per day.
Standard criteria (symptoms, test results, time and place) that decide who counts as a case in an outbreak investigation.
A histogram of the number of cases by date of illness onset; its shape suggests a point source, a continuing source or person-to-person spread.
The fraction of a group exposed to a possible cause (such as a food) who became ill during an outbreak.
The ratio of the risk (or attack rate) in an exposed group to the risk in an unexposed group; values well above 1 point to the exposure as a cause.
An infectious disease that spreads between animals and people, such as rabies, Lyme disease or avian influenza.
The population of animals (or the environment) in which a pathogen normally lives and multiplies, from which it can spill over into people.
Coordinated efforts to use antibiotics only when they help, choosing the right drug, dose and duration, to slow the spread of antibiotic resistance.
The normal rate at which species go extinct outside mass extinctions, roughly 0.1 extinctions per million species-years (E/MSY).
MacArthur and Wilson's theory that the number of species on an island is an equilibrium between immigration (lower for distant islands) and extinction (higher for small islands).
The pattern that larger areas hold more species, usually described by $S = cA^z$, with $z$ about 0.2–0.35 for islands.
Future extinctions that are already "owed" because habitat has been lost, even though the species still survive for now in remnants too small to support them in the long run.
The breaking of a continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches separated by farms, roads or towns.
Changed conditions near a habitat boundary (more light, wind, drying, invasive species and nest predators) that make the edge zone unsuitable for interior species.
The smallest population with a high chance (for example 95%) of persisting for a set time (for example 100 years) despite demographic, environmental and genetic chance events.
The size of an ideal population that would lose genetic diversity at the same rate as the real one; usually smaller than the census count. With unequal sexes, $N_e = 4N_mN_f/(N_m + N_f)$.
Reduced survival and fertility in the offspring of related parents, mainly because inbreeding makes harmful recessive alleles homozygous.
The feedback loop in which a small population suffers inbreeding, drift and lost diversity, which lowers survival and reproduction and makes it smaller still.

Bringing individuals from another population into a small, inbred population to restore genetic diversity and reduce inbreeding depression (for example, Texas pumas released among Florida panthers in 1995).
A model that uses data on survival, reproduction and their variation to simulate a population's future many times and estimate its risk of extinction under different management options.
Controlling a pest or invasive species with one of its natural enemies (a predator, parasite or pathogen); modern programs first test that the enemy will not harm other species.
The maintenance of stable internal conditions (temperature, water, pH, sugar levels) within the range cells need, despite changes outside; usually achieved by negative feedback.
A property that appears at a higher level of organization from the way the parts are arranged and interact, and that the parts alone do not have, such as a heart's ability to pump.
A proposed, testable and falsifiable explanation for an observation, often leading to an "if…then" prediction.
The one factor an experimenter deliberately changes between groups; plotted on the x-axis.
The factor measured in an experiment to see the effect of the independent variable; plotted on the y-axis.
A factor that could affect the result and is kept the same in every group, so that only the independent variable differs.
The group of subjects that does not receive the treatment being tested (or receives the standard condition) and serves as a baseline for comparison.
In science, a broad, well-tested explanation that ties together many observations and has survived repeated attempts to disprove it. Not a guess; a law describes a pattern, a theory explains it.
Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur: the six elements that make up about 98% of the mass of living things.
A molecule with an uneven distribution of charge, slightly negative at one end and slightly positive at another, as in water.
A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom on one polar molecule and a slightly negative oxygen or nitrogen atom on another (or on another part of the same large molecule).
The attraction of water molecules to one another through hydrogen bonds; it causes surface tension and holds water columns together in plants. (Adhesion is attraction of water to other substances.)
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C; about 4.18 J/(g·°C) for water, which is unusually high.
A measure of hydrogen ion concentration: $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$. Below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; each unit is a tenfold change.
A pair of chemicals that resists changes in pH by taking up H⁺ when acid is added and releasing H⁺ when base is added, such as the bicarbonate buffer in blood.
A small molecule that can bond to others like it to form a polymer, such as a glucose, an amino acid or a nucleotide.
A large molecule made of many monomers bonded in a chain.
A reaction that joins two monomers with a covalent bond and releases a water molecule; $n$ monomers in a chain release $n - 1$ waters.
A reaction that breaks a bond in a polymer by adding a water molecule across it; the reverse of dehydration synthesis, and the basis of digestion.
A sugar or polymer of sugars made of C, H and O (about 1:2:1), used for quick energy (glucose), storage (starch, glycogen) and structure (cellulose, chitin).
A member of a diverse group of mostly nonpolar molecules that do not dissolve in water, including fats, phospholipids and steroids; not a true polymer.
A polymer of amino acids folded into a specific 3-D shape that determines its job, such as an enzyme, transporter, antibody or structural fiber.
The monomer of proteins: a central carbon with an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable R group. There are 20 common amino acids.
A polymer of nucleotides (each a sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogen base) that stores and transmits genetic information: DNA or RNA.
Deoxyribonucleic acid: the double-stranded nucleic acid that stores hereditary information, with the sugar deoxyribose and the bases A, T, G and C.
Ribonucleic acid: a usually single-stranded nucleic acid with the sugar ribose and the bases A, U, G and C; it helps carry out genetic instructions.
A biological catalyst, almost always a protein, that speeds up a specific reaction by lowering its activation energy and is not used up.
The molecule an enzyme acts on; it binds to the enzyme's active site.
The pocket or groove on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place; its shape and chemistry make the enzyme specific.
The energy needed to start a chemical reaction; enzymes lower it without changing the overall energy released or absorbed.
Loss of a protein's 3-D shape (and so its function) caused by high temperature, extreme pH or certain chemicals; usually permanent.
A molecule that reduces an enzyme's activity. A competitive inhibitor blocks the active site (overcome by adding substrate); a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape.
The covalent C–N bond joining the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the amino nitrogen of the next. It has partial double-bond character, so it is flat and does not rotate.
A right-handed coil of protein backbone held by hydrogen bonds between each C=O and the N–H four amino acids along; 3.6 amino acids per turn, rising 0.15 nm per amino acid.
A protein secondary structure made of extended strands (about 0.34 nm per amino acid) lying side by side, parallel or antiparallel, and hydrogen bonded through their backbones.
The tendency of nonpolar groups to cluster together in water, because hiding them frees the ordered water around them; the main driving force of protein folding and membrane formation.
A covalent S–S bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine side chains; it stabilizes the tertiary or quaternary structure of many proteins that work outside cells.
A compact region of a protein, typically 50–250 amino acids, that folds on its own and often has its own function; domains are reused in many proteins.
A protein that helps other proteins fold by shielding exposed hydrophobic regions and preventing aggregation; it does not supply the shape, which is coded in the sequence.
An infectious, misfolded form of a normal protein (PrP) that converts normal copies into the misfolded form; causes diseases such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and BSE.
The rate law $v = \dfrac{V_{\max}[\text{S}]}{K_m + [\text{S}]}$ for the initial rate of a simple enzyme reaction at substrate concentration [S].
The maximum initial rate of an enzyme reaction, reached when all enzyme molecules are saturated with substrate; proportional to the amount of enzyme.
The substrate concentration at which an enzyme works at half its maximum rate ($K_m$); a property of the enzyme and substrate, not of the amount of enzyme.
The number of substrate molecules one enzyme molecule converts per second when saturated: $k_{\text{cat}} = V_{\max}/[\text{E}]_{\text{total}}$.
The ratio $k_{\text{cat}}/K_m$, which measures how well an enzyme works at low substrate concentration; it cannot exceed the diffusion limit of about $10^8$–$10^9$ per molar per second.
A graph of $1/v$ against $1/[\text{S}]$ that turns the Michaelis–Menten curve into a straight line: slope $K_m/V_{\max}$, $y$-intercept $1/V_{\max}$, $x$-intercept $-1/K_m$.
A reversible inhibitor that binds only the enzyme–substrate complex, lowering both $V_{\max}$ and $K_m$.
An inhibitor that bonds covalently to an enzyme, usually at the active site, and inactivates it permanently, such as aspirin on cyclooxygenase or penicillin on bacterial wall enzymes.
Control of an enzyme by a molecule binding at a regulatory (allosteric) site separate from the active site, shifting the enzyme between more and less active shapes.
In a protein with several subunits, binding at one site makes binding at the others easier, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve; seen in hemoglobin and allosteric enzymes.
Regulation in which the end product of a pathway inhibits an enzyme early in the pathway, usually the first committed step, so production slows when the product is plentiful.
An inactive enzyme precursor that is activated by cutting off part of its chain, such as trypsinogen, which becomes trypsin in the small intestine.
A living part of an ecosystem, or material made by living things: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, fallen leaves, dung.
A nonliving condition in an ecosystem, such as sunlight, temperature, water, soil minerals, pH or salinity.
An organism that makes its own organic molecules from an outside energy source, usually by photosynthesis (plants, algae, cyanobacteria) or by chemosynthesis. Producers form the first trophic level.
An organism, mainly a bacterium or fungus, that breaks down dead material and wastes and returns simple nutrients to the soil and water.
A feeding step in a food chain: producers are level 1, primary consumers (herbivores) level 2, secondary consumers level 3, and so on.
All the feeding relationships in a community, drawn as many interlinked food chains. Arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it.

The rate at which producers store energy as new biomass, after subtracting their own respiration from gross primary productivity (GPP): NPP = GPP − respiration. It is the energy available to consumers.
The total dry mass of living organisms in an area or trophic level, usually given in g per m².
The rule of thumb that about 10% (typically 1–20%) of the energy at one trophic level becomes available to the next; most of the rest is lost as heat from respiration.
The path an element or compound (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, water) takes as it moves between living things and the air, water, soil and rocks.
The conversion of nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia or ammonium that organisms can use, done by certain bacteria (some in legume root nodules), by lightning, and industrially by the Haber–Bosch process.
The conversion of nitrate back to nitrogen gas by bacteria in low-oxygen soils and sediments, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere.
Population growth in which the increase is proportional to the population size, $dN/dt = rN$ (or $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$), giving a J-shaped curve. It occurs only while resources are unlimited.
Population growth that slows as the population nears carrying capacity, $dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K$, giving an S-shaped curve that is steepest at $N = K/2$.
The largest population of a species that an environment can support over the long term, written $K$.
A limiting factor whose effect grows stronger as population density rises, such as competition, predation, disease and parasites.
A limiting factor that affects a population the same way whatever its density, such as a freeze, drought, flood or fire.
A method of estimating population size: mark $M$ animals, later catch $C$ animals of which $R$ are marked, and estimate $N = MC/R$.
The role a species plays in its community: what it eats, where and when it feeds, the conditions it tolerates, and what eats it.
An interaction in which one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey); it benefits the predator and harms the prey (+/−).
A close relationship between two species in which both benefit (+/+), such as legumes and nitrogen-fixing bacteria, or flowers and pollinators.
A close relationship in which one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (+/0), such as barnacles on a whale.
A close relationship in which one species (the parasite) lives on or in another (the host) and feeds on it, harming but usually not quickly killing it (+/−).
A species whose effect on its community is far larger than its abundance suggests, so removing it changes the community greatly (for example, the sea star Pisaster or sea otters).

The gradual, fairly predictable change in the species of a community after a disturbance. Primary succession starts without soil (bare rock); secondary succession starts with soil in place (after fire or farming).
A large region with a characteristic climate and the community of organisms adapted to it, such as tundra, desert or tropical rainforest.
The variety of life, measured at three levels: genetic diversity within species, species diversity within communities, and ecosystem diversity across regions.
A measure of species diversity that accounts for richness and evenness: $D = 1 - \sum n(n-1)/[N(N-1)]$, the probability that two individuals picked at random belong to different species.
A species introduced to a region outside its native range that spreads and causes ecological or economic harm, often because its natural predators and competitors are missing.

A table that records, age by age, how many individuals of a population survive and die (and often how many offspring they have), giving survivorship $l_x$, mortality rate $q_x$ and life expectancy $e_x$.
A group of individuals born at about the same time and followed together through their lives, as in a cohort life table.
The average number of further years an individual of a given age can expect to live, $e_x = T_x / n_x$ in a life table.
A graph of the number of survivors of a cohort (usually on a log scale) against age. Type I: most die old; Type II: a constant fraction dies at each age; Type III: most die young.
The average number of offspring (in life tables, usually female offspring) produced by an individual of a given age, written $m_x$.
The average number of daughters a newborn female produces over her lifetime, $R_0 = \sum l_x m_x$. The population grows if $R_0 > 1$ and shrinks if $R_0 < 1$.
A species' schedule of growth, reproduction and survival: age at first breeding, number and size of offspring, and life span, shaped by trade-offs.

Species with traits favored when populations are usually below carrying capacity: early maturity, many small offspring, little parental care, short lives. One end of a continuum, not a strict category.
