Split each mRNA into codons from AUG and translate. Original: `AUG GAC AAU CUG GCG UCU UAA` = Met–Asp–Asn–Leu–Ala–Ser. Mutated protein: Met–Asp–Asn–Leu–Ala–Ser, then stop.

Codon 6 changed from UCU to UCC, but both code for Ser. The protein is unchanged: **silent** (1).

Split each mRNA into codons from AUG and translate. Original: `AUG CAG CCU CCC AAA UCU UAA` = Met–Gln–Pro–Pro–Lys–Ser. Mutated protein: Met–Gln–Pro–Pro–Lys–Ser, then stop.

Codon 6 changed from UCU to UCA, but both code for Ser. The protein is unchanged: **silent** (1).

Split each mRNA into codons from AUG and translate. Original: `AUG ACU GAG UAC AGG ACU UAA` = Met–Thr–Glu–Tyr–Arg–Thr. Mutated protein: Met–Thr–Glu–Ser–Gly–Leu (no stop codon in this stretch).

The mutation is deleting the A at position 11. One base added or lost shifts the reading frame: re-read in threes from AUG, `AUG ACU GAG UCA GGA CUU`, and every codon after the change is different. **Frameshift** (4).

Split each mRNA into codons from AUG and translate. Original: `AUG GAG UCU GUG CCG UGC UAA` = Met–Glu–Ser–Val–Pro–Cys. Mutated protein: Met–Glu–Ser–Val–Pro–Cys, then stop.

Codon 3 changed from UCU to UCC, but both code for Ser. The protein is unchanged: **silent** (1).

Split each mRNA into codons from AUG and translate. Original: `AUG AUU AAC CGC GCG UGU UAA` = Met–Ile–Asn–Arg–Ala–Cys. Mutated protein: Met–Ile–Thr–Arg–Ala–Cys, then stop.

Codon 3 changed from AAC (Asn) to ACC (Thr). One amino acid is replaced: **missense** (2).

Split each mRNA into codons from AUG and translate. Original: `AUG UUA CCG AAG UCC AGU UAA` = Met–Leu–Pro–Lys–Ser–Ser. Mutated protein: Met–Leu–Arg–Lys–Ser–Ser, then stop.

Codon 3 changed from CCG (Pro) to CGG (Arg). One amino acid is replaced: **missense** (2).

Split each mRNA into codons from AUG and translate. Original: `AUG GAC UUG GCU GUA GUC UAA` = Met–Asp–Leu–Ala–Val–Val. Mutated protein: Met–Asp, then stop.

Codon 3 changed from UUG (Leu) to UAG, a stop codon. The protein is cut short: **nonsense** (3).

drills.solution: {sol}

drills.title: Copies after PCR cycles
drills.prompt: A PCR reaction starts with {n0} copies of a target DNA sequence. Assuming the number of copies doubles every cycle, how many copies are there after {cyc} cycles? Give 3 significant figures (scientific notation such as 1.05e9 is fine).
drills.solution:
Each cycle doubles the count, so after $n$ cycles $N = N_0 \times 2^n$.

$N = {n0} \times 2^{{cyc}}$, and $2^{{cyc}}$ = {tw:int}, so $N =$ **{N:int}** copies, about ${man:num2} \times 10^{{ex}}$.

drills.title: Estimate fragment size from a DNA ladder
drills.prompt:
A DNA ladder on a gel gives these bands (size in base pairs, distance from the well in mm):

| Size (bp) | 10,000 | 5,000 | 2,000 | 1,000 | 500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance (mm) | {d10} | {d5} | {d2} | {d1} | {d05} |

An unknown fragment traveled {du} mm. Distance falls on a straight line against the logarithm of size. Estimate the fragment's size in base pairs (within 5%).
drills.solution:
From 10,000 bp ({d10} mm) to 1,000 bp ({d1} mm) is a factor of 10 in size over {k} mm, so each {k} mm of travel is one step in $\log_{10}$ of size.

The unknown band is ${d1} - {du}$ mm closer to the wells than the 1,000 bp band (if that difference is negative, it is farther, so smaller than 1,000 bp). $\log_{10}(\text{size}) = 3 + \dfrac{{d1} - {du}}{{k}} \approx {lg}$, so size $\approx 10^{{lg}} \approx$ **{est:int} bp**.

drills.title: Restriction fragment sizes
drills.prompt: A linear DNA molecule {L} bp long is cut with a restriction enzyme that has sites at positions {c1} and {c2} (counted from the left end). Give the three fragment sizes from left to right. Then suppose the same DNA were a circle with the same two sites: give the size of the piece between the sites that contains positions {c1} to {c2}, and of the other piece.
drills.solution:
Linear: two cuts make three pieces. Left end to first cut: **{f1}** bp. Between cuts: {c2} − {c1} = **{f2}** bp. Second cut to right end: {L} − {c2} = **{f3}** bp. (Check: they add to {L}.)

Circle: there are no ends, so two cuts make two pieces: **{ca}** bp between the sites, and {L} − {ca} = **{cb}** bp for the rest (the left and right pieces joined).

drills.title: Counting alternatively spliced mRNAs

choices.label: one optional cassette exon, which can be included or skipped
two optional cassette exons, each of which can be included or skipped independently
three optional cassette exons, each of which can be included or skipped independently

drills.prompt: A gene has three clusters of mutually exclusive exons, with {c1}, {c2} and {c3} alternatives. Every mRNA includes exactly one exon from each cluster. The gene also has {ncas}. How many different mRNAs can the gene make?
drills.solution:
Independent choices multiply. The three clusters give ${c1} \times {c2} \times {c3} = {base}$ combinations. Each optional cassette exon doubles the count, so the cassette exons multiply it by $2^{{nc}} = {pw}$.

Total: ${base} \times {pw} =$ **{tot:int}** different mRNAs.

drills.title: Reads needed for sequencing coverage

choices.label: a bacterial genome of 5 million base pairs
a yeast genome of 12 million base pairs
a fruit fly genome of 140 million base pairs
a human genome of 3,100 million base pairs

drills.prompt: You want an average coverage of {cov}× for {org}, using reads {rlen} bases long. How many reads do you need, in millions? Give 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Coverage is $C = \dfrac{\text{number of reads} \times \text{read length}}{\text{genome size}}$, so the number of reads is $\dfrac{C \times \text{genome size}}{\text{read length}}$.

Reads $= \dfrac{{cov} \times {gm} \text{ million}}{{rlen}} =$ **{nr:sig3} million**.

drills.title: Chance matches of a short sequence in a genome
drills.prompt: A genome has {gs} base pairs. If its sequence were random, how many times would one particular {k}-base sequence be expected to appear by chance, counting both strands? Give 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Every position on each strand starts one {k}-base window, so there are about ${pos:texsci}$ windows. A random window matches a given sequence with probability $1/4^{{k}}$, and $4^{{k}} = {seqs:int}$.

Expected matches $= \dfrac{{pos:texsci}}{{seqs:int}} \approx$ **{ex:sig3}**.

drills.title: Percent identity of an alignment
drills.prompt: Two DNA sequences are aligned over {alen} positions, counting gap positions. The alignment has {mm} mismatches and {gp} gap positions, and every other position is identical. What is the percent identity? Give one decimal place.
drills.solution:
Identical positions: ${alen} - {mm} - {gp} = {idn}$.

Percent identity $= \dfrac{{idn}}{{alen}} \times 100 =$ **{pid:num1}%**.

drills.title: Carbon-14 dating
drills.prompt: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. A piece of charcoal has {pct:num4}% of the carbon-14 found in living wood. How many half-lives have passed, and how old is the charcoal in years?
drills.solution:
{pct:num4}% is $\tfrac{1}{{den}} = \left(\tfrac12\right)^{{h}}$, so **{h}** half-lives have passed.

Age $= {h} \times 5{,}730 =$ **{age:int} years**.

drills.title: Potassium-40 dating of volcanic rock
drills.prompt: Potassium-40 has a half-life of 1.25 billion years. A volcanic ash layer contains {pct}% of its original potassium-40. How old is the ash layer, in billions of years?
drills.solution:
{pct:num4}% remaining is $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{{h}}$: {h} half-lives.

Age $= {h} \times 1.25 =$ **{age} billion years**. A fossil just below this ash would be at least that old; one just above it, younger.

drills.title: Phenotype frequency after selection
drills.prompt: A moth population has {nL} light moths and {nD} dark moths. In one season, {sL}% of light moths and {sD}% of dark moths survive to reproduce. What percent of the population was dark before selection, and what percent of the survivors are dark? Give percents to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
Before: $\dfrac{{nD}}{{nL} + {nD}} =$ **{before:num1}%** dark.

Survivors: light ${nL} \times {sL}\% = {svL:sig6}$, dark ${nD} \times {sD}\% = {svD:sig6}$, total {tot:sig6}.

Dark among survivors: $\dfrac{{svD:sig6}}{{tot:sig6}} =$ **{after:num1}%**.

drills.title: Hardy-Weinberg: allele and genotype frequencies
drills.prompt: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, {q2}% of individuals show a recessive phenotype ($aa$). Find $q$, $p$ and the frequency of heterozygotes $2pq$ (as decimals), and the expected number of heterozygotes in a population of {N}.
drills.solution:
The recessive phenotype is $aa$, so $q^2 = {q2}\% = {q2d:num2}$, and $q = \sqrt{{q2d:num2}} =$ **{q}**.

$p = 1 - q =$ **{p:num1}**. $2pq = 2({p:num1})({q}) =$ **{het:num2}**.

Expected heterozygotes: ${het:num2} \times {N} =$ **{nhet:int}**.

drills.title: Carriers of a recessive disorder
drills.prompt: A recessive disorder affects 1 in {M:int} people in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the frequency $q$ of the disease allele (as an exact fraction), and what percent of people are carriers ($Aa$)? Give the percent to 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Affected people are $aa$: $q^2 = \dfrac{1}{{M:dp0}}$, so $q = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{{M:dp0}}} =$ **1/{r}**.

$p = 1 - q = {pp:num4}$. Carriers: $2pq = 2 \times \tfrac{1}{{r}} \times {pp:num4} = {car:num4}\%$, about **{car:num2}%**, roughly 1 person in {oneIn:int}.

drills.title: Allele frequencies from genotype counts
drills.prompt: A population has {AA} $AA$, {Aa} $Aa$ and {aa} $aa$ individuals. Find the allele frequencies $p$ (of $A$) and $q$ (of $a$) as decimals, and the number of heterozygotes expected if the population were in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (to the nearest whole number).
drills.solution:
There are {N} individuals, so $2 \times {N:dp0} = {tot:dp0}$ gene copies. Copies of $A$: $2({AA}) + {Aa} = {cA}$.

$p = \dfrac{{cA:dp0}}{{tot:dp0}} =$ **{p:dp3}**, and $q = 1 - p =$ **{q:dp3}**.

Expected heterozygotes: $2pq \times {N:dp0} = 2({p:dp3})({q:dp3})({N:dp0}) \approx$ **{eAa:int}** (observed: {Aa}).

drills.title: Earth's history on a 24-hour clock

choices.label: The earliest widely accepted fossils (3,500 million years ago)
The Great Oxidation Event (2,400 million years ago)
The first eukaryotes (about 2,000 million years ago)
The start of the Cambrian explosion (539 million years ago)
The first land plants (about 470 million years ago)
The end-Permian extinction (252 million years ago)
The first dinosaurs (about 230 million years ago)
The end-Cretaceous extinction (66 million years ago)

drills.prompt:
Squeeze Earth's 4,540 million years into a single 24-hour day, with Earth forming at midnight (0 hours) and the present at the next midnight (24 hours).

Event: {ev}.

How many hours after midnight does this event fall on the clock? Give hours to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
Elapsed time before the event: $4{,}540 - {ev:dp0} = {el:dp0}$ million years.

Clock time $= 24 \times \dfrac{{el:dp0}}{4{,}540} \approx$ **{hr:num1} hours** after midnight, which is {left:num2} hours before the end of the day.

drills.title: One generation of selection against a recessive phenotype
drills.prompt: A population starts in Hardy-Weinberg proportions with $q = {q}$, the frequency of allele $a$. Relative fitnesses are $w_{AA} = w_{Aa} = 1$ and $w_{aa} = {w}$. Find the mean fitness $\bar w$ and the frequency $q'$ of $a$ among the breeding adults after one generation of selection. Give both to 3 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Zygotes: $AA$ ${zAA:dp4}$, $Aa$ ${zAa:dp4}$, $aa$ ${zaa:dp4}$.

Multiply by fitness: only $aa$ changes, to ${zaa:dp4} \times {w} = {caa:dp4}$.

Mean fitness: $\bar w = {zAA:dp4} + {zAa:dp4} + {caa:dp4} =$ **{wbar:dp3}**.

New frequency: $q' = \dfrac{q^2 w_{aa} + pq}{\bar w} = \dfrac{{caa:dp4} + {pq:dp4}}{{wbar:dp4}} =$ **{qn:dp3}**, down from {q}.

drills.title: Effective size through a bottleneck
drills.prompt: Over five generations a population has {big}, {big}, {nb}, {big} and {big} breeding adults. Find its effective population size $N_e$ over the five generations (1 decimal place), and the fraction of its starting heterozygosity expected to remain after the five generations, multiplying $\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2N}\right)$ for each generation (3 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Use the harmonic mean: $N_e = \dfrac{5}{\tfrac{4}{{big}} + \tfrac{1}{{nb}}} = \dfrac{5}{{inv:sig4}} =$ **{ne:num1}**, far below the ordinary average of {am:num1}.

Heterozygosity left: $\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2 \times {big}}\right)^4 \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2 \times {nb}}\right) =$ **{keep:dp3}**. The single bottleneck generation alone removes {lossb:num1}% of the heterozygosity, while each large generation removes only {lossg:num2}%.

drills.title: Chi-square test of Hardy-Weinberg proportions
drills.prompt: A sample of 400 individuals has {nAA} $AA$, {nAa} $Aa$ and {naa} $aa$. Find $p$, the frequency of allele $A$ (2 decimal places), and the chi-square value for a test of Hardy-Weinberg proportions (2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$p = \dfrac{2({nAA}) + {nAa}}{800} = \dfrac{{cA}}{800} =$ **{p:dp2}**, and $q = {q:dp2}$.

Expected counts: $AA$: ${p:dp2}^2 \times 400 = {eAA}$; $Aa$: $2({p:dp2})({q:dp2}) \times 400 = {eAa}$; $aa$: ${q:dp2}^2 \times 400 = {eaa}$.

$\chi^2 = \dfrac{({nAA} - {eAA})^2}{{eAA}} + \dfrac{({nAa} - {eAa})^2}{{eAa}} + \dfrac{({naa} - {eaa})^2}{{eaa}} =$ **{chi:dp2}**.

Compare with 3.84 (df = 1, because $p$ was estimated from the same counts): 3.84 or more means reject Hardy-Weinberg proportions; less means the counts are consistent with them.

drills.title: Calibrating and using a molecular clock
drills.prompt: Fossils show that two lineages split {tcal} million years ago, and a gene differs between them at {dcal:num2}% of sites. Two other species in the same group differ in this gene at {dnew:num2}% of sites. Find the rate of change per lineage (percent per million years) and the time since the two species split (millions of years).

answers.name: rate
answers.label: Rate per lineage (% per million years)

drills.solution:
Both lineages change after a split, so the difference grows at twice the per-lineage rate.

Rate: $r = \dfrac{d}{2T} = \dfrac{{dcal:num2}}{2 \times {tcal}} =$ **{rate}% per million years** in each lineage.

Time: $T = \dfrac{d}{2r} = \dfrac{{dnew:num2}}{2 \times {rate}} =$ **{tnew} million years**.

drills.title: Exponential growth of bacteria
drills.prompt: A broth culture starts with {N0} bacterial cells, and under these conditions the generation time is {gt} minutes. Assuming exponential growth with no cell death, how many generations occur in {t} minutes, and how many cells are there at the end? Give whole numbers.
drills.solution:
Generations $=$ elapsed time $\div$ generation time $= {t} \div {gt} =$ **{n}**.

Each generation doubles the population, so $N = N_0 \times 2^{\,n} = {N0} \times 2^{{n}}$ = **{N:int}** cells. (Multiplying by {n} instead of by $2^{{n}}$ is the usual mistake.)

drills.title: Counting bacteria by serial dilution
drills.prompt: A sample is diluted to $10^{-{dexp}}$ of its original concentration, and {vol} mL of the dilution is spread on a nutrient plate. After incubation, {col} colonies grow. How many colony-forming units (CFU) per mL were in the original sample? You can type scientific notation, such as 2.5e6.
drills.solution:
Each colony grew from one cell, so the plated {vol} mL held {col} CFU: that's ${col} \div {vol}$ CFU per mL of the dilution.

The dilution was $10^{-{dexp}}$, so multiply by $10^{{dexp}}$ to undo it:

$\text{CFU/mL} = \dfrac{\text{colonies}}{\text{dilution} \times \text{volume}} = \dfrac{{col}}{10^{-{dexp}} \times {vol}} =$ **{cfu:sci}** CFU/mL.

drills.title: Transpiration rate from a potometer
drills.prompt: In a potometer, the air bubble moves {dist} mm in {tmin} minutes along a capillary tube with a cross-sectional area of {area} mm². Find the volume of water taken up (mm³) and the rate of uptake (mm³ per minute). Give answers to 2 decimal places where needed.
drills.solution:
The water drawn in fills a cylinder of the tube: volume $=$ area $\times$ distance $= {area} \times {dist} =$ **{vol:num2} mm³**.

Rate $=$ volume $\div$ time $= {vol:num2} \div {tmin} =$ **{rate:num2} mm³/min**. Because the shoot uses little of the water it absorbs, this approximates the transpiration rate.

drills.title: Stomatal density from a leaf imprint
drills.prompt: A nail-polish imprint of a leaf's lower surface is viewed under a microscope. The field of view is {diam} mm in diameter, and {count} stomata are visible in it. Find the area of the field of view (mm², 4 decimal places) and the stomatal density (stomata per mm², to the nearest whole number).
drills.solution:
The radius is half the diameter: $r = {diam} \div 2 = {rad:num4}$ mm.

Area $= \pi r^2 = \pi({rad:num4})^2 =$ **{fov:num4} mm²**.

Density $= {count} \div {fov:num4} \approx$ **{dens:int} stomata per mm²**.

drills.title: How hard the xylem must pull
drills.prompt: A tree is {h} m tall. The soil water near its roots has a water potential of {soil} MPa, and friction in the xylem along the path costs a further {fr} MPa. Using $\rho = 1000$ kg/m³ and $g = 9.81$ m/s², find (a) the pressure difference needed just to hold up a water column {h} m tall, and (b) the water potential at the top of the tree. Give both in MPa to 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
(a) $\rho g h = 1000 \times 9.81 \times {h} = {grav:num4} \times 10^{6}$ Pa $=$ **{grav:num2} MPa** (about 0.01 MPa per meter).

(b) Start from the soil and subtract what gravity and friction cost on the way up: ${soil} - {grav:num2} - {fr} =$ **{top:num2} MPa**. The answer is negative: the water at the top is under tension, pulled up by transpiration.

drills.title: Burst size from a plaque count
drills.prompt: A culture contains ${inf} \times 10^{5}$ infected bacteria per mL. After all of them have burst, a sample is diluted to $10^{-{dexp}}$ and {vol} mL is plated with fresh bacteria, giving {plq} plaques. Find the phage concentration (PFU per mL) and the burst size (phages released per infected cell, 1 decimal place). You can type scientific notation, such as 6.2e7.
drills.solution:
Each plaque came from one phage, so

$\text{PFU/mL} = \dfrac{\text{plaques}}{\text{dilution} \times \text{volume}} = \dfrac{{plq}}{10^{-{dexp}} \times {vol}} =$ **{pfu:sci}** PFU/mL.

Burst size $= \dfrac{\text{phages released}}{\text{infected cells}} = \dfrac{{pfu:sci}}{{inf} \times 10^{5}} =$ **{burst:num1}** phages per cell.

drills.title: Resistant mutants and combination therapy
drills.prompt: An infection contains $10^{{nexp}}$ bacteria. Resistance to drug A arises in 1 cell in $10^{{aexp}}$, and resistance to drug B in 1 cell in $10^{{bexp}}$, independently. Find (a) the expected number of cells resistant to drug A, (b) the expected number resistant to both drugs, and (c) how many doublings the drug-A-resistant cells need to regrow to $10^{{nexp}}$ cells if drug A alone is used (1 decimal place). You can type scientific notation, such as 1e-4.
drills.solution:
(a) $10^{{nexp}} \times 10^{-{aexp}} =$ **{ra}** cells. Under drug A alone, these survive.

(b) Both mutations must occur in the same cell: $10^{-{aexp}} \times 10^{-{bexp}}$ per cell, so the expected number is $10^{{nexp}} \times 10^{-{aexp}} \times 10^{-{bexp}} =$ **{dbl:sci}**. A number far below 1 means almost certainly no doubly resistant cell exists, which is why combination therapy works.

(c) Doublings needed: $2^{n} = 10^{{nexp}} \div {ra}$, so $n = \log_2(10^{{aexp}}) = {aexp} \times \log_2 10 \approx$ **{dbls:num1}** doublings.

drills.title: Negative feedback returns glucose to its set point
drills.prompt: After a meal, a person's blood glucose is {peak} mg/dL; the set point is {sp} mg/dL. In a simple model of negative feedback, insulin action removes {kp}% of the excess above the set point in every 30-minute interval. After {mins} minutes, what is the excess above the set point and what is the blood glucose level? Give answers to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
The starting excess is ${peak} - {sp} = {ex0}$ mg/dL. Each interval keeps $1 - {kp}\% = {keep}$ of it, and {mins} minutes is {n} interval(s):

excess $= {ex0} \times {keep}^{{n}} =$ **{exn:num1} mg/dL**, so glucose $= {sp} + {exn:num1} =$ **{glu:num1} mg/dL**.

The correction gets smaller as the level nears the set point: the hallmark of negative feedback.

drills.title: Nerve conduction speed (Helmholtz's method)
drills.prompt: A nerve is stimulated {far} mm from the muscle it controls, and the muscle twitches {t2:num2} ms later. Stimulated {near} mm from the muscle, it twitches after {t1:num2} ms. Find the conduction speed in m/s, and the time in ms an impulse at that speed would take to travel 1 m.
drills.solution:
The muscle's own delay is the same in both trials, so subtract: extra distance $= {far} - {near} = {gap}$ mm, extra time $= {t2:num2} - {t1:num2} = {dt:num2}$ ms.

Speed $= {gap} \text{ mm} \div {dt:num2} \text{ ms} =$ **{v} m/s** (1 mm/ms = 1 m/s).

Time for 1 m $= 1000 \text{ mm} \div {v} \text{ mm/ms} =$ **{tm:num2} ms**.

drills.title: Stroke volume and cardiac output
drills.prompt: At the end of filling, a left ventricle holds {edv} mL of blood; after it contracts, {esv} mL remain. The heart rate is {hr} beats per minute. Find the stroke volume (mL) and the cardiac output (L/min, 2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Stroke volume is the blood pumped out in one beat: ${edv} - {esv} =$ **{sv} mL**.

Cardiac output $=$ heart rate $\times$ stroke volume $= {hr} \times {sv} = {mlm}$ mL/min $=$ **{co:num2} L/min** (divide by 1000 to change mL to L).

drills.title: Metabolic rate from oxygen use
drills.prompt: A {mass} kg person uses {vo2} mL of oxygen per kilogram per minute (3.5 is a typical resting value). About 20 kJ of energy is released per liter of oxygen used. Find the total oxygen use (L/min), the energy use per minute (kJ/min), and per hour (kJ/h). Give 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Oxygen: ${mass} \times {vo2} = {mlo:num1}$ mL/min $=$ **{lpm:sig3} L/min**.

Energy: ${lpm:sig3} \times 20 =$ **{kjm:sig3} kJ/min**, and $\times 60$ gives **{kjh:sig3} kJ/h**.

drills.title: Minute and alveolar ventilation
drills.prompt: A person takes {rr} breaths per minute with a tidal volume of {tv} mL. Dead space (air that only fills the airways) is {ds} mL per breath. Find the minute ventilation and the alveolar ventilation, in L/min to 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Minute ventilation $=$ tidal volume $\times$ rate $= {tv} \times {rr}$ mL/min $=$ **{ve:num2} L/min**.

Only ${tv} - {ds}$ mL of each breath reaches the alveoli: $({tv} - {ds}) \times {rr}$ mL/min $=$ **{va:num2} L/min**.

drills.title: Energy in food
drills.prompt: A food contains {carb} g of carbohydrate, {prot} g of protein and {fat} g of fat. Using 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal/g for fat, find its total energy (kcal) and the percentage of that energy that comes from fat (1 decimal place).
drills.solution:
Energy $= 4({carb}) + 4({prot}) + 9({fat}) =$ **{kcal} kcal**.

From fat: $9 \times {fat} \div {kcal} \times 100 =$ **{pfat:num1}%**.

drills.title: Herd immunity threshold and vaccine coverage
drills.prompt: A disease has a basic reproduction number $R_0 = {R0}$. A vaccine protects {eff}% of the people who receive it. What percentage of the population must be immune to reach the herd immunity threshold, and what percentage must be vaccinated to get there? Give percentages to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
Threshold $= 1 - \dfrac{1}{R_0} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{{R0}}$, which is **{hit:num1}%** of the population.

Only {eff}% of those vaccinated become immune, so coverage $= {hit:num1}\% \div {eff}\% \times 100 =$ **{cov:num1}%**.

drills.title: Equilibrium potential (Nernst equation)
drills.prompt: A neuron has {ion} at {co} mM outside and {ci} mM inside. Using the Nernst equation at 37 °C, $E = 61.5 \log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{out}]}{[\text{in}]}$ mV (for an ion with charge +1), find the equilibrium potential of {ion} in mV, to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
$E = 61.5 \log_{10}\dfrac{{co}}{{ci}} = 61.5 \times ({lg:dp3}) =$ **{emv:num1} mV**.

The sign tells the direction: a negative value means the inside must be negative to stop the ion leaking out (as for K⁺); a positive value means the ion keeps flowing in until the inside is positive (as for Na⁺).

drills.title: Reflex time from conduction speed and synaptic delay
drills.prompt: A reflex arc has a sensory axon and a motor axon, each {len} m long, both conducting at {spd} m/s, with {syn} synapse(s) in the spinal cord, each adding 0.5 ms of delay. Ignoring muscle contraction time, find the total reflex time in ms (2 decimal places). Then find the conduction time alone, in seconds, if both axons were unmyelinated and conducted at 1 m/s.
drills.solution:
Total path $= 2 \times {len} = {path:num1}$ m. Conduction time $= {path:num1} \div {spd} = {tcond:num2}$ ms (multiply seconds by 1000).

Synaptic delay $= {syn} \times 0.5 = {tsyn:num1}$ ms, so the reflex time is $\approx$ **{ttot:num2} ms**.

At 1 m/s, conduction alone would take ${path:num1} \div 1 =$ **{tslow:num1} s**, far too slow for a reflex. Myelin makes the difference.

drills.title: Antibody diversity from gene segments
drills.prompt: Suppose a species has {vh} V, {dh} D and {jh} J heavy-chain segments; {vk} V and {jk} J kappa light-chain segments; and {vl} V and {jl} J lambda light-chain segments. Each B cell makes one heavy chain and one light chain (kappa or lambda). Counting segment choices only, how many different heavy chains, light chains, and heavy-light pairs are possible?
drills.solution:
Heavy chains: one V, one D and one J, so ${vh} \times {dh} \times {jh} =$ **{heavy}**.

Light chains: kappa ${vk} \times {jk} = {kap}$, lambda ${vl} \times {jl} = {lam}$. A cell uses one or the other, so add: **{light}**.

Pairs: ${heavy} \times {light} =$ **{pairs}**. Imprecise joining multiplies this many times more.

drills.title: Effective reproduction number and vaccine coverage
drills.prompt: A disease has $R_0 = {R0}$. In a town, {cov}% of people are vaccinated with a vaccine that protects {veff}% of those who receive it; no one else is immune. Find $R_{\text{eff}}$ (2 decimal places) and the vaccination coverage needed to reach the herd immunity threshold (percent, 1 decimal place).
drills.solution:
Immune fraction $= {cov}\% \times {veff}\% = {imm:dp3}$, so the susceptible fraction is $1 - {imm:dp3}$.

$R_{\text{eff}} = {R0} \times (1 - {imm:dp3}) =$ **{reff:num2}** (the outbreak grows if this is above 1, shrinks if below).

Threshold $= 1 - \dfrac{1}{{R0}}$; dividing by the effectiveness, coverage needed $= \dfrac{1 - 1/{R0}}{{veff}/100} =$ **{need:num1}%**.

drills.title: Hormone clearance and half-life
drills.prompt: A hormone is at {c0} units in the blood when its secretion stops. Its half-life in the blood is {hl} minutes. What is its level after {tm} minutes, and what percentage of the original remains? Give 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Number of half-lives $= {tm} \div {hl} = {nh:num2}$.

Level $= {c0} \times (1/2)^{{nh:num2}} =$ **{conc:num2} units**, which is **{pct:num2}%** of the original.

drills.title: Minimum urine volume and diabetes insipidus
drills.prompt: A person must excrete {sol} mOsm of solutes a day. With plenty of ADH, the kidneys can concentrate urine to {umax} mOsm per liter. With diabetes insipidus, urine stays at {udi} mOsm per liter. Find the smallest possible daily urine volume in each case, in liters (2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Volume $=$ solute load $\div$ urine concentration.

With ADH: ${sol} \div {umax} =$ **{vmin:num2} L/day**. With diabetes insipidus: ${sol} \div {udi} =$ **{vdi:num2} L/day**, which the person must replace by drinking.

drills.title: Net primary productivity
drills.prompt: The producers in an ecosystem capture {gpp} kJ per m² per year (gross primary productivity) and use {resp} kJ per m² per year in their own cellular respiration. What is the net primary productivity, in kJ per m² per year?
drills.solution:
Net primary productivity is what is left after the producers' own respiration:

$$\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R = {gpp:dp0} - {resp:dp0} = {npp:dp0}$$

So NPP = **{npp} kJ per m² per year**, the energy available to consumers.

drills.title: Energy up the food chain (10% rule)
drills.prompt: The producers in a food chain store {e0} kJ of energy per m² per year. Using the ten percent rule, how much energy (in kJ per m² per year) is available to the {lev}?
drills.solution:
The {lev} are {steps} feeding step(s) above the producers, and each transfer keeps 10%:

$${e0:dp0} \times 0.1^{{steps}} = {ek:dp0}$$

About **{ek} kJ per m² per year** reaches them.

drills.title: Ecological efficiency between two levels
drills.prompt: Herbivores in a meadow take in energy at {lower} kJ per m² per year and the carnivores that eat them get {upper} kJ per m² per year. What percent of the herbivores' energy is transferred to the carnivores? (Answer as a percent, without the % sign.)
drills.solution:
Efficiency = energy at the higher level ÷ energy at the lower level × 100:

$$\frac{{upper}}{{lower}} \times 100 = {p}$$

The transfer efficiency is **{p}%**.

drills.title: Biomass from quadrat samples
drills.prompt: To estimate the plant biomass of a {ha}-hectare field (1 hectare = 10,000 m²), a student clips, dries and weighs the plants in four {q} m² quadrats: {m1} g, {m2} g, {m3} g and {m4} g. Find the biomass per m² (g) and the total dry biomass of the field (kg).
drills.solution:
Mean per quadrat: $\dfrac{{m1} + {m2:dp0} + {m3:dp0} + {m4}}{4} = {avg:dp0}$ g.

Per square meter: ${avg:dp0} \div {q} =$ **{dens} g per m²**.

Field area: ${ha:dp0} \times 10{,}000 = {area:dp0}$ m². Total: ${dens:dp0} \times {area:dp0} = {grams:dp0}$ g, which is **{kg} kg** of dry biomass.

drills.title: Exponential growth, N = N₀λᵗ
drills.prompt: A population of {n0} animals is multiplied by $\lambda = {lam}$ each year. Using $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$, how many will there be after {t} years? (Round to the nearest whole animal.)
drills.solution:
$$N_{{t}} = {n0:dp0} \times {lam}^{{t}} = {n0:dp0} \times {fac:num4} = {nt:dp1}$$

Rounded to a whole animal: **{ntr}**. (A $\lambda$ below 1 means the population is shrinking; above 1, growing.)

drills.title: Logistic growth rate
drills.prompt: A population grows logistically with $r = {r}$ per year and carrying capacity $K = {cap:dp0}$. Using $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN\,\dfrac{K - N}{K}$, how many individuals per year is it adding when $N = {n:dp0}$?
drills.solution:
$$\frac{dN}{dt} = {r} \times {n:dp0} \times \frac{{cap:dp0} - {n:dp0}}{{cap:dp0}} = {r} \times {n:dp0} \times \frac{{left:dp0}}{{cap:dp0}} = {rate:dp2}$$

The population is adding about **{rate:num2} individuals per year**. (Growth is fastest at $N = K/2$.)

drills.title: Mark–recapture estimate
drills.prompt: Ecologists capture, mark and release {mk} lizards. A week later they capture {cc} lizards, and {rr} of them are marked. Use the Lincoln–Petersen method to estimate the population size.
drills.solution:
The fraction marked in the second sample should match the fraction marked in the population: $\dfrac{R}{C} = \dfrac{M}{N}$, so

$$N = \frac{M \times C}{R} = \frac{{mk} \times {cc}}{{rr}} = \frac{{prod:dp0}}{{rr}} = {pop:dp0}$$

Estimated population: **{pop} lizards**.

drills.title: Births, deaths, and migration
drills.prompt: A town's squirrel population is {n0} at the start of a year. During the year there are {b} births, {dd} deaths, {im} immigrants and {em} emigrants. Find the population at the end of the year and its percent change (negative if it shrank, to 1 decimal place, without the % sign).
drills.solution:
$$N_{\text{end}} = N_0 + B - D + I - E = {n0:dp0} + {b:dp0} - {dd:dp0} + {im:dp0} - {em:dp0} = {n1:dp0}$$

Change: ${n1:dp0} - {n0:dp0} = {chg:dp0}$, and $\dfrac{{chg:dp0}}{{n0:dp0}} \times 100 = {pct:dp1}$.

End population **{n1}**, a change of **{pct:num1}%**.

drills.title: Simpson's diversity index
drills.prompt: A pond sample contains four species of invertebrates: {n1}, {n2}, {n3} and {n4} individuals. Calculate Simpson's diversity index $D = 1 - \dfrac{\sum n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}$ to 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Total: $N = {n1:dp0} + {n2} + {n3} + {n4} = {tot:dp0}$, so $N(N-1) = {tot:dp0} \times ({tot:dp0} - 1) = {den:dp0}$.

$\sum n(n-1) = {n1:dp0}({n1:dp0}-1) + {n2}({n2}-1) + {n3}({n3}-1) + {n4}({n4}-1) = {s:dp0}$.

$$D = 1 - \frac{{s:dp0}}{{den:dp0}} = {dval:dp2}$$

So **D = {dval:num2}**. Values near 1 mean many evenly represented species; values near 0 mean one species dominates.

drills.title: Survivorship and mortality rate from a life table
drills.prompt: A cohort of {n0} newborn voles is followed until all have died. At the start of age {age} (years), {nx} are still alive; at the start of age {age1}, {nxt} are alive. Find the survivorship $l_x$ at age {age} and the age-specific mortality rate $q_x$ during age {age}. (Decimals, 3 places.)
drills.solution:
Survivorship is the fraction of the original cohort still alive: $l_x = \dfrac{n_x}{n_0} = \dfrac{{nx}}{{n0}} =$ **{lx:dp3}**.

Deaths during age {age}: $d_x = {nx} - {nxt} = {dd}$. The mortality rate uses the number alive at the start of that age: $q_x = \dfrac{d_x}{n_x} = \dfrac{{dd}}{{nx}} =$ **{qx:dp3}**.

drills.title: Life expectancy from a cohort life table
drills.prompt: A cohort of 1,000 birds is followed from hatching. Numbers alive at the start of ages 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years are 1,000, {na}, {nb}, {nc}, {nd} and 0. Using $L_x = (n_x + n_{x+1})/2$ for the bird-years lived during each age, find the life expectancy at hatching, $e_0$, and at age 1, $e_1$. (Years, 2 decimal places.)
drills.solution:
Adding the $L_x$ from age 0 onward, each middle count appears twice with weight $\tfrac12$, so $T_0 = \tfrac{1000}{2} + {na} + {nb} + {nc} + {nd} = {big:dp1}$ bird-years, and $e_0 = \dfrac{{big:dp1}}{1000} =$ **{e0:dp2} years**.

From age 1 on: $T_1 = \tfrac{{na}}{2} + {nb} + {nc} + {nd} = {t1:dp1}$, so $e_1 = \dfrac{{t1:dp1}}{{na}} =$ **{e1:dp2} years**.

drills.title: Net reproductive rate R₀
drills.prompt: A plant population has survivorship $l_x$ = 1, {la}, {lb}, {lc} at ages 0, 1, 2, 3 (none live past 3) and fecundity $m_x$ = 0, {ma}, {mb}, {mc} female seedlings per plant at those ages. Find the net reproductive rate $R_0$ (2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$R_0 = \sum l_x m_x = 1(0) + {la}({ma}) + {lb}({mb}) + {lc}({mc}) = 0 + {pa:num4} + {pb:num4} + {pc:num4} =$ **{rnot:dp2}**.

If $R_0 > 1$ the population grows, if $R_0 < 1$ it shrinks, and $R_0 = 1$ means each plant just replaces itself.

drills.title: Light and dark bottle productivity
drills.prompt: Lake water starts with {init:dp1} mg of dissolved O₂ per liter. A clear bottle and a dark bottle of the water are hung in the lake for {hrs} hours. Afterward the light bottle has {light:dp1} mg/L and the dark bottle {dark:dp1} mg/L. Find respiration, net production and gross primary productivity for the run (mg O₂ per liter).
drills.solution:
Respiration (dark bottle loss): ${init:dp1} - {dark:dp1} =$ **{resp:dp1}**.

Net production (light bottle gain): ${light:dp1} - {init:dp1} =$ **{net:dp1}**.

GPP adds back respiration: light − dark $= {light:dp1} - {dark:dp1} =$ **{gpp:dp1}** mg O₂/L (check: {net:dp1} + {resp:dp1}).

drills.title: From carbon emissions to a CO₂ rise
drills.prompt: In a year, human activities emit {emis:dp1} billion tonnes of carbon (GtC) as CO₂, and the airborne fraction is {af}. How many GtC stay in the atmosphere, and by how many ppm does atmospheric CO₂ rise? (1 ppm of CO₂ contains about 2.12 GtC. Give 2 decimal places.)
drills.solution:
Carbon staying in the air: ${emis:dp1} \times {af} =$ **{added:dp2} GtC**. The rest goes into the ocean and land sinks.

Rise in concentration: ${added:dp2} \div 2.12 =$ **{ppm:dp2} ppm**.
